papers.title: Intervenable Concept Dynamics for Video Activity Forecasting
papers.abstract: Concept bottleneck models route predictions through human-understandable concepts, making their intermediate states inspectable and editable. Extending this model family to forecasting requires modeling how concept activations evolve over time as objects, actions, and their interactions change, yet existing CBMs ground concepts only in observed inputs and do not forecast their future evolution. We study this problem using videos of ongoing activities and forecast future activities through a named-concept state. We propose TRACE-CBM (Temporal Relational Activity Concept Evolution), which first refines observed concept activations with sparse spatio-temporal graphs. It then recursively predicts future concept states, conditioning each transition on the prior activity distribution, and decodes both observed and predicted states with a shared activity classifier. At inference time, the model supports editing concept values, activity activations, and learned edges without parameter updates, exposing the relational spatio-temporal dependencies used for forecasting. Across multiple datasets, TRACE improves observed-activity Top-1 accuracy over concept-based methods by 1.2-8.5 percentage points and attains H3 forecast Top-1 accuracy within 1.9-2.2 points of matched black-box forecasters. Intervention experiments show concept-node edits correct 25.6-34.4% of initially incorrect H3 forecasts without flipping initially correct ones, and concept steering achieves the requested target activity in up to 90.0% of cases.

papers.intro:
Concept-based forecasting needs a semantic interface. Concept bottleneck models (CBMs) route predictions through human-understandable intermediate concepts (Koh et al., 2020). Therefore, these models expose the semantic evidence behind a prediction that supports inspection and targeted model intervention (Yuksekgonul et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023; Steinmann et al., 2025; Knab et al., 2026b).

Concept-based forecasting needs a semantic interface. Concept bottleneck models (CBMs) route predictions through human-understandable intermediate concepts (Koh et al., 2020). Therefore, these models expose the semantic evidence behind a prediction that supports inspection and targeted model intervention (Yuksekgonul et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023; Steinmann et al., 2025; Knab et al., 2026b).

However, CBMs typically encode concepts as a static representation of an observed input, without modeling their evolution over time (Oikarinen et al., 2023; Prasse et al., 2025). Forecasting requires modeling this evolution, as future predictions can also depend on the future semantic state. If this evolution takes place in an opaque latent space, the semantic interface is lost, making it difficult to debug forecast errors or steer predictions at inference time (De Felice et al., 2026). An intervenable CBM for forecasting should therefore not only expose its current concept state, but preserve a meaningful and editable concept state throughout the prediction horizon.

An intervenable CBM for forecasting should therefore not only expose its current concept state, but preserve a meaningful and editable concept state throughout the prediction horizon.

Videos are challenging for persistent concept forecasting. Activity recognition requires models not only to recognize observed video content, but also to anticipate future activities (Feichtenhofer et al., 2019; Bertasius et al., 2021). To do this, strong video forecasting models commonly propagate latent features whose future evolution cannot be directly inspected or controlled (Liu et al., 2022; Girdhar and Grauman, 2021; Gong et al., 2022). We study whether an explicit concept interface can be maintained while semantically aligned concepts are recursively forecast into the future. In contrast, existing video CBMs learn semantically-isolated concepts for video classification (Lee et al., 2025; Knab et al., 2026a), but do not forecast future concept states or define how interventions propagate over time. Black-box video forecasters can predict future activities, but typically evolve opaque latent representations without a named, editable state (Assran et al., 2023) (see Figure 1). Consequently, no existing approaches provide mechanisms to provide interpretable forecasts nor have a clear mechanism to correct future concept states and thus steer future activity corrections.

In contrast, existing video CBMs learn semantically-isolated concepts for video classification (Lee et al., 2025; Knab et al., 2026a), but do not forecast future concept states or define how interventions propagate over time. Consequently, no existing approaches provide mechanisms to provide interpretable forecasts nor have a clear mechanism to correct future concept states and thus steer future activity corrections.

Intervenable concept-space forecasting. To address this limitation, we propose TRACE (Temporal Relational Activity Concept Evolution), an autoregressive concept bottleneck model for video activity forecasting that recursively updates named concept states, rather than opaque latent representations (see Figure 1). Our method learns spatio-temporal graphs on concept states that refine observed concept activations and represent learned within-window (spatial) and cross-window (spatio-temporal) dependencies. We use a graph because its explicit relation-based propagation lets an edit to one concept propagate to other concepts, rather than treating concept edits in isolation. The model then recursively predicts future concept states and conditions each transition on the activity distribution predicted at the previous window. A shared concept-to-activity classifier decodes both observed and forecasted states on the same semantic space. This design allows for model edits on concept nodes, activity beliefs, and learned edges without changing model weights. Because the architecture exposes editable concept states during forecasting, we evaluate whether these edits can correct or steer future activity predictions. Our main contributions are as follows:

papers.title: Euclid Quick Data Release (Q1). Mass-to-light ratio of elliptical galaxies: constraints from strong lensing
papers.abstract: Mass is among the most fundamental properties describing a galaxy. The relation between the luminosity and the total mass of a galaxy contains information on the efficiency of the star formation process and on the distribution of dark matter. We used strong gravitational lensing data from the Euclid Quick Data Release 1 (Q1) to constrain the total mass enclosed within an aperture of $5\,h^{-1}$kpc, $M_5$, of elliptical galaxies. Our analysis is based on a sample of 95 lenses, which we built by ensuring that their selection function is reproducible. This enabled us to correct our inference for selection effects. The average $\log_{10}{(M_5\,h\,M_\odot^{-1})}$ for a galaxy with an $r$-band luminosity of $10^{10.7}L_{\odot}\,h^{-2}$ at $z=0.5$ is $11.30\pm0.02$. The mass $M_5$ scales with luminosity to the power $\beta_\mathrm{L}=0.71\pm0.07$, and decreases with increasing redshift at fixed luminosity. Assuming a scenario in which galaxies grow by mergers and stellar populations evolve passively, these correlations imply that $M_5$ increases with time for individual galaxies. These measurements provide a useful benchmark for testing models of galaxy structure and evolution that make predictions on the distribution of total mass on the scales of $5\,h^{-1}$kpc.

papers.intro:
Elliptical galaxies are some of the best-studied objects in the Universe. The properties of their luminous component are known in great detail. However, key aspects of their inner mass structure, such as the distribution of dark matter, are still uncertain. Mass is the quantity that is most robustly predicted in simulations of galaxies. Therefore, observations that directly trace mass offer a better chance for making accurate comparisons between theoretical models and observations. Models with different recipes for processes dominated by baryons, such as star formation or the ejection of gas from active galactic nuclei, make different predictions on the inner mass distribution (Duffy et al. 2010; Peirani et al. 2017, e.g.), and so do simulations with different models of dark matter (Despali et al. 2026). Therefore, precise measurements of mass can help us to build more realistic models of galaxies.

Therefore, precise measurements of mass can help us to build more realistic models of galaxies.

Strong gravitational lensing offers the most direct means of obtaining measurements of mass in galaxies. A strong lens can provide a direct estimate of the total projected mass enclosed within the multiple images of the lensed background source, with a precision on the order of 1%1\%. Hundreds of such measurements have been obtained so far (Auger et al. 2009; Brownstein et al. 2012; Sonnenfeld et al. 2013a; Shu et al. 2015; Oldham et al. 2017). However, there are two aspects of strong lensing observations that complicate their interpretation. The first one is the fact that the Einstein radius, which is the main observable in strong lensing, is not purely an intrinsic property of the foreground lens galaxy, but also depends on the redshift of the background source. Consequently, comparing theoretical models to strong lensing data is not as simple as doing this with more traditional observations, such as the stellar mass or the half-light radius. To overcome this obstacle, it is helpful to have a model for the density profile of the lens galaxies. The most commonly adopted model of this type is a power law, in which the density is assumed to scale as ρ⁡(r)∝r−γ\rho(r)\propto r^{-\gamma}. The density slope γ\gamma of early-type galaxies has been the focus of several strong lensing-based observational studies (Koopmans et al. 2006; Auger et al. 2010; Bolton et al. 2012; Sonnenfeld et al. 2013b; Tan et al. 2024; Sahu et al. 2024), and also of kinematics-only analyses (Tortora et al. 2014; Cappellari et al. 2015). The second obstacle in the interpretation of strong lensing data is the fact that strong lenses are a biased subset of the general population of galaxies. Therefore, in order to generalise measurements obtained on strong lenses to the full population of galaxies, selection effects must be taken into account.

The Euclid satellite (Euclid Collaboration: Mellier et al. 2025) is revolutionising the field of strong lensing. Hundreds of new galaxy-scale strong lenses were discovered in the first Euclid Quick Data Release (Euclid Quick Release Q1 2025; Euclid Collaboration: Walmsley et al. 2026; Euclid Collaboration: Rojas et al. 2026; Euclid Collaboration: Lines et al. 2026; Euclid Collaboration: Li et al. 2026; Euclid Collaboration: Holloway et al. 2026, Q1;). The Q1 data cover an area of 6363 deg2 (Euclid Collaboration: Aussel et al. 2026), meaning that more than 10510^{5} lenses are expected to be discovered in the entire Euclid Wide Survey (which will ultimately cover an area of 14 00014\,000 deg2). In this work, we use the Q1 Euclid strong lensing data to carry out a statistical study of the mass distribution in elliptical galaxies, including a detailed treatment of selection effects. The Q1 strong lens sample is sufficiently large to produce competitive statistical measurements, while sufficiently small to allow for human-led lens modelling, which at this stage is a necessary step in our analysis. The results obtained in this work will help us guide in the analysis of the much larger sample of lenses from the Data Release 1.

The main quantity that we seek to constrain is the total projected mass enclosed within a cylinder of fixed physical radius. We set this radius to 5​h−1​kpc5\,h^{-1}\,\mathrm{kpc}, as this is close to the average Einstein radius of the lenses in the Euclid sample. We want to measure how the total fixed-aperture mass varies with luminosity, half-light radius, and redshift, across the population of elliptical galaxies. We choose to work with luminosity, rather than stellar mass, because it can be determined much more robustly. Our main result is therefore a measurement of the mass-to-light ratio integrated within an aperture, 5​h−1​kpc5\,h^{-1}\,\mathrm{kpc}, where baryons and dark matter contribute with comparable amounts to the total mass of a typical massive elliptical galaxy (Auger et al. 2010). As this quantity can be readily predicted with hydrodynamical simulations, our measurement offers one of the most direct ways of comparing models of galaxy evolution with observations.

papers.title: Efficient Interpolation of the Bethe-Salpeter Hamiltonian at Arbitrary Momenta
papers.abstract: We develop an efficient reciprocal-space method to reconstruct the static Bethe-Salpeter (BSE) Hamiltonian at arbitrary crystal momenta from coarse first-principles grids. Bloch states are interpolated within an optimally smooth Wannier subspace, while the screened Coulomb interaction is reconstructed from the dielectric response. This decouples the electron-hole transition momenta and transferred momentum from the underlying ab initio sampling. We benchmark the method on monolayer hBN, monolayer MoS$_2$, and bulk GaAs against explicit ab initio calculations, finding excellent agreement for dense-grid Bloch states, dielectric screening, and BSE optical spectra. Furthermore, our cost analysis estimates speedups of up to $22\times$ on the grids considered here. Arbitrary transferred-momentum sampling gives direct access to the long-wavelength exciton dispersion: in hBN and MoS$_2$, we resolve the nonanalytic behaviour induced by long-range electron-hole exchange at momenta well below the spacing of practical uniform grids. For bulk GaAs, locally refined transition-momentum sampling yields a converged binding energy for the threefold-degenerate lowest exciton, in close agreement with experiment and reference calculations, using far fewer BSE points than conventional uniform meshes. As the present framework provides exciton energies and amplitudes at arbitrary crystal momenta, it opens the way to incorporating ab initio excitonic effects into nonlocal electron-phonon vertices and to extensions towards exciton-phonon interactions and nonequilibrium exciton dynamics.

papers.intro:
The Bethe–Salpeter equation (BSE) provides a standard first-principles description of neutral excitations in solids, including optical spectra, exciton binding energies, and correlated electron–hole states [85, 2, 74, 63]. Its predictive accuracy, however, comes with a substantial computational cost. The electron–hole Hamiltonian couples transitions throughout the Brillouin zone, and converged calculations often require dense momentum sampling, particularly for spatially extended excitons [26, 4]. The screened Coulomb interaction introduces a further sampling bottleneck, since its momentum dependence can vary rapidly in the long-wavelength limit, especially in low-dimensional systems [39, 69].

The Bethe–Salpeter equation (BSE) provides a standard first-principles description of neutral excitations in solids, including optical spectra, exciton binding energies, and correlated electron–hole states [85, 2, 74, 63]. Its predictive accuracy, however, comes with a substantial computational cost. The electron–hole Hamiltonian couples transitions throughout the Brillouin zone, and converged calculations often require dense momentum sampling, particularly for spatially extended excitons [26, 4]. The screened Coulomb interaction introduces a further sampling bottleneck, since its momentum dependence can vary rapidly in the long-wavelength limit, especially in low-dimensional systems [39, 69].

The need for flexible momentum sampling becomes even more apparent away from the optical limit. Standard first-principles implementations rely on regular electronic momentum meshes, so a finite-momentum BSE calculation can be performed directly only when the electronic states required for a given transferred momentum 𝐐\mathbf{Q}, corresponding to the total crystal momentum of the electron–hole pair, are represented on those grids. An arbitrary 𝐐\mathbf{Q} will generally not satisfy this condition, and accessing it may require a new, typically denser, underlying calculation. This becomes particularly restrictive close to Γ\Gamma in two-dimensional systems, where long-range electron–hole exchange gives rise to a nonanalytic exciton dispersion and distinct longitudinal and transverse branches [6, 68, 19]. Resolving this regime requires transferred momenta well below the spacing of typical ab initio meshes, as recently demonstrated by the direct observation of a linear exciton dispersion in monolayer hBN [46, 38].

Dense interpolation in reciprocal space is already widely used in first-principles calculations. Maximally localised Wannier functions [54, 82, 53] provide a smooth representation of Bloch states from which band structures can be reconstructed on dense momentum grids. The same framework was subsequently extended to electron–phonon matrix elements [30, 13], while more recent work has shown that reciprocal-space quantities can be interpolated directly within an optimally smooth Wannier subspace, without an intermediate transformation to real space [89]. These developments now underpin dense-grid first-principles calculations of electron–phonon coupling, transport, spectroscopy, and carrier dynamics [45, 91, 14, 51].

A common smooth electronic representation becomes especially important when several interactions are treated within the same computational framework. Transport and nonequilibrium calculations require electronic states and interaction vertices to be evaluated on compatible dense momentum grids. This is the case, for example, in coupled Boltzmann treatments including both electron–phonon and electron–electron scattering [47], and in real-time descriptions of carrier dynamics in which both scattering channels are treated simultaneously [49, 78, 65, 83, 57]. Beyond interpolation, a common Wannier representation allows matrix elements associated with different interactions to be combined consistently.

The same requirement arises when excitons are coupled to lattice degrees of freedom. First-principles exciton–phonon frameworks combine BSE amplitudes at different transferred momenta with electron–phonon matrix elements to describe scattering and relaxation [16, 7], phonon-assisted absorption and emission [64], dynamical spectral renormalisation and phonon sidebands [20], exciton lifetimes and optical linewidths [15], and phonon-driven exciton dynamics and thermalisation in real time [84, 10]. The symmetry properties of finite-momentum excitons further constrain these processes through selection rules for exciton–phonon coupling [59]. Recent formulations have also addressed the consistent combination of excitonic and electron–phonon quantities within a common electronic representation [5, 50]. More broadly, the interplay between electronic correlations and lattice dynamics motivates a common treatment of the corresponding interaction vertices [34]. The ability to reconstruct the BSE interaction at arbitrary momenta within the same smooth electronic representation as other interaction vertices is therefore relevant not only for equilibrium excitonic properties, but also for exciton transport and nonequilibrium dynamics.

Making such calculations practical also requires reducing the cost of constructing and solving the underlying many-body problem. Compact representations of the polarisation based on localised orbitals and formulations avoiding explicit sums over empty states have been developed for G​WGW calculations [86, 87]. Lanczos-chain and response-based approaches avoid explicit diagonalisation of the full response problem [70, 8], while density-matrix [71, 72] and finite-field formulations [62] reduce or eliminate explicit summations over virtual states and dielectric matrices.

papers.title: Density functionals for the Pauli-Fierz Hamiltonian
papers.abstract: We develop a density-functional theory for the Pauli-Fierz Hamiltonian of nonrelativistic quantum electrodynamics in the spirit of the convex-analytic formulation of Lieb. We consider finitely many electrons, subject to external scalar and vector potentials, coupled to the full continuum of massless transverse photons with an ultraviolet cutoff. The natural basic variables are the standard electron density and a combined current density, the sum of the paramagnetic current density and a field-induced current density generated by the quantized vector potential. We prove representability results for these density-current pairs and show that the mixed-state constrained-search functional attains its infimum and coincides with the Lieb functional obtained by convex conjugation. Since arbitrarily soft photons purify mixed states at a negligible energy cost without changing their density and combined current density, the pure-state Levy-Lieb functional equals the Lieb functional and is therefore convex, even though its infimum need not be attained. In addition, we establish the zero-coupling limit, which recovers the mixed-state Vignale-Rasolt functional of current-density-functional theory. Finally, we consider the long-wavelength (dipole) limit and show that the limiting functional can be written as a constrained search for the well-known length-gauge dipole Hamiltonian.

papers.intro:
Strong coupling of molecules and solids to the quantized electromagnetic field of an optical cavity has been reported to modify chemical and material properties [12, 5, 15, 6]. At the energy scales of chemistry and condensed-matter physics, such effects are described by nonrelativistic quantum electrodynamics (QED) in the form of the Pauli–Fierz Hamiltonian [40, 54], in which electrons are minimally coupled to the quantized transverse vector potential. To treat realistic systems, density-functional theory (DFT) has been extended to this setting as quantum-electrodynamical DFT (QEDFT) [57, 46, 45]. See [13, 49] for approximate functionals and [48, 47] for reviews. Strong coupling of molecules and solids to the quantized electromagnetic field of an optical cavity has been reported to modify chemical and material properties [12, 5, 15, 6]. At the energy scales of chemistry and condensed-matter physics, such effects are described by nonrelativistic quantum electrodynamics (QED) in the form of the Pauli–Fierz Hamiltonian [40, 54], in which electrons are minimally coupled to the quantized transverse vector potential. To treat realistic systems, density-functional theory (DFT) has been extended to this setting as quantum-electrodynamical DFT (QEDFT) [57, 46, 45]. papers.title: Two-Dimensional Search for a Moving Target on Rectangular and Cylindrical Grids
papers.abstract: We study how precisely a moving target can be localized on finite rectangular grids and their cylindrical counterparts. Each query asks whether the target lies in a chosen subset of vertices and receives a noiseless answer. Queries may depend on previous answers. Between successive queries, the target may stay in place or move along one horizontal or vertical edge. Accuracy is measured by the number of positions still possible immediately after the final answer, with no subsequent movement. A strategy achieves accuracy $s$ if it always terminates with at most $s$ possible positions, whatever admissible trajectory the target follows. Thus $s=1$ means exact localization. We denote by $s^*(M,N)$ the smallest value of $s$ achievable by a finite adaptive strategy on a finite grid. Our main result shows that every finite rectangular grid admits a strategy that localizes the target to at most eight positions, regardless of the grid dimensions: $s^*(M,N)\leq8$. The construction uses nine local query patterns and their vertical reflections. Its termination follows from the progress these patterns force toward the finite grid boundaries. We also prove the dimension-dependent bound $s^*(M,N)\leq\min\{M+1,N+1\}$. For finite cylindrical grids $P_M\square C_N$, where the columns are periodic but the first and last rows remain boundaries, we introduce the corresponding accuracy parameter and state the proposed dimension-independent bound $s^*_{\mathrm{cyl}}(M,N)\leq9$.

papers.intro:
Combinatorial search concerns the identification or localization of an unknown object through successive queries. For a stationary object, subset tests lead naturally to separating systems and related information-theoretic questions. Katona’s work on restricted separating systems [6], his survey of combinatorial search problems [7], and his discussion of Rényi’s contributions [8] form part of the classical foundation of this subject. General treatments of combinatorial search include [1, 2].

When the object can change its position during the search, information acquired through a test may be partly lost before the next one. Moving-target search already appears in Koopman’s probabilistic formulation of search and screening [10]. A combinatorial model of two-sided search on graphs was developed by Aydinian, Cicalese, Deppe, and V. Lebedev [3, 4]. In that model the searcher queries subsets of the vertices, while the unobserved target may move along an edge between tests. A. Lebedev and V. Lebedev investigated the related problem of minimizing the total cardinality of tests when searching for a moving element [11]. Faster targets and the relation between adaptive and non-adaptive tests have been investigated by A. Lebedev and Deppe [12]. Other graph-search games also involve hidden moving objects. For example, Beluhov and Kolev [5] studied a chase game that includes rectangular grids, but with a different query and capture rule. Such differences in observations and success criteria are important when comparing results.

The searcher may query an arbitrary subset of the vertices and adapt subsequent queries to previous answers. We measure the remaining uncertainty immediately after the final answer, with no subsequent movement. With the complete grid as initial uncertainty, the same answer histories arise if movement is placed after each nonterminal test instead. The terminal accuracy criterion used here differs from the one in [3, 4, 12], which includes a target movement after the final test. In our notation, that criterion measures |Γ⁡(Dτ)||\Gamma(D_{\tau})|, whereas we measure |Dτ||D_{\tau}|. The accuracy parameters of the two models must therefore be distinguished. In contrast to a stationary search problem, the effectiveness of a query depends on the geometry of the resulting candidate set, since movement expands this set through its graph neighborhood. In two dimensions, horizontal and vertical expansion interact, while the finite boundary may restrict both.

An application motivating this abstraction is adaptive localization and tracking in wireless systems employing reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RISs). These surfaces can modify radio propagation and are being investigated for wireless sensing and localization; an overview is given by Zhang et al. [15]. RIS-assisted hierarchical beam training uses successively refined spatial or angular probing patterns to reduce training overhead [14]. Moreover, RIS-aided user localization and tracking have been studied with explicit mobility models, for example by Teng et al. [13] and Keykhosravi et al. [9].

The connection is particularly transparent in a discretized service area. Each grid vertex may represent a possible user location, and with a suitable spatial discretization and sampling interval, mobility can be idealized by a stay-or-one-edge constraint. A sequence of suitably designed sensing configurations can then progressively reduce the set of plausible locations, while user mobility enlarges it again before the next observation. The binary subset queries in the present paper idealize this process: we assume noiseless answers and permit arbitrary test subsets. A physical RIS or beam pattern generally cannot implement all such subsets exactly, and practical measurements are affected by noise, multipath, hardware restrictions, and finite angular resolution. Thus our results provide combinatorial benchmarks for mobility-aware adaptive localization, not performance guarantees for a particular RIS architecture.

papers.title: Search-Aware On-Policy Self-Distillation with Sibling Alignment for Generative Recommendation
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation retrieves items by autoregressively generating semantic IDs, typically via beam search. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) enhances training supervision by transferring privileged self-teacher knowledge at student-generated states. However, beam-search retention depends on competition among prefixes: visited states differ in importance, and initially reliable decisions may approach the pruning boundary as training evolves. Moreover, conventional distribution matching couples target-token confidence with preferences among competing continuations, potentially weakening relational supervision when the self-teacher strongly favors the target. To address these challenges, we propose Search-Aware On-Policy Self-Distillation (SA-OPSD), a framework that transfers privileged self-teacher knowledge to the states visited during the student's own beam search. Specifically, we introduce Evolving-Boundary Sampling, which prioritizes search-critical states by considering both current pruning-boundary proximity and initial-reference retention-margin decline under a controlled distillation budget. Furthermore, we develop Confidence-Decoupled Branch Distillation, which separates target-probability calibration from informative sibling relations to better preserve the teacher's preferences among competing branches. Experiments on Industrial, Office, and Instruments demonstrate strong performance for SA-OPSD.

papers.intro:
Generative recommendation (GR) formulates next-item prediction as the autoregressive generation of semantic ID (SID) tokens conditioned on a user’s interaction history (Rajput et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024). Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers preference knowledge to student recommenders during training (Hinton et al., 2015; Tang and Wang, 2018b; Cui et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b). Here, we study on-policy self-distillation for students deployed with beam search, keeping their architecture and decoding procedure unchanged. Beam search expands candidate SID prefixes and retains the highest-scoring ones at each decoding step (Yu et al., 2026). In Web-based product discovery, generative recommenders must efficiently retrieve and rank relevant products from large catalogs. Since beam-search pruning determines which candidates remain available for ranking, distillation should reflect the student’s actual decoding decisions.

Knowledge distillation has been extensively investigated in recommendation, from ranking-based knowledge transfer (Tang and Wang, 2018b; Kang et al., 2023) to LLM-based recommendation distillation (Cui et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025) and generative recommendation models (Zhang et al., 2026b). Beyond conventional teacher-forcing supervision, on-policy distillation (OPD) transfers teacher knowledge at states induced by the student (Agarwal et al., 2024). Recent recommendation research has also explored on-policy distillation for latent reasoning (Zhuang et al., 2026). Meanwhile, self-distillation provides another direction for exploiting richer supervision, with privileged information from future interactions or reasoning contexts guiding recommendation models (Tang et al., 2026; Jiang et al., 2026a). On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) further combines student-generated trajectories with privileged self-teacher supervision (Zhao et al., 2026). Related recommendation research also explores student-aware reasoning distillation (Shahgir et al., 2026). These advances offer a promising foundation for transferring richer preference knowledge to generative recommenders.

Beyond conventional teacher-forcing supervision, on-policy distillation (OPD) transfers teacher knowledge at states induced by the student (Agarwal et al., 2024). Meanwhile, self-distillation provides another direction for exploiting richer supervision, with privileged information from future interactions or reasoning contexts guiding recommendation models (Tang et al., 2026; Jiang et al., 2026a). On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) further combines student-generated trajectories with privileged self-teacher supervision (Zhao et al., 2026). Related recommendation research also explores student-aware reasoning distillation (Shahgir et al., 2026). These advances offer a promising foundation for transferring richer preference knowledge to generative recommenders.

On-policy distillation grounds supervision in states generated by the student, making the rollout procedure central to knowledge transfer. For beam-decoded recommendation, the student’s own beam-search rollouts expose competing prefixes whose continuations contend for shared beam slots. Candidates are retained according to their cumulative path scores, and a target prefix may be pruned even when its local continuation probability is relatively high. Moreover, changes to competing continuations can alter a target’s rank even when its own score is fixed. Recent studies have explicitly incorporated such search behavior into recommendation learning. APAO (Yu et al., 2026) optimizes target-prefix survival, BEAR (Yang et al., 2026) introduces beam-search-aware regularization, and SmartGR (Zhang et al., 2026b) transfers teacher-beam ranking preferences. These studies highlight the importance of search-level optimization. Consistent with this motivation, the rollout comparison in Table 3 shows higher NDCG@10 for dense beam-search supervision than for single- and multi-rollout distillation, motivating supervision over competing student-visited states.

Consistent with this motivation, the rollout comparison in Table 3 shows higher NDCG@10 for dense beam-search supervision than for single- and multi-rollout distillation, motivating supervision over competing student-visited states.

Although OPSD enables supervision over student-generated states, directly extending it to beam-search prefixes introduces two coupled challenges. First, where should a limited distillation budget be spent? Student beam search produces numerous parent states with different influences on candidate retention. Selection should therefore balance broad coverage with attention to parents whose children lie near the pruning threshold, where small score changes can affect retention. Moreover, as the student policy evolves, target prefixes retained at initialization may gradually lose their retention margins, suggesting that initial-reference retention-margin decline can further inform the selection of search-critical states. Second, what self-teacher knowledge should be transferred at the selected states? At ground-truth-prefix (GT-prefix) states, whose prefixes match the beginning of the target SID, full KL couples target-probability calibration with conditional preferences among non-target siblings, which are the other legal next-token children of the same parent (Zhao et al., 2022). When the privileged self-teacher assigns high confidence to the observed target, the relative contribution of non-target relational supervision can become small, even though preferences among competing continuations remain informative for search ranking. This motivates separate treatment of target-probability calibration and sibling-relation knowledge.

Although OPSD enables supervision over student-generated states, directly extending it to beam-search prefixes introduces two coupled challenges. First, where should a limited distillation budget be spent? Student beam search produces numerous parent states with different influences on candidate retention. Selection should therefore balance broad coverage with attention to parents whose children lie near the pruning threshold, where small score changes can affect retention. Moreover, as the student policy evolves, target prefixes retained at initialization may gradually lose their retention margins, suggesting that initial-reference retention-margin decline can further inform the selection of search-critical states. Second, what self-teacher knowledge should be transferred at the selected states? At ground-truth-prefix (GT-prefix) states, whose prefixes match the beginning of the target SID, full KL couples target-probability calibration with conditional preferences among non-target siblings, which are the other legal next-token children of the same parent (Zhao et al., 2022). This motivates separate treatment of target-probability calibration and sibling-relation knowledge.

To address these challenges, we propose Search-Aware On-Policy Self-Distillation (SA-OPSD). For knowledge transfer, Confidence-Decoupled Branch Distillation (CDBD) separates target-probability calibration from the teacher’s conditional preferences among non-target siblings, allowing informative branch relations to receive effective supervision even when the self-teacher strongly favors the observed target. Supported non-GT-prefix states receive full KL supervision. The unified objective combines target-SID learning with privileged self-teacher guidance over the student’s search states.

papers.title: Communication with Adversarial Users: Byzantine Models in Multi-User Information Theory
papers.abstract: We consider communication systems operating in environments where some participating users cannot be trusted. This motivates the study of Byzantine communication models, in which users may behave adversarially. In this survey, we provide a unified information-theoretic perspective on communication with adversarial users in multi-user settings. We review recent advances in Byzantine multiple access channels, including reliable communication, adversary identification, and distributed function computation. Furthermore, we discuss extensions to classical-quantum channels and highlight fundamental differences between classical and quantum models. Finally, we outline key open problems and future research directions at the intersection of communication, computation, and security.

papers.intro:
Modern communication systems, such as wireless Internet-of-Things (IoT) networks and large-scale distributed sensing architectures, consist of devices with heterogeneous capabilities and varying levels of trust [17, 8]. Since these devices share a common communication medium, a compromised device may attempt to disrupt the communication process from within the system. This raises fundamental questions about reliable communication in the presence of adversarial users, i.e., users who do not follow the prescribed protocol and may act maliciously. A natural information-theoretic framework for studying such communication systems is the Byzantine Multiple Access Channel (Byzantine MAC), which extends the classical Multiple Access Channel (MAC) to accommodate adversarial users. A MAC models communication between multiple senders and a single receiver over a shared communication medium. In Byzantine MAC, one or more of the users may deviate arbitrarily from the given protocol. The receiver, however, is unaware of whether any user is adversarial and does not know the identity of such users. A distinguishing feature of this model is that the adversary is not an external entity but rather one or more of the legitimate participants in the communication system.

The receiver, however, is unaware of whether any user is adversarial and does not know the identity of such users. A distinguishing feature of this model is that the adversary is not an external entity but rather one or more of the legitimate participants in the communication system.

This Byzantine perspective differs substantially from classical adversarial models in information theory. In the wiretap channel [42], the adversary is passive and observes a noisy version of the communication, while the goal is to ensure reliability and secrecy. In arbitrarily varying channels (AVCs) [13, 29], the adversary is active and controls the channel state in order to jam communication. The multi-user extension, arbitrarily varying multiple access channels (AV-MACs), has been studied extensively [27, 25, 5, 40, 33, 11]. In all these models, however, the adversary is external to the system. In contrast, Byzantine models capture internal adversaries, i.e., one of the “legitimate” users that may behave maliciously (cf. Section 2.1).

Over the past years, a sequence of works has developed an information-theoretic understanding of such systems. Reliable communication in Byzantine MACs has been studied in [36]. The objective is to decode all trustworthy users’ messages despite adversarial interference. This line of work reveals that the presence of adversarial users fundamentally alters the structure of the capacity region and introduces new feasibility conditions that do not arise in conventional AV-MACs. The notion of authenticated communication in Byzantine MACs was introduced in [36]. In this model, the decoder is required to either reliably decode the messages of the trustworthy users or detect the presence of adversarial interference. Thus, unlike in the reliable communication model, the decoder is allowed to forgo decoding when an adversarial attack occurs. An intermediate model, termed communication with adversary identification, was introduced in [37]. In this model, the decoder may declare adversarial interference instead of decoding the trustworthy users’ messages, but must additionally identify the adversarial user (in two user Byzantine MAC) when doing so. A detailed comparison between all these models is given in [35]. More recently, Byzantine distributed function computation has been investigated in [9], where the objective shifts from message transmission to robust recovery of functions of distributed data in the presence of adversarial users.

A unifying phenomenon underlying all these models is the presence of competing adversarial explanations for the same received observation. In the classical communication setting, an adversarial user may generate channel input that imitate plausible honest behavior, thereby creating ambiguity at the decoder. In distributed function computation, different set of adversarial users may induce statistically indistinguishable observations while leading to different function values. Consequently, reliable communication or computation is fundamentally possible only for quantities that remain invariant under all adversarial scenarios that are indistinguishable to the decoder.

While these developments already exhibit rich and fundamentally new phenomena in the classical setting, the situation becomes even more intricate when moving to quantum communication systems. In the quantum scenario, many new challenges arise that have no direct classical analogue. Most importantly, quantum measurements are inherently invasive: every measurement may change the quantum state. As a consequence, not only the input of an adversarial sender may disrupt the communication process, but also previously applied decoding operations can influence subsequent decoding steps. This creates a fundamentally different interaction between encoding, decoding, and adversarial behavior compared to the classical systems.

Furthermore, the role of randomness in coding theory changes significantly between classical and quantum setting. In the classical setting, it is well known that the capacity of arbitrarily varying channels can be achieved by deterministic codes under suitable conditions [19]. Similarly, for arbitrarily varying multiple access channels, deterministic coding schemes have been constructed [5]. In contrast, for quantum arbitrarily varying channels, only random coding techniques are currently available [4, 20]. This indicates a fundamental limitation in transferring classical derandomization and robustness techniques to the quantum domain.

These differences have profound implications for Byzantine communication. Many classical techniques developed for Byzantine MACs, including deterministic verification procedures and identification-based decoding methods, do not directly extend to quantum channels. In particular, an unknown quantum state generally cannot be verified with certainty: even an invalid quantum state may pass a decoding measurement with non-vanishing probability. Consequently, fundamentally new coding and decoding techniques are required for quantum Byzantine communication.

papers.title: Spade-SLAM: Sparse Correspondence Anchors for Dense Self-Supervised Visual SLAM
papers.abstract: We introduce Spade-SLAM, a self-supervised dense visual SLAM framework that substantially narrows the long-standing performance gap to supervised methods in a zero-shot setting. By demonstrating that high-fidelity tracking can be achieved without explicit ground-truth pose and depth labels, our approach offers a highly effective and label-efficient alternative to fully supervised pretraining. Our core contribution is a complementary sparse-to-dense training regime: While a warping-based photometric loss provides a dense training signal, we stabilize the optimization and suppress drift in ambiguous regions using a sparse correspondence loss derived from image feature matches. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Spade-SLAM significantly improves robustness and accuracy compared to existing self-supervised baselines, closely rivaling SLAM systems trained with explicit pose and depth supervision. The code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/JulianPSchmitt/Spade-SLAM.

papers.intro:
Recent years have witnessed rapid progress in dense visual simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), driven by the growing demand for reliable 3D perception in robotics [1], augmented reality [2], and autonomous navigation [3]. Unlike traditional sparse methods that rely on discrete feature keypoints [4, 3], dense SLAM systems reconstruct detailed geometry, enabling richer spatial understanding for downstream tasks [5]. While classical geometry-based methods laid strong foundations, recent advances increasingly leverage deep learning [6, 7, 8] to improve robustness in texture-less regions, under motion blur, and across challenging lighting conditions, pushing dense SLAM closer to real-world deployment.

Unlike traditional sparse methods that rely on discrete feature keypoints [4, 3], dense SLAM systems reconstruct detailed geometry, enabling richer spatial understanding for downstream tasks [5]. While classical geometry-based methods laid strong foundations, recent advances increasingly leverage deep learning [6, 7, 8] to improve robustness in texture-less regions, under motion blur, and across challenging lighting conditions, pushing dense SLAM closer to real-world deployment.

Despite their strong performance, state-of-the-art learning-based SLAM systems rely heavily on supervised training with ground-truth poses and dense depth annotations [6]. Acquiring such comprehensive ground truth is costly and often restricted to synthetic environments or specialized capture setups, making label-efficient alternatives highly desirable. Self-supervised learning offers a compelling direction by typically replacing explicit labels with photometric warping as a dense training signal [9, 10, 11]. However, photometric consistency can be a fragile assumption: it breaks down under illumination changes, non-Lambertian surfaces, and in texture-less regions. Consequently, pure photometric methods have struggled to match the accuracy and robustness of their supervised counterparts, leaving a performance gap that limits their practical utility [12].

Consequently, pure photometric methods have struggled to match the accuracy and robustness of their supervised counterparts, leaving a performance gap that limits their practical utility [12].

In this work, we aim to narrow this gap by demonstrating that self-supervised learning can achieve performance competitive with fully supervised baselines, even when constrained to identical training data volumes. We introduce Spade-SLAM, a self-supervised SLAM framework built upon a complementary sparse-to-dense training regime. Our key insight is that while dense photometric alignment can be prone to local minima, sparse point correspondences provide reliable and illumination-robust geometric cues. By incorporating a sparse correspondences reprojection loss alongside a robust brightness-aligned photometric objective, we introduce strong geometric anchors that stabilize optimization and suppress drift in ambiguous regions, without the need for ground-truth camera poses or dense depth supervision.

papers.title: When Does Triadic Balance Reduce to Pairwise Order?
papers.abstract: Structural-balance interactions are naturally defined on triads, but when pair affinities are themselves generated by continuous node attributes, it is not clear whether the resulting interaction remains genuinely higher order. Here we address this question for agents represented by unit vectors in an attribute space, with pair affinity given by their scalar product and a Heider product assigned to each triangle. For planar attributes, we show that the triadic interaction reduces exactly, at finite system size, to a pairwise Curie--Weiss XY model of the doubled angles. The ordered phase is therefore nematic and undergoes a continuous mean-field $O(2)$ transition at $k_{\mathrm B}T_c=J/8$. The same reduction reveals a local $\mathbb Z_2$ degeneracy: each nematically ordered state corresponds to $2^N$ polar assignments, whose binomial multiplicities make two nearly equal opposite groups typical at low temperature. Monte Carlo simulations support the exact critical temperature, the mean-field Binder-cumulant value, and the predicted complete-graph finite-size scaling. Finally, a tensor representation of the interaction shows that the planar reduction is dimension specific: in two dimensions the cubic invariant is constrained by lower-order invariants, whereas for $d\geq3$ it is generically independent. These results identify when attribute-induced triadic balance is effectively pairwise and when genuinely higher-order structure can remain.

papers.intro:
Heider’s balance theory organizes signed relations through a constraint on triangles: a triad is balanced when the product of its three link signs is positive [11, 12]. On a complete graph this condition leads to either an all-positive “paradise” state or a partition into two internally friendly and mutually antagonistic factions [7, 3, 4]. Large signed-network data sets have provided empirical tests of balance and related signed-triad patterns [28, 8, 16, 2]. Statistical-physics formulations promote imbalance to an energy and use stochastic or thermal dynamics to study ordering, metastability, and phase transitions. Thermal Heider models with link degrees of freedom can exhibit discontinuous balance–disorder transitions, whereas coupling node and link variables can instead produce a continuous transition [13]. Recent extensions to multiplex, Erdős–Rényi, and planar networks further show how balance transitions depend on interlayer coupling, connectivity, and local triangle topology [18, 22, 23, 19]. A recent complementary result shows that, within the structurally balanced sector, binary Heider links can be represented by products of Ising spins on complete and arbitrary graphs [6]. That correspondence concerns binary link variables subject to structural balance, whereas the reduction derived below is a configuration-by-configuration identity for continuous affinities generated by node attributes.

A distinct but complementary question concerns the origin of the links themselves. Continuous-link formulations allow the strength of friendship or hostility to vary [15, 20], while homophily-based models generate relations from similarities between multidimensional attributes or opinions. Attribute-based balance models explicitly couple triadic balance to agent features [10, 25]; multidimensional attributes have also been used to expose signatures of Heider dynamics in empirical and model networks [17, 24, 21]; dyadic homophily alone can reproduce characteristic triad statistics [26]; and multidimensional spin descriptions have been used to study homophilic group formation [14]. Agbanusi and Bronski studied an energy-based model with continuous node positions and edge opinions, obtaining consensus and balanced two-group states [1]. These results motivate a sharper structural question: when affinities are induced by continuous node attributes but the Hamiltonian is imposed on triads, does the apparent three-body interaction contain an irreducible higher-order degree of freedom?

papers.title: Molecular Communication for Plaque Sensing in a Vascular Bifurcation with Receiver Constraints
papers.abstract: Future molecular communication (MC) networks are envisioned to use the human cardiovascular system as a channel. Disease-related changes affect particle transport, allowing an MC receiver to also act as a sensor. In this work, we investigate plaque formation in a carotid bifurcation through a systematic fluid-dynamics simulation study with non-Newtonian blood rheology. We analyze how plaque geometry changes branch-specific particle reception and timing, and use these observations to estimate plaque-induced channel obstruction. At an illustrative reference of only 128 emitted particles, a 250 ms observation window and 50 ms temporal resolution, a Ridge detector estimates maximum local channel-width reduction with a mean absolute error of 8.30 percentage points. We evaluate robustness across system constraints like particle budgets, observation windows, branch access, detection efficiency, count resolution, and synchronization. Coarse counting has little effect when timing features remain available, whereas limited temporal resolution and clock uncertainty substantially affect short-window estimates. Extending the observation window to 1 s reduces these timing-related penalties. The results establish a baseline for plaque sensing from constrained MC observations and identify receiver capabilities relevant to the Internet of Bio-Nano Things.

Atherosclerosis is characterized by the formation of plaque inside arterial walls, progressively narrowing and obstructing the blood vessel [11]. The carotid artery and its bifurcation are important sites for investigating plaque-related changes [13]. Monitoring these changes is a potential application of the Internet of Bio-Nano Things, in which bio-nano machines communicate and cooperate to support tasks inside the human body [2, 10, 4].

Changes in the propagation environment also affect the received signal. Plaque formation therefore connects molecular communication with sensing. papers.title: SurgPace: Complexity-Aware Progressive Distillation for Surgical Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have shown strong potential in robotic surgery for question answering, scene understanding, and grounded assistance, but their high computational cost limits real clinical deployment. Knowledge distillation provides a practical way to build compact surgical MLLMs, yet direct distillation is not well suited to surgical data because surgical samples vary greatly in difficulty, visual ambiguity, and required clinical context, making uniform teacher-student transfer unstable. In addition, the role of supervision changes during training: early stages require stronger teacher guidance for multimodal alignment, while later stages rely more on task supervision for effective optimization. To address these challenges, we propose SurgPace, a complexity-aware continuous curriculum framework for progressive distillation of surgical vision-language models. SurgPace estimates sample complexity using predictive confidence and Lorentz geometric consistency, and uses the fused score to guide a continuous easy-to-hard training process. We further introduce hierarchical representation alignment, which aligns the student with the teacher at the feature, logit, and probability levels, while gradually shifting the training focus from teacher imitation to task supervision. This design separates sample-level curriculum from objective-level scheduling, leading to more stable and effective distillation. We evaluate SurgPace on Surg-396K, a benchmark built from four public surgical datasets and covering five dialogue paradigms. SurgPace consistently outperforms strong MLLM distillation baselines, demonstrating its effectiveness for building compact, memory-efficient surgical MLLMs with faster decoding under controlled benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/hezhicheng2002/SurgPace.

papers.intro:
Modern surgical care increasingly relies on digital imaging and video streams to support clinical decision-making [36, 29]. During minimally invasive procedures, large volumes of visual data are generated, including endoscopic videos, surgical tool trajectories, and intraoperative imaging. These data encode rich information about anatomical structures, surgical actions, and instrument-tissue interactions. Surgeons must continuously interpret these visual signals to infer the current surgical state and make timely decisions [53, 2]. As surgical procedures become more complex, the volume and heterogeneity of visual data increase rapidly, which further elevates the cognitive burden on clinicians. In recent years, multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for interpreting such complex medical data [22, 19, 57]. By integrating visual perception with language understanding, these models can analyze surgical scenes while interacting with clinicians through natural language. This capability supports applications such as surgical question answering, workflow understanding, procedure summarization, and clinical dialogue assistance. As a result, MLLMs are increasingly regarded as a potential foundation for intelligent surgical assistants that can observe procedures, interpret context, and communicate clinically relevant information during operations [39, 45, 14, 13].

Despite this promise, the practical deployment of MLLMs in surgical environments remains challenging [32, 15, 9]. Modern MLLMs typically rely on large vision encoders and deep language backbones, which incur substantial computational overhead. These architectures require considerable memory, high-end GPUs, and long inference time [44]. Such demands conflict with the constraints of real clinical systems, where latency, hardware resources, and system reliability are strictly limited. In operating rooms and robotic surgery platforms, intelligent systems must respond rapidly and reliably, as surgeons often require immediate feedback during critical procedural steps [56, 28]. However, MLLMs are usually developed in research settings with abundant computational resources. Their translation into real clinical workflows therefore remains nontrivial [21]. This gap between model capability and deployment feasibility has become a major barrier to practical surgical multimodal intelligence in real clinical settings.

Transferring multimodal capability from a high-capacity teacher model to a resource-efficient student model remains a fundamental challenge for surgical MLLM systems. Knowledge distillation provides a practical route for compressing MLLMs into compact models with lower computational demands [10, 11, 59]. However, directly applying standard distillation strategies to surgical multimodal tasks often leads to unstable optimization and suboptimal transfer. Several aspects of surgical multimodal learning make this transfer difficult. First, surgical samples differ widely in visual clarity, question complexity, and required clinical context [31, 33]. Treating all samples in the same way can cause hard cases to dominate early training and reduce training stability. Second, surgical tasks require joint reasoning over visual appearance, instruments, anatomy, spatial relations, actions, and procedural context [54]. Distilling only final responses can overlook intermediate cues that support reliable surgical understanding. Third, the useful supervision signal changes during training. Early stages benefit more from teacher-guided supervision for visual and multimodal alignment, while later stages need stronger task supervision to refine final answers. A fixed objective cannot model this change well. These issues limit reliable knowledge transfer in resource-constrained surgical systems, such as operating rooms and robotic platforms.

The student is aligned with the teacher at probability, logit, and hidden-representation levels, while the balance between distillation loss and task loss changes over time. papers.title: From Simulation to Sustainable Urban Mobility: A Purpose-Driven Framework for Advanced EV Charging Technology Transfer
papers.abstract: The integration of electric vehicles (EVs) into urban mobility systems offers both opportunities and challenges for cities pursuing sustainability and energy efficiency. While simulation-based approaches have demonstrated the technical feasibility of advanced charging strategies, such as smart charging, bidirectional charging, and Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G), their real-world impact is often constrained by policy, business models, and stakeholder engagement. This paper introduces a purpose-driven technology transfer (PDTT) framework that systematically connects simulation insights with the needs of urban stakeholders. Leveraging a modular simulation architecture based on Simulation of Urban Mobility (SUMO), we evaluate the operational and sustainability impacts of advanced EV charging in complex urban scenarios, assessing indicators such as energy efficiency and CO2 emissions. The PDTT framework guides the translation of simulation results into actionable pathways for deployment, policy design, and market innovation, supporting co-creation with city planners, utilities, and communities. Our findings highlight the value of simulation as a diagnostic and engagement tool, and demonstrate how a multidimensional, stakeholder-centered approach can accelerate the sustainable adoption of advanced EV charging technologies in smart city contexts.

papers.intro:
The integration of electric vehicles (EVs) into urban transportation systems presents both significant challenges and transformative opportunities for cities striving to achieve sustainability goals and optimize energy usage [2, 13, 24, 23]. While technical solutions such as smart charging, which optimizes charging times and power based on grid conditions, and bidirectional charging are increasingly available [19], their real-world impact is often limited by factors beyond engineering, such as business model viability, stakeholder alignment, and the complexity of urban ecosystems [23]. Bidirectional charging enables not only the charging of EVs but also the ability for EVs to discharge electricity back to the grid or other systems. This capability is commonly referred to as Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G), where EVs act as distributed energy resources, supporting grid stability and flexibility [23, 15].

papers.title: AnchorComplete: Recovering Complete Scene Meshes from Partial Point Clouds
papers.abstract: Most image-based 3D reconstructors primarily recover visible surfaces, producing partial point clouds with large holes and leaving unobserved geometry unresolved. To address this limitation, we introduce AnchorComplete, a framework that reconstructs complete scene meshes from partial point clouds while preserving observed geometry and supporting scenes of varying scales. Building on TRELLIS.2, our method combines partial-point conditioning, which integrates global scene tokens with local spatial evidence to anchor generation to the input, and metric-scale coarse-to-fine generation, which progressively refines scene geometry within fixed-size windows while maintaining global structural consistency. Experiments on Replica and SCRREAM demonstrate that AnchorComplete consistently outperforms strong baselines in complete-scene reconstruction, particularly under sparse-view settings.

We study the problem of recovering a complete 3D mesh of a scene given only a partial observation, such as the output of a 3D reconstructor or a 3D scanner. A robust solution to this problem would benefit downstream applications such as novel-view AR/VR rendering (Xie et al., 2026), large-scale physical simulation (Savva et al., 2019; Szot et al., 2021), and robotics (Liu et al., 2023a), where complete scene meshes are often required for rendering, collision detection, and physical interaction.

However, completion is not part of their formulation, so unobserved regions remain large holes, limiting their applicability in many downstream applications.

papers.title: Fast Self-Triggering and Segment-Fitting of Cosmic Muons with a small-Diameter Monitored Drift Tube Detector
papers.abstract: We present a fast self-triggering and segment-fitting algorithm that identifies cosmic muons and reconstructs their directions using a small-diameter Monitored Drift Tube (sMDT) chamber without an external trigger detector. The muon arrival time is determined using a Legendre-based algorithm combined with coarse- and fine-grid searches. We implement the algorithm in FPGA firmware on an ATLAS MDT miniDAQ board and evaluate its efficiency, resolution, and latency. The results demonstrate standalone sMDT triggering and trigger-level reconstruction of muon directions, providing a solution for chamber commissioning and potentially MDT-based triggers for charged massive stable particle searches at the High Luminosity-LHC.

papers.intro:
Drift-tube detectors are widely used for precision tracking in particle and nuclear physics experiments, with several recent applications documented in [4, 14, 1, 19, 9, 5, 15, 7, 6, 13]. When a charged particle traverses a drift tube at time t0t_{0}, electrons produced in primary and secondary ionizations drift toward the central wire. The time difference between the earliest signal arrival at the wire (tst_{s}) and the reference time (t0t_{0}) defines the hit drift time, tdrift=ts−t0t_{\mathrm{drift}}=t_{s}-t_{0}, which is then converted into a drift radius using a time-to-radius (R⁡(t)R(t)) relation[17]. In a multilayer chamber, the hit tubes provide multiple drift circle measurements, and the particle trajectory is reconstructed as the line tangent to these circles. Drift tube detectors typically achieve a spatial resolution of approximately 100 μ\mum per tube, with drift times ranging from 100 ns to 1 μ\mus, depending on the gas mixture, operating pressure, and applied high voltage.

In the NA62 experiment, the straw tube tracker was integrated into the first-level trigger system by exploiting the similar arrival times of electrons produced near the walls of tubes traversed by the same charged particle [9]. However, because drift tube detectors have relatively long drift times and cannot readily determine t0t_{0} independently, they are generally not used for triggering in collider experiments and specific trigger detectors are needed. For example, for the planned ATLAS upgrade for the High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) [11], the barrel resistive plate chamber (RPC) and endcap thin-gap chamber (TGC) trigger detectors will provide t0t_{0} measurements and define regions of interest for identifying tubes that may have been traversed by charged particles. A fast segment-finding and track-fitting algorithm will then process the selected tubes to estimate the charged particle’s momentum at the first-level trigger. This approach reduces the number of candidate hits that must be analyzed in real time and allows the trigger system to incorporate precise tracking information from the drift tube chambers within its stringent latency constraints.

A fast segment-finding and track-fitting algorithm will then process the selected tubes to estimate the charged particle’s momentum at the first-level trigger. This approach reduces the number of candidate hits that must be analyzed in real time and allows the trigger system to incorporate precise tracking information from the drift tube chambers within its stringent latency constraints.

This article presents the development of a fast self-triggering and segment-fitting algorithm to trigger on cosmic muon events and determine their directions in real time using a Legendre-transform-based method. The algorithm is implemented in firmware and executed on the field-programmable gate array (FPGA) of a mini data-acquisition (miniDAQ) system [12] to collect cosmic muon events with an ATLAS small-diameter Monitored Drift Tube (sMDT) detector [21, 3]. The algorithm’s performance is evaluated in terms of trigger efficiency, segment-direction and t0t_{0} resolutions, spatial resolution per tube, and latency.

Although the cosmic muon event rate is substantially lower than the event rate encountered under LHC collision conditions, self-triggering on cosmic muons presents significant challenges. Cosmic muons can traverse the chamber at arbitrary angles, whereas muons produced in LHC collisions typically originate from the interaction point. In addition, cosmic muons arrive asynchronously and may traverse the detector at any time relative to the system clock. By contrast, muons at the LHC are produced in p​ppp collisions synchronized with the accelerator bunch crossings, and their presence is identified by dedicated trigger devices. For cosmic muon events, no external timing reference is available, and t0t_{0} must instead be inferred directly from the drift-tube signals in real time. Our algorithm addresses this challenge by simultaneously identifying a consistent pattern of tube hits, estimating the muon arrival time, and reconstructing the corresponding track segment. This capability provides a low-latency solution for standalone cosmic muon triggering and may facilitate detector commissioning, calibration, testing, and performance studies when external trigger devices, such as dedicated trigger chambers or scintillator detectors, are unavailable. It also has the potential to be used to trigger on slow-moving charged particles produced in collider experiments.

papers.title: Newtonian Dynamics in Metric Spaces
papers.abstract: We develop a variational framework for second-order, frictionless (Newtonian) dynamics in metric spaces, extending the metric theory of curves of maximal slope from gradient flows to evolutions with inertia. The construction rests on three pillars, mirroring the first-order theory. First, we introduce a class of second-order absolutely continuous curves, characterized by a geometric--variational inequality on families of tangent geodesics, and define a metric notion of acceleration. Second, we define curves of Newtonian motion as the curves achieving equality in an energy inequality involving an upper gradient--Hessian pair, which in Hilbert spaces is equivalent to Newton's equation $\ddot\gamma = -\nabla E(\gamma)$. Third, we propose a two-step predictor--corrector minimizing movement scheme and show that its discrete interpolants satisfy approximate versions of these inequalities. Under extendability and interceptor conditions on geodesics---which are satisfied, for instance, by geodesically uniformly complete, locally compact spaces with curvature bounded below---and under suitable regularity assumptions on the energy, we prove that the scheme converges, up to subsequences, to a curve of Newtonian motion. As an illustration, we recover the linear wave equation as a curve of Newtonian motion driven by the Dirichlet energy. This paper is complemented by the companion paper [Fornasier, Klemenc, Scagliotti, "A Lions Lift Framework for Gradient and Newtonian Evolutions in Wasserstein spaces"], which specifies and adapts the results to the Wasserstein metric space $(\mathcal{P}_2,W_2)$ through Lions lift, which explains Vlasov equations as Newtonian flows on spaces of probability measures.

papers.title: Evaluating Uncertainty Calibration in Probabilistic Time Series Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) are increasingly used for probabilistic forecasting across diverse domains, yet the reliability of their uncertainty estimates remains poorly understood. In this work, we study uncertainty calibration in probabilistic TSFMs from a broader methodological and empirical perspective. We introduce a taxonomy of how TSFMs represent predictive uncertainty and develop a fine-grained evaluation framework for calibration in multi-horizon forecasting that distinguishes pooled, horizon-wise, and stronger conditional notions of calibration. Using this framework, we conduct a comprehensive empirical evaluation of popular TSFMs across diverse datasets and show that current models exhibit distinct and systematic patterns of miscalibration that standard metrics often obscure. We further analyze common post-hoc recalibration methods and characterize which forms of calibration they can improve and which tend to persist. Our results provide practical guidance for evaluating and improving uncertainty calibration in TSFMs and highlight important limitations of current practice.

Time series foundation models (TSFMs) are progressively emerging as a general-purpose approach to forecasting Liang et al. (2024). Pretrained on large and heterogeneous collections of time series, they can often be applied in a zero-shot manner to unseen datasets, frequencies, and domains while remaining competitive with specialized forecasting systems Ansari et al. (2024a); Woo et al. (2024); Das et al. (2024). As their adoption grows in high-stakes applications such as healthcare Gu et al. (2025), energy systems Meyer et al. (2025), and finance Zhu et al. (2025), it becomes increasingly important that they not only produce accurate forecasts but also communicate uncertainty in a trustworthy manner.

In many of these settings, decisions depend not only on the predicted outcome itself but also on how likely adverse outcomes are. This makes the quality of uncertainty estimates an important practical objective beyond predictive accuracy. However, such estimates are useful only if their stated confidence levels can be interpreted reliably. In particular, a prediction interval reported at 90%90\% confidence for a forecast should contain the realized outcome about 90%90\% of the time. This notion of reliability is commonly captured by calibration, meaning that predicted probabilities agree with observed frequencies Gneiting et al. (2007); Gruber and Buettner (2022); Kuleshov et al. (2018); Song et al. (2019). A model might therefore achieve strong forecasting accuracy while still providing uncertainty estimates that are misleading in practice.

Although TSFMs increasingly support uncertainty-aware forecasting, calibration in this setting is still only partially understood. Recent work has begun to examine this question empirically Adler et al. (2026), providing an important first view of calibration in modern forecasting models. At the same time, calibration is a subtle property in multi-horizon forecasting, where conclusions can depend on how forecasts are represented, how behavior varies across horizon steps, and how results are aggregated across instances. This creates the need for a more systematic evaluation framework that supports comparison across heterogeneous TSFMs and reveals forms of miscalibration that may be hidden by standard aggregate metrics.

papers.title: Supporting Viewpoint Coordination for Compliance by Design with an Artifact Model for Regulatory Requirements Engineering
papers.abstract: Regulatory compliance has become an essential software requirement Legal demands for compliance by design CbD call for requirements engineering RE approaches that derive requirements and support compliance implementation in subsequent software engineering SE processes such as software design The complexity of the legal knowledge demanded in regulatory RE makes it important to involve legal experts and ensure the relevant specifications are valid and usable for them Regulatory requirements must support compliance implementation in software design However there is a lack of approaches bridging legal and SE viewpoints and interaction challenges between the two persist To address engineeringlegal coordination in specification of regulatory requirements we propose the Artifact Model for Regulatory Requirements Engineering AM4RRE operationalized through templates AM4RRE was positively evaluated by most of the 37 practitioners for coordination in regulatory RE and for supporting requirements quality Results from a quasiexperiment with 34 of them in 10 groups indicated that templateguided coordination was associated with on average shorter total specification time when executed first and higher requirements quality in most groups in which it varied Existing RE research and practice provide little attention and support for viewpoint coordination in regulatory RE for CbD Artifactoriented approaches such as AM4RRE have the potential to guide coordination in RE for better RE results and contribute to concretizing the role and contribution of RE to CbD

papers.intro:
In recent years, countries worldwide have enacted multiple sophisticated regulations affecting software engineering (SE) Green Software Foundation (2023); Osborne Clarke (2025) across domains. Consequently, regulatory compliance has emerged as a cross-cutting software quality requirement that demands legally verifiable conformance. Recently introduced compliance by design (CbD) obligations demand integrating regulatory requirements into software design rather than addressing them as an afterthought. To address the challenge of systematically accounting for regulations and supporting compliance implementation in SE, regulatory requirements engineering (RE) approaches must both derive requirements from regulations and support their implementation throughout software engineering processes Hjerppe et al. (2019); Kempe and Massey (2021). In practice, awareness and adoption of regulatory RE approaches remain limited Klymenko et al. (2022); Kosenkov et al. (2025b). We argue this is because two conditions tied to core RE challenges are overlooked.
