papers.title: A Systematic Analysis of Live Intraoperative Surgical Expert Narrations
papers.abstract: Manual annotation remains the principal bottleneck in surgical video understanding. Live intraoperative narration by the operating surgeon is a scalable alternative that requires no manual annotation, but the information it contains has not been characterized. We analyzed 13 endoscopic lumbar spine decompression procedures (13.2 h) by two senior spine surgeons, using time-synchronized close-mic German audio. An annotation-free pipeline (word-level speech recognition, deterministic correction of surgical-term errors, utterance fusion, LLM-based translation to English, and relevance filtering) converted speech into time-stamped procedural cues labelled with the surgical entities they reference and their speech act. Of 3,171 utterances, 1,201 (37.9%) were retained as procedural cues, while 57.6% were non-procedural and removed. Retained cues referenced instruments (60.7%), anatomy (48.0%) and surgical actions (57.1%), and 98.5% carried at least one of these. 39% of cues (472 of 1,201) were directives, mainly instrument requests and commands. All 467 manually verified instrument requests preceded the instrument's appearance in the field, by a median of 8.2 s. Domain-term transcription corruption affected 18.0% of retained cues. Live narration is thus a dense, annotation-free supervisory signal describing instruments, anatomy, actions and team coordination, but it is noisy and temporally displaced from the events it names, and this displacement must be modelled before safe downstream use.

papers.title: SAMP: Self-Adaptive Margin Prioritization For Robust Diffusion Watermarking
papers.abstract: Diffusion models have made high-fidelity visual generation widely accessible, while also lowering the barrier to producing convincing visual forgeries and complicating content provenance. Existing watermarking methods typically use a fixed embedding strength throughout denoising or treat all watermark dimensions equally. As a result, they may introduce unnecessary distortion when some watermark dimensions are already reliable, while failing to sufficiently reinforce those that are more vulnerable to subsequent perturbations. Therefore, robust watermarking requires adapting both the embedding strength during denoising and the optimization priority across watermark dimensions. To address this problem, we present SAMP, a self-adaptive framework consisting of global margin regulation and vulnerability-sensitive allocation. Global margin regulation adjusts the embedding strength according to the separation between the target codeword and competing codewords, together with the estimated effects of common attacks. Vulnerability-sensitive allocation identifies watermark dimensions that are more easily weakened by local perturbations and gives them higher optimization priority. Experimental results demonstrate that SAMP achieves an average information recovery accuracy of 0.993. Compared with state-of-the-art methods, SAMP improves PSNR by 16.8% and reduces LPIPS by 47.1%. These results validate the effectiveness of SAMP for reliable and high-quality diffusion watermarking.
papers.intro:
Diffusion models enable high quality visual content generation from simple user inputs, while also lowering the barrier to producing convincing visual forgeries. As generated content becomes increasingly common, distinguishing its origin and verifying its authenticity become more difficult. Digital watermarking provides a direct means of associating provenance information with visual content, supporting source tracing and authenticity verification.

Early diffusion watermarking methods embed watermark information by modifying the latent state that initializes the generation process. Tree Ring [10] introduces structured Fourier patterns into the initial noise for watermark verification. Gaussian Shading [11] encodes watermark information into latent representations while preserving the original latent distribution. RingID [2] extends latent-space watermarking to multi-channel identification, while WIND [1] and PRC [3] explore latent-space embedding strategies for improving robustness and generation quality.

Recent methods further move watermark embedding into the denoising trajectory to achieve finer control over the generation process. LFLDW [5] injects watermark signals into selected latent-frequency components during intermediate denoising steps. GROW [7] extends this idea by progressively guiding the predicted clean latent across multiple denoising steps. However, existing trajectory-based methods still rely on predefined embedding strategies and cannot adapt the intervention strength to the current watermark reliability or prioritize more vulnerable watermark dimensions. Therefore, robust diffusion watermarking requires adaptive control over both embedding strength and optimization priority.

Specifically, SAMP adjusts the watermark update process by controlling the modification magnitude and the optimization priority of different watermark dimensions. SAMP’s global margin regulation mechanism estimates the required latent modification by measuring the separation between the target watermark code and competing codewords. It further incorporates lightweight attack-aligned perturbations to improve the reliability of this estimation. The proposed vulnerability-sensitive allocation mechanism analyzes the sensitivity of different watermark dimensions to local perturbations and assigns higher optimization priority to vulnerable dimensions. papers.title: HideOut - User Protection Against Localization with Throughput Guarantees in Mobile Networks
papers.abstract: Channel state information (CSI) in cellular networks is primarily used to maintain quality of service (QoS), yet it leaks privacy-sensitive information, in particular the user equipment's (UE) location. CSI is reported in plaintext on a publicly available schedule; thus, capturing it on the air and using a well trained AI model to localize the UE is straightforward. This simplicity in the attack execution makes it a serious privacy vulnerability. Using conventional privacy enhancing techniques, such as additive perturbation from differential privacy, to protect location data can potentially degrade the downlink communication quality. We present HideOut, a client-side defense mechanism that preserves the user's location from neural-based localization methods, while maintaining their downlink Spectral Efficiency (SE). Unlike generic adversarial attacks, HideOut treats downlink SE as a strict constraint in an optimization setting. Under maximum ratio transmission (MRT) beamforming, we show that a user-selected SE loss budget can be converted into an angular rate-feasible constraint on the reported channel vector. HideOut then performs gradient-based localization obfuscation while projecting each update onto this rate-feasible set. We evaluate HideOut against four CSI-based localization architectures under both white-box and black-box assumptions. Across models, HideOut increases localization ambiguity (error) from approximately $1--2$ m to $72--85$ m while keeping downlink SE loss within a $1\%$ budget. These results show that CSI-based localization can be substantially degraded at negligible communication quality loss when adversarial perturbations are made aware of the wireless link.

papers.intro:
Cellular networks are becoming sensing systems as well as communication systems. In 5G-Advanced and emerging 6G deployments, the same radio measurements that support beamforming and link adaptation can also be used to infer a User Equipment’s (UE’s) location. The 3GPP architecture already includes a Location Management Function (LMF) that collects positioning-related measurements from UEs (3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP), 2024). Recent learning-based positioning systems further strengthen this capability. Neural networks can map channel state information (CSI) directly to UE coordinates, exploiting multipath, blockage, and other propagation effects that are highly location-dependent (Colpaert et al., 2023; Vuckovic et al., 2024; Pan et al., 2025). Thus, CSI is no longer only a communication primitive, but also a high-resolution location signal.

This dual use creates a privacy risk. A UE must report CSI to receive efficient downlink service, but that same report may allow a network-side localization service to infer the UE’s precise position. Such location information can reveal sensitive attributes such as home and workplace, mobility routines, social relationships, and visits to sensitive places (Wang et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2025). Protecting only the location record after LMF is therefore insufficient: if the localization service can infer location directly from CSI, then privacy must be enforced before or during CSI reporting.

papers.title: The liquid-phase xenon purification system of the XENONnT dark matter experiment
papers.abstract: The XENONnT dark matter experiment utilizes a dual-phase time projection chamber (TPC) housed in a cryostat filled with 8.5 t of ultra-pure liquid xenon. To achieve optimal sensitivity, free electrons generated by particle interactions are required to drift across the 1.5-meter detector under an electric field. Dissolved impurities, particularly oxygen (O$_2$), can attenuate the resulting charge signal due to electron attachment. XENONnT demands an O$_2$-equivalent concentration below 100 parts per trillion (ppt) to enable its dark matter sensitivity reach. A novel liquid-phase xenon purification system was developed that continuously circulates liquid xenon through custom-designed, packed-bed sorbent purifier units at a volumetric flow rate of $\sim$2 liters per minute (L/min) at a cryogenic temperature around 175 K. With a purification time constant of approximately 25 h, the system reached the required purity within five days. The purification strategy employs a two-step approach: For an initial cleanup, a purifier based on a copper catalyst on high-surface-area alumina support (Q5) removes impurities from the liquid xenon bulk with nearly 100% efficiency, ideal for initial detector filling or after long-term maintenance. However, the high $^{222}$Rn emanation rate of the Q5 catalyst leads to increased background in the detector. In a second step, a purifier with sintered pellets of non-evaporable getter alloy (St707) ensures sustained purity with negligible background impact. The St707-based purifier exhibits a 55% efficiency, sufficient for normal operation. Following system commissioning, XENONnT achieved an O$_2$-equivalent concentration in liquid xenon below 19 ppt during its first science run. With this exceptional purity, over 86% of generated electrons survive a full drift across the TPC.

Particle interactions within a TPC generate both primary scintillation photons and ionization electrons. A uniform electric field is applied to drift the ionization electrons upwards towards the liquid-gas interface. Upon reaching the surface, these electrons are extracted into the gaseous xenon (GXe) phase by a stronger electric field, where they are accelerated to produce secondary scintillation photons through electroluminescence Dolgoshein et al. (1970). However, impurities dissolved in the LXe can hinder this process by capturing drifting electrons or absorbing both primary and secondary scintillation photons before they are detected by photomultiplier tubes (PMTs) arranged in arrays at the top and bottom of the TPC. These detrimental effects lead to attenuated signals, worsening the low-energy threshold of TPCs and increasing response variations within the sensitive LXe volume, ultimately impacting their sensitivity to potential WIMP interactions.

papers.title: Galaxy cluster thermodynamics at z=1.7: Resolved tSZ and X-ray analysis of CL J0459.6-4946
papers.abstract: Measurements of the entropy and temperature distribution of the intracluster medium (ICM) of local clusters have proven pivotal for the study of cluster astrophysics. Here, we extend these measurements to $z=1.7$ with a resolved analysis of the ICM in ACT/SPT-CL J0459.6-4946. By combining high-resolution thermal Sunyaev-Zeldovich measurements using new, deep ALMA Band 1 and 3 observations, with archival X-ray data, we conclude that the cluster has (i) an ICM with a flat and relatively high ($\approx 200$ keV cm$^2$) entropy distribution out to $\approx 0.3\,r_{500,\mathrm{c}}$, (ii) a hot core ($T_{\mathrm{e}} \simeq 14$ keV) with a declining temperature profile, (iii) a short effective path length along the line of sight of $l_{\mathrm{eff}} \simeq (0.75 \pm 0.05) \times r_{500,\mathrm{c}}$, and (iv) a clumpiness factor $C = \langle n_{\mathrm{e}}^2 \rangle / \langle n_{\mathrm{e}} \rangle^2 \simeq 1.17 \pm 0.05$ within $r_{500,\mathrm{c}}$. Its dynamic nature and high redshift suggest that the cluster is still thermalising its ICM, consistent with a relatively large hydrostatic mass bias of $b = 1 - M_{500,\mathrm{c,HE}}/M_{500,\mathrm{c,WL}} = 0.27^{+0.32}_{-0.67}$ that we measure with respect to the weak lensing mass. Furthermore, a region with low entropy and high density to the south of the cluster centre is observed in the X-rays yet absent in the Compton-$y$ map, indicating pressure equilibrium; we interpret this as a sloshing cold front -- the first such detection at high redshifts. This case study demonstrates that $\approx 3$h-long ALMA observations, combined with comparatively "short" X-ray exposures ($\approx 122$ ks), can fully characterise the ICM at high redshift, opening a path towards the thermodynamics of young and distant galaxy clusters for larger samples.

Since Zwicky (1933)’s work, observations of individual clusters of galaxies have been pivotal for the study of cosmology and for understanding the physics of the most massive overdensities formed in the Universe. It nevertheless took three more decades to detect (Byram et al., 1966; Gursky et al., 1971), and another to characterise (Mitchell et al., 1976; Serlemitsos et al., 1977), the hot intracluster medium (ICM), in which most of the clusters’ baryonic mass resides. Since then, measurements of the ICM’s thermodynamic properties have informed research on topics such as feedback by active galactic nuclei (AGN), low-density plasma physics, and cosmology (Sarazin, 1986; Voit, 2005; Pratt et al., 2019, for reviews, see;).

These observations of the ICM, however, have largely been limited to the nearby Universe (z<0.5z<0.5), mainly because the observed X-ray surface brightness suffers from cosmological dimming. This has not halted attempts to characterise the thermodynamic distribution of the ICM at early epochs (z>1.5z>1.5; see, for instance, McDonald et al. 2017; Mantz et al. 2020; Tozzi et al. 2022; Mantz et al. 2026), but such observations require Chandra and/or XMM-Newton integration times approaching the megasecond regime. These long integrations are essential for obtaining spectroscopic temperature estimates of the hot electrons in the ICM by fitting a plasma model to the observed X-ray spectrum. The temperature estimates, in turn, are crucial for accurately inferring cosmological parameters (Pratt et al., 2019) and for studying astrophysical phenomenon in clusters, such as shock fronts, cooling flows, and sloshing motions (Markevitch and Vikhlinin, 2007; McNamara and Nulsen, 2012, e.g.,).

The mm-wave regime probes the hot ICM through inverse Compton scattering of cosmic microwave background (CMB) photons, a phenomenon known as the thermal Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect (tSZ effect; Sunyaev and Zeldovich 1972; for a review of the tSZ effect and its applications in astrophysical studies, see Mroczkowski et al. 2019). Because the tSZ effect probes the integrated thermal electron pressure along the line of sight, and the surface brightness of the X-ray emission is roughly proportional to the line-of-sight integral of the square of the thermal electron density, one can infer a temperature map of the ICM using the ideal gas law. Therefore, the ratio of the tSZ flux to the square root of the X-ray flux yields a pseudo, electron-density-weighted temperature distribution at a much higher angular resolution than usually achievable when deploying the X-ray-only spectroscopic method (Wicker et al., 2026, see also,).

papers.title: Dust-induced reversal of the optical wavelength dependence of spiral-arm pitch angles
papers.abstract: The classical density-wave scenario predicts a blue-to-red age--colour gradient across the spiral arms of disc galaxies as a consequence of shock-induced star formation. However, observations of spiral-arm pitch angles at different wavelengths sometimes suggest the opposite trend, namely a red-to-blue ``colour jump''. The origin of this apparent contradiction remains unclear. In this work, we investigate the effects of dust attenuation on post-shock stellar emission, together with the streamline motions of gas and stellar populations. We find that dust attenuation in regions with relatively high optical depths, $\hat{\tau}_{V} \gtrsim 0.2$, can produce an apparent red-to-blue spatial sequence, with respect to the shock location, by reversing the relative positions of the flux maxima of stellar populations observed in different bands. Moreover, streamline motions confine post-shock stellar populations near the spiral arms for longer than in a circular-orbit model, thereby modifying the spatial distribution of the emitted light. We conclude that the apparent red-to-blue colour jump does not necessarily contradict the classical density-wave scenario. Instead, it can arise from the same post-shock stellar populations that intrinsically produce a blue-to-red age--colour gradient if their emission is modified by dust attenuation.

papers.intro:
The origin and nature of spiral structure in disc galaxies remain a central problem in astrophysics. Among the proposed mechanisms, the density wave (DW) theory (Lin & Shu, 1964; Bertin et al., 1989; Shu, 2016) has historically provided a compelling framework, describing spiral arms as long-lived quasi-stationary patterns that rotate with a constant angular speed. In this scenario, large-scale shocks compress the interstellar medium, triggering star formation near the spiral potential minimum (Roberts, 1969). As a consequence, newly formed stars drift away from their birthplaces, producing observable azimuthal age (or colour, blue-to-red) gradients across spiral arms.

The origin and nature of spiral structure in disc galaxies remain a central problem in astrophysics. Among the proposed mechanisms, the density wave (DW) theory (Lin & Shu, 1964; Bertin et al., 1989; Shu, 2016) has historically provided a compelling framework, describing spiral arms as long-lived quasi-stationary patterns that rotate with a constant angular speed. In this scenario, large-scale shocks compress the interstellar medium, triggering star formation near the spiral potential minimum (Roberts, 1969). papers.title: The MAGPI Survey: the evolution of galaxy spin-filament alignments since z~0.3
papers.abstract: We present measurements of galaxy spin-filament alignments at 0.20<z<0.42 using the MAGPI Survey, exploiting resolved stellar and ionised gas kinematics to reconstruct 3D spin axes. Cosmic filaments are identified using a stellar mass-matched constant-number-density population from the GAMA, MAGPI Redshift Survey and DESI datasets. We detect a flipping of the statistical alignment signal at z~0.3 as a function of M*: low-mass galaxies preferentially exhibit spins parallel to the direction of their host filaments, while high-mass galaxies tend towards perpendicular orientations. The transition mass is measured to be log(M{*,t}/Msun)~10.8, approximately 0.6 dex higher than the value for the SAMI Galaxy Survey at z~0.05. Bootstrap analysis gives 99.5% confidence that the transition mass is higher for MAGPI than SAMI. At fixed stellar mass MAGPI galaxies exhibit stronger parallel alignments than their SAMI counterparts, suggesting evolution of spin-filament alignments over the past ~3 Gyr. The gaseous component in MAGPI galaxies is more closely aligned with filaments than the stellar component, relative to a M*-matched SAMI sample. This indicates a stronger coupling between ionised gas and the large-scale structure at z~0.3, consistent with coherent gas accretion onto filaments remaining efficient at higher M*. At z~0 we detect a transition toward perpendicular alignments at lower M*, while the gas and stellar components exhibit similar alignments relative to filaments, likely due to the cumulative effects of mergers and secular evolution.

Understanding how galaxies acquire their angular momentum is fundamental for a complete picture of galaxy formation and evolution. According to tidal torque theory, galaxies acquire their spin through torques exerted by the surrounding large-scale structure during the early phases of halo collapse, leading to correlations between galaxy angular momentum and the cosmic web (Hoyle, 1951; Peebles, 1969; Doroshkevich, 1970; White, 1984; Porciani et al., 2002; Schäfer, 2009). Detecting these correlations can help us to provide insights into the processes driving galaxy growth.

Understanding how galaxies acquire their angular momentum is fundamental for a complete picture of galaxy formation and evolution. According to tidal torque theory, galaxies acquire their spin through torques exerted by the surrounding large-scale structure during the early phases of halo collapse, leading to correlations between galaxy angular momentum and the cosmic web (Hoyle, 1951; Peebles, 1969; Doroshkevich, 1970; White, 1984; Porciani et al., 2002; Schäfer, 2009). Detecting these correlations can help us to provide insights into the processes driving galaxy growth.

Large-scale cosmological hydrodynamic simulations find that the orientation between the galaxy spins and their closest filament depends on stellar mass (Dubois et al., 2014; Laigle et al., 2015; Codis et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018; Kraljic et al., 2020). Low-mass galaxies tend to align parallel to direction of their closest filament, consistent with growth dominated by smooth gas accretion, whereas more massive galaxies show perpendicular alignments associated with merger-driven angular momentum reorientation (Welker et al., 2014). The transition between parallel and perpendicular alignments is therefore linked to a ‘transition mass’ that has been found to be redshift-dependent for dark matter halos (Codis et al., 2012; Codis et al., 2015; Tobar et al., 2026). Different galaxy formation models predict different transition masses between parallel and perpendicular orientations (Krolewski et al., 2019; Kraljic et al., 2019; Ganeshaiah Veena et al., 2019), but this transition mass so far has remained unconstrained beyond zz ∼\sim 0 by current spin observations.

This paper is organised as follows. We present our MAGPI galaxy sample, including stellar and ionised gas kinematics and galaxy parameters in Section 2. We also provide a brief summary of the SAMI Galaxy Survey and the zz ∼\sim 0 reference sample for galaxy spin–filament alignments from Barsanti et al. (2022). In Section 3 we describe the reconstruction of the cosmic filaments. In Section 4 we identify the orientation of the spin axes. In Section 5 we present our results on the alignments, their correlations with stellar mass, the measured transition mass, and the comparison with SAMI galaxy spin–filament alignments at zz ∼\sim 0. In Section 6 we compare our findings to previous studies, and we discuss their physical interpretations. Finally, we summarise our findings and state our conclusions in Section 7. papers.title: The L1157 filament as traced in HNCO by the LMT
papers.abstract: Context. The L1157 outflow is a prototype of chemically active outflows where to look for molecular species linked to complex chemistry. Aims. With the aim of imaging the large (parsec) scale structure of key prebiotic molecules, we have mapped the whole blue-lobe of the L1157 outflow with the Large Millimeter Telescope (LMT), proving the potential of this facility to detect weak and extended molecular emission. Methods. Isocyanic acid, HNCO, an important precursor of complex chemistry, was chosen to be observed in its (4_0,4-3_0-3) transition at 87.925 GHz with the SEQUOIA focal-plane array, covering an area of 3x3 arcmin2 centered at the position of the main shock L1157-B1, which included a large portion of the vicinity of the protostellar region. Results. The HNCO emission was detected not only from the outflow but it also was found tracing a structure of about 0.3 pc in length, corresponding to the filament from which the protostellar system was born. Conclusions. The HNCO molecule was found to be a tracer of the densest part of filaments in molecular clouds, and given its importance in the formation of more complex molecules, its presence in the cold, quiescent filamentary gas indicates that the building blocks of complex chemistry are already well established in stages prior to protostellar warming or shocks. By allowing the detection of structures related with the filament, these observations proved the LMT potentialities to map weak and extended components in molecular clouds.

papers.intro:
The current view of stellar birth considers the formation of filaments as a natural consequence of supersonic turbulence during cloud collapse, and that the processes leading to filament shaping and its evolution set the initial conditions for star formation (Hacar et al. 2023; Pineda et al. 2023, for recent reviews, see). Observations in the far-infrared, sub-mm/mm and radio waves have revealed a widespread presence of filaments in the interstellar medium, with the latest census counting nearly 23 000 filamentary structures in our own Galaxy, covering a wide range of scales (Hacar et al. 2023). Typical tracers of the filamentary structure are the submm/mm continuum, the HI line, and rotational transitions of molecules such as 13CO, C18O, HCN, and N2H+, the later of which tracing preferentially denser gas (Priestley et al. 2023).

L1157 is part of a complex of molecular clouds named L1147/L1158 located in Cepheus at estimated distances in the range of ∼\sim 330-370 pc (352±\pm18 pc reported by Zucker et al. (2019), while 340±\pm3 pc was determined by Sharma et al. (2020)). Large-scale maps of the far-infrared emission show that the coma-shaped dark cloud named LDN 1157 breaks into a filamentary structure of about 1.2 pc in length and 0.09 pc in width, in which one half runs from east to west and the other half change to a north-south direction (Sharma et al. 2020, see figure 1). Two high-density clumps are identified within the filament, named C1 and C2 (Sharma et al. 2020, with peak values of dust column densities of 1.3×\times1022 and 9×\times1021 cm-2, respectively, according to). Almost at the eastern end of the east-west segment lies the C1 clump that harbors the L1157-mm protostellar object that has recently been revealed as a binary system (Tobin et al. 2022). At the southern end of the north-south segment and beyond the L1157-mm blue-lobe outflow, resides the C2 clump, which is less dense than C1 and, given the absence of detectable 70μ\mum emission, it is thought to be a starless core.

The L1157-mm protostellar system drives a precessing and episodic jet of matter at supersonic velocity (Gueth et al. 1996; Zhang et al. 2000; Nisini et al. 2010; Podio et al. 2016). Most of the studies have focused on the bright blue shifted southern outflow lobe, in which the jet has excavated two main cavities, the apices of which are called B1 and B2. Located at the apex of the more recent cavity, the bright bow shock B1 has a kinematical age of ∼\sim1000 years (Podio et al. 2016) and its intense chemical activity has been revealed by numerous investigations (Bachiller et al. 2001; Arce et al. 2008; Yamaguchi et al. 2012; Benedettini et al. 2013; Burkhardt et al. 2016; Lefloch et al. 2017; López-Sepulcre et al. 2024, e.g.). On the other hand, the B2 shock is thought to be an older event (Podio et al. 2016, ∼\sim1800 years:), with less chemical diversity than B1 (Bachiller et al. 2001). This older shock, on the plane of the sky, is located close to the C2 clump, at its northern end.

Millimeter continuum, 12CO, C18O, and N2H+ observations have revealed the detailed physical and chemical characteristic of the L1157 filament and its cores (Sharma et al. 2020). The emission of 12 CO that traces diffuse and external gas shows double-peaked line profiles all along the filament. The C18O peak velocities show a remarkable velocity coherence of the filament, with LSR values of 2.65±\pm0.05 km s-1. In contrast, the N2H+ molecule shows line profiles with peak LSR velocities in the range of 2.64 to 2.78 km s-1, indicative of the internal kinematics of the cores, the velocities of which are 2.62 km s-1(C1) and 2.72 km s-1 (C2). In addition, interferometric observations have shown that the emission from C1 is coincident with the elongated absorption feature at 8μ\mum that has been suggested to be the flattened envelope of the protostellar system (Chiang et al. 2010). The millimeter continuum and N2H+ are stronger in C1 than in C2, and the opposite tendency is found for C18O, which suggests that CO is more depleted in C1 than in C2, which in turn suggests that C2 is chemically younger than C1 (Sharma et al. 2020).

By utilizing the LMT, we sample the 3mm line emission with a beam approximately two times smaller than that of the IRAM 30m. The increased sensitivity and resolution allow us to recover the filament/envelope-scale emission that interferometers mostly miss, while providing the clarity needed to resolve intermediate-scale structures. As demonstrated here, this capability has been crucial for identifying the filamentary emission of the HNCO molecule, targeted in this study as a key precursor of complex organic chemistry, and underscores the LMT’s important role in connecting disparate spatial scales in star formation regions.

papers.title: Behavior Graphs: Unsupervised Graph Structures for Interpreting Robot Deployment Data
papers.abstract: Data flywheels promise continuous improvement via insights from deployment data. Understanding how the deployed model succeeds and fails can steer subsequent data collection towards patching failures and reinforcing successes. However, robot deployments create large volumes of high-dimensional rollout data, which is challenging to understand and confidently ground data collection decisions in. To make deployment data easier to analyze and act on, we propose behavior graphs, which compress policy rollouts into a single interpretable, directed graph. We construct the graphs by learning to identify similar behavior modes across rollouts, connecting the behaviors temporally, and finally linking them to outcomes. In a user study on three real-world tasks, where participants analyzed rollouts to choose a data collection strategy, 16 of 18 preferred behavior graphs to rollout videos, reaching comparable conclusions with 40.3% lower perceived temporal demand and 37.6% lower effort. Beyond interpretability for deployment data, behavior graphs are capable progress predictors: across 43 datasets, they improve the rank correlation between predicted progress and true temporal order by 22.9% and reduce mean absolute error by 53.5% relative to the strongest baseline. As the number of deployed robots grows, behavior graphs lend structure to high-dimensional policy rollouts and make deployment data easier to interpret and reason about.

papers.intro:
Imitation learning has become a standard approach for training robotic manipulation policies [1, 2]. As policies move toward real-world deployment, improving them after initial training relies on the data flywheel: deploy the policy, observe its rollout behavior, collect new demonstrations that address observed shortcomings, and retrain. Closing this loop effectively is difficult. Operators must identify not just that a policy fails, but which execution strategies are responsible, whether those failures stem from missing or low-quality training data, and what new demonstrations would meaningfully change the policy’s behavior distribution. Without a structured account of policy behavior, these decisions reduce to intuition. This raises two problems as robots move from labs to deployments: rollout data quickly outgrows what operators can review, and intuition is hard to communicate, compare, or verify. Closing the data flywheel requires methods that condense deployment data into a shared basis for understanding and reasoning about policy behavior.

Active data collection approaches such as DAgger [9, 10] are effective, but expensive to scale, as they require constant monitoring and human experts to collect recovery data. papers.title: A multiprobe $\Lambda$CDM consistency analysis with gravitational-wave standard sirens
papers.abstract: Multi-messenger cosmology offers an independent path to stress-test the $\Lambda$CDM model as gravitational wave (GW) catalogs grow in size. We present the first multiprobe assessment of $\Lambda$CDM tensions incorporating GW standard sirens: LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA Collaboration (LVK) fifth Gravitational-Wave Transient Catalog (GWTC-5.0) standard sirens are combined with Dark Energy Survey (DES) Year 6 weak lensing and galaxy clustering (3$\times$2pt), baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO), and type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia), together with Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) BAO, and confronted with primary cosmic microwave background (CMB) measurements from Planck, the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT), and the South Pole Telescope (SPT). All probes are analyzed under homogeneous priors and combined via normalizing flows, and we quantify the $S_8$ discrepancy and $H_0$ tension with respect to CMB. Adding standard sirens to the 3$\times$2pt analysis improves the constraints in the $\Omega_m$-$S_8$ plane by $\sim$30%, while constraining $H_0$ to 6.2%. We present cosmological constraints from the low-redshift probes including standard sirens, yielding $S_8 = 0.793 \pm 0.010$, $\Omega_m = 0.308^{+0.007}_{-0.006}$, and $H_0 = 69.4^{+4.1}_{-4.4}$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$. At current GW sensitivity, however, both the $S_8$ discrepancy and the $H_0$ tension remain essentially unchanged. Our analysis nonetheless delivers the first assessment of $\Lambda$CDM tensions computed with standard sirens included among the probes, and establishes them as a mature cosmological probe -- ready to be combined on equal footing with established datasets in forthcoming surveys such as the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), Euclid, and Roman.

The Λ\LambdaCDM model, comprising a cosmological constant (Λ\Lambda) and CDM (CDM) that seeds large-scale structure, remains the standard framework for cosmic history and dynamics. papers.title: FESTiVE: Self-calibrated Spatial-temporal Gradient Characterization for Non-cartesian Imaging on High Performance Systems
papers.abstract: Gradient imperfections disrupt the encoding benefits of long-readout imaging applications on high-performance systems. Currently, external field monitoring hardware provides the only reliable solution for general spatial-temporal gradient characterization. We present FESTiVE, a data-driven alternative to higher-order field monitoring. FESTiVE leverages parallel imaging to both implicitly model and explicitly recover field imperfections. Using a fast k-t mapping calibration scan, FESTiVE formulates a time-varying GRAPPA problem which maps k-space data corrupted by a time-varying gradient imperfection against a clean reference. This mapping is represented compactly with an implicit neural representation, from which the spatial-temporal fields are recovered in image space using coil sensitivities. In phantom, FESTiVE produces comparable field measurements to a Skope field camera across multiple non-cartesian 2D acquisition strategies and gradient specifications. In vivo, FESTiVE achieves state-of-the-art image quality for a high-performance diffusion spiral protocol on the head-only MAGNUS 3T, where higher-order phase imperfections are significant. At 7T, on the head-only Siemens TerraX system, FESTiVE enables 300{\mu}m spiral imaging where conventional field camera-based approaches fall below probe dephasing limits. In conclusion, FESTiVE enables robust high-resolution non-cartesian imaging on high-performance gradients, characterizing gradient imperfections using parallel imaging rather than field monitoring hardware.

(2022), or thermal dependencesNussbaum et al. (2022). Geometry-dependent concomitant fields unique to asymmetric head-only gradientsAbad et al. (2023) additionally confound LTI assumptions. papers.title: Physics-informed X-ray tomography of magnetization and material parameters
papers.abstract: Three-dimensional spin textures are stabilized by microscopic interactions within their host materials. X-ray vector tomography can image these nanoscale structures, but weak magnetic contrast and a limited range of viewing angles often leave parts of the magnetization poorly determined. Here we show that a reconstruction constrained by the micromagnetic energy recovers the three-dimensional magnetization from such data and gains sensitivity to the underlying material interactions. Applied to the chiral magnet Co$_8$Zn$_9$Mn$_3$, the method resolves the three-dimensional helical texture even from a small fraction of the dual-axis projections typically required for a successful tomographic reconstruction, or from a single tilt axis alone. By testing which ratio of exchange to Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction in the reconstruction best reproduces the measured projections, we obtain a value for the sample that differs by about 10 % from the literature value derived from the helical winding period. Taken together, our findings suggest a way to reduce the time needed for vector tomography and to extend it to determining fundamental magnetic interactions in a material.

papers.title: Fluid Limits and Upper Bounds for Randomized Greedy Matching
papers.abstract:
The Modified Randomized Greedy (MRG) algorithm [Tinhofer (1984), Aronson-Dyer-Frieze-Suen (1995)] is a classical greedy algorithm for finding approximate maximum matchings. MRG repeatedly picks a uniformly random unmatched vertex and matches it to a uniformly random unmatched neighbor, if one exists. Since 1991, the best upper bound on its approximation ratio has been $2/3$, given by the Bomb graphs of [Dyer and Frieze (1991)]. We improve this bound to $0.6569$ on general graphs and $0.6607$ on bipartite graphs.
  Our constructions consist of copies of small gadgets, with specified vertex classes joined completely. We track each algorithm by counting gadget copies with each possible configuration of remaining vertices. Wormald's differential equation method [Wormald (1995)] shows that these counts, scaled by the size parameter of the construction, converge to a deterministic trajectory known as the \textit{fluid limit}, which is described by ordinary differential equations. This fluid limit approximation holds while the relevant vertex classes have positive density, and so we devise a separate counting argument determines the contribution from the end of the run.
  Furthermore, we apply our framework to Random Decision Order (RDO), in which vertices are processed in uniformly random order and choose unmatched neighbors according to fixed adversarial preferences. On bipartite graphs, we determine the exact limiting ratio on the Double-Bomb family of [Tang-Wu-Zhang (2020)]. Its minimum is $31/48$, confirming their numerical estimate of about $0.646$.On general graphs, we improve their upper bound of $5/8$, given by the paw graph, to $0.5946$ on a new family. Finally, we give one possible explanation for why $2/3$ seemed to be optimal for MRG in the concluding remarks.

A matching in a graph GG is a set of vertex-disjoint edges, and ν⁡(G)\nu(G) denotes the size of a maximum matching. Any maximal matching (matching that cannot be extended by adding new edges) has at least ν⁡(G)/2\nu(G)/2 edges, and so the simplest greedy algorithm, which adds edges one at a time as long as possible, is a 1/21/2-approximation. A long line of work asks how much randomness helps such greedy algorithms (Tin, 84; DF, 91; ADFS, 95; PS, 12; CCWZ, 18; GT, 12; BP, 17; TWZ, 23; DY, 26). Besides being natural, these algorithms are oblivious and local, i.e. they never look at the graph beyond the neighbors of the current vertex (without full knowledge of the graph). This matters when matches must be made as requests stream in, long before a maximum matching could be computed. In search advertising, an ad must be chosen for each query as it arrives, as in the AdWords problem of search engines such as Google (MSVV, 07; Meh, 13), and in real-time bidding each display impression is auctioned within 1010 to 100100 milliseconds (YWZ, 13; YWLQ, 14). Ride-sharing platforms assign riders to vehicles in batches collected over windows of about 3030 seconds (AMSW+, 17), and randomized online assignment is a standard way to balance load in distributed systems (ABKU, 99). A greedy rule that processes vertices in random order uses only local information at each step, and its approximation ratio measures what is lost by not computing the optimum.

MRG is an algorithm for the randomized greedy matching problem, also called the oblivious matching problem (GT, 12; TWZ, 23). The algorithm chooses the order in which it tries vertex pairs without looking at the graph, adds every tried pair that is an edge between two unmatched vertices, and its quality is defined by the worst-case ratio 𝔼​|M|/ν⁡(G)\mathbb{E}|M|/\nu(G). The point of MRG is that a vertex with few available neighbors is matched along one of them with correspondingly large probability.

papers.title: How Much Can Approximate Equilibria Change the Social Cost of Selfish Routing?
papers.abstract:
We study approximate Nash equilibria in nonatomic congestion games, with the goal of understanding how much the social cost can change when the equilibrium condition is relaxed. We consider $\epsilon$-approximate Nash equilibria ($\epsilon$-NE), in which each player uses a strategy whose cost is at most $1 + \epsilon$ times the minimum available cost. We compare the social costs of $\epsilon$-NE and exact Nash equilibria. This lets us quantify, for example, how much a navigation app can reduce total travel time when drivers tolerate routes slightly slower than the fastest available route.
  For degree-$d$ polynomial latencies in both general nonatomic congestion games and single-commodity routing games on series-parallel networks, we give tight lower and upper bounds on the relative change in social cost from an exact Nash equilibrium to any $\epsilon$-NE, with matching instances for every $\epsilon$. For small $\epsilon$, the largest possible relative reduction and increase in general congestion games are both $\Theta(\sqrt{d\epsilon})$, independently of the number of resources and populations. In contrast, on series-parallel networks of depth $h$, the largest possible relative reduction is $\Theta(h\epsilon)$, while the largest possible relative increase is known to be $\epsilon$. For the classes of games we study, these results give a tight and quantitative characterization of the possible changes in social cost and establish a separation between general and series-parallel networks.

papers.intro:
Nonatomic routing games are a fundamental model in algorithmic game theory. In this model, a continuum of infinitesimal drivers travels through a network, and the latency (travel time) of each edge depends on the total traffic using it. A flow specifies how the traffic is split among the available routes. A Nash equilibrium, also called a Nash flow or Wardrop equilibrium [65], is a flow in which every driver uses a route of minimum latency under the resulting traffic pattern. The social cost of a flow is the total travel time of all drivers. The classical examples of Pigou [52] and Braess [12] show that a Nash flow need not minimize the social cost. The seminal work on the Price of Anarchy (PoA) [40, 54, 58] quantifies this inefficiency as the worst-case ratio of the social cost of a Nash flow to the optimal social cost.

The exact Nash equilibrium condition, however, is often too restrictive as a model of drivers’ behavior. In many scenarios, drivers may lack accurate and timely estimates of travel times, perceive routes with slight travel time differences as equally good, or prefer a familiar route even if it is slightly slower. Drivers may also be willing to follow a navigation app’s recommendation as long as its estimated travel time is close to that of the fastest route. Routing platforms could use this tolerance to steer traffic toward more desirable flows. This motivates us to study ϵ\epsilon-approximate Nash equilibria (ϵ\epsilon-NE), in which every driver uses a route whose latency is at most 1+ϵ1+\epsilon times that of the fastest available route under the resulting traffic pattern.

papers.title: Uncertainty-Aware Coordinated Multi-Ramp Metering Based on an Action-Conditioned Traffic Prediction Operator Under Sparse Observations
papers.abstract: Coordinated multi-ramp metering (CRM) is an important approach to mitigating freeway congestion, but sparse observations in practice complicate the state estimation and model calibration required by predictive control. This study develops an Action-Conditioned Traffic Prediction Operator (ATPO) driven by sparse, heterogeneous observations and candidate multi-ramp actions, and embeds it in an uncertainty-aware CRM framework (ATPOUCRM). ATPO forms a four-channel history from the density and speed measurements of fixed detectors and probe vehicles and their separate observation masks. Queries at future spatiotemporal points attend to all valid historical observations before incorporating upstream mainline demand and on-ramp queue information. Candidate metering actions condition the latent field through feature-wise linear modulation, a spatial Fourier operator, and a causal temporal kernel. The operator produces action-conditioned predictive distributions of future density and speed throughout the corridor; a bootstrap ensemble additionally characterizes disagreement among models. Using these predictions, ATPOUCRM primarily minimizes expected total time spent, including mainline travel and on-ramp waiting, while penalizing predictive uncertainty near merge areas. It uses the cross-entropy method to search candidate actions and applies a safety filter before execution. For five-minute global traffic state prediction on a simulated 7-km freeway corridor, ATPO achieves root mean square errors of 2.54 veh/km/lane, 4.56 km/h, and 0.76 veh*h for density, speed, and total time spent over the forecast horizon, respectively, outperforming the comparison methods. Across 100 control scenarios, ATPOUCRM reduces mean total time spent by 26.17% relative to no control. ATPO also generates predictions on finer spatiotemporal grids without retraining.

papers.intro:
Freeways are essential corridors for urban and intercity travel. Increasing vehicle ownership, however, has contributed to recurrent congestion that reduces network efficiency and service reliability. Ramp metering regulates the flow entering the mainline, reduces density near merge areas, and thereby limits the formation and propagation of bottleneck congestion. Its practical value was demonstrated by the local-ramp feedback controller ALINEA (Papageorgiou et al., 1991). Yet local benefits from metering one ramp may come at the expense of downstream traffic conditions or longer on-ramp queues. This has motivated Coordinated multi-Ramp Metering (CRM), which allocates metering and queue storage across ramps to improve corridor-wide performance. The field deployment of HERO (Papamichail et al., 2010b) further showed that coordination among adjacent ramps can improve traffic operations along an entire freeway corridor.

The field deployment of HERO (Papamichail et al., 2010b) further showed that coordination among adjacent ramps can improve traffic operations along an entire freeway corridor.

CRM can be organized into three methods according to the information and predictive model used for decision-making. The first coordinates local feedback controllers through predefined rules. HERO uses ALINEA locally and links upstream and downstream ramps according to mainline occupancy and on-ramp queues, drawing on upstream queue storage to relieve a downstream bottleneck. Such controllers require only real-time measurements at ramps and nearby mainline locations, rather than online traffic-model optimization or demand forecasts. Their heuristic rules, however, do not directly maximize network-wide throughput (Papamichail et al., 2010b). The second approach optimizes predicted traffic evolution with a traffic-flow model. AMOC and subsequent model predictive control (MPC) methods simulate candidate metering sequences and optimize multiple ramps subject to demand, queue, and control constraints (Kotsialos et al., 2002, 2004; Hegyi et al., 2005; Papamichail et al., 2010a). This provides a systematic framework for anticipatory coordination, but the ranking of candidate actions depends on accurate estimates of the current network state, model parameters, and boundary demand. Performance can deteriorate when these conditions depart from the model assumptions. The third approach learns action-driven traffic dynamics from data and uses the learned model for predictive optimization. Gu et al. (2023) learned ramp-action-dependent transitions of link-aggregated states with a deep Koopman model and embedded it in MPC for coordinated ramp metering. Zhou et al. (2026) additionally learned latent dynamics, reward, and value functions for offline planning. These methods reduce reliance on explicit traffic-flow equations, but their training and control use state vectors covering all modeled links, which are difficult to obtain under sparse real-world observations.

papers.title: CuriousTogether: Implications of Curiosity and Cultural Grounding in Multi-Agent LLM Interactions
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent settings, exhibiting emergent collective behaviors, yet the role of curiosity as a driver of such dynamics remains understudied. We introduce CuriousTogether, a framework evaluating curiosity-driven multi-agent LLM interactions across three complementary dimensions: novelty-seeking, epistemic and social curiosity. Across eight tasks spanning reasoning, creative generation, and social bias mitigation, curiosity-guided multi-agent settings yield improvements over non-curious ones on seven out of eight tasks, with gains of up to 20.6% in story generation (semantic diversity) and a 14.9 pp reduction in stereotype rates. Furthermore, country-conditioned cultural grounding show benefits for story generation and social tasks, but can hurt precision-oriented reasoning. Finally, we show that inference-time multi-agent curiosity-based approach offers favorable quality-token trade-offs, compared with single-agent baselines. Together, these findings support curiosity-guided interaction as a practical mechanism for improving multi-agent collaboration, with downstream benefits for reasoning, creative, and societal tasks.

papers.intro:
Curiosity drives learning, exploration, and innovation in humans (Loewenstein, 1994), functioning as a fundamental engine of intellectual and creative progress (Kashdan, 2009). In group settings, questions about uncertain situations propagate through social networks, shaping shared attention and exploration strategies (Berlyne, 1960). In social psychology, this phenomenon is called curiosity contagion, where observing others ask questions increases one’s own motivation (Litman, 2005; Edmondson, 1999). Further, curiosity is shaped by cultural background and social norms (Borah et al., 2025b), with cultures varying in how they encourage questioning and reward exploration. This means that a group’s collective curiosity is inherently tied to its cultural composition (Leung et al., 2008; Maddux and Galinsky, 2009). At the collective level, culturally-grounded curiosity leads to richer information exchange, supports perspective-taking and enables communities to generate, challenge, and refine knowledge over time (Hong and Page, 2004). Furthermore, it has been linked to creative problem-solving, and adaptive learning in complex environments (Mussel, 2013a; Mussel, 2013b), properties that are increasingly relevant as LLMs are designed to reason and interact at scale.

LLMs are increasingly used in multi-agent setups across diverse applications such as planning (Wang et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2022), tool-use (Schick et al., 2023; Qin et al., 2023), safety evaluation (Feffer et al., 2024), and human-AI collaboration (Wu et al., 2024; Park et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2023). While such settings reveal emergent behaviors, they also sometimes show undesirable collective behaviors, including bias amplification (Borah and Mihalcea, 2024), echo-chamber effects (Nehring et al., 2024a; Borah et al., 2025c), and sycophantic conformity to majority beliefs (Andriushchenko et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2025). These behaviors can systematically undermine the reliability and downstream utility of multi-agent LLMs. Curiosity can help counter this by encouraging exploration and novelty-seeking over conformity (Weng et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2026). Cultural diversity among agents can further amplify this effect: agents grounded in different cultural priors bring heterogeneous perspectives to collective reasoning (Bai et al., 2025). In reinforcement learning, similar curiosity-driven exploration has been shown to improve coordination and achieve higher returns than standard baselines (Zheng et al., 2021; Reyes et al., 2022; Dai et al., 2025). Overall, these insights motivate studying collective curiosity and its interplay with cultural grounding in multi-agent LLMs as a way to promote better reasoning, reduce conformity bias, and improve the robustness of LLM interaction.

Prior work on curiosity in LLMs has primarily focused on single-agent settings, exploring aspects such as cross-cultural variations (Borah et al., 2025b) and patterns of human questioning and causal inquiry (Ceraolo et al., 2025). Separately, recent work has shown that culturally grounded multi-agent systems produce richer, more diverse outputs in tasks such as image captioning (Bai et al., 2025), suggesting that cultural context is a meaningful axis of agent heterogeneity. However, little attention has been given to how curiosity and cultural grounding jointly improve multi-agent performance. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to systematically investigate the impact of curiosity and culture in multi-agent LLMs, addressing three key questions: (1) How can curiosity be effectively introduced in multi-agent LLM interactions? (2) How does the optimal level and form of curiosity change based on the task at hand? and (3) How do curiosity- and culture-grounded multi-agent LLMs fare against single-agent baselines across performance and token efficiency? Importantly, we treat “curiosity” and “culture” as operational prompting constructs rather than human-like trait or faithful representations of real cultures. Our goal is to study how these design mechanisms shape information exchange and downstream performance in multi-agent LLM interactions.

papers.title: Witnessing pre-processing at intermediate redshift: observational evidence of infalling groups onto a merging galaxy cluster
papers.abstract: The fraction of quenched galaxies increases with local density, and part of this trend is thought to arise in groups before cluster accretion (pre-processing). In merging clusters, this is difficult to separate from star formation triggered or suppressed by the cluster merger itself. We investigate whether five high-velocity galaxies in the merging cluster SPT-CL~J0307-6225 ($z=0.579$), distributed in two candidate infalling groups, show signs of group-scale environmental processing prior to accretion. We combine MUSE integral-field spectroscopy and HST imaging to derive [\ion{O}{ii}] kinematic maps, spectral classes, and star-formation rates (SFR), to understand the properties of the galaxies. We further use the Magneticum simulations and the phase-space information to determine if these galaxies are part of two groups, and if they will be accreted onto the merging cluster. Group~1 is a morphologically disturbed interacting pair bound to the cluster, with at least one galaxy classified as dusty starburst. Group~2 is a compact triplet at $\sim$4$\sigma_v$ from the cluster, in which two galaxies share a common [\ion{O}{ii}] envelope and the dominant member, an e(b) starburst, shows an elevated ionised-gas velocity dispersion. The SFR of both starburst galaxies lie within the scatter of the field star-forming main sequence, as expected for modest, interaction-triggered bursts. Close pairs at the phase-space position of group~2 occur for $\sim$1\% of comparable-mass cluster galaxies in Magneticum, so it is not unlikely for the group to be bound. Both groups show spatially resolved signatures of galaxy--galaxy interactions alongside ongoing star formation, supporting a pre-processing scenario in the environment of a merging cluster. Such group-scale interactions may contribute to the enhanced star formation reported in merging clusters.

papers.intro:
Many studies separate galaxies in two fundamental types: actively star-forming, and quiescent (or “quenched”) systems. A correlation between the local number density and the fraction of quiescent galaxies, has been observed out to z∼1.5z\sim 1.5 (Dressler, 1980; Dressler et al., 1997; Postman et al., 2005; Holden et al., 2007; van der Wel et al., 2007; Mei et al., 2012; Fritz et al., 2014; Paulino-Afonso et al., 2020), where the fraction of quiescent galaxies is substantially higher in the densest environments, such as galaxy clusters, compared to those in the field (Nantais et al., 2017). Environmental mechanisms such as ram-pressure stripping (RPS) and tidal interactions drive galaxy evolution within clusters (Bahé et al., 2013; Jaffé et al., 2015; Marasco et al., 2016; Pallero et al., 2022). One of the most direct forms of galaxy evolution is gravitational interactions between galaxies, such as mergers (Gunn & Gott, 1972). The relatively large velocities of galaxies within a cluster make it hard for them to directly interact with each other. However, galaxy groups, which have lower velocity dispersions and are sometimes comprised of as few as 2-3 members, provide the perfect environment for such interactions to happen (Moran et al., 2007). The phenomenon in which galaxies are quenched in groups before being accreted by larger galaxy clusters is known as “pre-processing” (Fujita, 2004).

(2014) found an increase of Hα\alpha emission in star-forming galaxies in the ‘Sausage’ (CIZA J2242.8+5301) merging cluster and, by comparing with the more evolved merger cluster ‘Toothbrush’ (1RXS J0603.3+4213), concluded that merger shocks enhance the star formation activity of galaxies, exhausting their gas reservoirs faster (Stroe et al., 2015). Aldás et al. (2025) used simulations to study galaxies in clusters with different dynamical states, with one key finding being that at the beginning of interaction, in the case of merging galaxy clusters, there is a boost in the star formation rate, followed by a suppression as the cluster reaches the equilibrium state.

Given the perturbed dynamical state of galaxy clusters, distinguishing galaxies in infalling groups from those that are part of the merging clusters is challenging. One common technique to distinguish between galaxies in different stages of accretion is with the use of the phase-space diagram (Jaffé et al., 2015; Rhee et al., 2017; Ivleva et al., 2026, PSD,). In the PSD, line-of-sight (LoS) velocities (commonly normalized by the velocity dispersion) and projected cluster-centric distance (normalized by the virial radius) are used to determine the accretion history of galaxy clusters. Thus, the need for unbiased, high-S/N galaxy spectra and high-resolution imaging are crucial to disentangle environmental factors in galaxy evolution, such as pre-processing and the effects of cluster mergers, as well as determining the accretion history of the system.

papers.title: Leveraging high-performance head-only gradients to enable ~2-fold higher multiband acceleration in SMS-EPI and SMS-EPTI
papers.abstract: High-performance head-only gradient systems can substantially reduce echo spacing (ESP) in echo-planar imaging (EPI), but the resulting encoding speed is typically used to shorten readouts and reduce distortion. Here, we instead leverage the increased echo budget to enable denser k-space sampling and higher simultaneous-multislice (SMS) acceleration in SMS-EPI and SMS-EPTI. Fast k-space traversal with denser ky-kz sampling is achieved using peripheral nerve stimulation (PNS)-optimized gradient waveforms, while high-quality reconstruction is obtained using field-correcting GRAPPA (FCG). The resulting ESPs on MAGNUS 3T and Impulse 7T are approximately half those of high-performance whole-body systems, enabling approximately 2-fold higher multiband (MB) acceleration. This facilitates high-quality 2.5-mm isotropic whole-brain resting-state fMRI at 7T with MB28 and a repetition time (TR) of 123 ms.

papers.title: Robust Appointment Scheduling with Heterogeneous Costs
papers.abstract:
Designing simple appointment systems that under uncertainty in service times, try to achieve both high utilization of expensive medical equipment and personnel as well as short waiting time for patients, has long been an interesting and challenging problem in health care. We consider a robust version of the appointment scheduling problem, introduced by Mittal et al.\ (2014), with the goal of finding simple and easy-to-use algorithms. Previous work focused on the special case where per-unit costs due to under-utilization of equipment/personnel are homogeneous i.e., costs are linear and identical. We consider the heterogeneous case and devise an LP that has a simple closed-form solution. This solution yields the first constant-factor approximation for the problem. We also find special cases beyond homogeneous costs where the LP leads to closed form optimal schedules. Our approach and results extend more generally to convex piece-wise linear costs.
  For the case where the order of patients is changeable, we focus on linear costs and show that the problem is strongly NP-hard when the under-utilization costs are heterogeneous. For changeable order with homogeneous under-utilization costs, it was previously shown that an EPTAS exists. We instead find an extremely simple, ratio-based ordering that is 1.0604 approximate.

papers.intro:
Consider the problem of scheduling appointments in service operations where customers are served sequentially by a single server. Service times of customers are uncertain, and we wish to assign time slots for serving the customers in advance. An important practical setting where this problem arises everyday is in health care services, where there are numerous instances that require efficient scheduling of appointments, such as scheduling outpatient appointments in primary care and specialty clinics, scheduling surgeries for operating rooms, or appointments for MRI scans. Often in these settings the order in which patients undergo the procedure is known in advance. Then a day before the procedures, a hospital manager determines planned start times and how much time to allot to each procedure. If the manager allots too small an interval to a procedure, it could easily go overtime and delay the next procedure. The inconvenience and costs resulting from such a delay are referred to as the overage cost for that procedure. On the contrary, if the manager assigns a very large interval, then the procedure will likely end much sooner. In this case the hospital incurs an underage cost as the equipment and personnel may be left idle until the scheduled start of the next procedure. We would like to design an appointment schedule that can achieve the desired trade-off between overage and underage costs.

In an influential survey on outpatient scheduling, Cayirli and Veral [6] concluded that the “biggest challenge for future research will be to develop easy-to-use heuristics”. Traditionally, most models for the problem are stochastic in nature and assume distributional knowledge of the uncertain service times. While such models are very powerful, estimating distributions accurately can require large amounts of data. There are many settings where such data is in fact available but, in applications related to health care appointment scheduling there is evidence (ref. [19, 20, 8]) that the amount of data available by surgery types, let alone by surgery types and surgeons, is extremely limited. Moreover, computing an objective function that involves finding the expectation of a high dimensional non-linear function can be computationally burdensome. Further, Mak et al. [20] and Mittal et al. Instead, it uses deterministic uncertainty sets and performs a worst-case analysis w.r.t. to the uncertainty. Referring to the procedures/services in any given context simply as ‘jobs’, in the robust appointment scheduling problem we are given nn jobs with uncertain service times {ti}\{t_{i}\}. Assume that the time tit_{i} for job ii can be anything in the range [pi−δ^i,pi+δi][p_{i}-\hat{\delta}_{i},p_{i}+\delta_{i}]. The range is known to us but the value of tit_{i} can be chosen adversarially. Our task is to propose an appointment start time for each job. A job will be available to process after this start time and jobs will be served in order of increasing index ii. The order in which jobs are processed is fixed a priori. Due to uncertainty in service times, a job may have to wait to be processed after its appointed start time. The overage cost incurred per unit of wait is given by oi≥0o_{i}\geq 0. Similarly, ui≥0u_{i}\geq 0 is the per-unit underage cost associated with job ii. Given a set of appointment start times, an adversary chooses the worst possible instantiation of service durations tit_{i} i.e., one that maximizes the overall overage/underage cost. We seek start times to minimize this worst case total cost.

Robust Appointment Scheduling (RAS): We explore the structure of optimal appointment schedules and find several properties that all optimal schedules must satisfy. Somewhat surprisingly, we find that in every optimal appointment schedule, the case of all jobs underaged as well as the case of all jobs overaged are always worst-cases for the adversary’s problem. papers.title: Fredholm approximations to the Bethe-Salpeter equation with spherical-Bessel kernels for Wannier-Mott excitons
papers.abstract: We develop a deterministic radial approximation to the static Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE), designed for rapid preliminary screening of Wannier-Mott exciton binding across direct-gap bulk materials. The approximation replaces the electron-hole transition problem by small radial eigenvalue problems that require no stochastic sampling. Starting from the four-point BSE and its matrix representation in a Bloch electron-hole basis, we retain one valence and one conduction band in the effective-mass limit within the Tamm-Dancoff approximation. We introduce a central projection of the screened direct interaction and omit bare electron-hole exchange. The resulting model applies to spatially extended excitons whose envelopes vary slowly on the scale of the unit cell, provided that the effective-mass description and central screened interaction adequately represent the exciton of interest. A partial-wave decomposition separates the angular-momentum channels and expresses their interaction kernels as spherical-Bessel transforms of the real-space screened Coulomb interaction. Nystr\"{o}m discretization produces real symmetric radial matrices suitable for standard eigensolvers. Their dimension is set by the radial grid independently of the Brillouin-zone sampling used to calculate screening. We implement the formulation in the all-electron, full-potential code $\texttt{exciting}$. For bulk GaAs, the compact radial problem reproduces the corresponding conventional matrix-BSE binding energy within $(1~\mathrm{meV})$ at matched sampling. Further refinement achieves finite-mesh stability within the same tolerance on denser screening meshes without increasing the radial matrix size.

papers.intro:
Neutral excitations in solids, in particular bound electron-hole pairs (excitons), give rise to prominent features in the optical spectra of semiconductors, insulators, and low-dimensional materials. Their reliable quantitative description generally requires an excplicit treatment of the electron-hole interaction beyond the independent-particle picture and commonly uses adiabatic approximations to time-dependent density-functional theory (TDDFT). The most widely used approach today is many-body perturbation theory (MBPT) in the G​WGW+Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) framework, where quasiparticle energies obtained from the G​WGW approach are combined with a BSE for the two-particle Green’s function[32, 43, 35, 6]. This scheme has become a de facto standard for calculating excitons and optical spectra in bulk and low-dimensional systems[32, 42, 13, 27], and has also been successfully applied to molecules and complex environments[6, 12].

Neutral excitations in solids, in particular bound electron-hole pairs (excitons), give rise to prominent features in the optical spectra of semiconductors, insulators, and low-dimensional materials. Their reliable quantitative description generally requires an excplicit treatment of the electron-hole interaction beyond the independent-particle picture and commonly uses adiabatic approximations to time-dependent density-functional theory (TDDFT). The most widely used approach today is many-body perturbation theory (MBPT) in the G​WGW+Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) framework, where quasiparticle energies obtained from the G​WGW approach are combined with a BSE for the two-particle Green’s function[32, 43, 35, 6]. This scheme has become a de facto standard for calculating excitons and optical spectra in bulk and low-dimensional systems[32, 42, 13, 27], and has also been successfully applied to molecules and complex environments[6, 12].

Historically, the BSE was introduced in relativistic quantum field theory to describe two-particle bound states in quantum electrodynamics, with an interaction kernel constructed from propagators and interaction vertices[38, 39]. In condensed-matter and quantum-chemical applications, the same formal structure is typically recast into an equal-time (Salpeter-like) equation adapted to electron-hole excitations in crystalline or finite systems[32, 6, 35, 25, 9]. In all these settings, the BSE is fundamentally an integral equation for a two-particle amplitude with a nonlocal interaction kernel. In practical solid-state calculations, however, the BSE is almost always implemented in matrix form as an effective electron-hole Hamiltonian acting in the space of Bloch transitions[32, 43, 35]. The diagonal part contains quasiparticle transition energies, while the off-diagonal elements arise from the screened direct (attractive) and bare exchange (repulsive) Coulomb interactions[43, 1, 36]. This formulation has been implemented in many ab initio codes and applied to bulk semiconductors, molecular crystals, nanostructures, and two-dimensional materials,[32, 40, 14, 15, 37]. Since its computational cost grows rapidly with the number of bands and 𝐤\mathbf{k}-points, and storing and constructing the full kernel can become a serious bottleneck, which has triggered intensive work on more efficient solvers and kernel representations: Haydock-type time-evolution schemes[20, 18], reduced-scaling and tensor-based diagonalization [41, 13, 5], finite-field methods [29] and stochastic approaches [7], as well as low-rank and interpolative kernel decompositions[21, 5]. Recent developments include real-time BSE propagation [26], GPU-accelerated BSE implementations in planewave codes [44], data-driven low-rank kernels in time-dependent G​WGW-based schemes [22], and subspace or model-reduction strategies tailored to specific excitations[34]. Nevertheless, these advances do not alter the underlying mathematical character of the BSE as an integral equation for bound excitons.

From a mathematical perspective, once momentum space is restricted to a bounded domain and the interaction kernel is regularized so that it is square-integrable on the corresponding product domain, the associated integral operator is Hilbert-Schmidt and therefore compact. This compactness provides a basis for isolating bound-state eigenvalues and constructing systematic finite-rank approximations [24, 19, 3, 11]. Such Fredholm techniques have a long history in relativistic Bethe-Salpeter studies: early work by Graves-Morris, Broido and Taylor, Greenman, Bauhoff, and others explicitly constructed “Fredholm approximations” by projecting the kernel onto finite-dimensional subspaces and analyzing convergence of the resulting matrix problems [16, 8, 17, 4, 10, 23]. These ideas, however, have not been systematically brought into the modern solid-state G​WGW+BSE framework. In parallel, full matrix-BSE solvers have been connected to simpler effective descriptions in terms of Wannier-Mott excitons and effective-mass Hamiltonians[13, 27, 6]. In the Wannier-Mott regime, where the exciton radius spans many unit cells, the exciton behaves as a hydrogenic quasiparticle whose relative motion is governed by a screened Coulomb potential with material-dependent effective masses and dielectric constant [27]. In the continuum limit, this leads to a Wannier equation for the exciton envelope in real or momentum space, and the effective-mass BSE becomes explicitly a three-dimensional integral equation [17, 25, 9]. In this language, the link to Fredholm theory follows naturally.

In this work, we develop a radial Fredholm approximation to the solid-state BSE for rapid preliminary screening of direct-gap bulk materials through their Wannier-Mott exciton binding energies. Our strategy reduces the physical description to small radial eigenvalue problems while retaining material-dependent effective masses and microscopic screening. The radial matrices are solved deterministically, without the sampling uncertainty associated with stochastic BSE formulations [7]. Their dimension is controlled independently of the Brillouin-zone sampling used to calculate the screened Coulomb interaction, allowing denser screening meshes without enlarging the exciton matrices. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews the BSE and its matrix representation in a Bloch electron-hole basis. Section III derives the momentum-space Wannier equation and its Fredholm formulation. Section IV introduces the partial-wave decomposition and the spherical-Bessel representation of the central kernel. Section V describes the Nyström discretization and matrix symmetrization. Section VI validates the implementation against the conventional matrix BSE and shows its numerical stability for the example of bulk GaAs. Finally, Section VII summarizes the results and their range of applicability.

papers.title: Detection Instead of Inversion: T1-T2 Microstructure Quantification With Detection Transformers
papers.abstract: T1-T2 correlation MRI has strong potential to quantify microstructural compartments without imposing a biological model. Traditionally, full T1-T2 spectra per voxel are reconstructed with an ill-conditioned and time-consuming Inverse Laplace Transform. We propose to view this challenge as an object detection task: A Detection Transformer (DETR) takes 64 TI/TE signals and directly predicts a set of compartments specified by T1, T2, and signal fraction. We achieve a mean average precision mAP@10 of 76.8% on simulated data, outperforming both our previous model design (53.8%) and regularized NNLS (66.1%). We show that our DETR approach outperforms NNLS in almost every setting across compartment count, compartmental signal fraction, and SNR. Reconstruction is orders of magnitude faster than NNLS. The results are fully reproducible from our public code: github.com/SebastianEndtTHI/t1t2-detr
papers.intro:
Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) voxels contain a mixture of microstructural compartments, such as intra- and extracellular water, myelin water, and free water – each with distinct relaxation properties. Multidimensional correlation MRI, e.g., T1-T2 correlation imaging, can distinguish these compartments [6, 1, 9]. Conventionally, full multidimensional parameter spectra are reconstructed for each voxel. This ill-posed Inverse Laplace Transform (ILT) is usually solved using regularized NNLS algorithms.

papers.title: FADE: A Flow-Based Approach for Multichannel Tail Estimation
papers.abstract: Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communication (URLLC) is vulnerable to rare low-received-power events, and the spatial-diversity benefits of multiple receivers can be significantly reduced when they experience simultaneous deep fading. Multivariate Extreme Value Theory (MEVT) provides a principled framework for characterizing such joint tail behavior. However, conventional MEVT methods often rely on restrictive parametric assumptions or discrete representations of the dependence structure, which may not fully capture complex multivariate tail behavior. This paper proposes Flow-based Angular Density Estimation (FADE), a flow-based approach for characterizing the dependence between extreme events across receivers within the MEVT framework. FADE transforms multivariate extremes into a standard extreme-value representation and uses a flow-based density estimator to learn the dependence structure from the transformed data without imposing a predefined parametric form. The proposed framework is evaluated using experimentally collected data from a UAV communication system, in which the UAV serves as the transmitter and communicates with two ground receivers. FADE provides closer agreement with the empirical joint CDF, achieving reductions of up to 22.4% in MAE compared with the state-of-the-art Logistic and Maximum Empirical Likelihood (MEL) methods, while also improving distributional agreement and reducing absolute bias.

URLLC (URLLC) is intended for wireless applications where communication must remain highly reliable, including autonomous systems, industrial automation and remote control [1]. URLLC operates at packet error rates between 10−910^{-9} and 10−510^{-5}, with communication delays constrained to only a few milliseconds or less [2]. Utilizing multiple antennas can improve reliability through spatial diversity. Therefore, characterizing the joint occurrence of extreme channel observations across receivers is important for ultra-reliable communication.
