EVT (EVT) provides tools for studying observations in the tails of a distribution, making it suitable for characterizing rare channel outages [3]. Its application to wireless channels has enabled tail-aware channel modeling for URLLC [4] and has subsequently been used for EVT-based channel prediction in wireless systems [5]. MEVT (MEVT) additionally provides tools for modeling the extremes of multiple receivers and describing the dependence between extreme observations across receivers [6]. In this framework, the dependence between extreme observations is characterized by the angular, or spectral, distribution, which describes the relative contribution of each variable to the joint extremes [3]. Several approaches have been proposed to model multivariate extreme dependence. The logistic model provides a compact parametric description of the dependence structure but imposes a specific functional form on the dependence between extreme observations [3, 6]. MEL (MEL) avoids this parametric restriction by estimating the spectral measure directly from extreme observations [7]. However, its discrete representation of the spectral measure can limit its scalability and ability to represent complex dependence structures. These limitations motivate a data-driven approach for modeling the dependence structure while retaining the probabilistic formulation required by MEVT.

papers.title: Metabolic heat and moisture reuse with climate-adaptive control for energy-efficient black soldier fly bioconversion in modular container farms
papers.abstract: Black soldier fly larvae (BSFL, Hermetia illucens) convert organic residues into feed ingredients and fertiliser. Climate control is a major contributor to the energy demand of container-based bioconversion. We developed a control-oriented dynamic model linking larval growth, substrate dynamics and container climate to heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC). A two-level Model Predictive Control (MPC) strategy planned climate trajectories and tracked them through HVAC actuation. Four simulation studies examined controller selection, HVAC configuration, larval age pairing and inter-container coupling, using subsets of eight climate scenarios. Across the four scenarios tested for controller selection, dynamic MPC reduced specific energy consumption (SEC) by 31 to 61% and increased predicted dry biomass at harvest by up to 27.5% relative to single fixed setpoints. Under the tested controller settings, active cooling was required in the two hot scenarios, whereas dehumidification provided no additional operational benefit. Pairing larval ages four days apart within one container reduced SEC by up to 33% in the tested non-hot scenarios. In the Cooldry scenario, two age-separated containers connected by an actuated air duct produced 9.0% more biomass and achieved 3.9% lower SEC than two independent containers with mixed ages, despite using 4.6% more total HVAC energy. The simulations suggest that dynamic climate control and metabolic heat and moisture reuse can improve the energy intensity of BSFL bioconversion. The quantitative estimates and hardware recommendations require experimental validation before application to industrial facilities.

papers.title: Clock Offsets and Ranges from Optical Pseudoranges
papers.abstract: This note describes the estimation of ranges and clock offsets from measured pseudoranges in the context of the Kepler Navigation System. The latter system continuously adapts the frequency of its clocks to ensure that they all show the same time independently of where they are. In Medium Earth Orbits, the joint problem of estimating ranges and clock offsets can then be factorized.

papers.title: Nonlinear adiabatic theorem for the Gross-Pitaevskii equation
papers.abstract: We prove a nonlinear adiabatic theorem for the repulsive Gross-Pitaevskii (GP) equation with a time-dependent trapping potential $V(x,t)$. If either (i) $V(\cdot,t)$ is smooth, subquadratic in space and with uniformly bounded spatial derivatives of order $\geq 2$, or (ii) $V(\cdot,t)$ is a uniformly bounded perturbation of a fixed non-negative potential which is asymptotically $|x|^m, m\geq 2$, then the GP equation has a global solution, which remains uniformly close to the instantaneous minimizer of the time-independent GP functional, provided the initial condition is a ground state. In fact, we show that the existence of a solution of the GP equation is the real bottleneck: If existence is assumed, then adiabaticity holds under very minimal assumptions.

papers.title: $P$-stationary structural equation modeling: Causal effect identification under temporally incomplete observations
papers.abstract: Causal modeling of discrete-time processes often involves the assumption that the modeled processes are stationary. A general class of linear causal models for discrete-time stationary processes are structural equation processes (SEP), which generalize the well known structural equation model for i.i.d. observations. In this paper, we extend the SEP model from stationary to $P$-stationary processes, which are non-stationary processes whose $P$-periodically sampled subprocesses are jointly stationary. We will use this model to approach the problem of causal effect identification under temporally incomplete observations from a graphical modeling perspective. To have a notion of generic identifiability, we restrict our analysis to $P$-stationary structural vector autoregressive (SVAR) processes, which are SVAR processes whose underlying coefficients can vary $P$-periodically over time. Our findings allow to detect, in any given temporally incomplete observational setting, if a certain set of instrumental processes qualifies to identify a causal effect between $P$-periodic subprocesses, and if this is the case, that effect admits an explicit expression as a rational function evaluated at the observational spectral density.

papers.intro:
Causal inference [32, 41] is about modeling cause and effect relations in the presence of randomness. The fundamental concept in causal inference is that of a causal model. A causal model has an associated directed graph whose vertices represent the entities between which causal relations are to be modeled, and whose directed links specify the immediate cause and effect relations. In addition to the graph, a causal model contains a set of functions compatible with the directed links, and a random noise object for each vertex. If the model is well defined, it gives rise to a probability distribution, also known as the observational distribution, over the random variables indexed by the vertices of the graph. The question of what information about the causal model can be recovered from the observational distribution drives a major stream of research in causal inference, including the present paper.

Time is intrinsic to causal relations in that an effect cannot precede its cause, i.e., cause and effect are ordered by time. When defining a causal model which obeys the ordering of time, a discrete set of time points is often assumed. Structural equation processes [33, 34] provide a broad class of linear causal models for discrete time processes. The qualitative causal structure of an SEP is encoded by a finite directed graph. Every vertex on that graph has an independent stationary noise process, and every directed link has an associated infinite sequence, which quantifies how the past of the causing process linearly influences the present state of the caused one. The structural equation process defines a linear equation system, which is uniquely solved by the (stationary) observational process of the SEP.

In particular, stationary SEPs are not capable of modeling time-varying interactions. The underlying observation to our approach is that any temporally incomplete observation of an PP-stationary SEP can be represented, for an appropriate integer RR, as a finite collection of R​PRP-periodic subsamplings. Then we will show that every PP-stationary SEP has an equivalent R​PRP-stationary SEP, which is equipped with a latent structure rendering every missing subsample as latent. Taking this approach, we analyze the problem of identifying causal effects, i.e., link filters, in PP-stationary SEPs from temporally incomplete observations. Following previous work [36, 34], we will study the problem in the frequency domain, where the algebraic relations are more tractable. The identification of a given effect in the PP-stationary SEP using a set of instrumental processes relies on the availability of certain entries in the spectral density. However, for temporally incomplete observations the spectral density can generally not be computed, so that identification via instrumental processes seems infeasible. By providing an explicit recovery formula, we will characterize the temporally incomplete observations for which it is possible to recover a given entry in the spectral density. Accordingly, in a setting of temporally incomplete observations, we detect a given effect to be identifiable if there is a suitable set of instrumental processes while the temporal incompleteness of the observations is such that all the entries in the spectral density that are required for identification via that set of instrumental processes can be recovered. For technical reasons, we restrict our analysis to PP-stationary structural vector autoregressive processes, i.e., SVAR processes whose coefficients are allowed to vary periodically over time with periodicity PP.

papers.title: M3Former: Fine-Grained Cross-Layer Mixing for Transformers
papers.abstract: Residual connections give each Transformer block access to all earlier layers only through one fixed sum, broadcast to all of the block's inputs. This broadcast bottleneck imposes three constraints: the query, key, value and residual inputs of a block, which we call its roles, read the same vector; all hidden dimensions within a role share one set of weights over earlier layers; and every earlier layer has the same fixed weight for every token. We propose the Multi-Role Multi-Group Mixing Residual (M3), which removes all three: every role, and every group of hidden dimensions within a role, reads its own token-dependent mixture of all earlier layers. M3 starts as an exact residual connection and adds as little as 1.4% parameters and 1.8% FLOPs. From 100M to 1.4B parameters, M3Former outperforms the Transformer and coarse-grained cross-layer connections at every size, matching a Transformer 1.19-1.34x the size of the one it modifies, trained with 1.4-1.8x the compute. Relaxing only some of the constraints recovers only part of this gain. M3Former also improves sparse mixture-of-experts models of up to 4.6B parameters and trains more stably in deeper networks. Code: https://github.com/Kingchet10/m3former

papers.intro:
Residual connections (He et al., 2016) allow Transformers (Vaswani et al., 2017) to be trained at great depth. Each block adds its output to a running sum, and the next block reads this sum as its input. In a pre-norm Transformer, the input of a block is thus the token embedding plus the updates of all earlier blocks. This running sum, often called the residual stream, is the only path through which a block can use what earlier layers have computed (Elhage et al., 2021). Although language models have grown to billions of parameters (Brown et al., 2020; Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022), nearly all of them still connect their blocks in this way.

(1) Roles: queries and keys decide where to attend, values decide what to move, and the residual path carries the state that the block updates (Vaswani et al., 2017; Elhage et al., 2021), yet all four read the same vector. (2) Groups: different subspaces of the stream carry different features (Elhage et al., 2021), and heads and layers specialize in different functions (Voita et al., 2019; Clark et al., 2019b; Tenney et al., 2019; Jawahar et al., 2019), yet all hidden dimensions of a role share one set of weights over earlier layers. We call these constraints the broadcast bottleneck.

papers.title: Regularizing the Navier-Stokes Equations by One Noise Component
papers.abstract: We study the three-dimensional incompressible Navier--Stokes equations on the torus with multiplicative It\^o noise which is driven by a single Brownian motion and acts only through the vertical velocity component. Such a noise is strongly degenerate: An infinite-dimensional part of the velocity field is not forced at all. We show that it nevertheless has a regularizing effect. For a linear noise, strong solutions whose initial data have no unforced part are global with probability tending to one as the noise intensity grows. For a suitable nonlinear noise, the same holds for arbitrary $\mathrm{H}^1$ data, together with smallness of the space-time $\mathrm{L}^6$-norm of the vertical velocity. As a deterministic counterpart, we give a self-contained proof that a quintic damping of the vertical component yields global regularity, and the same argument shows that, under the linear noise, blow-up can only occur if the vertical velocity leaves $\mathrm{L}^6_{t,x}$.

papers.intro:
Whether smooth solutions of the three-dimensional incompressible Navier–Stokes equations remain smooth for all times is a well-known open problem. A useful way of isolating what is missing is to ask which additional mechanism, as weak as possible, would suffice for global regularity. In this paper we look at regularizing mechanisms acting only on a single velocity component.

A useful way of isolating what is missing is to ask which additional mechanism, as weak as possible, would suffice for global regularity. In this paper we look at regularizing mechanisms acting only on a single velocity component.

Regularization by noise, the phenomenon that a suitable random perturbation improves the well-posedness of an evolution equation, has attracted considerable attention in recent years. For the three-dimensional Euler and Navier–Stokes equations and related models, several noise mechanisms are now known to prevent blow-up with high probability, among them large linear and superlinear multiplicative noise and transport noise [14, 23, 13, 7, 15]. In all of these results, the noise acts on the whole velocity field. We show that much less suffices: A noise acting only through the vertical velocity component, which leaves an infinite-dimensional part of the velocity field entirely unforced, still produces global strong solutions with probability close to one when its intensity is large (for arbitrary H1\mathrm{H}^{1} data in the nonlinear case).

papers.title: Environmental seismology: What can we learn on earth surface processes with ambient noise?
papers.abstract: Environmental seismology investigates mechanical vibrations generated by external processes or influenced by phenomena originating outside the solid Earth. It encompasses interactions between the solid Earth and other environmental systems, including the cryosphere, hydrosphere, and anthroposphere, as well as the specific sources of seismic vibrations associated with these systems. This field also examines how environmental factors, such as temperature fluctuations and hydrological variations, affect seismic wave propagation. Recent advances in data-processing techniques, combined with increased computational capabilities and the growing density of seismic sensor networks, have enabled novel observations and contributed to the emergence of environmental seismology as a distinct research field. This article reviews how subtle changes in the Earth's subsurface can be detected and interpreted through variations in seismic wave propagation induced by external environmental processes, with applications to geomechanics, hydrology, and natural hazard assessment. In particular, we demonstrate how ambient seismic noise can be used to monitor: (1) thermal variations in the subsurface, within buildings, and in rock columns; (2) the temporal and spatial evolution of groundwater levels; and (3) changes in the rigidity of the material forming a landslide, with particular emphasis on the reduction in rigidity that may precede slope failure.

papers.title: An Empirical Temperature Relation for Chemical Abundances in AGN
papers.abstract: We present for the very first time the empirical temperature structure of the narrow line region (NLR) clouds of active galactic nuclei (AGNs) based on a sample of [N II] and [O III] auroral line measurements. The scaling of Te([N II]) with Te([O III]), expressed as the t2-t3 relation, is key to deriving accurate chemical abundances, in AGNs and other line-emitting nebulae, particularly when only one auroral line is observed. Here, we provide the first robust empirical description of t2-t3 for AGNs: t2(10^4 K)=1.285*t3(10^4 K)+0.799. We find substantial changes in 12+log(O/H) when compared to other t2-t3 calibrations when using the direct, or Te, method with only the [O III] 4363 auroral line. We find that adopting our t2-t3 most accurately recovers the fully direct method 12+log(O/H). To interpret the physical mechanisms behind the AGN t2-t3, we compare the observed distribution of [N II] 6584/5755 and [O III] 5007/4363 flux ratios to a variety of ionization model predictions. We find evidence for power law density gradients, pressure stratification, and (sometimes significant) contributions from astrophysical shocks driving much of the dispersion on these flux ratios while metal cooling dominates the primary shape of the distribution. With more accurate t2-t3 and 12+log(O/H), the properties of the interstellar medium photoionized by AGN can be better characterized and understood across a wide range of cosmic time and may bring better context for novel observations at z>6 with JWST, with implications for understanding chemical enrichment in the earliest stages of galaxy evolution.

papers.intro:
Accurate inference of gas-phase metallicity is critical to appropriately interpreting the physical conditions of active galactic nuclei (AGNs) and the role these objects play in galaxy evolution. Metallicity can place key constraints on physical conditions within the AGN narrow line region (NLRs) such as the gas cooling rate (Ferland and Mushotzky, 1984; Sutherland and Dopita, 1993; Flury and Moran, 2020, Flury et al. in prep) and hardness of the ionizing spectrum (Thomas et al., 2016). Moreover, robustly accurate chemical abundances determine where AGNs populate the fundamental mass-metallicity relation (e.g., Thomas et al. 2019; Dors et al. 2019; Pérez-Díaz et al. 2021; Carr et al. 2023; Li et al. 2024), an empirical indicator of galaxy evolution (e.g., Lequeux et al. 1979; Tremonti et al. 2004; Mannucci et al. 2010), thereby informing the possible role of AGNs in galaxy evolution.

Moreover, robustly accurate chemical abundances determine where AGNs populate the fundamental mass-metallicity relation (e.g., Thomas et al. 2019; Dors et al. 2019; Pérez-Díaz et al. 2021; Carr et al. 2023; Li et al. 2024), an empirical indicator of galaxy evolution (e.g., Lequeux et al. 1979; Tremonti et al. 2004; Mannucci et al. 2010), thereby informing the possible role of AGNs in galaxy evolution.

Extensive studies of extragalactic star-forming regions (SFs; H ii regions, H ii galaxies) have resulted in a wealth of direct-method estimates of the gas phase metallicity of SFs in the local Universe (e.g., Peimbert et al. 1978; Torres-Peimbert et al. 1989; van Zee et al. 1998; Kennicutt et al. 2003; Hägele et al. 2008; Esteban et al. 2020; Rogers et al. 2021) and at higher redshifts (z≳ 1z\>\ga\>1, e.g., Sanders et al. 2016; Sanders et al. 2020; Sanders et al. 2024; Gburek et al. 2019; Arellano-Córdova et al. 2022). After extensive assessment (Hägele et al., 2006, e.g.,), general consensus is that the most reliable metallicity (ZZ) or chemical abundance estimates of individual heavy elements (e.g. O, N, S, etc) are those based on the direct, or TeT_{\rm e}, method, which relies on measurements of auroral emission line fluxes like [O iii]λ\lambda4363, [N ii]λ\lambda5755, and [S iii]λ\lambda6312 to determine state excitation, or electron, temperature TeT_{\rm e} and, in turn, the ionic emissivities and related abundances (for a review see, e.g., Peimbert et al. 2017; Pérez-Montero 2017; Nicholls et al. 2020). While the physical justification for the direct method stems from atomic physics, good agreement between direct estimates in nebulae located in the solar neighborhood and those derived from observations of the weak interstellar O iλ\lambda1356 line towards stars (see Pilyugin 2003 and references therein) as well as by estimates in H ii regions and in B-type stars in the Milky Way and in other galaxies (e.g. Toribio San Cipriano et al. 2017) provides empirical evidence that the direct method yields accurate chemical abundance estimates. While temperature inhomogeneities (as proposed by Peimbert 1967) may bias direct method abundances in H ii regions and star-forming galaxies (Méndez-Delgado et al., 2023, e.g.,), the presence of such phenomena in AGN, though proposed (Dors et al., 2020b; Binette et al., 2024, e.g.,), has yet to be demonstrated empirically. Other effects, such as contamination from shocks (Dors et al., 2021, e.g.,) may instead play a dominant role.

papers.title: On some positivity properties of the Riemann $\Xi$ function
papers.abstract: We prove strict log-concavity of the positive functions $\Theta$ and $\Lambda$ with one-sided and bilateral Laplace transforms $1/\xi(\tfrac12+\sqrt s)$ and $1/\Xi$, respectively, where $\Xi(z)=\xi(\tfrac12+iz)$. For either function, log-concavity is the P\'olya frequency property of order two (PF$_2$). Without assuming the Riemann hypothesis (RH), but using its published verification up to height about $3\cdot10^{12}$, we further prove that both densities are PF$_{k_*}$ for $k_*=1\,810\,540\,931\,075$. The proof views $\Theta$ as a small signed perturbation of a density that is PF of every order, with an error bound independent of the order, so the numerical check reduces to scalar inequalities. Since $\Lambda$ is a Gaussian mixture of $\Theta$, it inherits the same order. Conversely, a pole obstruction shows that if either density is PF$_k$, then every zeta zero lower than the $(k+2)$-nd lies on the critical line. Finally, we prove that if RH holds up to height $T>\tfrac12$, then $\Xi$ satisfies the generalized Laguerre inequalities $L_n[\Xi](x)\ge0$ of every order $n$ for $|x|\le T-\tfrac12$, extending the case $n=1$ of Csordas, Ruttan and Varga (1991).
papers.intro:
For a connoisseur of positivity, the Riemann Ξ\Xi function offers a tantalizing array of questions. While the hardest of these are equivalent to the Riemann hypothesis (RH) itself, we find that even weak necessary conditions for RH already repay study. The ideas permeating our study are classical: Fourier–Laplace transforms, the Laguerre–Pólya class, Pólya frequency functions, among others. Our goal is a richer understanding of these positivity properties without assuming RH, and ideally with as little information about the zeta zeros as possible.

papers.title: Frequency-domain spin-wave logic gate based on three-magnon confluence
papers.abstract: Spin-wave-based information processing provides a promising platform for low-power nanoscale computing by exploiting coherent magnon dynamics and intrinsic nonlinear interactions. A key advantage of wave-based processing for efficient miniaturization is the ability to perform operations in the frequency domain without requiring separate propagation paths for the input and output signals. Here, we demonstrate a frequency-domain spin-wave logic gate based on resonant, non-degenerate three-magnon confluence in an yttrium iron garnet nanowaveguide. Under resonant conditions, two input spin waves at different frequencies efficiently generate an output spin wave at the sum frequency, which occurs only when both input signals are present, thereby directly implementing an AND logic operation. We further show that the output intensity scales linearly with each input intensity and is therefore proportional to their product, enabling analog multiplication of two signals. These results demonstrate nonlinear magnon confluence as a versatile mechanism for frequency-domain spin-wave logic and analog signal processing.

papers.title: CUA-Master: Scaling Computer-use Agents through Open-World Recursive Improvements
papers.abstract: Despite recent advances in CUAs, their development remains constrained by the limited diversity, controllability, and reliability of interaction data. Moreover, conventional optimization pipelines lack iterative feedback, while existing recursive improvement approaches often rely on self-generated experiences, limiting ability expansion and yielding diminishing returns. To address these challenges, we introduce CUA-Master, a nested double-loop recursive improvement framework. At the system level, an outer world-data-model flywheel continuously incorporates open-world corpus and leverages evolving model weaknesses to guide subsequent data construction and optimization iterations. At the data level, an inner flywheel couples open-world seeding and autocatalytic propagation. The former mines authentic workflows as seed tasks from instructional videos, and employs visual-semantic dual-path trajectory reconstruction; The latter transforms these seeds into reusable primitives for controllable synthesis of diverse, complex, and verifiable tasks. To enable efficient and reliable trajectory collection, we further introduce a feedback-guided snapshot-rollback retry mechanism in various real environments. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CUA-Master-27B achieves competitive performance across GUI-only and GUI-CLI hybrid benchmarks, scoring 80.2 on OSWorld Verified, 36.9 on OSWorld 2.0, 43.9 on WeaveBench, and 25.0 on Agents' Last Exam. Our framework also substantially improves the quality and efficiency of data synthesis, and exhibits continuous gains across recursive iterations.

papers.intro:
Computer-use agents (CUAs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for automating real-world workflows across diverse software applications, and unlocking new levels of digital productivity. Recent advances in both foundation models [37, 30, 47, 40, 32, 3] and specialized agents [51, 49, 17, 28, 9] have substantially improved their capabilities not only grounding of computer scenarios, but also in interactive reasoning and long-horizon execution. Besides, early CUAs operate predominantly via graphical user interfaces (GUIs), while subsequent works extend their capability scope by incorporating command-line interfaces (CLIs) [8, 24, 45, 42] and extensible tools [16, 19]. Nevertheless, developing powerful CUAs capable of reliably executing diverse, long-horizon, and cross-application workflows remains challenging.

Recent advances in both foundation models [37, 30, 47, 40, 32, 3] and specialized agents [51, 49, 17, 28, 9] have substantially improved their capabilities not only grounding of computer scenarios, but also in interactive reasoning and long-horizon execution. Besides, early CUAs operate predominantly via graphical user interfaces (GUIs), while subsequent works extend their capability scope by incorporating command-line interfaces (CLIs) [8, 24, 45, 42] and extensible tools [16, 19]. Nevertheless, developing powerful CUAs capable of reliably executing diverse, long-horizon, and cross-application workflows remains challenging.

A fundamental bottleneck lies in how data construction and model optimization are coupled and recursively improved. Many existing pipelines follow a unidirectional paradigm of data generation followed by model training [51, 49, 28, 18], where data construction is insufficiently informed by the evolving weaknesses. Consequently, additional data may provide lopsided benefits without addressing persistent capability gaps. Recent recursive improvement approaches partially address this issue by incorporating iteratively self-generated data [50, 33, 75]. However, their exploration remains closed-world optimization, where such cycles still predominantly rely on the own knowledge and capabilities of the model itself. It is bounded by existing capabilities, potentially reinforcing distributional biases, and yielding diminishing marginal returns. These observations fundamentally motivate us to build a recursive system that continuously acquires new open-world knowledge, and systematically expands the performance boundary of the whole system.

Beyond system-level limitations, a more concrete concern is the availability of large-scale, high-quality data that adequately captures the diversity and complexity of real-world trajectories. While human-annotated trajectories provide high-quality supervision, their substantial annotation costs and limited application coverage make large-scale collection impractical [51, 20, 25, 50, 13]. Therefore, synthetic data generation emerges as a promising alternative [44, 60, 39, 21, 41]. However, existing approaches face three intertwined challenges. First, diversity: tasks derived from restricted and similar sources often exhibit substantial homogeneity, leading to insufficient ability coverage and fast improvement saturation as data volume increases. Second, controllability: direct instruction rewriting and template-based generation offer limited control over operational abilities, complexity, and task dependencies, particularly for long-horizon and cross-application workflows. Third, reliability: scaling the collection of verified trajectories across diverse real-world environments becomes increasingly challenging as task complexity grows, leading to lower rollout success rates and frequent execution failures. Collectively, these limitations constrain not only the quantity of synthetic data, but also its effective coverage of the capabilities required by general-purpose CUAs.

At the data level, the inner flywheel couples open-world seeding and autocatalytic propagation as two complementary driving forces. papers.title: Mechano-chemical control of enzymatic activity in crowded environments
papers.abstract: Macromolecular crowding has long been known to alter biochemical equilibria and enzyme kinetics, with reported catalytic activities that may increase, decrease, or vary non-monotonically with crowder concentration. Classical Michaelis--Menten kinetics does not by itself identify which of these responses should occur for a conformationally active enzyme. Here, we develop a minimal non-equilibrium mechano-chemical theory for a fueled enzyme embedded in a bath of passive crowders and uncover a fluctuation-induced effective force dipole acting on the enzyme subunits, akin to a generalized form of dispersion or depletion interaction. Since the preferred conformation of the model enzyme varies through the catalytic cycle, the fluctuation-induced mechanical load affects the relevant kinetic activation barriers and is sufficient to produce both monotonic inhibition and non-monotonic modification of turnover. The framework provides a thermodynamically consistent route for linking crowded environments to catalytic currents, suggesting how mechanical design principles could be leveraged to control enzymatic pathways.

papers.title: Kernelized Stable Fluids for simulating physically accurate solutions
papers.abstract: The Stable Fluids algorithm is a fractional step method for solving the incompressible Navier-Stokes (NS) equations in an unconditionally stable way. It was initially developed for visual effects and allows real-time simulations because of its low computational complexity. The method solves the advection step by using the method of characteristics which is implemented via linear interpolation. This results in excessive diffusion of vorticity and is one of the main reasons for the physical inaccuracy of the algorithm. We propose Kernelized Stable Fluids with Sparse Cholesky Preconditioning (KSF-Chol) in order to address this shortcoming and make the algorithm thereby suitable for engineering problems and scientific computing. The algorithm is modified by replacing the linear interpolation approach with kernel interpolation in the advection step. We accelerate the computationally expensive kernel interpolation by using sparse Cholesky preconditioning and a near-/far-field approach and optimize both methods for computations on a uniform Cartesian grid. KSF-Chol achieves per time step a near-linear computational complexity of $\mathcal{O}(N\log^d(N/\varepsilon_{\mathrm{chol}}))$ in space and time. We test KSF-Chol against reference solvers and numerical reference data on multiple 2D and 3D benchmarks and demonstrate a significantly reduced numerical diffusion as well as a competitive accuracy concerning the computation of relevant flow quantities.

papers.intro:
The dynamics of viscous incompressible fluids are governed by the NS equations. Numerical approaches for solving these equations usually demand a discretization of the governing equations through Finite Volumes (FV), Finite Elements (FE) or Finite Difference (FD) methods [18]. To circumvent the ill-conditioning of these methods for large time steps and achieve unconditional stability Jos Stam introduced the Stable Fluids algorithm [44], which is a fractional step method and uses the method of characteristics for fluid advection. During each time step, the Stable Fluids algorithm successively applies a forcing, the solution operations for the advection and diffusion step and finally performs a projection in order to achieve a divergence free velocity field. The numerical stability of Stable Fluids comes at the cost of numerical dissipation, which arises mainly during the advection step. The step is solved by tracing characteristics backward in time and evaluating the velocity field at the resulting off-grid points. These evaluations are performed by linear interpolation on a regular Cartesian grid and are therefore a weak point of the solver’s architecture that we want to improve. While dissipation of vorticity can be often acceptable for visually plausible fluid animations, it limits the applicability of the original Stable Fluids algorithm when quantitatively accurate simulations for scientific applications are required.

papers.title: Specificity Bias and the Wikipedia Paradox: An xAI Analysis of AI Text Detectors under Domain Shift
papers.abstract: The widespread adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) demands reliable detection of human-authored versus synthetic text. However, current Transformer-based detectors often experience severe performance degradation during domain shifts and operate as opaque classifiers. This paper investigates the robustness and interpretability of fine-tuned Transformer models (DistilBERT, RoBERTa) by evaluating them against a custom out-of-distribution (OOD) dataset of hyper-local news synthesized via open-source LLMs (Llama 3, Mistral, Gemma). To analyze model decision boundaries, we apply a tripartite Explainable AI (xAI) framework using SHAP. Our analysis reveals three key phenomena: First, detectors often rely on a "Call-to-Action" syndrome inherent to instruction-tuned LLMs rather than generic machine text. Second, we observe a "Specificity Bias," where LLMs successfully bypass detection by hallucinating specific named entities and mimicking conversational imperfection. Finally, we illustrate the "Wikipedia Paradox," wherein formal, objective human writing is frequently misclassified as AI due to its low statistical burstiness. These findings demonstrate that purely statistical detection paradigms face systematic limitations in highly structured human domains, emphasizing the critical need for semantically-aware, interpretable detection architectures.

papers.title: MultiInpaintCOCO: Fine-Grained Visual Understanding in Multiple Languages
papers.abstract: Previous research shows that vision-language (VL) models struggle to understand fine-grained image details and tend to focus on the overall layout. Moreover, any weakness in English tends to be further amplified in the multilingual setting. To study that, we extend InpaintCOCO, an English dataset focused on fine-grained visual details, to 13 typologically diverse languages across five language families, creating MultiInpaintCOCO - a new multilingual benchmark of 953 minimal-pair examples. We further test several state-of-the-art models in multilingual multimodal retrieval, considering both light VL CLIP-like encoders and large language models. Our results show that performance degrades substantially for lower-resource languages, with the strongest predictor being the data resources available for the languages rather than typological similarity to English. In cross-lingual retrieval, most models exhibit a systematic bias toward English: when given a correct caption in a non-English language and an incorrect one in English, models preferentially select the English caption. This bias varies considerably across architectures. Among the tested models, Gemma 3 shows the strongest English preference while Qwen 3 is the least biased, despite both reaching similar monolingual accuracy across languages. The code is available at https://github.com/ufal/multi-inpaint-coco.

papers.intro:
Vision-language (VL) models take both images and text as input. Depending on the task, two main types of models are currently used. Dual encoders, such as CLIP (Radford et al., 2021) and SigLIP 2 (Tschannen et al., 2025), encode images and texts independently into a shared embedding space; they are the standard choice for retrieval and similarity tasks. Decoder-only models, such as Gemma 3 (Team et al., 2025) and Qwen 2.5-VL (Bai et al., 2025b), are decoder-based and generate text conditioned on both visual and textual input. Both model types are pre-trained on large image-text corpora using objectives (contrastive or generative) that do not require distinguishing between images or captions that differ only in fine-grained details.

Dual encoders, such as CLIP (Radford et al., 2021) and SigLIP 2 (Tschannen et al., 2025), encode images and texts independently into a shared embedding space; they are the standard choice for retrieval and similarity tasks. Decoder-only models, such as Gemma 3 (Team et al., 2025) and Qwen 2.5-VL (Bai et al., 2025b), are decoder-based and generate text conditioned on both visual and textual input. Both model types are pre-trained on large image-text corpora using objectives (contrastive or generative) that do not require distinguishing between images or captions that differ only in fine-grained details.

Several studies have shown that VL models fail to capture fine-grained visual information and instead rely on coarse features, such as global scene layout or the most salient objects (Fu et al., 2025). To probe this limitation precisely, Rösch et al. (2024) proposes minimal pairs: each example consists of two images that differ by a single inpainted object and two captions that differ by exactly one keyword, so that the correct answer cannot be reached without identifying the specific visual detail. A similar strategy applied at the caption level underlies benchmarks such as SugarCrepe (Dumpala et al., 2024). The image-editing approach has a key advantage: it introduces genuine visual ambiguity, because neither the image nor the caption alone is sufficient to determine the correct match.

All of this work is English-only. It is well established that VL model performance drops substantially when moving from English to lower-resource languages (Liu et al., 2021; Bugliarello et al., 2022a), and that multilingual models are not equally calibrated across languages. Errors in less-resourced languages may therefore not only be more frequent but also qualitatively different. The combination of fine-grained visual understanding and multilingual evaluation is therefore almost entirely unexplored. To close this gap, we extend InpaintCOCO (Rösch et al., 2024) to 13 typologically diverse languages (Azerbaijani, Arabic, Czech, German, Greek, Hindi, Italian, Japanese, Romanian, Russian, Slovak, Ukrainian, Vietnamese), producing the MultiInpaintCOCO dataset. Captions were first translated automatically and then post-edited by native speakers.

We evaluate several state-of-the-art dual-encoder and generative decoder models on MultiInpaintCOCO and report two main findings. First, performance on lower-resource languages is substantially worse than on English and other high-resource languages, confirming that fine-grained retrieval is harder in the multilingual setting. Second, and more surprisingly, when a model is given one correct caption in a non-English language and one incorrect caption in English, most models systematically prefer the English caption. This bias appears in both dual-encoder and generative decoder-only models, with Azerbaijani the least favored language. The strength of the bias varies considerably across models: Gemma 3 exhibits the strongest preference for English, while Qwen 3 is the least biased. This is not just a reflection of lower overall accuracy in weaker languages. It reveals a systematic preference for English that persists even when the model is otherwise capable of making the correct match.

papers.title: Regular Separability for Bidirected VASS
papers.abstract: The regular separability problem asks, given two languages, whether there exists a regular language that contains one of them and is disjoint from the other. We study regular separability for bidirected VASS. We first show that the problem remains Ackermann-complete when the input consists of two languages recognised by bidrected VASS. To find a subclass of VASS in which the problem has lower complexity we define alphabetically bidirected VASS as ones where bidirectedness is also visible in the input letters. Our main result establishes that regular separability for alphabetically bidirected VASS is EXPSPACE-complete. The key to this result is that, in this setting, regular separability coincides with disjointness. As a first ingredient in this equivalence, we also show that for alphabetically bidirected Z-VASS, regular separability and disjointness are equivalent. Consequently, regular separability for these systems is in polynomial-time. In fact, it is log-space inter-reducible with non-solvability of integer linear Diophantine equation systems. Finally, we observe that the picture changes dramatically in the presence of a zero test, namely, we show that regular separability for alphabetically bidirected one-counter automata is undecidable.
papers.intro:
Regular separability is a decision problem for two given languages L1,L2⊆Σ∗L_{1},L_{2}\subseteq\Sigma^{*}, and it asks whether they are regularly separable, i.e. whether there is a regular language S⊆Σ∗S\subseteq\Sigma^{*} such that L1⊆SL_{1}\subseteq S and L2∩S=∅L_{2}\cap S=\emptyset. Regular separability has received a significant amount of attention. After some discouraging undecidability results on context-free languages in the 1970s [29, 17], regular separability has been studied intensively over the last decade for vector addition systems with states (VASS), which have finite many control states with access to counters that can be incremented and decremented, but not zero-tested. Moreover, the counters have to stay negative during the run. Regular separability has been studied for integer VASS [4, 7], combination of VASS and subclasses [11], Büchi VASS [1], and VASS coverability languages (more generally, well-structured transition systems) [10, 8], VASS reachability sets [5], and one-dimensional VASS [9]. This culminated in the celebrated decidability result for regular separability of general VASS [19].

papers.title: Certifying Graph Neural Networks Against Label and Structure Poisoning
papers.abstract: Robust machine learning for graph-structured data has made significant progress against test-time attacks, yet certified robustness to poisoning - where adversaries manipulate the training data - remains largely underexplored. For image data, state-of-the-art poisoning certificates rely on partitioning-and-aggregation schemes. However, we show that these methods fail when applied in the graph domain due to the inherent label and structure sparsity found in common graph datasets, making effective graph-partitioning difficult. To address this challenge, we propose a novel semi-supervised learning framework called deep Self-Training Graph Partition Aggregation (ST-GPA), which enriches each graph partition with informative pseudo-labels and synthetic edges, enabling effective certification against node-label and graph-structure poisoning under sparse conditions. Our method is architecture-agnostic, scales to large numbers of partitions, and consistently and significantly improves robustness guarantees against both label and structure poisoning across multiple benchmarks, while maintaining strong clean accuracy. Overall, our results establish a promising direction for certifiably robust learning on graph-structured data against poisoning under sparse conditions.

papers.intro:
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are highly susceptible to adversarial perturbations in their input graph applied at test or training time (Zügner et al., 2018; Dai et al., 2018). Subsequently developed empirical defenses are at the continual risk of being rendered ineffective by more sophisticated ways to choose adversarial perturbations (Koh et al., 2022; Mujkanovic et al., 2022). This motivates the development of robustness certificates, which provide provable guarantees about the stability of predictions under worst-case data perturbations, allowing to rigorously assess and mitigate adversarial vulnerabilities. While significant advances in providing such provable guarantees for GNNs against test-time attacks have been made (Günnemann, 2022; Hojny et al., 2024), certifying robustness of GNNs against data poisoning, where an adversary can manipulate the graph structure (Zügner & Günnemann, 2019) or node-labels (Lingam et al., 2024) at training time, remains largely underexplored.

papers.title: First- and second-order constrained optimisation for inverse homogenisation of unidirectionally varying microstructure
papers.abstract: This paper is concerned with inverse homogenisation problems that aim to identify microstructure features of a body from macroscopic measurements. The unknown microstructure is assumed to vary macroscopically in one spatial direction and affects the effective tensor in an elliptic partial differential equation that governs the behaviour of the body on the macroscale. We establish the well-posedness of the PDE-constrained minimisation problems that model the task of identifying the microstructure, derive first-order necessary optimality conditions, and prove the convergence of a gradient-projection algorithm for the studied problem class in an infinite-dimensional setting. We moreover demonstrate that recently obtained results on generalised differentiability properties of solution maps of bilateral obstacle problems make it possible to set up and analyse a novel semismooth Newton method in the considered situation. The functional analytic setting that we use for our investigation is chosen such that it covers various elliptic PDEs simultaneously (classical second-order equations, bi-Laplace problems, linear elasticity, etc.) and explicitly exploits the problem structure to obtain global convergence guarantees for the studied solution algorithms in terms of the Lipschitz constants of the involved operators. Our analysis is accompanied by numerical experiments which show that the new semismooth Newton approach requires far less expensive projection evaluations than the gradient-descent method and, thus, offers a significant speedup.

For the durability assessment and/or quality inspection of structures whose properties arise from microscopic features, it is often of vital importance to be able to detect and identify defects and macroscopic variations of microstructural properties (fibre-densities, perforation patterns, etc.). As microscopic defects can rarely be measured directly, these types of variations often have to be identified based on the macroscopic behaviour that they induce, for instance, altered load-bearing capabilities or a changed response to mechanical excitations. Periodic microstructures that are slowly modulated macroscopically in only one spatial direction are of particular relevance in this context. They arise, for example, in additive manufacturing processes that rely on a layer-wise printing procedure, or when laminates are considered. In metamaterial applications, unidirectionally slowly modulated microstructures (typically called graded in this context) are also often leveraged to increase the bandwidth of desired effects, e.g. rainbow trapping or rainbow reflection [6, 17].

papers.title: PET Attenuation Map Generation for Brain Imaging from Virtual Non-Contrast and Virtual Non-Iodine Images Obtained with Photon Counting CT Scanners
papers.abstract: This study presents a transformation scheme for converting measured Hounsfield units (HUs) into linear attenuation coefficients (LACs) for 511 keV gamma photons in iodine contrast-enhanced angiographic CT images. The method is based on spectral CT data acquired from tissue-equivalent inserts of the Sun Nuclear electron density phantom. The resulting transformation will be used to develop an attenuation map template for our in-house developed BrainPET 7T system. Three approaches were used to obtain the attenuation maps. The first approach is based on angiographic spectral CT scans with iodinated contrast agent administration, and the computation of virtual non contrast (VNC) and virtual non-iodine (VNI) images. In this case, two images are combined: bone regions are segmented from the VNI images, and the corresponding voxel values in the VNC images are replaced, yielding a single quantitative monochromatic CT image. The second approach relies exclusively on VNC images, whereas the third approach uses only VNI images. The transformation schemes from HUs to LACs were established for different tube voltages (120 kV and 140 kV) and virtual monochromatic energies (64 keV, 67 keV, 70 keV, 76 keV, 80 keV, and 100 keV), showing the HUs dependency on the energy setting of the reconstructed virtual monochromatic energies. The accuracy and precision of the proposed transformation scheme were further evaluated using previously acquired angiographic CT datasets. Spectral CT can be expected to minimize the systematic error when converting HUs to LACs for 511 keV gamma rays using virtual monochromatic images (VMIs).

They also facilitate the computation of virtual monoenergetic images (VMIs), providing an inherently more robust derivation of LACs from polyenergetic CT data across diverse kVp settings.

In typical PET/CT workflows, the CT scan used for attenuation map generation is acquired shortly before the PET acquisition. In contrast, hybrid PET/MR systems, such as our in-house developed 7T BrainPET, integrate PET with magnetic resonance imaging. This combination provides superior soft tissue contrast and advanced functional imaging, without the need for ionizing radiation. However, because MR does not provide the information available from CT, the established HU-to-LAC transformation used in PET/CT cannot be directly applied to PET/MR. As a result, attenuation map generation is performed using either previously acquired CT images from the same patient, or— more commonly—segmentation, atlas-based, or template-based methods LADEFOGED2017346; wagenknechtMRIAttenuationCorrection2013; KopsTemplateBasedAttenuationCorrection; LeeReviewDeep-Learning_AC.

When generating attenuation atlases or templates for head PET/MR imaging with CT acquisitions, particular care must be taken regarding the eye lenses, as they are highly sensitive to ionizing radiation DoseLimit_EyeLens. To address this concern, dedicated head CT scans are often performed with special techniques to protect the eye lenses. Common approaches include the use of bismuth eye shields or gantry tilting. For instance, Zhang et al. zhangQuantitativeAccuracyCT2018 reported bias values of up to 10 %10\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} for low-dose CT scans. papers.title: Align Once to Explain: Feature Alignment for Scalable B-cosification of Foundational Vision Transformers
papers.abstract: Foundational vision models have become the de facto standard for many vision tasks due to their strong performance. However, they are notoriously opaque and remain hard to interpret. We present ALOE (ALign Once to Explain), a one-time, label-free feature alignment approach that efficiently converts foundational vision models into inherently interpretable B-cos variants. Once aligned, the B-cos backbone is used as a drop-in replacement across several downstream tasks-amortizing the cost of interpretability. ALOE is robust across pre-training paradigms (supervised, self-supervised, vision-language) and can preserve teacher-level generalization with orders of magnitude less data than training from scratch. On classification, it strongly outperforms vanilla B-cosification (e.g., +10.5 p.p. top-1 on ImageNet for DINOv3 ViT-B/16), retains strong linear probing, k-NN, and zero-shot transfer competitive with foundational backbones (DINOv3, SigLIP2) across diverse downstream datasets. It also preserves spatially structured features useful for dense prediction, while yielding well-localized and highly human-interpretable explanations by design.

papers.intro:
Large-scale vision foundation models, including self-supervised encoders in the DINO family [12, 55, 72] and contrastive vision–language models such as CLIP [60] and SigLIP [80, 76], are powerful and versatile feature extractors that achieve state-of-the-art performance across a diverse set of downstream tasks. Trained on billions of images and image–text pairs, these models serve as general-purpose building blocks across various domains, from fine-grained recognition to medical imaging, often replacing their fully supervised, domain-specific counterparts [72]. However, their decision-making processes remain largely opaque, which hinders their use in sensitive and safety-critical applications. Post-hoc explanation methods aim to mitigate this issue, but can be noisy and not always faithful to the underlying model being explained [2, 61, 3].

Post-hoc explanation methods aim to mitigate this issue, but can be noisy and not always faithful to the underlying model being explained [2, 61, 3].

An alternative line of work develops inherently interpretable architectures that yield model-faithful explanations by design. They introduce architectural constraints that lead to human-interpretable, faithful summaries of the model’s computations; examples include prototype-based models [17, 24, 51], dynamic linear models [6, 7], and concept-bottleneck models [37, 54, 62]. A prominent example is the family of B-cos Networks [7, 8], which replace linear transforms with bias-free B-cos transforms that promote weight-input alignment to enhance interpretability and enable a faithful summary of the model’s decision. To avoid training these models from scratch, recent work proposed ‘B-cosification’ [4], an approach that efficiently transforms existing models to their B-cos variants post-hoc at a fraction of the full training cost. However, despite strong gains on fully-supervised convolutional backbones and competitive results on a CLIP ResNet [32] backbone, the B-cosification recipe provides only modest improvements for Vision Transformers (ViTs) [25], sometimes failing to match the performance of training from scratch. Since most modern foundation models are ViT-based, this significantly limits its practical utility and broader adoption.

papers.title: A Bayesian Framework for Safe Optimal Control of Unknown Systems from Input-Output Data
papers.abstract: As control engineering is applied to increasingly complex systems, learning-based control, which uses empirical data to reduce the reliance on first-principles models, has emerged as a promising paradigm. However, such approaches must cope with nonlinear and stochastic dynamics, the absence of state measurements, and scarce data, while ensuring safe operation under constraints, which requires rigorous uncertainty quantification. Whereas existing methods treat these challenges in isolation, this article proposes a Bayesian framework that jointly addresses them. A prior in state-space form is updated from input-output data using particle Markov chain Monte Carlo methods, yielding a representation of joint uncertainty over dynamics and latent states. Building on this representation, a validation procedure is developed that provides probabilistic guarantees for constraint satisfaction under arbitrary causal control laws. For control synthesis, a formulation penalizing the conditional value-at-risk of the constraint function is proposed, together with an adaptive calibration mechanism that adjusts the performance-robustness trade-off to achieve a desired robustness level. The probability of successful certification is characterized theoretically. The framework is extended to a receding-horizon setting, where posterior updates from new measurements allow the controller to progressively reduce uncertainty and improve performance. The approach is demonstrated on the optimal control of a vertical farm.

papers.intro:
Learning-based optimal control aims to enable the high-performance operation of systems with unknown dynamics by learning models from empirical data. This paradigm is particularly relevant in applications where pure first-principles modeling is infeasible or prohibitively expensive, such as soft robotic actuators, systems involving human interaction, and biological processes. In real-world applications, several challenges arise jointly that fundamentally shape the learning-based control problem: 1. Nonlinear and stochastic dynamics: Real-world systems are inherently nonlinear and affected by both process noise, which alters the system trajectory, and measurement noise, which only corrupts observations. 2. Absence of state measurements: In many applications, the system state is latent, i.e., it cannot be measured directly due to limited sensing capabilities. Consequently, methods must operate solely on input–output data. 3. Scarce data: In engineering applications, data are often scarce due to costly and time-consuming experiments, making the incorporation of structural knowledge from first principles essential for data efficiency and generalization. 4. Rigorous safety guarantees: In safety-critical applications, constraint satisfaction must be ensured with high confidence despite the challenges posed by (1)–(3). This necessitates the rigorous quantification of both the irreducible aleatoric uncertainty introduced by process and measurement noise and the reducible epistemic uncertainty about the dynamics and latent states that arises from limited data. Despite the practical importance of these challenges, existing approaches address individual aspects only, while their combined treatment remains largely unresolved. In the following, we briefly review existing approaches and their limitations with respect to these challenges.

Data-driven control methods rooted in behavioral systems theory [4] formulate optimal control problems directly from input–output data without requiring measurements of the underlying system state. These approaches have primarily been developed for linear time-invariant systems, and although extensions to stochastic and nonlinear settings have been proposed, their guarantees rely on specific system classes or local approximations.

These approaches have primarily been developed for linear time-invariant systems, and although extensions to stochastic and nonlinear settings have been proposed, their guarantees rely on specific system classes or local approximations.

Nonlinear input–output models, such as nonlinear autoregressive exogenous (NARX) models, learn a mapping from past inputs and outputs to future system behavior. Bayesian formulations, for instance Gaussian process (GP) NARX models [21], systematically quantify both epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty through a posterior distribution over this mapping, potentially enabling control with probabilistic safety guarantees. However, input–output models lack an internal state and therefore cannot distinguish process noise from measurement noise, treating all stochastic variability as a single lumped disturbance. This can lead to biased and increasingly inaccurate multi-step predictions over the horizons relevant for optimal control [28]. Moreover, prior knowledge from first principles, such as conservation laws or kinematic relations, is naturally expressed in terms of state variables and cannot be straightforwardly encoded in input–output mappings.

Moreover, prior knowledge from first principles, such as conservation laws or kinematic relations, is naturally expressed in terms of state variables and cannot be straightforwardly encoded in input–output mappings.

State-space models are a compelling foundation for learning-based optimal control, as they can describe nonlinear dynamics, inherently separate process and measurement noise, and allow the direct integration of prior knowledge from first principles. In their Bayesian formulation, for instance as GP state-space models, they further provide a principled framework for quantifying both epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty, which several works have exploited for robust learning-based control [25]. These approaches, however, rely on full state measurements, which are unavailable in many applications. Without them, learning the dynamics no longer reduces to fitting a function to observed state transitions, and predictions over a planning horizon depend on a current state that is itself unknown. The unknown dynamics and the latent states must therefore be estimated jointly. While several works provide point estimates of both [27, 26], quantifying the remaining uncertainty is substantially more challenging because the uncertainties of the dynamics and the latent states are coupled and their joint posterior is generally intractable. To the best of our knowledge, no existing control method for nonlinear systems accounts for this joint uncertainty and translates it into certifiable probabilistic guarantees, except for our preliminary work [17].

papers.title: Toward the one- and two-loop EFTofLSS for Simons Observatory CMB lensing
papers.abstract: Cosmic microwave background (CMB) lensing observations are becoming sensitive to non-linear structure formation and baryonic feedback scenarios. The effective field theory of large-scale structure (EFTofLSS) provides a systematic description of matter clustering in the mildly non-linear regime, accounting for baryonic effects through counterterms and offering a consistent framework for cross-correlations with other observables. We perform a Fisher forecast for the joint Simons Observatory temperature, polarization, and CMB lensing likelihood using noiseless data vectors with different baryonic feedback scenarios, modelling non-linear structure formation using the one- and two-loop EFTofLSS. We find that, with a single additional parameter, obtained through a principal-component analysis of the EFTofLSS counterterms, both the one- and two-loop EFTofLSS provide a good fit across the baryonic feedback scenarios considered. This parameter is closely aligned with the effective AGN heating temperature $T_{\rm AGN}$. Both loop orders reduce cosmological parameter biases, with only a small loss in marginalized precision at fixed scale cuts. We find that the one-loop EFTofLSS yields unbiased estimates over a range of scales similar to the dark-matter-only model, while the two-loop EFTofLSS extends this range to smaller scales and accommodates different feedback scenarios more robustly. When each model is evaluated at the smallest scales for which its cosmological parameter estimates remain unbiased, the two-loop EFTofLSS yields stronger constraints than the dark-matter-only model.

papers.intro:
The Simons Observatory (SO) [4] and other CMB surveys such as the South Pole Telescope [45, 11] and the Atacama Cosmology Telescope [34, 14, 29] measure the cosmic microwave background (CMB) at high multipoles with unprecedented precision. The CMB signal is distorted by gravitational lensing of CMB photons by the large-scale structure (LSS) of the Universe [32]. Gravitational lensing affects a wide range of multipoles by smoothing the acoustic peaks and transferring power into the damping tail, where the lensing contribution can dominate over the unlensed CMB signal. CMB lensing is an important probe of late-time structure formation and can constrain dark matter and dark energy physics through their effects on structure growth and the expansion history [46].

The CMB signal is distorted by gravitational lensing of CMB photons by the large-scale structure (LSS) of the Universe [32]. Gravitational lensing affects a wide range of multipoles by smoothing the acoustic peaks and transferring power into the damping tail, where the lensing contribution can dominate over the unlensed CMB signal. CMB lensing is an important probe of late-time structure formation and can constrain dark matter and dark energy physics through their effects on structure growth and the expansion history [46].

It has been shown, however, that for SO and next-generation surveys, inconsistent modelling of non-linear clustering and baryonic effects can systematically bias cosmological parameter inference [38, 55, 37]. The effective field theory of large-scale structure (EFTofLSS) [10, 16, 15, 27, 24] can mitigate this by providing a consistent framework for describing the matter power spectrum in the mildly non-linear regime. It combines perturbative calculations of long-wavelength modes with counterterms that parameterize the large-scale effects of unresolved small-scale dynamics, including both non-linear gravitational evolution and baryonic physics [13]. While marginalizing over the counterterm coefficients can broaden cosmological parameter constraints, higher-order computations can extend the range of scales accurately described by the theory, providing access to additional cosmological information.

Recent work has explored two-loop predictions for two-point statistics in galaxy clustering and weak lensing [50, 17, 25, 43, 7, 8, 9], making two-loop calculations a promising route to extracting more cosmological information from smaller scales within the perturbative regime. In this manuscript, we apply the EFTofLSS to a joint forecast for SO lensed CMB temperature and polarization power spectra and the CMB lensing power spectrum. We investigate whether one-loop and two-loop EFTofLSS predictions for the non-linear matter power spectrum yield unbiased cosmological parameter estimates and assess the precision of these constraints under different scale cuts.

papers.title: Single-pass stochastic cooling for electron microscopy
papers.abstract: Scientific applications of free electrons, such as in electron microscopes and particle accelerators, are limited by the brightness of available electron sources. Accelerators can use phase space cooling to surpass these source limitations, whereas electron microscopes can only rely on particle filtering to increase beam coherence at the cost of reduced brightness. We show that strong electron-light coupling in nanophotonic structures makes it possible to achieve single-pass stochastic cooling inside an electron microscope for a lossless improvement of longitudinal emittance. This approach is laser-free and compatible with normal CW operation of electron microscopes. We derive a fully quantum mechanical model of stochastic cooling valid in the strong coupling regime, finding an analytic asymptotic formula for the optimal cooled energy spread $\sigma_{E_f}\simeq0.88(\hbar\omega)^{2/3}\sigma_{E_0}^{1/3}$, with $\hbar \omega$ the cooling photon energy and $\sigma_{E_0}$ the initial energy spread. Numerical simulations confirm that the energy spread reduction is reflected in an increase in the purity of the electron's quantum state and a reduction of the longitudinal phase space area. Our work paves a path towards even brighter beams for electron microscopy, promising higher image quality, enhanced spectral resolution, and a route to reaching fundamental quantum limits on electron beam phase space area.

papers.title: Exact Fusion of Softmax Attention Heads Can Require Exponentially Many Atoms
papers.abstract: Fusing independently normalized attention heads can increase the number of explicit key-value entries, or atoms, needed to preserve their output. We prove a sharp separation for $W_d(q)=\sum_{j=1}^d\sigma(q_j)$: its $d$ two-atom heads use $2d$ head-atom terms, whereas its minimum single-head representation has exactly $2^d$ atoms, even with arbitrary fixed replacement keys, scalar values, and positive masses. The same lower bound holds for every fixed uniform error below $1/2$ on $\mathbb R^d$, and the threshold is sharp. The proof uses exposed-key normal cones; exact equality on any nonempty open query domain inherits the bound. The resulting atom bound for a fixed head count is tight when that count divides $d$. A normalized family retains its exponential exact minimum while approaching a constant on fixed-radius query balls. For pretrained-model caches, a classical affine-rank bound and a certified instance exclude exact vector preservation at a specified atom count. Learned-cache comparisons on two disjoint banks of 64 contexts show budget-dependent reversals and calibration effects.

papers.title: GIST: Location-Dependent Uplink Path Structure Transfer for FDD Downlink Channel Estimation
papers.abstract: A key challenge of downlink (DL) channel estimation in frequency division duplex (FDD) massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems is the pilot overhead, which grows with the numbers of antennas and subcarriers. However, a prior on path delays and directions shared by the uplink (UL) and DL channels can reduce this overhead. A model trained only on UL channels measured at a base station (BS) can predict the path structure (delays, directions and power gains) from the location of a user equipment (UE) and thereby assist DL channel estimation. In this paper, we propose Gaussian-Informed Structure Transfer (GIST), in which each Gaussian primitive models one propagation path, whose delay, directions and power gain are predicted from the UE location relative to the primitive center. The complex gains of the predicted paths are estimated from DL pilots by linear minimum mean square error estimation with this prior. Experiments on a ray-traced and a measured dataset show that GIST outperforms all baselines, reaching a lower DL estimation error with fewer pilot subcarriers. Further experiments demonstrate its robustness to UE location errors, its low storage and computational requirements.

papers.intro:
In frequency division duplex (FDD) systems, the uplink (UL) and downlink (DL) occupy different carrier frequencies, separated by more than the coherence bandwidth. Since the phase of each propagation path depends on the carrier frequency, instantaneous reciprocity is lost and the base station (BS) cannot directly reuse its UL channel estimate as the DL channel. Especially in FDD massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems, the pilot overhead is substantial, as conventional estimators such as least squares require DL pilots scaling with the number of BS antennas [1, 2]. Nevertheless, UL and DL signals propagate along the same paths, sharing frequency-independent delays and directions, a property known as partial reciprocity [3, 2]. Delays and directions from the UL can thus assist DL estimation and reduce the pilot overhead.

Delays and directions from the UL can thus assist DL estimation and reduce the pilot overhead.

An intuitive approach to avoid the pilot overhead is to predict the DL channel directly from the UL channel [4, 5, 6] or the location [7, 8] of the user equipment (UE). However, the instantaneous DL channel predicted without DL pilots may contain phase errors and deviations caused by small environmental changes or UE location errors. Another way is to obtain the path delays and directions from UL channels as the prior of pilot-based DL estimation, as in parametric reconstruction methods [2, 9]. Per-UE path extraction at runtime in these methods, however, can challenge real-time operation. In a covariance-based method proposed in [1], the channel is estimated from the DL pilots along a few beam directions selected from a UL covariance extrapolated to the DL, while the path delays remain unknown. In addition, these methods still rely on recent UL sounding of each UE.

papers.title: Vector incremental treatment effects
papers.abstract: Causal questions involving multiple binary treatments are poorly served by standard causal approaches. Potential outcomes grow exponentially with the number of treatments, many treatment combinations are rarely or never observed, and fixing everyone to one combination can require implausible positivity assumptions. We extend incremental propensity score interventions to vector-valued binary treatments, defining causal effects through counterfactual distributions that scale the odds of each treatment by a user-specified factor. Because marginal odds constraints do not uniquely determine the joint distribution, we define it as the minimum-divergence projection of the observed law onto the constrained set, for a user-specified separable divergence, preserving the observed conditional support. The resulting counterfactual mean outcome is identified under consistency and conditional mean exchangeability, without requiring every treatment combination to have positive conditional probability. For a class of smooth divergences, we derive the efficient influence function and construct cross-fitted one-step estimators that are consistent at the parametric rate and asymptotically normal when marginal treatment probabilities are exactly 0, exactly 1, or bounded away from those values. We relax this requirement by specifying a different estimand and deriving a corresponding estimator, which is asymptotically normal under a convergence-rate condition on the estimated active set. We also extend sensitivity analysis to address unmeasured confounding. Applying the framework to 159,466 New York Medicaid beneficiaries with serious mental illness, we estimate how healthcare costs would change under uniform improvements in the odds of six recommended quality-of-care processes. Increasing recommended care is associated with lower total, inpatient, and mental-health cost and higher outpatient cost.

papers.intro:
Researchers are often interested in causal effects when many binary treatments or exposures act together—for example, when policies shift several factors at once, when interactions among treatments matter, or when the intervention is best described as a vector of binary components rather than a single (possibly multi-valued) variable. The same structure arises when a construct of interest (e.g. quality of health care) is not directly measurable and we only observe a series of binary indicators. We may then ask how downstream outcomes such as mortality or comorbidity would change if that construct improved. Such questions often arise in epidemiology, policy evaluation, and the social sciences, yet standard causal contrasts are poorly suited to this setting.

papers.title: Anticyclotomic Iwasawa theory at potentially ordinary primes
papers.abstract: We study anticyclotomic Iwasawa theory for self-dual twists of $p$-ordinary modular forms of weight two with nebentype $\epsilon^2$, where $\epsilon$ is a non-trivial Dirichlet character of conductor $p$. Under a generalized Heegner hypothesis and suitable residual hypotheses, we prove one divisibility in the anticyclotomic main conjecture in both the definite and indefinite settings. The prime $p$ may split, remain inert, or ramify in the imaginary quadratic field. Our proofs use a compatible bipartite Euler system of Heegner classes and theta elements, together with a comparison with the $p$-adic $L$-functions of Kohen--Pacetti. In the definite case, we prove cotorsion of the Selmer group and the characteristic-ideal divisibility by the $p$-adic $L$-function. In the indefinite case, we prove a rank-one statement and the corresponding divisibility in terms of the Heegner class. We also discuss criteria for equality and their relation to Kolyvagin's conjecture. Specialization gives finite-level Bloch--Kato Selmer bounds with local terms, and applications to Mordell--Weil ranks and $p$-primary Tate--Shafarevich groups for elliptic curves that have potentially ordinary reduction at $p$ satisfying our hypotheses.

papers.title: EMBER: A Little Red Dot Candidate at $z_{\rm spec}=10.36$ in the Seed Black Hole Era
papers.abstract: Little red dots (LRDs) are a newly discovered population that may trace rapidly growing black holes (BHs) and provide a link between seed BHs and luminous active galactic nuclei (AGNs). However, no LRD had previously been spectroscopically confirmed at $z>10$, leaving this earliest phase observationally unexplored. Using JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy from the EMBER program, we measure a spectroscopic redshift of $z_{\rm spec}=10.361^{+0.003}_{-0.002}$ for \target, the highest-redshift LRD candidate known to date. The redshift is constrained by a prominent Ly$\alpha$ break and multiple tentative emission lines, including C\,{\sc iv}\,$\lambda\lambda1549,1551$ and [O\,{\sc iii}]\,$\lambda4363$ detected at $S/N=3.9$ and $3.6$, respectively. Its extreme NIRCam-MIRI color of $m_{\rm F444W}-m_{\rm F770W}=1.82\pm0.1$, characteristic V-shaped continuum with a turnover near the Balmer limit, and continuum slopes of $\beta_{\rm UV}=-2.26^{+0.11}_{-0.11}$ and $\beta_{\rm opt}=1.17^{+0.74}_{-0.70}$ all support its LRD nature. A possible iron complex at $\lambda_{\rm rest}\sim0.24$--$0.25\,{\rm \mu m}$ and a possibly high $\log\left([{\rm O\,III]\,\lambda4363/\rm H\gamma}\right)=0.17^{+0.24}_{-0.22}$ further support an AGN-like interpretation, as seen in previously known LRDs. Tentative detection of Ly$\alpha$ emission may indicate enhanced Ly$\alpha$ transmission at $z\sim10$. Our findings extend the observational frontier of BH growth into the seed-BH formation era, and upcoming MIRI spectroscopy will further establish the physical nature of the source.
