Supermassive black holes (SMBHs) are ubiquitous in massive galaxies in the local Universe and are thought to co-evolve with their host galaxies [57, e.g.,]. However, the origin of SMBHs remains one of the major unsolved problems in modern astrophysics [111, 39, 87, e.g.,].

Supermassive black holes (SMBHs) are ubiquitous in massive galaxies in the local Universe and are thought to co-evolve with their host galaxies [57, e.g.,]. However, the origin of SMBHs remains one of the major unsolved problems in modern astrophysics [111, 39, 87, e.g.,].

As a possible key population for uncovering the origin of SMBHs, “little red dots” (LRDs) have recently attracted significant attention (e.g., Labbé et al. 60, Furtak et al. 24, Matthee et al. 73, Kocevski et al. 53, Harikane et al. 31, Barro et al. 5, Akins et al. 1, Hainline et al. 30, Hviding et al. 34, Inayoshi and Ho 36). LRDs were first revealed by JWST thanks to its unprecedented sensitivity at infrared wavelengths [88] and are characterized by rest-optical compact morphologies and a unique V-shaped spectral energy distribution (SED), with a blue rest-UV component and a steep, red rest-optical component [60, 24, 73, 53, 5, 1, e.g.,]. These components transition near the Balmer limit [93, e.g.,] and often show a Balmer break [55, 59, 112, e.g.,], and in some cases exhibit an extremely strong Balmer break that cannot be explained by stellar populations alone [18, 77, 103, e.g.,].

These components transition near the Balmer limit [93, e.g.,] and often show a Balmer break [55, 59, 112, e.g.,], and in some cases exhibit an extremely strong Balmer break that cannot be explained by stellar populations alone [18, 77, 103, e.g.,].

Spectroscopic observations have revealed broad Balmer emission lines with absorption features in many LRDs [58, 24, 73, 28, e.g.,]. Despite having broad Balmer lines similar to those of type-I active galactic nuclei (AGN), LRDs show several unusual properties that distinguish them from typical AGNs. First, most LRDs are undetected in X-rays [118, 2, 69, 1], with rare exceptions including objects proposed to be in transition from LRDs to conventional AGNs [33, 23]. LRDs are also generally undetected in radio [1, 85, 74, 27], although radio emission has been detected in some low-zz LRD analogs [90, 91]. Recent studies have revealed hot-dust emission in individual LRDs and stacked samples [19, 64, 43, 84, 7]. However, the detection of hot-dust emission does not necessarily imply that dust attenuation is responsible for the steep red rest-optical continua of LRDs, and the relative contributions of dust attenuation and other emission mechanisms remain uncertain [19, 94]. Many LRDs have not shown significant photometric variability [56, 119, 104, 122], although photometric variability has been reported in gravitationally lensed high-redshift LRDs in a century time-scale [120] and low-zz analogs [63]. Multi-epoch observations have also revealed variations in broad Balmer-line equivalent widths and emission-line fluxes in individual LRDs [25, 44, 61, 8, 77], whereas recent systematic monitoring studies have found substantially weaker Hα\alpha variability in LRDs than expected for typical AGNs [66, 98]. In summary, these unusual properties leave their physical nature uncertain.

One proposed framework is the BH envelope (or BH-star) model [77, 51, 38, e.g.,], in which a BH rapidly grows from a seed, possibly through super-Eddington accretion, while surrounded by dense, optically thick gas with an effective temperature of ∼4000− 5000​K\sim 4000\,\mathchar 45\,5000\,{\rm K}. The rest-optical-to-near-infrared SEDs of LRDs can be reproduced by blackbody-like emission from BH envelopes, whose Wien tails explain the steep rest-optical continua [64, 51, 16, 108, e.g.,]. Furthermore, dense, predominantly neutral gas (nH≳109​cm−3n_{\rm H}\gtrsim 10^{9}\,{\rm cm^{-3}}) can produce strong Balmer absorption and a Balmer break through collisional excitation of hydrogen to the n=2n=2 state [37, 116]. However, the geometry and physical properties of the surrounding gas remain uncertain, and the gas may have a covering factor below unity, as in some clumpy, disk-like, or toroidal configurations [83, 102, 45, 14, 121, 117]. In addition, dense ionized gas with electron column densities of Ne∼1024​cm−2N_{\rm e}\sim 10^{24}\,{\rm cm^{-2}} may contribute to broad Balmer-line profiles through electron scattering [92], suggesting that the emitting, absorbing, and scattering regions may not be identical. Other models invoke nebular emission from ionized gas cocoons [96, 97], dense accretion flows around direct-collapse BHs [82], or dust-reddened AGN emission [68, 67] to explain the characteristic red rest-optical continua of LRDs. Therefore, we have not yet achieved a unified model of the nature of LRDs.

Furthermore, dense, predominantly neutral gas (nH≳109​cm−3n_{\rm H}\gtrsim 10^{9}\,{\rm cm^{-3}}) can produce strong Balmer absorption and a Balmer break through collisional excitation of hydrogen to the n=2n=2 state [37, 116]. However, the geometry and physical properties of the surrounding gas remain uncertain, and the gas may have a covering factor below unity, as in some clumpy, disk-like, or toroidal configurations [83, 102, 45, 14, 121, 117]. In addition, dense ionized gas with electron column densities of Ne∼1024​cm−2N_{\rm e}\sim 10^{24}\,{\rm cm^{-2}} may contribute to broad Balmer-line profiles through electron scattering [92], suggesting that the emitting, absorbing, and scattering regions may not be identical. Other models invoke nebular emission from ionized gas cocoons [96, 97], dense accretion flows around direct-collapse BHs [82], or dust-reddened AGN emission [68, 67] to explain the characteristic red rest-optical continua of LRDs. Therefore, we have not yet achieved a unified model of the nature of LRDs.

Regardless of the specific physical framework invoked to explain their unusual properties, LRDs may trace an early stage of BH growth, potentially close to the epoch of BH seeding. This picture is supported by Inayoshi [40], who compared the number density evolution of LRDs with that of non-LRD AGNs and suggested that LRDs may represent the first episode of BH growth after seed BH formation. Therefore, LRDs provide a crucial population for observationally probing seed BHs, which have long been a theoretical target of study [111, 39, 87]. However, almost all previous LRD studies have been limited to z<9z<9. Prior to this work, the most distant LRD with a spectroscopic redshift was CAPERS-LRD-z9 at z=9.288z=9.288 with a broad Hβ\beta detection [103]. More recently, Cai et al. [10] reported a broad-line AGN at z=9.984z=9.984 and discussed its possible classification as an LRD. Extending LRD studies to z>10z>10 is crucial for constraining their number-density evolution during their emergence and for uncovering when and through which mechanisms seed BHs formed, a regime that has remained observationally inaccessible until now.

papers.title: Characterisation of surface layers formed on plasma-facing components in controlled fusion devices: Role of heavy ion elastic recoil detection
papers.abstract: Wall components retrieved from the TEXTOR tokamak after tracer experiments with nitrogen-15 and molybdenum hexafluoride (MoF6) injection were studied to determine deposition patterns and, by this, to conclude on material migration. Toroidal limiter tiles made of carbon fibre composites and fine grain graphite were examined using time-of-flight heavy ion elastic recoil detection analysis. Molybdenum deposition patterns indicated migration based on erosion and prompt re-deposition. Nitrogen-15 was trapped together with the deposited molybdenum. Some information on the depth distribution of species in the top 400 nm layer of the limiters was obtained; however surface roughness of the samples strongly limited resolution. In the case of molybdenum, the largest concentration was found in the 100 nm outermost layer, whereas fluorine and nitrogen-15 displayed more irregular profiles. Other species, besides deuterium fuel and carbon-12, were also identified: boron-10 and boron-11 originating from boronisations, carbon-13 from earlier tracer experiments, nitrogen-14 from plasma edge cooling and metals eroded from the Inconel wall.

papers.title: MARTA: A "little" black hole hidden in a clumpy, metal-poor galaxy at z~3.8
papers.abstract: JWST has extended the search for accreting black holes into the high-redshift, low-mass regime. We report a low-mass black hole candidate in MARTA 3887, a clumpy, metal-poor galaxy at $z=3.7694$, combining deep JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy, HST and JWST imaging, and archival VLT/MUSE data. We detect a broad H$\alpha$ component with $L_{\rm H\alpha,b}=2.35\times10^{41}$ erg s$^{-1}$ and FWHM $=1270^{+260}_{-250}$ km s$^{-1}$, with no [O III] counterpart of comparable width. Under a broad-line-region interpretation, virial calibrations give $\log(M_{\rm BH}/M_\odot)=6.52^{+0.18}_{-0.23}$ and $\lambda_{\rm Edd}=0.07$, or up to 0.38 for alternative calibrations. The host comprises at least three compact clumps, with $\log(M_\star/M_\odot)=8.16^{+0.09}_{-0.10}$. If stellar photoionization dominates the narrow lines, the gas is highly ionized and metal poor, with $12+\log({\rm O/H})=7.68\pm0.04$ ($\simeq0.10\,Z_\odot$). The inferred $M_{\rm BH}/M_\star=2.3\%$ lies about 2 dex above the extrapolated local relation, suggesting that black-hole growth has outpaced the assembly of the observed host. If growth began only when the first 10% of the observed stellar mass had formed ($t_{10}=92$ Myr ago), a $10^2\,M_\odot$ seed would require a lifetime-mean Eddington ratio $\simeq5.7$; earlier growth or a more massive, e.g. direct-collapse, seed would allow sub-Eddington mean accretion. MUSE reveals extended Ly$\alpha$ emission ($\simeq6.5$-6.9 proper kpc), offset by $+64^{+10}_{-8}$ km s$^{-1}$ from systemic, with a provisional escape fraction of $\simeq0.44$. Together with a Mg II doublet ratio close to the optically thin limit and a high [O III]/[O II] ratio, this makes MARTA 3887 a laboratory to study black-hole growth, stellar assembly, and ionizing-photon escape jointly.

The origin of the first massive black holes remains a central problem in galaxy evolution. The existence of ∼109​M⊙{\sim}10^{9}\,M_{\odot} quasars within the first billion years requires massive seeds, sustained near-Eddington accretion, super-Eddington episodes, or a combination of these processes (Inayoshi et al., 2020). Luminous quasars, however, sample only the high-mass tail of the distribution, while black holes with MBH∼105M_{\rm BH}\sim 10^{5}–107​M⊙10^{7}\,M_{\odot} in lower-mass galaxies provide complementary constraints on the early phases of seeding and black-hole-galaxy co-evolution.

Luminous quasars, however, sample only the high-mass tail of the distribution, while black holes with MBH∼105M_{\rm BH}\sim 10^{5}–107​M⊙10^{7}\,M_{\odot} in lower-mass galaxies provide complementary constraints on the early phases of seeding and black-hole-galaxy co-evolution.

JWST/NIRSpec has extended the search and characterization of early black holes exactly into this regime. Broad-line AGN with MBH∼106M_{\rm BH}\sim 10^{6}–108​M⊙10^{8}\,M_{\odot} are now being routinely identified at high redshift, well below the luminosities accessible to pre-JWST quasar surveys (Harikane et al., 2023; Kocevski et al., 2023; Larson et al., 2023; Übler et al., 2023; Matthee et al., 2024; Maiolino et al., 2024a; Greene et al., 2024; Juodžbalis et al., 2026; Geris et al., 2026). Many of the newly discovered black holes have large inferred MBH/M⋆M_{\rm BH}/M_{\star} ratios relative to local scaling relations (Reines & Volonteri, 2015; Kormendy & Ho, 2013; Pacucci et al., 2023), suggesting that black-hole growth might precede the assembly of the dominant stellar component. Strong selection effects related to flux and line-width sensitivity thresholds favour the detection of massive and/or rapidly accreting black holes at fixed host mass, while measurement scatter further enhances the detected upper envelope (Lauer et al., 2007; Li et al., 2025). Selection-aware analyses indicate that the intrinsic high-redshift MBHM_{\rm BH}–M⋆M_{\star} relation may be consistent with the local relation, but with substantially larger scatter capable of producing the observed high-MBH/M⋆M_{\rm BH}/M_{\star} tail (Ziparo et al., 2026). Even if individual detections preferentially sample this upper envelope, the existence and frequency of such overmassive systems remain informative about black-hole formation and early growth. Models predict different low-mass distributions and scatter depending on their prescriptions for seeding, accretion, and feedback (Habouzit et al., 2022; Volonteri et al., 2023; Trinca et al., 2026); well-characterized systems at the boundaries of the observed parameter space therefore provide complementary constraints on these processes.

The identification of the faintest candidates requires particular care. Broad Balmer emission without an associated forbidden-line component of comparable width is a standard signature of a broad-line region (BLR), but at low luminosity it can also arise from interacting supernovae, shocks, outflows, or spatially unresolved galaxy structure (Maiolino et al., 2025; Geris et al., 2026). Classical optical narrow-line diagnostics are also poorly discriminating in the metal-poor, highly ionized ISM regime common at high redshift: metal-poor narrow-line regions overlap with the star-forming sequence, while extreme stellar populations can approach classical AGN-classification boundaries (Feltre et al., 2016; Gutkin et al., 2016; Kewley et al., 2013; Mazzolari et al., 2024).

The combined effect of accretion supplying additional hard ionizing photons and radiative or mechanical AGN feedback lowering the neutral-gas covering fraction could open channels through which both AGN- and stellar-produced Lyman-continuum (LyC) photons can escape. However, this is not an inevitable consequence of hosting an AGN: simulations of high-redshift dwarf galaxies find that supernova feedback can dominate the structure of the ISM and that black-hole activity does not necessarily increase the LyC escape fraction (Trebitsch et al., 2018). Direct measurements at z≃3z\simeq 3–4 span a broad range, from sub-unity average escape fractions in moderate-luminosity AGN to high values in luminous quasars (Grazian et al., 2018; Iwata et al., 2022). Compactness, high [O iii]/[O ii], and the presence of strong emission in resonant lines such as Ly​α{\rm Ly}\alpha and Mg II probing the physical conditions associated with low neutral gas column densities or porous sightlines can therefore test whether active black-hole growth coexists with favourable ionizing radiation escape channels (Jaskot & Oey, 2013; Nakajima & Ouchi, 2014; Verhamme et al., 2015; Henry et al., 2018; Chisholm et al., 2020; Izotov et al., 2018; Flury et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2023; Naidu et al., 2022). Systems combining these features offer a view of the interplay between black-hole growth, stellar feedback, and ionizing radiation escape. papers.title: A VLT/CRIRES+ study of helium 1.083$\mu$m absorption features towards the inner Orion Nebula
papers.abstract: JWST NIRCam F115W observations towards the inner Orion Nebula revealed a diverse array of previously unknown dark features. The most likely cause was absorption or suppressed emission of the helium 1.083$\mu$m triplet which lies in that filter. We have obtained VLT/CRIRES+ high-resolution spectrographic observations over a selection of different dark targets, confirming that the features are indeed explained by a reduction in the flux of the helium 1.083$\mu$m triplet, a reduction that is fairly uniform across the line. The Orion Nebula is a blister HII region, with a dense, bright ionised layer on the far side from the observer near the Orion A molecular cloud and lower density gas elsewhere. Using a simple radiative transfer model, we show that dark features arise when emission from the dense layer is absorbed by intermediate density helium (e.g. in clumps, globules, or winds from objects like proplyds) on the near side of the dense layer.

papers.intro:
The Orion Nebula H II region, the eponymous Orion Nebula Cluster (often referred to as the ONC), and the inner Trapezium Cluster comprise one of the nearest (Kounkel et al., 2017; Maíz Apellániz et al., 2022, d∼390d\sim 390\,pc, e.g.) and best-studied massive star-forming regions. It has played an important role in the study of feedback from massive stars (Zuckerman, 1973; Hillenbrand, 1997, e.g.), photochemistry (Tielens et al., 1993; Berné et al., 2022, e.g.), and the external photoevaporation of protoplanetary discs (Winter & Haworth, 2022; Allen et al., 2025). The region has been studied extensively for many years, with recent works including those in the optical with HST, VLT/MUSE (Weilbacher et al., 2015; O’Dell et al., 2017a), in the infrared with JWST, Spitzer, SOFIA, and Herschel (Megeath et al., 2012; Pabst et al., 2019; McCaughrean & Pearson, 2023, e.g.), in the sub-millimetre with ALMA (Boyden & Eisner, 2020; Otter et al., 2021; van Terwisga et al., 2022, particularly for the study of discs, e.g.), in the radio with the VLA (Vargas-González et al., 2021), and in X-rays with Chandra (Getman et al., 2005; Kastner et al., 2005, e.g.). Despite this intense, long-term examination, the region still holds many mysteries and surprises.

Despite this intense, long-term examination, the region still holds many mysteries and surprises.

What is fairly well known is the general structure of the region. At the heart of the Trapezium Cluster are the four massive and multiple OB stars known as the Trapezium, with the main source of ionisation being the O6V star θ1\theta^{1} Ori C. They sit on the far side of the nebula, in front of the background Orion A molecular cloud and associated main ionisation front which separates them (O’Dell et al., 2017a; O’Dell et al., 2020; O’Dell & Abel, 2025, e.g.). To the north-east of the Trapezium, part of the molecular cloud overlays the H II region to create the Dark Bay. To the south-east, the molecular cloud structure curves upwards towards the observer, yielding the prominent photodissociation region (PDR) known as the Orion Bar. This has been subject to photochemical studies for many years (Tielens et al., 1993; van der Werf et al., 1996; Bernard-Salas et al., 2012, e.g.), studies that have intensified since the recent advent of JWST observations (Berné et al., 2022, e.g.).

These dark features typically exhibit a reduction in F115W flux on the order of 10–30 per cent relative to their surroundings, and display a variety of morphologies. Some appear as ragged and isolated small globules or clouds, while others are more linear features associated with jets and outflows from young stars. But majority appear as irregular bubble-like structures roughly centred on young stellar objects in the region and particularly those associated with photoevaporating discs or proplyds. Continuum dust absorption is ruled out as the cause of the dark features, as they only appear in the F115W filter and not in adjacent longer-wavelength JWST or shorter-wavelength HST observations. papers.title: exoALMA XXV: A Statistical Analysis of Gaseous Substructure in Low-Inclination Disks
papers.abstract: Protoplanetary disks exhibit complex structure in both their gas dynamics and their temperature. Characterizing it has proven challenging, owing to the mismatch between the observed complexity and the relatively simple semi-analytical models typically used to interpret it. To augment these analyses, we apply the second-order structure function to the velocity and temperature perturbations of four low-inclination sources from the exoALMA program, each measured against a noise-only null built from the data themselves. All exhibit correlated structure. Its radial correlation length is limited by the beam in every case, which excludes non-axisymmetric structure on radial scales larger than ~1.5 pressure scale heights. In three of the four disks the structure is instead resolved and elongated in azimuth, by factors of 1.6-2.3, as expected of small-scale perturbations sheared out by Keplerian rotation. We further introduce two statistics that characterize spiral structure without tracing an arm crest: a modal power spectrum, measuring the periodicity of the azimuthal structure, and a winding contrast, measuring the radial dependence of its phase. The velocity residuals of three disks are significantly wound. MWC 758 is the only source in which the winding is coherent across the disk and shared by the temperature field. Its trailing m=1 temperature structure is consistent with the illumination of a warp, while its velocity field carries small-scale, sheared structure that could redistribute angular momentum. Because neither statistic requires a crest, both extend a quantitative description of winding to the flocculent regime, where a spiral cannot be parameterized.

papers.intro:
High-resolution ALMA observations have established that the gas in a protoplanetary disk does not simply rotate in a Keplerian fashion. Once an axisymmetric model is subtracted, the line-of-sight velocity retains residuals at the few per cent level relative to the background Keplerian rotation, and the emission surface retains temperature variations of a few Kelvin, ≈5{\approx}5–10%10\% of the azimuthally averaged surface temperature, both organized on scales comparable to the disk’s own radial extent [46]. The exoALMA program, Teague et al. [48], was designed to characterize exactly this component, and its atlases of non-Keplerian deviations and of vertical flows found spiral-like features, arcs, rings and localized flows across the majority of the sample [16, 7].

Interpreting that residual component is harder than detecting it. The residual velocity field is usually compared against a parametric expectation (the wake of an embedded planet, a warp, a vortex, a gravitationally unstable arm) and individual disks have been interpreted convincingly in each of these ways [40, 41, 9, 42, 54, 55, 20, 33, 43, 44, 27, e.g.,]. Two difficulties arise. The first is that these models are not easily distinguished from one another on the basis of a residual map, since each predicts a pattern of comparable amplitude on comparable scales. The second, and the one that motivates this work, is that a substantial part of what the data show cannot be described by these parametric expectations. Although the structure is correlated over a finite range of scales, it is neither periodic, ordered, nor traceable as a crest.

A complementary approach is to describe the field statistically rather than parametrically. The second-order structure function, S2S_{2}, measures the mean square difference of a field between pairs of points as a function of their separation, and so characterizes the amplitude and the characteristic scales of a correlated field without reference to any particular morphology. It has a long history in the study of turbulence [31, 37], and has been applied extensively to the interstellar medium [32, 39, 24, 12] and the solar wind [8], including specifically to velocity centroid maps of the kind we analyze here [13]. Its appeal in the present context is that it makes no assumption of a crest, a mode number or a pitch angle, and returns a measurement whether or not the field is ordered.

Teague et al. [45] developed this framework for disk velocity residuals and established what can and cannot be recovered from noisy data. Structure is detectable well below the amplitude at which it can be determined by eye, and the dominant correlation scales and the degree of anisotropy can be constrained, provided that significance is assessed against a noise model with properties matched to the data rather than against an idealized noise model. Application to numerical simulations of the vertical shear instability, the gravitational instability and the magneto-rotational instability demonstrated that this analysis was able to differentiate between models, however not uniquely identify them. This application also identified the framework’s principal limitation: a wound field, i.e., a spiral, imprints its winding on the off-diagonal structure of S2S_{2}, where an annulus-by-annulus analysis, as used to characterize the scale of the perturbations, averages it away. In effect, the presence of spiral structure dilutes the significance of the scale parameters.

papers.title: Targeting the future of spectroscopic galaxy surveys -- A cosmological study case with the Wide-field Spectroscopic Telescope
papers.abstract: The next generation of Stage-V spectroscopic surveys are designed to measure hundreds of millions of galaxy and quasar spectra, extending precision large-scale-structure cosmology to redshifts and volumes well beyond the reach of current Stage-IV facilities. Realising this potential requires revisiting the target selection strategies and designing them explicitly around the depth, multiplexing, and survey time of the new instruments, rather than a direct extrapolation of existing recipes. This work develops and characterises new strategies for the Wide-field Spectroscopic Telescope (WST), a proposed 12-metre, highly multiplexed facility expected to operate in the 2040s. Using deep multi-band photometry, including COSMOS-field data from CLAUDS and HSC, we revisit low-redshift $z<1.6$ tracer selection of SDSS, BOSS/eBOSS, DESI and 4MOST-CRS -- Bright Galaxies, Luminous Red Galaxies, Emission Line Galaxies and quasars -- to photometric depth achievable in the WST era, and introduce a purely magnitude-limited sample (MagMax) exploiting three-dimensional colour-colour star-galaxy separation, and a set of Lyman-Break Galaxy dropout samples extending target selection to $z>2$. Using Fisher-matrix forecasts, we showcase the constraining power of a WST-like cosmological survey on BAO distance parameters $\alpha_\parallel$ and $\alpha_\perp$, the growth rate $f$, the evolving dark energy equation $w_0w_a$, the local-type primordial non-Gaussianity $f_{\rm NL}^{\rm loc}$, and the sum of the neutrino mass $\Sigma m_\nu$. The main outcome of this work is an optimisation framework that directly links instrumental capabilities and observing time to cosmological constraining power, providing a science-driven template applicable to the design of future generations of Stage-V spectroscopic surveys.

papers.intro:
Optical spectroscopy has been a cornerstone of modern cosmology for the past three decades, with the advent of multi-fibre instruments. The Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS; York et al. 2000) and the 2 degree Field Galaxy Redshift Survey (2dFGRS; Colless et al. 2001) revolutionized wide-area 3D mapping of the galaxy distribution and measurements of galaxy clustering. In parallel, deep, high-density galaxy surveys but limited in sky area, like the VIMOS Public Extragalactic Redshift Survey (VIPERS; Guzzo et al. 2014) extending the accessible redshift range provided dedicated study of galaxy clustering, redshift-space distortions, growth of structure, and the cosmic web (Bel et al., 2014). For two decades, these surveys and there extensions (e.g. 6dFGRS Beutler et al. 2012, eBOSS Dawson et al. 2016) map millions of extra-galactic objects including bright galaxies (BGs), luminous red galaxies (LRGs), emission-line galaxies (ELGs), and quasi-stellar objects (QSOs), to trace the expansion history of the Universe out to redshift z=2.2z=2.2 and z<3.5z<3.5 using the Lyman-alpha forest of QSOs, achieving percent-level precision on cosmological parameters (Tegmark et al., 2006; Alam et al., 2021; Cole et al., 2005). Today, the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI, Levi et al. 2013) observes a third of the sky with a target density at least 2.5 times higher than SDSS, allowing it to reach sub-per cent-precision cosmological measurements of the Baryon Acoustic Oscillation (BAO) distances (Abdul Karim et al., 2025). DESI has already completed its nominal five-year survey and has begun a three-year extension, increasing both target density and sky area (DESI Collaboration, in prep.). Other forthcoming Stage-IV redshift surveys —the 4-metre Multi-Object Spectroscopic Telescope (4MOST; de Jong et al. 2012 with the cosmology redshift survey (CRS; Richard et al. 2019; Verdier et al. 2026), the Subaru Prime Focus Spectrograph (PFS; Tamura et al. 2016), and the Euclid space mission (Euclid Collaboration et al., 2025c)—will complement DESI in redshift range and sky coverage.

The recent results from DESI, combined with other cosmological probes, have revealed hints of an evolving dark energy model that challenge our current Λ\LambdaCDM paradigm (Adame et al., 2025b; Abdul Karim et al., 2025), well established since the 1980s (Lahav and Shah, 2026). Beyond differentiating between dark energy models, spectroscopic surveys also probe more recent questions in cosmology: is the assumption of a Gaussian primordial Universe valid? What is the neutrino mass hierarchy? To address these questions, the redshift-survey community is advocating for Stage-V spectroscopic surveys. Several projects have been proposed, including the MUltiplexed Survey Telescope (MUST; Zhao et al. 2024), Spec-S5 (Besuner et al., 2025), and the Wide-field Spectroscopic Telescope11 1 https://wstelescope.eu (WST; Bacon et al. 2024; Mainieri et al. 2024). Using large-aperture telescopes with highly multiplexed spectroscopic instruments, these surveys plan to reinforce the density of low-redshift tracers at redshift z<1.6z<1.6, along with targeting high-redshift galaxies such as Lyman-break galaxies (LBGs; Steidel et al. 1996) and Lyman-α\alpha emitters (LAEs; Ouchi et al. 2020), extending precise mapping of the Universe out to redshift 5 over the coming decades, enabling observation of the linear modes in the primordial Universe. As a pilot for these future projects, the DESI collaboration is preparing DESI Run 2 (Schlegel et al., 2022), an extension of DESI Run 1, aiming to start in 2029 and to significantly extend the science reach of its predecessor, collecting 40 million spectra at higher density and higher redshift than DESI Run 1, while serving as a pathfinder for a future Stage-V survey. Stage-V surveys (Spec-S5, WST) expect to measure hundreds of millions of redshifts, opening a new and largely uncharted discovery space. Executing such large-scale spectroscopic campaigns depends critically on available imaging surveys with sufficient sky coverage, wavelength range, and depth to identify suitable targets. Over the coming decade, large photometric surveys such as the Rubin Observatory’s Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST; LSST Science Collaboration et al. 2009), the Euclid sattelite (Euclid Collaboration et al., 2025c), the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope (Akeson et al., 2019), and the China Space Station Telescope (CSST; CSST Collaboration et al. 2026) will cover a wide spectral range from the optical to the infrared, enabling hundreds of millions of tracers to be selected for Stage-V experiments. Together, these new datasets will allow us to probe the mechanisms driving the accelerated expansion of the Universe—both in its earliest moments (inflation) and at late times (dark energy)—while also addressing the neutrino mass problem and the internal tensions within the Λ\LambdaCDM paradigm, which have been brought into sharper focus by recent DESI results. A key challenge in cosmology with redshift surveys is to provide galaxy or quasar samples with both high density and high purity, in order to optimise the scientific return of these experiments. In this paper, we explore new target-selection strategies for future Stage-V spectroscopic surveys that extend current tracer-selection approaches. At redshift z<1.6z<1.6, we propose an alternative to the traditional, DESI-like tracer-based strategy, selecting magnitude-limited samples instead. In a second part, we optimise these selections for the specific case of a WST-like instrument. We examine the survey design of WST and its implications for the selection of WST tracers, and we present cosmological forecasts to quantify what WST could deliver. For the high-redshift survey, given by LBGs primarily, we propose to define the target selection using a science-driven approach, in which the magnitude limits are directly constrained by the scientific return of the survey.

papers.title: GALACTIC CENTERS AS TRACERS OF GALAXY EVOLUTION: Zooming from galaxy large-scale properties into their central massive black holes
papers.abstract: During the workshop ''Galactic Centers as tracers of galaxy evolution'' (Lorentz Center, Leiden), we reviewed one of the most debated questions in the field of galaxy evolution: the connection between galactic central regions and the evolution of galaxies at a global scale. We gathered different research communities to reveal the connection channels between central massive black holes (MBHs), nuclear structures, and evolutionary processes at a global scale, such as gas inflows and outflows and galaxy-galaxy interactions. Special focus was dedicated to MBH seeding, formation and growth, active galactic nuclei feedback, and the formation of nuclear stellar structures, without missing a global perspective. Participants from these different fields introduced us to the state of the art in numerical simulations, as well as cutting-edge observational techniques. In addition to achieving a deep understanding of these topics, we set up plans to exploit future facilities such as the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT). In this paper, we briefly summarize the highlights of the workshop, identify the open questions that emerged during the workshop discussions, and discuss what observations and simulations will be needed to address them.

papers.intro:
In the last few decades, the astrophysical community has made great progress in understanding the formation and evolution of galaxies, shedding light on the combination of internal and external processes, such as secular evolution (Kormendy and Ho, 2013; Kormendy, 2015, e.g.,) and galaxy mergers (Lotz et al., 2008; Hopkins et al., 2010; Chilingarian et al., 2010, e.g.,), which have resulted in the present day diversity of morphologies (e.g., Pillepich et al. 2018).

In the last few decades, the astrophysical community has made great progress in understanding the formation and evolution of galaxies, shedding light on the combination of internal and external processes, such as secular evolution (Kormendy and Ho, 2013; Kormendy, 2015, e.g.,) and galaxy mergers (Lotz et al., 2008; Hopkins et al., 2010; Chilingarian et al., 2010, e.g.,), which have resulted in the present day diversity of morphologies (e.g., Pillepich et al. 2018).

Complexity is also prominent in the central regions of galaxies, where a variety of distinct stellar systems form, often coexisting with central massive black holes (MBHs). Together with the gas in the central regions, these stellar systems are important tracers of the dynamical state and overall evolution of the host galaxy. Studying these structures not only reveals their formation and growth but can also point to the mechanisms that funnel stars and gas to the center, which can lead to the seeding and growth of MBHs and to the appearance of active galactic nuclei (AGNs, e.g., Bonoli et al. 2014; Neumayer et al. 2020). When MBHs undergo an active phase, they interact with the host galaxy through black-hole feedback. This can be positive and foster or trigger star formation, or negative and be responsible for quenching (Combes, 2021; Cazzoli, 2017; Ramos Almeida et al., 2023). The tight connection of galactic nuclei with large-scale processes makes them key to understanding galaxy evolution in general.

When MBHs undergo an active phase, they interact with the host galaxy through black-hole feedback. This can be positive and foster or trigger star formation, or negative and be responsible for quenching (Combes, 2021; Cazzoli, 2017; Ramos Almeida et al., 2023). The tight connection of galactic nuclei with large-scale processes makes them key to understanding galaxy evolution in general.

Nuclear star clusters (NSCs) and nuclear stellar disks and rings (NDRs), are the most prominent stellar structures in galactic nuclei. The latter may also be observed in the forms of nuclear bars or spirals (Márquez et al., 2000; Martini et al., 2001; de Lorenzo-Cáceres et al., 2020; Nitschai et al., 2020). NSCs are compact, with sizes of a few parsecs, and come in a variety of shapes (e.g., Sánchez-Janssen et al. 2019; Neumayer et al. 2020), while NDRs can be more extended, up to a few hundred parsecs, and are rotationally supported structures (Pizzella et al., 2002; Gadotti et al., 2020). With small sizes and masses between 10510^{5} and 10810^{8}M⊙M_{\odot}, NSCs and NSDs are very dense. Between 60 and 80% of galaxies with stellar masses between 10810^{8} and 101010^{10} M⊙M_{\odot} host an NSC, while NDRs have been found in about 20% of disk galaxies (Comerón et al., 2010b; Neumayer et al., 2020). The distinction between these structures is sometimes difficult, and in fact they have much in common with each other: sometimes similar masses, ages and metallicities, and complex stellar populations.

NSCs can form mainly via two different channels: 1) the inspiral of star clusters, formed elsewhere, towards the center due to dynamical friction and 2) in-situ star formation after gas inflow. These scenarios are not mutually exclusive, and several observational studies have suggested that both mechanisms contribute to the formation and growth of NSCs (e.g. Fahrion et al. 2021; Fahrion et al. 2022; Fahrion et al. 2024). However, there is no overall agreement on their relative contribution, nor on the dominant formation scenarios for galaxies with different morphological types (Pinna et al., 2021). Most studies on NDRs support an in-situ formation from gas funneled to the center by a bar, although an external origin has been invoked for those showing counter-rotation (Bittner et al., 2020).

The coevolution of galaxies and their nuclei is also traced by peculiar objects that are thought to be the stripped remnants of their progenitor galaxies, as a consequence of past galaxy-galaxy interactions. The most massive globular clusters in the Milky Way (e.g., M54 and Omega Centauri) show complex kinematics and stellar populations (Alfaro-Cuello et al., 2019; Clontz et al., 2024) and likely host MBHs in their centers (Häberle et al., 2024b). Their properties, similar to NSCs, suggest they were the stellar nuclei of accreted dwarf galaxies. On the other hand, ultra-compact dwarf galaxies (UCDs) are compact stellar systems more massive than the most massive globular clusters, and more compact than dwarf galaxies of similar masses. They also show complex stellar populations and often an MBH in their center, which is over-massive (as predicted by the relation between MBH mass and galaxy mass, e.g.,Ferrarese and Merritt 2000). This can be explained if they are the nuclear remnants of much more massive progenitors that were tidally stripped (Seth et al., 2014; Ahn et al., 2018; Ferré-Mateu et al., 2021).

As mentioned above, the evolution of nuclear stellar and gaseous structures, especially NSCs, appears to be intimately connected to MBHs. In particular, both NSCs and central MBHs share mass scaling relations with their host galaxy (e.g., Ferrarese et al. 2006), suggesting that the formation of both is driven by processes that affect the evolution of their entire host galaxy. The very high density of NSCs favors merging events of objects such as lower-mass BHs, producing gravitational waves. These events may give birth to potential seeds of MBHs (intermediate mass black holes, IMBHs), which later grow through gas accretion and tidal disruption events, favored by the dense NSC environment (e.g., Neumayer et al. 2020). Thus, MBHs may form and grow in NSCs, while the same large-scale processes (e.g., rejuvenation after galaxy mergers) may play a key role in both triggering nuclear starbursts and feeding MBHs (Levy et al., 2022; Levy et al., 2024; Askar et al., 2021; Askar et al., 2023; Bellocchi et al., 2023). Gas inflow and subsequent in-situ star formation is one key mechanism to form nuclear structures, while AGN winds and outflows can wipe out all gas at galactic centers and prevent in-situ star formation. Thus, the fueling cycle of MBHs is intimately connected to the formation of stellar structures in the center of galaxies.

papers.title: Chemical and dynamical evolution of prestellar cores, the dawn of star and planet formation
papers.abstract: Studying prestellar cores is crucial to understanding the formation of stellar and planetary systems. To date, we lack a comprehensive survey of their density and velocity structure at small scales (100-1000 au), the gas ionisation state, their lifetimes, and how these properties are influenced by the environment. A deep study into this critical stage of star formation requires a large single-dish (sub)millimetre telescope like AtLAST.

papers.title: A temporally clustered gravitational wave pair and a Type IIb supernova
papers.abstract: Compact object mergers are generally expected long after the stellar collapse that forms their remnants. Here we report two marginal gravitational wave (GW) candidates, S190910d and S190910h, separated by 7.1 hr, whose three-dimensional localizations overlap at the position and distance of the Type IIb supernova SN 2019rsq. The GW pair lies in the extreme tail of the joint distribution of temporal separation and localization overlap, with a pairwise null probability of $7.6 \times 10^{-5}$ under our Monte Carlo null test. Independent re-analyses recover both as signal-like candidates. Under a common-origin hypothesis, S190910h remains consistent with a low-mass compact binary with source-frame masses near $2.5 + 1.3\,M_\odot$, whereas S190910d favours a strongly asymmetric $\sim 34 + 3\,M_\odot$ system whose observed amplitude is compatible with the supernova distance. SN 2019rsq is a rapidly evolving stripped-envelope Type IIb explosion whose light curve is consistent with stellar collapse occurring near the GW activity. Although the supernova coincidence alone is not statistically rare, its timing and physical properties provide a stellar collapse anchor for the unusual GW pair. A fragmenting collapsar disk provides a plausible framework that can accommodate the component masses, hour-scale delays and supernova properties, raising the possibility that multiple compact object mergers can accompany a single stellar collapse episode.

papers.title: Beyond Source Compatibility: WebAssembly as a Stable ABI for ARINC 653 Applications
papers.abstract: Thirty years ago, ARINC 653 was introduced to provide a vendor-independent platform for software applications in Integrated Modular Avionics (IMA). A platform is characterized by a well-defined interface abstracting over implementation details; in the case of ARINC 653 this is an Application Programming Interface (API), defined on the source-code level. However, several aspects of this API - such as the memory layout and partially also the integer bit width of data types - remain implementation dependent, so portability across Operating Systems (OSs) requires recompilation, and often also source code adaptation. Our contribution is three-fold; first, we refine the ARINC 653 header file, eliminating remaining ambiguities. Second, building on WebAssembly (Wasm), we define an OS- and processor-architecture-agnostic Application Binary Interface (ABI) at the object-code level, resolving differences in data layout, endianness, and function-pointer representation between host and guest environments. Third, we demonstrate a Wasm-VM-agnostic shim-library that executes ARINC 653 partitions, compiled to Wasm bytecode and following our ABI, on multiple processor architectures using two independent Wasm runtimes.

With the push towards IMA, multiple software applications are executed together on the same computer module. Between applications, partitioning is of utmost importance to avoid cascading failures [8]. This partitioning is provided by specialized OS, offering an API for scheduling, IPC, external I/O, health management, etc. Software applications are often tightly coupled to an OS and hardware / module type, hindering portability between such OS. To enable software re-use, ARINC 653 was developed [4].

This partitioning is provided by specialized OS, offering an API for scheduling, IPC, external I/O, health management, etc. Software applications are often tightly coupled to an OS and hardware / module type, hindering portability between such OS. To enable software re-use, ARINC 653 was developed [4].

ARINC 653 is a modular standard that specifies OS interfaces and configuration aspects for the partitioning. Multiple OS implement (subsets of) the ARINC 653 API, e.g. PikeOS, VxWorks, DEOS, LynxOS-178 & Integrity-178. However, various aspects of the ARINC 653 API are implementation dependent; for example, the order of struct fields or the bit width of id types (such as APEX_LONG_INTEGER). Consequently, even applications relying only on the specified behavior of the ARINC 653 API still require recompilation for a port to a new compliant OS to accommodate these implementation-dependent aspects [5]. Although Cook [5] frames this as “[…] facilitating portability via recompilation of the application source […],” recompilation is necessary but insufficient to guarantee portability: Cook presupposes access to source code, a matching toolchain, and the absence of implicit reliance on non-standardized behavior. In practice, applications are likely to implicitly rely on such non-standardized aspects, further raising the risk and cost of porting to a new OS. In particular in IMA settings, depending on history and relationship between function supplier and airframer, the source code might not be available (any more) to the airframer.

This is not a novel idea, and has been briefly discussed already in section 4.b of [38]. However, various minute implementation details are merely glanced over by that publication, leaving it up to this paper to fill in the gaps.

papers.title: Universality of Large-Scale Geometry For Critical Random-Cluster Models
papers.abstract: The understanding of the behaviour of critical lattice models in two dimensions has made immense progress in the past couple of decades, with conformal invariance as its conjectured end goal. We consider here the critical random-cluster model (or FK-percolation) on a large class of graphs --- namely bi-periodic isoradial graphs --- with cluster-weight~$q \in [1,4]$. Following up on the establishment of rotational invariance at criticality in \cite{Rotation}, we prove that the large scale behaviour of these models is asymptotically the same on all such graphs. These include the critical homogeneous models on the square, triangular and hexagonal lattices.

papers.title: Synchronization of Enriched Spin Glasses
papers.abstract: We show that enriching a non-convex multi-species Hamiltonian by a uniform Ruelle probability cascade implies synchronization of the joint overlap array without an additional regularizing perturbation. In particular, we show that any limit point of the overlap array is a deterministic non-decreasing function of a uniform Ruelle probability cascade.

In this short note, we show that the enrichment of the free energy with a uniform Ruelle probability cascade (RPC) [29, 7] plays the role of a macroscopic perturbation that forces synchronization in the limit without the need of an additional perturbation argument. The form of the enrichment is special in the sense that it is rich enough to capture the underlying ultrametric [25] structure of the spin configurations in the limit, making it a natural candidate to synchronize with the configurations. One might expect that the synchronization is only possible for optimal enrichments that match the limiting structure, but this is not the case and it holds for any regular (see Definition 1.1) enrichment path.

papers.title: Interpretable Multiple-Instance Learning of Glomerular Pathomics and Subtype Ratios for eGFR Classification
papers.abstract: Chronic kidney disease is characterized by structural alterations in renal tissue and progressive loss of kidney function. While glomerular subtype ratios provide a compact and clinically meaningful summary of glomerular composition, representing pathomic information using whole-slide image (WSI)-level mean values diminishes glomerulus-level heterogeneity and the contribution of less prevalent patterns. In this proof-of-concept study, we investigated whether modeling individual glomeruli using multiple-instance learning (MIL) could provide complementary information to conventional subtype ratios for estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) classification. We analyzed 162 kidney-biopsy WSIs from 162 patients, categorizing renal function as eGFR < 60 or >= 60 mL/min/1.73 m^2. Quantitative size, shape, intensity, and texture features were extracted from segmented glomeruli, representing each patient as a bag of glomerular instances. An attention-based MIL model was trained to aggregate these heterogeneous pathomic profiles. We evaluated subtype ratios, pathomics, and their combination using ABMIL, with a mean-pooled multilayer perceptron baseline. In five-fold cross-validation, the subtype-ratio-only model achieved an AUC of 0.7262 +/- 0.0596. MIL using pathomics alone achieved an AUC of 0.7362 +/- 0.0788, whereas integrating pathomics with subtype ratios produced the highest mean AUC of 0.7630 +/- 0.0665. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) were used to examine individual feature contributions. These results demonstrate that MIL-based pathomics can complement established glomerular subtype ratios by capturing additional glomerulus-level information for quantitative kidney-biopsy analysis.
papers.intro:
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a major global health burden associated with progressive loss of renal function, increased cardiovascular risk, and substantial healthcare costs [10, 20]. Accurate assessment of chronic kidney injury is therefore important for diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment planning. In routine renal pathology, whole-slide images (WSIs) of kidney biopsies provide important histological evidence for evaluating disease severity. Glomeruli are particularly informative because their structural alterations are associated with the development and progression of many renal diseases [26, 12, 14]. In quantitative renal pathology, the proportions of different glomerular subtypes, particularly the percentage of globally sclerotic glomeruli, are well-established measures of chronic renal injury and have demonstrated clinical and prognostic value in both native and transplant kidney disease [6, 7, 8]. These subtype ratios provide a compact and interpretable summary of the glomerular composition of a biopsy. In addition to subtype composition, individual glomeruli exhibit quantitative variations in size, shape, staining characteristics, texture, and structural organization [29, 7]. These variations may reflect differences among glomeruli assigned to the same pathological subtype and could provide information complementary to established subtype ratios. Preserving and analyzing this glomerulus-level heterogeneity may therefore provide a more comprehensive quantitative characterization of renal injury [9, 18, 8].

Recent advances in computational pathology have enabled the systematic extraction of quantitative features, commonly referred to as pathomics [1, 27], from segmented histopathological structures [2, 4, 31, 3]. Pathomic analysis has shown potential for disease classification, outcome prediction, and biomarker discovery by quantifying tissue characteristics that may not be fully represented by categorical labels [28]. A common implementation summarizes instance-level pathomic features using slide-level statistics, such as their mean or variance. Although these representations are concise and computationally efficient, mean pooling assigns equal importance to all glomeruli and may reduce subtle information from less prevalent but potentially informative glomerular patterns. Multiple-instance learning (MIL) provides an alternative framework in which each patient is represented as a bag of individual glomerular instances while requiring only a patient-level label [22, 5]. In computational pathology, MIL has been widely applied using image patches or learned image embeddings as instances [30, 5]. However, relatively few studies have investigated MIL using handcrafted pathomic features extracted from biologically defined structures such as glomeruli. Attention-based multiple-instance learning (ABMIL) can learn the relative importance of individual glomeruli while preserving the quantitative meaning of the original pathomic features [11, 15, 13]. Whether ABMIL-based glomerular pathomics can provide additional information for kidney-biopsy analysis, particularly in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) classification, remains insufficiently investigated.

In this proof-of-concept study, we develop an interpretable ABMIL framework for eGFR classification using glomerulus-level pathomic features extracted from kidney-biopsy WSIs. Individual glomeruli are first identified and classified into pathological subtypes, after which quantitative pathomic features are extracted from each glomerulus. Instead of representing these features only through slide-level averages, the proposed framework treats each glomerulus as an instance and learns to aggregate heterogeneous glomerular profiles into a patient-level representation. We compare ABMIL with a multilayer perceptron (MLP) using mean-pooled pathomic features. The MLP is evaluated using three input settings: glomerular subtype ratios only, pathomics only, and their combination. ABMIL is evaluated using pathomics alone and pathomics combined with subtype ratios. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) are further used to examine the contributions of individual quantitative features, as depicted in the schematic overview of the experimental settings (Fig. 1). Through these experiments, we investigate whether MIL-based glomerular pathomics provides information complementary to established subtype ratios for quantitative kidney-biopsy assessment.

papers.title: NovaFilter - A Rule-Based ETL Staging Framework for Fault-Tolerant Relational Databases
papers.abstract: NovaFilter is a completely new approach to deriving structured relational data from heterogeneous input data in different data formats. It combines consistency checks, rule-based data transformation, and a human-in-the-loop example discussion. Using these three components, NovaFilter stores all transformation knowledge in an explicit rule base, which is continuously expanded through the example discussion with the user. The resulting data transformation process is deterministic, transparent, and reusable. As a result, the method can replace conventional ETL scripts and offers a completely new strategy for transforming data between different data models and schemas. Its main advantage is that users without programming skills (e.g. domain experts) can answer the example discussion and thus it is a building block for democratization of ETL script developement.

papers.title: Get Permanent Results Faster by Counting Stars
papers.abstract: We show that $n \times n$ permanents can be computed with $O^*{(2-\varepsilon)^n}$ arithmetic operations over every commutative ring, for $\varepsilon = 10^{-40}$. This solves a problem stated in Knuth's The Art of Computer Programming. Our algorithm implements the classical Binet--Minc identity with dynamic programming and careful bookkeeping. It also gives algebraic branching programs of size $O^*{(2-\varepsilon)^n}$.

papers.title: Homomorphisms on a product of free convex semilattices
papers.abstract: Convex semilattices form an equational class that combines convex algebras and semilattices by a distributive law. For a set $I$ let $\mathcal FI$ be the free convex semilattice with basis $I$. A product $\mathcal FI\times\mathcal FJ$ is generated by $I\times J$, but is not free. Hence, not every map from $I\times J$ into an arbitrary convex semilattice $X$ extends uniquely to a homomorphism from $\mathcal FI\times\mathcal FJ$ to $X$. We investigate a condition on a map $\varphi$ of $I\times J$ into some convex semilattice $X$ that is always necessary and often sufficient for $\varphi$ to have such an extension to a homomorphism $\Phi$ of $\mathcal FI\times\mathcal FJ$ into $X$.

papers.intro:
A convex semilattice is a combination of a convex algebra and a semilattice, imposing a distributive law that rules the interplay between these structures (we refer to Section 2.2 for all definitions). This kind of algebras has a more abstract background, namely as the Eilenberg-Moore algebras of a certain monad, and has recently attracted attention in theoretical computer science, in the context of traces of transition systems with nondeterminism and probability, see [2], see also [14, 13] for quantitative extensions. From a different viewpoint, algebras whose operations distribute over a semilattice operation have been studied e.g. in [16, 18, 9].

Our main focus in the present paper lies on the equational class of convex semilattices. In this class the situation is different: we prove in Theorem 4.1 that for each two sets I,JI,J having at least two points, the relation θ\theta does not generate ker⁡Λ\ker\Lambda. This is our first main result. It emphasises that convex semilattices have a more complicated structure than their two ingredients – convex algebras and semilattices – separately. We prove this in Theorem 5.9 which is our second main result. A possible intuition is that requiring that XX is not too wild compensates for the deficiency that θ\theta does not generate ker⁡Λ\ker\Lambda.

A distinctive feature of nonlocal equations is that the local behavior of solutions is influenced by their values at arbitrarily large distances. Consequently, any local regularity estimate must necessarily involve suitable global quantities measuring the long-range interactions encoded by the operator. For the fractional heat equation, the weighted space-time integral appearing on the right-hand side of (1.1)–(1.2) is precisely the natural quantity entering the definition of local weak solutions. The main point of the present paper is that this quantity completely controls their interior regularity up to C1C^{1}-level.

Kassmann and Weidner [14] proved the local boundedness estimate of the form (1.1) for solutions to a general equation modeled on the fractional heat equation, having measurable coefficients; see also [6] in a different context. They also established Hölder continuity of solutions under the stronger assumption of L1+εL^{1+\varepsilon}-time-integrability and showed that Hölder continuity may fail under the natural L1L^{1}-time-integrability assumption. This left open the question of whether continuity itself still follows from the minimal integrability required in the weak formulation. The question was answered affirmatively in [18], where a quantitative modulus of continuity of the form (1.2) was established for solutions.

papers.title: Allen--Cahn Residual-Constrained Topology Optimization via an Augmented Lagrangian Method
papers.abstract: This paper presents a residual-constrained topology optimization framework that controls interface transition bandwidth without requiring external density filters. The steady conserved Allen--Cahn (AC) equation is formulated as an equality residual constraint and solved via a mass-weighted Augmented Lagrangian Method (ALM) coupled with the Method of Moving Asymptotes (MMA). A closed-form chemical potential projection eliminates the constant residual mode, ensuring algebraic compatibility with external volume targets. Variational sensitivity analysis reveals a symmetric-plus-rank-one Jacobian that yields matrix-free sensitivities without additional adjoint PDE solves, reducing residual sensitivity overhead to only 0.11% of the state elasticity solve time in 3D. Systematic 2D benchmarks confirm that interface bandwidth is governed intrinsically by reaction--diffusion parameters across mesh refinements. While diffuse interfaces incur a continuous compliance elevation (1.4%--12.3%), a volume-preserving 0/1 post-processing audit across 48 benchmark cases demonstrates that this gap stems primarily from intermediate-density penalization: binarized AC-ALM designs achieve equal or superior stiffness in 45 configurations (averaging 1.2% stiffer than SIMP). Simultaneously, single-node hinges and strut fragmentation are substantially suppressed compared to unregularized baselines. Three-dimensional benchmarks further demonstrate practical spatial viability for complex structures.

papers.title: From Local Skills to Long-Horizon Web Tasks: Progressive Skill Exploration for LLM Web Agents
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are driving autonomous agents toward real-world environments, with the Web emerging as one of the most representative interaction scenarios. However, training Web agents with naive exploration remains challenging: successful trajectories are rare, and the sparse terminal rewards make it difficult for agents to obtain useful feedback from failed trajectories. Inspired by skill acquisition theory, we propose Skill-Composed Progressive Exploration (SCOPE), a short-to-long learning framework for long-horizon Web agents that decomposes complex task exploration into a gradual expansion process from local skills to complete task-solving capability. Specifically, SCOPE iteratively explores around local skills: Skill Discovery extracts reusable local skills and failure experiences from historical rollouts; Skill Orchestration composes discovered skills into high-level skill chains; and Skill Expansion leverages failure experiences aligned with the current skill chain to guide the agent toward exploring new subskills. Through this process, SCOPE progressively constructs task-completing skill chains across rollouts and internalizes them into the policy parameters through agentic on-policy distillation. Extensive experiments on WebArena, WebVoyager, and WebShop show that SCOPE consistently improves exploration dynamics and achieves 3.9% to 18.6% relative gains over the strongest baselines in each setting.

papers.intro:
Large language models (LLMs) (Qwen et al., 2025; Grattafiori et al., 2024) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in language understanding, commonsense reasoning, and complex planning (Xu et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2024), laying an important foundation for autonomous agents (Wang et al., 2024). In this context, Web agents that interact with real-world websites (Zhou et al., 2024; He et al., 2024; Yao et al., preprint) have become a highly promising research direction, as they hold the potential to bridge human natural language instructions and the operational workflows of traditional computer systems. Unlike conventional single-step text generation tasks, LLM-based Web agents must continuously perceive complex and dynamically changing Web environments and make long-horizon decisions throughout interaction, which poses substantially greater technical challenges.

To improve Web agents on long-horizon tasks, recent studies have begun to explore agentic reinforcement learning paradigms (Qi et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2025). The central idea is to enable agents to interact directly with online environments, collect trajectories, and optimize their policy parameters using task rewards. However, the naive exploration strategies used in existing agent training are often ineffective: (1) Sparse Successes: long-horizon interactions and dynamic webpage states make it difficult for agents to obtain successful trajectories through naive end-to-end exploration; (2) Unexploited Failures: rewards in Web environments are typically sparse, so failed trajectories are often discarded entirely. As a result, when successful trajectories are difficult to obtain, failed attempts provide little guidance for later exploration, often leading to repetitive trial-and-error failures. This raises a key question: how can we support effective and sustained exploration for long-horizon tasks when successful trajectories are difficult to obtain through naive exploration?

Fitts and Posner’s skill acquisition theory (Fitts and Posner, 1967) provides an instructive perspective for addressing these exploration challenges: complex skills are not acquired through a single end-to-end attempt, but are progressively composed from simpler skills. This perspective naturally fits long-horizon Web tasks, which typically exhibit an inherent compositional structure. Specifically, such tasks can often be decomposed into a sequence of subtasks that are locally verifiable through environmental feedback. For example, when a human first visits a shopping website, she may find it difficult to find orders with a specific status in a single attempt. However, even if the overall task fails, environmental feedback can still reveal useful sub-skills and informative failure experiences in the trajectory, such as navigating to the order page or entering irrelevant pages. In the next attempt, the former can serve as a basis for more complex skills like order sorting, while the latter can help the agent avoid repeating ineffective actions. In this way, learning a long-horizon task is decomposed into a progressive expansion process from local skills to complete task-solving capability.

papers.title: Getting a Grip: Operating Human-Agent Software Teams Through Governed Messages
papers.abstract: Software is increasingly developed by teams in which several people direct many coding agents from different vendors. Such teams must establish who may request what from whom, which messages start work, which decisions bind, and who caused a change. We propose to govern a human-agent team through its message protocol and present yoars, a relay in which humans and agents are authenticated principals that exchange typed, addressed messages in rooms holding goals, decision rules, routing and an attributable, append-only record. This report gives the architecture, the full controlled study and the field material. In 926 controlled runs (899 analyzable), small agent teams built programs under varied room rules, some with a hostile member planting a backdoor. Revising which messages start work, bundled with limits on repeated messages, was followed by a drop in total coordination failure from 42% to 13% (p = .0063, adjusted p = .057 over nine registered tests). Instructed roles and votes did not reliably produce the intended process, and no defense inside the conversation reliably prevented the backdoor. An auditor read the records of 96 runs with a confirmed backdoor. In the 25 runs where the attacker had persuaded a teammate to write it, the auditor named the persuader in all 25, but it also flagged 24 of 40 honest runs. In a four-week field study, up to nineteen agents and two people developed a distributed system through yoars, producing 7,457 acts. Human attention and decision making emerged as the critical resource: requests waited mainly for the human-run coordinator and for approvals, while agents answered within minutes. Most governance requirements emerged from operation, and holding context dominated token cost. We report twenty-six failures of our own instruments, derive seven lessons and a checklist, and release the corpus, the redacted room ledger and the analysis scripts.

Coding agents now author hundreds of thousands of pull requests in public repositories (Li et al., 2025), and developers run several agents in parallel while struggling to coordinate and monitor them (Long et al., 2026; Dhanorkar et al., 2026). The next step is already visible in practice. Several people direct many agents, the agents come from different vendors and run in different tools, and they work on components that depend on each other. A change to one component may require coordinated actions by several agents and people, each with different responsibilities and authority.

Such a team must answer questions that a single agent never raises. Who may ask whom for what? Which messages should start an agent’s work, and which only inform it? Which decisions bind later work? Who asked for a change, and who wrote it? Prompts alone neither enforce these rules nor ensure an attributable record of compliance. Security makes these questions pressing. Agents write and ship code, and in a team of agents from different vendors a single compromised or misaligned member can plant a vulnerability that its peers accept (Wang et al., 2026; Greenblatt et al., 2024). The team must then be able to tell who introduced it and on whose request.

Software engineering research shows that coordination across team boundaries slows work (Herbsleb and Grinter, 1999; Herbsleb and Mockus, 2003) and that productivity depends on matching communication to technical dependencies (Cataldo et al., 2008). Multi-agent frameworks for software development coordinate agents inside one program through instructed roles and standard procedures (Hong et al., 2024; Qian et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2023). Their failures are dominated by misaligned agents and missing verification (Cemri et al., 2025). Agent protocols connect a client to tools (Model Context Protocol, 2025) or delegate a task to one remote agent (A2A Project, 2025).

These approaches provide parts of what such a team needs, but not a persistent, governed space in which several people and independently hosted agents exchange obligations, take decisions and leave an auditable record. It is also open whether such structure, once built into the communication layer, controls how agents behave, and what operating such a team looks like over weeks of real work. We therefore ask three questions: • RQ1 (controllability). Which rules of the shared room change how agent teams coordinate: the description of the workspace, the rules that decide which messages start work, assigned roles, or voting? • RQ2 (transparency). When one team member is hostile, do defenses inside the conversation prevent a planted security hole, and does a transparent, attributable record allow the hole and its originator to be found afterwards? • RQ3 (operation). When a heterogeneous fleet of agents and two people develops a complex system through the protocol, where does work wait, which collaboration patterns help or hurt, how do the requirements change, and where do tokens and context go?

The field study exposes a bottleneck absent from the controlled tasks: access to human attention and decisions. Component agents usually answered within minutes. Requests to coordinators in human-operated sessions, and approvals, waited longer as the team grew. In our experience as the operators, most waiting decisions were simple once seen, such as an approval or the order of two tasks, and with more stakeholders we expect this bottleneck to grow. The team responded organizationally, by adding decision makers and delegating authority. We therefore treat human attention and decision making as a central design concern for human–agent teams.

Scope of this report. This report gives four things. First, it describes the architecture of the relay and the design decisions that shaped it (Section 4). For each decision we give the problem that forced it, the alternatives we rejected where the records name them, and when it was built relative to the controlled and the field study. Second, it gives the full method of the controlled study: task material, run protocol, measures, statistics and the rules that decide whether a run counts (Section 5 and Appendix C). Third, it reports the detailed results behind each of the four findings (Section 6). These include comparisons whose results we withdrew, the results across model families, and a single-agent baseline. Fourth, it gives the field material in full (Section 7 and Appendix B). This material comprises threads from the record, the problems a coordinator logged, and an early session in which capability and instruction could not be told apart. It also includes a measurement of what context costs in a resident fleet, whose agents stay in one room for weeks. Appendix D separately describes three designs that follow from the results and have not been tested.

papers.title: A Tool in the Forward Pass: Frozen Tape Modules as Layers of a Small Language Model
papers.abstract: Calling a tool through generated text adds decoding steps, even when the computation itself is short. We study an alternative: a small neural module that runs inside a language model's forward pass. A learned writer turns hidden states into a symbolic tape, a short sequence of discrete symbols that encodes the computation. The module, trained separately and then frozen, reduces the tape to a result, and a learned reader returns that result to the model. We evaluate arithmetic and object tracking in gemma-3-1b-it. With a writer trained on labelled tapes, the layer answers all 750 items of BIG-Bench Hard's tracking shuffled objects correctly. At seven people it needs about 1/10 of the GPU kernel time of a text-tool baseline that uses the same host model and exact code, with accuracy 1.00 against 0.99. The writer can also be learned from answers alone, guided by a hand-written copying prior, but less reliably: 5 of 6 runs succeed in the 1B host and 2 of 4 in the 4B host. Two independently trained layers keep their task accuracy when attached to one model, and a learned gate keeps them silent on the tested general-text and look-alike prompts. The results support a narrow use case: a bounded computation that returns one symbol can avoid the decoding cost of a textual tool call. Extracting the right input reliably, and deciding when to act, remain the main open problems.

A language model that uses a calculator, an interpreter or a database writes the call as text, waits for the result and reads it back (Schick et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023). This interface is flexible, but generating the call requires sequential decoding steps. The returned result must also be processed by the model, although its tokens can be processed together. For a short computation inside a longer answer — arithmetic in a word problem, the state of a few objects in a story — the call can cost more than the answer.

A tool can instead sit inside the forward pass (Figure 1, a–b against c). A writer reads hidden states and hands the tool its input, the tool computes, and a reader writes the result back, all in one pass. Earlier work has shown this with exact code as the tool and a writer supervised on annotated operands (Dietz and Klakow, 2025; Dhanraj and Eliasmith, 2025), and with a symbolic network steered from hidden states (Dugan et al., 2024). We examine four questions in this setting. Can the tool be a learned module, trained on its own and frozen, so that modules can be developed and exchanged independently (RQ1, and RQ5 for several modules)? What does a tool in the forward pass save against the same tool used through text, at near-equal accuracy (RQ2)? How can the model learn what to hand the tool when nobody labels the tool’s input (RQ3)? And does the interface read wording it was never trained on (RQ4)?

A tape module is a small network that rewrites the tape step by step, each step replacing a few neighbouring cells by one, until a single cell holds the result. In arithmetic, the tape is the expression itself, such as 3+4*2, and the module evaluates it. This is the development task on which the layer was designed. In tracking shuffled objects from BIG-Bench Hard (BBH), a benchmark of hard reasoning tasks (Suzgun et al., 2023), people exchange objects and the question asks what one of them holds at the end. The tape lists who swaps with whom, followed by the person asked about (Figure 1c). We chose this task after developing the arithmetic architecture. Its benchmark items are excluded from training, but later interface decisions were informed by experiments on this task. It is therefore a transfer case study, not a completely untouched test of the final design.

The central result is a cost reduction at near-equal accuracy: the layer performs the computation during prompt processing, while the text-tool baseline generates its inputs token by token. Our contributions are: • A learned tool that the model uses (RQ1). The tool is a small network trained alone on tapes, then frozen. One check shows that it computes correctly on the tapes the model writes: replacing it by exact code of the same computation gives the same accuracy. A second shows that the answer depends on it: removing its result from the hidden state drops accuracy to chance (§5.1). • Length extrapolation (RQ1). The module applies one small rule round after round, so a longer input needs more rounds, not new parameters. Trained on up to six operators, it reaches 0.97–1.00 at twenty-four. As a layer, the model answers 1.00 at twelve operators, where the same model with adapters alone answers 0.10–0.12, and it is exact on seven exchanges after training on at most five (§5.1). • A tool call without generated tokens (RQ2). On seven-person object tracking, the layer is as accurate as the same model calling exact code through text (1.00 against 0.99) at 1/101/10 of its GPU kernel time per item at batch size one (§5.2). • Which tokens to hand the tool, learned from answers (RQ3). Without labelled tapes, rewarding tapes whose result is right trains the writer: 5 of 6 runs in gemma-3-1b-it and 2 of 4 in gemma-3-4b-it become exact. A hand-written prior supplies each token’s symbol (digits and operators, a fixed name-to-index lexicon), so reward learns which tokens to mark, for example to leave out the story’s introduction, not what the symbols mean. Gradients through the frozen module destroy the writer instead (§5.3). • Unseen wording (RQ4). On benchmark items rewritten by another language model, writers on the frozen model reach 0.87–0.96, while gemma-3-4b-it with chain of thought falls from 0.96 to 0.71 at seven people (§5.4). • Tools added independently (RQ5). It does not establish a general tool interface or an advantage of learned execution over exact code. On both tasks exact code would have served as well. The learned module is a feasibility result for tools that have no code, or that should be trained and exchanged independently.
