papers.title: Wrong Together: Shared Bias in User Simulation
papers.abstract: User simulators generate responses in place of human participants, allowing researchers to estimate the result of a study. To use these estimates before collecting human responses, researchers need a way to assess their reliability. We test whether disagreement among simulators can identify unreliable estimates of a group's response proportions and of differences between groups. We evaluate this signal using 6 language-model simulators and existing GlobalOpinionQA responses for 60 questions in 12 countries. Disagreement predicts invalidity more accurately for differences between two groups than for a single group's response proportions (AUC 0.87 versus 0.71). Errors shared by the simulators remain invisible to this signal. When such an error affects both groups equally, it cancels in the comparison, helping explain the stronger result for group differences. We test this explanation by estimating the shared bias using one set of groups and subtracting it from predictions for a separate set. This correction reduces prediction error without changing disagreement among the simulators. In a retrospective analysis, we simulate referring the 20% of group comparisons with the greatest disagreement for human assessment. Among the remaining comparisons with a conclusive validity judgment, 54.8% are judged invalid, compared with 63.7% before referral.

Researchers use language models to generate responses on behalf of study participants and estimate how a population would respond. This silicon-sampling approach (Argyle et al., 2023; Santurkar et al., 2023) can reduce the work of collecting human responses, provided the simulated estimates support the conclusions researchers would draw from human data. We focus on survey respondents, complementing work on simulated users of search, recommender, and dialogue systems (Zhou et al., 2026; Chen, 2026; Zerhoudi et al., 2026b). A survey study may estimate the proportion choosing an option in one population, which we call a level, or the difference in that proportion between two populations, a contrast.

papers.title: A hitting-time version of Kotzig's conjecture in random graphs
papers.abstract:
A family of perfect matchings on the same vertex set is said to have the Kotzig property if the union of any pair of matchings forms a Hamilton cycle. Kotzig famously conjectured that, when $n$ is even, the complete graph on $n$ vertices can be decomposed into $n-1$ perfect matchings with the Kotzig property. A closely related conjecture of Wormald states that, for fixed $d \ge 3$, whp a random $d$-regular graph contains $d$ perfect matchings with the Kotzig property. Recently, the first and third authors considered a version of these problems for the binomial random graph $G(n,p)$ and proved that, for every fixed $k$, there is $C=C(k)$ such that whp $G(n,C\log n/n)$ contains $k$ perfect matchings with the Kotzig property. We strengthen this result by showing a hitting time version: for every fixed $k$, whp the hitting time in the random graph process for finding $k$ edge-disjoint perfect matchings with the Kotzig property is the same as the hitting time for a graph with minimum degree $k$. This is a generalisation of the celebrated result of Bollob\'as and Frieze for even $n$ establishing the hitting time for $k$ edge-disjoint Hamilton cycles.
  The proof uses several ideas. We first design a coupling, via a randomised algorithm, of the random graph at the hitting time with $k$ almost-independent perfect matchings and a set of random reservoir edges, which may be of independent interest. We then prove various statistical properties of these matchings, in particular concerning the cycle structure of the $2$-factors formed by pairs of matchings. This includes a novel concept of ``shuffledness'', which we establish through a careful exposure argument and a concentration inequality for random permutations. Finally, we show that the initial $2$-factors can be merged into Hamilton cycles, using the random reservoir edges, by analysing certain P\'osa-type rotations via branching processes.

papers.title: Ferroelectric Switching in x-cut MgO-doped Thin-Film Lithium Niobate: Implications for Periodic Poling and Domain-Wall Electronics
papers.abstract: Thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) revives a mature ferroelectric as a wafer-scale platform for integrated photonics and, increasingly, for domain-wall electronics such as nonvolatile memories and memristors. Both applications rely on controlled ferroelectric switching, which is poorly understood in TFLN: periodic poling consistently requires electric fields above 30~kV/mm, far above the coercive fields of about 21~kV/mm and 4.5~kV/mm of bulk congruent and 5~mol\% MgO-doped lithium niobate, respectively. Here, we present systematic ferroelectric hysteresis measurements on x-cut, 5~mol\% MgO-doped TFLN with coplanar electrodes as used for periodic poling, combining the positive-up-negative-down (PUND) method with second-harmonic microscopy (SHM). We obtain a spontaneous polarization of $(0.72\pm0.02)$~C/m$^2$, consistent with bulk values, while the coercive field varies between 24 and 40~kV/mm with the voltage ramp rate and depends on the electrode geometry. We identify three contributions to the high coercive fields: (i) fast voltage ramps, (ii) finger electrodes, and (iii) the coplanar surface-electrode geometry. Together with bulk data, the coercive field follows a single power law of the ramp rate over five orders of magnitude, showing that the high fields are dominated by switching dynamics rather than by intrinsic thin-film properties. Moreover, the apparent internal field depends on the electrode geometry, and reverse switching leaves buried, electrically isolated domains. These results provide guidelines for scalable, fab-compatible periodic poling---one of the principal bottlenecks of TFLN device integration---and for the write and erase operation of TFLN domain-wall devices.

papers.intro:
Lithium niobate (LN) and lithium tantalate (LT) are among the most established ferroelectric single crystals. They are grown as large single crystals for more than six decades and are used on an industrial scale, e.g., in surface-acoustic-wave filters for mobile communication or for electro-optic and nonlinear optical devices [1, 2, 3]. With the commercial availability of single-crystalline thin films on insulator on wafer scale over the last decade, LN and LT have seen a remarkable revival. Thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) has revolutionized integrated photonics by combining strong ferroelectric properties with large electro-optic and nonlinear-optical coefficients, a high refractive-index contrast, and commercial wafer-scale availability [4, 5, 6, 7, 8]. This enables applications ranging from high-speed optical modulation for data communication [9, 10], terahertz and microwave-to-optical conversion [11, 12], laser-frequency conversion [13, 14], and frequency-comb generation [15] to numerous quantum-optical applications in quantum communication, quantum simulation, or quantum computing [16, 17, 18]. At the same time, TFLN is compatible with hybrid and heterogeneous integration with silicon photonics, silicon nitride, and silicon electronics [19, 20, 21], and it enables new acoustic devices at improved frequencies and decreased footprint [22].

At the same time, TFLN is compatible with hybrid and heterogeneous integration with silicon photonics, silicon nitride, and silicon electronics [19, 20, 21], and it enables new acoustic devices at improved frequencies and decreased footprint [22].

A key feature that distinguishes LN from many other photonic and electronic materials, like silicon or many III-V systems, is its ferroelectricity: the direction of the spontaneous polarization can be switched locally and nonvolatilely by an electric field. This domain engineering provides electric, reconfigurable control over all properties that depend on the sign of the polarization, such as the second-order nonlinear and electro-optic coefficients, the piezoelectric response, and surface and wall charges [23, 6]. In TFLN, two major fields of application exploit this capability: domain-wall (DW) electronics and periodic poling for nonlinear optics.

This domain engineering provides electric, reconfigurable control over all properties that depend on the sign of the polarization, such as the second-order nonlinear and electro-optic coefficients, the piezoelectric response, and surface and wall charges [23, 6]. In TFLN, two major fields of application exploit this capability: domain-wall (DW) electronics and periodic poling for nonlinear optics.

Owing to its wide band gap, single-domain LN is highly insulating, whereas charged DWs can be conductive by many orders of magnitude [24, 25, 26, 27, 28]. Because DWs can be written, moved, modified, and erased by voltage pulses, they act as reconfigurable, nanoscale conducting channels [29, 30, 31]. In LN thin films, this has enabled nonvolatile DW memories integrated on Si with high on/off ratios and endurance [32, 33], DW memristors with many conductance states and synaptic plasticity for neuromorphic computing [34, 35], tunable DW memories [36], and multilevel DW devices for in-memory computing [37]. Many of these concepts use in-plane domains written by coplanar electrodes on x- or y-cut films due to the ease of structuring by 2D lithography [32]. In all of them, the write voltage and speed, the retention, and the reliability of the erase operation are determined by the switching process, i.e., by the coercive field and its dependence on the pulse parameters, by internal fields (imprint), defects, and by the completeness of reverse switching. Here, poling needs to be understood locally to determine performance and lifetimes of DW-based devices. As for emergent ferroelectrics, such as doped HfO2 or AlScN [38, 39, 40], the quantitative understanding and control of these parameters remain key challenges. These might be well characterized for bulk LN, but remain only loosely explored for TFLN and in-plane switching with surface electrodes.

In nonlinear optics, periodic poling creates quasi-phase-matching (QPM) structures for efficient frequency conversion by compensating the phase mismatch between the interacting waves [41, 19, 8, 7]. Here, the challenge is of a different kind: domain gratings with periods of a few micrometers have to be inverted homogeneously over lengths of millimeters to centimeters, typically with short, high-field pulses far from quasi-static switching conditions, and the device performance depends directly on the shape, homogeneity and duty cycle of the domains on this large scale. Therefore, the fabrication, scaling, and understanding of periodic poling are key enabling technologies in TFLN integrated photonics [42, 43, 44, 45].

Therefore, the fabrication, scaling, and understanding of periodic poling are key enabling technologies in TFLN integrated photonics [42, 43, 44, 45].

Highly efficient QPM nonlinear-optical frequency converters are regularly reported, showing that poling processes have been developed successfully by numerous groups [65, 76, 77, 73, 8, 13, 14, 72, 78]. Nevertheless, the fabrication of periodically poled TFLN (PPTFLN) remains challenging, e.g., regarding the reproducibility and homogeneity of the domains or the realization of small poling periods. Hence, still numerous works deal with various improvements ranging from (pre-)annealing over pre-pulses to ultra-small poling periods by sidewall poling [71, 69, 72, 65]. Moreover, the poling process itself remains poorly understood from a solid-state-physics perspective, which hinders systematic, theory-guided optimization.

Moreover, the poling process itself remains poorly understood from a solid-state-physics perspective, which hinders systematic, theory-guided optimization.

The most common technique for ferroelectric domain inversion is electric-field poling via lithographically structured electrodes [79, 68], which can be scaled with standard nanofabrication techniques [79, 68, 57, 73, 80]. During periodic poling, an electric field exceeding the coercive field of the crystal is applied via the periodic electrodes, which locally inverts the spontaneous polarization [79, 68]. For bulk 5 mol% MgO-doped and congruent lithium niobate (LN), the coercive fields are reported to be about 4.5 kV/mm and 21–22 kV/mm, respectively [23, 54]. In bulk periodic poling, fields slightly above the coercive field are commonly applied, and the process is stopped before full inversion has taken place. The poling result can be monitored ex situ by domain-visualization techniques [81, 82, 83, 84, 85, 86, 87, 88], or in situ, e.g., by optical imaging [88, 89, 90] or by monitoring the poling current and stopping at a predefined charge [91]. Table 1 summarizes typical poling conditions for bulk z-cut LN and x-cut TFLN of congruent and MgO-doped composition. Since these are poling recipes rather than coercive-field measurements, the listed fields are naturally larger than the coercive fields. Strikingly, however, while for bulk z-cut crystals fields only 1–2 kV/mm above the coercive field are reported, the fields applied to TFLN regularly exceed the bulk coercive field by 20 kV/mm or more. This is especially pronounced for MgO-doped TFLN, where the applied fields exceed the bulk coercive field by a factor of six to ten.

papers.title: Second order Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle for solenoidal fields: sharp constants, optimizers and sharp stability
papers.abstract:
The second order Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle of Cazacu, Flynn and Lam is the uncertainty principle for the gradient of a function. Motivated by the question of Maz'ya on the uncertainty principle for divergence-free vector fields, solved by Cazacu, Flynn and Lam for $N=2$ and by Hamamoto for $N\ge3$, we study the second order principle for divergence-free fields $\mathbf{U}$ on $\mathbb{R}^N$. We prove that $\int|\Delta\mathbf{U}|^2dx\int|x|^2|
abla\mathbf{U}|^2dx\ge C_N^2(\int|
abla\mathbf{U}|^2dx)^2$, where $C_N=1+ rac12\sqrt{N^2+8}$ for $N\ge3$ and $C_2=1+\sqrt2$. For the velocity of an incompressible flow, $\int|
abla\mathbf{U}|^2$ and $\int|\Delta\mathbf{U}|^2$ are, up to constant factors, the enstrophy and the palinstrophy, so the inequality bounds the palinstrophy from below in terms of the enstrophy and the spatial spread of the velocity gradient. The constant $C_N$ is sharp and larger than the constant $ rac{N+2}{2}$ for general fields, and all the optimizers are explicit fields with Kummer function profiles. We also obtain the sharp constants on the poloidal and the toroidal fields of each degree. Then we prove the sharp stability of the inequality. In sum form, the deficit controls a chain of squared distances to explicit families of poloidal and toroidal fields, with all the constants sharp. In product form, we find the sharp stability constant in all dimensions. For $N\ge4$ it is $ rac12(\sqrt{N^2+4N-4}-\sqrt{N^2+8})$, and it is attained by swirling flows, the toroidal fields of degree one. On the Fourier side, the sixth order poloidal problem becomes a first order Caffarelli-Kohn-Nirenberg inequality for radial functions, and its stability follows from weighted Poincar'e inequalities with Gaussian type measures.

papers.title: Stochastic learning flow: moment equations for stochastic gradient descent at finite step size
papers.abstract: Analytical theories of learning in deep networks often assume gradient flow, discarding the finite step size and batch noise of stochastic gradient descent (SGD). Starting from the discrete update, we derive continuous-time equations for the mean and covariance of the parameter distribution under a Gaussian closure for a general stochastic learning, to first order in the learning rate $\eta$. Applying these stochastic learning flow (SLF) equations to SGD, we show that the mean descends an effective loss regularized by the covariance and loss curvature, while the covariance, unlike in stochastic differential equation approximations, becomes unstable at curvature $2/\eta$. In SGD ensembles of linear and nonlinear networks, SLF predicts learning curves and mean trajectories more accurately than gradient flow and captures the covariance dynamics, failing where the parameter distribution becomes strongly non-Gaussian. In the full-batch limit, the edge of stability corresponds to a stationary point of the coupled sharpness-covariance dynamics, recovering self-stabilization and central flow, and batch-to-batch curvature fluctuations lower this threshold under SGD.

papers.intro:
Many of the most successful analytical theories of learning in deep networks, including exact solutions for deep linear networks [41, 42] and the neural tangent kernel [18], are formulated in the continuous-time limit of gradient flow. This limit makes the tools of dynamical systems theory available, but at the cost of discarding the finite step size and the sampling noise of stochastic, iterative algorithms such as stochastic gradient descent (SGD). These are not small corrections in practice. The learning rate and batch size change which solutions training finds and how well they generalize [21, 20, 45, 30], large learning rates produce qualitatively new dynamics [28, 12], and networks trained with gradient descent typically operate at the edge of stability, where the product of the learning rate and the largest Hessian eigenvalue is close to 22, far from the regime in which gradient flow applies [8].

A widely used approach approximates SGD by a stochastic differential equation (SDE), in which gradient flow is augmented by a diffusion term matched to the covariance of the minibatch gradient noise [33, 20, 5, 29]. Higher-order versions add deterministic finite-step corrections to the drift [29, 3, 44, 24], but as expansions in the product of the learning rate and the curvature, which break down where that product is of order one. In particular, these descriptions contain no instability at curvature 2/η2/\eta, and SDE surrogates of SGD do not stabilize where SGD does [2].

Ensembles of stochastic learners have also been described directly at the level of the parameter distribution. Kramers–Moyal expansions of the master equation for on-line learning at constant learning rate have long been used to describe the parameter distribution of stochastic learners, focusing on Fokker–Planck dynamics and their equilibria [26] or on moment equations with random update times [16]. Working instead from the discrete update, Yaida [48] derived exact fluctuation–dissipation relations at stationarity, and Liu et al. What is missing is a continuous-time description of the parameter distribution that retains the deterministic effects of finite step size and the stochastic effects of minibatch sampling together, without expanding in the product of learning rate and curvature.

papers.title: Movable Antenna-Assisted Secret Key Generation over Temporally Correlated Channels
papers.abstract: Physical-layer key generation (PLKG) exploits reciprocal channel dynamics to generate symmetric keys, addressing the key distribution problem in wireless communications. However, strong temporal correlation in slow-fading environments limits fresh randomness and results in low key generation rates. Movable antennas (MAs) introduce spatial degrees of freedom through antenna repositioning, providing a new approach to addressing the limitation. This paper investigates MA-assisted PLKG over temporally correlated channels. A first-order Gauss-Markov process is utilized to characterize the temporal correlation of multipath gains. We characterize the full-sequence mutual information (MI) over temporally correlated channels. For fixed antenna positions and beamforming, we establish a finite-horizon approximation error bound that vanishes as both effective signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) increase. We derive a closed-form expression for the one-step conditional MI and adopt it as a tractable key-information metric. A nonconvex problem is formulated to jointly optimize antenna positions and per-slot beamforming under transmit-power and minimum-spacing constraints. We develop an alternating optimization algorithm, combining an exact principal-eigenvector beamforming solution with feasible SCA-based projected gradient position updates. Simulation results demonstrate that the MA-assisted scheme outperforms the fixed-position antenna baseline. At a high temporal correlation coefficient, position optimization achieves approximately $51\%$ higher rates than fixed antennas. Joint position and beamforming optimization provides a further $106\%$ gain over position optimization alone, demonstrating more pronounced gains under strong temporal correlation.
papers.intro:
With the evolution toward beyond-fifth-generation (B5G) and sixth-generation (6G) networks, future wireless systems are expected to support massive connectivity [1]. The growing number of devices, limited radio resources, and heterogeneous network conditions motivate lightweight security mechanisms [2]. Conventional upper-layer cryptographic mechanisms typically rely on computational hardness and pre-established long-term secret keys, which can become inefficient or impractical in highly dynamic wireless environments [3]. In particular, limited computational capabilities, frequent topology variations, and the absence of centralized key-management infrastructure pose fundamental challenges to secure and timely key distribution for emerging wireless devices.

In particular, limited computational capabilities, frequent topology variations, and the absence of centralized key-management infrastructure pose fundamental challenges to secure and timely key distribution for emerging wireless devices.

Physical-layer secret key generation (PLKG) provides a promising alternative by exploiting reciprocal wireless channels to establish symmetric keys [4, 5, 6]. By exchanging pilots within a channel coherence interval, legitimate terminals obtain correlated observations of the same propagation channel, although receiver noise introduces discrepancies between their estimates. PLKG derives secret material from the shared propagation environment rather than pre-distributed keys, making it attractive for resource-constrained and latency-sensitive devices [7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12]. A typical PLKG procedure consists of reciprocal channel probing, quantization, information reconciliation, and privacy amplification [13, 14, 15]. Quantization converts channel measurements into bit sequences, reconciliation corrects disagreements, and privacy amplification compresses the reconciled bits to limit information available to an eavesdropper, including leakage from public reconciliation. The resulting key material depends on both the quality of the reciprocal observations and the channel randomness available for extraction.

From an information-theoretic perspective, the achievable secret key rate (SKR) depends on the common randomness shared by the legitimate terminals and the information available to an eavesdropper, and is closely related to the mutual information (MI) between their channel observations [16, 17, 18]. However, in slowly varying channels, successive probes can be strongly correlated, reducing the temporal innovation available for each new key segment and lowering the SKR [19, 20]. This limitation is particularly severe when the channel remains static or quasi-static over the coherence interval: although the legitimate terminals can still obtain high-quality observations, the amount of fresh randomness is limited.

To improve the randomness available for PLKG, existing studies have considered reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RISs) and precoding optimization in massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems [21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26]. RIS-based designs can require deploying and controlling additional reflecting elements, while precoding shapes observations using a fixed array geometry. Depending on the architecture, additional hardware, control, or energy overhead accompanies these approaches. This motivates a complementary degree of freedom that directly adjusts the spatial channel response at the legitimate transmitter without relying on additional reflecting infrastructure.

Movable antenna (MA) technology provides this degree of freedom [27]. Unlike fixed-position antenna (FPA) arrays, MA arrays allow element locations to be adjusted within a prescribed region, making antenna position an additional design variable [28, 29, 30]. Under the field-response model, antenna coordinates alter the phases of resolvable multipath components and thereby reshape the spatial channel response and correlation structure [31, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36]. Even when propagation angles and path-gain statistics remain unchanged over the movable region, different layouts produce different combinations of the multipath components at the antenna elements. Position selection consequently determines the spatial observations available to the array, while beamforming controls how these observations are combined. Their joint design allows the effective channel to be adjusted through both antenna geometry and signal processing.

MA reconfiguration has been studied in secure transmission [37, 38, 39, 40, 41, 42], covert communication [43, 44], and integrated sensing and communication [45, 46]. For PLKG, position selection offers a means to improve the observation of available channel fluctuations, even if the selected layout remains fixed during probing. The relevant information then depends on both the current observation quality and its dependence on earlier probes. In [47], random antenna repositioning introduces additional randomness in quasi-static environments with fixed propagation parameters. However, the setting does not address temporally evolving path gains or the interaction with joint multi-antenna position and beamforming optimization. A configuration that maximizes the MI in one slot does not necessarily maximize the additional shared information available in the next slot. Temporal correlation creates dependence between consecutive observation pairs. Accounting for the preceding observations is necessary to evaluate the additional shared information provided by the next probe. Addressing the problem involves two coupled technical challenges. The first challenge is to derive a tractable conditional MI expression that accounts for temporal dependence and to quantify its approximation error relative to the full-sequence joint MI. Second, antenna positions and consecutive-slot beamforming jointly determine both the current channel power and the component predictable from earlier observations. This coupling produces a nonconvex objective, while minimum-spacing constraints further restrict feasible position updates.

papers.title: JABER: Sequential Quality Control for Human-AI Data Annotation under Shared Bias
papers.abstract: High-quality annotations are essential for training and evaluating artificial intelligence (AI) systems. Quality control (QC) often acquires additional human or AI judgments before accepting a label. Nevertheless, shared biases can cause correlated judgments, leading conventional methods to mistake repeated agreement for independent evidence of correctness. To address this challenge, we propose JABER (Joint Alias-Preserving Belief for Evidence Routing), a bias-aware sequential QC framework that maintains a joint Bayesian posterior over label correctness and shared biases to guide evidence acquisition and termination decisions. Building on this posterior, we develop a finite-horizon algorithm that selects evidence-acquisition and termination actions to minimize expected QC loss under resource constraints. Our theoretical analysis shows that conditional-independence updating can become arbitrarily confident in an incorrect label under persistent shared bias. We further identify when repeated inspections cannot distinguish a correct label from an incorrect label supported by shared bias, when obtaining a new label can resolve this ambiguity, and why modeling the dependence between label correctness and shared bias can be necessary for QC decisions. Our experiments show that JABER reduces expected QC loss by an average of 4.65% compared with a method maintaining separate label correctness and bias probabilities when shared bias makes repeated inspections unreliable. Further, JABER's finite-horizon planning, which evaluates outcomes of successive QC actions, reduces expected QC loss by an average of 10.05% compared with a one-step lookahead method. In real-API experiments on FEVER, JABER achieves zero labeling errors while reducing QC costs by 2.67% and 16.99% compared with marginal-based belief modeling and one-step lookahead methods, respectively.

papers.intro:
THE increasing deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) in high-stakes applications has made reliable data annotation essential. Modern annotation pipelines increasingly combine human annotators, large language model (LLM) labelers, and LLM-as-a-judge systems for dataset construction, preference assessment, and model evaluation [1, 2, 3]. However, such human–AI collaboration can introduce shared biases that lead to correlated judgments, making it difficult for quality control (QC) mechanisms to distinguish independent evidence of label correctness from agreement driven by common biases. This challenge is particularly pronounced in LLM-assisted annotation, as evaluators may exhibit correlated judgments due to shared pretraining data, model families, prompts, or evaluation criteria. Similarly, human annotators may exhibit correlated judgments when exposed to common interfaces and task contexts. Such dependencies can be further amplified by task-level cues, including response length, presentation order, and model provenance. Consequently, high agreement among annotators may reflect shared biases rather than independent evidence of label correctness [4, 5, 6], effectively reducing the number of independent judgments [7, 8].

Modern annotation pipelines increasingly combine human annotators, large language model (LLM) labelers, and LLM-as-a-judge systems for dataset construction, preference assessment, and model evaluation [1, 2, 3]. However, such human–AI collaboration can introduce shared biases that lead to correlated judgments, making it difficult for quality control (QC) mechanisms to distinguish independent evidence of label correctness from agreement driven by common biases. This challenge is particularly pronounced in LLM-assisted annotation, as evaluators may exhibit correlated judgments due to shared pretraining data, model families, prompts, or evaluation criteria. Similarly, human annotators may exhibit correlated judgments when exposed to common interfaces and task contexts. Such dependencies can be further amplified by task-level cues, including response length, presentation order, and model provenance. Consequently, high agreement among annotators may reflect shared biases rather than independent evidence of label correctness [4, 5, 6], effectively reducing the number of independent judgments [7, 8].

Moreover, human and AI errors are not necessarily complementary [3], making correlated judgments particularly problematic in sequential QC. For instance, when multiple annotators agree on a label because of a shared bias, conventional methods that assume independent judgments may mistakenly interpret this agreement as strong evidence of correctness. As a result, the system may become overly confident and accept an incorrect label. Although existing dependence-aware methods account for such correlations when combining a fixed set of judgments [5, 4], post-annotation QC introduces an additional challenge: deciding what to do after each new judgment. Specifically, the system must determine whether to accept the current label, request another inspection, obtain a replacement label, seek arbitration, or leave the task unresolved. Since these actions differ in cost, reliability, and sensitivity to shared bias, choosing the best action requires considering both the evidence already collected and the potential value of acquiring further evidence. Thus, accounting for shared bias is essential not only for accurately assessing label correctness but also for determining when and how to continue QC.

For instance, when multiple annotators agree on a label because of a shared bias, conventional methods that assume independent judgments may mistakenly interpret this agreement as strong evidence of correctness. As a result, the system may become overly confident and accept an incorrect label. Although existing dependence-aware methods account for such correlations when combining a fixed set of judgments [5, 4], post-annotation QC introduces an additional challenge: deciding what to do after each new judgment. Specifically, the system must determine whether to accept the current label, request another inspection, obtain a replacement label, seek arbitration, or leave the task unresolved. Since these actions differ in cost, reliability, and sensitivity to shared bias, choosing the best action requires considering both the evidence already collected and the potential value of acquiring further evidence. Thus, accounting for shared bias is essential not only for accurately assessing label correctness but also for determining when and how to continue QC.

• RQ1: How should evidence from human and AI annotators be evaluated during QC when agreement on a label may result from shared bias rather than independent support for its correctness? However, repeated agreement can reflect either label correctness or a persistent bias favoring an incorrect label. When a QC action produces identical observation probabilities under these two explanations, the action cannot distinguish between them, a phenomenon known as aliasing.

Existing methods account for correlations among human and AI judgments when combining multiple annotations to estimate label correctness [5, 4]. However, repeated agreement can reflect either label correctness or a persistent bias favoring an incorrect label. When a QC action produces identical observation probabilities under these two explanations, the action cannot distinguish between them, a phenomenon known as aliasing.

• RQ2: When should sequential annotation QC stop collecting additional judgments and instead use a more informative evidence source to resolve uncertainty about label correctness? Collecting additional judgments is useful only when they provide new information about whether the current label is correct. However, under persistent shared bias, repeated reviews of the same label may produce similar judgments regardless of its actual correctness, making further inspections ineffective at resolving uncertainty. In such cases, the system may benefit from switching to a different QC action.

Choosing the best QC action requires considering not only its immediate cost and outcome but also how it may improve subsequent decisions. The remaining budget and decision steps also constrain which follow-up actions remain available.

papers.title: Defining Autonomous Weapon Systems: A schematic framework for refined purpose-driven definitions
papers.abstract: The literature on autonomous weapon systems (AWS) includes many proposed definitions for these (types of) systems, with core disagreements between scholars, governments, and international regulatory bodies. In this article, we present and critique prevailing (classes of) definitions, arguing that what is needed is not a singular definition, but rather a definitional framework which allows one to classify different sorts of AWS within the same conceptual family. Recognizing we cannot foresee all future AWS, we show how variations on a broadly accepted definition can be used to produce a definitional schema which can be easily modified in order to classify various concepts belonging to the class of AWS.

As of writing this, it has been over a decade since regulatory discussions around autonomous weapon systems (AWS) began in Geneva under the auspices of the United Nations Convention on Conventional Weapons (CCW),11 1 Fully, the “Convention on Prohibitions or Restrictions on the Use of Certain Conventional Weapons Which May be Deemed to be Excessively Injurious or to Have Indiscriminate Effects”. For a brief historical overview of the work at the CCW, see https://dig.watch/processes/gge-laws, accessed July 31, 2026. For the rolling text from those efforts, see Group of Governmental Experts on Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems (2025). and ethical discussions have been ongoing far longer.22 2 Early discussion of ethical and doctrinal aspects of autonomous weapons can be found in, e.g., Guetlein (2005); Sharkey (2007); Sharkey (2008); Sparrow (2007); Lin et al. (2008). In that time, many definitions of AWS have been put forward,33 3 E.g., Roff (2013), pp. 353–354; International Committee of the Red Cross (2014), p. 5; Williams (2015); Boothby (2016), pp. 247–257; Caron (2020); International Committee of the Red Cross (2021b), p. 1; Taddeo and Blanchard (2022); US Department of Defense (2023), p. 21. See Wood (2023b); Pacholska (2024) for broader discussion of definitions and definitional worries. and while some have gained wider acceptance, there is still no broadly agreed view. Moreover, the range of existing definitions all admit weaknesses in need of addressing. This article seeks to remedy this by developing not a singular definition of AWS, but rather a conceptual definitional framework for defining specific (types of) autonomous systems used in various military roles. In doing so, the article pays heed to a core reality of autonomy in systems, namely that it can be leveraged for a variety of purposes, with a variety of technical, operational, legal, and ethical challenges, and with various attendant technical, operational, legal, and ethical approaches for mitigating those challenges.44 4 Scharre (2023), p. 3; Wood et al. (2026). Thus, given the need for specificity, the article builds toward a modular definitional schema where scholars, policy-makers, and defense professionals can “plug in” definitional components as needed, befitting both the system they are considering and their definitional needs. This latter concern is of relevance given that not all definitions serve the same purpose, and in a domain as politically charged and with as significant of consequences as this, being able to craft purpose-built definitions for specific applications holds immense value.

To develop these arguments, the article begins (Section 2) by canvassing general points on definitions, laying out the methodological assumptions guiding this work and tying these to the underlying purpose of the article. With these in place, Section 3 then presents and critiques two strands of definition one can find in the literature from scholars, states, and international bodies, what we call the “standard view” and the “demanding view”. Building from these critiques, Section 4 lays out base definitions of both “autonomous systems” and “autonomous weapon systems”, stressing that these are base definitions. That is, they are not to be treated as complete, as demarcating every relevant feature of some system, or as not needing further refinement. Before moving onto the arguments themselves though, there are two preliminary points to be addressed. First, it is worth clarifying and stressing at the outset that the purpose of this work is to add clarity to the ongoing debates surrounding autonomous (weapon) systems and to reduce the risks of scholars and practitioners “talking past one another”. papers.title: Evolving Explanations: Complexity-Adaptive Refinement of Faithful Explanations for Symbolic Regression
papers.abstract: Natural-language explanations generated by large language models (LLMs) for machine learning models often seem fluent but are not necessarily faithful to the underlying model. We formalize this mismatch as a faithfulness gap and propose a complexity-adaptive refinement framework for symbolic regression that iteratively generates and validates explanations until numerical agreement with the target expression is achieved. The approach follows a two-stage pipeline: an explainer LLM produces textual descriptions at increasing levels of detail, while an independent validator LLM extracts a symbolic expression that is compared against the original model. This process is framed as a discrete search over explanation space, where complexity is minimized subject to a faithfulness constraint. We evaluate the method on real-world and synthetic datasets, with a total of 250 runs across varying model complexities. The explanation refinement loop achieves an overall pass rate of 84.0%, with most explanations converging at low complexity levels and only a small fraction requiring detailed descriptions. Our results demonstrate that faithful explanations can be obtained with minimal necessary complexity by explicitly closing the explanation loop through symbolic validation.

Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely used to generate text for various tasks, including explanations of machine learning (ML) models [14, 3]. Despite the widespread use of LLMs for explanation generation, their faithfulness to the underlying model is rarely verified. An unfaithful explanation is worse than no explanation: it can cause a domain expert to trust or reject a model for the wrong reasons, violating the core purpose of explainability [12]. This is particularly problematic for symbolic regression (SR) models. Unlike black-box models, SR produces an explicit mathematical expression that can in principle be explained precisely, yet LLMs tend to paraphrase, round coefficients, or omit interaction terms, producing explanations that sound plausible but do not faithfully reflect the discovered formula [1].

papers.title: Supporting Orthographic Recall of Chinese Characters through Self-Generated Compositional Mnemonic Stories: A Mixed-Methods Pilot Study
papers.abstract: Mnemonic studies on Chinese characters have mostly tested provided mnemonics against writing outcomes and self-generated mnemonics against meaning recall; whether writing one's own component-based story helps learners write the character has received little attention. I present Nuome, a tool that shows a character's component decomposition next to an editor in which learners write their own story, with live checks on whether the story covers every component and the character's meaning. In a within-subjects pilot, eight L2 learners each learned four self-chosen characters with the story builder and four with a read-only panel showing the same decomposition, with identical writing practice. Descriptively, partial-credit written-recall scores favoured the story builder by 18.8 percentage points immediately (N = 8) and 17.9 points after two days (N = 7); mean study time per character was 1.69 times as long (n = 6); usability was high (SUS 88.1). Interviews yielded three themes: participants felt that composing a story made them attend to components; knowing the components is not the same as being able to write them; and characters differ in how well they suit a story.

papers.title: Vision-based Sensing of Urban Environment using Hardware-Software co-design at Scale
papers.abstract: Urban environmental monitoring is crucial for climate-adaptive cities, yet current approaches rely heavily on human inspection, overhead remote sensing, or limited terrestrial RGB imagery, thereby lacking comprehensive multispectral perspectives at street level. To bridge this gap, this paper introduces UrbanScapes, an adaptable and flexible hardware-software co-design platform for large-scale, vision-based sensing of urban environments. Built on a modular architecture, UrbanScapes seamlessly integrates multispectral imaging channels, including Red, Green, Blue (RGB), Near-Infrared, and Thermal, to capture multispectral street-level imagery. The system is designed for both opportunistic deployment on bicycles, vehicles, or pedestrians and targeted deployments on municipal fleets, ensuring high spatio-temporal scalability without requiring hardware redesigns. Crucially, the platform utilizes on-device deep learning models to automatically remove personally identifiable information (PII) at the edge, addressing privacy concerns inherent in street-level data collection. By combining this multispectral street-level imagery with overhead multispectral remote sensing imagery, UrbanScapes enables scalable calculation of physics-based environmental indices, providing a foundational tool for advanced citywide analysis.

papers.intro:
Urban environmental monitoring is vital for the development of climate-resilient cities. Existing approaches, largely comprising remote sensing imagery and manual human inspections, are limited to overhead views and non-scalable, respectively. In this work, we demonstrate an integrated hardware-software platform, UrbanScapes, for opportunistic sensing to collect multispectral street level data. This data can be combined with overhead remote sensing imagery, enabling comprehensive monitoring of urban environmental parameters at city-wide scales. Specifically, the UrbanScapes hardware comprises Red, Green, and Blue (RGB), near-infrared, and thermal imaging sensors that collect multispectral street-level imagery synchronously at high spatial and temporal resolutions. Data quality is ensured by utilizing similar imaging channels available in overhead remote sensing imagery, which is later processed using computer vision-based deep learning models to understand and quantify various urban environmental parameters. For instance, in the urban city context, one can identify different building façade materials using near-infrared channels, analyze urban greenery using a combination of vision and near-infrared channels or analyze energy leakage from building façades using thermal channels. The device is designed for flexible deployment via magnets on bikes, cars, and buses, and can also be carried by humans. Thus, it is suitable both for participatory citizen-science based sensing and opportunistic municipal sensing. Further, all personally identifiable information (PII) is removed on-device using a deep learning model. Hence, enabling comprehensive analysis of urban environmental parameters at scale supported by explainable physics-based indices. In this paper, we highlight the design of the system, architecture of the system, and demonstrate capabilities possible from multispectral street-level data collected by this device. The device was deployed in real-world across 4 urban areas inside the Netherlands collecting synchronized multi-spectral imagery, generating a dataset of 17k street-level images, and available openly as the Spectrascapes dataset [1].

papers.title: Analog and hybrid computing in the 21st century
papers.abstract: Analog computers solve problems through physical representations of mathematical variables and relations, often using the dynamics of electronic circuits and their associated signals. Many analog computers directly represent nonlinear dynamical systems; they encode their solutions in the signals that they generate. Although most modern scientific computing relies on digital architectures with inherently discrete-valued representations and algorithmic approaches, the design constraints of such architectures increasingly limit both performance and energy efficiency. Analog systems can circumvent some of these constraints; they execute specific computations very efficiently by mapping them directly onto physical processes using smaller and simpler computing elements than the ones in digital architectures. In this article, we provide an interdisciplinary perspective on modern analog and hybrid (i.e., analog-digital) computing. We discuss how modern scientific computing workflows can leverage analog approaches in various applications, such as in simulating dynamical systems, performing optimization, and enabling more energy-efficient implementations of artificial intelligence.

What is an analog computer, and how does it differ from our now-ubiquitous digital computers? A digital computer, which is more aptly called a “stored-program digital computer”, is a machine with a fixed internal structure that solves problems by executing sequences of simple instructions that operate on data that is represented digitally using binary values.[175] This concept is incredibly powerful, as such a machine can carry out any computation that is describable by an algorithm if there are sufficient time and memory resources. It rests on both Turing’s universal-machine construction and the Church–Turing thesis, which identifies algorithmic solvability with computability by a Turing machine.[222, 49] We will return to this thesis and to its analog counterpart in Sec. II.

In the context of integration density, the term “technology node” historically referred approximately to a characteristic feature size that is measured in nanometers (nm). However, semiconductor manufacturers now use node names such as “5 nm” and “2 nm”, even though these numbers no longer correspond directly to any specific physical dimensions of underlying integrated circuits.[15] As critical device and interconnect dimensions approach the nanometer regime, heat dissipation and quantum effects impose increasingly severe constraints. Accordingly, continued increases in integration density will become both more difficult and more costly.

Clock frequencies of digital computers have essentially stalled in the few-gigahertz (GHz) range over the last two decades, primarily because the energy of digital circuits increases faster than linearly with clock frequencies.[247] In practice, doubling the clock rate from 3 GHz to 6 GHz typically results in more than twice the power consumption. This is not only inefficient but also a technological challenge, as the electrical power that is consumed by a chip is converted into heat, which then must be dissipated from a rather small chip area.[72, 106]

The current demand for computing power, which is driven in part by the rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI), is leading to increasingly large data centers with substantial energy consumption. This has sparked discussions about recommissioning old nuclear power plants or building new nuclear reactors that are dedicated to individual data centers.[97] Although these are interesting from a technological point of view, their widespread deployment entails substantial economic and environmental challenges.[189] Accordingly, to satisfy current and future demand for computing power, it is necessary to explore different computational paradigms beyond the usual digital computing. One of these paradigms is “analog computing”, which is the focus of our perspective article.

An analog computer differs fundamentally from a digital computer. First, in an analog computer, values are typically not represented by binary digits; instead, they are encoded by magnitudes of physical processes (e.g., by voltages or currents). Second, an analog computer consists of a potentially large number of computing elements, which each implement a specific basic mathematical operation (such as summation, multiplication, and time integration). One then connects these computing elements with each other, thereby implementing an electronic model (i.e., an ‘‘analogue’’) of a problem that one seeks to solve. This model-based approach to computing gave rise to the name ‘‘analog computing".11 1 Unfortunately, many people perceive the notion of “analog computing” as being old-school, slow, or otherwise suboptimal. Accordingly, it may be worthwhile to abandon the name “analog computer” for future discussions and replace it by terms such as “natural computing” or “physical computing”.

What is it that actually makes analog computing a notion of computing? What makes it similar enough to the digital-computing paradigm to count as computation, yet different enough to make it a distinct type of computation? In other words, what is computation in general, such that digital computing is one type and analog computing is another type?22 2 We are going to entirely avoid discussing quantum computing in this context. The answer that seems to best fit this perspective is that computation involves the following items: • physical representations or variables (which can represent physical systems or mathematical systems), which • are manipulated by physical mechanisms • and change the values of those representations or variables by manipulating the physical properties that are responsible for representing them. Digital computers use digital representations, which are manipulated by electronic mechanisms in terms of discrete voltages that are controlled by a sequentially executed algorithm. Analog computers do not employ such algorithms; instead, they rely on setting up a model. Electronic analog computers are mechanisms that manipulate continuous representations in terms of voltages. 33 3 See Ref. 145 for a philosophical account of analog computing.

papers.title: A Representation Theorem for Fractional Viscoelastic Networks
papers.abstract: We prove a representation theorem for finite series-parallel viscoelastic networks composed of springs and spring-pots of a common order $0<\alpha<1$. The associated complex shear modulus, expressed in an appropriately chosen auxiliary variable, is rational and admits a finite partial-fraction representation with simple poles on the negative real axis and negative residues. Its reciprocal admits an analogous representation with positive residues and a possible additional pole at the origin. Inverting the corresponding Laplace transforms gives finite fractional Prony representations of the relaxation modulus and creep compliance with non-negative amplitudes. These results provide a rigorous proof of a corrected version of the Mainardi-Spada conjecture for this network class. A six-element network illustrates the construction.

papers.title: Statistical mechanics of spontaneous behavior
papers.abstract: Why do a few behaviors fill most of an animal's time? The usual answer is that these behaviors are started more often, because learning and reinforcement favor them. Here we show that how long a behavior lasts can, by itself, explain much of what is observed. We consider a system that runs until it meets a constraint, such as a wall, and then resets. The fraction of time it spends in each behavior then follows the Boltzmann law, and the partition function is the mean time between resets. The four laws of thermodynamics follow as theorems from four postulates, and critical points that act as bottlenecks become the most occupied states. In 47 multi-day recordings of fruit flies, the dominant behavior accounts for only $13\%$ of bout starts yet fills $49\%$ of the time, and its typical duration identifies the individual fly. These results lay the groundwork for a statistical mechanics of behavior.

papers.title: The Tower of Babel in artificial intelligence: who should speak, and when it pays to listen
papers.abstract: Two machines can each recognize an object well and still fail together. We study classifiers that see different parts of one object and send short messages to a receiver that identifies its class. Coordination asks how to design messages together; cooperation asks whether the team outperforms one sender given the whole budget. On three digit datasets, messages designed together beat messages designed apart by 18.07 to 22.68 percentage points on average with two-bit messages, with gains in all 24 configurations. A fixed agreement, you report the row and I the column, recovers about half this gain, with only the receiver learned. Senders that draw the same distinctions waste a narrow vocabulary, and senders whose distinctions cross multiply it. A team has no more possible messages than one sender with the same budget, so a partner must bring evidence the first lacks. A solvable model shows individual statistics alone cannot determine whether a partnership helps. On MNIST digits, six shared bits remove 49.54 percent of the strongest tested solo's errors on average. Paired measurements correctly predicted most sensor teams would reduce average accuracy on new participants. Who should speak is a property of the pair, and must be measured in pairs.

papers.intro:
In the old story, the tower of Babel is abandoned when its builders can no longer understand one another. Every collective that must pool what its members know meets a version of that difficulty. Animal groups combine observations made by different individuals, and human teams combine abilities that no member has in full [1, 2]. What a group achieves depends on how its members’ information is used, as well as on how much each member holds [3]. The same question arises in teams of artificial systems. Frameworks assemble teams of language-model agents [4], and exchanges between agents improve answers on some reasoning tasks [5]. Yet multi-agent systems fail in characteristic ways [6], a single agent with the same budget often matches or beats the team [7], and human–machine teams often perform below their stronger member [8].

Yet multi-agent systems fail in characteristic ways [6], a single agent with the same budget often matches or beats the team [7], and human–machine teams often perform below their stronger member [8].

The members of such a collective hold private representations shaped by distinct views and histories [9]. Even when members establish common ground on the meanings of task outcomes [10, 11], a fundamental bottleneck remains. Cells within an organism and animals in a group coordinate through compressed signals [12, 13], just as sensors, neural modules, and AI agents must exchange information under strict limits on bandwidth, time, or token budgets [7, 14, 15, 16, 17]. A narrow channel that carries only a few bits forces each member to compress what it knows into coarse categories, and forces the group to decide whether sharing the channel beats giving the entire budget to one capable speaker.

We treat it as a game of common interest. The members share one goal and hold private information and private codes, as in the signalling games of Lewis and the team problems of Marschak and Radner [18, 19, 20]. Without any conflict of interest, two problems remain. One is coordination. Which convention should divide the vocabulary between the senders, so that a receiver can use their messages together? The other is cooperation in the sense of resources. Is a partner’s share of the channel worth more than the same bits in the hands of one capable member? In this game, cooperation carries no dilemma: the senders share a goal, and the cost of a partner is the share of the channel it takes. Decentralized detection designs the reports of several sensors jointly and, under a shared rate, has asked how many identical sensors should speak and with how many bits each [21, 22, 23, 24, 25]. Coding for computing preserves the information that one answer needs [26, 27], and task-oriented and emergent communication extend both to learned systems [16, 28, 15, 29]. For systems learned from data, we must make this decision from samples of senders that may differ substantially. We ask how to determine, before deployment, whether sharing the budget improves on giving it to one capable sender.

To isolate the mechanics of bandwidth sharing from the confounders of free-text generation and prompt heuristics, we study communication through controlled discrete bottlenecks. Classifiers and supervised readouts of frozen language and vision models observe different views of the same object and send short bit-limited messages to a receiver that predicts the object’s class. Holding the encoders’ underlying representations fixed while varying only their message rules and bit allocations separates communication design from individual capability. Alongside an exactly solvable model of synergistic evidence, we evaluate teams across handwritten digits, hierarchical text abstracts, tabular morphology, multi-modal bird and research-paper archives, and wearable sensor recordings.

We find a sharp divergence between learning to speak together and beating a solo speaker. Coordination is large and cheap, with capacity limits set by combinatorial counting: at representative budgets, joint code design raises team accuracy by 18 to 39 percentage points across domains, and on the digit datasets a data-blind convention recovers roughly half of that improvement without learning the encoders. Yet large coordination gains routinely mask cooperation failures. In our solvable model, identical individual statistics can make partnership either useless or error-free depending on how observations couple. Empirically, sharing the bit budget beats the strongest tested equal-budget solo on complementary digit views—eliminating 49.54% of solo errors on average at six total bits on split MNIST digits—while often losing to or tying the solo on text halves, tabular features, and wearable sensors despite massive coordination gains. Furthermore, predictions of team benefit derived from separate member statistics mistakenly approve partnerships on text and dry-bean tasks, whereas paired calibration on the same objects correctly predicts whether sensor teams improve or degrade average performance on new participants. Who should speak is an irreducible property of the pair, and we identify the comparisons and measurements needed to assess it.

papers.title: Quantizing Recurrent Language Models Is Easier Than You Think
papers.abstract: Linear recurrences are becoming an increasingly common building block in large language models, replacing the growing KV cache of softmax attention with a fixed-size recurrent state that enables efficient decoding. However, the quantization stack has largely been developed around softmax Transformers, whose numerical properties and inference state differ from those of recurrent models. Our goal is to understand these differences and study the design space of quantization methods for recurrent models. In our analysis, we differentiate between two targets. First, extra-state quantization concerns weights and activations outside the recurrent state, whose distributions are shaped indirectly by the sequence mixer during training. In controlled 1.3B parameter models, we find that decayed recurrences develop weaker residual outlier channels than softmax attention and are therefore easier to quantize without incoherence processing. Second, intra-state quantization concerns the recurrent state itself during decode, where repeated updates create a different numerical problem from KV cache quantization. We instantiate our findings as LoReS, a state quantization pipeline combining value-axis scale grouping to match output channel magnitude, decay-based mixed-precision to protect slowly decaying heads or channels, and stochastic rounding to limit error accumulation under repeated requantization. Across Qwen-3.5 9B, Nemotron-H 8B, and Kimi-Linear 48B-A3B, LoReS supports robust 8-bit state quantization and lower effective precision on shorter decode horizons. We implement LoReS in vLLM and demonstrate end-to-end decode speedups.

Softmax attention has shaped the architecture of large language models, as well as the deployment stack built around them. This is particularly true for post-training quantization (PTQ). A large body of prior work investigates quantization of the weights and activations of softmax Transformers (Frantar et al., 2022; Xiao et al., 2023; Ashkboos et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025), while a complementary line studies quantization of the key-value cache that grows during autoregressive generation (Liu et al., 2024; Hooper et al., 2024; Duanmu et al., 2024).

Linear attention and state-space models replace softmax attention with linear recurrences (Katharopoulos et al., 2020; Dao and Gu, 2024; Yang et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025; Tumma et al., 2026a), and recent large-scale hybrid models interleave recurrent and softmax layers within the same architecture (Blakeman et al., 2025; Team et al., 2025; Qwen Team, 2026). As these hybrid models become increasingly common, the inference stack developed for softmax Transformers must be adapted accordingly.

Compared with softmax attention, however, the behavior of recurrent language models under quantization remains poorly understood. Existing work has begun to adapt quantization to recurrent architectures (Chiang et al., 2025b; Chiang et al., 2025a; Xu et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2026; Chandiramani et al., 2026), but has focused on particular architectures and quantization targets. In this work, we instead ask the more general question: how does replacing softmax attention with a linear recurrent sequence mixer change the quantization problem? We argue that this replacement matters along two distinct axes. First, the choice of sequence mixer changes the training dynamics of the model and therefore the distributions of the weights and activations learned throughout the network. We refer to quantization of these tensors as extra-state weight/activation (W/A) quantization. Second, softmax attention and recurrent mixers maintain fundamentally different objects during inference. Softmax attention stores a growing cache of keys and values, whereas a recurrent mixer repeatedly updates a fixed-size state in place. We refer to quantization of this object as (intra-)state quantization. Together, these two settings separate the implicit effect of the sequence mixer on the rest of the model from the explicit effect of quantizing the mixer state itself. Our main contributions can be summarized as follows: • For extra-state W/A quantization, we show that decayed linear recurrences develop substantially weaker residual outlier channels than softmax attention, making them more robust to W/A quantization before incoherence processing. We instantiate our findings as LoReS (Low-bit Recurrent State), combining value-axis grouping, stochastic rounding and decay-based mixed precision for integer state quantization. • We implement LoReS in vLLM, demonstrating end-to-end decode speedups at scale.

papers.title: Omni-iEEG Planner: an open-source Python platform integrating multimodal neuroimaging and intracranial EEG data for epilepsy surgery research
papers.abstract: Multimodal intracranial EEG (iEEG) research for epilepsy surgery combines anatomical and functional imaging, implanted electrode locations, interictal biomarkers, and functional mapping--outputs produced by different applications and reconciled by hand before they can be viewed on the same anatomy. Omni-iEEG Planner is an open-source Python platform that brings these inputs into one patient coordinate frame for research data analysis. The workflow starts from the preoperative T1-weighted MRI, from which FreeSurfer provides the cortical surface and anatomical labels; CT, PET and diffusion MRI are then co-registered to that reference, electrode contacts are detected automatically on the postimplantation CT and reviewed by the analyst, and tractography is reconstructed within the application. Channel-indexed results computed outside the platform, such as high-frequency oscillation counts from pyHFO or time-resolved gamma responses, are projected onto the contacts and the cortical surface with their source units preserved, and interictal and functional evidence remain separate layers. We describe the design and demonstrate representative workflows on de-identified patient data. The platform is not proposed as a method for every laboratory; it is a worked example of how one research group combined multimodal integration with an AI-assisted iEEG analysis tool, pyHFO, in a single open environment that others can adapt to their own pipelines. The design will accommodate further evidence types--model-derived contact scores, virtual implantation and hypothetical resection studies, group-level analyses--as they are implemented. The software is released under the MIT license for research and educational use, not clinical decision-making.

papers.title: SPARQLcirc: Probabilistic Query Evaluation with Provenance Circuits
papers.abstract: Probabilistic query evaluation (PQE) computes the probability of every answer of a query over a tuple-independent probabilistic knowledge graph. We study exact PQE for SPARQL over graphs accessed through SPARQL 1.1 endpoints. Shared triples among the derivations of an answer make exact PQE #P-hard in general. Knowledge compilation of the Boolean provenance of every answer yields exact probabilities, and the provenance formulas of different answers can share subformulas. We propose SPARQLcirc, which rewrites a SPARQL query into CONSTRUCT queries that name every gate by its content, so that the results of independent queries form one Boolean provenance circuit for all answers. The rewriting covers joins, unions, projection, filters, OPTIONAL, difference, and transitive closures. SPARQLcirc compiles the circuit and computes the exact probability of every answer by weighted model counting. For the evaluation, we draw random probabilities for the triples of WatDiv and gMark and the statements of Wikidata and evaluate the CONSTRUCT queries on GraphDB, Fuseki, and Oxigraph. The ratio of the end-to-end time of PQE with SPARQLcirc to that of PQE by compiling the provenance expressions of the SPARQL provenance rewriting NPCS decreases with the number of derivations.

Information extraction and link prediction produce triples with confidence scores (Etzioni et al., 2004; Carlson et al., 2010; Dong et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2019), and statistical signal detection derives drug interactions with association scores from adverse-event reports (Tatonetti et al., 2012). A probabilistic knowledge graph treats every score as the probability that the triple holds (Ceylan et al., 2021). In RDF, the probability annotates the triple through standard reification, named graphs, RDF-star or Wikidata statement nodes (Brickley and Guha, 2014; Carroll et al., 2005; Hartig et al., 2021; Kellogg et al., 2026; Malyshev et al., 2018). In Figure 1, every :interactsWith triple carries an identifier pip_{i} and a probability. Knowledge graphs with annotated triples, such as Wikidata, are queried through SPARQL endpoints (Vrandečić and Krötzsch, 2014; Malyshev et al., 2018). A SPARQL query can return the probabilities of the matched triples, but the SPARQL semantics assigns no probability to an answer (Harris and Seaborne, 2013). A public SPARQL endpoint accepts only SPARQL requests, and the endpoint administrator alone can extend the query engine. For a probabilistic knowledge graph accessed only through a public endpoint on the Web, the probability of every answer must therefore be computed from the results of SPARQL queries.

Top-k query evaluation ranks the answers by marginal probability (Ré et al., 2007). The Boolean provenance of an answer is the Boolean function over the triples that is true exactly in the worlds in which the answer occurs, so the marginal probability is the probability that the Boolean provenance is true (Suciu et al., 2011). In Figure 1, the walks of :Aspirin :interactsWith+ ?y from Aspirin to Warfarin can repeat the cycle. Provenance that counts the walks becomes a power series with infinitely many terms (Green et al., 2007), and the series for Warfarin is p1+p12​p6​p7​p8+⋯p_{1}+p_{1}^{2}p_{6}p_{7}p_{8}+\cdots. SPARQLprov and NPCS rewrite a query into SPARQL queries, so that an endpoint without extensions returns the provenance of every answer (Hernández et al., 2021; Asma et al., 2026). SPARQLprov returns tables that encode expression structure and node identifiers. NPCS constructs and aggregates expression strings inside the endpoint. Both rewritings return one provenance expression per answer, and a subexpression that several answers share is therefore repeated in each expression. The probability of every answer is then computed by compiling its expression outside the endpoint. A SPARQL property path returns only the pairs of nodes that its walks connect, and SPARQLprov and NPCS cover only patterns without transitive closures. In relational databases, ProvSQL covers recursive reachability queries, builds one circuit for all answers and names every inner gate by hashing its operator and operands (Senellart et al., 2018; Sen et al., 2026; Senellart and others, 2026). ProvSQL runs inside PostgreSQL as an engine extension, but engine extensions on a public endpoint can be installed only by its administrator.

papers.title: Wideband Channel Measurements in the Lower FR3 Band (6-12 GHz) for Industrial Environments
papers.abstract: The upper mid-band, also known as Frequency Range 3 (FR3), spans 7.125-24.25 GHz and is a key candidate band for sixth-generation (6G) wireless communications. However, channel measurements in industrial environments remain scarce, and the 3GPP indoor-factory (InF) channel model, developed for omnidirectional antennas, has yet to be validated across the FR3 band. This paper presents a wideband channel measurement campaign in an industrial production hall, covering 135 line-of-sight (LOS) positions at 1-18 m and 30 non-line-of-sight (NLOS) positions behind an industrial robot at 2.5-16.5 m across 6-12 GHz. In LOS, the path-loss exponent ranged from 1.87 to 2.12, and the close-in fits agreed with the 3GPP InF-LOS model to within approximately 2 dB. However, shadow fading was only 1.4-1.7 dB, compared with the model's 4.3 dB. In NLOS, the robot caused an excess loss that increased from 10.3 to 13.0 dB between 6.5 and 11.5 GHz, consistent with diffraction. Blocking the direct path raised the mean directional delay spread from approximately 5 to 25 ns, close to omnidirectional values. These results indicate that the 3GPP InF model captures mean LOS path loss well but overestimates the variability of beam-aligned FR3 links, and that blockage loss in FR3 is frequency dependent. The dataset and processing code are publicly available.

papers.intro:
Identifying spectrum that balances capacity and coverage is an important step towards sixth-generation (6G) mobile networks. The upper mid-band, commonly referred to as frequency range 3 (FR3) and spanning approximately 7–24 GHz, offers the potential for wider contiguous bandwidths than sub-6 GHz bands while retaining more favourable propagation conditions than millimetre-wave bands [1, 2]. Interest in this range is reflected in international spectrum studies in preparation for the World Radiocommunication Conference 2027 [3]. In parallel, the Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) has undertaken dedicated work to validate and enhance channel models for this range [4, 5]. For private industrial networks supporting automation, collaborative robotics and extended-reality applications, reliable deployment requires channel models validated under representative factory conditions [6, 7].

For private industrial networks supporting automation, collaborative robotics and extended-reality applications, reliable deployment requires channel models validated under representative factory conditions [6, 7].

Industrial environments, such as factory halls, combine open production areas with large metallic structures, including machinery, shelving and enclosures. These structures give rise to strong specular reflections and can partially or completely obstruct direct propagation paths [8]. The indoor-factory (InF) model in 3GPP TR 38.901 [4] provides statistical descriptions of path loss, shadow fading and delay spread for omnidirectional channels. However, the scarcity of industrial FR3 measurements limits the empirical basis for assessing its underlying assumptions. In particular, further measurements are needed to assess whether the model’s frequency-independent path-loss exponents and delay-spread statistics adequately describe industrial propagation across FR3.

Previous industrial channel measurements at sub-6 GHz and millimetre-wave frequencies have highlighted the importance of metallic reflectors and the differences between directional and omnidirectional channel statistics [9, 10]. More recent studies have examined frequencies within and adjacent to FR3. Factory measurements at 6.75 and 16.95 GHz across 12 transmitter–receiver locations provided directional and omnidirectional channel statistics, revealing frequency-dependent delay and angular spreads that differ from the 3GPP model [11]. An omnidirectional measurement campaign covering 254 links at 10–12 GHz found that the sparse-clutter InF model described NLOS path loss better than the dense-clutter model [12]. Outside industrial environments, continuous wideband measurements over 6–14 GHz demonstrated frequency-resolved channel characterisation in an urban microcell, although the campaign covered 11 receiver positions [13]. 11 1 Dataset on GitHub: https://github.com/FaiZanRaUf00/fr3-inf-zess-dataset. To complement industrial measurements at isolated carrier frequencies or over narrower bands, this paper combines contiguous frequency coverage with extensive spatial sampling under a consistent beam-aligned configuration. A measurement campaign using a vector network analyser (VNA) and boresight-aligned double-ridged horn antennas covers 135 line-of-sight (LOS) receiver positions and 30 non-line-of-sight (NLOS) positions behind an industrial robot in an industrial production hall of the Center for the Engineering of Smart Product-Service Systems (ZESS) at Ruhr University Bochum, Germany. Analysis in six contiguous 1-GHz sub-bands over 6–12 GHz characterises the close-in (CI) path-loss exponent [14], shadow fading, blockage-induced excess loss and root mean square (RMS) delay spread. The path-loss exponent and directional delay spread show no systematic frequency trend, while the 3GPP TR 38.901 InF-LOS model captures mean path loss well but overestimates shadow fading for the measured beam-aligned links. In NLOS, the excess loss caused by the robot increases with frequency, consistent with diffraction, and the directional delay spread rises to values close to omnidirectional ones. The dataset, including raw S-parameters, receiver positions and calibration data, is made publicly available together with the processing code

papers.title: Closed-Form Gaussian Mixture Representations of d-Dimensional Triangulated Domains
papers.abstract: We derive a Gaussian Mixture (GM) representation of a full-dimensional subset of Euclidean space with finite volume from a finite simplicial triangulation in closed form. On each simplex, we replace the uniform probability density function (PDF) with a Gaussian PDF that minimizes the Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence, arriving at the information projection onto the family of Gaussian PDFs. By exploiting affine isomorphisms between simplices, the joint convexity and bijection invariance properties of the KL divergence, identities for Dirichlet PDFs, and a partition-of-unity argument, we establish a dimension-dependent but geometry-independent sharp upper bound on the global KL divergence between the resulting GM PDF and the uniform PDF on the original domain. Numerical examples illustrate the construction and demonstrate its potential in practical applications.
