papers.intro:
Grain-oriented (GO) as well as non-oriented (NO) electrical steel sheets are widely used as core material in power transformers and generators. The design and optimization of such devices requires accurate simulation and, thus, to appropriately take into account the complex behavior of ferromagnetic materials, including hysteresis, saturation, and anisotropy. While various approaches to model these phenomena have been reported in literature, a systematic description of anisotropic nonlinear magnetic behavior and its efficient and reliable incorporation into practical simulation workflows seems not available to date [1, 2, 3]. The present paper provides a new methodology to model anisotropic material behavior that is theoretically and mathematically sound and suitable for incorporation into standard finite-element methods.

papers.title: Pretraining Data Scale Reverses the Muon-AdamW Fine-Tuning Gap
papers.abstract: Muon has recently emerged as a promising optimizer for pretraining large language models, offering a speedup over AdamW in minimizing pretraining loss. However, it remains unclear whether Muon's advantage persists after fine-tuning. In this paper, we study the downstream behavior of Muon and AdamW and uncover a surprising trend: beyond a sufficiently large pretraining data budget, AdamW outperforms Muon after fine-tuning. Moreover, as model size increases, AdamW overtakes Muon at progressively smaller pretraining token-parameter ratios. To explain this reversal, we view fine-tuning as a perturbation of the outputs and introduce the margin-to-spread ratio, which measures how far the correct logit lies above the wrong ones relative to how widely the wrong logits are spread. In language models, Muon has the larger margin-to-spread ratio at small data budgets and AdamW at large ones, mirroring the fine-tuning trend. In a linear associative memory, we prove that after one update the margin-to-spread ratio of gradient descent gains on that of Muon as the data budget grows, and simulations show that this trend persists after extended training.

At larger budgets, this trend reverses: AdamW achieves a better learning–forgetting tradeoff than Muon, and the fine-tuning gap becomes positive.

To quantify sensitivity to output perturbations, we introduce the margin-to-spread ratio (MSR), a simple metric derived from the model’s output logits that characterizes robustness. For each prediction, the MSR is the difference between the correct logit and the average of the incorrect logits, normalized by the spread of the incorrect logits (Section 4.1): a prediction is more robust when the MSR is larger.

papers.title: From Natural Language to Exact Cover: A Neuro-Symbolic Approach to Zebra Puzzles
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) generation has substantially improved the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) on complex reasoning tasks, including code generation, data analysis, and exam-style question answering. Despite these advances, purely neural LLMs continue to struggle with elementary logical reasoning problems and lack the determinism, soundness, and reliability characteristic of symbolic reasoning systems. Conversely, classical symbolic methods such as SAT solving and exact cover guarantee correctness and completeness, but require problems to be expressed in highly specialized formal encodings, limiting their applicability to natural language inputs. In this work, we present a synergistic neuro-symbolic framework that bridges this gap by combining neural semantic parsing with deterministic exact cover reasoning. Given a Zebra-style logic puzzle in natural language, an LLM translates entities and constraints into structured tool calls that construct an exact cover instance. A symbolic solver then computes the solution and provides feedback to iteratively refine invalid, under- or overconstrained encodings, exploiting the uniqueness property of Zebra puzzles. We conduct a comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple parameter scales, post-training paradigms, and LLM families. The results demonstrate that our hybrid approach consistently outperforms strong plain neural baselines, including CoT prompting, as well as recent neuro-symbolic methods.

papers.intro:
Constraint Satisfaction Problems (CSPs) lie at the core of many real-world decision-making tasks, including scheduling, planning, resource allocation, and configuration, making them a fundamental abstraction in AI research (Russell and Norvig, 1995; Mackworth, 1977; Nadel, 1989; Knuth, 2016; Knuth, 2020; Knuth, 2025). While symbolic methods such as SAT and constraint solvers can guarantee correctness and completeness, their practical deployment critically depends on constructing effective formal encodings – a process that remains difficult even for domain experts (Heisinger et al., 2024). Translating informal problem descriptions into a structured encoding requires substantial modeling expertise as small representational choices can dramatically impact solver performance and tractability. As a result, research often studies simplified yet representative proxy domains such as logic puzzles (e.g. Sudoku or Zebra Puzzles), which capture essential combinatorial and relational reasoning challenges while providing clean semantics, controllable complexity, and objectively verifiable solutions (Dechter and Pearl, 1987; Prosser, 1993; Lin et al., 2025; White et al., 2025).

This reliance on structured benchmark domains aligns naturally with recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs), which are increasingly applied to tasks requiring the construction of structured symbolic solutions from unstructured inputs. Such domains include mathematical reasoning (Hendrycks et al., 2021b), programming (Hendrycks et al., 2021a), planning (Zhang et al., 2026), and logic puzzle solving (Lin et al., 2025; Chollet et al., 2025). A shared characteristic of these problems is that, although discovering solutions is challenging, their correctness can be verified algorithmically. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards post-training has therefore emerged as a standard approach for optimizing models directly against symbolic verifiers (Guo et al., 2025). The resulting thinking LLMs produce Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning traces enabling inference-time scaling.

Zebra Puzzles are among recent benchmarks to test the reasoning capabilities of LLMs (Lin et al., 2025; White et al., 2025). They consist of lists of entities, properties, and attributes as well as clues; the goal is to infer the relations of attributes and entities from the given information. Lin et al. (2025) find that scaling the model size does not help beyond a certain level of complexity which is defined by the puzzles’ solution space. This manifests in generalist LLMs faring extremely well on simple Zebra Puzzles while struggling with more complex ones. Longer reasoning traces appear to be more helpful with these problems than larger models. However, these longer traces present additional challenges such as high frequency noise (Radler et al., 2025) and increased chance of hallucination (Mei et al., 2025).

Prior work explores both agentic formulations that iteratively generate solver-compatible programs and solver-centric pipelines that translate natural language inputs into formal constraint specifications solved using SAT, SMT, CSP, or ASP techniques (Szeider, 2025; Pan et al., 2023; Ye et al., 2023; Eiter et al., 2025). This coupling of semantic parsing and symbolic solving consistently outperforms LLMs on Zebra Puzzle-style benchmarks.

papers.title: Mediating Human-Swarm Interactions Through a Robot Helper: A Shepherding-Inspired Approach
papers.abstract: This work investigates human-swarm interaction (HSI) for steering large collectives through an intermediary robot helper. While prior robot-swarm control and HSI techniques commonly assume swarm members are addressable, these assumptions often fail for ``ungovernable'' swarms such as wildlife flocks and schools of fish. Motivated by pastoral shepherding, we compare low-level teleoperation to a higher-autonomy motion-primitives interface in a virtual reality (VR) shepherding task under varied swarm cohesion dynamics. Results indicate that motion primitives that operate on collective shape (e.g., boundary-based control) improve task performance and reduce perceived workload.

papers.intro:
Large, naturally occurring collectives such as bird flocks and fish schools often exhibit the properties of ungovernable swarms: systems in which individual members cannot be pre-programmed or directly commanded, yet whose aggregate motion must still be influenced for safety or logistical reasons (e.g., airfield operations, aquaculture). At present, influencing of such swarms is largely achieved through passive or environmental interventions. In aviation, for example, wildlife hazard management commonly prioritizes habitat modification (e.g., reducing attractants such as food, water, and shelter) and exclusion methods to discourage birds from using the airfield environment [1, 2]. Only under particular contingencies do airports more frequently deploy reactive dispersal and direct-control tactics (e.g., hazing/harassment, pyrotechnics, or removal) [3, 4]. Although effective in many routine contexts, these approaches are difficult to apply with precision during time-critical disruptions. A canonical example where an “ungovernable” collective is influenced via a human-controlled helper agent is pastoral shepherding. Here, a handler issues compact, discrete commands (e.g., “come-bye”, “walk-up”) to a sheepdog. The sheepdog then transmits the human’s intent by shaping flock-level motion. This paradigm has inspired a substantial body of algorithmic and robotic shepherding research, in which one or more agents guide swarm members [5, 6].

Translating shepherding into human-robot interaction (HRI) raises a central interface-design question: how should the human’s interaction with the helper agent be structured? The designer must decide how much of the helper’s behavior should be specified explicitly by the human versus generated autonomously by the robot, and at what level of abstraction (e.g., continuous low-level control versus discrete, task-level commands). This choice directly determines the robot’s effective autonomy and, consequently, the operator’s role in the control loop. In HRI, “levels of robot autonomy” (LoRA) are consequential because they shape operator workload, situation awareness, and performance. Beer et al. formalize this idea via a 10-level taxonomy spanning teleoperation through full autonomy, enabling systematic reasoning about autonomy allocation and its human-factors implications [7].

Guided by the shepherding metaphor, we compare (i) a teleoperation condition, which provides direct, continuous control of the helper agent, with (ii) a shepherding condition with a motion-primitives based interface. This comparison is motivated by prior work on shared autonomy and primitive-based control which argues that elevating control from low-level actuation to higher-level task/motion primitives can reduce operator burden and improve efficiency while preserving meaningful human agency [8, 9, 10, 11].

papers.title: Multi-Trajectory Parallel-in-Iteration Optimization
papers.abstract: Previously, we developed a ``parallel-in-iteration'' optimization framework that uses multigrid reduction-in-time (MGRIT) to parallelize slowly converging optimization methods, such as gradient descent. Unlike time-dependent evolution problems, optimization requires only a final point with a sufficiently small gradient, rather than an accurate approximation of the entire trajectory of iterates. This motivates a different use of MGRIT: instead of repeatedly improving the approximation of a single long trajectory, we introduce restarted MGRIT (R-MGRIT), which performs one MGRIT iteration on a trajectory, takes the approximate final point as a new initial guess, and repeats the process on a new trajectory. Each restart thus defines a new all-at-once system, allowing progress toward the solution without accurately approximating the preceding trajectory. Moreover, we find that these trajectories can be shortened without increasing the number of restarts needed for convergence. We provide theoretical results comparing MGRIT and R-MGRIT for linear problems and demonstrate the convergence behavior of the shortened trajectories numerically for both linear and nonlinear problems. Shortening the trajectories increases the estimated parallel speedup while reducing the number of processors required.

papers.title: FastHeapDict: Permanent Slot Indexing for Efficient Decrease-Key Operations in Indexed Priority Queues
papers.abstract: Efficient decrease-key support remains an important practical concern in priority queues used by shortest-path and graph-processing algorithms. Although duplicate-entry heaps avoid explicit decrease-key operations and are simple to implement, they may accumulate many stale entries when tentative priorities are repeatedly improved. This paper presents FastHeapDict, an indexed binary min-heap based on permanent slot indexing. Instead of repeatedly locating keys through hash-table lookups during heap repair, FastHeapDict assigns each key a stable integer slot and stores that slot directly in heap entries. As a result, position updates during sift-up and sift-down operations are performed through integer indexing while preserving the usual indexed-heap interface. We evaluate FastHeapDict in both Python and C++20 using Dijkstra's algorithm as the primary experimental workload. The benchmarks include constructed dense stress graphs, randomized dense graph variants, and comparisons against duplicate-entry heaps and existing priority-queue alternatives. Across the tested Python workloads, FastHeapDict consistently outperforms the duplicate-entry heapq baseline and the tested heapdict and pqdict implementations. In the C++20 implementation, FastHeapDict also achieves strong constant-factor improvements over std::priority_queue duplicates, std::set-based decrease-key, and std::multiset duplicates. These results indicate that permanent slot indexing can provide a compact and effective implementation strategy for indexed priority queues in workloads where priority updates are frequent.

Priority queues are fundamental components of many graph algorithms and optimization problems. Among their most important operations is decrease-key, which allows the priority associated with an existing element to be updated efficiently without inserting duplicate entries. Algorithms such as Dijkstra’s single-source shortest-path algorithm rely heavily on this operation when tentative distances are repeatedly improved during execution [1].

Priority queues are fundamental components of many graph algorithms and optimization problems. Among their most important operations is decrease-key, which allows the priority associated with an existing element to be updated efficiently without inserting duplicate entries. Algorithms such as Dijkstra’s single-source shortest-path algorithm rely heavily on this operation when tentative distances are repeatedly improved during execution [1].

Despite the theoretical importance of decrease-key, many practical implementations of Dijkstra’s algorithm avoid supporting it explicitly. Instead, they rely on a duplicate-entry strategy in which every distance improvement inserts a new heap entry while obsolete entries are discarded only when they are eventually removed from the priority queue. This approach is simple, robust, and readily supported by widely used libraries such as Python’s heapq [2] and C++’s std::priority_queue [3]. However, when many priority updates occur before vertices are finalized, duplicate entries accumulate, increasing the number of heap operations, memory usage, and unnecessary processing of stale elements.

Indexed priority queues address this limitation [4] by maintaining exactly one live entry for each key and updating its priority in place. Traditional indexed heaps, however, typically maintain a mapping from keys to heap positions, requiring repeated hash-table or dictionary lookups whenever heap elements move during sift-up or sift-down operations. Although these lookups have expected constant-time complexity, they contribute additional constant-factor overhead in implementations where decrease-key operations occur frequently.

Unlike conventional indexed heaps that repeatedly recover heap positions through key-based hash-table accesses, FastHeapDict performs all subsequent heap maintenance through direct integer indexing once a permanent slot has been assigned. Each key is assigned a stable integer slot when it first appears, and heap entries store this slot together with the key and its priority. A separate position array maps slots to current heap locations, allowing heap repair operations to update positions through integer indexing rather than repeated key-based hash lookups. FastHeapDict does not change the theoretical complexity of indexed binary heaps; instead, it proposes a compact implementation strategy that reduces repeated hash-table access during heap maintenance. papers.title: X-World 1.6: Building Controllable Virtual Cities with World Models
papers.abstract: Deploying generative world models for end-to-end closed-loop evaluation and policy learning requires precise scenario control, consistent observations, and sustained generation quality during extended interactions. This report presents \emph{X-World~1.6}, advancing X-World~1.0 toward a more reliable and versatile driving simulator. The upgraded base model offers finer-grained control over traffic semantics, including traffic lights and road markings, together with improved spatial consistency across cameras. Virtual City capabilities broaden scenario construction through a family of models conditioned on diverse 2D and 3D references, including support for generating multi-camera future videos from a single image. An enhanced post-training framework enables efficient causal, few-step generation with stronger temporal coherence, better quality retention over longer rollouts, and improved alignment with human preferences. We also introduce a dedicated evaluation suite to support systematic assessment and guide model iteration. Together, these upgrades expand the scenarios X-World can simulate and improve the efficiency and reliability of its generated observations, supporting broader use in autonomous-driving development.

Stronger and broader scene control. We strengthen existing controls, add traffic-light positions and colors and road-surface markings, and improve geometric association across camera views. The principal extension beyond element-level control is absolute static scene control. Scene references from 3D Gaussian representations [11, 4, 30], point clouds, and visual observations constrain persistent geometry and appearance while ego trajectories and supported traffic conditions change. This provides evidence for buildings, roadside structures, and location-specific details that sparse road annotations do not determine. The objective is to preserve a specified place within the available reference coverage, while allowing scenario-dependent content to evolve. These conditioning paths use independently trained models; the common interface does not imply a single model accepting every reference modality.

papers.title: 4K Image Super-Resolution on Mobile NPUs: Mobile AI 2026 Challenge Report
papers.abstract: Image super-resolution is widely used on mobile devices for upscaling various types of image data. This creates a need for efficient deep learning-based models that are not only performant but can also be deployed on neural processing units (NPUs) present in the majority of mobile and IoT chipsets. In this Mobile AI challenge, we address this problem and propose the participants to design fast solutions that can upsample images from Full HD to 4K resolution while running on popular mobile NPUs from Qualcomm and MediaTek. For this, the participants were provided with the DIV2K dataset and trained models to do an efficient 3X image upscaling. The competition had two tracks: in the first track, the models had to be fully quantized (INT8), and the runtime of all models was evaluated on the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 NPU. In the second track, the participants were developing floating-point solutions that were evaluated on the MediaTek Dimensity 9500 NPU. Top solutions proposed in this challenge are able to reconstruct 4K images under 5 milliseconds while reaching a PSNR score of 30 dB. A comprehensive description of the models developed in the challenge is provided in this paper.

papers.intro:
Single-image super-resolution is a core computer vision task that aims to generate a high-resolution image from its downsampled version by restoring fine details and high-frequency information. Unlike the standard image interpolation techniques [61, 23, 82, 89, 90, 101, 102, 103, 28, 92], deep learning-based approaches are able to achieve significantly superior results in terms of both reconstruction fidelity and perceptual quality. In recent years, this task has gained significant attention due to its direct applications in telephoto image processing and AI-based digital zoom in smartphone cameras, enhancement of low-resolution media, frame interpolation in video games, or upscaling of images and videos to match the resolution of display panels. A wide range of deep learning-based methods have been proposed in the past to achieve high-fidelity image reconstruction [20, 19, 66, 73, 88, 91, 10, 77, 108, 56, 72, 14, 109, 13, 12, 84]. However, a primary limitation of these approaches is that they are typically focused on optimizing the restoration quality, while neglecting the computational efficiency required for mobile platforms, where resource constraints are a critical consideration. In this challenge, we directly address this problem and propose the participants to design efficient super-resolution models that can run on recent smartphone neural processing units (NPUs) from Qualcomm and MediaTek mobile chipsets.

Designing deep learning models that run efficiently on mobile devices — especially across different AI accelerators like NPUs — is a complex challenge. It demands careful analysis of hardware constraints such as limited operator support, restricted memory capacity and bandwidth, reduced accuracy for quantized models and specific driver behavior of NPUs. Even when certain layers or operations are technically supported, they may be executed inefficiently due to constraints related to NPU hardware architecture or its driver implementation, and thus create performance bottlenecks during inference. A striking example here would be the Google Tensor NPU present in all recent Google Pixel smartphones that, despite having quite high theoretical peak performance, is unable to efficiently accelerate the vast majority of even simplistic CNN-based models [45]. As a result, achieving low latency and energy efficiency often requires partial or complete redesigns of model architectures. For a more detailed discussion of these challenges and the performance of modern mobile AI accelerators we refer to [53, 50]. Overall, all these limitations require various adaptations of the standard deep learning models for their efficient deployment on mobile NPUs, including conventional optimizations like 16-bit / 8-bit [15, 63, 62, 104, 70, 79, 9, 85, 86, 74] and low-bit [11, 93, 5, 60, 76, 111, 6, 65, 18, 8, 68] quantization, network pruning and compression [15, 69, 75, 80, 64, 26, 110, 100, 67, 96], NPU-specific adaptations, platform-aware neural architecture search [27, 87, 98, 95, 78, 17, 107, 99, 16, 106], etc.

A striking example here would be the Google Tensor NPU present in all recent Google Pixel smartphones that, despite having quite high theoretical peak performance, is unable to efficiently accelerate the vast majority of even simplistic CNN-based models [45]. As a result, achieving low latency and energy efficiency often requires partial or complete redesigns of model architectures. For a more detailed discussion of these challenges and the performance of modern mobile AI accelerators we refer to [53, 50]. Overall, all these limitations require various adaptations of the standard deep learning models for their efficient deployment on mobile NPUs, including conventional optimizations like 16-bit / 8-bit [15, 63, 62, 104, 70, 79, 9, 85, 86, 74] and low-bit [11, 93, 5, 60, 76, 111, 6, 65, 18, 8, 68] quantization, network pruning and compression [15, 69, 75, 80, 64, 26, 110, 100, 67, 96], NPU-specific adaptations, platform-aware neural architecture search [27, 87, 98, 95, 78, 17, 107, 99, 16, 106], etc.

In this Mobile AI Challenge, the participants were proposed to develop efficient deep learning super-resolution models that can upscale Full HD images to 4K resolution directly on smartphone NPUs. The DIV2K [3] dataset containing diverse RGB images was provided for network training, a downscaling factor of 3 was considered in this competition. The competition had two tracks: the first one, where the standard floating-point (FP16) models were considered, and the second one, where all models had to be additionally INT8 quantized (both weights and activations) to ensure high efficiency and compatibility of the designed solutions with low-power edge NPUs. The runtime of the models was evaluated on the Dimensity 9500 NPU and the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 NPU in the 1st and 2nd tracks, respectively. Each submission was evaluated based on both image fidelity and runtime efficiency, thus balancing reconstruction quality with model efficiency. All solutions developed during this challenge are fully compatible with the LiteRT [81] (former TensorFlow Lite) framework, enabling deployment on a variety of Linux and Android-based IoT platforms, smartphones, and edge devices.

papers.title: Efficient Image Denoising on Smartphone GPUs: Mobile AI 2026 Challenge Report
papers.abstract: Image denoising is a fundamental problem in mobile photography. Despite a large number of solutions proposed for this task, the majority of them are trained on synthetically produced noisy images, and are additionally too computationally heavy for processing full-resolution images on mobile devices. This creates a need for efficient deep learning-based models that are not only performant but can also be deployed on constrained mobile hardware. In this Mobile AI challenge, we address this problem and propose the participants to design fast solutions that can denoise Full HD resolution photos while running on popular smartphone GPUs from Qualcomm and Arm. For this, the participants were provided with a large-scale dataset consisting of noisy-clean image pairs captured in the wild. The runtime of all models was evaluated on the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 and Dimensity 9500 chipsets with the Adreno and Mali GPUs, respectively. Top solutions proposed in this challenge are able to perform high-quality image denoising under 100 milliseconds on both platforms while reaching a PSNR score of over 37 dB. A comprehensive description of the models developed in the challenge is provided in this paper.

papers.intro:
Despite recent advancements in mobile imaging sensor technology, image denoising remains a significant challenge in the processing of mobile photo and video data. Physical and design constraints limit the ability to increase sensor size in mobile devices — when combined with the trend toward higher sensor resolutions and reduced pixel dimensions, these factors contribute to elevated noise levels, particularly under low-light conditions. To address this issue, numerous classical denoising methods have been proposed in the past [66, 75, 17, 8, 9, 81, 79, 88]. More recently, deep learning-based approaches have demonstrated substantially improved quantitative performance [23, 91, 112, 111, 1, 3, 73, 109, 13, 60, 71, 89, 24]. However, despite achieving high fidelity metrics, many of these methods rely on synthetically generated training and validation datasets [91, 112, 111, 73, 109, 13, 71, 89, 24], or are evaluated on limited collections of indoor imagery [2, 1, 3, 60], thereby restricting their generalizability to real-world noisy camera data. Another primary limitation of these approaches is that they are typically focused on optimizing the restoration quality, while neglecting the computational efficiency required for mobile platforms, where resource constraints are a critical consideration. In this challenge, we directly address this problem and propose the participants to use a real-world dataset and design efficient image denoising models that can run on recent smartphone GPUs.

papers.title: A localized packing lemma for sets of bounded $\operatorname{VC}_2$-dimension
papers.abstract:
In the setting of abelian groups, Haussler's packing lemma implies that any subset of bounded $\operatorname{VC}$-dimension can be approximated by one of a small number of representative translates. While this exact statement is provably false under the weaker hypothesis that $A$ has bounded $\operatorname{VC}_2$-dimension, we show that in $\mathbb{F}_p^n$ a similar statement does hold after localization to cosets of subspaces depending on the individual translates.
  More precisely, given $\epsilon>0$ and $A\subseteq \mathbb{F}_p^n$ with $\operatorname{VC}_2(A)<k$, we show that there exist $r\leq \epsilon^{-O_{k,p}(1)}$ and $g_1,\ldots, g_r\in \mathbb{F}_p^n$ with the property that for every $x\in \mathbb{F}_p^n$, there is a partition $\mathcal{C}_x$ of $\mathbb{F}_p^n$ into cosets of (possibly distinct) subgroups, each of index at most $\exp(\epsilon^{-O_{k,p}(1)})$, and a subcollection $\Omega_x\subseteq \mathcal{C}_x$ whose union has size at least $(1-\epsilon)|\mathbb{F}_p^n|$, such that on each $C\in \Omega_x$, the translate $A-x$ looks like one of $A-g_1,\ldots, A-g_r$, in the sense that $|((A-x)\Delta (A-g_{i_{x,C}}))\cap C|<\epsilon|C|$ for some $1\leq i_{x,C}\leq r$. We also prove a second version of this result in which each partition $\mathcal{C}_x$ is the set of cosets of a single subgroup $H_x$ of quasipolynomial index but where the bound on $r$ is a quadruple exponential.

papers.title: Asymmetric Little--Parks Oscillations as a Probe of Coupled Pairing Channels in Surface-Superconducting \texorpdfstring{PtBi$_2$}{PtBi2}
papers.abstract: Motivated by the recent discovery of unconventional surface superconductivity in PtBi$_{2}$, we theoretically study its signatures in the Little-Parks oscillations of a narrow ring made from the same material. Using a Ginzburg-Landau model with three coupled pairing channels allowed by the trigonal crystal symmetry, we show that a fixed in-plane magnetic field can make the mean-field transition temperature asymmetric under reversal of the normal flux through the ring, while preserving periodicity in the superconducting flux quantum. The leading weak-field contribution to this asymmetry is cubic in the in-plane field strength. The flux-odd component respects the threefold crystal symmetry and changes sign when the in-plane field is rotated by $\pi/3$ at fixed magnitude. Within the homogeneous ring model, this asymmetry is absent for a single pairing channel and arises from the coupling between the three channels. Our calculations further show that increasing the in-plane magnetic field can enhance the superconducting nucleation temperature through mixing of pairing channels, illustrating magnetic control of multicomponent superconductivity in mesoscopic rings. Little-Parks interferometry with independent control of flux and field direction thus offers a mesoscopic probe of the pairing state, complementary to spectroscopic studies of the gap structure.

The Little–Parks (LP) effect [19] is one of the clearest manifestations of macroscopic phase coherence in a multiply connected superconductor. In the conventional single-component Ginzburg–Landau (GL) description, fluxoid quantization makes the transition temperature periodic in the superconducting flux quantum Φ0=h​c/2​e\Phi_{0}=hc/2e, with a reciprocal response built from parabolic winding branches [31], Tc​(ϕ)=Tc​(−ϕ),T_{c}(\phi)=T_{c}(-\phi), with ϕ≡Φ/Φ0.\phi\equiv\Phi/\Phi_{0}. Moreover, LP interferometry is a phase-sensitive probe of unconventional and multicomponent superconductivity. A familiar example is the π\pi-shifted LP pattern, with extrema displaced from integer to half-integer flux, long discussed in connection with nontrivial pairing symmetry and multicomponent order [10, 14, 18, 2]. papers.title: Zero sets in spaces of analytic functions with $p$-summable Taylor coefficients
papers.abstract: A zero set for a space of analytic functions is a set on which some nonzero function in the space vanishes; it is exact if it coincides with the full zero set of such a function. We construct zero sets that are not exact in the classical coefficient spaces $\ell_A^p$ of functions analytic on the unit disk for every $1\le p<2$. For $1<p<2$, a single Blaschke set $W$ is a zero set for every $\ell_A^p$ in this range, but is not exact for any of them. The endpoint case $p=1$, corresponding to the analytic Wiener algebra $\ell_A^1$, requires a separate construction, yielding a non-exact zero set that accumulates at only one point of the unit circle. The proofs combine quadratic characters, finite-dimensional Clark transforms, and logarithmic estimates in zero-free regions. We also establish sharp moment duality and an exact summability criterion for a family of regular polygons. For $p>2$, we construct two disjoint exact zero sets whose union is a uniqueness set. For these exponents, suitably chosen rotations also yield a continuum-sized family of nonzero closed shift-invariant subspaces of $\ell^p$ with pairwise trivial intersections, recovering a known existence result.

papers.title: Blueprint2CAD: Benchmarking Foundation Models on Engineering Drawing-to-CAD Render Correspondence
papers.abstract: Engineering drawings specify mechanical parts through orthographic projections. Recognizing which part a drawing depicts underlies part search, design reuse, and digitization, yet no public benchmark measures whether vision models can do it. We introduce Blueprint2CAD, a benchmark for drawing-to-render correspondence: given an orthographic line drawing and a shaded render, usually from another viewpoint, decide whether they show the same part. Its data layer, BlueCAD-30K, applies an open drafting pipeline to 29,925 Zero-to-CAD models, adding view-aligned renders, clean and dimensioned drawings from six viewpoints, and surface-type metadata. Frozen encoders retrieve the matching part from a 10,000-model gallery with up to 65% Recall@1 when viewpoints are known but 43% when they are not, and the four encoders we test lie within six points of each other: viewpoint, not backbone, is the bottleneck. Six zero-shot vision-language models reach only 0.52-0.67 verification accuracy, with model-specific Yes/No biases that chain-of-thought shifts but does not remove; a quick LoRA fine-tuning on in-domain pairs improves verification accuracy by a few points but sharpens these biases and leaves the viewpoint failure intact.

The problem is harder than it looks. Mechanical components are textureless, symmetric, and repetitive, and their identity rests on small features such as holes, pockets, fillets, and chamfers. A drawing presents these as sparse line art with hidden lines and annotations layered on top, whereas a render shows a shaded surface, usually from another viewpoint. Deciding whether the two show the same part therefore means holding one projection and relating it to another across a change of view, a correspondence that is natural to carry as visual structure and awkward to spell out in words. Existing CAD datasets [39, 37, 82, 52] support shape retrieval and generative modeling, and SPARE3D [25] poses spatial-reasoning questions over three-view drawings, but none pairs engineering drawings with shaded renders of the same part under controlled cameras, so the encoders behind drawing-to-CAD reconstruction [81, 19], drawing digitization [58, 17], and CAD inspection [1] have never been measured on orthographic line art.

We introduce Blueprint2CAD, a benchmark that makes drawing-to-render correspondence a first-class task. Its scope is deliberately 2D: every task relates a line drawing to an image of the part it describes, and nothing is claimed about recovering 3D geometry. The data layer, BlueCAD-30K, adds no new geometry either. It is the output of an open drafting pipeline applied to 29,925 models of the Zero-to-CAD collection [5]: shaded renders together with clean and dimensioned projections from six canonical viewpoints under a shared camera rig, so that view correspondence holds by construction, plus B-rep-derived surface-type metadata and model-level training, validation, and test splits. The pipeline runs on any STEP collection, which is how we expect the benchmark to grow.

We evaluate the two paradigms a practitioner would reach for first. Five frozen vision foundation models (DINOv3 [72], SigLIP2 [75], I-JEPA [4], RADIO [66], TIPSv2 [11]) serve as embeddings for search over a 10,000-model gallery: when the camera direction of each projection is known, the four strongest reach 59–65% Recall@1 within six points of each other, while a hand-crafted silhouette descriptor already reaches 49%; without that knowledge the best encoder falls to 43%, still about twice the silhouette’s rate, two dimension lines per view cost at most seven points, and I-JEPA stays near chance under our protocol. Six vision-language models (Claude Sonnet 5 [2], Gemini 3.6 Flash [23], GPT-5.6 Luna [60], Mistral Small 3.2 24B [56], InternVL3.5 14B [80], Qwen3-VL 8B [8]) are queried zero-shot on binary verification and 4-way retrieval: none reaches 0.70 verification accuracy, even with chain-of-thought, each carries its own Yes/No prior that reasoning prompts redirect rather than remove, and correct matches become rare once the render is a top or bottom view. A tiny LoRA adapter trained on in-domain pairs lifts Qwen3-VL 8B by a few points without touching either failure mode. Read together, the two studies place drawing-to-render correspondence among the problems where an intermediate representation in language does not stand in for one that keeps the geometry: supplying the view relation directly, as the oracle alignment does for frozen encoders, is worth more than any change of backbone, while asking a Vision Language Model (VLM) to narrate that relation leaves its viewpoint failure where it was. papers.title: HistoTx: Early fusion of H&E images and spatial transcriptomics at varying spatial transcriptomics resolution with self-supervised learning
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics maps gene expression across tissue sections and, when integrated with whole slide images, jointly captures both morphological architecture and molecular activity to provide a rich, multimodal view of tissue biology. ML approaches combining spatial transcriptomics and WSIs typically learn a mapping from morphological features to molecular profiles via contrastive alignment or supervised fine-tuning of pathology foundation models. In both cases, transcriptomics serves as a training signal rather than a true input modality, leaving inference fundamentally image-driven. We propose an early-fusion vision transformer architecture in which transcript tokens are constructed at arbitrary spatial resolution, merged with image patch tokens, and jointly processed through a shared transformer stack for deep cross-modal interaction. Starting from a pretrained vision-only pathology foundation model, we train HistoTx by continuing self-supervised pretraining on paired image and spatial transcriptomics data and demonstrate that: 1) at inference with image only, performance remains on par with the baseline on most tasks while improving on tasks that inherently benefit from molecular knowledge, such as gene expression prediction; 2) when both modalities are available at inference, jointly providing image and transcript inputs outperforms either modality alone.

papers.intro:
Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained whole slide images (WSIs) are the gold standard for cancer diagnosis, routinely used for tumor detection, subtyping, and clinical decision making, yet their interpretation remains a labor-intensive task demanding years of specialized pathologist training (Thomas and Button, 2015). Recent advances in artificial intelligence have led to the emergence of large pathology foundation models trained on vast collections of WSIs, achieving strong performance across a broad range of clinically relevant tasks (Wang et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2024), yet their capabilities remain limited for tasks that could benefit from additional molecular knowledge.

Recent advances in artificial intelligence have led to the emergence of large pathology foundation models trained on vast collections of WSIs, achieving strong performance across a broad range of clinically relevant tasks (Wang et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2024), yet their capabilities remain limited for tasks that could benefit from additional molecular knowledge.

In parallel, advances in spatial transcriptomics (ST) technologies now enable molecular profiling directly on tissue sections, facilitating precise cell type identification, detection of functional cell states, and richer tumor characterization (Jain and Eadon, 2024). ST data comes in different formats depending on the platform. For example, high-resolution Xenium data consists of individual transcript detections, each annotated with its spatial location and gene identity but limited to a fixed gene panel. By contrast, Visium data is whole-transcriptome based and consists of a regular grid of barcoded spots, each with a diameter of 55 µm, where transcripts are aggregated into a single expression profile per spot. Due to the different nature and granularity of the ST data it is nontrivial to train a model on both Xenium and Visium data. In fact most models use only on spot-based (Chen et al., 2025; Chung et al., 2024; Pang et al., 2021; Xie et al., ; Hemker et al., 2026; Zhan et al., ) or probe-based data (Fu et al., 2025; Martinelli et al., 2026; Gindra et al., 2025) for training. To our best knowledge, only MINT (Lee et al., 2026) is able to encode both modalities with one model, however this model is limited to one learnable ST token.

To leverage molecular information alongside histology, early approaches trained supervised models to predict gene expression directly from H&E images (Schmauch et al., 2025; Chung et al., 2024; Nonchev et al., 2025; Pang et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2026). More recently, methods inspired by CLIP have employed contrastive learning to align image and ST embeddings in a shared latent space, using the transcriptomic modality merely as a supervision signal to guide visual representation learning (Chen et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026; Xie et al., ; Hemker et al., 2026). Multimodal fusion is reduced to late-stage feature-level concatenation or averaging, rather than being deeply integrated into the model architecture. We argue that this image-centric strategy is well motivated in practice: given the high cost of ST, molecular profiles are rarely available in routine clinical workflows, whereas H&E images are inexpensive and virtually ubiquitous. Leveraging limited ST data as a supervision signal to endow the image encoder with molecular knowledge is therefore a natural and clinically practical design choice. However, existing contrastive approaches apply this supervision crudely, typically at the coarse patch level, failing to exploit the fine-grained spatial correspondence between transcript distributions and image content. At the same time, in the cases where transcriptomics data are available at inference, deeper and more principled multimodal fusion beyond simple concatenation or averaging remains desirable to fully exploit the complementary information carried by both modalities, as can be achieved by early-fusion (Martinelli et al., 2026).

We present HistoTx, an early-fusion multimodal transformer building on (Martinelli et al., 2026) that integrates H&E images and ST. We extend the architecture to accommodate both Visium and Xenium platforms by constructing spatially aligned image and transcript tokens at multiple spatial resolutions, merging them into a joint token sequence, and processing them through a shared transformer stack for deep cross-modal interaction. HistoTx is trained by continuing DINOv2 (Oquab et al., 2024) self-supervised pretraining on paired image and ST data, warm-started from a pretrained vision-only pathology foundation model. By constructing tokens at multiple spatial resolutions, the model captures biological structures across scales, from subcellular transcript patterns to tissue-level morphology. The two main contributions of this work are: • Multimodal self-supervised pretraining: a training strategy that continues DINOv2 pretraining on paired image and ST data from a vision-only pathology foundation model, yielding a model that retains strong image-only performance, improves on tasks requiring molecular knowledge, and further benefits when both modalities are available at inference. • Flexible transcript tokenization strategy: This enables a single backbone to handle both Xenium and Visium data, allowing training on the full HEST-1k (Jaume et al., 2024) dataset and broadening exposure to diverse tissues, gene panels, and spatial scales.

papers.title: Y2CdX4 (X = S, Se, Te) Semiconductors: A First-Principles Study of Structural, Electronic, Optical, and Energy-Related Properties
papers.abstract: We present a comprehensive density functional theory (DFT) investigation of the structural, mechanical, electronic, optical, thermoelectric, and bonding properties of Y2CdX4 (X = S, Se, Te) compounds for potential optoelectronic and energy-conversion applications. Structural optimization reveals a systematic expansion of the equilibrium lattice parameters from S to Te. The calculated bulk moduli decrease from 83 GPa for Y2CdS4 to 68 GPa for Y2CdSe4 and 54 GPa for Y2CdTe4, indicating progressive lattice softening. Electronic band-structure calculations predict indirect band gaps of 2.42, 2.08, and 1.71 eV for Y2CdS4, Y2CdSe4, and Y2CdTe4, respectively, with further narrowing upon inclusion of spin-orbit coupling. The calculated dielectric functions, refractive indices, absorption coefficients, reflectivity, optical conductivities, and electron energy-loss spectra reveal systematic changes in optical response across the chalcogen series. The absorption onset shifts toward lower photon energies, from approximately 2.4 eV in Y2CdS4 to 1.7 eV in Y2CdTe4. Thermoelectric calculations indicate promising Seebeck coefficients and power factors, with Y2CdSe4 exhibiting a favorable balance of transport properties. Charge-density distributions, electron localization functions, and Bader charge analyses suggest increasing covalent bonding contributions from sulfide to telluride. These findings highlight the potential of Y2CdX4 compounds for tunable optoelectronic and energy-conversion applications.

papers.title: ReGATE: Recurrent Gated Visual Fusion for Reactive Humanoid-Object Interaction
papers.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinating object acquisition, transport, and release from onboard sensing while responding to user commands and incomplete visual observations. We present ReGATE, a whole-body controller that combines egocentric depth, proprioception, and online locomotion and contact commands. Built on a teacher-student framework, ReGATE integrates interaction-state estimation through a recurrent adapter that predicts object geometry and physical contact without an external object-pose estimator. Head-wise and global gates regulate visual updates to a proprioceptive pathway. A visual-grounding and corruption curriculum trains the adapter, while phase-aware initialization increases coverage of brief contact transitions. In simulation, ReGATE achieves 85.2% success across 330 static-object acquisition trials, compared with 48.5% for VisualMimic under the same protocol, and 85.9% across 440 moving-object acquisition trials. Deployment on a Unitree G1 demonstrates commanded grasp-transport-release sequences and acquisition of laterally displaced boxes. A qualitative hardware experiment further demonstrates successful box acquisition when the camera is occluded after an initial observation and before the contact command. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to extend recurrent gated fusion of onboard depth and proprioception from perceptive locomotion to humanoid loco-manipulation under interrupted visual sensing.

papers.intro:
Humanoid robots offer the potential to perform object interaction in human-centered environments [1, 2]. Their embodiment enables coordinated whole-body behaviors that integrate locomotion, grasping, and object transport [3, 4]. A deployable controller must coordinate these stages from onboard sensing and support user-specified locomotion and contact commands. Learning-based methods have enabled increasingly robust humanoid–object interaction through reinforcement learning and motion imitation [5, 6, 7, 2, 8]. However, many existing systems either track predefined interaction motions [6, 7] or rely on object states obtained from external motion-capture systems [8], limiting their deployment outside instrumented environments. Recent methods address this limitation using perceptive closed-loop control. Some estimate object states through explicit perception pipelines [9, 4, 1], while others distill privileged interaction policies into visuomotor students operating from onboard observations [10, 3]. Despite this progress, executing a complete interaction remains challenging when the controller must perceive the object for closed-loop interaction and adapt the interaction online to user commands.

Three challenges are particularly important for robust HOI. First, obtaining object states through external perception packages introduces additional engineering dependencies and may propagate estimation errors to the controller. An end-to-end policy should instead infer the task-relevant object state directly from onboard depth and proprioceptive history. Second, the reliability of depth observations changes throughout an interaction. Occlusion by the object or the robot body, missing measurements, latency, and frozen frames can make visual evidence unreliable, requiring the controller to preserve a stable proprioceptive interaction belief while selectively incorporating useful visual information. Third, the controller must respond to user-defined locomotion and contact commands rather than rigidly replaying a reference trajectory. This requires coordinated adaptation of whole-body motion and contact behavior across different stages of object manipulation.

ReGATE operates from onboard proprioception and egocentric depth, together with a user command specifying planar velocity, yaw rate, and desired contact state, allowing the user to adjust robot movement and contact timing during deployment. At the core of ReGATE is a recurrent gated fusion adapter that estimates task-relevant object state directly from depth observations and proprioceptive history. The adapter augments each depth frame with image coordinates and encodes it into spatial tokens using a convolutional encoder and recurrent visual memory. Cross-attention retrieves visual evidence conditioned on the current proprioceptive state and user command. Head-wise and global gates regulate the contribution of this fused evidence, while an always-active proprioceptive pathway maintains the interaction representation when depth becomes unreliable. The fused representation is decoded under auxiliary supervision into object pose and physical contact. These predictions are then temporally aggregated to reconstruct the interaction latent learned by the privileged teacher. A visual curriculum first grounds the depth pathway under clean observations and subsequently introduces occlusion and sensing corruption. We evaluate ReGATE on a box pickup and carrying HOI task under online command variations, contact transitions, and visual degradation. Across the tested box-picking scenarios, ReGATE localizes the object from onboard depth and completes commanded grasp–transport–release sequences under both nominal and degraded visual observations.

papers.title: Flux vector splittings and semi-implicit finite volume schemes for an isentropic two-phase flow model
papers.abstract: We present two new semi-implicit finite volume schemes for the 1D hyperbolic and thermodynamically compatible (HTC) isentropic two-phase flow model of Romenski et al., written in terms of mixture density, volume fraction, partial gas density, mixture momentum and the relative phase velocity. In gas-liquid mixtures, the sound speed of the weakly compressible liquid is much larger than the gas sound speed and flow velocity, so the time step of fully explicit discretizations is dictated by liquid acoustic waves, even when the interest lies in the dynamics of the gas. To overcome this difficulty, the model's flux is split at the continuous level into an explicit subsystem (gas dynamics) and an implicit subsystem (liquid acoustic waves), leading to a nonlinear system for liquid pressure solved with the Newton method. In the first splitting the entire liquid phase is treated implicitly, while in the second the liquid convective terms are moved to the explicit subsystem, so only liquid acoustic waves are treated implicitly and nested Picard iterations are avoided. Thus, the time step of both schemes is restricted only by flow velocities and gas sound speed, independent of liquid sound speed. We prove and numerically confirm that both schemes exactly preserve the Abgrall condition (uniform velocity and pressure across material interfaces). For well-prepared initial data, both schemes are consistent with the volume balance of the liquid's low Mach number limit. Riemann problems, pressure equilibrium tests and acoustic tests show that in non-stiff regimes the semi-implicit schemes reproduce the results of a fully explicit scheme, while in the stiff regime they allow time steps that are up to 3-4 orders of magnitude larger, avoiding the excessive numerical dissipation of explicit schemes whose numerical viscosity is dictated by liquid sound speed.

Multi-phase flows have been widely investigated over the last decades in order to describe different types of phenomena involving interactions between different phases, such as gas–liquid flows in energy systems, particle-laden flows in environmental applications, and reactive flows in chemical engineering [20, 28, 19, 14]. Many multi-phase systems are described using diffuse interface models, in which the interface is represented as a thin transition region of finite width rather than as a sharp boundary. The seminal Baer–Nunziato model introduced in [2] is the cornerstone of the description of compressible two-phase flows and has inspired many alternative models, which differ in the closure relations and in the relaxation parameters, see [8, 11, 12, 15, 16, 23, 34, 35, 36]. Among the various approaches, the hyperbolic and thermodynamically compatible (HTC) two-phase flow model of Romenski et al. [33, 32, 31] is of particular interest because it admits a conservative formulation, which is advantageous for the theoretical analysis. The first derivation of this model is based on the theory of symmetric hyperbolic thermodynamically compatible systems [17]. Since then, several studies have been devoted to the analytical and numerical investigation of this model [37, 22, 38, 30], and in [14] it has been extended to an arbitrary number of phases, including viscous fluids and elastoplastic solids. In a recent work [29], the model has been derived from the multispecies Boltzmann equation, which yields explicit expressions for the coefficients and the evolution equation of the volume fraction directly from kinetic theory.

For classical explicit finite volume schemes the time step is restricted by the fastest waves of both phases [33, 31], and schemes of Rusanov type, whose numerical viscosity is proportional to the largest signal speed, become very dissipative on the slow gas and material waves, so that very fine grids are needed to achieve acceptable accuracy. Several strategies have been proposed to overcome this difficulty, see e.g. [22], where acoustic waves and material waves are treated separately by a semi-implicit approach. The time step is then restricted only by the material waves, which therefore remain well resolved. In the present work, instead, the gas phase is discretized entirely explicitly, and only the liquid phase, or only its acoustic waves, is treated implicitly. A different remedy, which keeps a fully explicit discretization and hence the acoustic restriction of the time step, has recently been proposed in [13] for the HTC multiphase model, where the numerical viscosity dissipates the jumps of the volume fractions only on the scale of the material velocity and the jumps of the thermodynamic state of each phase on the acoustic scale.

The idea of treating the pressure terms implicitly, while the nonlinear convective terms are discretized explicitly, goes back to the pressure method of Casulli and Greenspan for transient compressible flows [5] and to the semi-implicit finite difference schemes of Casulli for the shallow water equations [7], in which the free surface elevation is obtained from a discrete wave equation, so that the time step is no longer restricted by the celerity of the surface gravity waves. For the compressible Euler equations at low Mach number, Klein, Munz and co-workers have derived semi-implicit schemes from a multiple pressure variables asymptotic analysis, which reduce to a projection method for the incompressible Euler equations in the zero Mach number limit [21, 24]. Within this line of research, Park and Munz [27] proposed the first conservative flow solver for all Mach numbers based on a pressure-based semi-implicit scheme on a staggered grid, in which the physical flux of the Euler equations is split at the continuous level into an advection system, discretized explicitly, and a pressure system, discretized implicitly. papers.title: Sentiment sensing: comparative analysis of multilingual sentiment dynamics
papers.abstract: Cross-country sentiment analysis faces three fundamental challenges: language-specific biases distort comparisons, compositional data constraints invalidate standard statistics and temporal dynamics lack rigorous testing frameworks. We introduce sentiment sensing, a framework that addresses these gaps through integrated statistical methods. By combining compositional data analysis, functional data methods, and non-parametric inference, sentiment sensing enables valid multilingual comparisons and statistically defensible detection of sentiment shifts. Our framework has been tested in two case studies, analyzing news articles from the 27 countries of the European Union on the topics of energy and artificial intelligence. Sentiment sensing focuses on multilingual sentiment analysis enabling rigorous comparative science.
papers.intro:
Sentiment analysis has grown remarkably (Rodríguez-Ibánez et al.,, 2023), driven by huge volumes of social media data and proven utility across diverse domains including marketing, politics, economics, health, and crisis management. Recent applications have demonstrated sentiment analysis’s capacity to detect emotional responses during the COVID-19 pandemic across more than 100 countries (Wang et al.,, 2022), detect the impact of major events such as volcanic eruptions in real-time social media streams (Farquharson,, 2025), and reveal long-term trends in news media negativity spanning two decades (Rozado et al.,, 2022).

Sentiment analysis has grown remarkably (Rodríguez-Ibánez et al.,, 2023), driven by huge volumes of social media data and proven utility across diverse domains including marketing, politics, economics, health, and crisis management. Recent applications have demonstrated sentiment analysis’s capacity to detect emotional responses during the COVID-19 pandemic across more than 100 countries (Wang et al.,, 2022), detect the impact of major events such as volcanic eruptions in real-time social media streams (Farquharson,, 2025), and reveal long-term trends in news media negativity spanning two decades (Rozado et al.,, 2022).

Despite these advances, significant methodological gaps remain in comparative sentiment analysis, particularly for multilingual corpora across countries, languages, and cultural contexts. Existing approaches are hindered by language-specific biases, lack standardized methods for temporal comparison, and provide limited statistical support for detecting significant sentiment shifts across heterogeneous corpora. These limitations become especially problematic when comparing sentiment trends across countries with different languages, media ecosystems, and baseline sentiment distributions—precisely the scenario in European Union discourse analysis.

Most sentiment analysis research has focused on improving classification accuracy (improving the ability of models to label text as positive, neutral, or negative) achieving remarkable advances in model architectures, from lexica to transformers (A Semary et al.,, 2024; Stefanovitch et al.,, 2022; Jabbari Tofighi and Alhajj,, 2025). Far less attention has been paid to the problem of how to analyze the resulting sentiment labels. As a consequence, different commercial and academic tools often produce substantially different outputs on the same data, with companies not providing detailed information on how their results and analyses are obtained (Rodríguez-Ibánez et al.,, 2023). As a matter of fact, research has focused on comparing architectures, reporting benchmark accuracies, and fine-tuning for specific domains (Rodríguez-Ibánez et al.,, 2023; Wang et al.,, 2022; Rozado et al.,, 2022; Farquharson,, 2025; Jabbari Tofighi and Alhajj,, 2025). Once sentiment labels are assigned, analysis frequently consists of plotting proportions over time, computing descriptive statistics, visually inspecting trends, or using Granger causality (Granger,, 1969). Our framework improves on these approaches, making it easy to perform statistically meaningful comparisons across languages.

Our framework improves on these approaches, making it easy to perform statistically meaningful comparisons across languages.

In multilingual settings, multilinguality is seen as important as it enables sentiment classification for low-resource languages (Zhao et al.,, 2024; Přibáň et al.,, 2024). Beyond performance differences across languages (Wang et al.,, 2022), sentiment classifiers exhibit systematic, language-dependent biases that distort cross-country comparisons. For example, if a model assigns 80% neutral labels to German texts but only 40% to French texts with identical sentiment distributions, then a direct comparison of sentiment proportions becomes misleading. Standard accuracy metrics applied to the classifier predictions are not designed to detect or correct for such distributional biases, and therefore provide limited guidance for comparative analysis.

A further challenge arises from the compositional nature of sentiment data: outputs are proportions summing to one, belonging to a constrained simplex rather than unconstrained Euclidean space. Many standard statistical methods cannot be used with compositional data. Nevertheless, sentiment is often aggregated using raw proportions, net sentiment score11 1 An industry convention, e.g. used in Medallia https://docs.medallia.com/en/medallia-agile-research/text-analysis/net-sentiment-score-nss., or compound metrics such as those produced by the VADER tool (Youvan,, 2024). These approaches ignore compositional constraints, violating standard statistical assumptions. Compositional data analysis addresses this limitation through logratio transformations that map proportions to unconstrained real-valued spaces (Pawlowsky-Glahn et al.,, 2015). Recent studies have begun applying such transformations to sentiment analysis, enabling valid regression and hypothesis testing while preserving relative information (Marti-Ochoa et al.,, 2025; Haines et al.,, 2025).

Finally, most sentiment studies lack a comparison with a baseline. Analyzing sentiment within a topic in isolation cannot distinguish topic-specific patterns from global media shifts. For example, a drop in positive sentiment about energy may reflect the topic itself, seasonal effects, or wide changes in journalistic tone. Comparing topic-specific sentiment against a reference baseline drawn from general discourse provides a way to control for such confounders. In addition, comparing per-country baselines and the topic-specific data addresses any potential language-dependent bias.

These limitations are increasingly consequential as organizations and policymakers rely on sentiment analysis for critical decisions (Rodríguez-Ibánez et al.,, 2023). While classifiers produce labels, it is the subsequent analysis that produces understanding, determining whether observed sentiment levels are unusual, change over time, or differ systematically across groups. To address these gaps, we present sentiment sensing, an integrated statistical framework which focuses on what to do with the sentiment labels, providing a statistically-sound framework for quantitative inter-country (inter-language) sentiment analysis via intra-country comparisons, answering the questions: (i) How different is the sentiment of the thematic corpus from the sentiment of the baseline corpus in the period considered? papers.title: A multivariate unsupervised lognormal-GPD mixture for dependent losses
papers.abstract: We propose a multivariate two-population mixture distribution for heavy-tailed and positively skewed non-negative data. The first mixture population is a multivariate lognormal, while the second is a distribution obtained by joining univariate zero-mean generalized Pareto densities via a Gumbel copula. The model is unsupervised, since no threshold has to be set or estimated. We derive some properties of the distribution and develop an Expectation-Conditional Maximization algorithm for maximum likelihood estimation, which is found to perform well in multivariate contexts beyond the bivariate case. The finite-sample properties of the estimators are assessed by means of simulation experiments, and an empirical application to aggregated commercial property-casualty insurance claims illustrates the impact of dependence on risk estimation. All the methods are implemented in the R package MultLognGPD, available on Github.

papers.intro:
Spliced and mixture distributions are commonly used models for losses in non-life insurance applications. Indeed, in many cases, no single probability distribution is flexible enough to fit all the data, since the bulk and the upper tail exhibit different features. On one hand, many “small” losses can be fitted by classical size distributions, such as the lognormal, the Weibull or the gamma (see, e.g., Kleiber and Kotz,, 2003). On the other hand, the upper tail is typically heavy, with the largest observations well modeled by a Pareto-type distribution (Embrechts et al.,, 1997; Panjer,, 2006). In addition, accurately estimating, and possibly extrapolating, the tail is crucial for risk management purposes, where the focus is on the largest losses.

In addition, accurately estimating, and possibly extrapolating, the tail is crucial for risk management purposes, where the focus is on the largest losses.

The extension of spliced and mixture models to the multivariate case is challenging and therefore less studied, despite the fact that losses are often not independent. To fill this gap, we propose a mixture of a multivariate lognormal and a multivariate distribution with Generalized Pareto univariate marginals. Building a tail model based on the Generalized Pareto distribution (GPD) constitutes a well-grounded approach to rare events estimation, motivated by a wide body of Extreme Value Theory (EVT) theoretical results, which provide us with a very effective theoretical framework for these tasks (Beirlant et al.,, 1994).

We show that maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) can be carried out by means of an Expectation-Conditional Maximization algorithm. Despite the large number of parameters, this method works well even in large dimensions, thanks to the better separation of the two populations when the dimension increases. This feature, which will be discussed and checked via simulation in the following, is a distinctive trait of mixture distributions, which mitigates the “curse of dimensionality” issues often associated to large-dimensional single-population distributions.

papers.title: Depth Anyviewpoint? Evaluating Monocular Depth Over Viewpoint Sequences
papers.abstract: Monocular depth estimation aims to predict depth maps from single RGB images (forgoing the need for stereo camera pairs) and has seen impressive leaps in performance in recent work due to the introduction of affine-invariant losses and the use of foundation model features. These monocular depth models predict affine-invariant depth, which describes the relative positions of objects in the scene instead of absolute depth. While these models demonstrate strong performance on single image benchmarks and qualitatively consistent predictions in video, their effectiveness at preserving consistent spatial structure has been less thoroughly explored. Many potential real-world applications, such as handling video streams as input, rely on coherent three dimensional consistency in scenes. Further, anchoring relative depth predictions to a metric reference for a given scene is a key challenge for applying monocular depth models to real-world situations. We develop a novel evaluation protocol for monocular depth models using video sequences with moving camera positions to test the consistency of prediction across variation in viewpoint. We demonstrate this methodology over diverse, real-world video sequences where we are able to anchor depth model output to metric depth values using structure from motion. Our work demonstrates open challenges in the development of broadly applicable monocular depth foundation models, particularly with their ability to provide temporal consistency over long time frames. We also identify challenges in the straightforward adoption of structure-from-motion as a metric grounding tool for monocular depth estimation models.

papers.intro:
In a wide array of computer vision applications, depth information from a camera system is vital. To produce depth maps, the two most common approaches are stereoscopic depth and structure from motion. Stereoscopic depth relies on a calibrated pair of cameras, which may be infeasible for applications without control over the hardware (such as arbitrary non-stereo datasets) or in which stereoscopic hardware may be cost or weight prohibitive. Structure-from-motion (SfM) can reconstruct depth from a single camera, but it requires multiple camera views which may be time consuming or impractical to acquire for some tasks [1].

To produce depth maps, the two most common approaches are stereoscopic depth and structure from motion. Stereoscopic depth relies on a calibrated pair of cameras, which may be infeasible for applications without control over the hardware (such as arbitrary non-stereo datasets) or in which stereoscopic hardware may be cost or weight prohibitive. Structure-from-motion (SfM) can reconstruct depth from a single camera, but it requires multiple camera views which may be time consuming or impractical to acquire for some tasks [1].

Monocular depth estimation (MDE) aims to provide an alternative method for retrieving depth information by predicting depth from a single RGB image. Recent innovations make use of affine-invariant loss and pre-trained foundation models to greatly improve the effectiveness of monocular depth models [2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. While the ability to directly recover metric depth is limited with these models, they have shown remarkable promise in recovering relative depth within a scene. Additionally, although relative depth has inherent limitations for many real-world situations and tasks, MDE models show particular strengths in providing high density depth maps, even in low-texture areas, showcasing distinct advantages over traditional depth estimation methods. There is therefore significant promise for the application of monocular depth models in robotics and other scene understanding tasks due to their potential for high resolution with cheap inference [3, 6].

Standard metrics for evaluating monocular depth models include absolute relative error (AbsRel) and proportion of pixels not exceeding 25% relative error (δ1\delta_{1}) [4, 2, 3, 6]. While these metrics together effectively convey performance over a given image, they are typically calculated by treating test images as independent, and may potentially missing biases in model effectiveness for less well represented viewpoints. Additionally, testing individual frames does not provide an estimate of model spatial coherence for a static scene as the viewpoint changes. Recent work has considered the need for spatial coherence in adapting monocular depth prediction to video [4, 7, 8], introducing coherence measures to both loss and evaluation. However, the spatial coherence of the depth predictions has been assessed only across adjacent frames or through qualitative assessment. This focus on short-term consistency could potentially be missing accumulated errors over the entire video sequence. Similarly, these metrics are reported as averages, ignoring potentially rare but significant short-term errors in spatiotemporal consistency that could substantially reduce MDE reliability in the real world.

Similarly, these metrics are reported as averages, ignoring potentially rare but significant short-term errors in spatiotemporal consistency that could substantially reduce MDE reliability in the real world.

papers.title: Learning Purposeful Co-designs of Bio-inspired Quadrupedal Robots
papers.abstract: Treating morphology and control as separate design problems has constrained the efficiency and adaptability of quadrupedal robots, while current co-design approaches are often constrained by restricted design spaces. We overcome this limit by introducing Dogger, a bio-inspired quadruped with modular three-segment legs, four-bar linkages and adjustable passive knee compliance. A two-stage framework combining reinforcement learning and Bayesian optimization is developed: the morphology-conditioned control policy is trained across designs and then held fixed during task-specific design selection. The resulting designs and policies deployed zero-shot reduce the cost of transport by 18.6% and 35.7% for inspection and payload-carrying tasks. Comparisons demonstrate that full geometry-compliance co-design outperforms fixed and restricted design scopes. Cross-task tests further reveal distinct task-specific morphologies with shared mechanical trade-offs. These results provide hardware-level evidence that expanding the physical design space alongside learned control is essential to realize the full potential of task-driven morphology-control co-design in legged robotics.

Animals exhibit diverse forms of agile, efficient and adaptable locomotion through the close integration of morphology, neural control and behaviour. This coupling continues to inspire the design of legged robots capable of meeting different task demands [46, 42, 14, 23].

Inspired by the natural muscle-skeleton system, passive elastic actuators, especially parallel elastic actuators (PEAs), are incorporated into the quadrupedal design, improving robustness, reducing energy consumption or generating highly dynamic motions [7, 45, 44, 6, 2, 39]. On the other hand, learning-based controllers have enabled quadrupeds to traverse challenging terrain [33, 27, 29], locomote over deformable surfaces [10], and perform agile or adaptive multi-skill behaviours [24, 21, 26, 49]. Yet these controllers are typically developed for a specified mechanical platform, whose leg geometry and passive mechanics shape the dynamics and energy exchanges underlying locomotion. Changes to these properties may therefore require policy retraining or hardware-specific adjustment. Physical legged robots provide concrete examples: Badri-Spröwitz et al. developed BirdBot, which uses avian-inspired geometry and passive clutching to support energy-efficient locomotion with minimal active control [3]; Ruppert and Badri-Spröwitz matched a closed-loop central pattern generator (CPG) to passive elastic dynamics [39]; and Stella et al. embedded behavioral synergies in tendon routing, pulley geometry, and joint stiffness [46]. Together, these studies highlight the importance of coordinating mechanical structure and control, as further illustrated by the system-level energy-efficiency improvements demonstrated by RAIBO2 [28]. They motivate a broader design question: How should morphology and control be jointly optimized to meet different task demands?

Morphology-control co-design offers a promising way to address this question. Evolutionary approaches search mechanical design and gait or controller parameters [12], while trajectory-optimization and control-aware methods incorporate design variables into motion optimization [20, 11, 13]. Reinforcement learning (RL) approaches have explored concurrent learning of agent design and behaviour, including frameworks that couple online and offline learning [40, 19, 48, 32, 9]. Other approaches combine learning with trajectory optimization or evolutionary search [17, 18], or couple evolutionary design search with optimal control [15]. Meta-RL and design-conditioned policies further support the evaluation of candidate morphologies by reusing learned control across designs [5, 6]. Collectively, these approaches have broadened the available optimization strategies. However, an algorithmic formulation alone does not determine which mechanical variables can be changed in a real robot, how readily candidate designs can be fabricated and exchanged, or whether predicted improvements persist after hardware deployment.
