Most directly related to this work, Bjelonic et al. combined a design-conditioned RL policy with Bayesian optimization (BO) to co-design passive knee elasticity and locomotion control on ANYmal [6]. Their study demonstrated learning-based physical co-design with a mechanical search focused on passive knee elasticity. Design optimization used a teacher policy, whereas a distilled student policy was deployed on hardware. These advances demonstrate the practical value of co-design, while leaving open how different mechanical design freedoms should be combined for a given task. In particular, optimizing passive compliance within a prescribed leg geometry does not establish whether jointly varying geometry and compliance yields additional benefits, or how these benefits change across tasks. Systematically investigating these questions on hardware calls for a platform that supports controlled variation of geometry and compliance, together with a control framework for evaluating candidate designs and deploying the selected configurations.

By aligning an expressive physical substrate with advanced co-design algorithms, we provide a systematic real-world demonstration that morphology–control co-design yields substantial gains in quadrupedal locomotion under specific task requirements. This overarching contribution unfolds through three key technical advances: • Modular quadruped Dogger. We introduce a modular quadruped for systematic morphological variation. papers.title: Algorithmic Intervention Decreases Polarization in Content Moderation
papers.abstract: Crowd-based moderation relies on people's collective judgments to combat misinformation, but raters bring their own ideological biases to the task, shaping how they moderate each other's contributions. We ask whether an algorithmic redesign can counteract this bias, using X's Community Notes, where contributors write context for potentially misleading posts and rate each other's notes. Community Notes replaced simple majority voting with an algorithm that instead rewards agreement across people with different ideological viewpoints. Comparing 8,805 notes and 4,367 contributors before and after this change, we find that ideological polarization decreased in the algorithm's estimates of contributor and note positions. Although negative interactions increased, contributors became less structurally aligned, indicating that negative interactions were less organized along partisan lines. These findings show that algorithmic incentives can reshape both the social structure and behavioral dynamics of crowds, extending beyond their intended effects on content moderation.

papers.intro:
Social media algorithms are often blamed for amplifying the societal harms of social media. By prioritizing rapid information diffusion [1] and personalizing content based on user behavior [2], these algorithms have been linked to the spread of misinformation, political polarization, and the erosion of public discourse [3], with consequences for public health [4, 5] and democratic processes [6, 7]. But what happens when an algorithm is designed to reduce polarization rather than amplify it? This question is particularly important for content moderation systems, where platforms must respond to harmful content at the speed and scale at which it spreads, without sacrificing accuracy, user trust, or freedom of expression.

But what happens when an algorithm is designed to reduce polarization rather than amplify it? This question is particularly important for content moderation systems, where platforms must respond to harmful content at the speed and scale at which it spreads, without sacrificing accuracy, user trust, or freedom of expression.

Social media platforms have relied on professional fact-checkers to fight misinformation. This approach has proven effective: fact-checking can reduce the spread of false information and improve the accuracy of users’ beliefs [8, 9]. However, its limitations are equally well documented. Professional fact-checking is labor-intensive, operates slowly relative to the speed at which content can go viral, and is difficult to scale to the volume of claims circulating daily on large platforms [10, 11]. Fact-checking has also faced criticism regarding potential political and cultural bias. A 2019 survey found that approximately half of Americans believed that fact-checkers were biased, with this perception being substantially more prevalent among Republicans than Democrats [12]. Such perceptions can undermine the perceived legitimacy of moderation systems.

In response to these limitations, several major platforms have begun shifting from expert-driven moderation towards community-based systems, in which users themselves can act as fact-checkers by collectively evaluating and annotating potentially misleading content. A prominent example of such initiatives is Community Notes (Birdwatch), which was first introduced on X (Twitter) [13] and is currently being implemented by Meta [14]. In Community Notes, contributors write notes to add missing context or correct potentially misleading information. Other contributors rate the helpfulness of these notes, and an algorithm uses these ratings to determine which notes are displayed to users [15].

Early evidence suggests that Community Notes can achieve levels of accuracy comparable to those of professional fact-checkers [16, 17], while offering a more scalable and cost-effective alternative to expert-based models [18, 19]. Community-based notes may also be more persuasive because users tend to prefer contextual explanations over authoritative declarations of truth [20]. Moreover, Community Notes are a less intrusive intervention, as users retain the autonomy to engage with or disregard the information in the notes [21].

To address this problem, X replaced the majority rule with a bridging algorithm [27]. The algorithm uses historical rating patterns to estimate latent positions for contributors and notes, which are then used to weight ratings when calculating a note’s helpfulness. Consequently, positive ratings from contributors who have disagreed with each other in the past, carry more weight than the ones who usually agree. The redesign therefore shifted the aggregation mechanism from relying primarily on the proportion of positive ratings toward accounting for the diversity of rating patterns.

papers.title: CrowdForge: Effects of Audio and Visual Audience Participation Modalities on Agency, Collaboration, and Engagement in AI-Mediated MR Performances
papers.abstract: Technology-mediated audience participation (TMAP) enables audiences to influence live performances, yet balancing interaction with meaningful agency remains challenging. While AI-generated music and MR enable new forms of audio and visual audience participation, little is known about how these participation modalities influence audience experiences during live musical performance. In particular, it remains unclear how they shape perceived agency, collaboration, and engagement, and how they complement one another within TMAP systems. We present CrowdForge, an AI- and MR-mediated paradigm where audiences collectively control generative music and virtual environments during a live performance featuring a guitarist and DJ. Through a mixedmethods concert study evaluating three interaction conditions (audio, visual, and combined audio-visual), we demonstrate that observability is the primary driver of audience agency. While visual interaction provided easily observable feedback, audio parameters offered macro-structural control over the music. Audiences tended to use the control enabled by AI audio generation to test musical boundaries, introducing a productive adversarial tension between the crowd and the musicians. This dynamic pushed creative limits, deepened engagement, and generated moments of musical coherence when performers successfully resolved audience-induced challenges. We argue future TMAP systems should prioritize human-centered, highly observable interactions to build agency, while combining the expressiveness of music with the clarity of visual feedback.

papers.intro:
Traditional live music performances are predominantly unidirectional experiences, with minimal interaction between the audience and performers [1]. Participatory music experiences shift this focus and prioritize aspects such as collaborative creativity and community building [2, 3]. Though participatory music experiences are ubiquitous across cultures, and come in many different forms [1, 4, 5], in recent years, the role of technology in facilitating audience participation has become an area of academic and artistic interest [6, 2, 7]. These interdisciplinary artistic works ask us to reconceptualize the traditional paradigm, shifting the experience of music performance towards an exploratory and communal effort. The field of technology-mediated audience participation (TMAP) in live music performance [8] simultaneously celebrates the artistry of trained live musicians and the use of technology as a means of communicating the intentions and sentiments of an audience, thus contributing to the creative process.

As technologies became more sophisticated and interconnected [9, 10], engineers, designers, and artists alike have contributed to this growing field by utilizing a myriad of technological tools [6, 11, 12, 13, 14]. With the growing prevalence of networking, reliance on visual media (e.g., mixed reality, interactive visualizations), and complex engineered systems, TMAPs have begun to touch on many questions central to the musical metaverse [15, 16].

papers.title: Non-backtracking Laplacian for hypergraphs
papers.abstract: We extend the non-backtracking Laplacian for graphs, introduced by Jost, Mulas and Torres, to hypergraphs. The operator is defined on the permutations of the edges and is normalized by the number of edges through which a non-backtracking walk can continue. We show that it satisfies a symmetry that generalizes the graph case, and that it can be obtained from the random walk Laplacian of a directed graph by rescaling if and only if all edges have the same cardinality. Moreover, we show that, up to copies of the eigenvalue $1$, its spectrum can be computed from a much smaller matrix indexed by the incidences of the hypergraph, and we use this reduction to bound the remaining eigenvalues away from $1$.

Spectral graph theory studies the structural properties of a graph that are encoded in the eigenvalues of its associated operators, such as the adjacency matrix and the various Laplacians [15, 12, 21]. Among these, the non-backtracking matrix is of theoretical interest [18, 38, 37] and has proved remarkably effective in applications ranging from community detection [11, 22, 31, 9, 10] to node centrality [4, 23, 24, 36] and percolation [33, 13, 25]. Moreover, in [20], Jost, Mulas and Torres introduced the non-backtracking Laplacian and showed, computationally for graphs with a small number of nodes, that cospectral pairs are rarer for this operator than for the adjacency matrix, the Kirchhoff Laplacian, the normalized Laplacian and the non-backtracking matrix. Further spectral properties of this operator were established in [28], and a graph coloring number arising from that work was studied in [29].

The closest object appears in the literature on hypergraph sampling: Nakajima, Kodakari and Aida [30] consider a non-backtracking walk that avoids both the previously visited node and the previously traversed edge, and derive its stochastic transition matrix on the incidences, together with its stationary distribution, with the aim of obtaining unbiased estimators of structural properties of large hypergraphs. Such a transition matrix does induce a Laplacian; being row-stochastic by construction, however, it is the random walk Laplacian of a weighted directed graph on the incidences, and its spectral theory is therefore that of a directed graph. papers.title: Generative Forecasting from Coarse-Grained Observations: When Does Cascading Help?
papers.abstract: We study probabilistic forecasting of dynamical systems such as fluids and waves from coarse observations. Since the unseen fine scales influence the dynamics, the same coarse initial state can evolve into a whole distribution of futures. Generative forecasters may produce visually plausible samples, but it is hard to tell whether they sample the right conditional distribution, since trajectory data contain a single future for each initial state. We address this problem by generating reference data in a hierarchical way: for each coarse initial state, we generate many different fine-scale components and numerically evolve the full states. Using these conditional ensembles, we show that standard diffusion models and stochastic interpolants make substantial distributional errors. We then show that cascading shorter forecasts greatly reduces these errors for the turbulent flows and waves we study, but we also find and characterize cases in which it hurts. Since the coarse process is not Markov, cascading discards information about the unresolved fine scales even with exact transitions. To understand this, we propose a solvable analytic model which shows that the optimal cascade depth decreases as the coupling between the unresolved and observed scales gets stronger, and increases as the dependence of the forecast on the observation becomes more oscillatory. Consistent with our experiments, cascading is detrimental when the direct forecast is ``easy'' to learn, for example Gaussian as in the passive scalar case. We release our datasets as a first benchmark for probabilistic forecasting with ground-truth conditional ensembles.

papers.title: Outstrumental Variable Regression
papers.abstract: Estimating the causal effect of a treatment $X$ on an outcome $Y$ from observational data in the presence of unobserved confounding requires additional structure or assumptions. Existing identification strategies such as instrumental variable regression exploit exogenous variation in only the treatment. We show that the causal effect can also be identified if the outcome mechanism varies across a finite set of environments, even if the treatment distribution is unchanged. Concretely, we introduce Outstrumental Variable Regression (OVR), which proceeds in three steps: (i) compute the conditional expectation of $Y$ given $X$ in each environment; (ii) form the vector of differences in these conditional expectations between all environments and a reference environment (we call this vector contrast); and (iii) regress $Y$ on $X$ while adjusting for the contrast and environment. We prove that this yields the true causal effect if the following two conditions hold: inclusion restriction, i.e., the contrast determines the conditional confounding bias; and positivity, i.e., the treatment varies sufficiently strongly after adjustment. We prove that a finite-sample version of OVR is consistent under regularity conditions and demonstrate the procedure's effectiveness on synthetic and real-world data.

Estimating the causal effect of a treatment XX on an outcome YY is a central goal of empirical science. Randomized controlled trials (Fisher, 1935) provide a direct solution, but are often infeasible, unethical, or too costly. When only observational data is available, unobserved confounding usually renders causal effects unidentifiable without additional assumptions.

One of the most widely used approaches to this problem is instrumental variable (IV) regression, which has played a central role in estimating causal effects from natural experiments and policy changes (Angrist et al., 1996; Angrist & Pischke, 2009). We propose a complementary identification approach that exploits a different source of information: variation in the ‘outcome channel’, that is, E→YE\to Y (see Fig. 2). Assume EE is categorical and corresponds to different environments in which we observe the data (for example, different sites, time periods, experimental conditions, or policy regimes). papers.title: The Skin Detector System of the LZ Dark Matter Experiment
papers.abstract: This paper presents the design, calibration, and performance of the Skin Detector component of the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) dark matter experiment. The Skin Detector consists of approximately 2 tonnes of liquid xenon instrumented with 131 photomultiplier tubes, surrounding the central time-projection chamber and functions as an active veto system for background rejection. Energy calibration with monoenergetic gamma sources established a position-dependent energy scale and determined prompt and delayed veto thresholds. Radon decays in the Skin can be identified with less than 15~mm spatial resolution, revealing stable convective flow patterns with measured velocities ranging from 2-4 mm/s that persisted throughout extended data-taking periods. The achieved Skin veto threshold meets or exceeds the design goal of 100~keV throughout the Skin volume. The prompt veto efficiency for gamma rays emitted following electron capture in $^{127}$Xe is found to be ($88 \pm 2$)\%, consistent with the simulated value of ($90.4 \pm 0.6$)\%. M-shell EC decays are used to validate the LZ detector sensitivity for low-mass dark matter during the first science run.

In this article, we describe the design and performance of the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) Skin Detector. The LZ experiment [1] is a dark matter direct detection experiment designed to achieve unprecedented sensitivity to weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs), one of the leading candidates for dark matter. Located at the 4850-foot level of the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF) in Lead, South Dakota, USA, LZ utilizes a dual-phase xenon time projection chamber (TPC) to detect nuclear recoils from WIMP interactions. To date, LZ has published results from three science runs, referred to as WS2022 [2], WS2024 [3], and WS2025 [4], with world-leading constraints on spin-independent and spin-dependent WIMP-nucleon cross sections. Figure 1 shows the layout of the LZ experiment.

To date, LZ has published results from three science runs, referred to as WS2022 [2], WS2024 [3], and WS2025 [4], with world-leading constraints on spin-independent and spin-dependent WIMP-nucleon cross sections. Figure 1 shows the layout of the LZ experiment.

Ionizing interactions in the TPC produce two distinct signals: a prompt scintillation pulse (S1) and a delayed electroluminescence pulse (S2) from ionization electrons extracted into the gas phase. Voltages applied to three wire-mesh grid electrodes (cathode, gate, and anode) create the electric field configuration necessary for electron drift, extraction and electroluminescence. The S1 and S2 signals are detected by two arrays of photomultiplier tubes (PMTs) located above and below the LXe TPC volume. The timing and spatial distribution of S1 and S2 allow for three-dimensional event reconstruction, and their relative sizes allow discrimination between nuclear and electronic recoils. However, given the extreme rarity of potential WIMP interactions, additional background suppression is essential. To this end, LZ employs both passive shielding and two active veto systems, the xenon Skin Detector and the Outer Detector (OD).

The Skin Detector, regions 1 and 2 in Fig. 2, refers to the instrumented LXe volume outside the TPC field cage but within the inner cryostat vessel (ICV). The TPC electrodes and the grounded ICV create a horizontal electric field in the Skin volume, approximately within the range 3–6 kV/cm in WS2022 and from 1.5–2 kV/cm in WS2024 and WS2025. With no electroluminescence region, the Skin Detector produces only S1-like signals.

The Skin Detector serves a dual purpose: electrically, it provides the necessary standoff between the biased TPC components and the grounded ICV; functionally, it acts as an active veto for background events. A gamma-ray that Compton scatters in the TPC and then deposits additional energy in the Skin will produce a coincident signal that is inconsistent with the expected single-scatter topology of a WIMP interaction. Similarly, neutrons that scatter in the TPC and are subsequently captured in the Skin or OD can be identified through delayed coincidences. By rejecting such events, the Skin significantly enhances the background rejection capability of the experiment, especially for events near the edge of the detector volume where external backgrounds are more likely to penetrate.

In addition to its veto function, the Skin Detector serves as a diagnostic tool for characterizing the background environment of the experiment. With sufficient light collection and timing resolution, the Skin enables energy and position reconstruction of interactions within its volume. This allows for the identification of radioactive contaminants, such as gamma rays from detector materials, neutron captures, and alpha decays from radon progeny. Notably, the Skin has demonstrated sensitivity to decay chains from 222Rn and 220Rn, enabling spatial mapping of the liquid flow by tracking the decay pairs. The Skin has also been used to tag electron capture decays of xenon isotopes such as 127Xe, which produce low energy Auger electrons and X-rays with associated gamma-ray emission [5].

Section 2 describes the detector geometry, PMT configuration, and readout system. Section 3 details the methods used to calibrate the Skin position and energy scales using external and internal gamma-ray sources. papers.title: A Computational Journey Toward an Optimal Design for Metamaterial Epicardial Passive Sleeves
papers.abstract: Heart failure (HF) following myocardial infarction (MI) is a major clinical challenge with severe complications. Epicardial sleeves and patches are increasingly investigated to improve heart function post-MI, yet their passive mechanical effects remain underexplored. This has resulted in limited insight into how sleeves mechanically interact with the infarct and remote myocardium. This study used 3-D in-silico cardiac models to examine how sleeve shape, material properties, and architecture affect global and regional mechanics. A high-fidelity biventricular model is used to investigate how a continuum cardiac sleeve alters function. Designs that improve regional mechanics successfully limited pathological bulging, modulated fiber strains, and influenced torsional behavior without over-constraining remote tissue, whereas overly restrictive and stiff sleeves penalized healthy myocardium and reduced the intended relief of infarct bulging. These findings highlight the importance of considering regional biomechanical markers when developing sleeve designs. Building on these continuum sleeve insights, a spheroidal left ventricle model demonstrated the proof-of-concept advantage of an "auxetic" metamaterial sleeve, engineered with a negative Poisson ratio. This programmed architecture provided region-specific benefits beyond those of conventional continuum sleeves. Ultimately, this work contributes to an improved understanding of passive sleeve-heart interactions and improves the targeted biomechanical support therapies following MI.

papers.intro:
Myocardial infarction (MI) leads to considerable adverse effects, significantly compromising patients’ quality of life and long-term outcomes. Despite advancements in diagnostic, therapeutic, and post-MI care, nearly 35% of patients go on to develop heart failure (HF), with nearly half of these cases diagnosed within the first three days following infarction [1]. Among this population, the five-year mortality rate remains alarmingly high, reaching up to 40% [2]. The progression of MI to HF contributes significantly to morbidity, mortality, and reduced quality of life [3, 4, 5]. These challenges underscore the critical need for effective therapeutic strategies and the development of innovative, tailored interventions.

Among this population, the five-year mortality rate remains alarmingly high, reaching up to 40% [2]. The progression of MI to HF contributes significantly to morbidity, mortality, and reduced quality of life [3, 4, 5]. These challenges underscore the critical need for effective therapeutic strategies and the development of innovative, tailored interventions.

Current treatments for HF following MI range from pharmacological therapies to advanced implantable devices. Pharmacological therapies such as diuretics, angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, beta-blockers, and angiotensin receptor blockers remain foundational tools for HF management, optimizing cardiac function and reducing workload to manage symptoms effectively [6, 7, 8, 9, 10] while implantable devices play a role through electrical and/or mechanical intervention strategies such as pacemakers, implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD), and cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) devices, offer solutions for regulating heart rhythm, correcting arrhythmias, and stabilizing pumping efficiency [11, 12, 13, 14]. Moreover, emerging technologies such as acellular cardiac patches and epicardial sleeves have shown promise in promoting healing of damaged heart tissue after infarction [15, 16].

Moreover, emerging technologies such as acellular cardiac patches and epicardial sleeves have shown promise in promoting healing of damaged heart tissue after infarction [15, 16].

Despite recent improvements in the therapies available for HF post-MI, those that are characterized by mechanical intervention rely on actuators to mimic or assist with cardiac function, overlooking the potential of passive devices. A significant gap exists in the holistic understanding of the impact of passive implantable devices, particularly passive epicardial sleeves and cardiac patches. Recent innovations in epicardial sleeves include the development of electroconductive patches with auxetic structures [17] and hybrid materials combining bioresorbable materials and polymers [18, 19]. Despite these advancements, the effect of implants and sleeves designed to prevent excessive dilation and limit maladaptive remodeling following HF remains underexplored [20]. Such mechanical restraints may positively affect the local biomechanical environment of the myocardium, reducing the physical maladaptive alterations of heart structure post-MI [15, 16]. Therefore, a pressing need exists to bridge this gap, focusing on a detailed exploration of passive epicardial sleeves and their capacity to guide cardiac remodeling post-MI through meticulously considered design parameters.

In this in-silico study, we investigate how key passive sleeve design parameters, including geometry, mechanical anisotropy, stiffness, and material architecture, influence both infarcted and remote myocardial regions. We analyze two distinct sleeve families: continuum sleeves, which are modeled as transversely isotropic continua with tunable stiffness and fiber orientation, and auxetic sleeves, whose unit-cell geometry generates material behavior with a negative Poisson’s ratio (ν<0\nu<0). By integrating organ-level functional markers, such as ejection fraction and stroke volume, with regional indices, such as fiber strain, our computational framework provides a multiscale view of how design modifications impact cardiac function. This methodical exploration of a broad design space is crucial for enabling patient-specific optimization and for guiding future experimental validation of promising designs. Ultimately, tailored implantable devices could provide regional mechanical support to promote adaptive remodeling of the myocardium in HF patients following MI.

papers.title: DiffStent: Surrogate Adjoint Differentiation for Stent Deployment in Anisotropic Arteries
papers.abstract: We present DiffStent, a differentiable finite element framework for simulating arterial deformation during in silico stent deployment, where nearly incompressible, anisotropic vessel walls undergo large deformation and frictional contact with the stent. DiffStent combines the fiber-reinforced Holzapfel-Gasser-Ogden constitutive model with an implicit discrete adjoint that differentiates the converged mechanical equilibrium without unrolling the nonlinear solver, thus reducing the memory cost by three orders of magnitude. We identify three mechanisms that can lead to inaccurate, unstable, or uninformative gradients: nonsmooth switching, state mismatch, and gradient cancellation. To address these, we apply a contact surrogate in the backward pass while retaining the original physical model in the forward pass. We show superior gradient accuracy of our method over AutoDiff and finite differencing across constitutive benchmarks, idealized stented vessels, and patient-specific calcified coronary anatomies, and use the resulting sensitivities to quantify how tissue properties and calcification patterns govern lumen expansion and arterial wall stress. Finally, we demonstrate that DiffStent enables gradient-based system identification from retrospective clinical images of atherosclerotic coronary anatomy. Together, these results establish a practical approach for differentiating through nonlinear biomechanical simulations with stiff constitutive laws and nonsmooth contact, enabling patient-specific parameter inference and optimization in computational cardiovascular mechanics.

papers.intro:
Predicting how soft tissues deform under mechanical contact is necessary for planning interventions, designing endovascular devices, and simulating surgery. These deformations depend on the tissue’s material properties and fiber architecture: arteries distend under pressure (Taheri et al., 2026), ventricular myocardium twists during a cardiac pulse (Li et al., 2025a), and skeletal muscle bulges during contraction (Guzman et al., 2025). The properties governing these responses are difficult to measure directly, but can be inferred from observed deformation. This inference requires determining how sensitive a simulated result, like lumen gain, is to changes in tissue properties. One method of obtaining these sensitivities is differential simulation, which enables efficient gradient-based optimization to recover material information from a forward model deployment. Although differentiable simulators have been developed for rigid bodies, articulated robots, fluids, and elastic solids (Hu et al., 2020; Qiao et al., 2020; Du et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2021; Li et al., 2022; Li et al., 2024), computing reliable sensitivities for anisotropic tissues undergoing large deformation and device contact remains challenging.

For anisotropic tissues, these sensitivities must account for cross-linking fiber orientations, spatially varying material properties, and mechanical loads transmitted through device contact. Existing methods address parts of this problem. Neural Modular Physics (Li et al., 2025b) learns constitutive and time-integration modules and adapts to unknown material behavior and external forces from observed motion, but does not provide accurate gradients for fiber-reinforced anisotropic tissues interacting with devices. Fiber-reinforced constitutive laws (Holzapfel et al., 2000; Gasser et al., 2005; Holzapfel & Ogden, 2009) govern tissue mechanics, but merely computing deformation does not provide the sensitivities needed to infer tissue parameters from observed deformation or to select a balloon pressure that achieves the desired lumen expansion while limiting wall stress. Unrolling every step of a physics solver to obtain these gradients is computationally prohibitive as the cost scales with the number of model parameters. Moreover, exponential stiffening and mathematical discontinuities can compromise simulation gradients (Suh et al., 2022). Recent contact methods respond with surrogate gradients that sidestep the pathologies of the forward model (Paulus et al., 2026). However, these models face additional difficulties within the tissue: tension-only fiber recruitment can make the tangent stiffness discontinuous, while near-incompressibility can make the equilibrium system ill-conditioned. During stent deployment, these material effects interact with contact activation as the balloon expands the stent against the artery. We therefore ask: can we develop a method for accurate yet efficient computation of gradients in fiber-reinforced tissues under contact to enable tissue parameter identification from observed deformation and balloon-pressure optimization for a desired clinical outcome?

papers.title: OPALX: A performance-portable framework for particle accelerator simulations
papers.abstract: Accurate charged-particle beam simulations require self-consistent collective fields and realistic accelerator models, while their computational cost motivates efficient use of heterogeneous computing systems. We present OPALX, a performance-portable accelerator simulation framework that builds on the beam-dynamics capabilities of OPAL. Its modular architecture uses the Independent Parallel Particle Layer (IPPL) and Kokkos to support distributed-memory execution on multicore CPUs and GPUs from a common codebase. The framework combines relativistic particle tracking with prescribed accelerator fields, particle-in-cell space charge calculations, and spin tracking. We describe the physical and numerical models and their integration into the simulation workflow. The implementation is assessed using disorder-induced heating and frozen-spin test cases, together with comparisons of spin evolution with G4Beamline and beam transport with TraceWin. A three-dimensional space charge benchmark evaluates throughput on CPU and GPU systems, reaching approximately $10^9$ macroparticles per second on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU for this benchmark. These results provide initial verification of the implemented models and demonstrate CPU and GPU execution of self-consistent space charge calculations. OPALX provides a common foundation for extending accelerator models and numerical methods across heterogeneous computing platforms.

papers.intro:
Numerical simulations are essential to the design and operation of particle accelerators. For high-intensity and high-brightness beams, accurate predictions require realistic accelerator fields and a self-consistent treatment of collective effects. Space charge can modify beam sizes, emittances, halo formation, and particle losses, particularly in low-energy accelerators and injectors [37, 16]. In dense beams, discrete Coulomb interactions can introduce additional evolution beyond the smooth space charge field [33, 26]. The interplay between space charge and intrabeam scattering (IBS) can further affect beam evolution in regimes where both collective and collisional effects are significant [49, 48]. Resolving these processes can require large particle ensembles, fine meshes, and many integration steps, making efficient parallel computation an integral part of accelerator modeling [36, 17].

The increasing use of heterogeneous computing systems creates a need to execute these calculations efficiently on both multicore CPUs and GPUs. OPALX addresses this challenge through a modular computational framework based on the Independent Parallel Particle Layer (IPPL) [27] and Kokkos [41]. IPPL supplies distributed particle and field data structures, particle–mesh operations, and field solvers; Kokkos provides abstractions for parallel execution and memory management within each process. Together with communication through the Message Passing Interface (MPI) [25], these dependencies allow accelerator models to use a common source implementation across CPU and GPU platforms.

The program organizes particle advancement, accelerator components, external-field evaluation, collective-field calculations, and diagnostics through common interfaces. papers.title: Feedback Stability of Discrete-Time LTI Systems via Frequency-Wise Scaled Relative Graphs
papers.abstract: This paper studies the stability of negative-feedback interconnections of proper, stable discrete-time multivariable linear time-invariant (LTI) systems using scaled relative graphs (SRGs). We propose a frequency-wise condition that compares the SRGs of the two subsystems'frequency-response matrices only at the same frequency along a feedback-scaling homotopy. We prove that this condition guarantees well-posedness along the homotopy and $\ell_2$-stability for both single-input single-output (SISO) and multi-input multi-output (MIMO) subsystems, without requiring the chord property or nonsingular frequency-response matrices. An equivalent form exchanges scaling and geometric inversion. We also derive an operator-level condition from the SRG closures of the convolution operators and show that it implies the frequency-wise condition. Numerical examples show that the operator-level condition is more conservative because it depends on intersections between responses at different frequencies.

In data-driven control, controllers are designed directly from data rather than from a model, and certifying closed-loop stability without an accurate model remains difficult. SRGs are promising for this purpose because the SRG of a discrete-time LTI system can be computed directly from input–output data, and a robust SRG computed from noisy data is guaranteed to contain the true system’s SRG [18]. However, existing work on discrete-time SRGs has focused on their computation [18, 19], and SRG-based stability conditions for discrete-time feedback interconnections have received little attention.

papers.title: Quantization of Large Models with Weight Outliers and Sparsity
papers.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces the memory burden of large model deployment by casting the high precision trained weights to fewer bits. While this promotes memory-efficient inference, it also incurs quantization error that impairs model performance. To compensate for quantization error, the present contribution decomposes the original trained weights into a quantized matrix, a low-rank component, and a sparse matrix that accounts for outlier rows in the weights. Due to analytical intractability and the discrete structure of the decomposition, a simulated annealing search is employed to explore candidate decompositions while avoiding poor local minima. Numerical tests demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach across a broad suite of large language models, including Llama 3.2 1B, Llama 3.2 3B, Llama 3.1 8B, and Qwen2.5 7B, evaluated on natural language generation benchmarks using 4-bit NF4 and FP4 quantizers. The novel method can markedly outperform direct quantization while incurring minimal memory overhead.

Large language models (LLMs) [16, 15] have demonstrated remarkable effectiveness across a wide range of tasks, including natural language understanding [22], code generation [5], and reasoning [4]. Underpinning these capabilities are models with billions of parameters, typically represented in 16-bit floating-point formats (e.g. FP16, BF16). Although training such models requires substantial computational and energy resources, this process is typically performed once. In contrast, the subsequent LLM deployment requires sustained memory and bandwidth throughout the model’s lifetime. As models scale, memory-efficient deployment has become an increasingly important challenge, particularly in resource-constrained and latency-sensitive environments such as edge devices and the cloud.

To address this, several model compression techniques have been advocated. For example; pruning [1] reduces the parameter count by removing weights; knowledge distillation [10] transfers knowledge to a smaller student model; and quantization [7, 12] maps model parameters to lower-precision numerical formats. Among these approaches, low-bit quantization is particularly attractive because it can markedly curtail memory footprint and bandwidth requirements.

Post-training quantization (PTQ) is a popular paradigm because it applies quantization to a model after training, as opposed to alternative paradigms that incorporate quantization during pretraining [19] or fine-tuning [23]. Conventional PTQ typically leverages a calibration dataset to determine the quantization parameters [11, 12], whereas zero-shot PTQ directly quantizes model parameters without additional data. This distinction establishes zero-shot PTQ as remarkably attractive in scenarios where representative calibration data is unavailable. However, a central challenge in PTQ is coping with the associated quantization error, especially when compressing to 4 bits or less. For LLMs, the performance impairment can be exacerbated because errors propagate in the transformer layers and across output tokens in long-sequence inference [7, 9].

A major source of quantization error is the presence of high-magnitude outliers in LLM weight distributions, which can exhibit structured patterns [7, 9]. Directly quantizing such outliers is challenging because they enlarge the quantization range and thereby reduce quantization fidelity for the majority of weights, especially in low-bit regimes. As a result, outliers can contribute disproportionately to quantization error and lead to downstream performance degradation. Prior work has proposed several strategies to mitigate this issue. For instance, Gpt3.int8() [7] and SPQR [9] isolate high-magnitude activation or weight outliers and retain them in higher precision. SmoothQuant [24] transfers activation outliers to weights using per-channel scaling, while AWQ [18] performs saliency-aware weight quantization. QuaRot [2] instead applies rotation matrices to redistribute activation magnitude. Many of these approaches, however, rely on calibration data and can thus be less suitable in fully calibration-free/zero-shot deployment settings.

Rather than directly quantizing pretrained weights, we adopt a calibration-free mixed-precision decomposition framework that factorizes high-precision pretrained weights into three complementary components: a quantized backbone, a high-precision sparse component, and a high-precision low-rank factor. This decomposition is motivated by the observation that, once the high-energy outliers are isolated, the remaining reconstruction error often admits an efficient low-rank approximation capturing the dominant singular directions. Together, the sparse and low-rank components improve reconstruction fidelity while incurring minimal memory overhead and inference latency. Since a global search for an optimal decomposition scales exponentially with weight matrix dimensions, the present contribution leverages a simulated annealing algorithm to explore candidate decompositions while avoiding poor local minima. Experiments on zero-shot natural language generation tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach across a wide range of popular large language models quantized to 4-bit NF4 and FP4 formats.

papers.title: Evidence for topological flat band magnetism in Co$_3$Sn$_2$S$_2$
papers.abstract: Correlations and topology are central pillars in the study of emergent electronic phases. Topological flat bands near the Fermi level unite these concepts, providing a route towards correlated topological phenomena and unconventional magnetism. Despite theoretical predictions, momentum-resolved observation of a topological flat band at the Fermi level has remained elusive. Using angle resolved photoemission spectroscopy, we observe a flat band at the Fermi level within the topologically non-trivial electronic structure of the magnetic kagome Weyl semimetal Co$_3$Sn$_2$S$_2$. We further uncover a strong temperature dependence in which the flat band shifts across the Fermi level, accompanied by a reconstruction of the Fermi surface. Strikingly, this evolution occurs on the same temperature scale as previously reported anomalies in the magnetic response. Together, these results provide evidence for topological flat band magnetism in Co$_3$Sn$_2$S$_2$, establishing a microscopic setting in which topology, electronic correlations, and magnetism become intertwined.

papers.title: Modeling CO Line Luminosity with FIRE simulations: II. Comparison With Observations, CO Luminosity Functions and Redshift Evolution
papers.abstract: We present predictions for the CO(1-0) and CO(2-1) luminosities of 765, 850, 887 and 915 galaxies at z=0, 1, 2 and 3, respectively, drawn from the Feedback in Realistic Environments (FIRE-2) simulations and post-processed with SKIRT radiative transfer and CLOUDY line emission calculations. We compare our CO line luminosity predictions with existing observations. At z=0, our predictions reproduce the observed scatter and mean relation between star formation rate (SFR) and CO(1-0) luminosity for both massive star-forming galaxies and low-metallicity dwarf galaxies. We also reproduce the observed superlinear power-law slope between CO(1-0) luminosity and metallicity. At z=1, our CO(2-1) predictions scatter to much lower luminosities than observed, which likely reflects the limited sensitivity of current surveys. At fixed SFR, our CO(1-0) luminosities decrease by roughly an order of magnitude per unit increase in redshift. This decline is likely driven by the decrease in metallicity with increasing redshift, since FIRE-2 galaxies with comparable SFR and metallicity produce similar CO(1-0) luminosities regardless of redshift. At fixed stellar mass, the predicted luminosities show no redshift dependence. These results show that our FIRE-2 predictions reproduce the observed scaling relations between CO(1-0) luminosity and galaxy properties wherever the observed galaxies are robustly detected. This gives us confidence in our predictions for the regime where no observational data exist, and suggests that our luminosity predictions can be used to build predictive models for CO line intensity mapping experiments.

papers.intro:
Line intensity mapping (LIM) has emerged as a promising alternative to galaxy surveys, probing the large scale structure (LSS). LIM trades angular resolution for mapping speed. Rather than cataloging galaxies, it measures spatial fluctuations in the integrated emission of a spectral line, or lines, from many unresolved sources, including faint objects undetectable in standard galaxy surveys. Since they measure the redshift of emission along the line of sight, LIM experiments yield a three-dimensional tomographic map of the LSS over a broad range of redshifts, at a fraction of total observing time required for galaxy surveys [90, 89, 13]. Many of these lines trace star formation and/or conditions in the interstellar medium (ISM) of galaxies. Thus, LIM surveys provide information about astrophysics as well as cosmology. For example, they could provide a more complete census of star formation across cosmic time than galaxy surveys, e.g., Visbal and Loeb [149], Kovetz et al. [90], Kovetz et al. [89], Bernal et al. [13], Chang and Lidz [27].

In this series of three papers, we focus on the rotational transitions of carbon monoxide, with an eye toward the CO Mapping Array Project (COMAP, Cleary et al. 32), which is currently underway. It targets CO(1-0) at z∼3z\sim 3 and has progressively tightening the upper limits of the CO power spectrum through its first two observing seasons [30, 29], but a confirmed detection has yet to made. Interpreting these measurements, first as upper limits and eventually as a detection, requires a physically grounded model of how CO emission from the ISM of galaxies traces the underlying dark matter distribution. This is the second in a series of three papers describing such a model, using state of the art MHD cosmological galaxy simulations from the FIRE project, post-processed with radiative transfer calculations using SKIRT and emission line calculations using CLOUDY, all described briefly in [143] (hereafter 143). In this paper we test the predictions of our model using a number of different observations. 144 (in prep.) presents simple analytic models, or response functions, that can be used in combination with large scale N-body or halo models to produce mock maps of CO emission from large volumes of the universe. These mock maps can then be compared quantitatively to maps made by LIM surveys.

In the current literature these response functions are constructed either from empirical calibrations [101, 116, 100, 81, 30] or semi-analytical models of galaxy formation [62, 94, 133, 156, 108, 134] which are tuned to match observed scaling laws. The empirical route typically follows a chain of calibrated relationships between halo mass and CO(1-0) luminosity (LCO⁡(1−0)′L^{\prime}_{{\rm CO}(1-0)}) using a correlation measured in observed galaxies [138, 158, 26, 78]. Each link is informed by real data, which is the principal strength of this approach. However, this is also its principal limitation, as the currently available data are dominated by the most luminous galaxies, with CO detections preferentially are from massive, actively star-forming, and metal-rich systems as we discuss below. Luminous galaxies at z∼1z\sim 1 to 3 do appear to follow a relation similar to local ones [26], but for the faint, low mass galaxies that dominate by number the assumption is untested, because they lie below current sensitivity limits. Partly as a result, published CO models differ by one to two orders of magnitude at the redshifts targeted by COMAP [21, 20, 29].

In the local Universe, dwarf galaxies with low metallicity are notoriously faint in CO, and even deep observations with sensitive telescopes detect only a minority of them [127]. Also see Krumholz et al. [93] for a compilation of low-metallicity dwarf galaxies. CO has nonetheless been detected in dwarfs with gas phase oxygen abundances of 12+log⁡(O/H)≈7.812+\log({\rm O/H})\approx 7.8 [44, 120] and even ≈7.5\approx 7.5 [128], far below the solar value of 8.69±0.048.69\pm 0.04 [3]. Across larger samples, the CO detection rate increases with stellar mass, star formation rate, visual extinction (AVA_{V}), and most strongly with metallicity [31], so observations of metal poor systems frequently yield only upper limits. For a review for CO observations at local Universe see [122].

papers.title: A geometry-aware framework for electromagnetic fields in GATE 10
papers.abstract:
Objective. An increasing number of medical-physics applications require the modelling of charged-particle transport in electromagnetic (EM) fields. We aim to provide GATE 10 users with a flexible mechanism for defining such fields in Monte Carlo simulations while preserving the native Geant4 particle-transport machinery.
  Approach. Our framework separates the handling of coordinates from EM field evaluation. Fields are attached to geometry volumes, defined in their local frame, and represented by analytic expressions, field maps, or arbitrary Python functions. They automatically follow the position and orientation of these volumes, including in nested and dynamic geometries. We validated the framework against native Geant4 transport and tested coordinate transformations, nested volumes, and dynamic geometry. We also compared the computational cost of the three field representations.
  Main results. The framework reproduced the native Geant4 trajectories exactly for all tested field types with direct Geant4 counterparts. Coordinate transformations introduced only floating-point-level differences, while simulations with dynamically changing geometry reproduced the equivalent static configurations exactly. All three representations produced equivalent transport. Mapped fields added at most 18% to the single-threaded runtime of analytic fields, while Python functions required 6.9 times as much. The compiled representations scaled with the number of threads, whereas Python functions became slower as threads were added.
  Significance. The framework adds flexible, geometry-aware EM field definitions to GATE 10 without modifying the underlying Geant4 transport machinery, and is part of the open-source GATE 10 codebase. It also provides a basis for extending GATE 10 with additional field representations in the future.

papers.intro:
Monte Carlo (MC) particle-transport simulations are an essential tool in research and treatment planning in radiotherapy, providing a high-fidelity description of radiation transport and energy deposition in complex, heterogeneous media. GATE, an open-source layer built on top of the Geant4 toolkit (Agostinelli et al., 2003; Allison et al., 2006; Allison et al., 2016), has been widely adopted across imaging and dosimetry (Sarrut et al., 2014; Sarrut et al., 2021; Sarrut et al., 2022). The latest version, GATE 10, replaces the legacy macro interface with an accessible Python-based interface while retaining the capabilities of Geant4 (Sarrut et al., 2026; Krah et al., 2026).

The latest version, GATE 10, replaces the legacy macro interface with an accessible Python-based interface while retaining the capabilities of Geant4 (Sarrut et al., 2026; Krah et al., 2026).

An increasing number of medical-physics applications require the modelling of charged-particle transport in electromagnetic (EM) fields. A prominent example is magnetic-resonance-guided radiotherapy (MRgRT), where magnetic fields deflect charged-particle trajectories and can therefore alter dose distributions: in photon therapy through the deflection of secondary electrons (Raaijmakers et al., 2005; Raaijmakers et al., 2008), and in proton therapy through the deflection of the primary beam itself (Schellhammer & Hoffmann, 2017; Schellhammer et al., 2018). Beyond MRgRT, dipoles and quadrupoles steer and focus beams in accelerators and treatment beamlines, where modelling beam losses requires charged-particle transport through these fields together with interactions in the surrounding material (Nevay et al., 2020). Electric and magnetic fields also play a central role in radiation detectors, where they act directly on the secondary charged particles that determine the detector signal. For instance, in Faraday cups used for proton dosimetry, electric and magnetic fields are applied to control secondary-electron contributions, which can limit the accuracy of the collected charge unless corrected for (Winterhalter et al., 2021; Ehwald et al., 2023). These applications differ not only in the fields involved, but also in how fields relate to the simulation geometry: a single field can encompass an entire patient, a beamline might contain several independently positioned field-producing elements, and a detector may contain a field confined to a single component. A general and well-validated capability for EM field transport in a medical-physics Monte Carlo framework is therefore of broad interest.

Geant4 provides a general framework for defining EM fields and for tracking charged particles through them. GATE has historically provided access to a subset of these capabilities through interfaces shaped by the applications that motivated them. Uniform magnetic fields were introduced in early versions of GATE for emission-tomography studies in which a single field encompasses the whole scanner, and were subsequently used to quantify the effect of magnetic fields on positron range in PET/MR (Soultanidis et al., 2011; Barati et al., 2021). Spatially varying fields were later introduced in GATE 8 through three-dimensional field maps supplied as look-up tables and interpolated over the extent of the grid (Padilla-Cabal et al., 2020). These capabilities were retained in GATE 9 and used, for example, to commission a beamline with an integrated dipole for MR-guided proton and carbon-ion radiotherapy (Fuchs et al., 2023). However, neither interface was ported to GATE 10 during the transition to the Python-based architecture. This created a need to reintroduce EM field transport in GATE 10, and an opportunity to provide a more general mechanism for defining fields in relation to the simulation geometry, while preserving the native Geant4 particle-transport machinery.

In this work, we introduce a framework for defining EM fields in GATE 10 and associating them directly with simulation volumes. The framework separates the handling of coordinates from EM field evaluation, allowing the same geometry-dependent coordinate treatment to be used with different field representations. Three interchangeable approaches are provided: analytic fields for closed-form descriptions, mapped fields for fields defined on regular grids, and Python functions for arbitrary user-defined spatial dependencies. Fields are defined in the local coordinate system of their associated volume and automatically follow its position and orientation, including when the geometry is nested or dynamically modified. We validate the framework against native Geant4 transport, test its behaviour under translations, rotations, and nested and dynamic geometries, and compare the computational cost of the three field representations.

papers.title: Power-Optimal Risk Control via Standardized Margin Calibration
papers.abstract: Machine learning can screen far more candidates than can be experimentally validated, creating a need for selection procedures that identify promising candidates while controlling risk before costly experimental validation. We propose Uncertainty-Normalized Empirical Calibration (UNEC), a p-value-free framework that ranks candidates by uncertainty-normalized predictive margins and directly calibrates a selection cutoff using held-out losses. UNEC supports flexible prediction models, general bounded losses, and diverse selection targets. We study marginal discovery risk (MDR) and selective discovery risk (SDR), with SDR reducing to the false discovery rate under binary loss. We establish finite-sample MDR control for an adjusted rule and asymptotic SDR control with explicit limiting risk and power. Under a location--scale model with a common one-sided binary target, we further show that UNEC asymptotically attains the oracle power benchmark among observation-wise selection rules. Simulations and molecular screening applications in solubility, toxicity, and lipophilicity demonstrate favorable risk--power trade-offs and substantial computational gains across binary and graded-loss settings.
papers.intro:
Machine learning increasingly guides decisions about which candidates deserve further investigation and which predictions can be acted upon. Applications include prioritizing antibacterial compounds for experimental testing (Stokes et al., 2020), screening generated proteins for desired biological activity (Madani et al., 2023), identifying stable crystal structures (Merchant et al., 2023), selecting patients likely to benefit from treatment (Lei and Candès, 2021), and accepting trustworthy outputs from large language models (Gui et al., 2024). These decisions must be made before the relevant outcomes or quality assessments are available, while unsuitable selections can waste resources or compromise downstream decisions.

Applications include prioritizing antibacterial compounds for experimental testing (Stokes et al., 2020), screening generated proteins for desired biological activity (Madani et al., 2023), identifying stable crystal structures (Merchant et al., 2023), selecting patients likely to benefit from treatment (Lei and Candès, 2021), and accepting trustworthy outputs from large language models (Gui et al., 2024). These decisions must be made before the relevant outcomes or quality assessments are available, while unsuitable selections can waste resources or compromise downstream decisions.

This motivates the problem of risk-controlled selection: selecting promising observations while controlling a prespecified measure of selection risk. Much of the existing literature focuses on binary false-selection errors. Conformal selection (CS), for example, combines conformal pp-values with multiple-testing procedures to control the false discovery rate (FDR) (Jin and Candès, 2023). In many applications, however, the cost or extent of an error matters. Drug candidates differ in synthesis cost (Fromer and Coley, 2024), so counting inactive selections alone does not capture the resources wasted. Likewise, generated responses may contain different proportions of unsupported factual claims (Min et al., 2023). These considerations motivate general bounded losses that quantify costs or graded errors beyond binary false-selection indicators.

Recent work such as SCoRE provides finite-sample selective risk control for general bounded losses through conformal ee-values (Bai and Jin, 2026). We pursue a complementary direction: can risk-controlled selection be achieved directly from predictions and held-out losses, without constructing conformal pp- or ee-values? Such an alternative is particularly attractive if it remains flexible and computationally efficient across different losses and selection targets.

We propose uncertainty-normalized empirical calibration (UNEC), a simple pp-value-free framework combining standardized-margin ranking with direct empirical risk calibration. By normalizing predicted target margins by local uncertainty, UNEC provides a flexible construction supporting general bounded losses, observation-specific thresholds, and interval targets. Calibration uses sorted scores and cumulative losses, offering substantial computational savings over the evaluated SCoRE implementations. Our theory establishes finite-sample marginal discovery risk (MDR) control for an adjusted rule and asymptotic selective discovery risk (SDR) control under suitable conditions. For binary loss with a common one-sided target, we further establish asymptotic power optimality under a location–scale model and appropriate estimation conditions. Simulations and molecular screening applications demonstrate the effectiveness of UNEC, with competitive risk–power performance and substantial computational gains.

papers.title: XLA from the Trenches: Correctness on TPU Workloads at Scale
papers.abstract: Accelerating modern foundational models has pushed domain-specific compilers toward increasingly complex, multi-tiered optimization pipelines. However, this heavy optimization focus introduces delicate tradeoffs between peak execution performance and correctness. Subtle codegen defects can trigger numerical degradation and memory or buffer corruption, invalidating multi-million-dollar training runs and degrading live serving quality without raising obvious compiler errors. In this paper, we present a battle-tested methodology for verifying and triaging Google's XLA:TPU compiler at hyperscale. We leverage fuzzing techniques, combining synthetic program generation with real production traces, while orchestrating AI agent swarms to autonomously generate stress tests, reproduce failures, and draft fixes. To pinpoint root causes in full workloads, we pair this with a hierarchical differential pipeline that bisects large graphs down to individual failing operations inside fused kernels. Deployed in production, our framework has already driven the resolution of over 142 compiler bugs (with 103 additional findings under review), from which we distill pragmatic lessons learned.

papers.intro:
Optimizing machine learning (ML) workloads has become one of the defining computational challenges of our era. At the center of this revolution lie domain-specific ML compilers, such as XLA Sabne (2020), TVM Chen et al. (2018a), Triton Tillet et al. (2019), Glow Rotem et al. (2018), which bridge the gap between high-level framework representations and custom accelerator architectures like Google’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) Jouppi et al. (2017) and modern GPUs. To unlock the physical compute limits of hardware, modern ML compilers rely heavily on aggressive, hardware-specific optimization passes. Crucial to this process are tiled fusions, where the compiler merges multiple operations into unified execution kernels and partitions them into smaller tiles, streaming intermediate data through fast on-chip caches or scratchpad memory rather than materializing it in off-chip High Bandwidth Memory (HBM).

To unlock the physical compute limits of hardware, modern ML compilers rely heavily on aggressive, hardware-specific optimization passes. Crucial to this process are tiled fusions, where the compiler merges multiple operations into unified execution kernels and partitions them into smaller tiles, streaming intermediate data through fast on-chip caches or scratchpad memory rather than materializing it in off-chip High Bandwidth Memory (HBM).

While substantial literature and industrial efforts in ML compilation focus on performance—maximizing FLOP utilization, minimizing memory footprint, and automating tuning heuristics Adams et al. (2019); Chen et al. (2018a); Chen et al. (2018b); Cano et al. (2026)—an equally vital requirement is compiler correctness. In the era of frontier foundational models and safety-critical autonomous systems, a compiler defect can have severe, widespread repercussions. Beyond explicit failures like segmentation faults or fatal assertions, ML compiler bugs frequently manifest as silent numerical drift or subtle data corruption. A single miscompiled index offset, improper loop accumulator revisit, or packing error can silently alter tensor outputs, causing multi-million-dollar training runs to diverge after weeks of compute, or injecting subtle hallucinations into live inference services McAllister et al. (2025); Roune (2025).

(2025); Roune (2025).

Guaranteeing correctness in a production ML compiler faces several distinct challenges. First, code generation for accelerators involves a combinatorial explosion of interacting knobs (e.g., tensor shapes, tile sizes, buffering levels, layouts) creating an optimization space where standard regression suites barely scratch the surface. Second, modern production workloads compile into large computational graphs, making whole-model triage of numerical divergence a significant bottleneck that can take weeks of manual toil. Third, while differential testing against an unoptimized reference interpreter is theoretically sound, naive synthetic inputs trigger undefined floating-point math and hardware alignment violations, generating false-positive noise that undermines automated isolation. Finally, even after isolating an anomaly to a single fusion node, pipelined kernels execute intermediate values purely in hardware vector registers (without materializing them in HBM), turning fusions into opaque black boxes that blind standard debugging tools.

Third, while differential testing against an unoptimized reference interpreter is theoretically sound, naive synthetic inputs trigger undefined floating-point math and hardware alignment violations, generating false-positive noise that undermines automated isolation. Finally, even after isolating an anomaly to a single fusion node, pipelined kernels execute intermediate values purely in hardware vector registers (without materializing them in HBM), turning fusions into opaque black boxes that blind standard debugging tools.

To address these challenges, we introduce a cohesive reliability framework for the XLA:TPU compiler that tackles correctness both proactively and reactively. Proactively, we improve bug detection via hybrid fuzzing. Rather than relying solely on (unrepresentative) synthetic graphs, we piggyback differential correctness checks onto our existing production autotuning pipeline Cano et al. (2026), stress-testing boundary conditions across real fleet operations at near-zero marginal infrastructure cost. To further amplify this approach, we leverage AI to systematically expand test coverage across the fleet and scale both the findings and the generation of compiler fixes. Reactively, we establish a hierarchical differential isolation pipeline spanning from macro-graphs down to fused kernels. At the graph level, we recursively navigate large computational graphs to pinpoint failing operations while reducing false positives using reverse constraint propagation. At the kernel level, we inspect intermediate tensors directly inside fused kernels to pinpoint the exact sub-operation where hardware execution diverges from the reference semantics.

papers.title: Optimal portfolio and consumption under no-shorting constraints: The exploratory formulation and reinforcement learning
papers.abstract: We develop a reinforcement-learning framework for the continuous-time optimal portfolio-consumption via utility maximization under no-shorting portfolio constraints. We adopt the exploratory formulation under entropy regularization and impose no-shorting constraint through a componentwise nonnegative conditional-mean constraint on the class of admissible randomized policies, while the sampled actions are allowed to be negative during the training. For CRRA utility, we derive the homothetic value function and the optimal Gaussian portfolio and Gibbs consumption policies under some model conditions and establish a verification theorem. These results allow compatible parameterizations in actor, critic, and $q$ functions for a constrained policy-iteration algorithm. Policy evaluation uses trajectory-based moment conditions, and policy improvement uses fitted coefficients to solve a convex quadratic program over the nonnegative orthant without requiring market coefficients as inputs. The mean constraint preserves tractable Gaussian exploration throughout parameter learning, while modal deployment converts the learned randomized policies into deterministic controls. In particular, the Gaussian mode coincides with its constrained mean and hence satisfies no-shorting constraint, and the Gibbs mode determines the deployed consumption rule.

Continuous-time utility maximization for optimal portfolio and consumption has been a core research topic with extensive studies. Along this direction, no-shorting portfolio constraint has attracted considerable attention due to the practical risk and regulation concerns. Some empirical studies on the impact of no-shorting constraint on financial stability have been conducted in Allen et al. (1993), Gómez and Sharma (2006), Beber and Pagano (2013), Grullon et al. (2015), to name a few. Theoretical developments in portfolio optimization under no-shorting constraints can be found in Xu and Shreve (1992), Shirakawa (1994), Cvitanić and Karatzas (1992), Wang et al. (2024), and references therein.

The primary goal of this paper is to address this challenge in the context of finite-horizon utility maximization for portfolio and consumption management. We consider the market model consisting of multiple correlated risky assets with unknown constant market coefficients. We impose no-shorting through a componentwise nonnegative conditional-mean constraint on the randomized portfolio policy and first solve the full-information exploratory problem under CRRA and logarithmic utility. We then show the connection between the optimal randomized policy and the solution to the classical constrained Merton problem, which allows us to develop a constrained martingale policy-iteration scheme. The proposed algorithm evaluates policies from observed trajectories, updates the portfolio through a nonnegative-orthant quadratic program, and deploys the modes of the learned policy densities.

Entropy regularization is the first ingredient of this construction. In our exploratory utility maximization problem, pointwise maximization of the entropy-regularized Hamiltonian intrinsically produces a Gibbs density whose exponent is determined by the local reward and the value derivatives. The quadratic portfolio Hamiltonian yields a Gaussian policy, and the consumption Hamiltonian yields a Gibbs policy under CRRA utility and a Gamma policy under logarithmic utility. Their forms determine the portfolio covariance jointly with the value function and supply compatible actor, critic, and little-qq parameterizations for learning.

The second ingredient is the constraint on conditional-mean of portfolio policies. In the same utility maximization setting, Chau et al. (2026) imposed an interval support constraint on a single-asset policy and obtain a truncated Gaussian policy. For correlated multi-asset setting, the analogous orthant truncation has a generally nonfactorizable normalizer, which may entail multivariate Gaussian-probability calculations and complicated sampling. We instead consider the constraint on conditional mean in this work, in which the maximizer remains a full Gaussian for multiple assets. Its mean solves a covariance-coupled convex quadratic program over the nonnegative orthant, and the required portfolio-action moments stay explicit. The quadratic program resolves binding constraints jointly across correlated assets rather than clipping an unconstrained portfolio. Recently, Li et al. (2026) considered the same policy-mean constraint in an unregularized auxiliary problem for mean–variance selection with a time-varying and unknown investment opportunity set, where the Gaussian covariance is specified externally. In our model, entropy regularization determines the covariance jointly with the value function, and the mean constraint reappears in policy improvement through the nonnegative-orthant quadratic program.

papers.title: Fast and Exact Relative-Position Attention via Structure-Aware Kernels
papers.abstract: Relative-position attention mechanisms offer compelling alternatives to RoPE across various transformer architectures, delivering superior performance in domains such as audio. These mechanisms typically modify attention scores by adding content-position or bias-position terms. Unlike RoPE, which encodes position via per-token rotations directly on the queries and keys, relative-position terms generally require pairwise offset-dependent computation or lookups, complicating their integration into fused attention kernels and introducing severe memory, bandwidth, and compute overheads as sequences scale. To address this bottleneck, we propose an exact attention algorithm that incorporates additive relative-position terms into FlashAttention-style tiled computation. Our method (1) uses offset-aware tiling to avoid redundant indexing and memory accesses, (2) computes only the necessary key/query-relation products and reuses them across token pairs in both forward and backward passes, and (3) uses offset-based gradient sharding and aggregation, eliminating atomic contention. We provide a unified, efficient Triton implementation across diverse relative-position attention mechanisms and evaluate it against naive and specialized implementations. For 8K-token sequences, our method speeds up the forward (backward) pass by 1.8-6.4$\times$ (2.0-21$\times$) and reduces peak memory up to 2.9-128$\times$ (1.4-54$\times$) over the strongest baseline for each mechanism, enabling long-context end-to-end transcription that is 1.8$\times$ faster and uses 2.4$\times$ less memory. Our method thus provides a drop-in, hardware-efficient solution for scaling relative-position attention transformers.
papers.intro:
The Transformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017) has revolutionized modern machine learning, from large language models (LLMs) in natural language processing to foundation models in speech, vision, and biology. At its core is the scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) mechanism, which allows input tokens to directly attend to each other and aggregate mutual information. However, scaling these models to larger inputs introduces two fundamental challenges, namely injecting scalable positional information into the network, and keeping the computation and memory footprint of SDPA tractable despite its quadratic complexity.

However, scaling these models to larger inputs introduces two fundamental challenges, namely injecting scalable positional information into the network, and keeping the computation and memory footprint of SDPA tractable despite its quadratic complexity.

For standard content-based attention, IO-aware kernels such as FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022; Dao, 2024) resolved the quadratic memory bottleneck by streaming blocks of tokens through fast on-chip SRAM, avoiding the materialization of the full N×NN\times N score matrix in GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM). Paired with parameter-free, token-wise rotary position embeddings (RoPE) (Su et al., 2024), which can be seamlessly integrated into fused kernels, this pipeline now serves as the backbone of most autoregressive LLMs.

Parameter-free positional encodings, such as RoPE and ALiBi (Press et al., 2022), are not without drawbacks. Despite their computational efficiency, they often fail to use context beyond the sequence lengths seen during training (Kazemnejad et al., 2023; Hua et al., 2025), where learned relative biases such as T5’s generalize better (Kazemnejad et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024). Consequently, learnable relative-position encodings remain an enticing alternative for Transformer models. This class of mechanisms additively augments attention scores with learnable terms that depend on the relative distance i−ji-j between query and key tokens, either through content-to-position projections or scalar biases. This allows modeling explicit, shift-invariant relationships across sequences, and has remained enticing for speech models (Barrault et al., 2023; Sekoyan et al., 2025; Abouelenin et al., 2025), text encoding (He et al., 2023; Zaratiana et al., 2025), proteomics (Elnaggar et al., 2022), and genomics (Linder et al., 2025).

papers.title: Learning Agile Humanoid Dodgeball with Onboard Monocular Vision
papers.abstract: Humanoid robots operating in shared, dynamic environments must respond to rapidly approaching objects while maintaining balance. We study dodgeball as a controlled test of this capability, coupling visual threat assessment with whole-body evasion, recovery, and target reacquisition. We develop a system that integrates onboard monocular perception, temporal ball-state and threat-flag estimation, and learned whole-body control. A ball detector supplies bounding-box histories, and a temporal estimator predicts relative ball position and a binary threat flag. Separate dodge/recovery and search/track policies share this interface and are composed to support repeated encounters. A three-stage curriculum first trains control with privileged ball states, then starts estimator supervision from stable policy rollouts, and finally replaces the actor's privileged inputs with estimator outputs. Analytic projection and perception randomization provide detector-like training observations without image rendering. Across approach-angle bins in controlled simulation, dodge success ranges from 97.8--100.0% for 5.0 m launches at 6 m/s to 33.2--40.8% for 2.5 m launches at 10 m/s, with 1000 throws per speed--distance condition. On a physical Unitree G1, controlled single-throw success exceeds 85% over more than 15 trials. A hardware sequence demonstrates full-azimuth target reacquisition followed by another dodge. These results demonstrate an integrated onboard-monocular-vision system under highly dynamic motions.
