papers.intro:
Humanoid robots are intended to operate in environments where people and objects move unpredictably. An accidentally thrown or falling object can enter the robot’s immediate workspace before a nominal task controller has time to respond. Avoiding such an object requires the robot to alter its whole-body motion while preserving balance, then recover a posture from which it can continue operating. For a biped, an evasive action that avoids contact but causes a fall is not a successful response. Fast-object avoidance therefore provides a concrete setting for studying reactive whole-body behavior under simultaneous sensing and balance constraints.

Humanoid robots are intended to operate in environments where people and objects move unpredictably. An accidentally thrown or falling object can enter the robot’s immediate workspace before a nominal task controller has time to respond. Avoiding such an object requires the robot to alter its whole-body motion while preserving balance, then recover a posture from which it can continue operating. For a biped, an evasive action that avoids contact but causes a fall is not a successful response. Fast-object avoidance therefore provides a concrete setting for studying reactive whole-body behavior under simultaneous sensing and balance constraints.

We study humanoid dodgeball as a controlled experimental task for this capability. Ball launches make approach speed, distance, and direction explicit, enabling repeatable tests of the time available for perception and movement. The task extends beyond an isolated dodge: the robot must find the ball, assess its approach, evade it, recover, and reacquire a target for the next encounter. A torso-mounted camera makes these requirements interdependent. Turning the body changes visibility, but rapid turning can also degrade the images needed to guide subsequent motion. The tested ball and launch conditions define the scope of our evaluation; they do not establish avoidance of arbitrary projectiles.

Fast-object avoidance has been demonstrated on aerial robots with frame and event cameras [1, 2, 3, 4], and quadruped systems combine learned evasion with active sensing [5, 6]. Humanoid ball-interaction systems demonstrate agile whole-body skills [7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12]. Closely related, PAC-MAN combines perception-aware control-barrier-function guidance and reinforcement learning for humanoid dodgeball [13]. These advances motivate examining the complete sensing-to-action loop, including recovery and target reacquisition with a moving onboard camera.

A three-stage curriculum separates control acquisition from estimator learning before closing the perception–control loop: the actor first learns from ground-truth ball states, estimator supervision begins after stable rollouts emerge, and the actor then switches to estimated states. The bounding-box interface supports this transition while matching the output available from the deployed detector.

The main contributions are: • We combine analytic 2D bounding-box projection and perception randomization with temporal estimation of relative ball position and a binary threat flag. • We develop a humanoid dodgeball system using onboard monocular vision, separate dodge/recovery and search/track policies, and a three-stage curriculum. • We validate perception, estimation, and avoidance in simulation and on a physical Unitree G1 across controlled launch speeds, distances, and directions.

papers.title: Gromov-Witten theory of the local model of the standard flop
papers.abstract: We conjecture that the generating series of equivariant Gromov-Witten invariants of the local Calabi-Yau $(2n-1)$-fold $\operatorname{Tot} \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{n-1}} (-1)^{\oplus n}$ at fixed genus can be presented as a linear combination of polylogarithms, generalising a well-known property of the resolved conifold. We prove this conjecture for two specialisations of the equivariant parameters. In the first, the parameters are specialised to roots of unity and the proof proceeds via Givental-Teleman reconstruction. In the second, we obtain a closed-form evaluation of the generating series from which the conjecture follows. For $n=3$, the resulting closed formula establishes a special case of a Gopakumar-Vafa-type conjecture for Calabi-Yau fivefolds.

papers.title: The Verifier Is Part of the Simulator: Evidence-View Gaming in Agentic Equation Discovery
papers.abstract: A growing number of agentic pipelines search for governing equations: an agent proposes laws and a verifier checks them against simulated trajectories. The verifier sees only a numerical summary: integrals against test functions on a time grid. That summary carries its own discretization error, making the verifier part of the simulator. We freeze the trajectory, candidate library, verifier and thresholds, leaving the agent one move: which permitted summary to admit. Without scores or language models, finer time grids reduce numerical discrepancies and false library rejections. On PDEBench, the verifier instead accepts equations missing diffusion on score-selected summaries. Maximizing a public score rewarding decisive verdicts and larger mismatches when rejecting the library wrongly rejects all 1,500 in-library cases; retrospectively retuning score constants on a separate bank reduces errors to 13/180 at best. We call this evidence-view gaming: reward hacking by choice of permitted summary. In single-turn forced-choice tests, Claude models rarely choose summaries giving wrong verdicts when asked to be accurate, but often do so when asked to maximize the score or report missing physics. In separate trust prompts, they often rank those harmful summaries least trustworthy. Requiring several summaries to agree reduces errors but often withholds a verdict and performs worse than a fixed fine view on PDEBench: a safeguard, not a certificate. Evidence chosen after its verdict is known cannot alone authorize a claim.

papers.intro:
Scientific agents use evaluator feedback to propose laws, run candidate-model code, and adjust experiments [45, 30, 24]. We study one link in that loop: which numerical summary is admitted as evidence by the verifier. Checking a candidate means integrating the trajectory against test functions on a time grid. The check has its own discretization, with settings the interface leaves open. The generating law and stored trajectory are held fixed: changing the summary alone can make a complete candidate library appear misspecified or an incomplete equation appear adequate. We ask whether an agent rewarded for decisiveness selects a harmful view, and whether prescribed agreement prevents it.

Weak-form variants avoid pointwise differentiation by integrating against test functions [25, 37, 10, 16], while stability selection addresses noisy model selection [23]. papers.title: Artificial spin ice on the CaVO lattice: a tricritical bridge from square to kagome
papers.abstract: Artificial spin ices (ASIs) are arrays of interacting nanomagnets in which phase transitions can be imaged and controlled. Studies of the thermodynamic have focused mainly on the square and kagome lattices, and on their variants. Here we study artificial spin ice on the CaVO lattice, formed of squares and octagons. At fixed lattice constant, the ratio $r$ of the square and octagon link lengths tunes the interactions strongly while changing the geometry only slightly. Magnetic force microscopy and Monte Carlo simulations show a continuous bridge from square-ice-like to kagome-like behavior. At small $r$ the system has a single ordering transition, whereas at large $r$ it passes from a correlated paramagnet to charge order and then long-range order. The two regimes meet in a multicritical region, accurately modeled by a Blume-Capel model of the octagon toroidal moments. From this picture, we design a comparative magnetometry protocol that unambiguously separates interaction effects from single-nanomagnet effects in thermally active samples. Finally, the charge-ordered region maps onto a tunable dimer model, with a Coulomb phase and pinch points along the line between two ordered dimer phases. The CaVO ASI thus provides access to a rich phase diagram only through geometric tuning, without requiring extreme experimental conditions.

papers.title: Approximation Algorithms for Maximum-Weight Degree-Bounded Forests
papers.abstract:
In the maximum-weight degree-bounded forest problem, we are given a graph with nonnegative edge weights and a degree upper bound on each vertex. The objective is to find a maximum-weight forest satisfying the degree bounds. We show that this problem admits a simple $2$-approximation via the greedy algorithm. This already improves over the best-known guarantees obtained via a reduction to weighted $3$-matroid parity, and sets a baseline to improve upon.
  Our main result is an $\frac{8}{5}$-approximation algorithm for the maximum-weight degree-bounded forest problem. For the special case of uniform degree bounds, our algorithm achieves an approximation ratio of $\frac{3}{2}$. It computes two sets of edges, each of which we then restrict to a feasible solution in an optimal way, and finally returns the better of the two resulting solutions. To obtain the initial two edge sets, we first relax the degree bounds and leverage an algorithm by Lau and Singh [JACM'15] for degree-bounded spanning trees, and second we relax the forest constraints and employ an algorithm for maximum-weight $b$-matchings.

papers.intro:
The minimum-cost degree-bounded spanning tree problem is a seminal problem in combinatorial optimization and network design. Given a weighted graph G=(V,E,w)G=(V,E,w) and degree upper bounds bv∈ℕb_{v}\in\mathbb{N} for each vertex vv, it asks to find a minimum-cost spanning tree satisfying the given degree bounds. This line of work culminated in Lau and Singh’s iterative relaxation method [16] giving a polynomial time algorithm to obtain a spanning tree violating the degree bounds by an additive 11 while having a cost no more than that of an optimal solution (without violation). Their result is essentially the best possible. The iterative relaxation method was later applied and generalized to variants of this problem, for instance, higher connectivity [14], directed graphs [3], and matroidal constraints [12, 25].

papers.title: Pore-scale mechanisms of capillary imbibition in cement-based materials revealed by direct numerical simulations in a realistic FIB-SEM microstructure
papers.abstract:
Moisture transport in cement-based materials involves transient multiphase flow through highly irregular pore networks, where evolving air--water interfaces strongly influence liquid invasion and gas displacement. Here, pore-resolved, image-based direct numerical simulations (DNS) are used to investigate spontaneous imbibition in a FIB--SEM-reconstructed cementitious microstructure, resolving air--water interface dynamics at nanometre-to-micrometre spatial scales and nanosecond-to-microsecond timescales. As these dynamics remain inaccessible to direct experimental observation at such scales, the simulations provide, to the best of our knowledge, the first direct view of transient imbibition within the capillary porosity of a realistic cementitious microstructure.
  The three-dimensional simulations reveal highly heterogeneous wetting-front propagation, continuous interface reconfiguration, and progressive air entrapment, showing that local dynamics depend on evolving interface curvature and capillary-pressure fields rather than on characteristic pore size alone. Significant air entrapment develops even within the capillary pores and under perfectly water-wetting conditions, progressively reducing the saturation rate, while the capillary pressure of trapped-air clusters depends strongly on local interface geometry rather than gas volume alone. Controlled two-dimensional analyses show that the balance between capillary, viscous, inertial, and gravitational effects is strongly scale-dependent. Comparison with the three-dimensional simulations highlights the importance of out-of-plane interface curvature and pore-network connectivity. The framework also resolves moisture conditions at the steel--concrete interface, illustrating its potential for corrosion-relevant pore-scale analysis.

papers.intro:
Moisture transport plays a central role in the durability of cement-based materials because the amount and distribution of water within the pore structure strongly influence the transport of dissolved species, chemical reactions, freeze–thaw processes, and the conditions governing reinforcement corrosion [121, 96, 126, 5, 2]. Among the different modes of moisture transport, capillary imbibition governs the spontaneous uptake of liquid water driven by capillary forces and is relevant to a broad range of exposure situations encountered by cementitious materials [32, 94]. Predicting how water enters and redistributes within these materials is consequently a fundamental part of understanding their transport behaviour and long-term durability.

Predicting how water enters and redistributes within these materials is consequently a fundamental part of understanding their transport behaviour and long-term durability.

At the material and structural scales, moisture transport is commonly described through macroscopic state variables and effective transport properties. Experimental quantities such as water uptake and degree of saturation, together with effective transport properties such as sorptivity, permeability, and moisture diffusivity, provide practical measures of the overall transport response, while continuum models describe moisture redistribution using macroscopic conservation equations and constitutive relationships formulated in terms of the material moisture state [117, 43]. Depending on the formulation and conditions considered, these descriptions may represent liquid and vapour transport through different choices of state variables, constitutive relationships, and moisture-dependent transport properties [19, 22, 120, 110, 25, 118]. Such approaches are indispensable for engineering-scale prediction and provide effective descriptions of the underlying transport physics. However, continuum-scale descriptions inherently average over local fluid-solid configurations and interface dynamics, and therefore cannot resolve the pore-scale displacement and redistribution processes that collectively give rise to the observed macroscopic transport response [13].

However, continuum-scale descriptions inherently average over local fluid-solid configurations and interface dynamics, and therefore cannot resolve the pore-scale displacement and redistribution processes that collectively give rise to the observed macroscopic transport response [13].

At the pore scale, capillary imbibition is fundamentally a transient multiphase displacement process in which wetting water advances through the pore space and displaces the non-wetting air [73]. Classical descriptions such as the Lucas–Washburn equation provide an important physical reference by relating capillary driving pressure and viscous resistance in an idealized capillary [50, 99, 18]. In such simple geometries, pore size and wettability constrain meniscus curvature and therefore the associated capillary pressure. Real cementitious pore structures are considerably more irregular, forming interconnected networks of constrictions, expansions, dead ends, and ink-bottle-type pores with strongly varying local dimensions and connectivity. The limitations of representing capillary transport through simple parallel-pore concepts have long been recognized for cementitious materials [41, 67, 116]. As an air–water interface advances through such a network, its configuration continuously evolves with the local geometry, so that local curvature and capillary pressure cannot be related uniquely to a single characteristic pore size [6, 27, 61]. Consequently, macroscopic water uptake emerges as the collective outcome of local events involving interface deformation, pinning and depinning, bypassing, reconnection, gas entrapment, and associated pressure redistribution.

Experimental methods provide increasingly detailed information on water transport across different spatial and temporal scales, ranging from integral material response to spatially resolved moisture distributions and three-dimensional fluid configurations. Conventional absorption, sorptivity, and permeability measurements quantify the integral material response [32, 125], whereas magnetic-resonance techniques and neutron or X-ray radiography can provide spatially resolved information on moisture redistribution and wetting-front progression over time [83, 115, 37, 124]. In these measurements, however, the observed moisture state remains averaged over finite measurement volumes or, in the case of radiography, through the specimen thickness, so that the underlying pore-scale air–water interface dynamics are not resolved. Three-dimensional information can be obtained using neutron or X-ray computed tomography (CT), although the attainable spatial and temporal resolution is constrained by specimen size, acquisition time, and image quality [75]. Previous X-ray imaging studies provided evidence of water presence and filling in larger air voids, but represented the void state in a binary manner, as either empty or filled, without resolving intermediate filling states or the evolving air–water configuration within individual voids [66]. More recent X-ray CT studies have substantially advanced this capability by directly visualizing the moisture state and air–water configuration within macroscopic voids, including at the steel–concrete interface, and by following their evolution over prolonged exposure periods [79, 68]. Most recently, the saturation evolution of more than 5000 macro-voids larger than 100​μ100~\mum was tracked over several months, providing a statistically rich picture of long-term void filling and trapped-air evolution [31]. These studies provide valuable insight into long-term saturation of macroscopic voids and the secondary, slow stage of water uptake, but their spatial and temporal resolution remains insufficient to resolve the much faster primary capillary imbibition process within the finer capillary pore network.

papers.title: Superscalar Loop Processors
papers.abstract: To sustain the computational demands of modern ML and HPC workloads, programmable accelerators integrate large arrays of processing elements (PEs), typically built around single-issue in-order cores to maximize integration density and energy efficiency. As a result, each PE's instruction throughput is upper-bounded at one instruction per cycle (IPC), often suffering from significant underutilization of its functional units (FUs). Conventional superscalar processors can improve FU utilization by increasing IPC, but they typically incur substantial area and energy overheads. This work proposes the Superscalar Loop Processor (SLP) architecture, a lightweight approach to superscalar execution that targets regular, compute-intensive loop kernels. We present the SLP execution model, which exploits the static structure of these workloads to enable efficient multiple-issue execution without the complexity of dynamic out-of-order scheduling. We demonstrate the SLP architecture through an open-source prototype implementation, Schnizo, developed as an enhancement of a tiny RV32I core with floating-point support. Across several ML and HPC microkernels, Schnizo achieves substantially higher IPC and FPU utilization than the scalar baseline while retaining the efficiency of lightweight in-order designs. These results demonstrate that SLPs can provide an efficient architectural solution for programmable accelerators targeting regular, compute-intensive workloads.

The growth of machine learning (ML) workloads has created an unprecedented demand for computational capacity [1]. Empirical studies show that model quality improves predictably with additional compute [2, 3], driving rapid expansion of data centers and specialized accelerators. Recent analyses report that frontier-model training compute continues to grow at roughly 4-5×\times per year [4] and inference is scaling even faster due to the explosive increase in token generation linked to agentic workloads [5].

In this work, we propose Superscalar Loop Processors (SLPs) , a lightweight processor architecture that specializes superscalar execution for regular loop kernels. Rather than supporting general-purpose OoO execution, SLPs extract ILP exclusively within regular loop bodies. By constraining the scope of superscalar execution, SLPs achieve high FU utilization without incurring the overhead of OoO scheduling, bridging the gap between scalar efficiency and superscalar throughput for regular, compute-intensive workloads. We envision SLPs as an enhancement to the processing elements (PEs) of high-throughput programmable accelerators, such as GPUs and many-cores, where execution is dominated by regular loop kernels. They are not meant to replace OoO cores, which remain essential for latency-sensitive and irregular workloads.

papers.title: AgenticMobility: An Open-Source Platform for Multi-AI-Agent Mobility Dynamics
papers.abstract:
Understanding mobility dynamics and the effects of urban transportation management policies requires examining how individual travel decisions, traffic conditions, and policy interventions influence one another over time. We present AgenticMobility, an open-source experimental platform for studying how mobility AI agents and other AI agents interact, adapt through repeated experience, and collectively shape mobility outcomes. Persistent agents retain identities and relevant states across rounds, with explicit interfaces defining information access, admissible actions, and decision schedules; linked records trace decisions, execution, and feedback.
  In the current implementation, large language model (LLM) agents act as travelers choosing routes and departure times and as a manager periodically adjusting link charges within MATSim. A preliminary demonstration spans 100 simulated days in each of five configurations, with one run per configuration and a shared simulation seed. In the joint traveler--manager run, all 1,179,300 finalized target decisions satisfied action constraints; execution checks verified implementation of accepted choices and preservation of personal memories across days. Trajectories show stable route choices alongside departure-time adjustments and differences between controlled-trip and population-wide outcomes.
  The platform supports experiments on individual adaptation, collective outcomes, and management interventions by varying information access, retained experience, and management feedback. Source code is available at https://github.com/Agentic-City-Research/Agentic-Mobility

papers.title: Towards Self-Evolving Narrative Systems: Real-Time Adaptation and Long-Term Optimization with LLMs
papers.abstract: Traditional interactive narrative systems offer strong authorial control and structural coherence but often restrict player agency. In contrast, LLM-driven narratives enable open-ended generation and greater flexibility, yet frequently suffer from inconsistency and diminished narrative control. To navigate this trade-off, we propose a hybrid narrative framework that dynamically balances pre-authored content with real-time LLM generation via semantic similarity alignment. Additionally, sustaining narrative quality over extended gameplay remains a core challenge in LLM-based storytelling. To address this, we introduce a self-evolving, feedback-driven optimization framework that leverages in-context learning to iteratively refine prompts, eliminating the need for manual prompt engineering. Through a case study and participant-based evaluation, we show that our framework enhances narrative coherence while preserving player agency, effectively aligning generated content with both authorial intent and evolving player behavior.

papers.title: To Align Long, Plan Short: Simulating Diverse Profile-Aligned Students by Realizing Short-Term Plans in Long-Horizon Learning Environments
papers.abstract: Simulated students offer a scalable way to test learning platforms and AI tutors before deployment with real students and to augment scarce data for studying learning at scale. Existing LLM-based simulators primarily target short, language-centered interactions. In open-ended learning environments, however, student behavior emerges from patterns across long-horizon interaction trajectories, where turn-level prompting can drift from an assigned behavior profile. We introduce ALPS (Align Long-term by Planning Short-term), a hierarchical simulated student conditioned on observable, environment-specific behavior profiles. Rather than selecting every action independently, ALPS alternates between planning profile-aligned task segments and generating the corresponding actions. We evaluate ALPS in both data-sufficient and data-scarce settings, where supervision comes either from real student trajectories or from a teacher LLM. Across both settings, we compare in-context learning (ICL), supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reward-ranked fine-tuning (RAFT), and their sequential combination (SFT followed by RAFT). Experiments in an inquiry-based physics game and a pharmacy simulation evaluate behavioral density and coverage against held-out real data, and profile consistency using a human-aligned LLM judge. Across both settings, ALPS consistently outperforms turn-level generation, achieving comparable density and judge pass rates under scarce supervision, although coverage remains lower. These results show that hierarchical planning enables faithful, profile-aligned simulation over long interaction horizons, even with limited real student data.

papers.intro:
Interactive learning technologies increasingly rely on AI to provide personalized support, evaluate learning experiences, and guide adaptive interventions. Developing and validating such systems requires realistic student behavior: students who explore, pursue different strategies, and make mistakes, rather than merely records of success and failure. Collecting such behavior at scale is difficult. Classroom access, cost, and privacy constraints result in datasets that are small and skewed, with rare behavior patterns, often those of the students an intervention aims to support, being the least represented (Baker and Hawn 2022). Simulated learners, computational models that emulate how students interact with learning environments (Käser and Alexandron 2024), offer a scalable alternative for testing learning platforms and adaptive interventions before deployment (VanLehn, Ohlsson, and Nason 1994; Robinson, Jahanian, and Reich 2018; Nazaretsky, Hershkovitz, and Alexandron 2019) and augmenting datasets with rare but pedagogically important behaviors (Khalil, Liu, and Jovanovic 2025; Khalil et al. 2025; Liu et al. 2025). To fulfill this promise, simulated learners must be faithful, reproducing realistic student behavior, and diverse, representing the range of learner behaviors.

Earlier simulated learners were based on cognitive, rule-based, or probabilistic models learned from interaction logs (Li et al. 2011; MacLellan et al. 2016; Corbett and Anderson 2005; Faucon, Kidzinski, and Dillenbourg 2016; Botelho, Adjei, and Heffernan 2016). While these approaches provide interpretable and controllable models of student behavior, they typically rely on a small number of predefined states or parameters, limiting their ability to capture the richness of real student behavior (Käser and Alexandron 2024). More recently, large language models (LLMs) have enabled richer simulated learners. Existing LLM-based simulators, however, have primarily focused on short, language-centered interactions, including tutoring dialogues (Jin et al. 2025; Schmucker et al. 2023; Zhang et al. 2025; Xu et al. 2025; Scarlatos et al. 2026; Duan et al. 2026), misconceptions and errors (Ross and Andreas 2025; Fernandez et al. 2024; Sonkar et al. 2024; Daheim et al. 2024), assessment responses (Benedetto et al. 2024; Scarlatos et al. 2025; Nguyen et al. 2025; He-Yueya et al. 2024; Lu and Wang 2024), and mathematical or programming practices (Ross et al. 2025; Nguyen, Tschiatschek, and Singla 2024) (see Appendix A). Whether they can generate coherent, diverse behavioral trajectories in longer horizons remains largely unexplored.

Our work focuses on simulating learners in open-ended learning environments (OELEs), where students engage in long exploratory interaction trajectories rather than short exchanges. In this setting, behavior emerges from patterns across entire trajectories rather than individual actions. This shift from turn-level responses to trajectory-level behavior introduces three key challenges. First, maintaining a consistent behavior profile becomes more difficult. Because trajectories span hundreds of interactions, LLMs tend to drift from their assigned profiles (Abdulhai et al. 2025). Second, existing work typically conditions simulated learners on generic attributes such as knowledge states, personality traits, or demographics (Liu et al. 2024; Jin et al. 2025). These attributes describe the student, but not how the student behaves in a particular learning environment, leaving no observable basis for verifying generated trajectories. Many pedagogically meaningful behaviors are also environment-specific, arising from the available actions and constraints rather than general learner characteristics. Finally, the scarcity of student data that motivates simulated learners also constrains their development. New environments often provide only a handful of trajectories or none at all, making it difficult to learn environment-specific behavior profiles. Existing work shows that prompting performs poorly under such limited supervision (Scarlatos et al. 2026), leaving the development of faithful and diverse simulated learners an open problem.

papers.title: ClickSight: An LLM Framework for Interpreting Student Clickstreams Through Learning Strategies
papers.abstract: Digital learning environments produce rich clickstream data that can reveal how students approach learning tasks, yet interpreting these fine-grained traces often requires substantial expert effort. We introduce ClickSight, a framework for interpreting student clickstreams through learning strategies defined in the literature. Given a student clickstream and a predefined set of learning strategies, ClickSight uses a staged LLM-based pipeline to identify strategy-relevant evidence, assess adherence to each strategy, and generate an evidence-grounded interpretation of the student's behavior. We evaluate ClickSight across two learning environments, 365 students, and 12 model backbones using an expert-grounded quality rubric and an LLM judge calibrated with human-expert ratings. Our results show that ClickSight can generate high-quality strategy-based interpretations across different models and environments, with reasoning models performing more consistently than instruction-tuned counterparts. We further find that providing external clickstream-extracted guidance can improve interpretation quality for strategies that require precise quantitative information from the trace. By connecting fine-grained clickstreams with theoretically defined learning strategies and preserving the evidence underlying each judgment, ClickSight provides a flexible approach for studying student behavior in digital learning environments.

This reliance on expert-driven, often domain-specific processes makes it difficult to transfer such approaches across learning environments and limits their scalability.

Prior approaches include designing domain-specific features to capture strategy use (Shved et al., 2024; Käser and Schwartz, 2020; Perez et al., 2018; Fratamico et al., 2017), clustering student behaviors (Shved et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2016; Wei et al., 2025; Rohani et al., 2024; Cicchinelli et al., 2018), and applying sequential pattern mining to uncover common interaction traces (Park et al., 2017; Yürüm et al., 2023; Akpinar et al., 2020; Villalobos et al., 2024; Perez et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2022a). Other work has trained supervised models using expert-labeled data (Akpinar et al., 2020; Güres et al., 2025; Li et al., 2022) or applied knowledge-tracing techniques to infer latent student states (Rodrigues et al., 2024; Käser and Schwartz, 2020). While these approaches have successfully extracted meaningful patterns from clickstream data, translating low-level interactions into interpretable learning behaviors typically requires substantial expert input, for example to define features, construct labels, specify relevant patterns, or interpret the resulting representations. Large Language Models (LLMs) have the potential to alleviate these limitations by reducing the need for such expert effort, given their capabilities for pattern recognition, abstraction, and reasoning (Denny et al., 2024; Mirchandani et al., 2023). More recent work has begun applying LLMs to behavioral and non-textual educational data, but typically through fine-tuning, precomputed indicators, or engineered representations (Liu et al., 2025a; Moon et al., 2025; Davalos et al., 2025). It therefore remains underexplored whether LLMs can directly interpret clickstream data to derive higher-level behavioral insights grounded in theoretically defined learning strategies.

papers.title: SWE-Trail: History-Guided Trajectory Collection for Coding Agent Training
papers.abstract: Coding agents solve repository issues through long sequences of exploration, editing, and validation. These trajectories are increasingly used as post-training data, so how they are collected shapes what the trained model learns. A common approach is to sample multiple trajectories independently for each issue and then select or curate them. However, as more trajectories are sampled independently, later trajectories become increasingly redundant, even though earlier trajectories could guide where subsequent collection effort should be spent. A natural way to use this history is to expose it to the coding agent as advice. But training on such trajectories can make the model rely on advice that is unavailable at test time, creating a train-test mismatch. Instead, we argue that history should guide where collection effort is spent, while the coding agent decides what to generate. We introduce SWE-Trail, a trajectory collector that uses earlier trajectories to guide subsequent collection while keeping that history outside the coding agent's context. During a new rollout, SWE-Trail uses history to identify a state where additional collection effort may be useful. There, the coding agent proposes candidate next actions from its ordinary context, and SWE-Trail briefly executes them from the same checkpoint to decide which route continues. We evaluate collection approaches by training student models on the trajectories they produce. For a 124B student initialized from Ling-3.0-flash-base, SWE-Trail improves mean resolution over independent sampling by 2.33 and 1.60 percentage points on SWE-bench Multilingual and SWE-bench Pro, respectively. Without history, the same pipeline produces more resolved trajectories than independent sampling, but improves by only 0.11 points on Multilingual. These results show the value of using history to guide collection without exposing it to the coding agent.

Resolving a repository-level issue requires a coding agent to explore the repository, modify code, and validate its changes (Jimenez et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025a). These interactions form trajectories that record not only the final patch but also the agent’s reasoning and actions throughout the repair process. Such trajectories are increasingly used as post-training data, so the collection process directly affects their value for training (Chen et al., 2026; Han, 2026).

Such trajectories are increasingly used as post-training data, so the collection process directly affects their value for training (Chen et al., 2026; Han, 2026).

A common way to collect coding agent training trajectories is to sample several trajectories per issue and keep those that pass tests or a judge (Pan et al., 2025; Ehrlich et al., 2025; Jain et al., 2025). Some work also edits the kept trajectories, masking flawed tool calls or removing redundant steps (Tao et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2026a; Han et al., 2026; Xiao et al., 2026b). These methods operate after trajectories are collected, while trajectories for the same issue are still generated independently. However, later independent samples become increasingly redundant as more trajectories are collected. They often revisit repair targets and behaviors already explored earlier. Rather than ignoring this history, subsequent collection can use earlier trajectories to decide where additional collection effort should be spent. For example, disagreements between successful and failed trajectories can reveal decision points where alternative actions are worth comparing. We refer to such evidence as allocation signals and to the earlier trajectories for an issue as its history. Section 2 quantifies the redundancy of independent sampling and tests whether earlier trajectories provide such allocation signals. Since earlier trajectories can provide useful information for a new rollout, a natural way to use this history is to place it in the coding agent’s context as advice (Chen et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026b). This can help the current rollout, but the resulting training trajectories record reasoning and actions generated with access to the advice. This leads to our central question: How can history guide where collection effort is spent while the coding agent decides what to generate from its ordinary context?

During a new rollout, when the agent reaches such a state, it proposes candidate next actions from its ordinary context without access to the history. SWE-Trail then compares candidate actions by briefly executing them from the same checkpoint. It selects the route that is better supported by repository evidence. The coding agent then continues from the selected route to complete the trajectory. A concrete example illustrates this process. On a Rust issue, all prior failed trajectories made an edit and then continued reading without running tests. From this history, SWE-Trail determines that this state should receive additional collection effort when it appears again in a new rollout. When the rollout reaches such a state, the coding agent proposes different next actions from its ordinary context, including further reading and running tests. SWE-Trail briefly executes both choices from the same checkpoint and selects the test-running route based on the resulting evidence. The coding agent then continues from the selected route until the rollout ends.

papers.title: GoalDex: Learning Image-Goal-Conditioned Policies for Dexterous In-Hand Manipulation
papers.abstract: Dexterous in-hand manipulation is commonly formulated around explicit object pose estimation, yet reliable pose tracking is challenging under severe hand-object occlusions and often requires object-specific supervision. This dependence creates a bottleneck between perception and control that can limit robustness and scalability. We present an end-to-end visuomotor framework for dexterous in-hand reorientation that operates on RGB observations and proprioception without intermediate pose estimation. Our approach jointly learns visual representations and control policies through behavior distillation from privileged state teachers and auxiliary reconstruction objectives. Furthermore, we introduce image-goal-conditioned reorientation, allowing desired object configurations to be specified directly through images rather than canonical pose representations. We evaluate our approach across a diverse set of object geometries and instances in simulation, where it consistently outperforms pose-based methods and policies built on pretrained visual encoders. Finally, we demonstrate direct sim-to-real transfer of a single image-goal-conditioned policy across five real-world objects, showing that accurate dexterous reorientation can be achieved without explicit pose estimation. For videos and code release, please refer to the project website: https://rffr.leggedrobotics.com/works/goaldex/
papers.intro:
Manipulating objects into precise functional poses requires a high degree of dexterity. To succeed, a robot must infer object geometry, contact state, and motion despite severe hand-object occlusions. Most existing systems address this challenge through an explicit object pose interface that connects perception and control [1, 2]. While effective for individual objects, this abstraction introduces important limitations. Object pose discards rich information about local geometry and contact interactions. It also assumes a predefined canonical coordinate system for every object instance, both in the observation space and in the goal specification. As manipulation systems scale to diverse or unseen objects, defining such canonical frames becomes increasingly difficult and often ill-posed [3]. More fundamentally, object pose alone cannot capture the transient contact dynamics and local surface features that govern dexterous manipulation. These challenges motivate visuomotor representations that are coordinate-free, temporally grounded, and learned directly from sensory observations.

These challenges motivate visuomotor representations that are coordinate-free, temporally grounded, and learned directly from sensory observations.

End-to-end visual control has historically been difficult because pixel observations lack direct physical grounding [4]. Recent advances in reinforcement learning [5], visual rendering [6], and sim-to-real transfer [2] now make it possible to train RGB-based policies in simulation and deploy them on real hardware. A natural approach is to use pretrained visual encoders, which provide strong semantic and geometric priors [7, 8]. However, these models are trained for static visual understanding, not closed-loop physical interaction. Dexterous manipulation requires representations that capture contact, motion, and task-relevant geometry over time. These properties may not be readily accessible from generic visual features, motivating representations learned through interaction.

The framework combines privileged teacher–student distillation with a reconstruction objective on hidden system variables, encouraging the latent representation to capture object geometry, contact dynamics, and other task-relevant physical properties. We further scale training to 25 diverse objects in simulation. • We achieve direct sim-to-real transfer of a single policy trained in simulation on five objects to their real-world counterparts, with 80% success over 100 hardware trials compared with 27% for the strongest evaluated pose-based baseline.

papers.title: Built on Broken Assumptions (BOBA): Why Coding Agents Cannot Be Left Alone
papers.abstract: Coding agents are autonomous developers. Given a request, they change the code and report back when done. As such, they can handle not only independent requests but whole chains of them, each request built on the last. Agents are known to report wrong work as done, yet benchmarks still test them one request at a time, on human-written code, checked once. We build BOBA-Bench, 280 chains of 20 consecutive requests drawn from 140 real open-source projects, and evaluate ten coding agents on both. All ten do far worse on chains. On average, they complete 95% of requests taken one at a time, but when requests are chained together, they complete 51%. Worse code is not the cause. Once checked, agent code is nearly as good a base for later requests as human code. The cause is the mistakes agents miss. Coding agents declare a request done once their own tests pass, even when those tests miss a mistake. The next request then builds on broken code and fails about twice as often. The mistake is rarely found later. Nor can agents catch such mistakes by reviewing code. Asked whether an implementation is correct, they are right 53% of the time, barely better than a coin flip. Coding agents are therefore heavily dependent on access to verification. A single external ``that's wrong'' after a failed request and one repair round lift chain completion from 51% to 59%, and a repaired mistake no longer hurts the requests that follow. In simpler terms, coding agents are only as reliable as the checks they can reach: without verification, every request that follows is built on broken assumptions.
papers.intro:
Today’s coding agents (e.g., Codex (OpenAI, 2025), Claude Code (Anthropic, 2025), OpenHands (Wang et al., 2025)) let developers hand over a request and receive a finished change. Delegation promises to help not only when developers review each change before asking for the next, but also when they cannot, and each request then builds on code the agent wrote and reported complete (Liu et al., 2026a; Duma et al., 2026). Though trajectory studies confirm that agents rarely catch a mistake nothing flags for them (Rahman et al., 2026) and report wrong work as complete (Mehta, 2026; Advani, 2026; Smyth et al., 2026), they are typically evaluated on a single request, from human-written code, verified once (Jimenez et al., 2024; Deng et al., 2025).

Even though a growing body of work proposes to evaluate agents over successive requests (Deng et al., 2026; Lam et al., 2026; Orlanski et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026; Shastry et al., 2026; Jin et al., 2026; Shen et al., 2026; Sobal et al., 2026), we identify in our review (Section 2) that prior work either carries an agent’s verified and unverified work forward as one, even against an oracle control (Jin et al., 2026; Deng et al., 2026), so a later failure cannot be told apart as building on agent-written code or on a mistake nobody checked (Peng et al., 2026), or stops at the first failure (Shen et al., 2026; Sobal et al., 2026) and never continues from unverified work. In this work, we close this gap by creating a benchmark for continuous, unattended development – BOBA-Bench – built from the commit histories of 140 real repositories. At a high level, the chaining process we propose transforms a stretch of a repository’s history into a chain of 20 requests, specified from the tests the developers added, that jointly rebuild their changes. Autonomous evaluation then hands each request to the agent in a fresh conversation, on the state the previous request left behind, with hidden tests after every request telling verified work from a silent miss: the chain runs through all 20 requests, and the agent, told nothing and remembering nothing of the earlier requests, builds each one on whatever they left, verified or not.

papers.title: Partial Invariance for Classification under Structural Causal Models
papers.abstract: Making predictions in an unseen environment from data collected across multiple training environments is challenging. This challenge is particularly pronounced when the target-generating mechanism varies across environments. In this work, we introduce environment-label separation, a form of partial environmental invariance that decomposes the target conditional distribution into an environment-invariant component and a label-invariant component. We show that this partial invariance enables estimation of the target conditional distribution in an unseen environment when using labeled training data together with unlabeled test features. Within the structural causal model framework, we provide sufficient conditions for environment-label separation. Building on these conditions, we develop an algorithm, dIMP-Classifier, which jointly minimizes an estimate of the test risk and encourages invariance across environments. We further provide finite-sample guarantees that characterize the test risk in terms of deviations from invariance, estimation error, and sample complexity. Experiments on simulated data and the real-world light tunnel Causal Chamber data demonstrate that the proposed approach can perform under interventions on the target mechanism and consistently outperforms the considered standard and invariance-based baselines.

papers.title: Towards a Theory for the Design of Rules in Multi-Agent Systems: the case of Homogeneous Fleets
papers.abstract: The regulation of systems composed of many interacting decentralised agents is a long-standing problem. This problem has typically been resolved by the imposition of rules. Rules resolve the limitations of sub-optimal agents whilst simultaneously aligning the behaviour of the agents with the demands of society. Traffic laws, for example, let a driver cross a junction without seeing around the corner, and transport protocols such as TCP let applications share a network without knowing of one another. The problem is more pressing today, as autonomous systems are deployed in society. In this work, we establish the basis of a system-agnostic theory of rule design for multi-agent systems. We first state the rule design problem (RDP) in its generality. It relates a rule to the set of system performances, defined by the regulator, that the agents deployed under it can attain. However, it is not yet possible to solve the RDP in full generality. As such, we introduce the homogeneous rule design problem (HRDP), in which the agents in each environment are identical, and among other interesting properties, show that under worst-case aggregation the two problems have the same solution, bypassing the combinatorial complexity of the RDP. To solve the RDP under worst-case aggregation we propose Rule Branch and Bound (RuleBnB), an anytime branch-and-bound algorithm. Finally, we illustrate the value of solving the RDP on an autonomous driving case study.

papers.title: Optimal Annuitization, Consumption, and Investment with Costly Capital Injections
papers.abstract: We study a joint optimal decision of portfolio, consumption, and annuitization for a pension-plan manager who balances retirement consumption benefits against the cost of maintaining the solvency of pension account. The pension sponsor provides costly capital injection to prevent negative wealth. Annuity purchases are irreversible, and injected funds remain in the liquid account and earn interest. Using the Legendre transform, we derive a semi-explicit solution to the associated free-boundary problem and verify the optimality of the resulting strategies. We identify an endogenous annuity-income threshold separating injection-active and injection-inactive regions and characterize six policy regimes arising from the interplay between capital injections and consumption constraints. Compared with the no-injection benchmark, capital injections delay annuitization, alter the structure of the annuitization boundary, and permit positive holdings in risky assets even at zero liquid wealth. Numerical results further reveal that cheaper annuities may increase the expected capital contributions required from the pension sponsor.

After the seminal work Merton (1969); Merton (1971), continuous-time utility maximization for portfolio management and consumption planning has become a core research topic in quantitative finance. Taking into account the retirement planning, these decisions become more subtle because of longevity risk and the availability of life annuities, which convert liquid wealth into a guaranteed income stream for the remaining lifetime. As shown by Yaari (1965), actuarially fair annuities can be preferable to bonds in the absence of a bequest motive, while Davidoff et al. (2005) establish the welfare benefits of annuitization under more general conditions. These findings highlight the importance of jointly optimizing consumption, investment, and annuitization decisions in retirement planning.

Milevsky et al. Wang and Young (2012) extended this framework to commutable annuities with surrender charges. Downside protection is another important consideration in post-retirement pension management and annuitization, as adverse investment outcomes and the depletion of liquid wealth may threaten the sustainability of retirement consumption. In income-drawdown arrangements, retirees may remain invested during the decumulation phase rather than fully annuitizing their pension wealth, making protection against financial shortfalls particularly relevant. Gerrard et al. (2004) studied optimal post-retirement investment, while Gerrard et al. (2012) jointly examined consumption, investment, and annuitization timing. More explicitly incorporating downside protection, Di Giacinto et al. (2014) investigated income drawdown with a minimum guarantee, while Dadashi (2020) considered optimal investment and consumption under a minimum guarantee for future annuity income. These studies highlight the importance of balancing investment flexibility and annuitization decisions with protection against the risk of insufficient retirement wealth. However, they generally impose non-negative wealth as a hard state constraint or provide minimum retirement benefits, without explicitly modeling the capital contributions required to maintain solvency. In practice, pension sponsors may be required to make additional contributions when funding levels deteriorate, as illustrated by funding requirements for U.S. defined-benefit pension plans (Rauh, 2006).

The provision of such external financial support is closely related to the literature on costly capital injections and reflected surplus processes. In dividend and insurance models, capital injections are used to prevent insolvency, often leading to a lower reflecting boundary at zero (Lokka and Zervos, 2008; Eisenberg and Schmidli, 2009; Eisenberg and Schmidli, 2011; Ferrari and Schuhmann, 2019). Related portfolio optimization with benchmark-tracking (Bo et al., 2021; Bo et al., 2025a; Bo et al., 2025b; Bo et al., 2026a; Bo et al., 2026b) also utilized the capital support to maintain prescribed wealth floors, with the minimal regulator representing cumulative shortfalls. Building on these two strands of literature, we consider a post-retirement pension account with a sponsor-backed solvency guarantee. The pension-plan manager jointly determines consumption, portfolio allocation, and irreversible annuity purchases, aiming to maximize the retiree’s expected discounted consumption utility under constant absolute risk aversion (CARA) while accounting for the cost of external capital support. Whenever adverse investment outcomes or consumption withdrawals would otherwise drive liquid wealth below zero, the pension sponsor provides the minimum amount of capital required to maintain solvency. The injected funds remain in the pension account and earn interest with remaining wealth. Importantly, capital injections are available solely to fulfill the solvency guarantee and cannot be used as a discretionary borrowing facility. Unlike annuity purchases, which constitute a singular control chosen by the manager, capital injections are determined endogenously as the minimal reflecting process required to maintain non-negative liquid wealth. The resulting problem therefore involves a lower reflecting boundary associated with solvency protection and an upper intervention boundary governing irreversible annuity purchases.

papers.title: ETH is Dead, Long Live SH
papers.abstract: Impagliazzo and Paturi's 1999 Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH) is false, but Stearns and Hunt's 1990 Satisfiability Hypothesis (SH) remains plausible. We prove that SH is equivalent to the recently proposed Weak ETH which rules out $O(2^{n^{1-\varepsilon}})L^{O(1)}$-time 3SAT algorithms for every constant $\varepsilon>0$, where $L$ is the input length. We show that SH (or Weak ETH) preserves the typical process for lower bounds: a polynomial-time reduction from a 3SAT formula of size $s=\Theta(n+m)$ to an instance of size $N\le s^{b+o(1)}$, for fixed blowup exponent $b>0$, rules out $O(2^{N^{1/b-\varepsilon}})$-time algorithms for every constant $\varepsilon>0$. By comparison, for an $N=O(s^b)$ blowup, ETH would have ruled out $2^{o(N^{1/b})}$-time algorithms. The framework also yields parameterized lower bounds ruling out running times of the form $O(2^{k^{1/b-\varepsilon}})L^{O(1)}$. We also prove equivalence of the analogous counting hypotheses, #SH and Weak #ETH, and that they rule out $O(2^{(n+m)^{1-\varepsilon}})$-time algorithms for #2SAT for every constant $\varepsilon>0$.

papers.title: Closing the Dynamics Gap through Self-Directed Robotic Interaction
papers.abstract: Agentic Real2Sim2Real systems can reconstruct a scene in simulation from camera observations, but contact-rich dynamics such as friction and restitution cannot be observed without interaction. We call this the dynamics gap and present CUE, an agentic system that closes it by interacting with the environment itself. Given only a high-level instruction and no resets, the agent builds its own perception, identifies physical parameters, and targets interactions where its simulation is least accurate. On billiards, CUE reduces held-out ball-position error by 72% relative to the strongest baseline across 25 hidden-physics conditions in simulation, and we further deploy it on a real pool table. More details can be found on the project website: https://cue-dynamics.github.io/

papers.title: Training-Time Domain Transfer for Generator-Free Diagnostics on Novel Modalities in Computational Pathology
papers.abstract: Novel imaging modalities promise improved diagnostics, but AI development is constrained by scarce training data. Inference-time domain transfer can address this by mapping novel modalities to established ones, enabling reuse of existing diagnostic models. However, this introduces hallucination risks, computational overhead, and regulatory complexity. Inspired by sim-to-real transfer, we propose training-time domain transfer, generating synthetic target-domain training data from archived routine samples to enable direct diagnosis on real inputs without inference-time generation. Using unstained prostate histopathology as a proof-of-concept, we compare this approach with inference-time virtual staining and conventional H&E-based cancer detection. Training-time transfer achieved higher concordance with the conventional benchmark than virtual staining for both raw (Cohen's $\kappa$=0.59 vs. 0.37; Gwet's AC1=0.73 vs. 0.29) and deparaffinized tissue ($\kappa$=0.66 vs. 0.61; AC1=0.73 vs. 0.64), supporting its potential for emerging diagnostic modalities.
papers.intro:
Robust diagnostic AI requires large, annotated datasets, which are scarce for emerging imaging modalities. In pathology, e.g., unstained slides, spatial multiplex proteomics, or µ-CT lack large clinical datasets, whereas archives of conventional hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained slides enable large-scale AI studies. Computer vision addresses similar data scarcity through sim-to-real transfer, training models on synthetic data for direct deployment on real inputs, as demonstrated in autonomous driving [1] and robotics [2]. If a simulated domain, however imperfect, captures sufficient structure of the real target domain, a downstream model can be trained without real data. In medical imaging, this paradigm has been used to, e.g., synthesize MRI training data from annotated CT scans for radiotherapy contouring [3]. In pathology, the dominant response has been to deploy generative AI models to synthesize data. A prominent example is virtual staining [4], enabled by image-to-image translation [5] and explored, e.g., for prostate biopsies [6]. These approaches operate at inference time, translating images from a novel modality into a familiar one so that existing diagnostic models can be applied. However, generative AI models can hallucinate, and realistic hallucinations such as an incorrect number of nuclei can mislead diagnosis [7]. Combining generative and diagnostic models also increases regulatory complexity, requiring separate validation and revalidation after updates. We propose reversing this paradigm by restricting generative AI to training (training-time domain transfer, TTDT), following a sim-to-real approach (Fig. 1). As a proof-of-concept, we generate synthetic unstained training images from archived H&E slides for prostate cancer detection, while performing inference directly on real unstained tissue. To our knowledge, this approach is novel in computational pathology.

papers.title: SHq: Learnable Grids for LLM Weight Quantization
papers.abstract: Block-scaled lookup-table (LUT) formats, which represent weights as indices into a small value set (the grid), have become standard for low-bit LLM quantization, ranging from NF4 and BOF4 to the 3-bit LUT instruction in NVIDIA Rubin. While these formats leave the grid definition flexible, existing implementations rely on fixed grids derived either from numerical data types (INT, FP) or assumed weight distributions (NF, BOF). We demonstrate that no single fixed grid is universally optimal; the best fixed grid varies with bit-width: BOFS at 2 bits, NF at 4 and 5 bits, and INT at 6 bits. We introduce SHq, a closed-form family of grids parameterized by two critical degrees of freedom: a companding strength {\alpha} that interpolates level spacing from uniform to floating-point-like, and an offset c that introduces asymmetry. This offset allows the sign bit of the FP8 block scale, otherwise unused, to select between the grid and its mirror image, up to doubling the number of distinct values available per block. SHq modifies only the lookup table contents and serves as a drop-in replacement for the grid in any such format. Across five models ranging from 3B to 35B parameters, including a mixture-of-experts architecture, evaluated at 2-6 bits using RTN and GPTQ, SHq achieves the lowest KL divergence in every setting at 3 and 4 bits and in most settings at 2, 5 and 6 bits. It outperforms the best fixed grid by up to 34% and remains superior under mixed-precision configurations. At 4.5 bits per weight, the SHq format reduces the KL divergence of NVFP4 by 41-67% while improving downstream accuracy. Grid families incorporating both spacing and offset parameters perform comparably, whereas those lacking an offset exhibit clearly higher error, confirming that these two degrees of freedom drive the observed gains. We therefore propose SHq as the standard grid for block-scaled lookup-table formats.

Finding good grids for a given distribution is an old problem. The Lloyd–Max conditions are necessary conditions for the MSE-optimal scalar quantizer of a known source Lloyd (1982); Max (1960). In machine learning, ZipML was among the first to compute variance-optimal quantization levels directly from the data distribution Zhang et al. (2017). For LLM weights, this line of work has produced multiple families of grids: NF4 places its levels at quantiles of a normal distribution Dettmers et al. (2024a), BOF4 derives Lloyd-style codebooks that minimize the blockwise reconstruction error under absmax scaling Blumenberg et al. (2024), and recent formats go further, choosing between two grids for every block Cook et al. (2026); Egiazarian et al. (2026b). In most of these formats, the grids are fixed before the model is seen.

Fixing the grid in advance has three weaknesses. First, the optimal grid depends on the bit-width: in our experiments, the best fixed grid is BOFS at 2 bits, NF at 4 and 5 bits, and, in half of the settings, INT at 6 bits (Section 4), so no single fixed grid is a safe choice. Second, the optimal grid depends on the surrounding format as much as on the weights: the encoding of the block scale in E4M3 and the search over its values shift the error-minimizing grid (Section 2), whereas NF and BOF are derived from an assumed weight distribution under plain absmax scaling. Third, and more fundamentally, grids are fit to mean-squared error, possibly weighted by activation or curvature statistics; however, a lower layerwise error, weighted or not, does not necessarily yield a lower divergence of the model’s output Yvinec et al. (2023); Blumenberg et al. (2026). Learning the grid for every layer or channel Kim et al. (2024) removes the distributional assumption, but a learned codebook has 2q2^{q} free levels per layer and is in practice fit to a layerwise proxy.

First, the optimal grid depends on the bit-width: in our experiments, the best fixed grid is BOFS at 2 bits, NF at 4 and 5 bits, and, in half of the settings, INT at 6 bits (Section 4), so no single fixed grid is a safe choice. papers.title: KlaskTron-IL: A Contact-Rich Adversarial Imitation Learning Benchmark with a Validated Sim-to-Real Bridge
papers.abstract: KlaskTron is an open-hardware physical platform for two-player adversarial reinforcement learning, with a learned actuator model that supports zero-shot sim-to-real transfer of trained policies. Building on this platform, we contribute KlaskTron-IL: a multi-tier imitation learning dataset (80k human demonstration timesteps collected directly on the physical robot, 320k symmetry-augmented timesteps, and synthetic expert trajectories up to 5M steps generated by the zero-shot-validated PPO policy), and diagnostic baselines that expose three characteristic failure modes of standard IL methods under contact-rich adversarial dynamics: BC's data scaling plateau, GAIL's interpretable but weak-gradient discriminator (Spearman $\rho = -1.0$ peg-ball proximity recovery, but a logit span under 0.1), and an asymmetric BC-prior x reward-density interaction. Because the policy interface used throughout this paper is the same one the actuator model bridges to hardware, a policy trained on this benchmark can run unchanged on the physical robot, as we demonstrate zero-shot for the strongest BC baseline, so long as its commands respect the actuator model's $\pm 0.2$ m/s identification range.
papers.intro:
Physical adversarial multi-agent learning is bottlenecked by infrastructure. Industrial-grade platforms such as robotic table tennis [1] are inaccessible to most labs; cooperative manipulation benchmarks [2, 3, 4] avoid the high-speed contact and non-stationarity that adversarial play induces. KlaskTron addresses this with a <$2,500<\$2{,}500 open-hardware testbed based on the tabletop game Klask [5]: dual CoreXY gantries drive magnetic pegs beneath the board at 50 Hz, an overhead camera with EKF state estimation closes the perception loop, and a learned neural actuator model [6] bridges the simulator and the physical robot. Crucially, the platform supports zero-shot sim-to-real transfer: PPO policies trained in Isaac Lab deploy directly to hardware without further fine-tuning, even with domain randomization disabled [7].

Crucially, the platform supports zero-shot sim-to-real transfer: PPO policies trained in Isaac Lab deploy directly to hardware without further fine-tuning, even with domain randomization disabled [7].

This paper asks what happens when standard imitation learning is run on this platform. The same actuator network that enables PPO transfer also makes a policy with the same interface (12D state, 2D-velocity action) hardware-deployable, provided its commands stay within the action range the actuator model was identified on, so failure modes diagnosed in simulation are directly informative about what would fail on the robot. Three things go wrong, and they go wrong in interpretable ways: (a) Behavioral cloning exhibits a data-scaling plateau across 80k to 5M expert demonstrations, with performance statistically flat and well below expert parity regardless of dataset size – a signature that covariate shift, not data scarcity, is the binding constraint; (b) GAIL learns an interpretable but weak-gradient discriminator that recovers peg–ball proximity with perfect rank correlation (Spearman ρ=−1.0\rho=-1.0) but whose logit span is too narrow to serve as an informative reward in our configuration; (c) BC-bootstrapped RL displays an asymmetric demonstration-prior ×\times reward-density interaction – the BC prior stabilizes sparse-reward training but has no detectable effect under dense shaping.

papers.title: KlaskTron: An Open-Source Platform for Physical Adversarial Multi-Agent RL
papers.abstract: Progress in robot learning, particularly physical multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), is currently challenged by a limited availability of accessible, standardized benchmarks. While simulation-based MARL has produced remarkable emergent behaviors, from coordinated team play to complex tool use, translating these advances to physical systems remains difficult. A key barrier is infrastructural: physical platforms are often prohibitively expensive, require specialized facilities, or lack open mechanisms and designs for reproducibility. We introduce KlaskTron, an open-source, low-cost (<\$2500 USD), desktop-scale robotic testbed for adversarial MARL based on the dynamic tabletop game KLASK. The platform features dual CoreXY gantries with high-torque brushless motors, enabling the high-speed, precise manipulation required for competitive play. Crucially, we provide a complete ecosystem: hardware designs (CAD, BOM), a GPU-native digital twin in NVIDIA Isaac Lab for high-fidelity modeling and simulation, and a validated sim-to-real baseline using a learned neural actuator model. We demonstrate that this baseline enables zero-shot policy transfer, with trained agents exhibiting emergent adversarial behaviors. To ensure full reproducibility of our results, all project assets are released publicly: hardware CAD/BOM and assembly documentation at [https://idscethzurich.github.io/klask_hardware], inference software stack at [https://github.com/IDSCETHZurich/klask_software] and the simulation and MARL setup at [https://github.com/IDSCETHZurich/klask_rl].

papers.intro:
Robot Learning and Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) have achieved remarkable milestones in digital domains. From the superhuman coordination of AlphaGo [20], OpenAI Five in Dota 2 [1] and AlphaStar in StarCraft II [24], and foundational algorithms like MADDPG [16], agents have demonstrated that sophisticated long-horizon behaviors can emerge from simple reward signals given sufficient competitive pressure. These digital successes suggest a promising future for embodied intelligence. While these principles are well-established in digital environments, a critical challenge remains: the transition from abstract strategic reasoning to the high-stakes constraints of high-speed physical multi-robot play. A key barrier to this transition is infrastructural. Bridging the reality gap requires a benchmark that balances high-fidelity simulation with accessible hardware. While software environments enable millions of interactions per hour, physical MARL is often constrained by a lack of accessible high-fidelity benchmarks. Platforms in this domain are frequently either prohibitively expensive industrial systems [5] or limited to single-agent tasks.

We introduce KlaskTron (Fig. 1), a platform designed to bridge this gap. KlaskTron is an open-source, low-cost (<$2500 USD), desktop-scale robotic testbed explicitly built for physical adversarial MARL. It occupies a unique niche: more dynamic than static manipulation benchmarks, more accessible than industrial robotics, and designed for two-agent competitive interaction.

Why KLASK? KLASK instantiates a problem class we term high-speed, contact-rich adversarial MARL: a zero-sum, continuous-control task in which two agents must simultaneously attack, defend, and cope with explosive contact dynamics under long-horizon credit assignment. Unlike robotic air hockey or table tennis, KLASK requires no compressed-air infrastructure and fits on a standard desk, enabling fully automatic episode resets and continuous physical training without human intervention. Each ∼31{\sim}31-second episode contains on average 12.4 dynamic contacts (defensive blocks plus offensive strikes). With more than one million units sold worldwide, the rules are immediately intuitive to a broad audience, lowering the barrier to demonstration and community engagement.

papers.title: Controlling Sharpening in LLM Post-Training
papers.abstract: LLM post-training via reinforcement learning has shown consistent improvements in accuracy at the cost of reducing behavioral coverage - a phenomenon known as sharpening that can stall progress on difficult tasks. Repeated sampling objectives such as $\mathrm{pass@k}$ and $\mathrm{max@k}$ are known to mitigate sharpening, but the mechanism behind it remains poorly understood. Moreover, existing approaches for $\mathrm{@k}$ optimization use dedicated algorithms, and no general framework exists for adapting established policy optimization methods from $\mathrm{@}1$ to $\mathrm{@k}$. We derive the optimal policies for KL-regularized $\mathrm{pass@k}$ and $\mathrm{max@k}$ objectives in closed form. Our explicit solutions reveal that $\mathrm{@k}$ optimization naturally redistributes learning pressure based on prompt difficulty, directing it toward harder problems. Crucially, we show that standard $\mathrm{@}1$ objectives achieve these exact same optimal policies through prompt-adaptive regularization or reward transformation. Ultimately, this yields an optimizer-independent explanation for why $\mathrm{@k}$ objectives reduce sharpening on easy tasks while prioritizing success on harder ones. Building on these insights, we introduce $\mathrm{@k}$ Adaptive Pressure for Policy Optimization (KAPPO). Following a one-time reference calibration, KAPPO seamlessly adapts existing $\mathrm{@}1$ methods to $\mathrm{@k}$ via prompt-adaptive regularization or reward transformation, without otherwise altering their training procedures. Experiments with several RL methods on mathematical reasoning and code generation demonstrate that KAPPO provides direct control over sharpening. Crucially, we demonstrate that $\mathrm{@k}$ pressure can be fully realized with single completion training, matching the performance of multi-completion $\mathrm{@k}$ optimizers at a fraction of the cost.

papers.intro:
Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a central component of LLM post-training, producing substantial performance improvements in mathematical reasoning, code generation, and other verifiable domains (Shao et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025a; Yu et al., 2025). Yet, an increase in average performance does not by itself reveal how the model has improved. Pretrained LLMs contain extensive latent capabilities, and RL can affect them through two distinct mechanisms. It may uncover successful behavior that is rarely expressed by the base policy, or it may concentrate probability on solutions that are already readily available. The latter phenomenon, referred to as sharpening, improves single-trial success but often reduces the range of problems solvable by the model under repeated trials (Yue et al., 2025). Further capability progress thus depends on effectively controlling sharpening.

Recent studies confirm this exact limitation: RL post-training dynamics are indeed dominated by sharpening (Yue et al., 2025; Song et al., 2025). The impressive single-trial gains frequently diminish or reverse in multi-trial settings, as the generated reasoning paths are confined to a narrow subset of the base model’s original distribution. Counteracting this over-concentration is notoriously difficult. For example, simply injecting randomness or diversity at the token level rarely translates into meaningful diversity in high-level reasoning strategies (Walder and Karkhanis, 2025; Chen et al., 2025b).

papers.title: Anderson localisation in infinite and finite resonator crystals with long-range interactions
papers.abstract: We establish Anderson localisation for random capacitance operators and quantify concentration of individual modes of finite capacitance matrices for clusters of subwavelength high-contrast resonators. The underlying geometry is fully periodic in dimensions $d=2,3$, with one resonator per cell, and the inverse material factors are independent and uniformly distributed. We retain the full capacitance interaction, whose coefficients decay exponentially with lattice separation. Under coordinate reflection symmetry, spectral and dynamical localisation hold near the upper spectral edge for every fixed positive disorder strength. At weak disorder $W$, we obtain an explicit localisation window of energy width proportional to $W$; prescribed positive intervals are localised at sufficiently large disorder. A variational boundary comparison and a material-variable eigenvalue-spacing estimate transfer localisation from truncated matrices to individual modes of the finite capacitance matrix. In a bounded sample of cell size $\varepsilon$, with probability tending to one, all except for $O(\varepsilon^{1-d}\log(1/\varepsilon))$ modes in the localisation interval concentrate within radii $O(\varepsilon\log(1/\varepsilon))$. The estimates are uniform for the contrast-dependent capacitance family at small contrast. We also prove a common limiting density of states for the truncated and finite matrices and illustrate concentration numerically.

papers.title: Inferring Transferable Rewards via Active Inverse Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) aims to recover expert rewards that transfer across environments with differing dynamics. Prior work has shown that such transfer is possible when gathering expert demonstrations across sufficiently different dynamics. In practice, however, expert demonstrations are costly, making it critical to select the right dynamics to reduce the quantity of expert data required for learning transferable rewards. We propose a two-phase approach: we first cycle through the available dynamics to obtain a reliable reward estimate, then actively select dynamics to reduce our uncertainty about the expert reward. Crucially, this yields novel sample complexity guarantees on transfer that hold for any dynamics, with a rate independent of the number of available dynamics. Empirically, our method significantly reduces the number of expert demonstrations needed to learn a transferable reward.

Learning a transferable representation of expert behavior makes it possible to predict how the expert would act in previously unseen circumstances. Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) [1] formalizes this by inferring a reward function from expert demonstrations. Unlike imitation learning methods such as Behavior Cloning (BC) [2], which directly replicate observed behavior, IRL aims to recover the underlying objective the expert is optimizing. In contrast to a cloned policy tied to its training dynamics, a reward can, in principle, transfer to unseen dynamics.
