Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) [1] formalizes this by inferring a reward function from expert demonstrations. Unlike imitation learning methods such as Behavior Cloning (BC) [2], which directly replicate observed behavior, IRL aims to recover the underlying objective the expert is optimizing. In contrast to a cloned policy tied to its training dynamics, a reward can, in principle, transfer to unseen dynamics.

Despite its appeal, IRL is fundamentally ill-posed [1]. Under entropy regularization [3], the standard setting in identifiability works [4, 5], demonstrations from a fixed Markov decision process (MDP) identify the reward only up to subspace specific to that MDP. Consequently, such rewards transfer only to dynamics whose identifiable subspace sufficiently overlaps with that of the original MDP [6]. Recent works show that observing expert demonstrations in as few as two sufficiently different dynamics resolves this ambiguity [4, 5, 6]. However, these works leave open how to actively select such dynamics to reduce the ambiguity with as few expert demonstrations as possible.

This raises the following central question: How should we select dynamics to learn a transferable reward from a minimal number of expert demonstrations? To address this question, we propose an active IRL setting, in which the learner chooses the dynamics under which the expert demonstrates the task. This setting is natural whenever reconfiguring the environment is cheap compared to collecting expert demonstrations. For example, a robotics lab can cheaply vary the initial placement, mass, or friction of manipulated objects [7], or a driving simulator can vary road conditions [8]; collecting demonstrations, by contrast, requires a skilled human operator for each one [9].

papers.title: Circumventing Magnitude Collapse via Modular Two-Stage Open-Set Recognition
papers.abstract: Open-set recognition (OSR) requires neural networks to classify known classes while rejecting unknown samples, which is critical for real-world deployment. So far, OSR research studied and developed representation learning and postprocessing methods independently and their interactions remain unexplored. In this paper, we reconsider OSR as a modular two-stage pipeline and present the first systematic study of interactions between representation learning and postprocessing methods across dataset scales and usage of known unknown data. First, we discover a failure mode we term \emph{magnitude collapse}, where representation learning methods that utilize known unknown data can suffer performance degradation at large scale and irreversibly destroy discriminative information, despite excelling at small scale. Second, we study the modular interactions and reveal when they can be leveraged for modular performance gains via two-stage processing and where interaction effects amplify performance degradation due to magnitude collapse. Third, we show how these findings can be used to achieve state-of-the-art performance with a simple $K+1$ class classifier baseline and magnitude-aware postprocessing while circumventing magnitude collapse. Finally, our results demonstrate that small-scale evaluations with known unknown data are not predictive of large-scale performance, invalidating current best practices in OSR research. Code available at https://github.com/TwoDigitsOneNumber/Two-Stage-OSR.

papers.title: Intent2CAD: How Semantic-Parametric Supervision Shapes Text-to-CAD Generation
papers.abstract: Text-to-CAD generation aims to make CAD modeling more accessible by generating executable CAD programs from natural-language descriptions. However, practical CAD workflows require more than executable geometry: generated programs should also expose reusable structure that supports later modification. We introduce intent-oriented text-to-CAD generation, where design intent is expressed as recoverable code-level signals: semantic features, reusable parameters, and lightweight parametric relations. Rather than changing the model architecture or decoding procedure, we investigate how supervision representation granularity affects both CAD generation and zero-shot intent-preserving editing. To enable this study, we construct IntentCAD-100K, a 100K paired text--code dataset built by converting low-level CAD construction traces into executable CadQuery programs. We further construct IntentCAD-Edit-1K to evaluate zero-shot intent-preserving editing from the same representation perspective. Intent2CAD uses a two-stage conservative lifting pipeline: semantic lifting rewrites reliable primitive groups into feature-level operations, while parametric lifting exposes lightweight parametric relations. Under controlled fine-tuning, semantic lifting mainly improves generation reliability and feature recovery, reducing IR from 2.39% to 0.22% and achieving 99.96% API Recovery, while parametric lifting makes reusable relation structure explicit and further improves relation-aware zero-shot editing. Datasets and code are available at https://github.com/JinboYang94/Intent2CAD.

Computer-Aided Design (CAD) is a fundamental tool in modern engineering design and manufacturing, where designers create, refine, and iterate product designs throughout the development process [1, 2, 3]. Because traditional CAD workflows remain time-consuming and expertise-intensive [4], recent text-to-CAD research has explored how Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate CAD scripts from natural language descriptions [5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10]. This direction is promising, but practical CAD modeling is not only about producing a final shape. In parametric CAD modeling, a generated CAD program should support later reuse and modification, not just match the final shape.

Most existing text-to-CAD studies therefore leave an important gap. They primarily focus on geometric fidelity and program executability [5, 6, 7, 8, 9]. These criteria are necessary, but they do not fully capture the needs of parametric CAD workflows [11, 12, 13]. A program that approximates the target geometry with many low-level primitives may pass a shape metric, while still making a simple later edit, such as changing a shared radius or preserving symmetry, difficult to perform consistently. In this paper, we call this broader requirement intent-oriented text-to-CAD generation: the generated program should not only reproduce the requested shape, but also expose recoverable code-level intent signals that support reuse and local refinement.

papers.title: Expander Routing under Adversarial Deletions via Temporal Aggregation
papers.abstract:
In expander routing, we seek to establish paths in the expander graph between given source-target pairs while minimizing both dilation (maximum path length) and congestion (maximum edge load). We study this problem in a decremental dynamic setting where the underlying graph remains an expander despite ongoing edge deletions, and source-target pairs can be added or removed. Our goal is to maintain paths under these updates while keeping dilation and congestion low and performing low computation per update.
  We present a randomized algorithm that maintains paths with polylogarithmic dilation and congestion against an adaptive adversary, while incurring only polylogarithmic amortized computation per update, all with high probability. Our approach leverages a recent technique called Temporal Aggregation to maintain a collection of low-congestion, low-dilation random walks resilient to adaptive adversaries.

papers.title: Theory of the Ferroaxial Charge Density Wave in 1T-TiSe$_2$
papers.abstract: Recent experiments using strain to probe the charge-density wave (CDW) of 1T-TiSe$_2$ have uncovered additional transitions and broken symmetries inside the CDW state. The elastocaloric effect reveals a second transition below $T_\mathrm{CDW}$, which elastoresistivity shows to be associated with ferroaxial order, breaking all vertical mirror symmetries while preserving inversion. In addition, at even lower temperatures, a diverging nematic susceptibility has been reported through elastoresistivity. In this work, we argue that this rich phenomenology cannot be explained by the standard $L_1^-$ CDW order parameter, and instead requires the existence of a secondary CDW order parameter. Based on symmetry, microscopic, and diffraction considerations, we propose this subleading CDW to have $L_2^-$ symmetry. By analyzing the Landau theory of coupled $L_1^-$ and $L_2^-$ orders in the presence of strain, we reproduce the phase boundaries observed in the elastocaloric measurements and the emergence of ferroaxial order below the CDW transition. Moreover, the model supports a third threefold-rotational symmetry breaking transition at lower temperatures, consistent with the reported divergence of the nematic susceptibility.

papers.intro:
Phase transitions in quantum materials can be associated with the emergence of different types of ferroic order, such as the familiar ferroelectricity and ferromagnetism. Ferroaxiality is a more elusive type of ferroic order whose ferroic moment is a macroscopic time-reversal invariant axial vector [11, 20]. Classically, a non-zero ferroaxial (FA) moment, also known as an electric toroidal dipole or ferro-rotational moment, is generated by a non-irrotational electric polarization field (field with non-vanishing curl), such as a vortex-like distribution of electric dipoles. In a solid, it is an emergent order that can arise from electronic and/or lattice degrees of freedom.

Ferroaxiality is a more elusive type of ferroic order whose ferroic moment is a macroscopic time-reversal invariant axial vector [11, 20]. Classically, a non-zero ferroaxial (FA) moment, also known as an electric toroidal dipole or ferro-rotational moment, is generated by a non-irrotational electric polarization field (field with non-vanishing curl), such as a vortex-like distribution of electric dipoles. In a solid, it is an emergent order that can arise from electronic and/or lattice degrees of freedom.

Being even under time reversal, a ferroaxial moment cannot couple linearly to magnetic fields [40, 6, 8]. Unlike the ferroelectric moment, the ferroaxial moment is even under both inversion and a reflection with respect to the mirror perpendicular to it, whereas it is odd under reflections with respect to mirrors parallel to it. As such, electric fields cannot couple linearly with the ferroaxial moment either. Moreover, despite its non-irrotational nature, ferroaxiality is sharply distinct from chirality by the presence of inversion symmetry. In any crystal, a ferroaxial moment necessarily induces electric multipoles of higher angular momentum ll due to the breaking of continuous rotation symmetry [15]. Focusing on non-cubic crystals (axial groups) that are not themselves ferroaxial, an in-plane FA moment necessarily triggers an electric quadrupole moment (l=2l=2). However, an out-of-plane FA moment in these types of crystals only induces l>2l>2 multipoles for tetragonal, trigonal, and hexagonal groups. Consequently, strain, which transforms as an electric quadrupole, cannot couple linearly to the FA moment in these cases. Therefore, the absence of a simple field conjugate to ferroaxial moments (electric, magnetic, and strain fields) makes ferroaxial transitions difficult to detect [20]. Yet, renewed interest in the subject has recently uncovered several ferroaxial candidate materials and interesting ways to probe and manipulate ferroaxial moments [27, 16, 17, 14, 33, 1, 8, 50, 40, 2, 37]. Among these candidate materials, recent experiments reported evidence for ferroaxial order in the charge-density wave (CDW) phase of the trigonal transition-metal dichalcogenide 1T-TiSe2 [12, 26].

The symmetries broken by the CDW phase transition in 1T-TiSe2 have been the subject of a long debate. While the CDW was initially described in terms of a single 2×2×22\times 2\times 2 transition that doubles the lattice periodicity in all three directions (i.e., with wavevectors at the LL points of the hexagonal Brillouin zone) and breaks only translation symmetry [9, 21] (P​3¯​m​1→P​3¯​c​1P\bar{3}m1\rightarrow P\bar{3}c1), early scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) experiments reported the breaking of both threefold rotational C3C_{3} and vertical (dihedral) mirror σd\sigma_{d} symmetries, and characterized the CDW as chiral [25]. This led to theoretical proposals of a chiral CDW [43, 44], which was claimed to emerge at a second transition observed in specific heat measurements [4]. Subsequent experiments have both supported [22, 38, 48, 28, 29] and challenged [19, 32, 42, 51, 41] this claim, leading to a continued debate (see Ref. [35] for a more detailed account). It is important to note that, while the initial observations were interpreted in terms of a chiral CDW, several of them are equally consistent with ferroaxial order. In this case, it is not possible to unambiguously distinguish a chiral order parameter from a ferroaxial moment [31].

papers.title: Multiprobe strategies for Kinematic Lensing with the Roman Space Telescope High Latitude Wide Area Survey
papers.abstract: In its latest design, the High Latitude Wide Area Survey (HLWAS) Medium Tier comprises overlapping photometric and spectroscopic data across 2,300 square degrees. This dataset enables Kinematic Lensing (KL), a Weak Lensing (WL) technique that exploits galaxy kinematics to control for shape noise, the dominant statistical limitation of traditional WL. We present several simulated analyses quantifying the expected cosmological science return of a Roman KL analysis with the latest design of the HLWAS: We explore KL prospects with early Roman data from the Deep Tier fields and from the early Medium Tier fields; we demonstrate the impact of different roll-angle choices on the KL performance; we benchmark KL against traditional WL; we introduce a KL-based multiprobe analysis that jointly models KL, galaxy clustering, and galaxy-galaxy lensing. In these analyses, we consider systematics, including photometric uncertainties, shear calibration bias, galaxy bias, and baryonic feedback. Our results show that KL alone achieves a dark energy figure of merit (FoM) of 22.54, which is more than a factor of two improvement over a corresponding WL analysis. The KL multiprobe approach improves the full-survey FoM to 34.58, even assuming conservative scale cuts in the clustering and galaxy-galaxy lensing. For the HLWAS roll-angle strategy, we find that the current plan of 4 passes with rotations of approximately 0, 10, 170, 180 degrees are near optimal for KL.

While DESI’s BAO data alone remain consistent with Λ​CDM\Lambda\mathrm{CDM}, the joint analysis of BAO, CMB, and supernova (SN) favors a time-varying equation of state, w⁡(a)=w0+wa​(1−a)w(a)=w_{0}+w_{a}(1-a) (the Chevallier-Polarski-Linder or CPL parameterization; [12, 52]), deviating from the fixed w=−1w=-1 assumed in Λ​CDM\Lambda\mathrm{CDM} [54, 21, 23]. Since the release of DESI DR1, this result has been the subject of active debate [15, 16, 67, 25, 53, 64, 79, 24, 34, 82, 22].

Fully understanding the physics of dark energy and stress-testing the Λ​CDM\Lambda\mathrm{CDM} model requires additional independent measurements. For instance, the Euclid mission22 2 https://www.cosmos.esa.int/web/euclid is designed to measure BAO over similar redshift ranges as DESI, with distinctly different observational systematics [30]. Cross-checking DESI’s and Euclid’s BAO measurements will reveal whether unknown pipeline systematics exist. Similarly, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope (Roman33 3 https://science.nasa.gov/mission/roman-space-telescope/) and Rubin Observatory’s Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST44 4 https://www.lsst.org) are expected to observe thousands of Type Ia SNe in the coming years [45, 60], enabling studies to characterize the astrophysical systematics of SN light curves.

Complementary measurements offer another avenue to probe dark energy physics. Cosmic shear, Weak Lensing (WL) by the large-scale structure, probes the dark energy equation of state through lensing geometry and angular projection, providing information complementary to BAO’s standard-ruler measurement. Moreover, it provides additional constraints on structure growth and thus enables a growth-geometry-consistency test of the cosmological model. However, cosmic shear alone is subject to degeneracies between cosmology and nuisance parameters such as intrinsic alignment or photometric redshift uncertainties [4, 73, 3]. A typical way to improve cosmic shear constraints is to combine it with galaxy clustering and galaxy-galaxy lensing into a so-called 3×23\times 2pt analysis. This concept has been applied to the Stage-III photometric surveys such as the Dark Energy Survey (DES55 5 https://www.darkenergysurvey.org), the Kilo-Degree Survey (KiDS66 6 https://kids.strw.leidenuniv.nl), and the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program (HSC77 7 https://hsc-release.mtk.nao.ac.jp/doc/) [20, 35, 76, 61] to measure dark energy equation of state [19, 70].

Another way to improve cosmic shear constraints is Kinematic Lensing (KL). KL combines spectroscopic and imaging data with the Tully-Fisher relation [80] to extract the lensing signal at a much lower shape-noise level than the traditional WL [43, 84, 69]. Beyond reducing shape noise, KL is also immune to several WL systematics such as photometric redshift uncertainties and intrinsic alignment [42]. The KL concept has been demonstrated in cluster lensing using slit spectroscopy, achieving a shape-noise uncertainty of 0.026 per component [68]. Moreover, forecasts for several upcoming surveys, particularly Roman, suggest that KL has substantial potential to constrain cosmology [84, 86, 41, 51].

papers.title: SNAP: Semantic Navigation Among Pedestrians
papers.abstract: Navigating crowded urban environments requires robots to avoid pedestrians while adhering to social norms such as remaining on sidewalks. Existing approaches typically address either crowd avoidance or semantic path planning in isolation. We propose a reinforcement learning (RL) navigation policy that jointly reasons about semantic terrain and dynamic obstacles from a single semantically annotated bird's-eye-view (BEV) map, without relying on explicit human-state estimation. Our policy outperforms established crowd-navigation and semantic-aware baselines and transfers zero-shot to a legged robot, demonstrating socially compliant navigation in highly dynamic real-world scenarios.
papers.intro:
Robots operating in shared urban spaces must navigate not only safely but also predictably by adhering to social norms. More precisely, they are expected to respect personal space, adapt to surrounding pedestrians, and follow norms such as remaining on sidewalks or using crosswalks, otherwise causing disruptive behavior [1]. Such behavior is a prerequisite for applications like autonomous last-mile delivery [2] and, more broadly, the deployment of robots in urban environments.

Robots operating in shared urban spaces must navigate not only safely but also predictably by adhering to social norms. More precisely, they are expected to respect personal space, adapt to surrounding pedestrians, and follow norms such as remaining on sidewalks or using crosswalks, otherwise causing disruptive behavior [1]. Such behavior is a prerequisite for applications like autonomous last-mile delivery [2] and, more broadly, the deployment of robots in urban environments.

Crowd navigation, requiring a robot to reach a goal while avoiding dynamic obstacles, has been studied extensively [3, 4, 5]. Classical heuristic-based methods involve environment-specific tuning which limits generalization [6, 7]. Learning-based methods achieve higher success rates [3] but typically require explicit human-state information such as positions and velocities. Estimating these in real crowds is prone to occlusion and tracking failures [8], and the resulting modular pipelines add latency and propagate estimation errors. In parallel, semantic planners incorporate scene semantics into trajectory planning to follow social norms, such as preferring sidewalks or crosswalks [9, 10, 11]. However, they treat the environment as static or avoid pedestrians with reactive heuristics.

In parallel, semantic planners incorporate scene semantics into trajectory planning to follow social norms, such as preferring sidewalks or crosswalks [9, 10, 11]. However, they treat the environment as static or avoid pedestrians with reactive heuristics.

We bridge both lines of work with an RL policy that observes a robot-centric, semantically annotated bird’s-eye-view (BEV) map that encodes terrain classes alongside nearby dynamic obstacles. This unified observation lets the policy reason jointly about where to move and how to react to the crowd, without explicit pedestrian state estimation. We benchmark it against crowd-navigation and semantic-planning baselines, showing that BEV observations without explicit state estimation achieve better performance, and deploy it zero-shot on an ANYmal-D [12].

papers.title: Attacking P2P Networks: Liveness Attacks on the GossipSub and DOG Gossip Protocols
papers.abstract:
Peer-to-peer (P2P) networks form the communication layer of large decentralized systems such as Ethereum, and the correctness of higher-level protocols depends on the gossip layer delivering messages to honest nodes. We study the robustness of two gossip protocols against adversaries whose only goal is to violate liveness, that is, to prevent honest nodes from receiving fresh messages, without forging, altering, or invalidating any message.
  For GossipSub, the publish-subscribe protocol used by Ethereum, we show that an adversary operating a constant number of geographically distributed nodes with a fixed latency advantage can take over the ``First Message Deliveries'' peer-scoring term and separate a constant fraction of nodes from the honest mesh. We analyze the attack under a geographical model, address the random-peer and outbound-connection mechanisms, and show that the separation can be maintained under realistic churn.
  For DOG, a transaction-dissemination protocol designed for CometBFT, we first give simple counterexamples in which route filtering disconnects the dissemination graph even without failures or Byzantine participants, and then present a practical attack that uses only a single physical node with a constant number of identities and legitimate actions to disable every forwarding route, separating the full network while allowing only direct publisher-to-neighbor delivery. We verify the attack in a simulated network and analyze its cost, assumptions, and possible mitigations.
papers.intro:
Peer-to-peer (P2P) networks are distributed systems in which participating nodes communicate directly and collectively provide a service without relying on a single central coordinator. In large decentralized systems such as Ethereum, the P2P network forms the communication layer over which nodes disseminate transactions, blocks, and protocol-control messages. The correctness of higher-level mechanisms, including consensus, therefore depends not only on their own algorithms but also on the timely and reliable delivery of messages by the underlying P2P network.

Gossiping is a family of dissemination techniques in which each node forwards a newly received message to a selection of its peers, causing the message to propagate through the network by repeated local exchanges. In blockchain systems, gossip protocols are used to disseminate transactions, blocks, and consensus messages among nodes. For example, Ethereum relies on gossiping to propagate the information that validators and other nodes require to maintain a consistent view of the system and participate in consensus.

Although consensus protocols have received extensive formal analysis, the security properties of the P2P protocols that carry their messages are often understood less rigorously. This disparity is significant because a secure consensus protocol cannot compensate for a communication layer that prevents honest nodes from receiving the messages required to participate. An adversarial analysis of gossip protocols is therefore necessary to identify whether their optimization mechanisms introduce exploitable failure modes that can delay or suppress message delivery and thereby threaten the availability of the systems built upon them.

We say that the gossip layer satisfies liveness for a message if every continuously participating honest node that is intended to receive the message eventually receives it. papers.title: Stability of negative-regularity mixing and applications to stochastic fluids
papers.abstract: We consider mixing for a scalar advected by random vector fields, such as solutions to stochastic fluid equations. Our main abstract result is that contraction in expectation of a negative Sobolev norm of the scalar (negative-regularity mixing) is stable under perturbations of the joint scalar-velocity process. We apply the result in three settings: mixing for a hyperviscous Boussinesq-type system where the scalar actively drives the velocity, mixing for a passive scalar advected by two-dimensional Navier-Stokes driven by smooth-in-time stochastic forcing, and a black-box proof that negative-regularity mixing implies enhanced dissipation.

papers.title: High-order guaranteed lower bounds for the Schr\"odinger eigenvalue problem
papers.abstract: We compute unconditional guaranteed lower eigenvalue bounds for Schr\"odinger operators using a modified hybrid high-order method with built-in correction for the potential defect. The method assumes exact numerical integration and allows possibly unbounded potentials in $L^p$ for $p>n/2$ and $p\geq2$ on general polyhedral domains. We prove that the high-order correction preserves optimal a priori convergence orders, and derive reliable and efficient a posteriori error estimators. Numerical experiments provide striking evidence of optimal high-order convergence rates of the adaptive algorithm.

Guaranteed eigenvalue bounds are required whenever computed spectra enter rigorous statements, for instance in the assessment of critical loads and buckling in structural mechanics, the detection of spectral gaps, bifurcation and stability analysis, and computer-assisted existence proofs. Combined with the upper bounds from conforming Galerkin methods for self-adjoint problems, guaranteed lower bounds provide rigorous two-sided eigenvalue enclosures. For Schrödinger operators, such enclosures certify the quantum energy levels of ground and excited states.

papers.title: Ultrafast X-ray-induced dephasing of valence electrons
papers.abstract: Diffract-before-destroy schemes for atomic-scale electron mapping assume that ultrashort X-ray pulses outrun radiation damage. Although atomic cores move over tens of femtoseconds, outer electrons respond much faster, compromising their locations. We test this limit in elemental silicon using broadband, energy-chirped X-ray pulses to encode time with few-femtosecond resolution. Comparing valence-sensitive structurally forbidden reflections with simultaneously measured core-dominated Bragg peaks reveals valence-bond dephasing on sub-20-fs timescales even at pulse energies where direct ionization effects are negligible. Our findings demonstrate that crystallography where outer electrons contribute substantially to Bragg peaks requires pulses shorter than today's standard $\sim50\,fs$ standard. They also establish a path to disentangle valence electron and lattice contributions to order and dynamics with hard X-rays, enabling studies across molecular biology, quantum matter and devices.

papers.title: Mercury (Hg): a relativistic $N$-body simulation for Horndeski gravity
papers.abstract: We present Mercury, a relativistic $N$-body code for cosmological simulations in the $\alpha$-basis formulation of Horndeski gravity. Mercury extends a particle-mesh scheme by incorporating the dynamics of the additional scalar degree of freedom and the corresponding modified Einstein equations, expressed in terms of the time-dependent functions $\alpha_{\rm K}, \alpha_{\rm B}, \alpha_{\rm M}, \alpha_{\rm T}$ and the effective Planck mass $M_*^2$. This generalises our previous implementation of Horndeski subclass models, namely $k$-essence and kinetic gravity braiding (KGB), to the general linear Horndeski $\alpha$-basis. The code evolves the additional scalar degree of freedom and its effective stress--energy tensor alongside the nonlinear matter and metric fields, so that nonlinear structure formation sources the scalar-field evolution and feeds back on the gravitational potentials. Through its interface with hi_class, Mercury supports both phenomenological $\alpha$-function parametrisations and covariant Horndeski theories; we demonstrate the latter using nKGB, the Cubic Galileon, and Brans--Dicke models. We validate the implementation against hi_class in the linear regime and recover the expected nonlinear $k$-essence and KGB limits. For the luminal Horndeski models considered here, we show how a running effective Planck mass generates gravitational slip through the scalar anisotropic stress and modifies the friction terms governing the vector and tensor metric perturbations. The evolution of $M_*^2$ also modifies the normalisation and scale dependence of the effective dark-energy density contrast, leaving a corresponding imprint on its power spectrum. The present framework provides an intermediate step towards nonlinear Horndeski simulations, in which nonlinear scalar self-interactions and screening effects can be incorporated consistently within the same relativistic framework.

papers.intro:
Numerical tools have become an essential component in the study of cosmological perturbations and the interpretation of large-scale structure observations. Einstein–Boltzmann solvers such as CLASS (Blas et al., 2011) and CAMB Lewis (2026) provide accurate predictions for the evolution of linear perturbations and the corresponding cosmological observables in the standard cosmological framework. Extensions such as hi_class (Zumalacárregui et al., 2017; Bellini et al., 2020), mochi_class Cataneo and Bellini (2024), and EFTCAMB (Hu et al., 2014) have generalised this framework to scalar–tensor theories by incorporating Horndeski gravity (Horndeski, 1974), allowing the evolution of the background and linear perturbations to be computed for a broad range of dark-energy and modified-gravity models. In particular, hi_class provides two complementary descriptions of Horndeski theories: one based on the α\alpha functions introduced within the effective field theory description of dark energy (Bellini and Sawicki, 2014) and another based on the underlying covariant Lagrangian (Bellini et al., 2020). This has made it possible to confront a wide range of scalar–tensor theories with cosmological data.

In particular, hi_class provides two complementary descriptions of Horndeski theories: one based on the α\alpha functions introduced within the effective field theory description of dark energy (Bellini and Sawicki, 2014) and another based on the underlying covariant Lagrangian (Bellini et al., 2020). This has made it possible to confront a wide range of scalar–tensor theories with cosmological data.

While linear Einstein–Boltzmann calculations provide accurate predictions for a wide range of cosmological observables, current and forthcoming large-scale structure surveys, such as Euclid and DESI (Euclid Collaboration et al., 2025; Aghamousa et al., 2016), motivate the development of accurate predictions beyond the linear regime. In modified gravity theories, this requires numerical frameworks capable of following the coupled evolution of matter, metric perturbations, and additional degrees of freedom on nonlinear scales (Koyama, 2016). Relativistic NN-body simulations provide such a framework by extending conventional structure formation simulations with a consistent treatment of relativistic gravitational effects. The gevolution code (Adamek et al., 2016a; Adamek et al., 2016b; Adamek and Christiansen, 2026) incorporates relativistic metric perturbations within a weak-field formulation of general relativity and provides a relativistic description of cosmological structure formation.

The gevolution code (Adamek et al., 2016a; Adamek et al., 2016b; Adamek and Christiansen, 2026) incorporates relativistic metric perturbations within a weak-field formulation of general relativity and provides a relativistic description of cosmological structure formation.

A number of NN-body frameworks have been developed to study nonlinear structure formation in modified-gravity and scalar–tensor theories, including recent implementations based on the effective field theory of dark energy and Galileon-type models (Ganjoo and others, 2026; Atayde et al., 2026). Building upon the relativistic gevolution framework, several extensions have incorporated additional scalar-field dynamics, including kk-essence in kk-evolution (Hassani et al., 2019; Hassani et al., 2020) and scalar-field domain formation and associated relativistic signatures of the (a)symmetron model in Asimulation (Christiansen et al., 2023; Christiansen et al., 2024; Christiansen et al., 2025). More recently, we extended this framework in KGB-evolution to kinetic gravity braiding (KGB) models, incorporating the braiding interaction into the relativistic simulation framework and studying its signatures in nonlinear structure formation and relativistic observables (Nouri-Zonoz et al., 2026b; Nouri-Zonoz et al., 2026a). The progression from kk-evolution to KGB-evolution established the numerical workflow that we generalise here towards a broader treatment of Horndeski gravity.

In this work, we introduce Mercury, extending the KGB-evolution code to the general linear Horndeski α\alpha-basis. The code incorporates the Horndeski background and perturbation dynamics, with the linear perturbation sector described by the time-dependent α\alpha functions αK\alpha_{\rm K}, αB\alpha_{\rm B}, αM\alpha_{\rm M} and αT\alpha_{\rm T}, together with the evolution of the effective Planck mass M∗2M_{*}^{2}. The corresponding scalar contribution is implemented as an effective stress–energy tensor source on the simulation lattice, while the evolution of the effective Planck mass is consistently incorporated into the gravitational sector. Following the approach adopted in KGB-evolution, the additional scalar degree of freedom is evolved using the linear Horndeski equations while remaining consistently coupled to the nonlinear matter and metric sectors. A key feature of Mercury is its direct connection to the linear Horndeski framework implemented in hi_class (Zumalacárregui et al., 2017; Bellini et al., 2020). Following the same model description, Mercury supports both approaches available in hi_class: the effective-theory approach, in which the α\alpha functions are parametrised directly, and the covariant-theory approach, in which the model is specified through its underlying Horndeski Lagrangian and the corresponding α\alpha functions are determined from the covariant dynamics. We validate the implementation by recovering the known kk-essence and KGB limits, comparing the linear regime with hi_class predictions, and testing the framework using both effective-theory and covariant descriptions of Horndeski models.

The paper is organised as follows. In Sec. 2, we introduce the Horndeski framework and the description of the background and linear perturbation dynamics adopted in Mercury. Section 3 presents the implementation of the Horndeski contributions within the relativistic simulation framework, including the construction of the effective scalar sources in real space and the solution of the equations in Fourier space. In Sec. 4, we describe the numerical workflow of Mercury, from the specification of Horndeski models and the computation of the background evolution to the generation of initial conditions and the nonlinear evolution in the main simulation loop. papers.title: Quantitative $T_2^*$ Fidelity in Accelerated Radial Ultrashort-Echo-Time MRI of the Lumbar Cartilage Endplate: A Synthetic Computational Validation Study
papers.abstract: The lumbar cartilage endplate (CEP) is a short-$T_2^*$ structure whose composition has been linked to disc health. Ultrashort-echo-time (UTE) MRI enables direct CEP visualization, but acceleration and reconstruction may alter quantitative $T_2^*$ even when image quality improves. We evaluated how radial undersampling and reconstruction strategy affect CEP $T_2^*$ fidelity in a fully synthetic setting. A 96 x 96 sagittal lumbar phantom with five CEP levels (ground-truth $T_2^*$: 24, 22, 20, 18, and 16 ms) was simulated with six UTE echoes, eight receive coils, and radial sampling. Acceleration factors $R=1,2,4,6,8$ used 302, 151, 76, 50, and 38 spokes, respectively. Reconstructions were CG-SENSE, joint multi-echo FISTA, and direct model-based estimation from k-space. Twenty independent complex-noise realizations were evaluated per acceleration. Direct model-map RMSE increased from 0.172 ms at $R=1$ to 0.800 ms at $R=4$, 1.472 ms at $R=6$, and 2.256 ms at $R=8$. At $R=4$, joint-FISTA had lower image NRMSE than the direct model (0.132 vs. 0.203), while the direct map had lower level-wise $T_2^*$ RMSE than CG-SENSE and joint-FISTA ROI fits (0.800 vs. 1.448 and 1.288 ms; estimators differed). At $R=8$, CG-SENSE ROI fitting had the lowest $T_2^*$ RMSE (1.501 ms), whereas the direct model showed systematic underestimation (bias, -2.136 ms; CCC, 0.723). Image fidelity and quantitative biomarker fidelity therefore diverged under radial acceleration. In this synthetic framework, $R=4$ was a promising operating point for direct CEP $T_2^*$ mapping, whereas $R=8$ produced substantial bias and spatial instability. Scanner, phantom, and in vivo validation are required before clinical translation.

papers.title: Low Frequency Noise Identification for the SuperCDMS Experiment using Convolutional Neural Networks
papers.abstract: The SuperCDMS experiment uses semiconductor crystal detectors operated at cryogenic temperatures to search for low-mass dark matter. Vibrations observed during the SuperCDMS Soudan experiment generated broadband low-frequency noise (LFN), which due to its similarity in the pulse shape to the low-energy signal events is difficult to remove. In the final low ionization threshold analysis, CDMSlite Run 3, the strong event selection criterion applied to remove LFN events also significantly reduced the ability to identify signal events in the low energy region, thus reducing the sensitivity of the experiment to low-mass dark matter. Therefore, an LFN rejection criterion using machine learning (ML) aimed to improve the signal efficiency while maintaining the signal purity has now been developed. This paper presents a new method using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), its application to the CDMSlite Run 3 dataset, and its impact on dark matter sensitivities, with further investigation through case studies.

papers.title: Exploring Collaborative Debating Models for the future of science
papers.abstract: AI is expanding what researchers can produce. A substantial increase in scientific output would also change how that work is organised and distributed, as earlier shifts in the scale of science have done. This paper develops a thought experiment around Collaborative Debating Models (CDMs), topic-focused environments where researchers work with AI and one another to pursue questions and maintain an evolving account of their field. Individual contributions would remain attributable as ongoing debate and further analysis change the shared account. The paper considers how journals could evolve into these gathering places and how different forms of ownership would shape scientific agendas and the support for continuing work. CDMs could connect participants to remote laboratories and other research services to conduct new studies, with shared repositories making the resulting data available for further inquiry. The proposal links expanded scientific production to collective interpretation through continuing assessment and revision, while leaving room for disciplinary differences in how contributions are reviewed and recognised.

papers.title: Optical Acceptance Testing of Serenity-S1 Boards for the CMS HGCAL Phase-2 Backend Electronics
papers.abstract: The CMS Phase-2 upgrade includes a new high-granularity calorimeter. The calorimeter electronics will include around 300 Serenity-S1 FPGA boards that use Samtec FireFly electro-optical modules with a link speed of up to 25 Gbps. General production tests performed by the central Serenity group only validate the high-speed links via copper loopback cables. We present an optical acceptance test framework specifically designed for the calorimeter, providing comprehensive link and slow-control validation of installed FireFly modules under realistic operating conditions. This test combines loopback and board-to-board testing, extended bit error ratio measurements, and continuous module health monitoring within an automated workflow, delivering structured diagnostics and ensuring reliable large-scale system deployment.

papers.title: Machine Learning Aided Computational Discovery of Boride Substrates for Borophene Synthesis
papers.abstract: Borophene, a monolayer of boron, is distinctive among two-dimensional materials owing to its unique properties, including polymorphism and potential applications in quantum technologies and energy conversion and storage. Nevertheless, its applications are hindered by the strong binding of borophene to metal substrates, which impedes the realization of freestanding borophene. Alternative substrates with tunable binding to borophene are therefore highly desirable. Since boride layers arise during borophene synthesis on metals, borides provide potential alternative substrates for borophene synthesis. In this work, we investigate the binding energies and interactions between borophene and 1356 boride surfaces for two borophene phases (v1/6 and v1/9), using density functional theory (DFT) calculations and machine learning (ML). Importantly, incorporating ML-predicted charge transfer as an input feature to a subsequent ML model enables physics-informed predictions of binding energies. Additional DFT calculations on four representative cases were performed to validate the ML predictions. SHAP analysis reveals that the majority of key descriptors are associated with delocalized electrons, highlighting the role of electronic properties in governing binding strength. Combined DFT and ML screening identifies 65 and 73 promising boride surfaces for the v1/6 and v1/9 phases, respectively. Al- and Ag-based borides, including AlB2 and AgB2, emerge as predominant candidates for both phases. The computationally predicted candidate substrates and the deduced design guidelines provide a charge-transfer-informed ML strategy for substrate selection and represent promising steps toward the experimental realization of freestanding borophene.

papers.title: Subexponential-Time Exact-One Hitting Set
papers.abstract:
Exact-One Hitting Set is one of Karp's original 21 NP-complete problems: given an explicitly listed family of subsets of an $r$-element ground set, decide whether a subset meets every input set in exactly one element. Combining our reduction with the fixed-width exact-counting theorem of OpenAI (2026), we obtain a deterministic polynomial-space algorithm that computes the exact number of feasible selections in time $2^{O(r\log\log(r+16)/\sqrt{\log(r+16)})}\operatorname{poly}(L+1)=2^{o(r)}\operatorname{poly}(L+1)$, where $L$ is the input length. The number and widths of the input sets are unrestricted.
  Known row selection retains at most $r+1$ input constraints, but their total width may remain quadratic. Our path representation of two-query counting cancellation constructs two ordinary 3-CNF formulas with at most $2r$ variables and $O(r^2)$ clauses each, whose model counts differ by the desired answer. The auxiliary-variable budget depends on the number of simultaneous conditions, not on their widths or on the numbers of witnesses. We extend this construction to signed equations with fixed bounded demands and positive integer coefficients. We also represent every explicitly listed Boolean relation of VC dimension at most one by binary clauses and signed exact-one equations on its original variables, obtaining the same two-query variable bound for unrestricted overlaps among such local constraints. A bounded-term version further handles fixed finite/cofinite local degree rules on arbitrary graphs. The path representation is related by variable elimination to existing marker--parity cancellation.

papers.title: Leap-VLA: High-Rate Robot Control from a Low-Rate VLM Backbone
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models re-encode the full observation through a multi-billion-parameter vision-language model (VLM) at every control step, even though scene semantics evolve at roughly 1 Hz while reactive control requires 20-50 Hz. We present a VLA that decouples the two: a VLM runs as a low-frequency semantic anchor whose cached context is reused across control steps, while a flow-matching action expert operates at high frequency, consuming the cached semantics with a fresh, low-latency visual stream from a compact encoder pretrained on robot video with masked reconstruction, optical flow, and depth. The measured age $\tau$ of the cache conditions the expert through adaptive layer normalization. Reusing the cache makes the policy a function of its age, and training covers that function explicitly: cache ages sampled from real episode history, plus an age-ramped pixel corruption that erases the stale snapshot the way deployed staleness corrupts content. On the asynchronous deployment stack, the recipe closes most of the staleness gap: on LIBERO-Spatial, 61.4% to 95.5% at a 2 s semantic refresh (95.9% at 1 s, within 1.6 points of the frequency-matched anchor); averaged over the four LIBERO suites, the deployed policy holds 95.2% at a 1 s refresh and 94.5% at 2 s against a 96.3% matched anchor. A forward-only chunk-boundary correction (soft-nudge), an autograd-free reformulation of real-time-chunking guidance, carries per-control-step re-planning without loss (97.1%) at zero added latency. The same lens exposes a second defect: under an instruction-scene mismatch the policy keeps manipulating the scene, and a chain-of-thought verdict gate trained on zero-cost negative episodes freezes execution exactly on mismatched instructions without hurting feasible success.

papers.title: HiGenTrans: Hierarchical LLM Knowledge Transfer for Generative Recommendation
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation promises to simplify conventional multi-stage recommender systems by generating item Semantic IDs (SIDs) autoregressively. However, two obstacles limit its effective- ness in industrial settings: interaction-only supervision underuses the semantic knowledge encoded in pretrained language models, while beam-search likelihood ranks token sequences rather than directly estimating item relevance. To address these limitations, we propose HiGenTrans, a three-level framework that introduces LLM knowledge at the input, representation, and decision levels. First, Global Semantic Priming (GSP) adds an LLM-derived user representation to the beginning-of-sequence embedding, provid- ing a semantic prior before SID generation. Second, Hierarchi- cal Representation Transfer (HRT) aligns intermediate LLM representations with depth-matched GenRec layers through mean- centered projections and gated residual connections. Finally, Multi- Signal Decision Calibration (MDC) uses a lightweight mixture- of-experts calibrator to combine semantic relevance, generation confidence, and candidate-set context when reranking beam-search outputs. All semantic features are computed only from the observ- able interaction prefix, preventing target leakage, and can be cached offline. Experiments on three public benchmarks show that HiGen- Trans improves Recall@10 by up to 12.9% and NDCG@10 by up to 33.7% over the strongest baselines. These results demonstrate the value of transferring LLM knowledge at complementary stages of the generative recommendation pipeline.

papers.title: Evolutionary characterization of whole-genome doubling across human cancers
papers.abstract: Whole-genome doubling (WGD) is common across human cancers and is associated with tumour progression and adverse clinical outcomes. However, how genome-doubled tumours evolve across diverse cancer types remains poorly understood. Here we characterize WGD-associated tumour evolution by integrating genomic analyses of 41,332 tumours from 12 cancer types with evolutionary timing and multi-omic data. Several canonical driver mutations generally preceded WGD when both occurred, as did the onset of homologous recombination deficiency-associated mutagenesis. Notably, post-WGD chromosome-arm losses showed substantially weaker cancer-type dependence than pre-WGD losses, with 61-75% less variance explained by cancer type. Beyond chromosomal evolution, WGD+ tumours showed reduced interferon-response and HLA antigen-presentation programmes linked to epigenetic remodelling, without disproportionate enrichment of genetic immune-escape alterations. Our findings highlight WGD as a recurrent evolutionary transition associated with altered chromosomal evolution and epigenetically linked immune adaptation across cancers.

papers.title: Does Calibration Pick the Right Model? Likelihood Evidence from Income Risk
papers.abstract: Quantitative macroeconomics typically disciplines models by matching selected moments. We show how finite-state hidden Markov approximations make likelihood estimation and model selection feasible for nonlinear, non-Gaussian latent processes on short panels, without simulation. We illustrate the method with PSID earnings data. The calibrations that best match moments of earnings dynamics fit complete histories worse than a likelihood-estimated process with a Gaussian persistent component. In a standard saving model, calibrations of one process that fit the targets about equally well imply mean assets that differ by a factor of three. Close agreement with selected moments can leave economic predictions largely undetermined.

papers.title: NorthCUA Technical Report: Turbocharging Computer-Use Agents through Experience at Scale
papers.abstract: Scaling computer-use agents from individual actions to complex software work requires experience that connects decisions to complete outcomes. We present NorthCUA, an integrated system for turbocharging computer-use agents through experience at scale. Its Experience Flywheel supplies diverse executable tasks to the NorthCUA Harness, which sustains long interactions, records decisions, and checks task outcomes. The Flywheel uses these records to curate verified trajectories. For unsolved tasks, recursive self-improvement evolves reusable skills and preserves verified milestones so later attempts build on earlier progress. Staged Learning combines this experience with grounding data from the Flywheel to develop GUI competence through mid-training and long-horizon supervised fine-tuning. The policy then learns from fresh attempts in the same Harness through joint desktop-web reinforcement learning, closing the loop between experience production and policy improvement. The resulting Nano, Mini, and Pro family achieves state-of-the-art results among open-source models across GUI grounding, desktop execution, and Web interaction under the reported evaluation settings. For more responsive Web workflows, NorthCUA-Ultrafast pairs direct action selection with open-ended generation on pre-RL Nano, offering a measured quality-latency tradeoff. Together, these advances establish NorthCUA as a high-performing model family and a reusable foundation for agents that carry complex software work from intent to completion.

papers.title: RLiD: Reinforcement Learning in the Decision Plane for Language Agents and LLMs
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has improved the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) across a wide range of tasks. However, token-level RL assigns an action's advantage to the entire generated response, including tokens specifying the parsed action, reasoning chains, and malformed content. Although the environment executes only the parsed action, variation in how the action is expressed in natural language can introduce additional variance into policy-gradient estimates. We propose RLiD (Reinforcement Learning in the Decision plane), a framework that directly optimizes the probabilities of executable action options. RLiD compiles observations, an optional compact memory, and a labeled action menu into the model input, and uses a large decision model (LDM) to select an action in a single forward pass. By eliminating autoregressive token generation and bypassing action parsing, RLiD avoids invalid action outputs and improves RL rollout efficiency. Our analysis shows that, within a fixed text policy, marginalizing over alternative realizations of the same action removes a zero-mean gradient component without changing the expected update. We further distill trained LDM policies into generative LLMs through supervision on their action trajectories. Experiments on ARC, Countdown, and Sokoban demonstrate improved performance or lower computational cost across several settings. On ALFWorld, the complete training and distillation pipeline reaches 99.3% success in 12.7 H100 GPU-hours, compared with 86.6% in 17.3 GPU-hours for token-level RL of the same LLM. With compiled memory, our strongest Qwen2.5-1.5B LDM and distilled generative LLM achieve 100% success on all 134 unseen and 140 seen ALFWorld evaluation games.

papers.title: Validity of three-dimensional axisymmetric steady Prandtl expansion
papers.abstract: We study steady axisymmetric Navier--Stokes flows with swirl in the circular cylinder $\mathcal C_L=(0,L)\times B_2(0,1)$ with the no-slip condition on the stationary lateral wall. For the leading Euler velocity $(u_e^0,w_e^0,\theta_e^0)=(1,0,r K(r))$, where $K(r)=H(r^2)$ is a prescribed smooth radial function, we construct and justify a Prandtl expansion as $\varepsilon \to 0$ for sufficiently small fixed $L$. The expansion accounts for both axial and azimuthal boundary layers, including the case of a Blasius leading axial profile with nonzero swirl. Weighted estimates at the symmetry axis and coupled remainder estimates yield a uniform velocity error bound.

papers.title: Multi-Modal Multi-Agent System for Bridge Operation and Maintenance based on Large Language Model
papers.abstract: Bridges are critical transportation infrastructure, and reliable operation and maintenance (O&M) is essential for traffic safety and long-term structural performance. However, bridge O&M faces key bottlenecks: no unified architecture coordinates heterogeneous resources; model inferences lack clear links to physical-mechanical laws; and experts' tacit knowledge remains difficult to formalize. This study proposes a knowledge-enhanced autonomy formalization methodology and apply it to construct the Bridge O&M Multi-Modal Multi-Agent System (BOMMA), which integrates heterogeneous diagnostic actions, physics-mechanics-informed representations, long-term memory, and structured experiential knowledge within a coordinated multi-agent workflow, enabling interpretable and traceable scheduling, analysis, and decision-making. On 3,492 multi-source instructions, the proposed method achieves scheduling recalls of 85.37% for simple and 99.40% for composite tasks, with 95.35% BERT F1-score for O&M action reasoning. Ablation studies confirm the contributions of the components in the autonomy. This study bridges general LLM reasoning and specialized bridge O&M requirements.

papers.title: An optimal $\chi$-bound for $\{P_7, \text{diamond}\}$-free graphs
papers.abstract: A $\textit{diamond}$ is a graph obtained by removing an edge from the complete graph on four vertices. A graph is $\{P_7, \text{diamond}\}$-$\textit{free}$ if it contains no induced subgraph isomorphic to a seven-vertex path or a diamond. Schiermeyer (2020) asked whether there is a constant $c$ such that $\chi(G)\leq\omega(G)+c$ for every $\{P_7, \text{diamond}\}$-free graph $G$. We answer this question affirmatively by proving $\chi(G) \leq \omega(G)+3$. Moreover, the bound is optimal.

papers.title: Relativistic Kohn--Sham Theory of Paramagnetic Magnetic-Resonance Properties
papers.abstract: A general density functional theory based relativistic theory for paramagnetic NMR (pNMR) shifts, EPR g-tensors and hyperfine coupling tensors as well as magnetizabilities is derived. The formulation uses spin--orbit exact two-component (X2C) theory, gauge-including atomic orbitals, and generalized complex Kohn--Sham response equations with all ingredients being implemented analytically with the help of Goldstone modes and an orientation-constrained shielding. Additionally, we describe a two-component augmented Roothaan--Hall (ARH) solver for robust and stable convergence, which ensures that both a stationary point and a minimum are found. This is crucial for the convergence of the response equations for properties of paramagnetic systems. The extension of common population analyses for the two-component theory to aid in the interpretation of the spectra is further described. Using these new techniques, we are able to analyze the success and failure of density functional theory for relativistic open-shell systems including actinide complexes.

papers.title: Multi-GPU Acceleration of Interface Problems in FEniCS, with Application to Cardiac Modeling
papers.abstract: GPU acceleration of finite element assembly is well established for standard formulations, but mixed-dimensional problems, in which volumetric subdomains are coupled via lower-dimensional interfaces, remain unsupported in automated frameworks such as FEniCS. We extend cuDOLFINx, a GPU-enabled extension of the DOLFINx finite element framework, to assemble such interface problems on GPUs while preserving the high-level FEniCS programming model. Combined with GPU-resident Krylov solvers and algebraic multigrid preconditioning, this enables end-to-end GPU execution of the EMI (Extracellular--Membrane--Intracellular) model, an elliptic interface problem from cardiac modeling in which many intracellular subdomains are coupled through membranes. We compare the GPU implementation against a CPU-based one through strong and weak scaling experiments on regular and realistic 3D cardiac geometries with up to 8000 cells and 22 million degrees of freedom. In terms of assembly, a single GH200 node is roughly equivalent to two 144-core CPU nodes in strong scaling, and to two to three nodes in weak scaling, depending on geometry. For the linear solver, performance depends on geometry, preconditioning, and problem scale. On the regular geometry, GPU advantages emerge mainly at larger problem sizes and node counts. On the realistic geometry, with the same algebraic multigrid preconditioner for both architectures, the GPU is faster at all tested scales. The implementation is available as open-source software and applies to other problems with interface coupling.

papers.title: Coherent 1-{\mu}m-Band Co-Transmission with C+L-Band Channels over 50-km Hollow-Core Fiber
papers.abstract: We experimentally demonstrate simultaneous coherent transmission across 1-$\mu$m and C+L bands, carrying $54\times125$-GBaud PDM-16QAM C+L channels and $2\times15$-GBaud PDM-QPSK 1-$\mu$m channels over 50 km, highlighting 1 $\mu$m as a promising additional transmission window while avoiding gas-absorption constraints in C/L-band of HCFs.

papers.title: EgoActionBench: Benchmarking Dense Action Captioning for Egocentric Human Videos
papers.abstract: Learning from human data offers a scalable path toward embodied intelligence, yet it requires models to accurately understand fine-grained human actions from egocentric observations. However, existing benchmarks remain limited in action atomicity, temporal precision, and hand-action association. We introduce EgoActionBench, a benchmark that represents continuous human manipulation as temporally localized atomic actions associated with the left hand, right hand, or both hands. EgoActionBench contains 1,407 episodes with 41,132 human-refined action annotations. To evaluate such dense predictions, we propose an evaluation protocol that retrieves temporally eligible candidates, selects a prediction by content agreement, and scores semantic fidelity and temporal overlap alongside action precision and recall, jointly capturing what happens, when it happens, and which hand performs it. We benchmark 20 baseline models and systems on EgoActionBench and further adapt two backbones, Qwen3-VL-4B and LLaVA-OneVision-2-8B, through supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning on automatically annotated training episodes. EgoAction improves EgoActionScore by 15.9 and 23.2 points on the two backbones, and both adapted models outperform all open-source baselines. Our experiments reveal substantial limitations of current models in action atomicity, temporal precision, and hand-action association, highlighting the gap between general video understanding and the action understanding required for embodied intelligence.

papers.title: Contrastive Astromer: Two-Stage Contrastive Representation Learning for Astronomical Light Curve Classification
papers.abstract: Large astronomical surveys collect abundant light curves, but reliable class labels remain scarce. ASTROMER 2 learns from unlabeled light curves by reconstructing masked observations, yet this objective does not explicitly encourage class separation in a compact representation of each light curve. We introduce Contrastive Astromer, a two-stage approach that makes these representations more useful for classification without changing the ASTROMER 2 encoder architecture. First, unsupervised contrastive learning on single-band MACHO light curves brings together representations of augmented views of the same object. Supervised contrastive learning, supported by an auxiliary classification loss, then uses a separate labeled Alcock sample to strengthen class discrimination. We evaluate the resulting representations by freezing the encoder and training a separate classifier. On a held-out set of 600 objects, this classifier achieves a macro-F1 of 0.7943 with 500 labeled examples per class, exceeding our reproduction of the ASTROMER 2 finetune-and-classify pipeline by 5.10 percentage points. With downstream classifier training budgets of 20 and 100 examples per class, macro-F1 reaches 0.7078 and 0.7704, respectively, also surpassing this baseline. Embedding-space analyses further show that supervised adaptation improves local class consistency and global class separation. These results show that contrastive adaptation makes pretrained light-curve representations more effective for classification and more informative about the structure of variability classes.

papers.title: A Supermagnified Little Red Dot with a Resolved Host
papers.abstract: Little red dots (LRDs) are an intriguing new class of sources in the early universe discovered by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) characterized by V-shaped spectra and extremely compact sizes. Their underlying mechanisms still remain the subject of ongoing debate. We present JWST observations of a gravitationally lensed LRD nicknamed "Best Friend" at $z_{\rm spec} = 8.297\pm0.002$. Its high magnification factor of $\mu = 36^{+8}_{-12}$ makes it the highest magnified LRD reported to date and unveils both the resolved structure of its host and a central engine less than 7 pc in size. The spectrum of the central engine, in which broad lines are not detected, possibly owing to the limited S/N and spectral resolution, is better interpreted as black hole activity rather than a dense star cluster. The latter cannot be fully excluded, but if true, the resulting lower limit on stellar density would be $>1.25^{+0.4}_{-0.3}\cdot10^6 \mathrm{M_{\odot}/pc}^2$, which is around 2 orders of magnitude higher than stellar densities of typical clusters at high-z. By performing a spatially resolved analysis of NIRCam photometry and NIRSpec/PRISM spectroscopy, we find that the host stellar mass is $\log(M_\star/M_{\odot}) = 7.3^{+0.2}_{-0.8}$. Best Friend demonstrates the power of lensing to reveal the morphologies of LRDs.

papers.title: OmniPiano: Diverse Dexterous Piano-Playing Challenges for Standard, Robust, Safe, and Multi-Agent RL
papers.abstract: Dexterous robotic manipulation remains a major challenge in robotics, exemplified by piano playing, which requires coordinated control of fingers and provides a demanding testbed for reinforcement learning (RL). Although previous work established a benchmark for robotic piano playing, it is restricted to two hands and does not support unified evaluation. To address this gap, we introduce OmniPiano, a benchmark that provides one to up to five Shadow Hands and supports standard, robust, safe, and multi-agent RL within a shared piano-playing task family. OmniPiano is developed for scalable and diverse piano-playing tasks with configurable perturbations, explicit safety constraints, and decentralized cooperation settings. Particularly, to facilitate usability and extendability, OmniPiano adopts a highly modular design and provides comprehensive tasks to support RL study of task performance, robustness, safety, and cooperation in dexterous control. With at least 912 task settings and 36 baseline algorithms, OmniPiano further incorporates LLM-based agents to broaden the evaluation scope and reveal new insights. Extensive evaluations show that state-of-the-art RL algorithms and frontier LLM-based agents still struggle on challenging piano-playing tasks, even under standard RL settings, highlighting substantial room for improvement in dexterous control. The code, dataset, tutorial, and demo are available at https://sail-research-lab.github.io/omnipiano/.

papers.title: Two Isolated Microlensing Events Near the Upper Shore of Einstein Desert
papers.abstract: The Einstein desert is a deficit in the angular Einstein-radius ($\theta_{\rm E}$) distribution of isolated objects over the range $9 {\rm \mu as} < \theta_{\rm E}<26 {\rm \mu as}$. Although this interval contained no events when the desert was first identified, several subsequent detections have fallen within it, raising questions about its detailed structure and requiring a larger detection sample. In this paper, we report the observations and analyses of two microlensing events possibly caused by isolated giant planets or brown dwarfs whose $ \theta_{\rm E}$ lie near the upper shore of the desert. MOA-2021-BLG-145 has $ \theta_{\rm E} = 23.1\pm2.0 ~{\rm \mu as}$, placing it just inside the upper boundary, and KMT-2026-BLG-0357 has $ \theta_{\rm E} = 36.5\pm 3.7~{\rm \mu as}$, placing it above the desert. We also compare the $ \theta_{\rm E}$ distributions of isolated objects and bound planetary events. The bound population shows no corresponding deficit over the same range, suggesting that the Einstein desert may be associated with the formation or subsequent evolution of the isolated population. Furthermore, some FFPs may lie above the upper shore of the Einstein desert, indicating that a more complete understanding of the FFP population requires direct lens-mass measurements.

papers.title: The Tangled Web They Weave: Exploring Neural Representations with Directed Simplicial Complexes
papers.abstract: Understanding how artificial neural networks (ANNs) represent and combine features internally is a central challenge in mechanistic interpretability. Existing neural circuit-discovery methods represent neuron interactions as pairwise edges in a graph. But distributed neural representations consist of large groups of neurons that are inherently linked by higher-order causal dependencies: suppressing a subgroup of neurons in concert may shift the activation of other neurons in the feature representation. We propose a method to construct filtered directed simplicial complexes (DSCs) that give a topological representation of such dependencies, built from the activation profiles of an ANN on a given set of inputs. Our approach treats ANNs as structural causal models and uses counterfactual ablations to test for causal links between groups of internal neurons within specific input contexts. As a proof of concept, we apply the approach to a pair of small multilayer perceptron (MLP) architectures in a synthetic two-dimensional quadrant classification task. In these examples, DSCs recover the designed feature pathways and coordinated class transitions, and the complexes of trained networks are higher-dimensional than those of their handcrafted references. As validation, we compare our method with graph-based circuit-discovery baselines and find that their 1-skeletons agree within the relations that a weight graph can represent. These results support DSCs as context-dependent descriptions of multi-neuron computation and may thus provide a novel, orthogonal framework to study the phenomenon of distributed feature representations and polysemanticity.

papers.title: Cryogenic Optoelectronic Characterization of InGaAsP LEDs for Low-Energy Detector Calibration
papers.abstract: We measured the emission spectra and current-voltage (IV) characteristics of commercial InGaAsP LEDs in a cryostat over a temperature range from 7 K to 300 K. At a constant operating current of 3.3 mA, the peak emission wavelength of the 1200 nm (1650 nm) LED decreased from 1202.3 +/- 0.5 nm (1665.5 +/- 0.6 nm) at 300 K to 1143.1 +/- 0.3 nm (1539.5 +/- 2.2 nm) at 7 K, demonstrating a strong temperature dependence. The cut-in voltage increased systematically with decreasing temperature, in agreement with conventional diode theory. To assess junction self-heating effects, we conducted pulsed IV measurements at different duty cycles. The extracted apparent series resistance showed a clear duty-cycle dependence, whereas the cut-in voltage remained unchanged within experimental uncertainty, indicating that self-heating primarily influenced the IV slope rather than the cut-in voltage. These results quantitatively characterize the thermal behavior of both the spectral peak and key electrical parameters, supporting the application of InGaAsP LEDs as cryogenic calibration light sources.

papers.title: Chemical abundances of a Galactic Centre ejecta discovered in DESI
papers.abstract: Chemical abundances in the Galactic Centre (GC) are challenging to measure because of high extinction, crowding, and distance, and are typically limited to the brightest AGB and M giants observed in the near-infrared. In contrast, hypervelocity stars (HVSs) ejected from the GC by Sgr A* carry their natal composition into accessible regions such as the Milky Way halo, making them unique probes of GC chemistry. We present high-resolution optical Magellan/MIKE spectroscopy of DESI-312, a bound HVS candidate in the halo with super-solar metallicity ($[\mathrm{Fe/H}]=0.2\pm0.1$). This sets it apart from accreted halo populations on radial orbits and is most naturally explained by GC formation and Hills-mechanism ejection. Updated isochrone fits give an age of 7.4-11.3 Gyr; together with its metallicity and kinematics, this strengthens the case for a GC origin. Korg and Turbospectrum spectral synthesis yields $[\mathrm{X/Fe}]$ for 22 elements, plus Li from an independent line-by-line NLTE analysis. As DESI-312 is near the main sequence, its C, N, and O abundances are unaltered by dredge-up; to our knowledge, these are the first such measurements of unevolved GC material. Its abundance pattern lies where the nuclear star cluster (NSC), nuclear stellar disc (NSD), and inner-bulge sequences overlap, with a Na enhancement ($[\mathrm{Na/Fe}]=+0.16^{+0.03}_{-0.04}$) more modest than in NSC giants of similar metallicity. Chemistry alone thus cannot identify its progenitor; we nevertheless favour the NSC, given its large reservoir of old, metal-rich stars and the star's kinematics. Alongside WINERED-HVS1 and the S-star S0-6/S10, whose abundances point to different progenitors, this tentatively suggests multiple progenitor populations for the S-star cluster. DESI-312 is a test case for sampling GC chemistry with ejected dwarfs at optical wavelengths, complementing near-infrared studies of giants.

papers.title: Source-Resolved Collective Cognition in Robotics: Mathematical Foundations for Multimodal and Collective Estimation, and Their Reach across the Cognition Loop
papers.abstract:
The Generalized Singular Value Decomposition (GSVD) is a central tool for comparing two linear operators that act on the same unknown. Once the output metrics are fixed, it answers the basis-independent question "along which state directions does the first operator dominate the second, and by how much?".
  This foundational volume builds the GSVD and its surrounding estimation theory from the ground up. Part I re-derives every piece of linear algebra and statistical estimation machinery needed later -- inner products, the four subspaces, orthogonal matrices, the spectral theorem, quadratic forms, the ordinary SVD, Lie-group tangent perturbations, Jacobians, covariance, whitening, Fisher information, CCA, mutual information, discrimination criteria, and covariance intersection -- with self-contained derivations and worked numerical examples. Part II states the GSVD in both a transparent and a dimensionally general form, then proves it by two complementary routes. Part III works one small matrix pair through five different lenses, each computed by hand and verified numerically. Part IV separates information attribution, subspace geometry, statistical dependence, and decision-theoretic discrimination for collective systems. Part V evaluates the role and limits of the GSVD across the cognition loop. Part VI covers numerical practice, including a tested reference implementation.
  Every number printed in this document was verified in double precision. Where a statement is an assumption rather than a theorem, it is labelled as such.

papers.title: Sonar-MoE: In-Backward Expert Updates for Memory-Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Training
papers.abstract: Most parameters of a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model belong to its experts, and standard training keeps every expert gradient in GPU memory until the optimizer step. This memory grows with the number and size of the experts, so it rises as MoE models scale. We introduce Sonar-MoE, which updates each expert tensor during the backward pass and frees its gradient right away. It brings optimizer-in-backward from dense models to batched MoE expert tensors, so the GPU never holds more than one layer of expert gradients. When we fine-tune OLMoE-1B-7B and Granite-3.1-3B-A800M in bf16 with two expert-kernel backends, Sonar-MoE lowers peak memory by 19% to 22%. Its updates are bitwise identical to standard training without expert gradient clipping, and held-out loss stays within 0.003 of all baselines. Each step also takes 17% to 23% less time than standard training with global-norm clipping. Updating whole batched tensors rather than individual experts is what keeps Sonar-MoE fast, as it avoids a 20% to 72% slowdown while using the same memory. Sonar-MoE matches optimizer-in-backward over all parameters in memory and speed while still clipping the dense parameters.

papers.title: Reviso: Not All Visual Evidence Deserves Equal Attention in Video Captioning
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can generate detailed video captions, yet they may overemphasize minor details while overlooking essential context and key events. We argue that not all visual evidence deserves equal attention, as the importance of visual information depends on the content of each video. Motivated by this observation, we propose Reviso, an agentic video captioning framework that learns what to observe and how to gather relevant visual evidence. From a low-frame-rate global preview, Reviso constructs a hierarchical Context--Focus--Points (CFP) observation plan that identifies the video context, prioritizes key aspects, and defines concrete observation targets and corresponding tools. Guided by this plan, Reviso performs goal-directed active perception by selectively revisiting temporal segments and combining tools for fine-grained inspection. It interprets the acquired evidence, updates its plan as needed, and integrates global and local information to generate the final caption. To learn this observation strategy, we develop a verification-guided pipeline that constructs high-quality training trajectories through factual verification and teacher-guided refinement. We further train Reviso using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), incorporating a key-fact reward for caption quality, a Plan Alignment Reward (PAR) for identifying important observation targets, and an Unproductive Tool-Call Penalty (UTCP) that adjusts observation-cost penalties based on caption quality. Experiments across four video captioning benchmarks show that Reviso outperforms the evaluated open-source baselines, while its generated captions better support downstream video question answering. These findings highlight the effectiveness and potential of priority-guided active observation for video captioning.

papers.title: Nuclear Charge Radii from Precision Bound-Electron g-Factor Measurements
papers.abstract: An efficient method to determine absolute nuclear charge radii from high-precision bound-electron g-factor measurements in hydrogenlike ions is put forward. Assuming that a nuclear model independent radius determination is possible, we demonstrate that this method can improve the precision of the nuclear radius for several poorly known heavy isotopes by up to two orders of magnitude compared to current literature values, by utilizing recent breakthroughs in the quantum electrodynamics (QED) theory of the bound-electron g-factor [B. Sikora, V. A. Yerokhin, C. H. Keitel, and Z. Harman, Phys. Rev. Lett. 134, 123001 (2025)]. This opens a new, independent pathway for testing nuclear structure models and resolving nuclear structure anomalies.
