papers.title: Optimal bounds for design curves on the torus
papers.abstract:
A closed rectifiable curve on the torus $\mathbb T^d=\mathbb R^d/\mathbb Z^d$ is a $t$-design curve if normalized arclength integration is exact for trigonometric polynomials $e^{2\pi i \langle m,x\rangle}$ with frequencies $m\in\mathbb Z^d$ satisfying $\|m\|_\infty\le t$. For the arclength $L$ of such curves, we establish the sharp lower bound \begin{equation}\label{eq:abs} L\geq \Big(\frac{(t+1)^{2d}-1}{t(t+2)}\Big)^{1/2}. \end{equation} Equality is attained by the family of Korobov curves described in \cite{Kunis,Lindblad}.
  For even $t$, we also derive an explicit lower bound on the length of total-degree $t$-design curves, defined by the frequency condition $\|m\|_1\leq t$. This bound is sharp for $t=2$ in every dimension and for every even $t$ in dimension two.
  We determine the minimum length of hyperbolic cross $t^2$-design curves in dimension two. For $d\geq3$, we establish lower bounds of optimal order for the length of hyperbolic cross $t^d$-design curves.
  Finally, we obtain lower bounds of optimal order for the length of $t$-design curves associated with sparse frequency sets.

papers.title: Gradient flow formulation and discrete approximation of reaction-cross-diffusion systems with size exclusion
papers.abstract: We characterize a class of possibly degenerate nonlinear reaction-cross-diffusion systems with size exclusion as (non-metric) gradient flows in continuity-equation format driven by entropy. We then establish a connection between these systems and discrete reaction networks by proving an EDP-type lower limit inequality for the associated gradient systems. In the non-degenerate case, we show a chain rule identity that allows us to identify minimizers of the corresponding energy-dissipation functional as weak solutions to the PDE system. In conjunction with the lower limit, this yields an alternative proof of existence of weak solutions and their approximability by solutions to the proposed discrete ODE systems. Finally, we generalize our results to models including drift terms by extending the established framework to tilted energy landscapes.

papers.title: Library of Layers (LoL): Adaptively Ordering Transformer Layers at Runtime
papers.abstract: Computer programmers chain together the same reusable computational primitives, for example, conditional statements or loops, but in different orders to implement different algorithms. In contrast, existing language model architectures always execute their layers in the same order. We introduce Library of Layers (LoL), an architecture that dynamically orders its layers during inference to solve the problem at hand. LoL has a single hyperparameter, the size of its global library of transformer blocks, that allows it to transition seamlessly between parameter reuse and sparsity, generalizing the parameter-efficiency and FLOPs-efficiency tradeoffs of dense, depth-recurrent, and mixture of experts architectures in one unified family. We show that LoL achieves competitive performance with all three above baselines when pretrained on text data. On synthetic sudoku and maze data, we observe that the model employs distinct layer orderings to implement different solution strategies, and we can intervene on routing to force a model to apply a specific solution strategy to a problem instance. In a multilingual natural language setting, we find that LoL chooses different layer order patterns based on language and script. Similarly, we train LoL on safety data and fit probes to its router outputs, finding that these probes distinguish safe from unsafe text with high AUROC. LoL provides a path toward a future in which models dynamically compose their own computational graph, enabling more efficient and controllable reasoning.

papers.title: Detection of the Galaxy--Galaxy--Temperature Skewed Bispectrum
papers.abstract: We present the first measurement of the galaxy--galaxy--temperature skewed bispectrum, obtained by cross-correlating the squared, filtered unWISE galaxy overdensity with \textit{Planck} maps at 100, 143, 217, and 353~GHz. The signal is detected with high significance in all four channels. Its frequency dependence reveals contributions from hot gas through the thermal Sunyaev--Zel'dovich (tSZ) effect and from dust through the cosmic infrared background (CIB). With the galaxy occupation fixed, our halo-model fits favor higher integrated pressure and peak star-formation efficiency for the galaxy--temperature cross-spectra than for the skewed bispectrum. Comparisons with component-separated tSZ and CIB maps from the same \textit{Planck} observations indicate that this mismatch is not confined to the frequency-map fits. This difference motivates testing more flexible descriptions of gas pressure, CIB emission, and galaxy occupation. In particular, it could point to a mass dependence of the gas-pressure profile that our model does not fully capture. By giving greater weight to massive halos that host many galaxy pairs, the skewed bispectrum provides a complementary test of these descriptions, using information beyond two-point statistics at a comparable computational cost.

papers.title: Seismic study of soda straws exposed to nearby blasting vibrations
papers.abstract: This study aims to protect an exceptional population of soda straw stalactites from vibrations generated by nearby rock blasting activities. The Choranche Cave, located in the Vercors region of France, hosts thousands of remarkably slender soda straws, reaching several meters in length while measuring approximately 0.5 cm in diameter. These speleothems are particularly susceptible to vibrations because of their structural fragility and potential for dynamic amplification. Our analyses revealed that their fundamental natural frequencies fall within the frequency range of nearby blasting-induced vibrations, typically spanning tens to hundreds of hertz. To assess the effects of blasting, we combined in situ vibration measurements, laboratory-based material characterization, and dynamic two-dimensional finite element simulations to estimate the loads experienced by the soda straw population. The results indicate that resonance can amplify the induced loads by a factor of five. Consequently, shorter soda straws (0.1--1 m) were found to be more vulnerable to blasting-induced vibrations than longer speleothems (>1 m), despite the greater weight and inertial forces associated with the latter. Based on simulations of several blasting tests, we established an allowable peak particle velocity (PPV) threshold of 2.4 mm/s within the cave. Subsequent blasting operations were conducted in compliance with this limit, successfully protecting the soda straw population from damage. We also investigated the dynamic response of soda straws to regional earthquakes. In contrast to blasting-induced vibrations, the lower-frequency content of earthquake ground motions preferentially excites resonance in longer speleothe

papers.title: Systematic Evaluation of Robustness in Fine-tuned Models
papers.abstract: Our study systematically evaluates the robustness of fine-tuned pre-trained models across different datasets and attack types, aiming to provide insights for researchers in selecting pre-trained models for image classification tasks while prioritizing robustness against potential attacks. Our work explores the influence of fine-tuning pre-trained models with different datasets and attack types on their robustness and overview of the appropriate pre-trained model for image classification based on factors such as computation resources, memory usage, and accuracy on clean data. We fine-tune the models with weights. Evaluate the models on data before any attack and after different attack cases. The study utilizes publicly available image datasets such as MNIST, CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and SVHN to assess the robustness of pre-trained models. The results indicate that the robustness of fine-tuned models varies across different data distributions and sample sizes, emphasizing the need for tailored selection based on specific task requirements. The findings also highlight the varying performance of ResNet50, DenseNet, and MobileNet in defending against attacks on different datasets. Overall, this research provides valuable insights into the robustness of fine-tuned pre-trained models and their suitability for real-world applications in image classification.

papers.title: Playing Dumb: How a Chess Transformer Simulates Users Across Skill Levels
papers.abstract: Generative models increasingly simulate users at different skill levels in education and AI evaluation. Yet it remains unclear whether lower-skill behavior reflects less internal knowledge or a different use of retained knowledge. This distinction is difficult to study in natural language, where proficiency and relevant knowledge are hard to measure. In this work, we study Maia-2, a chess transformer that predicts human moves conditioned on player skill, using quantitative skill ratings and deterministically labeled chess concepts. We hold board positions and model weights fixed and analyze positions where skill conditioning changes the prediction from a blunder to the best move. First, we measure encoded knowledge by training probes to predict the presence of 172 chess concepts from Maia-2's internal states. Probe accuracy remains nearly constant across skill conditions, and probes trained at one level transfer accurately to the others. To test whether stronger decisions can be recovered from this retained knowledge, we fine-tune only Maia-2's final output layer, raising best-move accuracy in the lowest skill band from 14.4% to 82.8%. Training this layer only on highest-skill representations retains most of the improvement at lower levels, showing that recovery does not require direct training on lower-skill states. Steering concept-relevant features learned by a sparse autoencoder also improves lower-skill decisions while leaving probe-measured concept encoding practically unchanged. These results support an account in which skill conditioning changes how retained concept knowledge influences move selection, showing that weaker behavior can understate the knowledge available within a model.

papers.title: A power-saving asymptotic for a M\"obius-weighted GCD quadratic form
papers.abstract: For the M\"obius-weighted quadratic form $T(N)=\sum_{m,n\leq N}\mu(m)\mu(n)(m,n)^2/(mn)$, we prove that $T(N)=cN+O_{\varepsilon}(N^{2/3+\varepsilon})$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, where $c>0$ is given by an absolutely convergent series of finite M\"obius sums multiplied by a convergent Euler product. The proof combines the classical Jordan-totient decomposition of the GCD kernel with a mean-value estimate that is uniform in a coprimality parameter. Grouping the resulting squares according to $\lfloor N/d\rfloor$ gives the error term and a nonnegative series for $c$.

papers.title: Local or Escalate? Post-Training Expert Routing for Real-Time Duplex Speech Models
papers.abstract: A full-duplex model should answer easy questions immediately, but hard questions often need stronger reasoning, which may require waiting. The challenge is to choose between these paths at the moment the model begins to speak. Recent systems learn related mode decisions through special-token generation inside the dialogue model, coupling routing to turn-taking and temporally annotated full-duplex training. We study a post-training alternative. We freeze MiniCPM-o 4.5, using only its speech input and output, and fit a logistic failure readout on hidden states already available at its native listen-to-speak transition. The resulting gate requires no additional model generation and exposes thresholds that can be retuned without changing the duplex policy. A probe fitted on text-input states also reads the states of spoken questions, including unseen human recordings. On the internal benchmark, selective handoff improves answer accuracy by 27.1 points. Compared with always using the expert, it reduces mean server time to first answer audio by 31.5 percent. It also outperforms matched random routing across external speech question-answering pools, as well as a zero-shot GPT-5.4 mini router that rates the transcribed question. The training recipe also transfers to a second duplex model family. These results show that an existing duplex model can be equipped to answer easy turns immediately and wait for stronger reasoning or fresher knowledge on the turns that need it, without further duplex training.

papers.title: Reconstruction as Spatial Evaluation: Diagnosing Cross-View Spatial Intelligence in Large Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: The spatial intelligence of large vision-language models (LVLMs) requires the ability to combine local visual observations into a geometrically consistent representation of the physical world. Many static benchmarks assess isolated spatial judgments, such as relative direction or distance, while interactive embodied evaluations combine perception with exploration, planning, control, and simulator-specific execution. To bridge this gap, we introduce RECONSPATIAL, a benchmark centered on multi-view 3D scene reconstruction across indoor, tabletop, and outdoor environments. Given real multi-view images and target-object queries, LVLMs are required to jointly predict oriented 3D bounding boxes in a shared, camera-anchored metric coordinate frame. Reconstructions are evaluated along two complementary axes: Structure for relative layout and Metric for physical scale and camera-anchored placement. Nine atomic spatial QA tasks, grouped into Geometric Perception and Spatial Relations, probe spatial capabilities involved in joint reconstruction. Offline navigation extends evaluation to path planning. Evaluation of 18 frontier LVLMs reveals a consistent gap between relative scene structure and metric reconstruction; even GPT-6-Astra scores 81.4% on Structure but only 58.7% on Metric. Tracing this gap, diagnostic analyses link atomic spatial capabilities to reconstruction quality and show that relational consistency alone does not ensure metric accuracy. Experiments with 3D map injection further separate scene construction from path planning, revealing how these geometric errors limit navigation success. Finally, spatial fine-tuning yields broad transfer across both spatial and general vision-language benchmarks.

papers.title: Inhomogeneous Synthetic Fluxes in Optical Lattices
papers.abstract: Synthetic gauge fields in optical lattices are usually engineered to realize a uniform magnetic flux. Here, we propose a scheme to generate spatially inhomogeneous fluxes and demonstrate how such fluxes reshape the single-particle spectrum. Within Wannier--Stark-assisted tunneling, onsite modulation produces a plaquette flux that depends on the orientation of the static tilt, whereas laser-assisted tunneling (LAT) does not. Using LAT, two coherent Raman processes with different momentum transfers imprint a dimerized Peierls phase that alternates the flux between neighboring plaquettes of a square lattice while keeping the mean flux fixed. A bond-selective Raman phase extends the scheme to the kagome lattice, where a parameter $\xi$ redistributes the flux between triangles and hexagons at fixed flux per unit cell. The Hofstadter--Rammal spectrum of the bipartite square lattice retains chiral symmetry for all $\xi$, whereas the kagome lattice lacks this symmetry, and its flux periodicity and reflection symmetries survive only at special values of $\xi$. As $\xi$ is reduced, the anomalous Landau levels of the kagome singular flat band are compressed toward the flat-band energy and evolve into a degenerate zero-energy manifold at $\xi=0$ with compactly localized states. The dynamical structure factor, accessible through Bragg scattering, resolves this evolution as a Rydberg-like series of peaks whose spectral span tracks the width of the anomalous-level tower and vanishes as $\xi\to0$. We discuss the frequency resolution and temperature required for its observation.

papers.title: WebHarbor: Docking Real Websites for Evolving GUI Agent Environments
papers.abstract: GUI web agents require realistic and interactive environments that remain stable during both evaluation and training. Live website evaluation suffers from changing content, access restrictions, and limited coverage of authenticated workflows, while existing synthetic environments for training often lack functional depth and visual fidelity. We propose WebHarbor, a suite of 153 executable and dockerized website environments that faithfully reconstruct the visual interfaces, content, and functional workflows of real-world web services under deterministic control. We build WebHarbor through task-driven human-agent collaboration, where environments evolve as new tasks expand their functional scope, coding agents implement the required changes, and human contributors audit visual fidelity, functional correctness, and task validity. The resulting suite comprises 3,518 tasks spanning multi-step and post-authentication workflows, where existing works often fail to cover. Beyond reliable evaluation, WebHarbor provides high-fidelity synthetic web environments for cost-efficient reinforcement learning (RL). We demonstrate that a Qwen 4B-level GUI agent trained with RL in WebHarbor generalizes to unseen tasks and performs competitively with leading open-source GUI web agents across four benchmarks. The code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/aiming-lab/WebHarbor.

papers.title: Porteous Meets Walsh: Counting Critical Points for $\mathcal{H}_2$-Norm Model Order Reduction Using Algebraic Geometry Behind Multiparameter Eigenvalue Problems
papers.abstract: Several polynomial systems arising in systems and control have been shown to exhibit a partially linear structure, which allows them to be reformulated as a multiparameter eigenvalue problem (MEP). In this work, we show how such MEP formulations can be leveraged to obtain refined information about the solution set of the polynomial system. We demonstrate, in the setting of single-input single-output $\mathcal{H}_2$-norm model order reduction, how the Thom--Porteous formula can be used to derive an exact count of the complex solutions of the critical equations derived from Walsh's theorem. We prove, under suitable genericity assumptions, that their set of complex solutions is finite and that all solutions occur without multiplicity. Moreover, we derive an explicit formula for the total number of complex solutions as a function of the model orders. Throughout, we provide a self-contained and application-oriented exposition of the algebro-geometric tools required for our analysis, with the aim of making them accessible to the broader engineering community.

papers.title: From MHV Gravity Amplitudes and Hodges map to Pentad Varieties
papers.abstract: We study some geometric aspects behind the Hodges matrix appearing in the context of scattering amplitudes for the $\mathcal N=8$ supergravity. Through a vector bundle construction, we show that the Hodges matrix gives rise to a canonical rational map from the two-step flag variety to symmetric matrices, called the $\textit{Hodges map}$. This construction allows to define the amplitude geometrically: its vanishing locus is a divisor - the $\textit{MHV gravity divisor}$. Inspired by the Hodges map, we introduce the notion of Hadamard ratio of two varieties. In the case relevant to gravity, this is the ratio of two Grassmannians, which we call the $\textit{pentad variety}$, connecting it to the pentad constraint from algebraic statistics. Moreover, we show that the pentad variety is closely related to the combinatorial algebraic geometry of Martin's affine slope variety, and the phirotopes of Below, Krummeck, and Richter-Gebert.

papers.title: The Dirichlet problem for quaternionic Monge--Amp\`ere equations on flat quaternionic quotients
papers.abstract: We prove smooth solvability of the Dirichlet problem for quaternionic Monge--Amp\`ere equations on smooth relatively compact domains in ${\mathbb H}^m/\Gamma$, where $m\ge2$ and $\Gamma$ is a discrete additive subgroup: for a smooth positive density, the existence of a smooth strictly plurisubharmonic subsolution guarantees the existence and uniqueness of the smooth admissible solution. The technique of the proof is a simple adaptation from the Ph.D. Thesis of Jingyong Zhu [25] in 2017, supervised by Xinan Ma, which is a joint work of Ma and Zhu. The claim [22, Theorem A.1] by OpenAI on Sogge's local smoothing conjecture is a special case of our theorem.

papers.title: SketchBloom: Training-Free Vector Sketch Outpainting with Stroke-Level Style Control
papers.abstract: Outpainting sparse sketches while preserving contour coherence and stroke style remains challenging. We present SketchBloom, a training-free framework that combines pretrained raster outpainting and style-transfer guidance with per-instance vector optimization. Given a sketch, a scene prompt, and an optional reference style, it produces an editable Scalable Vector Graphic (SVG) composed of Bezier strokes. Adaptive latent blending balances content contours and reference texture without model retraining. A reference-derived stroke vocabulary initializes contour- and DINO-attention-guided strokes, which are optimized separately for structure and texture before contour-emphasizing multiply fusion. As in prior optimization-based vector sketching, no task-specific network is trained; our contribution is the synthesis design specialized to sketch outpainting. On LineArtOut-1K, comprising 1,024 input and style combinations, SketchBloom improves perceptual, semantic, and structural fidelity over the evaluated vector baselines when all methods vectorize the same outpainted raster. This protocol evaluates vector synthesis rather than end-to-end outpainting or reference-style superiority. Runtime is approximately six minutes per pair on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU. Project page: https://khangcntn123.github.io/SketchBloom/

papers.title: SketchForge: Training-Free Scene-to-Vector Sketching via Decoupled Structure and Texture Optimization
papers.abstract: Converting a raster image into a resolution-independent, stroke-editable vector sketch while faithfully preserving both structural contours and tonal texture remains challenging: raster-space rendering pipelines are difficult to edit at the stroke level, while generation-from-scratch vectorization methods struggle to remain faithful to an arbitrary input image. We present SketchForge, a training-free framework that converts an input raster image into a resolution-independent SVG sketch through per-instance test-time optimization of Bezier curves, requiring no additional training or fine-tuning. Strokes are seeded via a contour and attention-guided initialization, then refined by a vector-native differentiable rendering pipeline that decouples structural contour strokes from free-form texture strokes under dedicated objectives, composited via multiply-blend layering. Extensive experiments show that SketchForge consistently outperforms existing vector-based baselines in structural fidelity and generation quality. Project page: https://khangcntn123.github.io/SketchForge

papers.title: GEAR: Generative Editing for Scene-Conditioned Outfit Retrieval for VR Travel
papers.abstract: In virtual environments, choosing appropriate outfits requires contextual harmony with surrounding scenes, yet bridging the visual gap between 3D ambient views and catalog garment assets remains challenging. This paper investigates scene-conditioned outfit retrieval for interactive 3D environments, where a user's egocentric view serves as the retrieval signal. We present GEAR (Generative Editing for Asset Retrieval), a framework that bridges the cross-domain gap by synthesizing intermediate visual queries rather than predicting direct compatibility. GEAR uses a vision-language model to describe suitable clothing from a captured scene, employs an instruction-guided diffusion model to render the concept onto a standardized reference character, and utilizes the cropped clothing region to retrieve existing 2D outfit assets via embedding similarity. An interactive Unity prototype demonstrates real-time scene capture, asset retrieval, and in-engine 3D avatar fitting. We benchmark GEAR against direct visual similarity, aesthetic scoring, and VLM-based reranking on a controlled dataset using automated Swiss-system pairwise judgments, where GEAR achieves competitive top-ranked performance (mean Elo@5 of 1012.75 and top-10 overlap of 0.180) alongside 0.539 pairwise agreement. Furthermore, a user study across 20 virtual travel scenes demonstrates that GEAR achieves the highest overall participant preference in both visual appeal (34.5%) and contextual suitability (34.5%).

papers.title: A Living Leaderboard for Graph Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Graph machine learning benchmarking results are scattered across papers that use quite different sets of datasets and baseline methods, making it difficult to tell whether a reported gain reflects architectural progress or merely an outdated comparison or weakly tuned baseline. We introduce a living, graph-learning-specific leaderboard that organizes reported results by dataset, putting new results into context. As of 15 October 2026 our LLM-based extraction pipeline extracted 27,723 eligible results across 111 datasets from 885 peer-reviewed papers. Our analysis of these results quantifies concerns about graph-learning benchmarking: legacy datasets are still actively used and many result tables contain baseline results that are drastically lower than those already available in the literature, e.g. 45% Amazon-ratings tables and 37% for Peptides-struct. The leaderboard allows to quickly compare new results against compatible prior results, aiming to improve the overall quality of graph learning benchmarking.

papers.title: Optical Magnetic-Field Gating of Photon Avalanching Quantum Processes
papers.abstract: Highly nonlinear phenomena, where macroscopic changes are triggered by microscopic perturbations, are ubiquitous in complex systems ranging from epidemic spreading to neural networks. In optics, photon avalanching represents a prime manifestation of such highly nonlinear behavior, characterized by a steep nonlinear response (s) following an avalanche threshold. However, this nonlinearity is typically determined by material composition, making this behavior challenging to tune for adaptive sensing, imaging, and neuromorphic applications. Here, we demonstrate giant optical magnetic field gated threshold and nonlinearity in lanthanide doped nanoparticles. We exploit the distinct quantum selection rules of the avalanche process: while the energy looping cycles of excited state absorption and cross relaxation are primarily electrically driven, the seed excitation, ground state absorption, is a mixed transition permitting magnetic dipole interaction. By positioning the emitters within an optical standing wave to spatially partition the electromagnetic field, we tune the local magnetic to electric field balance to selectively regulate the seeding and amplification probabilities. This allows us to demonstrate an unprecedented dynamic range of control over the power threshold and nonlinearity, tuning the order from s = 15 to s = 62. Furthermore, we harness this spatial separation of electric and magnetic fields using tightly focused cylindrical vector beams to locally sculpt the nonlinearity of a single nanocluster, achieving sub wavelength super resolution imaging that substantially surpasses conventional photon avalanche imaging under Gaussian illumination. These findings establish the magnetic component of light as a practical knob to actively program nonlinear optical dynamics, sub diffraction nanoscopy, and critical quantum dynamics at the nanoscale.

papers.title: A Debiased Machine Learning Single-Imputation Framework for Item Nonresponse in Surveys
papers.abstract: Machine-learning methods offer flexible alternatives to parametric models for imputing missing survey values. However, using their predictions in the customary imputed estimator does not automatically yield valid inference. We explain why the error from estimating the regression function can prevent root-$n$ consistency and develop inference for a finite population mean using a cross-fitted augmented inverse-probability-weighted (AIPW) estimator. The analysis combines an imputation model, a sampling design, and a missing-at-random response mechanism, while allowing dependence among sampling indicators. We establish double robustness and show that, under suitable regularity conditions, consistency of both nuisance estimators together with a product-rate condition yields oracle equivalence and asymptotic normality. We also derive consistent variance estimators accounting for sampling and nonresponse. To obtain a completed survey variable, we construct adjusted imputed values that preserve observed responses and whose weighted mean reproduces the AIPW estimate exactly. We further discuss aggregation of nuisance learners and the conditions under which it preserves the prediction rates needed for inference. Simulations show that cross-fitting can substantially reduce undercoverage, but may increase mean squared error when nuisance predictions are inaccurate.

papers.title: Quantum dynamics of ultrasmall magnetic skyrmions in atomic-defect landscapes
papers.abstract: Magnetic skyrmions are prime candidates for future information technology, and their fate in devices is settled by the defects they encounter. In ultrathin films, skyrmions can be as small as a couple of nanometers, carrying only a few tens of magnetic moments, while atomic defects reshape their energy landscape on the atomic scale. Here, we demonstrate that such ultrasmall skyrmions can behave quantum mechanically and that their quantum dynamics is unusual. Since the gyrotropic force dominates, the two coordinates of a ferromagnetic skyrmion are canonically conjugate and the skyrmion behaves as a particle in the lowest Landau level of an effective magnetic field, with a magnetic length of 0.6~\AA. Utilizing skyrmion-defect interaction profiles of Cr and Fe adatoms and dimers in PdFe/Ir(111), obtained from atomistic spin simulations parametrized from first principles, we unveil quantized gyrotropic orbits with level spacings of 20--85~$\mu$eV, bound not only by pinning defects but also, counter-intuitively, by repulsive ones. Saddle points of the energy landscape act as quantum beam splitters for skyrmions, and quantum depinning reaches rates of 1--100~Hz below the critical current. Embedded impurities, in contrast, bind the skyrmion so strongly that it ceases to behave as a rigid particle, defining a strong-coupling regime. For the Gilbert damping typical of ultrathin films, the quantized levels remain well resolved. The thermal-to-quantum crossover lies between 40 and 160~mK, which is within reach of millikelvin scanning tunneling microscopy, where tip-induced escape statistics and electron spin resonance STM can reveal the quantized gyrotropic motion of skyrmions pinned at defects crafted atom by atom.

papers.title: Missingness-Aware Prior-Data Fitted Network for Irregular Clinical Time-Series
papers.abstract: Clinical time series are irregularly observed with laboratory measurements recorded at uneven intervals and observation patterns often reflecting patient state, clinical concern, and site-specific practice. Consequently, missingness is not merely a nuisance factor but an informative signal for prediction. We propose a Missingness-Aware Prior-Data Fitted Network (MA-PFN) for irregular clinical time-series prediction. MA-PFN first learns a diffusion-based prior over joint laboratory value and observation-mask trajectories from source-domain electronic health records, capturing both physiological dynamics and measurement processes. Synthetic trajectories sampled from this prior are then transformed into context-query tasks to train a PFN-style conditional predictor. Once trained, the model performs prediction for new admissions in a single forward pass, requiring neither retraining nor parameter adaptation on target datasets. The framework naturally supports both imputation and forecasting through different context-query constructions. We conduct internal validation on a held-out MIMIC-III test set and external validation on eICU, evaluating both imputation and forecasting and assessing cross-domain generalization under shifts in patient populations, clinical practices, and observation mechanisms. MA-PFN achieves the best performance across all evaluated settings, with Overall/Macro nRMSD ranging from (0.193/0.186) for internal imputation to (0.297/0.297) for external forecasting, without target-domain adaptation. These results demonstrate that learning missingness-aware task priors enables accurate and transferable clinical time-series prediction under informative missingness.

papers.title: Charge-Order pattern in $\kappa$-BEDT-TTF salts: A model independent, selection rule approach
papers.abstract: A well known vibrational selection rule is invoked to determine the charge order (CO) pattern displayed by the most interesting members of the widely studied class of $\kappa$-BEDT-TTF salts and their molecular analogues. The selection rule indicates that an easily identifiable Raman band should be present if intra-dimer charge disproportionation occurs, constituting a sort of model independent ``litmus test''. The absence of such a band in the available Raman spectra of $\kappa$-BEDT-TTF salts exhibiting static of fluctuating CO, strongly suggests that the CO pattern involves inter-dimer CO, in contrast with the universally accepted intra-dimer disprortionation. This paper therefore poses a challenge for the theoretical modeling of the concerned salts: either the lack of the Raman band sensitive to intra-dimer CO pattern is explained, or the modeling of the multivariate, unique physical properties of these $\kappa$-phase salts (spin frustration, electronic ferroelectricity etc.) has to start from the perspective of a different ground state.

papers.title: Charge-Balanced Control of Linear Systems: Controllability, Stabilizability, and Periodic Regulation
papers.abstract: Electrical neuromodulation is a therapeutic approach that regulates neural activity by delivering electrical currents to brain tissue to treat brain disorders, such as epilepsy and Parkinson's disease. A critical safety requirement is charge balance, which ensures zero net injected charge over each stimulation cycle. Despite its clinical importance, the implications of charge-balanced stimulation for system dynamics and control remain poorly understood. This article investigates the controllability, stabilizability, and regulation of discrete-time linear systems under charge-balanced input constraints, motivated by applications in electrical neuromodulation. We introduce novel notions of charge-balanced controllability and stabilizability and establish necessary and sufficient conditions for both properties. We further demonstrate that nonzero steady states cannot be maintained under charge-balanced inputs, motivating the introduction of charge-balanced periodic orbits as alternative control targets. We characterize the conditions under which convergence to such orbits is achievable and develop optimal feedback controllers to stabilize the origin and track optimal charge-balanced periodic orbits. Finally, we validate the proposed control framework using a Hodgkin-Huxley neuron model, demonstrating successful suppression of tonic spiking and highlighting the potential of our approach for controlling nonlinear dynamical systems.

papers.title: A Circuit Complexity Trichotomy For Regular Languages
papers.abstract:
We establish a trichotomy for the non-uniform, unbounded-fan-in circuit complexity of regular languages: the complexity of every regular language lies in exactly one of $O(1)$, $\Omega(\log n)\cap O(\log n\log\log n)$, or $\Omega(n)\cap O(n)$.
  Our main technical contribution is a characterization of the sublinear class in terms of algebra, word congruences, regular expressions, and logic. This class consists precisely of the regular languages computable by constant-depth circuits of size $O(\log^2 n)$, or, equivalently, by circuits of size $O(\log n\log\log n)$ and depth $O((\log\log n)^2)$. Consequently, every regular language of sublinear circuit complexity is definable in $\mathrm{FO}^2[\Sigma,<,\mathrm{mod}]$, which is contained in wire-linear $\mathbf{AC}^0$.
  For each of the three classes, deciding membership is $\mathbf{PSPACE}$-complete when the language is specified by a nondeterministic finite automaton. We also obtain a corresponding classification for regular languages with a neutral letter.

papers.title: Facility Location with Customer Incompatibilities
papers.abstract:
We study metric facility location with customer incompatibilities, where the clients assigned to each facility must satisfy prescribed independence constraints. We first consider the setting of facility-opening costs and where there is a single matroid $\mathcal M$ over the clients and the set of clients assigned to an open facility must be an independent set in $\mathcal M$. We develop a polynomial-time \((1+\sqrt{2}+\epsilon)\)-approximation algorithm for this setting. We further obtain a polynomial-time \((15+\epsilon)\)-approximation algorithm for the case of non-uniform facility-opening costs when $\mathcal M$ is a partition matroid that only permits $b_g$ clients to be assigned to a facility for each group $g$ in the partition. Both settings are substantial generalizations of Capacitated Facility Location with uniform capacities.
  Our algorithms are based on local search using add, delete, and single-swap operations. As with CFL, bounding the connection cost is reasonably straightforward using supermodularity of the minimum connection-cost function. However, bounding the facility opening costs requires novel arguments in both cases. We use a ``compression'' argument based on matroid exchange principles to identify a subset of the locally opened facilities whose size is no larger than that of an optimal facility set. The opening costs of facilities outside this subset can be bounded using supermodularity, while bounding the costs of the remaining facilities requires different arguments.
  It is natural to consider a variant where each possible facility $i$ has its own matroid $\mathcal M_i$ defining the subsets of clients it can feasibly serve. We also show problem is at least as hard to approximate as Set Cover even if all $\mathcal M_i$ are partition matroids that have the same partition of clients, just different group bounds $b_g$.

papers.title: Assessing Temporal Dispersion of Time-Varying Channel at 38 GHz for Different Reference Signals
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the influence of reference waveform selection on temporal dispersion estimation in a time-varying radio channel at 38 GHz. Three reference waveforms-numerically generated in MATLAB, measured through a conducted connection, and recorded in an anechoic chamber -are compared using the same wideband channel measurements conducted in a dynamic road environment. Their effects on the estimated power delay profiles (PDPs), mean delay, and root mean square (RMS) delay spread are evaluated. Despite noticeable differences in the time-domain and spectral characteristics of the reference waveforms, the resulting PDPs exhibit similar multipath structures, while the estimated temporal dispersion parameters show relatively small differences. The results indicate limited sensitivity to reference waveform selection under the investigated measurement conditions.

papers.title: Rubric-Based Assessment of Student Reports Using Small Language Models
papers.abstract: Language models can analyze and assess student texts using predefined rubrics and deliver structured feedback, reducing instructors' workload. However, existing solutions often rely on external services that are resource-intensive, costly, and raise privacy concerns, making them unsuitable for constrained environments. This study evaluates an automated assessment pipeline with three key aims: design for low-resource environments, privacy, and focus on a novel context in cybersecurity education. The pipeline integrates lightweight language models for textual evaluation and a vision-language model for image interpretation. Responses from 105 students were collected over two semesters of an undergraduate course during a cybersecurity exercise on incident response. Results across different hardware configurations show that small models in low-resource environments can achieve up to 97% accuracy in text-only and up to 94% in rich-text assessments. This rivals or even outperforms a large model while adding the benefits of locally hosted assessment. Our solution can help educators and practitioners who need grading assistance without replacing human oversight, especially in environments where cloud-based solutions may be impractical. This study contributes an open-source, locally deployable AI-assisted scoring pipeline that runs on affordable hardware and can be extended to various types of student reports in computing education. As a result, it makes automated assessment accessible to a broad range of educators and institutions.

papers.title: How Temporal Dispersion of Radio Channels Depends on Signal Bandwidth
papers.abstract: The degree of temporal dispersion of a radio channel is the basis for assessing its transmission capabilities. This paper addresses the practical issue of measuring the temporal parameters of a signal transmitted in the millimeter-wave (38 GHz) range. These parameters provide the basis for assessing the degree of dispersion of the received signal. The measurement results show that both the mean and RMS values of the delay spread depend on the distance between the transmitter and receiver as well as the bandwidth of the transmitted signals. The function description of these relationships (model) is determined based on a statistical analysis of the obtained measurement data obtained in a selected indoor corridor under line-of-sight conditions.

papers.title: Validating LLM-Generated Synthetic Survey Samples: A Use-Dependent Multi-Dimensional Framework for Social-Science Applications
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) make it increasingly feasible to generate synthetic survey respondents, but their empirical usefulness cannot be judged by a single notion of accuracy. A synthetic sample may perform weakly at the respondent level while still preserving distributional or substantive relationships relevant to social-science analysis. We develop a use-dependent, multi-dimensional validation framework distinguishing predictive, distributional, and substantive validity, and illustrate it using Eurobarometer data on attitudes toward artificial intelligence. Four off-the-shelf LLMs generate responses conditional on observed respondent profiles, while supervised machine learning provides a predictive reference for interpreting their performance. The results reveal substantial differences across validation dimensions: some LLM-generated samples preserve meaningful marginal heterogeneity, demographic ordering, cross-country variation, and predictor structure despite imperfect respondent-level correspondence. Performance varies across models and outcomes, but the broader picture is cautiously constructive. Synthetic samples should therefore be evaluated against the empirical properties required by their intended use.

papers.title: Answering Without Arriving: An Evidence Audit for Embodied Question Answering
papers.abstract: Embodied question answering asks an agent to navigate, observe, and then answer questions about what it saw, yet answer accuracy alone cannot tell whether any of this happened. A plausible answer can come from the question, the room label, or the answer choices, and a correct answer does not show that the supporting observation was ever made. We present a multi-room benchmark whose 200 test episodes and 800 questions are stratified by route extent, with an evaluation ladder that holds the questions fixed while varying only the evidence supplied to the answerer, from text-only probes through closed-loop agents to replay of the reference trajectory. Questions are generated from symbolic records of rooms, visible objects, and frames, so every answer can be traced to the observations that support it. A closed-loop vision-language agent reaches no target in 200 episodes yet answers 45.5% of questions, within 0.1 points of the same model given no images; replaying the reference trajectory raises the same model to 57.4%, so the evidence exists along the route but is not gathered. A family-level audit then shows that access to evidence is not the same as use of it. Four of eight families are largely answerable from text, one cites frames that cannot establish its own answer, and the oracle conditions reach 59.5% on Rooms-visited by counting the supplied images. Evidence acquisition, answer coverage, and shortcut sensitivity must therefore be established before an accuracy gain can be credited to memory.

authors.institution: University of Modena and Reggio Emilia

papers.title: Do Embodied VLMs Actually Use Their Scene-Graph Memory?
papers.abstract: Embodied agents that answer questions about their route need a memory of what they saw, and scene graphs are a natural form for it. A vision-language model (VLM) can receive such a graph as text or through a graph encoder, but accuracy alone cannot show whether the graph holds the episode's facts, reaches the model, or is actually relied on. In this diagnostic study, we introduce a graph-swap test for the last of these: each episode is given another episode's graph, and we count how many answers change. On an embodied question-answering benchmark with routes through two to seven rooms, we use it to compare ways of delivering scene-graph memory to a fine-tuned VLM. As text, the memory is used strongly, adding 30 points on route questions. As a graph, it is not, and we trace why: the encoder preserves the information, but standard pooled and late fusion discard it. Giving each node its own input token recovers part of it, a gain of 8.3 points on route questions that the swap test confirms comes from the graph. The test also exposes a shortcut that accuracy hides: when the same facts appear in the text, the model ignores its graph. The test thus offers a cheap check of whether a VLM uses its scene-graph memory, and our analysis points to how that memory should be delivered.

authors.name: Niyati Rawal
authors.institution: University of Modena and Reggio Emilia

papers.title: Agent Stack for ML Training Lifecycle: Generation, Validation, and Optimization
papers.abstract: Production model development requires repeated architecture design, platform integration, debugging, training, and evaluation. We present an agent stack deployed at LinkedIn with two independently usable agent loops: AutoTorch for model generation and migration, and AutoResearch for model optimization. AutoTorch generates PyTorch models and training pipelines for TensorFlow migration, XGBoost replacement, and new-model development. Executable validation hooks check platform API compliance, trainability, and conversion fidelity on sampled data, guiding iterative repair before engineer review and full-scale distributed training. AutoResearch explores architecture and training-configuration changes through expert-steered or autonomous experimentation. An external orchestrator manages parallel trials, experiment history, candidate selection, and wall-clock budgets across agent sessions. A shared runtime preserves execution state independently of agent reasoning and allocates GPUs separately from agent execution. Across ranking, content understanding, and recommendation workloads, AutoTorch completed generation and full-scale training in 92 of 115 workflow runs (80%). Of these, 77 (83.7%) produced models meeting post-training quality requirements. In a separate cohort, AutoResearch improved the primary task metric on held-out data for 28 of 100 production pipelines. Engineering teams estimate that the stack reduced elapsed end-to-end migration time from approximately eight weeks to two weeks, a 4x speedup.

authors.name: Tao Huang
authors.institution: Henan University of Science and Technology

authors.name: Santosh Jha
authors.institution: Council of Scientific and Industrial Research

papers.title: Beliefs in feedback: Factored representations of interacting agents in transformers
papers.abstract: Complex systems, from ecosystems to brains, are usually modeled as modular components coupled through feedback rather than as indivisible wholes. Can a transformer trained on the joint behavior of a group of interacting agents be understood in the same way? In this work, we develop a computational-mechanics framework to study agents interacting in feedback loops. We formally prove that any joint stochastic process can be presented as resulting from the behavior of agents interacting in feedback, and the resulting process is generated by a hidden Markov model whose Bayesian beliefs factorize into separate components per agent. Furthermore, our experiments show that transformers trained on such feedback sequences make use of this separability, disentangling the beliefs about the underlying factors into separate subspaces of their residual stream. This representation is found to scale linearly (instead of exponentially) with the number of agents. Moreover, interventions show that these representations are causally efficacious, allowing for targeted steering of individual agents' beliefs by selectively inserting counterfactuals. However, coarse-graining the behavior is found to disrupt the factorization, and can force a higher-dimensional representation. Together, the results establish both the dimensional advantage of a factorized representation and the ability of transformers to exploit it, laying the groundwork for investigating traces of compositional predictive architecture in pretrained models.

authors.name: David A. Ehrlich
authors.institution: Göttingen Campus Institut für Dynamic biologischer Netzwerke

papers.title: Constructing free subgroups of matrix groups
papers.abstract: The Tits alternative asserts that a finitely generated linear group is either solvable-by-finite or contains a non-abelian free subgroup. Given a non-solvable-by-finite subgroup G of GL(d, F), where F is the field of complex numbers or a non-archimedean local field, we present methods to construct explicitly a non-abelian 2-generator free subgroup of G in specific cases. Our implementations in the computeralgebra system Oscar are publicly available.

authors.name: Emmanuel Breuillard
authors.institution: Mathematical Institute of the Slovak Academy of Sciences

papers.title: Tracking the evolution of sub-Neptunes. I. Gyrochronology of planet hosting stars
papers.abstract:
Stellar age is fundamental for reconstructing planetary-system evolution but remains difficult to determine for unevolved main-sequence stars. Stellar rotation provides a sensitive age diagnostic and a temporal framework for investigating the evolution of close-in planets. This is the first paper in a series aimed at tracing the evolution of the sub-Neptune population through homogeneous ages of their host stars.
  We compiled rotation periods and stellar parameters for 4639 confirmed exoplanet hosts. Gyrochronological ages were inferred using a two-zone rotational evolution model and a Bayesian approach combining rotation periods, dereddened Gaia (BP-RP) colours, and literature stellar masses as Gaussian priors. Rotational tracks were extended to the terminal-age main sequence, beyond the empirical calibration range.
  We obtain gyrochronological constraints for 2204 host stars. Well-constrained ages have typical formal uncertainties of 10--15%, offering substantially greater precision than is generally achievable through isochrone fitting for unevolved stars. Inferred stellar masses agree with the literature priors, while model effective temperatures are consistent with independent determinations. Ages beyond the open-cluster calibration range remain model-dependent.
  The resulting homogeneous catalogue provides the age framework for investigating the evolution of sub-Neptune populations and the emergence of the radius valley. Stellar parameters, provenance, and gyrochronological results are publicly available through CDS.

authors.name: Isabella Pagano
authors.institution: The University of Texas at Austin

authors.name: Federico Spada
authors.institution: Max Planck Institute for Solar System Research

papers.title: TLAPS-Bench: Formally Proving Correctness of Real-World System Specifications with TLA+ Proof System
papers.abstract: TLAPS-Bench is a benchmark and execution harness for constructing machine-checked proofs for real-world system specifications in TLA+ with agentic AI. Proving correctness of complex system specifications requires discovering inductive invariants, reasoning about intricate state transitions, and decomposing proofs into tractable obligations. TLAPS-Bench provides a proof harness that supports iterative proof development atop the TLA+ Proof System (TLAPS), where agents are equipped with proof tools and libraries, with safeguards against reward hacking. Using the harness, we have employed AI agents to prove desired properties for important system specifications that were not proved before, spanning cache coherence, Byzantine consensus, and write-ahead logs. TLAPS-Bench contains 265 proof targets (each encodes a property to prove) from 95 TLA+ specifications of real-world systems. We evaluated frontier AI agents, represented by Codex with GPT models, on a subset of 70 proof targets across 12 specifications. The highest-scoring model, GPT-6.1 Sol (max), proved 31 (44.3%) proof targets. The results show challenges and opportunities in end-to-end proof development.

authors.name: Saad Mohammad Rafid Pial
authors.institution: Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology

authors.institution: Laboratoire Lorrain de Recherche en Informatique et ses Applications
