papers.title: Attribution-based diagnostics for single-cell foundation models
papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA foundation models (scFMs) are increasingly used for in-silico biological discovery, yet predictive performance alone does not reveal whether their decisions rely on biologically meaningful signals or model-specific shortcuts. We systematically investigate post-hoc attribution of downstream predictions across two tasks: cell-type annotation using pretrained Cell2Sentence and scGPT models, and perturbation prediction using scGPT+STATE in a controlled setting. For cell annotation, we use attribution to assess whether predictions rely on established marker genes and how their relevance varies with model architecture, expression rank, and the surrounding cellular context. For perturbation prediction, we compare attribution patterns with known regulatory ground-truth in a synthetic setting to assess what they reveal about the model's learned computations. Across these tasks, attribution reveals biological feature use, contextual interactions, contributions from different input pathways, learning progression, associations with prediction quality, and potential pitfalls that are not fully captured by standard performance metrics. Experiments with complete and limited regulatory knowledge further demonstrate that conclusions drawn from attribution depend strongly on the choice of biological reference, baseline, and null model. Together, these findings highlight the value of attribution as a flexible post-hoc diagnostic for understanding model behavior, identifying potential issues, and informing the development of scFMs.

authors.name: Farnoush Rezaei Jafari
authors.institution: Berlin Institute for the Foundations of Learning and Data

papers.title: k-uniform l-Eulerian hypergraphs
papers.abstract: We consider $l$-Euler trails and $l$-Euler circuits in finite $k$-uniform directed multihypergraphs, where $k\geq 2$ and $1\leq l<k$. Let $D$ be such a directed multihypergraph. The notions of $l$-connectivity and $l$-balance are defined in terms of the $l$-tails and $l$-heads of its hyperarcs. It is shown that $D$ is $l$-Eulerian if and only if $D$ is $l$-connected and $l$-balanced. Moreover, $D$ is $l$-semi-Eulerian if and only if $D$ is $l$-connected and has exactly two states with unequal $l$-indegrees and $l$-outdegrees, one with $l$-outdegree one greater than its $l$-indegree and the other with $l$-indegree one greater than its $l$-outdegree. The proofs are based on an $l$-transition digraph and the classical Euler theorem for directed multigraphs. The corresponding conditions for $k$-uniform multihypergraphs are also obtained in terms of their orientations. For a given orientation, an expected linear-time algorithm is provided to determine whether an $l$-Euler trail or an $l$-Euler circuit exists and to construct one when it does.

papers.title: Diagonal Equivalence in State Space Models: Characterization, Retrieval Rank, and Selective Extensions
papers.abstract: We classify real and complex state-space models (SSMs) with linear transitions, distinguishing fixed-basis diagonal equivalence from input-output equivalence and tracking coefficient-conditioning windows under coordinate changes. We characterize diagonal equivalence through commuting transition families whose members are diagonalizable over the chosen field. With time-shared token-local matrix maps, we identify this class's state-mediated kernels with unnormalized scalar-mode linear attention with multiplicative masks. Mamba 3's multiple-input, multiple-output (MIMO) construction lifts one value per local interface; SSD-MIMO routes independent values for local retrieval rank above one. HybridMamba combines Mamba 1's per-coordinate decay, Mamba 2-style heads and Mamba 3's complex rotations and two-endpoint writes, mixing real and rotating state blocks with different decay laws. They recover Mamba 1-3 single-input, single-output (SISO) configurations as exact special cases. On five large H100 bfloat16 workloads, our fused GPU kernels improve geometric-mean training time over official Mamba 1/3 in matched SISO recoveries, with Mamba 2 near parity at SSM-core scope. Memory tradeoffs depend on the baseline and metric: saved-for-backward versus peak allocation. In small-model multi-token recall experiments, both designs outperform Mamba 1-3 on the hardest tier; higher routing ranks perform best in gated or phase-diverse configurations. In single-seed language models with about 500M parameters, both improve on Mamba 1/2 in test loss at 2B tokens, but the routing gains do not translate into lower language-model loss. Our best configurations approach Mamba 3 SISO through 10B tokens while remaining behind it and Mamba 3 MIMO in language-model loss.

papers.title: Extreme Hard X-ray Variability in the TeV Blazar Mrk 421: Insights from NuSTAR Observations
papers.abstract: In this work, we investigate the hard X-ray variability of the TeV blazar Mrk 421 over both long-term and intra-day timescales to gain insights into the particle acceleration and cooling mechanisms driving its emission. Using 27 NuSTAR observations spanning 2012 to 2024, we conduct detailed spectral and timing analyses. Our findings reveal pronounced flux variability, with changes by up to a factor of 200 over the decade and a 10-fold increase within a period of 15 days during a flaring episode. The flux distribution exhibits a lognormal profile, and a linear root-mean-square (RMS)--flux relation suggests a multiplicative variability process. Spectral analysis indicates that a log-parabolic model best describes most observations, with a strong linear anti-correlation between the photon index and curvature parameter. We also identify a positive correlation between the synchrotron peak energy and flux, accompanied by a subtle ``harder-when-brighter'' trend. These results align with standard blazar emission models, supporting particle acceleration via shock fronts or magnetic reconnection in the relativistic jet.

papers.title: The Nuclear Dimension of Extensions and Graph $C^*$-Algebras
papers.abstract: We prove that the nuclear dimension of any graph $C^*$-algebra is at most two, and we compute the exact value of the nuclear dimension for a large class of graph $C^*$-algebras. In particular, this class covers all graphs with Condition (K). Our methods --- based on Szab\'o's recent $KK$-uniqueness theorem --- provide a unified approach to computing the nuclear dimension of various extensions. This includes the nuclear dimension of the Toeplitz algebra (first computed by Brake--Winter) and that of the Cuntz--Toeplitz algebras (first computed by Easo et al).

papers.title: Geometrization of Kottwitz-Shelstad transfer and Vogan's conjecture on local Arthur packets
papers.abstract: We give a geometric analogue of Kottwitz-Shelstad transfer for a general class of reductive groups over p-adic fields with cyclic component groups of trivial or prime order. We prove that this geometric transfer coincides with Kottwitz-Shelstad transfer, adapted to the language of disconnected groups, assuming the local Langlands correspondence satisfying certain desiderata, including the Kazhdan-Lusztig hypothesis for the ambient group and its endoscopic groups. As an application of this geometrization, we prove Vogan's conjecture on local Arthur packets over p-adic fields: for quasisplit classical groups and their pure inner forms, all local Arthur packets are ABV-packets, and the distributions attached to these ABV-packets of Arthur type satisfy Arthur's local conjectures on twisted endoscopic character relations. This demonstrates the following general principle: for any reductive group G over a local field, an Arthur packet should be defined as an ABV-packet of Arthur type, equipped with the endoscopic pairing calculated by traces of actions on vanishing cycles or microlocalizations.

papers.title: Aberration stabilized light bullets in normal dispersion injected Kerr resonators
papers.abstract: We investigate three-dimensional light bullets (LBs) in an optically injected, vertically emitting Kerr-Gires-Tournois interferometer operating in the normal dispersion regime. In the uniform field limit, the dynamics is governed by a generalized Lugiato-Lefever equation with third-order dispersion, paraxial diffraction, and fourth-order diffraction, stemming from lens and mirror aberrations close to the self-imaging condition. Using direct numerical simulations, we show that without aberration only transversely drifting, tilted multi-peak localized states (LSs) are stable in two dimensions, whereas no stable LBs exist in three dimensions. However, a small negative spherical aberration stabilizes a rich multistable family of two-dimensional LSs, including straight and tilted multi-peak LSs, oscillating states, and complex bound states, which persist even for negative paraxial diffraction. We identify an Andronov-Hopf bifurcation followed by a homoclinic transition toward tilted states, accompanied by hysteresis. Finally, we demonstrate that stable straight and tilted LBs exist in three dimensions in the presence of aberration, the latter forming a continuous family parametrized by the transverse tilt direction.

papers.title: The Golden Quadruple: Four Reals Whose Differences Form a Geometric Progression, Rigidity of the Golden Ratio, and a Bohr Almost Periodic Cosine Sum
papers.abstract:
Let $\varphi=(1+\sqrt5)/2$. The four-point set $\{0,\varphi,\varphi^2,\varphi^3\}$ is classical: up to a dilation it consists of the two endpoints and the two crossing points on a side of the regular pentagram (Euclid, Elements XIII.8), and, by the identity $\varphi^2=\varphi+1$, its six pairwise differences are $1,\varphi,\varphi^2,\varphi^3$, with multiplicities $1,2,2,1$. We write this configuration as the golden quadruple $S=(F, F-a, F-b, F-a-b)$, where $u>0$, $a=\varphi u$, $b=\varphi^2u$ and $F>a+b$, and study its extremal and rigidity properties. We prove that it is maximal and unique: no five distinct real numbers have all their positive differences in $\{u,\varphi u,\varphi^2u,\varphi^3u\}$ (indeed, not even in the whole set $\{u\varphi^n:n\in\mathbb{Z}\}$), and every four-element set with this property is a translate of $S$. We prove that the golden ratio is forced: $\varphi$ is the only ratio $x>1$ for which some four-point set of reals has the four-term progression $\{c,cx,cx^2,cx^3\}$ as its set of distinct differences. For the analogous quadruple with base $x>1$, $x
eq\varphi$, the failure is measured by two closure residues, $(x^2-x-1)u$ and $x(x^2-x-1)u$, which along Fibonacci quotients equal $\pm u/F_n^2$ and $\pm F_{n+1}u/F_n^3$. Finally, the cosine sum $C_S(t)=\sum\cos(2\pi d t)$ over the six differences equals $8\cos^2(\pi a t)\cos^2(\pi b t)-2$; it is not periodic, but it is almost periodic in the sense of Bohr, with explicit almost periods $F_n/u$. For an arbitrary scale $K>0$ the golden ladder $
u_n=K\varphi^{-n}$ realises the construction with $u=
u_{203}$, so that the differences are $
u_{200},\dots,
u_{203}$; we evaluate it for $K=\sqrt{c^5/(Gh)}$. We state explicitly what is classical and what is new, in relation to difference sets, Golomb rulers, Sidon sets, Fibonacci numbers, quasicrystals and almost periodic functions.

authors.name: Michał Przybylski
authors.institution: Wrocław University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Competing interaction driven broad magnetic entropy distribution in triangular net compounds \text{Ba$_3$RE(BO$_3$)$_3$}, RE= Dy and Ho
papers.abstract: Triangular magnetic lattices have attracted significant attention as a model platform for exploring frustrated magnetism and quantum spin liquids, particularly in rare-earth-based systems. These materials also hold considerable promise for cryogenic magnetic refrigeration. In this work, we investigate the magnetic and magnetocaloric properties of the rare-earth (RE) based compounds $\text{Ba}_3\text{RE}(\text{BO}_3)_3$ ($\text{RE} = \text{Dy}$ and $\text{Ho}$). Polycrystalline samples synthesized via a solid-state reaction method crystallize in a hexagonal structure with the space group $P6_3mc$, featuring triangular nets separated by approximately $8.8~\text{\AA}$ along the $c$-axis. Detailed magnetic investigation reveals a deviation from pure paramagnetic behavior at low temperatures ($T < 20\text{ K}$). This is further corroborated by isothermal magnetization measurements, which exhibit non-overlapping $M$ vs. $H/T$ plots and reduced magnetization moments, suggesting significant crystal electric field (CEF) splitting of localized $f$-states. For an applied magnetic field change of $70\text{ kOe}$, the maximum entropy change (Relative Cooling Power) reaches $4.2\text{ J kg}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$ ($204\text{ J kg}^{-1}$) and $7.3\text{ J kg}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$ ($230\text{ J kg}^{-1}$) for the Dy- and Ho-based compounds, respectively. Overall, the positive slopes of Arrott plots, the universal scaling behaviour of $\Delta S_{\text{m}}/\Delta S_{\text{m}}^{\text{max}}$ versus reduced temperature ($t$), and the field exponent $c$ of the RCP versus $H$ curves indicate a second-order nature of entropy distribution, making them promising candidates for magnetocalorics in the millikelvin range.

authors.name: Krishna Nand Prajapati
authors.institution: Indian Institute of Science Education and Research Thiruvananthapuram

authors.name: Prabuddha Kant Mishra
authors.institution: Włodzimierz Trzebiatowski Institute of Low Temperature and Structure Research

papers.title: TopoSteer: Topological Layer Selection for Activation Steering in LLMs
papers.abstract: Activation steering controls large language models at inference time by adding a vector to their internal representations. Most work asks how to build that vector, and far less attention has gone to where to add it, even though steering at a poorly chosen layer can be worse than not steering at all. Prior selectors choose a layer without ever steering the model to test it: they score how separable the target behavior is at that layer, and how consistently the individual examples point along the steering direction. We argue that what matters is not the separability of the two activation clouds, nor the alignment of individual displacements with their mean, but the extent of the cloud of per-example displacements that mean-difference steering averages. We propose a topology-based layer selection method, called TopoSteer, which scores a layer by the total H_0 persistence of its displacement cloud, computed as the length of the cloud's Euclidean minimum spanning tree. We show that the score focuses on the displacement cloud's relative geometry, while class separation affects it only through standardization. We also provide a theoretical explanation for our method by proving that, as example-level variation increases, TopoSteer and discriminability move in opposite directions, so the two criteria can rank layers in opposite ways. Across multiple language models and steering tasks, TopoSteer provides a principled alternative to discriminability- and separability-based layer selection and yields more effective steering without requiring held-out validation.

papers.title: Piezogyration and elastogyration in ternary chalcopyrites from first principles
papers.abstract: Natural optical activity arises from the spatial dispersion of the optical response and is described by the rank-two gyration pseudotensor. Its dependence on mechanical stress and strain, quantified by the piezogyration and elastogyration tensors, respectively, has been investigated experimentally for decades. However, a systematic first-principles description of these effects remains largely unexplored. Here we present a first-principles methodology to compute the full piezogyration and elastogyration tensors, and apply it to a set of representative ternary chalcopyrite crystals. The gyration of the unstrained crystal turns out to be a poor predictor of the magnitude of the elastogyration response, which we find to be a property inherited from their parent zinc-blende structures. The elastic compliance tensor further shapes the piezogyration response, with particularly pronounced effects in AgGaS$_2$, a well-known achiral yet optically active crystal. Finally, we explore strain-induced chirality through the trace of the gyration tensor, the only pseudoscalar contribution to the natural optical activity that is linear in the tensor components and encodes information about chirality.

authors.name: Asier Zabalo
authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

papers.title: Characterizing landslide dynamics from time-lapse time domain induced polarization and ground-based imaging: a case study of the MontGombert landslide (French, Alps)
papers.abstract: Electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) is widely used to investigate landslide morphology and dynamics. Landslide behavior is strongly influenced by clay content, pore pressure, and the spatial distribution of permeability. However, conventional direct current (DC) resistivity methods have limited capacity to characterize permeability, as materials with low electrical resistivity may exhibit either high or low permeability depending on their clay content and the relative contributions of surface and electrolytic conduction. Induced polarization (IP) offers a valuable complementary approach for investigating the petrophysical properties of geological materials. Despite its potential, IP has been rarely applied to landslide studies and has not yet been widely used for landslide monitoring. This study investigates the added value of IP measurements alongside conventional DC resistivity for landslide characterization and monitoring. Three time-domain induced polarization (TDIP) surveys were conducted at different time steps on an active landslide in the French Alps. Time-lapse inversions of resistivity and chargeability were performed, and spectral IP parameters were derived using Debye decomposition. The results were then compared with surface displacement estimates obtained from optical image processing. The findings demonstrate that TDIP is particularly valuable for delineating unstable volumes within the landslide. The geophysical results show strong agreement with independent measurements from piezometers and inclinometers. Furthermore, applying an empirical relationship between IP parameters and permeability enables the spatial distribution of permeability within the landslide to be estimated, as well as its seasonal variations. Overall, this study highlights the potential of combining IP and DC resistivity measurements to improve the characterization of landslide properties and support the monitoring of their temporal evolution.

authors.name: Pierre Bottelin
authors.institution: Institut des Sciences de la Terre

papers.title: Damage Assessment of Supporting Pillars in an Underground Cave Using Joint Inversion of Electrical Resistivity and P-wave Velocity, Burgundy (France)
papers.abstract: This study presents an integrated approach combining seismic refraction tomography and electrical resistivity tomography to evaluate the structural integrity of supporting pillars in an underground cave in Burgundy, France. A three-phase petrophysical joint inversion (P-JIv) was performed using a finite-element model on an unstructured triangular mesh. Compared with independent inversions, the joint inversion improved spatial resolution and enhanced the consistency between the two geophysical methods. The results revealed distinct zones of electrical resistivity and P-wave velocity, reflecting variations in rock fracturing and weathering. The geophysical interpretations showed strong agreement with visual inspections and borehole logs. Furthermore, rock porosity and water content were estimated from the P-JIv results. Finally, an automated clustering procedure was used to establish a proxy indicator of pillar integrity, enabling the prioritization of cave reinforcement measures.

authors.name: P. Bottelin
authors.institution: Institut des Sciences de la Terre

papers.title: Queering the Audits: Community-Based Auditing of AI Harms to Queer Communities
papers.abstract: AI systems embed majority-group defaults into training data, evaluation metrics, and category definitions, producing documented harms for queer communities including erasure, misclassification, and discrimination. Standard technical audits often rely on aggregate measures and cannot detect harms that be come visible only through the lived experience of affected communities. We conducted a participatory auditing workshop at EurIPS 2025 where 16 queer community members audited four case studies using the 4Cs harm taxonomy (Content, Conduct, Contact, Contract) applied across the AI lifecycle. Participants used structured worksheets and plenary synthesis to classify harms and trace them to their origins in the development pipeline. Across all four cases, participants traced harms to problem definition and data collection, and they identified contractual structures that extract value from vulnerable populations while providing minimal recourse. These findings illustrate that community-informed auditing surfaces concrete, identity-specific harms that aggregate evaluation methods risk overlooking.

papers.title: TRAILS: Trajectory Generation for Automated Indoor Locomotion Studies
papers.abstract: Virtual reality experiments involving navigation and simulated robot motion often require large, realistic environments and numerous distinct trajectories to avoid repetitive navigation while providing sufficient variation for controlled experiments. Designing such scenarios manually is labor-intensive, particularly when trajectories must satisfy predefined geometric and kinematic constraints while remaining diverse and comparable across experimental conditions. This paper presents TRAILS, an automated framework for generating complete virtual navigation scenarios consisting of an environment layout, a path, and a time-parameterized motion profile. The framework combines a constraint-based procedural environment generator inspired by Wave Function Collapse, trajectory generation using optimized cubic B\'ezier curves, and speed-profile generation subject to kinematic constraints. The generated scenarios provide diverse indoor environments with corridors, open spaces, and obstacles, together with trajectories of identical duration that vary in path geometry, wall proximity, and velocity profiles while minimizing systematic dependencies between these characteristics. The framework is designed as an easy-to-use tool requiring only a small number of intuitive user-defined parameters to automatically generate large sets of distinct navigation scenarios satisfying prescribed geometric and kinematic constraints. By relying on explicit, seed-controlled algorithmic procedures rather than data-driven models, the generated scenarios remain transparent, reproducible, and configurable, making the framework well suited for telepresence and human-subject experiments. The code is available at https://github.com/JucciK/Trails .

papers.title: Internal friction and frequency-dependent conductivity in the bivariate site energy model for the mixed alkali effect in glasses
papers.abstract: The mixed alkali effect is fundamental to understanding ion transport in glasses. It manifests itself in strong changes of various ionic transport properties when one type of ion is successively replaced by another type. Recently, we have developed a new theory of thermally activated hopping in bivariate random site energy landscapes that takes into account site occupation statistics according to generalized Fermi distributions and mixture kinetics in accordance with linear irreversible thermodynamics. The theory was successfully applied to predict the behavior of partial conductivities and their activation energies at low frequencies corresponding to the dc limit. Here we show that the theory is capable to capture the salient features of the mixed alkali effect observed in ac ion conductivities and in the peculiar behavior of the internal friction.

papers.title: What makes a theorem interesting? Operationalizing interestingness for open-ended exploration
papers.abstract: An agent that explores, whether it generates conjectures or research ideas, must decide which of them are worth keeping. This judgment of interestingness is usually delegated to a hand-picked proxy or to a language model, neither of which is known to correspond to what humans actually value. I study it for mathematical theorems, by observing which results mathematicians single out in formal libraries and in papers. I model each way of singling out results as an evaluator that weights features of a result's statement, its proof and dependencies, and split its weights into a shared and a subjective part. In formalized mathematics, ex-ante features predict these selections as well as a large language-model judge, and the two complement each other. Interestingness is also largely shared. One set of weights, carried mostly by structural features such as the length of the statement and of the proof and the subfields the proof draws on, accounts for most of the signal and transfers in part across formal libraries. What remains subjective depends on practices and individual authors more than on subfields. The judge's advantage lies in its knowledge of the canon, and neither the judge nor the features rely on memory of the papers. The approach, which infers what a community finds interesting from what it singles out, can be applied to other sciences.

papers.title: Electromagnetic Information Theory for Programmable Metasurfaces
papers.abstract: Programmable metasurfaces enable fine-grained control of electromagnetic waves and are creating new opportunities for information extraction, information transfer and information processing. Yet, despite exciting experimental demonstrations, their fundamental capabilities remain poorly understood. In this Perspective, we argue that programmable metasurfaces, and programmable wave systems more generally, call for an electromagnetic information theory that addresses limits at two levels, in a unified manner across applications like communications, sensing and computing. First, for a given physical platform, such a theory should bound achievable information manipulations, such as sensing precision, information-transfer rates, and computational performance. Second, at a more fundamental level, it should determine what non-programmable and programmable physical resources bound these system-specific limits, and what minimum resources are required to attain a prescribed level of performance. We discuss emerging theoretical approaches to these questions, and their connection to experimentally realizable systems. We examine how device thickness, programmable degrees of freedom, nonlocality, coupling and multiple scattering constrain these limits. Establishing the envisioned framework could clarify the ultimate capabilities of programmable metasurfaces and guide the design of future wave-based information systems.

authors.name: Philipp del Hougne
authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

papers.title: Chain on Demand: Deferred Evidence Organization for Long-Term Conversational Memory
papers.abstract: Long-term conversational memory faces a timing mismatch: write-time summaries and graphs organize history before a future query is known, while independent retrieval can allocate a limited evidence budget to redundant or fragmented turns. We introduce Chain on Demand (CoD), a query-time evidence organization framework over an unchanged turn-level memory. Given a broad candidate pool, CoD constructs a temporary evidence chain by allocating a fixed anchor budget according to query relevance, lexical diversity relative to selected anchors, and newly covered query terms, followed by deterministic restoration of each selected anchor's same-session neighborhood. The resulting chain is used only for the current query, while the underlying conversational memory remains unchanged. In a paired comparison over all 1,986 LoCoMo questions, CoD achieves 82.2% accuracy on 1,540 non-adversarial questions and 76.3% on all 1,986 questions. On LongMemEval-S, one fixed configuration that indexes both user and assistant turns obtains 86.6% across all 500 questions. These results show that long-term memory can preserve the original conversation while deferring evidence organization until the information need is known.

authors.name: Di Lu
authors.institution: Changchun University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Tail persistence of extremes at finite and asymptotic levels with Bayesian hierarchical inference
papers.abstract: Tail persistence characterizes the relative escalation of observations beyond an extreme threshold and complements conventional summaries such as return levels and tail indices. Existing literature is mainly distribution-based and does not account for uncertainty, nonstationarity, or covariate effects. We develop a Bayesian framework for modeling tail persistence under generalized extreme value and generalized Pareto models. We first make explicit the connection between tail persistence and the extreme value index under regular variation, which identifies the asymptotic persistence with $1/(1-\xi)$ and links persistence to tail heaviness. We then derive closed-form expressions for persistence at finite quantile levels under both models and show that, for any location--scale extreme value family with a common shape parameter, finite-level persistence depends on the location and scale parameters only through their ratio. Motivated by these results and by the weak identifiability of observation-specific shape parameters, we formulate a Bayesian hierarchical extreme value model in which the shape parameter is constant over time, while the location and scale parameters vary with covariates and latent effects. The asymptotic persistence is then a single, well-identified quantity, whereas finite-level persistence evolves over time through the location--scale structure. The framework provides posterior inference for both quantities, with credible intervals and probabilistic assessment of temporal evolution and covariate effects. Through simulation studies and real-data applications, we show that persistence provides an interpretable characterization of the escalation of extremes beyond high thresholds, complementing classical extreme value summaries with comprehensive uncertainty quantification in nonstationary settings. The methodology is implemented in an open-source \texttt{R} package.

papers.title: Cultural Evolution Drives the Emergence of Conventions in Neural Emergent Communication
papers.abstract: Recent studies of language evolution with neural agents often use models where agents can either speak or listen, where there are only two agents in the population, or where agents can share internal representations. These choices prevent the study of how language emerges through cultural evolution, i.e. through the cumulative adaptation of individual behaviours to fit the communicative needs of the community. We tackle this issue with a new model that trains populations of bi-directional neural agents in a fully distributed fashion to solve a referential game. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach on multiple image datasets and show that it is able to scale to large populations. We also show that more conventional languages are easier to learn, providing a direct advantage for cultural transmission. Overall, this work provides a novel approach to neural emergent communication that opens up new directions for evolutionary linguistics.

papers.title: First-principles calculations of far-wing absorption in He-broadened CO2 infrared spectra
papers.abstract: We report theoretical predictions and modeling of the far-wing absorption of CO2 broadened by He over a wide temperature range (200-1000 K), which are relevant for exoplanet atmosphere studies. Accurate modeling of He-broadened CO2 absorption is essential for opacity calculations used to characterize the composition, structure, and climate of exoplanet atmospheres. In particular, the strong CO2 band at 4.3 mum has been clearly identified in the spectra of several exoplanets observed with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). Requantized classical molecular dynamics simulations were first performed to predict absorption in the far wings of the 4.3 mum band of CO2. The resulting predictions show excellent agreement with available experimental data at room temperature. The theoretical predictions and measured data were then used to parameterize an impact energy-corrected sudden model, which allowed us to accurately reproduce the far-wing absorption of He-broadened CO2 in several infrared spectral regions over the (200-1000) K temperature range. Finally, for applications to exoplanet atmosphere opacity calculations, we derived temperature-dependent chi-factor corrections that account for the sub-Lorentzian behavior of the far wing of the major infrared bands of CO2.

papers.title: SNAPPerf: Software-Aware Tabular Foundation Model for Retraining-Free Performance Prediction of Configurable Systems
papers.abstract:
Modern software systems expose hundreds of configuration options whose combinations can substantially affect execution time, memory and energy usage. Measuring software performance resulting from a configuration set requires running a realistic workload. Since the configuration space grows exponentially, exhaustive benchmarking is infeasible. Prior work therefore trains models on a small set of measured configurations to predict the performance of the rest. Yet these models are specific to a particular software version, hardware platform, and workload, so changes require new measurements and retraining, and such changes are becoming more frequent with coding agents.
  We challenge this per-system training assumption with SNAPPERF (Software-aware, No-retraining, Adaptive Prediction), a sample-efficient tabular foundation model specialized for configurable software. SNAPPERF is pretrained once on synthetic data. Each new update only requires a few measured configurations as context to predict the rest without any per-system training or hyperparameter tuning. Across 39,866 configurations from 12 real-world systems, spanning 6 domains and 4 performance metrics, SNAPPERF reduces prediction error by 38% over the prior state of the art at the same measurement budget, and by 25% over the best general-purpose tabular foundation model. It matches the state of the art's accuracy with 54% fewer measurements on average. These results suggest that knowledge about software can be encoded in pretraining data rather than in per-system models, opening a new research direction in software-aware pretraining.

authors.name: Vadim Okun
authors.institution: National Institute of Standards and Technology

papers.title: The colors of protoplanetary disks - Impact of nonspherical dust particles on the polarized and total intensity colors
papers.abstract: Dust properties in protoplanetary disks remain poorly understood despite their central role in planet formation. Recent studies based on analyses of scattered-light images and phase functions provide promising insights into dust characterization, but the phase function alone is insufficient to constrain dust properties. Degeneracies between dust remain a major obstacle to linking observations to realistic dust models. We investigate the behavior of the disk color as a function of dust. We used MCFOST to generate synthetic scattered-light images from the visible to the near-infrared, in total and polarized intensity. We considered compact spherical grains using, irregular particles and compact and fractal aggregates using optical properties from the AggScatVIR database. Disk colors were measured from these images. For aggregates larger than the wavelength, monomer size influences color, whereas aggregate size has little effect, especially at low fractal dimensions. Polarized color is more sensitive to dust properties than total intensity color, because it combines the wavelength dependences of scattered intensity and polarization degree. Effective medium theory is reliable only for compact aggregates with small monomers, becoming inaccurate for highly porous aggregates or larger monomers. Effective albedo helps predict disk colors, but radiative transfer is needed to account for multiple scattering. For HD 100546, red optical-to-near-infrared colors exclude compact grains and organic-rich compositions but are consistent with amorphous-carbon aggregates, compact or fractal, containing large monomers. These results show that combining color measurements with polarized scattering phase functions offers a promising way to break degeneracies between dust models. Applying this approach to larger disk samples could better constrain dust properties and evolution.

authors.name: Ryo Tazaki
authors.institution: Institut de Planétologie et d'Astrophysique de Grenoble

papers.title: GSLM2: Multi-Stream Speech Representation Learning and Generative Spoken Language Modeling
papers.abstract: Generative spoken language models (SLMs) offer a route to learning linguistic structure purely from speech, yet they lag far behind text-based models in both capability and data scaling efficiency. We identify two bottlenecks underlying this gap: the limited linguistic quality of existing speech units and the reliance on a single stream of discrete units to represent speech. Multiple codebooks are widely used to encode acoustic features but rarely to represent speech semantics. We present GSLM2, which learns and models complementary properties of speech at multiple levels of abstraction. Its encoder, SpidR 2.0, uses self-supervised learning with differentiable prediction heads to induce high-quality discrete units at multiple levels. A multi-stream SLM then jointly models these units using a shared temporal backbone, stream-specific predictors, and an autoregressive head that captures cross-stream dependencies. Across training data sizes and model scales, up to 6M hours and 6.5B parameters, GSLM2 consistently improves linguistic competence while scaling more efficiently with data. As a result, it substantially narrows the gap between spoken and text-based LMs; across read and conversational speech domains, we shrink the gap by about two orders of magnitude on sWuggy, sBLIMP, and tSC, while also outperforming competitive speech-text systems on all three tasks. We open-source the training code and model checkpoints at https://github.com/facebookresearch/gslm2.

authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

authors.name: Mahi Luthra

papers.title: Coulomb Blockade in a One-Dimensional Array of Strong Josephson Junctions
papers.abstract: We measure current across a voltage-biased, long array of Josephson junctions. Current-voltage characteristics do not reveal any critical current and instead display the presence of threshold voltage and finite activation energy, consistent with the Coulomb blockade. However, the respective energy scale is well below the value prescribed by a single-island geometric capacitances. We explain it by strong quantum fluctuations of charge associated with a large value of Josephson energy, $E_J\gg E_C$, where $E_C$ is the charging energy associated with the inter-island capacitance. Comparison between the data and theory points to an exponential (in parameter $E_J/E_C$) suppression of the threshold. We achieve a quantitative agreement with theory by accounting for charge-$e$ solitons associated with the quasiparticles entering the array from its leads. This scenario however underestimates the current below threshold in comparison with the experiment.

papers.title: Original Insights Into Rock Slope Damage Processes Until Collapse From Passive Seismic Monitoring
papers.abstract: We conducted passive seismic monitoring of the unstable La Praz rock slope (approximately 14,000 m${}^3$) in the French Alps over a period of more than 10 years. During the six months preceding collapse, we observed a pronounced 24% decrease in the slope's fundamental resonance frequency ((f\_0)), indicating a reduction in the overall stiffness of the rock mass. Joint analysis of (f\_0) variations and slope deformation revealed alternating phases dominated by sudden brittle damage and more ductile behavior, potentially involving sliding. Seismic monitoring identified damage processes that were either ambiguous or undetectable through surface deformation measurements alone, while also highlighting critical periods of intensified damage. Although some of these periods coincided with identifiable external triggers, such as intense rainfall events, others could not be clearly linked to external forcing. These findings demonstrate the potential of passive seismic monitoring to provide insights into the internal structural condition of unstable rock slopes at depth. Combining surface deformation measurements with seismic tracking of rock mass stiffness could therefore improve the identification and characterization of active slopes undergoing progressive damage, contributing to the development of more effective slope monitoring systems.

papers.title: Mapping rockfall hazard and detecting precursory damage in rock slopes with passive seismic: Lessons from the La Praz case-study
papers.abstract: Repeated passive seismic surveys were conducted over more than a decade on the unstable La Praz rock slope in Savoie, France, which involved an estimated rock volume of approximately 13,000--15,000 m${}^3$. The final survey took place two months before the complete collapse of the slope in August 2023. The amplitude of the Horizontal-to-Vertical Spectral Ratio at the peak frequency (*aHVSR(fp)*) was used to distinguish stable and unstable areas and identify fractures associated with significant mechanical decoupling. Rock compartments were also classified according to their rockfall hazard. The compartments most susceptible to failure exhibited the highest *aHVSR(fp)* values, ranging from 26 to 157, compared with values of 7.5--19 in intermediate-hazard areas and 2.7 in the adjacent stable rock mass. The main HVSR peak frequency (*fp*) exhibited distinct decreases of 15%, 14%, and 11% in three unstable rock compartments before the collapse. These reductions substantially exceeded the range of environmentally induced resonance-frequency fluctuations observed at the site and commonly reported in the literature as a limitation of this method. The frequency decreases were interpreted as indicators of progressive damage extending into the rock slope. Notably, these changes were detected exclusively in the three compartments identified as the most susceptible to failure, which also exhibited the highest *aHVSR(fp)* values. This study demonstrates, for the first time, the potential of passive seismic monitoring to reveal progressive in-depth damage within a complex, heterogeneous, and highly fractured rock slope. The findings highlight the value of combining HVSR amplitude and peak-frequency variations to characterize unstable rock compartments and identify potential precursors to catastrophic slope failure.

papers.title: Quadratic Reconfiguration of Plane Spanning Paths on Two-Layer Point Sets
papers.abstract: Consider a crossing-free polygonal path with $n$ vertices and a flip operation that removes an edge and adds another one, without changing the vertex set and keeping the path crossing free. It is conjectured that any two such paths can be transformed into each other by a sequence of flips. Recently, Kleist et al. (2024) proved the conjecture for the special cases of vertices arranged in two convex layers. However, the number of flips in their proof may be exponential. In this paper, we show that $O(n^2)$ flips suffice. More precisely, for a two-layer point set $S=L_0\cup L_1$, where $L_0$ and $L_1$ denote the outer and inner layers, respectively, our method uses $O(|L_0|+|L_1|^2)$ flips.

papers.title: Autotuning GPU Thread Block Sizes for Large-Scale Stencil Applications Using the OPS DSL
papers.abstract: Large-scale structured-mesh stencil applications can run for hours or days on modern HPC GPU platforms, making launch-configuration choices important. OPS enables high-level stencil codes to target multiple GPU architectures, but its GPU backends rely on a default or user-selected global block/workgroup shape, even though different kernels, problem geometries, and architectures may favor different configurations. This paper presents a transparent per-kernel block/workgroup-shape autotuning extension for OPS. The extension explores valid block/workgroup shapes during execution, records the fastest configuration for each kernel, and enables precomputed replay of the selected configurations in subsequent runs. We evaluate the approach on structured-mesh proxy and academic research applications, covering 459 unique kernels across 3 NVIDIA and 2 AMD GPUs. The evaluation reports speedup distributions, representative wall-time summaries, timing variability, and input problem shape effects. Replaying the best per-kernel launch shapes improves 923 of 995 measured application/input/GPU cases over the default OPS shape. Depending on the GPU, the median speedup ranges from 1.02x to 1.18x, with individual configurations of LAPL2D, TTI3D, and OpenSBLI-based TGV solvers exceeding 1.5x. The results also show that performance sensitivity is not limited to launch shape. At fixed cell count, changing the input problem shape changes precomputed-replay runtime by 0.8-34.6% in representative cases, while kernel-level timing variability depends on the interaction between runtime contribution, input problem shape, and GPU/backend behavior. Overall, automatic per-kernel block/workgroup-shape selection improves OPS performance across GPUs, provided shape sensitivity and timing stability are interpreted together.

papers.title: Conjectures of Bernstein and Erd\H{o}s for weighted Lagrange interpolation with Hermite weight
papers.abstract:
The classical Bernstein and Erd\H{o}s Conjectures for algebraic Lagrange interpolation on a finite interval were settled in two consecutive papers by Kilgore and by de Boor and Pinkus in 1978. Extending these results to weighted interpolation on unbounded intervals has proved to be more difficult.
  In a previous work, we established the Bernstein and Erd\H os Conjectures, together with the ``modified'' de Boor--Pinkus intertwining theorem, for weighted Lagrange interpolation on the half-line with exponential weights. Here we continue this line of research by considering the Hermite weight on the whole real line. Our main result is the Hermite-weighted analogue of the Bernstein and Erd\H{o}s conjectures together with the appropriate version of the de Boor--Pinkus intertwining theorem.
  A key ingredient in the classical proofs is the nonsingularity of certain derivative matrices associated with the local maxima of the Lebesgue function. This property already breaks down in the exponentially weighted setting, although the resulting difficulties can still be resolved. In the Hermite-weighted setting, however, the situation becomes more intricate, requiring a substantial refinement of the previous approach.

papers.title: Scute: Exact Batched Serving for PEFT Adapters Beyond LoRA
papers.abstract: Existing serving systems for large language models batch requests for many different LoRA adapters on one GPU. However, these systems reject adapters from other parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods such as DoRA, (IA), VeRA and OFT. One solution to this is to convert these adapters to LoRA, but this induces a significant memory and accuracy cost. Instead, we show that, under some modifications, a batched LoRA kernel can serve all of these methods exactly and efficiently. We achieve this by writing each method in one normal form, a LoRA computation with six slots for an adapter's own vectors and matrices. Some slots can merge into an adapter's weights at load time; the others remain live and induce a cost. We give ways to efficiently pay this cost and predict it from a zero-parameter byte model. We package this system, Scute, and build it on top of vLLM. Scute serves all five methods, coming as checkpoints from the Hugging Face PEFT library, in one batch, and it matches that library with a mean error of at most 1.5% of each adapter's effect. Under a burst of requests on an RTX A6000, a mix of these methods takes 5-17% more decode time than the same number of LoRA adapters. Furthermore, using Scute, the same GPU can serve 64 to 1024 (IA) and VeRA adapters at 1.5x to at least 2.5x the request rate of their LoRA conversions.

papers.title: NAS-PO: Native Attention-Strategy Policy Optimization for Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become an effective post-training paradigm for vision-language models (VLMs). Standard RLVR, however, assigns identical outcome-derived credit to all generated tokens regardless of their perceptual relevance. Recent perception-aware methods estimate visual reliance through image perturbation or masking. These indirect proxies require perturbation branches, while corruption sensitivity does not necessarily identify the visual evidence used for reasoning. We instead shape model perception through native attention, an intrinsic model signal. Rather than treating attention as a post-hoc explanation, we formulate it as a reward-anchored, token-aligned routing signal that encourages attention patterns supporting visually grounded reasoning. To this end, we propose NAS-PO, a Native Attention-Strategy Policy Optimization framework. NAS-PO analyzes native attention with a visual mass policy that quantifies visual allocation and a conditional visual policy that captures spatial routing over visual tokens, making the optimization well-posed. Based on this, Native Attention-Strategy Advantage Shaping (NAS-AS) draws on the visual-mass policy to redistribute signed policy-gradient credit for visually engaged rollouts. The Adaptive Attention-Coupled (AAC) loss then aligns the visual-mass policy on all response tokens and the conditional visual policy on visually active ones, consolidating the visual-routing patterns that drive successful trajectories. Experiments demonstrate that NAS-PO substantially surpasses leading RL-tuned VLMs across 7 out-of-domain reasoning and perception benchmarks, with its effectiveness consistently validated across 8B and 32B. Visual-Routing Sensitivity (VRS) analysis further indicates that the optimized attention prioritizes visually load-bearing regions.

papers.title: Exploiting Textual Semantics for Robust Cross-View Object Correspondence
papers.abstract: Cross-view object correspondence (CVOC) aims to establish associations of the same target between query and search videos captured from different viewpoints. Existing methods often rely on visual cues for CVOC. Despite recent progress, these methods struggle in complicated scenarios with substantial viewpoint changes and appearance variations, due to lacking sufficient target information. Addressing this, we introduce TeSCo, a framework that exploits rich Textual Semantics of an object, in addition to its visual cues, for cross-view object Correspondence. Our key insight is, textual description of a target, by capturing diverse attributes such as category, texture, and color, provides viewpoint- and appearance-invariant semantics, which are complementary to visual cues and can hence enhance correspondence robustness in complicated scenes. Inspired by this, TeSCo first generates a textual expression of the target from the given query view using a vision-language model, and then extracts textual feature to enhance visual features for localization in the search view. To realize this, we introduce a text-conditioned cross-modal fusion (TCF) module that incorporates the textual feature into visual features with text-guided modulation, producing more robust multimodal target representation for object correspondence. Since not all textual cues are equally compatible with the target in current search-view frame, we propose an iterative textual feature refinement (ITFR) module that progressively adjusts textual feature using search-view information before the TCF module, enabling search-view-aware textual semantics to be fused into visual features and leading to better performance. In extensive experiments on Ego-Exo4D and HANDAL-X, TeSCo demonstrates state-of-the-art results and largely outperforms other models, validating its efficacy. Our code is released at https://github.com/VAIL-Fan/TeSCo.

papers.title: Keep on growing or change direction? Dependence of clonal plant survival on the probability of side-branching
papers.abstract: In clonal organisms, the genetic individual (genet) may consist of several physiological individuals (ramets). Clonal plants typically grow horizontally by means of stolons or other clonal growth organs. Some species grow linearly for several ramet generations, while others produce side branches frequently. We hypothesize that the probability of side-branching ($b$) affects genet survival ($G$) depending on the ramets' ratio of birth to death rates ($\lambda$). We used a spatially explicit model of ramet population dynamics to compare three growth strategies. In the neutral case, growing forward and side-branching were equally probable, whereas forward-growing and side-branching plants had lower and higher $b$, respectively. We found that the genet's survival threshold (the critical $\lambda_c$) strongly depended on the branching probability. The lowest threshold, and hence the broadest range of survival, occurred in moderately forward-growing plants, in which the average length of linear (non-branching) intervals was $1.89$ units. Above the threshold, the $G(b)$ relationship strongly depended on $\lambda$. Genet survival was promoted by forward growth in sparse ramet populations (low $\lambda$). However, this advantage gradually disappeared as $\lambda$ increased, and branching probability became effectively neutral across a broad parameter range encompassing both forward-growing and side-branching plants. This suggests strong selection for low branching intensity in unfavorable habitats, but weak or negligible selection in favorable habitats.

papers.title: Solar Wind Turbulence Spectra and Correlation Scale from 4 to 50 $r_\odot$: STEREO and PUNCH Observations
papers.abstract: We investigate the radial evolution of solar wind turbulence using remote-sensing brightness observations from the Solar Terrestrial Relations Observatory (STEREO) and the first science-ready images from the Polarimeter to Unify the Corona and Heliosphere (PUNCH) mission. Exploiting the combined wide fields of view of STEREO's COR2 coronagraph (4-9 r_sun) and PUNCH's Wide Field Imager (WFI, 21-50 r_sun), we track the radial evolution of the power spectral density and correlation scale of density fluctuations from 4 to 50 r_sun. Line-of-sight integration systematically steepens the "usual" turbulence scaling laws by a constant offset of about -0.5 across all resolved scales, so that the energy-containing range (nominally k^-1) and the inertial range (nominally k^-5/3) appear as k^-1.5 and k^-2.1, respectively -- consistent with previous synthetic-image simulations. The correlation scale increases with heliocentric distance across the full range of heliodistances probed, in accordance with previous theoretical models and observations at closer distances from the Sun.

papers.title: On Landau's "local method" for obtaining zero-free regions
papers.abstract: We extend Landau's local analytic method for the deduction of zero-free region to a very general setting, and as a particular consequence, obtain a zero-free region and corresponding Prime Number Theorem for Beurling number systems with well-behaved integers. We also discuss the sharpness of the method and prove estimates for the local number of zeros, as well as a clustering result, which roughly put says that zeros close to the 1-line cannot be isolated but must occur in clusters.

papers.title: $\mathsf{RCA}_0$ Proves the Collapse of the Intersection Principles Hierarchy
papers.abstract: This paper shows that the pairwise intersection principle ($2\mathrm{IP}$) implies, over $\mathsf{RCA}_0$, the existence of a Cohen $1$-generic real relative to every given set. Together with the known implications, this yields the equivalence over $\mathsf{RCA}_0$ of the finite intersection principle (FIP), $2\mathrm{IP}$, and $1$-GEN. In fact, FIP is equivalent to $n\mathrm{IP}$ for every fixed $n\geq 2$. These results give affirmative answers to Questions~1 and~2 of Cholak, Downey, and Igusa, and to Question~9.10.26 of Dzhafarov and Mummert. The proof uses cumulative, nested supports satisfying a finite Helly property and a decoding argument based on a least selected label. Neither $\Sigma^0_2$ induction nor $\Sigma^0_2$ bounding is required.

papers.title: 1-Genericity Is Not Weihrauch Reducible to the Finite Intersection Principle
papers.abstract: This paper shows that the problem of producing a Cohen $1$-generic real relative to a given oracle is not Weihrauch reducible to the finite intersection principle (FIP). More strongly, no nontrivial computable FIP instance admits a single Turing functional that produces an absolute $1$-generic real from every enumeration of every maximal centered set of indices. The argument combines a $1$-generic real that computes no perfect tree all of whose paths are $1$-generic with local constancy and a parametrization of maximal centered sets. This answers Question~9.10.25 of Dzhafarov and Mummert.

papers.title: Biunital Lie Semiheaps and Lie Triple Systems
papers.abstract: We examine the differential geometry of Lie semiheaps that admit biunital elements. Open Ol'shanskii semigroups, which appear widely across causal geometry and harmonic analysis, provide a large class of examples. It is shown that the subset of biunits is a smoothly embedded Lie subheap. Moreover, there is a canonical Lie triple algebroid associated with any proper biunital Lie semiheap. That is, there is a vector bundle over the manifold of biunits that comes equipped with a ternary bracket that satisfies the axioms of a Lie triple system together with a compatible `higher' anchor map. Although every Lie triple algebroid associated with a proper biunital Lie semiheap is trivialisable, it is not canonically so, unlike the case of the tangent bundle of a Lie group. As concrete examples, we examine the Lie semiheap of real $n\times n$ matrices, and the conformal causal Lie semiheap associated with the Lie group $\mathrm{SU}(2,2)$, which is a double cover of the conformal group of Minkowski spacetime, and the future-directed light cone.

papers.title: Ewald summation of doubly periodic 2- and 3-dimensional Stokes multipoles
papers.abstract: In spite of the qualitative differences between Stokes flows in 2 and 3 dimensions, most particle-resolved computational studies of microswimmers and other colloidal systems dominated by low-Re hydrodynamic interactions are carried out in triply periodic geometries, while the corresponding continuum descriptions are frequently solved in 2-dimensional doubly periodic domains. Furthermore, most experimental examples of biological and synthetic microswimmers are realised in confined, quasi-2-dimensional geometries with a finite thickness in one of the three dimensions. To enable studying the non-trivial differences between these system geometries, in this paper we systematically derive Ewald representations for periodic Stokes force multipoles in geometries with two periodic directions, treating both three-dimensional Stokes flow with one unbounded coordinate and intrinsically two-dimensional singularities. Starting from the periodic Stokeslet, we obtain explicit expressions for force dipoles and quadrupoles and analyse the non-trivial zero-wavevector contribution arising under partial periodicity. The analytical expressions are independently validated by comparing with results from an explicit lattice Boltzmann solver in each geometry.

papers.title: Robust Remote ECG Monitoring under Energy Constraints: Anomaly Filtering versus Predictive Uncertainty
papers.abstract: Machine learning for remote electrocardiogram monitoring must handle noise and diseases absent from training under tight resource constraints. We investigate whether upstream unsupervised anomaly detection can improve monitoring decisions more efficiently than classifier-derived uncertainty. We evaluate five detectors on PTB-XL and BUT QDB and compare a two-stage filter-classifier system with Monte Carlo Dropout and deep ensembles under unseen-disease and noise conditions. Performance is averaged over five training seeds. We measure single-pass energy, latency, and graph memory on a microcontroller's central processing unit (CPU) and neural processing unit (NPU). Per-score neural network costs account for repeated evaluations but exclude scoring outside deployed graphs. Energy equations relate filtering and rejection to avoided classifier execution. Across four disease scenarios, Deep Support Vector Data Description (Deep SVDD) achieves the highest mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve within all tested finite CPU energy budgets. On the NPU, it leads at 1 mJ, while Monte Carlo Dropout has slightly higher means at 10 and 100 mJ. With a narrow CPU classifier, the Deep SVDD two-stage system increases the fraction of correctly classified or correctly rejected inputs by 15.0-19.4 percentage points over classification without rejection. Estimated energy per input is 1.93-6.99 mJ, compared with 52.53 mJ for Monte Carlo Dropout and 8.76-17.51 mJ for deep ensembles, at each method's retrospectively selected test accuracy peak. These results support upstream filtering for efficient remote monitoring, while independent validation and complete-system measurements remain necessary.

papers.title: Controlling the Sign and Magnitude of the Thermoreflectance Coefficient of Gold-MoS$_2$ Metamaterials
papers.abstract: Heating a material changes how much light it reflects. This effect, quantified by the thermoreflectance coefficient $C_\mathrm{TR}$, enables temperature sensing, while it is a nuisance for situations where constant reflection is crucial. Whereas temperature detection requires a large $C_\mathrm{TR}$, the latter situation demands it to be as close to zero as possible. Controlling the $C_\mathrm{TR}$ has so far relied on the selection of materials and wavelengths, rather than engineering the coefficient itself. This work demonstrates that the $C_\mathrm{TR}$ of a 50 nm thin gold film on SiO$_2$/Si can be controlled in sign and magnitude by an ultrathin ($<$8 nm) MoS$_2$ film underneath it. Time-resolved thermoreflectance measurements reveal suppression, sign inversion, and revival of the thermoreflectance signal, controlled by three knobs: ($i$) the buried MoS$_2$ thickness, ($ii$) probe wavelength, and ($iii$) ambient temperature. Transfer-matrix simulations using temperature-dependent dielectric functions of gold and MoS$_2$ reproduce all experimental observations, demonstrating an optothermal metamaterial platform with controllable properties. In particular, these (anti-)thermoreflective metamaterial mirrors bring $C_\mathrm{TR}$ under the same interference design rules previously applied to the optical response itself, opening ways to maximize or minimize the temperature dependence of the optical reflectance, tailored to the specific application.

papers.title: Uncertainty-Aware 3D Position Reconstruction in CZT Drift-Strip Detectors
papers.abstract: Accurate three-dimensional interaction-position reconstruction is important for CZT drift-strip detectors, but conventional methods can suffer from degraded performance in challenging detector regions, while learned models provide limited information about prediction reliability. We investigate two uncertainty-aware approaches: deep ensembles of point-estimation networks and simulation-based inference (SBI), which estimates a posterior distribution over interaction position. Both approaches are trained on physics-based simulations and evaluated on both synthetic and experimental data. On synthetic data, uncertainty from both methods correlates with positioning error, with SBI showing a substantially stronger relationship. On experimental measurements, the deep ensemble achieves improved $z$-position resolution, while SBI provides more informative uncertainty estimates that highlight regions of reduced positional information and discrepancies between simulation and the physical detector. These results demonstrate the complementary strengths of ensemble-based reconstruction and posterior inference for uncertainty-aware detector position reconstruction.

papers.title: PRISM: RL-Based Rate Control for Low Latency and High Data Rate in Mobile Edge Networks
papers.abstract: Emerging delay-sensitive interactive services, such as extended reality and remote operation, demand advanced congestion control algorithms (CCAs) capable of maintaining high data rates while keeping latency low in mobile networks. Existing CCAs typically rely on congestion signals such as packet loss, delay, or explicit congestion notification (ECN) marks, which can be delayed, imprecise, or require extensive upgrades to the network infrastructure. To address these limitations, physical resource block (PRB) utilization has recently been proposed as a reliable early congestion signal in mobile networks [1]. This paper introduces PRISM, a reinforcement-learning-based CCA that uses peak PRB utilization to regulate the send rate under challenging mobility and fading conditions. NS3 simulation results show that, in a mobility scenario where two PRISM flows coexist with two TCP Cubic flows and one TCP BBR flow, PRISM maintains a per-packet mean one-way delay (OWD) of 6.3ms and a $p_{99}$ OWD of 44.6ms, with negligible (0.02%) packet loss, over a 20min high-contention interval. However, over the same interval, the coexisting TCP flows experience 60x higher mean OWDs of 371-390ms and $p_{99}$ OWDs of 563-578ms, with 0.1% packet loss. PRISM achieves a 31x improvement in goodput-over-latency performance, indicating a favorable tradeoff for delay-sensitive applications.

papers.title: QueueTrack: Framework for Detecting the Onset of Queueing in Mobile Networks
papers.abstract: In mobile networks, timely and accurate detection of the onset of queueing at path bottlenecks remains challenging for end-to-end congestion control algorithms (CCAs), where end hosts have limited visibility into queue status. Traditional congestion signals, such as packet loss, round-trip time (RTT), and one-way delay (OWD), have well-known limitations for early queue buildup detection. This paper presents QueueTrack, a practical end-host framework to detect the onset of queueing in mobile networks. QueueTrack computes a queue buildup indicator, denoted QBI, from endpoint-observable packet-level timing statistics, without requiring tight synchronization between end hosts or modifications to the existing network infrastructure. We develop and assess the complete QueueTrack machine learning (ML) pipeline, including data collection, labeling, model training, and testing, on a 5G testbed built on the OpenAirInterface platform, under a range of scenarios with competing TCP traffic. The experimental results show that QueueTrack can reliably detect the onset of queueing at the 5G base station using low-complexity classification models such as logistic regression. For example, QueueTrack achieves an F1 score of approximately 80% in a challenging mixed TCP/UDP scenario. These findings confirm that QueueTrack can serve as a practical framework for developing CCAs that target low delay, as well as for network telemetry and network monitoring in mobile networks.

papers.title: Evaluating autonomous self-healing against persistent cyber-attacks
papers.abstract: The need for autonomous cyber resilience (ACR) is strongly accelerating. The boost in cyber capabilities of advanced AI is speeding up the attacker-defender rat race to an unprecedented pace. As a result, the field of ACR must progress from early design and experimentation to hands-on evaluation and deployment. To illustrate what is needed for this transition, we put TNO's autonomous immune system-inspired Self-Healing for Cyber Security (SH4CS) software to the test. Our analytic and experimental evaluation results demonstrate that effective cyber resilience is achieved with SH4CS for (repeated) web application vulnerability exploits. Remaining challenges of SH4CS revolve around finding the right balance between predictable resilient behaviour, and adaptiveness to the large variety of cyber threats and applications-to-be-protected.
