papers.title: Policy Iteration over Terminal Cost Functions: From LQR to MPC
papers.abstract: Policy iteration is a classical method for successively improving control policies in optimal control and reinforcement learning. In this paper, we propose a policy iteration framework that refines receding-horizon control (RHC) and model predictive control (MPC) policies online by iteratively updating the terminal cost. We first develop the framework for the linear quadratic regulator (LQR) problem. We show that the Riccati map is a contraction in the Thompson metric on an explicitly constructed invariant order interval. Using this property, we prove convergence of approximate policy iteration for finite-horizon RHC, where the terminal cost is given by an approximate value function. From an initial terminal cost, we then construct a robust invariant order interval within which the RHC policy is refined online. We extend the analysis to constrained MPC and present a constructive algorithm for safely updating the terminal ingredients, which guarantees recursive feasibility and asymptotic stability of the closed loop throughout the iterations. These results connect classical Riccati theory with approximate policy iteration and provide a principled pathway toward learning MPC terminal ingredients. A numerical example illustrates the proposed method.

papers.title: IAMRAGBENCH: Benchmarking Authorization Expansions in LLM-Generated AWS IAM Policies under RAG Poisoning
papers.abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can synthesize Amazon Web Services (AWS) Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies from tasks and operational documents. Attacker-controlled context may induce provider-valid policies that exceed trusted authorization requirements. We present IAMRAGBENCH, a 60-case benchmark spanning scope, conditions, explicit denies, trust, permissions boundaries, and role delegation. It combines deterministic authorization-envelope scoring with case-specific validation, including request-level checks where supported. An attack requires a provider-valid clean policy that satisfies the task and a provider-valid treatment policy that violates the envelope, matches a predeclared goal, preserves an intended request, and newly authorizes a forbidden request.
  Across five endpoints, included-context exposure produces 49 exact authorization deltas, including 46 goal-matched attacks (46/292; 15.75\%). End-to-end BM25 over 720 documents retrieves the designated poison for all 60 tasks at \(k=5\) but produces 7/294 goal-matched attacks (2.38\%). Presenting the same weakening as a final security architecture exception produces 74/116 attacks in a frozen two-endpoint stress test (63.79\%) and 115/294 in a post hoc all-five extension using the same frozen prompts (39.12\%). In a replay of 194 provider-valid treatment policies that violate task requirements, AWS \texttt{CheckNoNewAccess} reports no new access for four of 168 goal-matched exact attacks. The full pre-deployment rule rejects all 171 exact deltas and routes five unresolved cases to review. These findings support treating IAM copilots as untrusted proposal generators whose outputs require independent authorization checks before deployment.

papers.title: Online Class Posteriors for Interpretable and Controllable Discrete Diffusion
papers.abstract: Discrete diffusion models remain far less understood than their continuous counterparts, despite recent breakthroughs across modalities, most notably in text. Leveraging tools from continuous diffusion, we formulate a theoretical framework to track the class-conditional posterior in an online manner by combining conditional and unconditional model predictions. In masked language modeling, this posterior offers highly interpretable dynamics: tokens aligned with a class boost the posterior, while contradictory ones suppress it. We also show that the posterior can be used for logical guidance operations (AND, OR, NOT) in discrete diffusion. These operations enable precise control over generation, such as avoiding specific classes. In addition, we discuss a mismatch in the formulation of classifier-free guidance between discrete and continuous settings: discrete models mix the data distributions, while continuous models mix the marginals. We validate our methods and discuss their potential applications on synthetic data, with all quantities analytically tractable, as well as on MNIST, text, and antibody sequences.

papers.title: Jet-QSparse: Accelerating Agentic LLM Inference with 4-Bit Sparse Attention
papers.abstract: Long-horizon reasoning and agentic workloads strain KV-cache capacity and decode attention throughput. We present Jet-QSparse, a training-free method that combines compact NVFP4 cache storage with native FP4 query-key computation on Blackwell tensor cores. A dense scan scores the full key history and selects 128-token blocks for sparse FP16 value aggregation with FP32 accumulation, preserving higher precision in the output-forming step while enabling contiguous tile loads. Calibrated key centering and at most two BF16 pages per sequence and layer address quantization error; FP8 prefill uses a temporary arena while the persistent cache is packed directly from BF16 activations. Across four hybrid LLMs, a budget of 128 blocks per KV head shows no detected accuracy loss on the evaluated mathematical reasoning, coding, and agentic benchmarks, although some smaller budgets incur losses. With 64 blocks, Qwen3.8-27B achieves a $1.94\times$ end-to-end decode speedup over dense BF16 at 128K context and batch size 16 on one GB300, and the measured Qwen KV pools provide $2.58$-$2.76\times$ BF16's token capacity.

authors.name: Shuo Yang
authors.institution: Kunming University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Spontaneous Geometric Structures in 2D MHD Flows
papers.abstract: Under suitable spatial decay assumptions on the initial data, we establish precise asymptotic expansions of the velocity and magnetic fields for two-dimensional incompressible MHD flows at each positive time. We identify in the far-field profile the hexagonal pattern previously discovered for the 2D Navier-Stokes equations by L. Brandolese \cite{Bra22}, characterized by six equally spaced directions of faster decay for each component of $u(x,t)-u_0(x)$. Surprisingly, the corresponding contribution to the magnetic field vanishes identically, owing to an exact cancellation associated with the antisymmetric structure of the magnetic nonlinearity. Thus, at order $|x|^{-3}$, the hexagonal structure appears only in the velocity field.

papers.title: The effect of local stacking fault fluctuations on dislocation glide and the interplay with solid solution strengthening in Al-Mg alloys
papers.abstract: Concentrated alloys are characterized by a random arrangement of solute atoms of different sizes, which generates spatially fluctuating displacement and stress fields with non-trivial correlations. This chemical disorder also induces local fluctuations in stacking-fault (SF) energies, giving rise to fluctuating SF forces acting on the partial dislocations bounding the SF. In this work, we investigate the characteristics of the SF noise, including spatial correlations and the impact of such SF energy fluctuations on dislocation glide. Specifically, the gliding behavior of screw, edge, and mixed dislocations in a model concentrated Al-Mg random alloy with varying Mg content is analyzed. The interplay between SF energy fluctuations and solid-solution noise is also discussed. We show that SF forces are spatially correlated, in close analogy with long-range elastic stresses, and exhibit a robust negative correlation along the slip direction. We identify the physical origin of these correlations and demonstrate that they significantly contribute to the critical resolved shear stress for dislocations to glide. In contrast, correlations in other directions are weaker but can still be non-negligible, depending on the underlying interatomic interactions.

papers.title: GeoGuesser Bench: Benchmarking Vision-Language Agents on Interactive Geolocation
papers.abstract: Vision-language model (VLM) agents that act in the open world need two abilities: world knowledge to interpret what they see, and exploration to find what they cannot yet see. We study how agents combine the two through interactive visual geolocation. GeoGuesser Bench contains 282 tasks in an offline Street View environment where agents rotate, zoom, and move between real panoramas. Its three task types shift the balance from knowledge to exploration: agents (1) report the coordinates of their starting location, (2) name the enclosing street, city, state, or country, or (3) find, read, and count nearby objects. The coordinate tasks in (1) also include 42 real GeoGuessr World Championship rounds, whose expert guesses provide a human reference. We evaluate 23 VLMs: the best accuracy is 62.5% on place naming and 35.0% on object finding, and the best agent averages 4352.4 GeoGuessr points on the championship rounds, against 4770.3 for the better expert in each round. Beyond these headline numbers, world knowledge and exploration are only weakly correlated across models: agents that localize well do not necessarily explore well. To understand where agents fail, we categorize their errors into vision, navigation, and tool-use failures. Further ablations show that the strongest agents, such as Claude Opus 4.8, still perform well with limited views, while weaker agents degrade; customizing the environment thus adjusts task difficulty. The environment's verifiable rewards and restorable state also support training, and our Planner-Worker-Compressor harness cuts planner tokens by 57-61% by compacting the interaction history. We hope GeoGuesser Bench and its environment serve as a high-quality foundation for simulating real-world exploration at scale.

papers.title: Rose: Efficient Embodied RL through Graph Optimization and GPU Compute Resource Control
papers.abstract:
Embodied reinforcement learning (RL) coordinates policy inference, simulation, and model training with highly heterogeneous resource demands. Although individual components frequently underutilize GPU compute during execution, existing systems only overlap work at coarse component boundaries (e.g., pipelining inference and simulation across simulator groups), leaving substantial low-activity GPU windows within subcomponent phases and nested loops. Exploiting these fine-grained windows manually requires tedious dependency analysis and workload-specific coordination. Furthermore, even when independent work is scheduled concurrently, cross-process GPU time slicing and streaming multiprocessor (SM) contention can negate the benefits of overlap.
  We present Rose, a runtime-aware system that automates fine-grained overlap and GPU resource management for embodied RL while preserving synchronous training semantics. Through a lightweight programmable interface that exposes execution hierarchy and state accesses, Rose tracks runtime data readiness and GPU activity to perform a two-stage optimization. First, a window-guided graph optimizer identifies low-activity windows and applies graph transformations to overlap complementary work across components and loop levels. Second, leveraging NVIDIA Multi-Process Service (MPS) for cross-process GPU concurrency, a slack-aware resource manager tunes process-level SM quotas by exploiting branch synchronization slack to mitigate interference on the critical path. Both stages combine local profiling with end-to-end iteration validation to guarantee throughput gains with minimal tuning overhead. Across diverse policies, simulators, RL algorithms, and GPU platforms, Rose achieves 1.20--1.92$\times$ training throughput improvement and increases average SM activity by 23.8--39.3\% compared with the state-of-the-art systems.

papers.title: The Siegel-Shidlovskii Method Revisited
papers.abstract: We revisit the classical Siegel-Shidlovskii method in transcendental number theory from a new perspective, in which functional relations play a central role. Within a single self-contained framework, we recover the foundational results in the theory of E-functions, including the Siegel-Shidlovskii theorem, Beukers' lifting theorem, and Andr{\'e}'s theorem on the singularities of the minimal differential operator annihilating an E-function. Notably, the latter is obtained without any recourse to the theory of Gfunctions. This unified approach also allows us to resolve a problem posed by Shidlovskii: we obtain a general algebraic independence measure extending the classical Siegel-Lang measure to an arbitrary algebraically independent family of E-values. We also provide a short elementary proof of a second theorem of Andr{\'e}, which has become an important tool in the theory of Efunctions and concerns the primality of the specialization, at a regular point, of the ideal of functional relations of a vector of E-functions satisfying a differential system.

authors.name: Colin Faverjon
authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

papers.title: Classification Aggregation with Multiple Memberships
papers.abstract: People face the problem of classifying objects into categories while aggregating their opinions. We axiomatically study such a classification aggregation problem with multiple memberships, meaning that each individual assigns one category to every object, whereas the resulting classification may assign more than one category. Under the natural settings and axioms (i.e., Independence and Supportiveness), each of our new axioms -- Responsibility, Split Stability and Rejection Stability -- characterises what we call the junta rules. The rules assign a category to an object exactly when some member of a fixed coalition does so. The coalitions that can secure an assignment form a grill, a topological structure implied by an ultrafilter. Hence, the study parallels the literature on Arrow's theorem characterised by the decisive coalition structures. An infinite population setting is also investigated to clarify the differences among the axioms.

papers.title: Ananas: A Networked Audio System for Distributed Spatial Audio Applications
papers.abstract: Spatial audio has an accessibility problem. Largescale spatial and immersive audio installations remain costly and exclusive, with high barriers to entry. We propose ''Ananas,'' a networked audio system consisting of network protocols, control software and microcontroller firmware, with the aim of rendering spatial audio applications accessible to a broad cohort of potential users. Based on a network of low-cost microcontroller development boards programmed in the Faust programming language, synchronised to nanosecond order via IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol, and controlled by approachable, digital audio workstation-based tooling, Ananas represents an opportunity to disrupt and democratise the spatial audio landscape. In this paper we demonstrate Ananas's protocols for audio and control data transmission and device discovery, its methods for media clock and presentation time recovery, and its applications to wave field synthesis and higher order ambisonics in a modular, scalable form.

papers.title: Phase-locked beam splitting with continuously tunable intensity ratio using stochastic phase masks
papers.abstract: We introduce a common-path beam splitter based on a randomly partitioned phase mask displayed on a spatial light modulator (SLM). The SLM aperture is divided into square patches, each randomly assigned to one of three phase ramps that steer light to three independent foci: two phase-locked beams and a dump that takes up the surplus power. We observe the beams in the focal plane of a lens. The fractions of patches assigned to each ramp set the focal intensities, with the focus positions controlled by the ramp slopes.We first demonstrate experimentally that the intensity ratio between the two foci can be tuned from 0 to 1 without distorting either of the spatial modes, and with their relative phase constant to within a few tens of mrad. We then derive a closed-form expression for the ensemble-averaged focal intensity, which decomposes into coherent foci of the desired pattern and a speckle background whose shape and amplitude are set by the patch size. The model is validated against experiment and against numerical Fraunhofer propagation, with quantitative agreement over about three orders of magnitude in intensity. We also identify the patch size as the central design parameter and characterize its experimental bounds.

papers.title: InSARFlow: Riemannian Flow Matching for Interferometric SAR
papers.abstract: Interferometric synthetic aperture radar (InSAR) enables the analysis of topological changes in natural sites or urban areas. This technique operates by recovering the surface displacement from the study of the phase difference (interferogram) between two or multiple SAR images of the same scene at different times. In practice, the use of phase denoising algorithms is necessary to extract relevant information from the interferograms, which motivated numerous developments in the past decade. Due to the inherent periodicity of phases, interferograms can naturally be represented as points on a Riemannian manifold (specifically, the flat torus). This strong prior knowledge motivates the design of learning-based methods that respect the interferogram's intrinsic geometric constraints. Building on this observation, this paper introduces InSARFlow: a generative modeling framework for the denoising and generation of interferograms. Unlike conventional deep learning approaches formulated in Euclidean spaces, which may violate phase periodicity and produce invalid estimates, this method leverages Riemannian flow matching to learn distributional transports directly on the torus. The interest of this approach is demonstrated on two use cases: (1) realistic interferogram generation, in which we model the transport between uniform noise on the torus to real-world interferograms; (2) interferogram denoising, where InSARFlow transports noisy interferograms to their denoised counterparts. Extensive experiments on a controlled synthetic dataset validate the effectiveness of InSARFlow for interferogram denoising. The proposed approach consistently outperforms studied baselines, highlighting the benefits of geometry-aware learning on the torus. Code and weights available at https://github.com/lebellig/insarflow.

authors.name: Arnaud Breloy

papers.title: Free energy of the Hopfield model
papers.abstract: We identify the limit of the free energy of the Hopfield model with independent symmetric Bernoulli patterns, for every temperature and loading ratio. A Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation reduces the problem to that of identifying the limit free energy of a bipartite spin glass with $\pm 1$ and spherical spins. One key difficulty is that the patterns, which become the coupling coefficients in the bipartite model, are Bernoulli instead of Gaussian, and the limit free energy is sensitive to the law of these coefficients. We show that the model is in fact equivalent to one involving Gaussian patterns and also subject to a finite number of Bernoulli random fields. We then solve this model by adapting the techniques recently introduced to identify the limit free energies of spin glasses with either $\pm 1$ or spherical spins.

papers.title: Muography Simulations for Carbon Capture and Storage Monitoring
papers.abstract: Muography can monitor CO2 storage through reservoir density changes, but site-scale simulations are costly: reservoirs can be deep and borehole detectors are small. We address both with two approaches. First, a two-stage workflow splits the kilometer-scale simulation: a fast code transports muons through the overburden, and a general-purpose Monte Carlo code through the reservoir and detectors. Second, a geometric filter at the source keeps only muons whose direction and position let them reach the detectors, within a margin for multiple scattering, and a range cut removes those with too little energy. Both are available in the UCMuon simulation suite for muon generation, filtering and transport. At a deep (800-1000 m) and a shallow (65 m) CO2 storage site, each approach reduces the computing time about 700-fold, and the filtered simulation gives the same hit rate as a full one, as long as the margin exceeds the muons' sideways scattering drift.

papers.title: On the representability of actions of algebras with several bilinear multiplications
papers.abstract: We study the representability of actions in varieties of algebras with $n \geq 1$ not necessarily associative bilinear multiplications. We first prove that, for homogeneous varieties, action accessibility is equivalent to being an Orzech category of interest. For an action accessible, operadic variety we then construct the external weak actor $\mathcal{E}(X)$ of an algebra $X$, an algebra with $n$ bilinear partial operations together with a natural monomorphism encoding the actions on $X$. We characterise the algebras admitting an actor in terms of $\mathcal{E}(X)$, and we deduce an obstruction to action representability: if, for some algebra $X$ with trivial multiplications, $\mathcal{E}(X)$ does not satisfy a multilinear identity of the variety, then the variety is not action representable. Computing the external weak actor explicitly, we obtain that associative and matching dialgebras are weakly action representable but not action representable, and that Poisson algebras, left-right non-commutative Poisson algebras and matching Lie algebras are not action representable. Finally, we introduce the reduced type $(p,q)$ of such a variety and prove that, over a field of characteristic different from $2$, an operadic variety of reduced type $(p,0)$, $(0,q)$ or $(1,1)$ is action representable if and only if it is term equivalent to the variety of Lie algebras or to that of abelian algebras. For the reduced types $(p,0)$ and $(0,q)$, the arguments require no assumption on the cardinality of the field, whereas the case $(1,1)$ requires the field to be infinite.

papers.title: Normalizers in the category of topological groups
papers.abstract: We show that the category of morphisms of topological groups admits split extension classifiers and hence the category of topological groups admits normalizers. We give explicit descriptions of both normalizers and of split extension classifiers of morphisms of topological groups in terms of split extension classifiers of topological groups.

papers.title: DBI Softens Stiff-Phase Gravitational-Wave Spectra
papers.abstract: We investigate the effect of non-canonical kinetic terms on the present-day density spectrum of primordial gravitational waves (GWs), by considering the dynamics of a scalar field governed by the Dirac--Born--Infeld (DBI) action and a runaway potential. The field, responsible for a period of inflation, subsequently enters a kinetically dominated regime, where the DBI structure reduces the equation-of-state parameter relative to the canonical kination result $w=1$, thereby softening the blue tilt of the GW spectrum. Simultaneously, the energy density of the field redshifts at a slower rate, delaying radiation domination and prolonging the stiff phase. The interplay between these two effects can lead to a potentially observable GW signal that would otherwise remain beyond the reach of future experiments in the canonical case. We test our predictions by numerically solving the background and perturbations, from inflation until radiation domination, and find viable parameter space compatible with cosmic microwave background and Big Bang Nucleosynthesis constraints.

papers.title: Lattice Green's functions for Poisson problems with two unbounded and one periodic direction
papers.abstract: Fourier-based Poisson solvers treat periodic directions spectrally and unbounded ones by the Hockney--Eastwood convolution with a free-space kernel. With two unbounded and one periodic direction, the setting of vortex tubes, wakes and jets, the kernel used so far by these solvers combines the two-dimensional kernel on the zero periodic mode with the symbol of the operator sampled on the doubled grid on every other mode. We show that the second ingredient is not exact: the error is the field of the periodic images of the source and independent of the mesh size. While the period $L_z$ is not much longer than the unbounded extent $L_x$, it is of order $\exp(-2\pi d/L_z)$, with $d$ the distance to the nearest image; beyond, it grows like $(L_z/L_x)^2$. The error is thus small on cubic domains, but larger than the solution itself on elongated ones. We remove the approximation by extending the integral representation of the exact second-order kernel of Hou and Colonius: the screened kernel of each mode is evaluated in closed form along one unbounded direction and by Gauss--Legendre quadrature along the other, for the high-order dimension-split and Mehrstellen stencils, at a one-off cost of about one solve. The kernels, implemented in the open-source library \flups{}, are verified by comparison with independent quadratures, by a padding test sensitive to the boundary condition enforced, and by convergence at the order of each stencil on an axially modulated tube source, on domains up to $64$ times longer than wide and up to $2.7\times10^{11}$ unknowns.

papers.title: Reinforcement Twinning via Twin-Calibrated Bayesian Policy Search and Replay-Driven Identification
papers.abstract: The feasibility of updating and synchronising digital twins of actuated systems from operational data depends strongly on how the system is controlled and, consequently, on the data generated during operation. This establishes a direct link between control actuation and model identifiability. This work presents a reinforcement-twinning framework that exploits this link through three computational components. A Gaussian-process surrogate of the physical return combines the twin prediction, used as a calibrated trend, with a discrepancy learned from measured returns, allowing Bayesian policy search to exploit the twin without being tied to its predictions. Candidate policies are proposed around the policy that is optimal for the twin, while measured returns can expand this region. The resulting physical episodes are replayed on the twin after observer-based synchronisation with sparse measurements, and its parameters are identified by combining Bayesian optimisation with gradient-based refinement. Selected information-oriented episodes deploy an excitation policy to improve parameter identifiability. The framework is demonstrated on a Burgers-flow analogue of dynamic-induction control in wind farms, with a deliberately misspecified model structure. Despite substantially biased return predictions, the twin provides a useful starting policy and search region, placing the guided search ahead of unguided Bayesian optimisation from its first physical evaluations. This advantage is maintained when the search region is allowed to expand in response to changes in measured returns, whereas searches over-constrained by the twin-defined region are eventually overtaken by the unguided alternatives. The results support reinforcement twinning as a framework for jointly adapting models and control policies when physical interaction is limited and model discrepancy cannot be neglected.

papers.title: Universality of monomial square forms
papers.abstract:
A monomial square form is a polynomial $F=\sum_{i=1}^k M_i^2$, where $M_1,\ldots,M_k$ are pairwise distinct squarefree monomials $\ne1$. We consider the problem of which of these forms are universal, i.e.\ represent every positive integer. We consider three classes of such forms:\\ (1) Forms $M_1^2+M_2^2+M_3^2+M_4^2$ ($k=4$),\\ (2) Forms $M_1^2+\ldots +M_5^2$ ($k=5$) in at most 5 variables,\\ (3) Forms where the monomials are products of consecutive variables of a fixed length:\\ $P_{m,d}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{d}(x_ix_{i+1}\cdots x_{i+m-1})^2,$ and its circular version\\ $C_{m,d}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_ix_{i+1}\cdots x_{i+m-1})^2\quad(n=m+d-1,\ x_{i+n}=x_i).$ We classify which of these are universal, possibly universal, or conditionally universal on a conjecture on the form $x^2+4y^2+5z^2$. This ternary form appears repeatedly and seems to play a central role.
  For forms (1), we also show that a form is universal if and only if it represents 14, 15, 29 and 9591 (partially conditional on $x^2+4y^2+5z^2$).

papers.title: Milliarcsecond-scale jet reorientations in GRS 1915+105 pointing towards a warped accretion disc
papers.abstract: The black hole X-ray binary GRS 1915+105 was persistently X-ray bright for over 26 years before entering a prolonged low X-ray flux state in 2018, while remaining bright at radio wavelengths. Multi-wavelength observations suggest this state results from a complex layer of absorbing material of unknown nature. Radio jet observations provide an unobstructed view of the physical changes during this phase, and recent Very Large Array and East Asian VLBI Network observations revealed substantial changes in the jet position angle (PA). We use higher-resolution VLBI observations to investigate the connection between the obscuration event and the jet behaviour close to the launch region. We observed GRS 1915+105 with the Very Long Baseline Array and European VLBI Network at four epochs during the early obscuration phase (2019-2021), sampling a diverse range of jet and accretion behaviours. We study the milliarcsecond jet morphology and PA changes and relate these to the reported X-ray behaviour. Many post-2018 PAs are significantly offset from the pre-obscuration jet axis, which has a weighted mean of $142^\circ \pm 7^\circ$ on milliarcsecond scales. We measure a maximum offset of $57^\circ \pm 8^\circ$, the largest reported for GRS 1915+105 to date. Our epochs reveal a variety of jet behaviour, ranging from a stable, compact source with a large PA offset, to a bright, flaring source with a similar offset, to an extended jet with a PA closer to the pre-obscuration axis, and a non-detection. The lack of measurable PA changes within individual 8-hour epochs rules out rapid Lense-Thirring precession of the inner disc as the direct driver of the jet reorientation. Instead, the timescales involved, the system geometry, and the apparent connection to the X-ray obscuration favour a radiation-driven warped accretion disc, a configuration that could naturally explain the persistent obscuration.

authors.name: S. E. Motta
authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

papers.title: Intranight optical monitoring of eight quasars with superluminal jets and low optical polarization: Probing the mechanism of rapid flux variability
papers.abstract: Intranight optical variability (INOV) of blazars whose emission arises predominantly from a relativistic jet, has been widely linked to a combination of two key observational diagnostics: the fractional optical polarization ($P_{opt}$) and the Doppler boost arising from relativistic beaming of the jet's emission. To discern which of these two factors plays the dominant role, we investigate INOV of a well-defined representative sample of 8 flat-spectrum radio quasars (FSRQs, which are `low-synchrotron-peaked' blazars) whose jets exhibit a low degree of polarization ($P_{opt}$ < 3$\%$) but a large superluminal motion with c$\beta_{app}$ = 5c $-$ 31c (median = 10c). We report sensitive optical monitoring of these 8 `low-polarization superluminal quasars' (LPSQs) using a 1.3-metre telescope, in 20 sessions of minimum 3-hour duration. These data were supplemented with similarly high-quality monitoring data/results available in the literature for this sample, thus adding another 19 sessions. Duty cycle (DC) of strong INOV (amplitude $\psi > 5\%$) is found to be zero, applying the normally used $F_{\eta}$ test, and $\sim 7\%$ using the more powerful `enhanced $F$-test'. The small DC, despite the strong Doppler boost expected from the observed high superluminality, shows that strong INOV is much rarer among LPSQs, compared to high-polarization quasars, for which DC $(\psi > 5\%$) is found to be around 30%, even using the $F_{\eta}$ test. This provides the first compelling evidence that optical polarization is the primary diagnostic of INOV, while relativistic beaming plays a supportive role. Possible implications for the proposed mechanisms for INOV are pointed out.

papers.title: VeilFL: Two-Stage Accountability for Anonymous Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Anonymous credentials can hide which registered client participates in federated learning, but their unlinkability also makes repeated misconduct difficult to associate. We present VeilFL, a two-aggregator protocol that adds staged accountability to PINE (USENIX Security '24). Each submission binds two private PINE messages, a round-specific pseudonym, and a tracing pair to the same hidden credential secret. This design enables detection of duplicate submissions within a round without introducing a persistent identifier for normal participation. VeilFL implements accountability in two stages. After a confirmed duplicate or joint PINE rejection, a threshold tracing committee reveals a stable handle that links faults associated with the same credential. The client's registered identity is recoverable only after the public log records the requisite number of linked faults and a separate threshold committee authorizes identification. Accepted and unopened submissions remain unlinkable under the stated assumptions. This work establishes submission binding and duplicate detection, anonymity, fault non-frameability, controlled two-stage opening, and preservation of PINE's privacy and validity guarantees. In the prototype implementation, creating a submission requires a median of 2.11 ms, while verification requires 3.01 ms. Batch verification reduces the cost to 1.86 ms per submission for a batch of 1,000. The public part of each submission is 608 bytes, with 1,248 bytes of additional VeilFL protocol data across the two aggregator submissions. Each opening stage completes within 4.3 ms for the different committee configurations.

papers.title: Alignment Flywheel-Guided Suppression Patching for Interactionless Inverse Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Learned reward models allow reinforcement-learning agents to use demonstrations, implicit feedback, safety constraints, social norms, or other sources that do not provide a complete hand-designed scalar reward. However, a learned reward model can assign high reward to unwanted behavior. A policy can exploit these errors during training. Later requirements can also identify additional regions where the deployed reward should change. We introduce \emph{flywheel-guided patching}, a mechanism for making such localized corrections without retraining the learned evaluator. An Alignment Flywheel identifies overgeneralized or constraint-violating regions and compiles verified findings into suppression patches. We instantiate the mechanism for Interactionless Inverse Reinforcement Learning using MoE-GUIDE, placing patches in the model's latent space and retrieving only a small local subset during online reward evaluation. In the main MuJoCo benchmark, we evaluate patching without expert-state reset warm starts. We also test whether operator-specified norms absent from the demonstrations can be compiled into the same reward interface and compare this with enforcing the corresponding rules online. The results show that localized corrective information can modify an existing learned reward without providing a complete replacement reward. Compilation can reuse judgments that are expensive or unavailable during control. Cheap deterministic rules may be simpler to check directly at each step. Code for MoE-GUIDE, Alignment Flywheel, and flywheel patching is at https://github.com/decide-ugent/Alignment-Flywheel.

papers.title: Origin of bias-voltage-dependent transient negative capacitance in PZT ferroelectric capacitor with labyrinthine-like domains
papers.abstract: We investigated how the bias-voltage-dependent variation in the ferroelectric domain switching pathways affects the transient negative capacitance in multidomain PZT ferroelectric capacitor with labyrinthine-like domains having, primarily, 90$^\circ$ walls. Using the vector piezoresponse force microscopy, x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, and energy dispersive x-ray spectroscopy, we show that, together with strain, local variation in composition results in the formation of labyrinthine domains in epitaxial films of thickness $\sim$1 $\mu$m. Clear signature of emergence of bias-voltage-dependent pathways could be observed in the Raman modes exhibiting splitting due to an intermediate state - different from the initial and final states - at the ``intermediate state of switching". The polarization relaxation patterns also show different states emerging depending on the bias voltage characteristics. The phase-field simulation of relaxation of ``intermediate state of switching" corroborates the experimental results and also exhibits dependence of the domain-wall area on the bias voltage and damping parameter. Combining the results of experiments and theoretical calculation, we show, therefore, that the variation of bias voltage leads to a change in the domain switching pathways and each pathway is associated with specific domain-wall area at the ``intermediate state of switching". Since, the net domain-wall area at the ``intermediate state of switching" governs the magnitude of transient negative capacitance, this work thus traces the origin of tunability of transient negative capacitance in PZT ferroelectric capacitor.

papers.title: Evolving Memory, Learning to Meta-Control: Test-Time Adaptation for Experience-augmented LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Self-evolving agents accumulate experience from task streams, but existing frameworks typically rely on fixed pipelines to retrieve and utilize this experience, neglecting when and how to deploy it. We introduce Online Meta-Control of Experience (OMCE), a framework that updates experience memory and learns a meta-control policy from task feedback during test-time adaptation. OMCE employs a lightweight contextual-bandit meta-controller that uses compact retrieval signals to select among four cognitive actions: DIRECT, EPISODE, GUIDE, and DISTILL. This routing mechanism operationalizes three coupled decisions: whether to invoke experience, which memory format to utilize, and when to consolidate new guidance. OMCE evolves online, leveraging task feedback to update the memory bank and refine the routing policy via contextual bandit updates. Experiments on four online adaptation benchmarks across four backbones show that OMCE improves first-attempt success by up to 20.5 percentage points over the strongest compared baseline, while reducing per-task token use by a factor of 5.7 to 62.5 relative to ACE with GPT-5.2. Controlled ablations further support the benefits of learned routing and continued routing policy adaptation.

authors.name: Peng Yu
authors.institution: Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications

papers.title: ParetoSaddler: Pareto-Guided Optimization of Agent Harnesses for Quality and Cost
papers.abstract: Harness optimization can substantially improve LLM agents without modifying model weights, but existing methods primarily optimize response quality. Extending them to joint quality--cost optimization introduces a challenge: applying the deployment preference during intermediate updates can prematurely reject candidates that are valuable for later improvements. We introduce ParetoSaddler, which addresses this mismatch by separating intermediate candidate promotion from final deployment selection. At each iteration, an optimizer updates a parent harness to produce a candidate, and then compares the two over repeated executions and uses Bayesian bootstrap Pareto support to promote candidates showing credible progress in either quality or cost. Promoted candidates receive broader development evaluation and remain available as parents for later optimization steps. We evaluate ParetoSaddler on ClawMark and GAIA2 using domain-disjoint splits. On ClawMark, ParetoSaddler improves quality from 70.86\% to 81.35\% while reducing cost from \$1.17 to \$1.01 per task; on GAIA2, it improves quality from 56.22\% to 62.89\% while reducing cost from \$0.78 to \$0.45 per task. The Pareto-selected harnesses also achieve higher quality at lower cost than quality-only harness optimization. Analysis shows that Pareto-aware optimization retains intermediate candidates that would be discarded by deployment preference but can support later improvements, while Bayesian bootstrap screening filters out candidates whose gains are weakly supported across runs.

papers.title: Protection challenges and solutions on power systems towards 100% inverter-based resources and energy storage systems
papers.abstract:
The decarbonization of the energy sector, driven by the Paris Agreement and the European Green Deal, is increasing the share of renewable energy sources (RES) in power systems. Unlike traditional systems, RES-based systems rely on power electronic converters, which creates unprecedented challenges for reliability and resilience. The future power system is expected to combine a low-level AC layer with an upper-level High Voltage Direct Current (HVDC) backbone, which requires new understanding of fault protection, stability, and interaction between AC and DC components, as well as new models and simulation tools. This is especially critical in systems moving towards 100 percent converter-based generation.
  Protection systems detect, locate, and isolate faults to protect assets while the rest of the system keeps operating. Traditionally, they rely on the large fault currents supplied by synchronous machines. In modern systems, converter controls limit the fault current contribution to about 120 percent of rated current, so relays that distinguish faults from normal overcurrents based on current level may operate incorrectly. In addition, inverter-based resources (IBR) may not inject enough negative and zero sequence current for directional relays to work properly, and converters hold the voltage at a fixed value only within their reach, beyond which it drops quickly. As a result, existing protection schemes may not provide the expected accuracy and reliability.
  This report reviews the protection challenges identified in recent academic literature for power systems with high shares of converter-based resources. It covers the specific characteristics of RES, the challenges for protection with intelligent electronic devices (IED), the challenges of converter control during faults, and the main solutions proposed in research over the last decade.

authors.name: Ahmar Farooque
authors.institution: Mehran University of Engineering and Technology

papers.title: Randomized Adaptive Sequential Allocation and the Limits of Bounded Exposure to Inferior Treatments
papers.abstract: A clinical trial must learn which treatment is superior while sparing its participants from the inferior one. Kundu et al. 2025 recently showed that a purely deterministic rule, which always assigns the treatment with the larger current sample mean, achieves a strong form of this ethical goal. The smaller allocation count stays almost surely finite and has all moments bounded uniformly in the sample size. Deterministic allocation is, however, predictable, and predictability invites selection bias. We ask whether this bounded-exposure phenomenon survives once the deterministic rule is replaced by a smooth randomized one. We show that it does not. Under any fixed non-degenerate symmetric randomization, both treatments are sampled infinitely often, the adaptive sample means are strongly consistent, and the inferior treatment draws a strictly positive limiting allocation proportion. Consequently, the inferior allocation count grows linearly and its moments are unbounded. We then study annealed randomization, in which the randomization scale cools with the accumulated information, and obtain summability and divergence criteria that separate finite, sublinear, and linear exposure. A forced-exploration variant identifies the superior treatment with probability one while keeping the inferior exposure sublinear, and thereby frees the annealed guarantees from any correct-stabilization event. We also treat normalized multi-treatment rules, ties, indifference zones, unequal variances, general response distributions, and local alternatives. Finally, we develop the post-trial asymptotic inference that each exposure regime permits. The results delineate the trade-off between allocation concealment, persistent exploration, and ethical concentration on the superior treatment.

papers.title: Paying for Fractional Error: Tight Constant-Round Approximation of Covering Problems with Short Broadcasts
papers.abstract:
We present a general framework for deterministic constant-round approximation of covering problems in sparse networks in the broadcast CONGEST model, where every vertex broadcasts the same $O(\log n)$-bit message to all its neighbors. The framework combines two independent tools. The first is a solver that computes a $(1+\delta)$-approximate solution of any local covering linear program with bounded positive integer costs on every class that excludes a fixed minor. The second is a rounding principle: a rounding rule that saves a fixed fraction of its own output, for every feasible input, pays for a solver error fixed in advance, so that an approximate fractional solution yields an exact coefficient.
  For ordinary domination, we achieve a $2a+1$ approximation against the fractional optimum $\gamma_f(G)$ for every fixed rational $a\ge1$, whenever every minor has a ratio of edges to vertices of at most $a$. On planar graphs this is seven, matching the lower bound of Hilke, Lenzen, and Suomela. The coefficients are also optimal at bounded treewidth and pathwidth, for $K_t$-minor-free graphs with $3\le t\le9$, on triangle-free planar graphs (five), and on planar graphs of large girth, where it approaches the optimal three. On every fixed surface the exact bound is $7\gamma(G)$, and we show that a bound of $7\gamma_f(G)$ is impossible on some fixed surfaces even sequentially.
  For total domination, on graphs without isolated vertices and under the same minor-density assumption, the exact coefficient is $2a$ against the fractional optimum, including the optimal six on planar graphs. Red-blue domination, and hence set cover and hitting set on planar incidence graphs, has the optimal limiting coefficient four. Our method also gives randomized constant-round and deterministic $O(\log^* n)$-round $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation schemes, with the randomized cost guarantee holding in expectation.

papers.title: CoworkOS:Scaling Agent Coworkers for Real-world Automation
papers.abstract: Rapid advances in cowork agents are shifting human-AI collaboration toward real-world automation, delivering software, designs, and other artifacts. However, such productivity work demands both high-quality delivery on complex productivity tasks and continued monitoring and decision-making over long horizons, a combination that remains an open challenge. We introduce CoworkOS, a general-purpose harness for long-horizon work that separates task strategy from execution management: the model decides actions, delegation, and acceptance, while the runtime maintains state and feedback. Its three-layer architecture enables direct execution or delegation to Subagents, synchronously or asynchronously, under stable responsibilities. Through a shared application layer, humans and agents inspect and revise the same evolving documents, presentations, CAD models, and Blender scenes, so human-in-the-loop participation can enter both through conversation and through direct modification of the work itself. To sustain continuity across agents and sessions, CoworkOS further introduces hierarchical workspaces and persistent semantic memory, so working files, key decisions, and long-running Job logs remain shareable, reusable, and resumable after interruption. Across 12 benchmarks and 6 categories of real-world applications, CoworkOS proves highly competitive with frontier agent applications such as Codex and DeepSeek Harness. As a sustained-work case study, CoworkOS uses GLM-5.3 as its backbone to conduct RSI-driven automated post-training on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. Over five rounds, the model's average score across eight benchmarks rose from 33.19 to 42.95 (+9.76). Looking ahead, we believe CoworkOS opens a meaningful path toward general cowork-agent intelligence.

papers.title: Refining Roadside 4D Radar Vehicle Classification Using Point-Cloud Dispersion
papers.abstract: Roadside sensing infrastructure is essential for Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS), but cameras and legacy sensors are limited in range, weather robustness, and depth accuracy. 4D radar complements these modalities by resolving range, azimuth, elevation, and radial velocity under adverse conditions, though its sparse, noisy point clouds make reliable classification difficult. We present a roadside multi-sensor platform combining a 4D radar and stereo depth camera under synchronized acquisition, used to collect a real-world dataset. Our analysis reveals a substantial class-distribution discrepancy between modalities, most notably a strong radar confusion between passenger cars and motorcycles (49.01% and\ 48.60% of the dataset). To address this, we propose a Neyman-Pearson-based binary classifier on the temporally-smoothed 2D positional standard deviation of radar point cloud clusters, reducing classification error from 52.1% to 42.7%. This lightweight and edge-deployable approach improves radar-only classification reliability and lays the foundation for future camera-radar fusion.

authors.name: Antonio Almeida
authors.institution: Federal University of São João del-Rei

papers.title: Fisher--Hartwig asymptotics and critical moments for the circular beta ensemble
papers.abstract:
We determine the joint moments of real powers of the absolute value of characteristic polynomials in the circular beta ensemble, for every $\beta>0$. At fixed distinct prescribed points, the Fisher--Hartwig formula holds for every exponent greater than $-1$, with explicit constants and a relative error bounded by a negative power of the matrix size $N$. For approaching points in the same integrable range, the error is bounded by a negative power of $N\delta_N$, provided that $N\delta_N\to\infty$ and the sum of the absolute values of the negative exponents is less than two. Here $\delta_N$ is the minimum distance between the prescribed points; this range includes every integrable pair of root exponents.
  For $q>0$ at the critical relation $pq^2=2\beta$, we prove the Keating--Wong asymptotic for the $p$th moment of the integral of the $q$th absolute power of the characteristic polynomial, for every real $p>1$. The leading asymptotic extends to every complex spatial weight in $L^p$. The proofs combine the recursion for orthogonal polynomials on the unit circle with conditional expectation identities for Gaussian multiplicative chaos and quantitative estimates for approaching singularities.

papers.title: Contrasting Eulerian and Lagrangian organization of turbulent dissipation
papers.abstract: The dissipation of turbulent kinetic energy is conventionally attributed to a scale-invariant spatial multiplicative cascade, with Lagrangian statistics inferred through bridge relations. Direct numerical simulations with tracers reveal instead that Eulerian coarse-grained dissipation has a squared-logarithmic cascade depth and scale-dependent multipliers, whereas time-averaged dissipation along trajectories displays multifractal scaling and an approximately scale-invariant temporal cascade. The classical bridge fails at the level of individual trajectories. Eulerian multipliers nevertheless possess a multifractal organization whose accumulation accounts for the squared-logarithmic spatial statistics. This contrast motivates a material-inheritance picture in which Eulerian dissipation statistics reflect the spatial assembly, deformation, and mixing of distinct Lagrangian histories. The results therefore distinguish the temporal cascade organization revealed along fluid trajectories from the non-stationary spatial refinement observed in the Eulerian frame.

papers.title: A Planar Switching Neuron Shares Logarithmic First-Spike Latency with Its Three-Dimensional Parent But Not Its Onset Mechanism
papers.abstract: Can a reduced neuron model reproduce first-spike latency scaling while changing how a stimulus initiates sustained firing? We compare a piecewise-linear planar Neurosimilator with its three-dimensional parent. Both exhibit logarithmic latency dependence over the investigated input intervals, with different fitted coefficients. The mechanisms differ. In the parent, sustained spiking and a stable resting focus coexist in a spiking--rest bistability regime. An abrupt step accesses spiking, while slow stimulation can retain rest at the same final input. Its step-induced firing threshold is therefore an operational basin-access threshold below the saddle-node limit point, not a loss of equilibrium stability. In the planar model, the resting equilibrium instead reaches a switching boundary while its subthreshold eigenvalues remain negative. We derive the planar latency law from this boundary approach. The model generates repetitive excursions without an imposed reset and admits exact trajectories within six switching regions. Similar measured latency scaling thus coexists with different mechanisms of access to firing. Validating a reduced model's mechanism of excitability requires examination of stimulus protocol and attractor access alongside equilibrium structure and spike timing.

papers.title: HALO-LP: A Homogeneous All-Shifted Non-Interior-Point Method for Linear Programming
papers.abstract: This letter introduces HALO-LP, a novel homogeneous all-shifted non-interior-point method for linear programming (LP). The proposed method combines a homogeneous self-dual (HSD) embedding with all-shifted nonlinear complementarity (NCP) functions and proximal primal-dual regularization, enabling arbitrary primal-dual warm starts without requiring strictly interior iterates. The resulting Newton equations admit a condensation based on a positive-definite matrix that can be efficiently factorized using Cholesky decomposition, while the HSD embedding enables primal and dual infeasibility detection through Farkas certificates. Numerical evaluations on perturbed LP instances derived from the Netlib test set demonstrate state-of-the-art warm-starting performance, outperforming the competing solvers in the evaluated setting. We further validate optimality and infeasibility detection on analytically characterized LP problems. Finally, we demonstrate HALO-LP's applicability to robotic optimal control through sequential linear programming (SLP) for centroidal walking and trotting of quadrupedal robots.

papers.title: Mathematical Formulation and Comparative Performance Evaluation of Machine Learning Algorithms for Maize Land Suitability Prediction
papers.abstract:
Addressing the food needs of a growing population is one of the major challenges of developing countries like Ethiopia. Various policies aimed at increasing food production have been enacted by governments and development partners. Although efforts in this regard have been made, there is still inadequate emphasis on increasing food production through the use of high technology practices. Precision agriculture using technology has been utilized to increase crop yield. Precision agriculture also relies on identifying land for a crop, which is a key factor that affects crop yield. Traditional methods of assessing land suitability for crop production are time-consuming, costly and unreliable. Against this background, the aim of this study was to assess the potential of machine learning (ML) in improving the speed and accuracy of assessing land suitability for maize, a staple crop in Ethiopia, as compared to traditional methods. The study is investigated in three areas (Burie, Shindi and Tilili) in the Amhara region. Data collection was done through the local agriculture offices and survey teams. The data were coded, scaled and balanced. Various feature extraction techniques, which included Univariate Feature Selection(UFS), Recursive Feature Elimination with Cross-Validation(RFECV) and Sequential Feature Selection(SFS), and various classifiers, which were K-nearest neighbor (KNN), gradient boosting (GB),random forest (RF) with mathematical formulations were employed. The best models were constructed through combining GBOOST and SFS and achieved an accuracy of 99.41% and 99.35% for both precision and recall. Our results showed that using machine learning is a reliable method of assessing land suitability for maize in Ethiopia.
  Keywords: Maize, Gradient boosting,Land suitability,Machine learning, Mathematical formulations

papers.title: Labor Market Returns to Education and Intra-family Educational Inequality: Theory and Experimental Evidence
papers.abstract: How do labor market conditions shape educational inequality within- and between families? A growing body of evidence documents convex wage returns to education in labor markets across the world. We develop a theoretical model that demonstrates that earnings convexity can increase or decrease between-sibling differences in investments and outcomes depending on the parameter of parental inequality aversion. We recover the distribution of this structural parameter from a highly-incentivized lab-in-the-field experiment with 246 parents in San Luis Potos\'i, Mexico, in which token allocations determine children's access to an AI course. Parents make allocation decisions across six scenarios that vary convexity in the payoff function and endowment-investment substitutability. We identify three types of parents: Rawlsian parents display perfect inequality aversion (12.6%), interior parents that are moderately inequality tolerant (76.8%), and Utilitarian parents who maximize total payoffs (10.6%). While these three groups respond to earnings convexity in heterogeneous ways, on average, greater convexity increases the share allocated to the high-endowed child, thereby widening within-family inequality.

papers.title: A Cooperative Game-Theoretic Framework for Real-Time Deviation Settlement in Local Energy Communities
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a cooperative game-theoretical framework for the financial settlement of real-time deviations in Community-Based Local Energy Markets (CB-LEMs). The real-time settlement process is modeled as a transferable-utility cooperative game, and the resulting Real-Time Local Energy Market (RTLEM) game is shown to be superadditive and balanced. We analyze two game-theoretical allocation mechanisms, the Shapley value and the nucleolus, and evaluate their efficiency, individual rationality, coalitional rationality, and temporal-aggregation properties. We subsequently compare these mechanisms with a settlement rule based on proportional imbalance responsibility. The three mechanisms are efficient and individually rational, but only the nucleolus is guaranteed to satisfy coalitional rationality for every RTLEM instance. The proposed framework is demonstrated using real-world data from a residential energy community in Amsterdam, showing the trade-offs among the three allocation mechanisms in terms of surplus distribution, coalitional stability, interpretability, and computational requirements.

papers.title: On the Conditional Consistency of the Bootstrap
papers.abstract: This paper focuses on the conditional consistency of the bootstrap. The target is the conditional law of a statistic given a common shock, and the bootstrap approximates it by the law of a resampled statistic conditional on the shock and the data. We call the bootstrap consistent if these laws are close in the Kolmogorov distance for almost every realization of the shock. The conditioning $\sigma$-algebras are allowed to be unrelated across sample sizes, and both the comparison law and the dimension of the data may vary with the sample size. We give sufficient conditions for consistency in this sense, show that they yield asymptotically correct conditional coverage for bootstrap quantiles, and provide a finite-sample bound on the coverage error. We also relate the Kolmogorov formulation to the merging of probability measures. The results are specialized to statistics depending smoothly on an estimator or on an estimated nuisance parameter.

papers.title: Invariant universal averages and Bertrand's paradox: a response to Shackel
papers.abstract: In 2014, with D. Aerts we proposed a solution to the hard problem of Bertrand's paradox by means of a universal average over different ways of randomizing an entity. In his recent monograph, N. Shackel raises objections concerning the approximation by cellular densities, the restrictions used in their construction, the apparently trivial limit of their averages, the choice of a second-order probability law, and the dependence of the result on the naming of chords. We revisit these objections using the invariance-based formulation of the universal average. The first objection is well taken, and the approximation argument is repaired: an explicit sequence of bivalent cellular densities provides weak approximation of any prescribed probability measure, with an error bound for intervals. We show that any second-order selection law invariant under rearrangements of equal-length cells has the same uniform barycenter, independently of the particular densities and weights employed. For cellular densities, this conclusion holds exactly at every finite resolution. Thus, non-uniqueness of the second-order law does not prevent uniqueness of the resulting average within the indifferent class. Finally, we prove that no probability measure can be invariant under both these rearrangements and arbitrary changes of interval lengths. The reference geometry therefore cannot be obtained by averaging alone: it must be supplied by the physical modelization of the randomized entity. These results clarify the scope, and the limitations, of our original distinction between the easy and hard problems of Bertrand's paradox.

papers.title: Enumeration of plane hypermaps with a mixed boundary II
papers.abstract: A plane hypermap with a boundary is a connected graph embedded in the plane with a distinguished face, and whose inner faces are properly face-bicolored. We say that such hypermaps are k-alternating if the colors of the faces adjacent to the distinguished face alternate at most 2k times when going counterclockwise. Eynard and Orantin, in [EO2005], have found a universal expression for the generating functions of k-alternating hypermaps as a surprisingly simple function of the generating function of 1-alternating hypermaps. In this article, we will provide combinatorial formulas for k-alternating hypermaps using specific subclasses of hypermaps in which each vertex can either be connected to a previously marked vertex, called accessible, or connected to all other vertices in what we call a blob. In particular, this method will allow us to derive the results from [EO2005] from a combinatorial perspective, and we anticipate that it will lead to the computation of asymptotics for hypermaps in future work. This article is naturally a sequel to, and most importantly a generalization of, the results in [BEL26], which deals essentially with the case of 1- and 2-alternating hypermaps.

papers.title: Programmable Droplets as Active Matter in a Reconfigurable Environment
papers.abstract: Exploring systems that bridge the gap between non living and living matter requires a reconfigurable environment coupled to synthetic systems capable of autonomous motion, adaptive behaviour and persistent dynamics. Self propelled droplets provide a minimal platform for such life like behaviour, but quantitative measures capturing both persistence and adaptability to enable closed loop reconfiguration remain lacking. Here we introduce an autonomous closed loop robotic platform to characterise and dynamically program the autonomous behaviour of multicomponent oil in water droplets. We explored two chemical composition spaces, with and without external pH perturbations, analysing droplet behaviour in real time and iteratively selecting formulations. To quantify this behaviour, we introduce two descriptors, persistence and diversity. Persistence is quantified by mapping temporal dynamics in a speed shape complexity space, where we identify a persistence domain that distinguishes active from inactive droplets. Diversity captures spontaneous or environmentally induced variation in motion and the propensity of droplets to reorient or adapt under perturbation. We show that persistence and diversity are constrained by a behavioural trade off: high persistence limits diversity, whereas high diversity reduces persistent activity. Our results provide a quantitative framework for navigating and programming life like behaviours in active droplets and show how closed-loop experimentation can uncover organising principles in complex active matter.

papers.title: Owning What Can Quit
papers.abstract: Academic journals are part of the infrastructure of science, yet most journal titles are owned by commercial publishers while their standing rests on editors and boards who can leave. This paper asks what that separation means for the governance of science. Using a coded dataset of all 57 editorial mass resignations recorded by Retraction Watch from 2015 to 2026, data on editor tenure at 110 economics, finance and accounting journals, and journal-level publication and revenue data, I document three patterns. First, resignation does not reverse an owner's decision: in none of the 19 episodes involving an editor's replacement did the owner back down after the board resigned, so editorial communities have influence only before they leave. Second, whether a departing board can take a journal's standing with it depends on institutions outside the board: successor journals follow most often where a scholarly society backs the board and rarely in medicine, where non-profit hosts are scarce, while journal ranking lists, which rate titles rather than the people who edit them, keep reputation with the owner. Third, a stated limit on editor tenure was applied at the publisher's discretion; where it was applied, output grew almost fourfold, a short-run gain whose long-run effect on the journal's standing is not yet known. I draw implications for scholarly societies, funders, publishers, and the bodies that compile journal rankings.

papers.title: Extending Aircraft Coverage of the Poll Schumann Model Using Public Data
papers.abstract: The Poll Schumann model requires airframe and engine parameters, but published tables cover only part of the fleet. Applications must obtain missing parameters, substitute another aircraft type or exclude unrepresented types. We reconstruct parameters using geometry from certification documents and manufacturer manuals, together with ICAO engine records. Published equations supply the physical parameters, regression estimates the propulsion efficiency scale. The inventory covers 90 type designators, including 22 absent from the direct pycontrails table and 18 without a listed substitute. Across 68 types, mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) against pycontrails was 7.38% for drag and 3.14% for design Mach. Across 66 types in 21 families, efficiency regression achieved 3.91% MAPE with the evaluated family excluded from input selection and fitting. On 100 recorded A320 flights, a type already represented in the published tables, cruise fuel flow MAPE for reconstructed and published parameter sets was 4.50% versus 4.68%, while mean absolute percentage error in integrated fuel over covered airborne intervals was 7.19% versus 6.82%. Public technical records can therefore extend Poll Schumann parameter coverage, with quantified agreement against published coefficients and comparable fuel prediction errors on the evaluated A320 flights.

papers.title: Intrinsic network dynamics catalyze switching in functional connectivity states of the brain
papers.abstract: Dynamic functional connectivity (dFC) reflects ongoing reconfiguration of large-scale brain networks, but the temporal organization and network processes underlying spontaneous state transitions remain poorly understood. We developed functional connectivity state switching (FCSS), a phase-coherence-based framework that tracks multiscale changes in dominant whole-brain connectivity configurations. In Human Connectome Project fMRI, FCSS was strongly evoked by cognitive state and condition switches, and distinct transition dynamics differentially predicted working-memory performance. During rest, spontaneous FCSS was characterized by progressive changes in network segregation, integration, and cross-network communication as connectivity approached a switching event. Critically, event-related analysis time-locked to spontaneous FCSS revealed opposing pre-switch dynamics: salience-network contribution increased while default-mode-network contribution decreased, suggesting coordinated engagement and disengagement of these networks before switching. This reciprocal reweighting may provide a network-level mechanism for spontaneous FC reconfiguration. Together, these findings identify both global reorganization and network-specific processes underlying spontaneous and task-evoked brain-state transitions in the human brain.

papers.title: Four-Dimensional Semi-Homogeneous Convex Cones: A Complete Classification
papers.abstract: We classify all four-dimensional semi-homogeneous convex cones, i.e., closed, pointed, full-dimensional cones whose connected automorphism group has principal orbits of codimension at most one. On such cones, the Monge-Amp\`ere equation defining the canonical barrier reduces to an ordinary differential equation. This makes this barrier computationally accessible. The semi-homogeneous cones can then be used in modeling by conic programs. An obvious subset of such cones are the homogeneous cones. The key point allowing the classification is that for all other cones, the automorphism group has a three-dimensional subgroup acting locally faithfully on the principal orbits. This subgroup must have a Lie algebra which is either abelian or a direct product of a 1-dimensional algebra and a two-dimensional algebra generated by $A,B$ satisfying $[A,B]=B$. In both cases we classify all 4-dimensional representations up to isomorphism, and for each representation all invariant convex cones. For every cone an orbit invariant is computed.
