TV has two limitations. Within each position, it assigns little corrective weight to severely undercovered target tokens, making it difficult to correct a draft that is initially poorly aligned with the target (Samarin et al., 2026). Across positions, an additive TV objective ignores that acceptance at each position depends on the preceding prefix surviving verification. For a fixed draft architecture and length, improving expected acceptance length (EAL) means generating more tokens for approximately the same drafting and verification cost. Under realizability, minimizing TV at every position also maximizes EAL, as both are optimized by q=pq=p. A drafter with limited capacity, however, must trade off errors across positions. This motivates optimizing EAL itself, but its gradients contain prefix products that weaken supervision at later positions when earlier tokens are rarely accepted.

We introduce TVP, a new family of losses derived from EAL that addresses both limitations. TVP replaces prefix products with additive supervision across draft positions and introduces a power parameter that controls the corrective weight assigned to undercovered tokens. Starting with stronger undercoverage correction helps train an initially misaligned draft. Annealing the power parameter toward one then shifts the objective toward acceptance as training progresses, keeping TV’s direct acceptance signal once the draft is aligned. We establish bounds connecting this family to EAL and local rejection probability, and show that annealing recovers both TV’s loss and its gradients.

papers.title: Multi-Estimate Elicitation Does Not Uniformly Debias Language Model Judgments
papers.abstract: Does eliciting five weighted estimates within a single response change how a language model responds to information? Across anchoring, hindsight, base-rate, conjunction, and status-quo/default tasks, we compare direct numerical answers with a multi-estimate response format, contrasting source framings, explicitly random cues, and probability-consistency constraints. We evaluate three completed configurations--gpt-6.1-sol, claude-sonnet-5.5, and Qwen3-8B (reasoning disabled, analyzed descriptively). In the first two configurations, direct elicitation yielded near-zero irrelevant-anchor indices and status-quo effects, while remaining responsive to informative sources and informed advice. Of 23 preregistered confirmatory tests, six rejected after Holm adjustment; however, all six absolute point estimates fell below their prespecified smallest effect sizes of interest without establishing equivalence. Moreover, while separate versus joint elicitation shifted conjunction judgments, interpretation is constrained by between-call noise. Ultimately, multi-estimate elicitation failed to produce uniform debiasing or response attenuation across tasks and models, though post hoc correlations between candidate spread and anchoring error motivate independent predictive validation. Materials: https://github.com/asj252/llm-judgment-studies

papers.title: Verification-Gated Redraw and Repair for Local Small Language Models: A Paired Evaluation
papers.abstract: Executable checks can reject incorrect model-generated programs, but rejection alone does not determine whether fresh sampling or diagnostic repair is preferable. We present a controlled, resource-bounded conceptual replication and extension of established recovery policies: a single answer (N), one verification-triggered redraw (R), and one diagnostic repair (D), for Ornith 1.5 9B and Gemma 4 E4B served locally in nominal 4-bit MLX format. The frozen evaluation contains 72 tasks: 40 HumanEval+ problems, 16 SQL tasks and 16 shell tasks. Policies share initial responses and use only public checks for online decisions; every candidate is model-generated. Each task has one stochastic trajectory per model, so the study does not estimate variation across independent sampling blocks. Redraw increases observed final-test success from 51.4% to 59.7% for Ornith and from 55.6% to 62.5% for Gemma. Diagnostic repair reaches 52.8% and 63.9%, respectively. None of four internally prespecified paired contrasts is significant after Holm correction (minimum adjusted p = 0.125). Public checks falsely accept 25 Ornith and 11 Gemma candidates, demonstrating that acceptance is not a correctness guarantee. A post-review audit of initial answers gives perfect-retry upper bounds of 76.4% and 87.5%, respectively: accepted initial errors cannot trigger recovery under the fixed gate. This one-block, resource-bounded study provides a finite-cohort experimental record, not policy equivalence, a general model ranking or universal reliability

Local small language models (SLMs) can generate executable solutions under explicit resource limits. A plausible program is not necessarily correct, and a public example set can accept a program that fails a held-out case. When a public verifier does reject a response, a recovery policy must decide whether to sample a fresh solution or ask the model to repair its rejected candidate.

We study two questions: does one verifier-triggered fresh sample improve selected-answer quality over a single response, and does diagnostic repair improve on that redraw? We distinguish the answer actually selected by a public policy from candidate availability, which uses a hidden oracle after collection. Only the former is deployable under the stated information boundary.

Shared initial candidates and diagnostic/final test separation are established controls, not new algorithms. papers.title: Polyteam logics for quantum contextuality
papers.abstract: We introduce logics of dependence and independence over polyteams (that is, databases with multiple relation schemes), in a similar way as in arXiv:1704.02158v3 [cs.LO]. On this basis, we develop a logical framework in which we can express (in formulas) relevant properties about the statistics of a repeated quantum experiment. In this framework, we formalize Bell's theorem, and the Kochen-Specker theorem as failure of logical entailments, as it was suggested in arXiv:2107.10817v3 [math.LO]. The key feature of polyteam logics in action here is their power to express both local and global properties, with respect to the set of possible measurements. The point of this is at least twofold. Firstly, as in arXiv:1102.0264v7 [quant-ph], it gives a high-level (information-theoretic) understanding of these physical phenomena, that is not intrinsic to the physical objects involved. Secondly, since logical entailment is often (partially) axiomatizable, this framework incites us to tackle the question of contextuality computationally. We also define semiring-weighted polyteams along with logics on them, and use them to recover the probabilistic versions of the contextuality theorems mentioned above.
papers.intro:
Quantum physics sometimes prevents us from measuring a set MM of attributes simultaneously, e.g. Heisenberg’s inequality for position and momentum. Thus, we are only left with local information : for each compatible C⊆MC\subseteq M, we may determine through experiment the statistical behavior of the attributes CC on a given system. This yields a set of tables, i.e. essentially a so called polyteam. Even though it is inaccessible to experiment, it is natural to think this local information is derived (by repeated projections) from one big table : the one describing the statistical behavior of the whole set of attributes MM. Quantum contextuality is the realization that this natural assumption turns out to be false, and the study of counter-examples.

This work tackles quantum contextuality through the lens of polyteam logics. It is the purpose of Section 1 to define teams, polyteams (Section 1.1), polyteam logics (Sections 1.2 and 1.3), and a polyteam-based framework for representing quantum experiments (Section 1.4). A logical analysis of quantum contextuality is interesting for several reasons : it is a higher level (information-theoretic) understanding of the phenomena (hence, more general and less intrinsic), and the restricted syntax prompts us into searching for axiomatizations of logical entailment.

(Poly)team logics feature atomic formulas such as =(x,y)=^{\!}\!(x,y) "xx determines yy", or x⟂yx\perp y "xx is independent from yy". These (in)dependence notions are very common in experimental sciences, hence we may expect polyteam formulas to reflect natural scientific discourse. It is the purpose of Section 2 to show most of the relevant physical properties of quantum experiments are expressible in polyteam formulas (Sections 2.2 and 2.4), and that Bell’s theorem and the Kochen-Specker theorem are formalizable as failure of entailments in polyteam logics (Section 2.5). There was already work in this area, and specifically about providing team-based accounts of contextuality. Section 2.6 discusses the relation between this contribution and previous literature. In short, we believe our polyteam account is at the same time efficient (formulas are somewhat expressive), consistent (no need to add alien atoms to the natural polyteam logics) and computation-friendly (polyteams are like databases).

papers.title: Spectral Theory and Continuum Norm Resolvent Convergence of a One-Sided Discrete Dirac-Type Operator
papers.abstract: We investigate a one-dimensional discrete Dirac-type operator $D_d$ acting on the Hilbert space $\big(\ell^2(\mathbb{Z};\mathbb{C})\big)^2$, obtained from the classical continuous free Dirac operator by replacing the spatial derivative with the one-sided backward difference operator $I - S_1$, where $S_1$ denotes the right shift on $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z};\mathbb{C})$. We establish the fundamental operator-theoretic and spectral properties of $D_d$: unlike symmetric or supersymmetric lattice discretizations, $D_d$ is bounded and non-normal for every non-zero rest mass $m > 0$, with self-commutator $[D_d, D_d^\dag] = -2mc^3(-\Delta_{\mathrm{disc}})\sigma_2$, yet it is quadratically normal. We compute the exact operator norm, determine the exact spectral radius in two mass regimes, and show via Fourier--Laurent analysis that the spectrum $\sigma(D_d)$ is purely continuous and lies on a two-component algebraic curve in the complex plane undergoing a topological transition at $mc^2 = 2c$. Finally, introducing a lattice spacing $h > 0$ and embedding $\big(\ell^2(h\mathbb{Z};\mathbb{C})\big)^2$ isometrically into $\big(L^2(\mathbb{R};\mathbb{C})\big)^2$ via Whittaker--Shannon band-limited interpolation, we prove that the scaled non-normal discrete Dirac-type operator $D_{d,h}$ converges to the continuous self-adjoint Dirac operator $D$ in the norm resolvent sense at the optimal rate $\mathcal{O}(h)$ as $h \to 0^+$, without requiring frequency cutoffs.

papers.title: Radial conditions for global compact finite propagation for divergence-form elliptic operators
papers.abstract: We study global compact finite propagation (GCFP) for the wave equation $u_{tt}=\operatorname{div}(A(x)\nabla u)$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$, that is, the property that a disturbance starting in a compact set cannot reach spatial infinity in finite time. For smooth strictly positive matrices $A$ we show that GCFP implies $\int_1^\infty a_*(r)^{-1/2}\,dr=\infty$, where $a_*(r)$ is the minimum over the sphere of radius $r$ of $\langle A\omega,\omega\rangle$; the proof uses the equivalence of GCFP with completeness of the Riemannian metric $A^{-1}$, of which we prove the necessary direction for the cosine family of the Friedrichs extension. We also prove that the analogous divergence condition with $a^*(r)$, the maximum over the sphere, is sufficient, and that this holds for measurable coefficients $A\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ with $A\ge I$. Finally, we construct a locally bounded measurable matrix with $a_*=a^*$ for which GCFP holds although the integral converges, so the necessary condition is not stable under the loss of continuity.

papers.title: The Exact Central-Index Profile of Groups with Bounded Noncommutativity
papers.abstract: For a finite group $G$, let $\omega(G)$ be the largest size of a pairwise noncommuting set and put $z(G)=[G:\mathrm Z(G)]$. We determine the maximum possible central index under $\omega(G)\le k$ for every integer $k\ge1$, giving an exact answer to Neumann's central-index question and sharpening Pyber's exponential upper bound. The maximum is $1$ for $k=1,2$, $(k-1)^2$ for $3\le k\le6$, $81$ for $k=7,8$, and $4^{\lfloor(k-1)/2\rfloor}$ for $k\ge9$. In the last range, with $r=\lfloor(k-1)/2\rfloor$, equality holds exactly when $G'\cong C_2$ and $G/\mathrm Z(G)\cong\mathbb F_2^{2r}$. We also obtain the sharp universal bound $z(G)\le(81/64)2^{\omega(G)-1}$. All maximizers are classified up to isoclinism. The results extend to arbitrary groups with finite clique number through finite isoclinic representatives.
papers.intro:
The size of a pairwise noncommuting set measures how many elements of a group can be mutually incompatible with commutativity. For a finite group GG, let ω⁡(G)\omega(G) be the largest size of such a set. We ask how strongly a bound on ω⁡(G)\omega(G) constrains the index of the centre. The order of GG itself cannot be bounded in this way: taking a direct product with an arbitrarily large abelian group changes neither ω⁡(G)\omega(G) nor the central index. The natural extremal quantities are therefore z(G)=[G:Z(G)],ζ(k)=sup{z(G):ω(G)≤k}.z(G)=[G:\mathrm{Z}(G)],\qquad\zeta(k)=\sup\{z(G):\omega(G)\leq k\}. Here the supremum is over finite groups. In graph-theoretic language, join two elements of GG when they do not commute; then ω⁡(G)\omega(G) is the clique number of this noncommuting graph. Thus the problem relates a combinatorial restriction to a structural invariant of the group.

The origin is a question posed by Erdős in 1975: if a group has no infinite pairwise noncommuting subset, must the sizes of its finite pairwise noncommuting subsets be bounded? Neumann answered this affirmatively in 1976 by proving the stronger statement that such a group has finite central quotient [20, Theorem 6]. We first solve the finite extremal problem and then extend the sharp bounds to arbitrary groups by isoclinism, as explained in Corollary 1.4 below. Neumann also explicitly asked how the central index can be bounded in terms of the largest noncommuting set. His proof gave log⁡z⁡(G)=O⁡(ω​(G)2)\log z(G)=O(\omega(G)^{2}), and he suggested a possible quadratic bound for z⁡(G)z(G) itself [20, Section 4].

Several parts of the literature supply information about the models and local estimates relevant to these questions. Isaacs’s formula, reported by Bertram, gives the clique numbers of extraspecial 22-groups [5, p. 40]; Chin studies noncommuting sets in extraspecial pp-groups [10]. Further results treat groups with derived subgroup of prime order and metacyclic pp-groups [18, 14]. For scalar commutator maps, noncommuting sets correspond to sets of pairwise nonorthogonal points in symplectic geometry. Results on partial ovoids therefore provide sharp information in some small odd-characteristic cases [7, 9]. Covering theorems provide a complementary tool: the centralizers of the elements of a maximum clique cover the group, so bounds for subgroup and coset covers can control the central index [19, 22, 8].

papers.title: Mutual-visibility colouring with two colours is NP-complete for every fixed diameter
papers.abstract: A mutual-visibility set in a graph $G$ is a set $S$ of vertices such that any two vertices of $S$ are connected by a shortest path with no internal vertex in $S$, and the mutual-visibility chromatic number $\chi_\mu(G)$ is the minimum number of mutual-visibility sets needed to partition $V(G)$. Babu, Di Stefano and Lakshmanan showed that it is NP-complete to decide whether $\chi_\mu(G)\le 2$ for graphs of diameter four. We show that the problem remains NP-complete for graphs of diameter $d$, for every fixed $d\ge2$; diameter two is the smallest diameter for which the problem is non-trivial. The proof rests on a reformulation of $\chi_\mu(G)\le 2$ for diameter-two graphs as the $2$-colourability of an associated hypergraph, and on a reduction from $2$-colourability of $3$-uniform hypergraphs without short cycles.
papers.intro:
Mutual visibility in graphs was introduced by Di Stefano [6]: a set S⊆V⁡(G)S\subseteq V(G) is called a mutual-visibility set (MV set) of GG if any two vertices u,v∈Su,v\in S are SS-visible, that is, joined by a shortest u,vu,v-path all of whose internal vertices lie outside SS. Klavžar, Kuziak, Valenzuela Tripodoro and Yero [9] introduced the corresponding colouring problem. A partition of V⁡(G)V(G) into MV sets is called a mutual-visibility colouring of GG, and the mutual-visibility chromatic number χμ​(G)\chi_{\mu}(G) is the minimum number of parts in such a partition. They asked about its computational complexity [9, Problem 8.1], and Babu, Di Stefano and Lakshmanan [1] proved that it is NP-complete to decide whether χμ​(G)≤2\chi_{\mu}(G)\leq 2, already for graphs of diameter four. Related variants (independent, total, dual and outer mutual-visibility colourings) are also known to be NP-complete [3, 2].

papers.title: TRIAGE: Reliability- and Load-Conditioned Escalation for Two-Tier LLM Serving with a Semantic Evidence Judge
papers.abstract: Two-tier LLM serving escalates selected requests from a small model to a large one, but prompt-based routers cannot see whether retrieved evidence supports an answer, and they treat the GPU cost of an escalation as constant. We study TRIAGE, which conditions escalation on a post-generation reliability state and on a load-dependent GPU price, and we report both what held and what did not on one A40 serving Qwen2.5-7B and 32B (AWQ) under VLLM. Escalation cost rose 21.9x from 1 to 10 requests/s but showed no monotone dependence on KV-cache headroom, and a pre-registered claim that the reliability state detects corrupted evidence (AUROC>=0.70) was falsified at 0.571, although any prompt-only router scores exactly 0.500 by construction. Post hoc, a semantic evidence judge raised detection to 0.846 (0.926 on never-served items) and predicted wrong small-model answers at AUROC 0.90-0.96 on RGB and three RouterBench model pairs; the resulting cascade stayed within about 3 pp of GPT-4 at 79.5% lower API cost for GPT-3.5->GPT-4, yet fell below random routing for open-model pairs with 2-3x price ratios. End to end, the 7B->32B pair showed only a +2.88 pp held-out gap, so the allocator rightly declined to escalate and the headline is a null that a small pre-launch gate failed to expose.

Serving a large language model (LLM) is expensive, and for many requests a smaller model is already correct. A common remedy is a two-tier system: a small model answers first and a large model is used only when it is likely to help (Chen et al., 2023; Jitkrittum et al., 2023; Ding et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2024; Ong et al., 2025). Most deployed routers decide from the prompt alone. Two properties of real deployments make that insufficient.

First, the information that decides correctness may not be in the prompt. In retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), the evidence attached to a question can be on-topic yet fail to contain the answer. A router that reads only the question sees an identical input whether the evidence is good or bad.

papers.title: Benchmark Study for Quantum Statevector Simulators for Scientific Computing
papers.abstract: Quantum circuit simulators are essential for quantum algorithm development, yet systematic runtime benchmarks comparing major frameworks across CPU and GPU backends are limited. We benchmark three open-source frameworks - Cirq (qsim), CUDA-Q, and Qiskit (Aer) - on statevector simulation of the 2D quantum acoustic wave equation, evolved via Trotterized Hamiltonian dynamics, for problem sizes from 7 to 29 qubits on a single Azure virtual machine. The evaluation spans four categories: CPU runtime versus qubit count, strong scalability on multi-core CPUs at 27 qubits, GPU runtime versus qubit count, and GPU-over-CPU speedup. Relative rankings shift from one category to the next. On CPU, Cirq is fastest up to 23 qubits (2.4x faster than Qiskit at 21 qubits), but Qiskit overtakes it at larger sizes and higher thread counts, sustaining 80% parallel efficiency at 16 threads. On GPU, CUDA-Q leads between 13 and 21 qubits, while Cirq becomes the fastest GPU backend at large problem sizes, achieving 1.5x and 2.3x speedups over CUDA-Q and Qiskit at 29 qubits. GPU-over-CPU speedup ratios should be interpreted alongside absolute GPU runtimes; CUDA-Q's 1500x at 21 qubits is largely driven by the limited scaling of its CPU backend (qpp), and the absolute GPU runtimes show that the three frameworks' GPU backends differ by less than these ratios alone suggest. These results indicate that no single framework dominates across configurations, and that backend selection for statevector simulation should be guided by both target hardware and problem size.

papers.title: The Prodigal Elephant Returns: Last-Return Laws in the Superdiffusive Regime
papers.abstract:
Let $(S_n)$ be the one-dimensional elephant random walk with memory parameter $p\in(3/4,1)$ and first-step probability $q=\mathbb{P}(S_1=1)\in[0,1]$. Set $a=2p-1$, and let $f_{q,a}$ denote the density of the almost-sure limit of $S_n/n^a$. We prove that the last return time $T_0=\sup\{m\geq0:S_m=0\}$ satisfies:
  $\mathbb{P}(T_0\geq n)\sim f_{q,a}(0)\sqrt{\frac{8}{\pi(2a-1)}}n^{-(a-1/2)}$.
  Reflection gives $f_{q,a}(0)=f_{1,a}(0)$, so the constant is independent of $q$. For future walks started from admissible states $(n,x_n)$ with $x_n/\sqrt n\to z$, we establish functional convergence of the centered martingale-normalized paths to a time-changed Brownian motion. Uniform control of late hitting times then gives the eventual-return kernel $2\Phi(-\sqrt{2a-1}|z|)$, uniformly on bounded scaled windows, where $\Phi$ is the standard normal distribution function. The same last-visit asymptotic holds uniformly for nonempty deterministic targets $F_n\subseteq[-r_n,r_n]\cap\mathbb{Z}$, $r_n=o(\sqrt n)$, held fixed during each trajectory. Conditionally on $T_0\geq n$, we identify the joint limit of $S_n/\sqrt n$, the next return divided by $n$, and the last return divided by the next return. The last ratio converges to $A^{-1/(2a-1)}$, independently of the other two limiting coordinates, where $A$ has the arcsine distribution on $(0,1)$.

papers.title: Same Function, Different Mechanism: Implementation-Local Geometry Beyond Accuracy
papers.abstract: Two models can make exactly the same predictions yet respond differently when their implementations are perturbed. A lookup table can change one case independently; a shared rule couples changes across cases. We compare these mechanisms through an implementation chart: a specified local family of logit perturbations around a fixed predictive distribution. Our main result counts the independent prediction changes allowed by exact finite-group sharing: the active dimension is the number of input-output orbits minus the number of input orbits. For softened modular addition, lookup and shared cyclic charts therefore have ranks $p^2(p-1)$ and $p-1$ despite identical predictions. The classical Fisher pullback connects these dimensions to local KL curvature; mechanism-preserving reparameterizations leave the rank unchanged. We also bound the spectral tail under approximate sharing and separate quadratic rank from higher-order learning coefficients. Trained modular-addition models verify that chart rank is measurable, while controlled compiled transformers distinguish compiler-supported intermediate charts from matched alternatives. Negative controls show where this discrimination fails. The framework evaluates specified mechanism hypotheses; it does not infer a unique mechanism from predictions or predict training dynamics.

papers.intro:
Suppose two systems answer every modular-addition question correctly, with exactly the same confidence. One stores a separate answer for each input pair. The other reuses one cyclic rule. Their predictions cannot distinguish them, but an intervention can: changing one stored answer need not affect another, whereas changing the shared rule affects many inputs together. This paper asks how to measure that difference while holding the predictive distribution fixed.

Their predictions cannot distinguish them, but an intervention can: changing one stored answer need not affect another, whereas changing the shared rule affects many inputs together. This paper asks how to measure that difference while holding the predictive distribution fixed.

The key quantity is the number of independent local changes to predictions that a specified mechanism permits. We call this its active dimension. To define it, we need more than the model’s outputs: we must say which parts of the implementation can change and which constraints remain in place. An implementation chart records that choice. For example, perturbing a convolutional kernel while preserving weight tying defines a different chart from independently perturbing its copies at every position. Both charts can pass through the same predictive distribution.

papers.title: An Odd-Arch Family of Perturbed Hofstadter Q-Recursions: Gaussian Profiles and Exact Frequency Laws
papers.abstract:
For every integer $p\ge2$, we construct a globally well-defined positive odd sequence $Q_p$ satisfying, after an explicit finite initial block, $Q_p(n)=Q_p(n-Q_p(n-1))+Q_p(n-Q_p(n-2))-(-1)^n$.
  Its binary block words admit the exact factorization $U_{p,k}=(A_k\overline{A}_{k+1})^{p-1}A_{k+2}$, producing exactly $2p-1$ alternating signed arches per natural block. The elementary word heights converge uniformly to the Gaussian isoperimetric profile $\varphi\circ\Phi^{-1}$.
  For each fixed $p$, this yields an explicit dyadic limiting profile with $2p-1$ sign transitions and a sharp relative-error constant $\Lambda_p=b_p/2$, where $b_p$ is determined by $b_p((3p-1)/2+\Phi(-b_p))=\varphi(b_p)$.
  We determine all zeros and parity crossings in sufficiently large dyadic blocks. For $p\ge3$, there are exactly $2p-1$ transverse even-index zeros, whereas the three-arch case $p=2$ exhibits an alternating four/six-zero pattern.
  An ordered frequency factorization gives exact dyadic histograms, moments, total-variation distances, and extremal multiplicities. The limiting frequency generating function $z^3/(2-z)$ is universal, although the highest finite multiplicities depend on $p$.
  Finally, the summatory function has main terms $N^2/4+(N/2)\log_2N$, an explicit parameter-dependent log-periodic term of order $N$, and remainder $O_p(N/\sqrt{\log N})$.

papers.title: Global straightening of solution manifolds for state-dependent delay equations
papers.abstract: Let $U$ be an arbitrary open subset of $C^1([-h,0],\mathbb R^n)$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuously differentiable. Suppose that each derivative $Df(\phi)$, $\phi\in U$, admits a continuous linear extension $D_ef(\phi):C([-h,0],\mathbb R^n)\to\mathbb R^n$, such that $D_ef(\phi)\chi$ depends jointly continuously on $\phi\in U$ and $\chi\in C([-h,0],\mathbb R^n)$. We construct a $C^1$ diffeomorphism of $U$ onto an open subset of $C^1([-h,0],\mathbb R^n)$ which maps the solution manifold of $x'(t)=f(x_t)$ onto an open subset of the closed subspace defined by $\phi'(0)=0$. This resolves an open problem posed by Walther concerning regularization of the entire solution manifold. The diffeomorphism preserves the value at zero and agrees with the original history on $[-h,-\tau]$ for any prescribed $\tau\in(0,h)$, and is uniformly arbitrarily close to the identity in the supremum norm. It is connected to the identity by a jointly $C^1$ family of diffeomorphisms. The same conclusions hold under the weaker assumption that the finite signed measures representing the derivatives of $f$ have no atom at zero. We also establish a corresponding theorem for separable real Hilbert-valued histories.

papers.title: The ball fixed point property for continuous functions on locally compact spaces
papers.abstract: Let $K$ be a compact Hausdorff space and $p\in K$. We prove that the Banach space $C(K,p)=\{f\in C(K,\mathbb R):f(p)=0\}$ fails the ball fixed point property (BFPP) whenever $p$ is non-isolated, answering a question of Avil\'es, Jap\'on, Lennard, Mart\'inez-Cervantes and Stawski. Consequently, $C_0(L)$ fails the BFPP for every noncompact locally compact Hausdorff space $L$. Together with Barroso's characterization for $C(K)$, this yields complete topological classifications of the BFPP for $C_0(L)$ and $C(K,p)$. We also resolve a second question of Avil\'es et al., showing that the BFPP of $C(K)$ implies that of $C(K,p)$ for every compact Hausdorff space $K$ and every $P$-point $p\in K$ if and only if there are no measurable cardinals.

papers.title: Order-Invariant CFO Contains Local-Order-Invariant FO
papers.abstract: Order-invariant cluster first-order logic (CFO) and local-order-invariant first-order logic are two fragments of order-invariant first-order logic, both motivated by the study of invariant logics on classes of bounded degree. Our main result is that order-invariant CFO contains local-order-invariant FO on arbitrary classes of finite structures, settling the conjecture of Ghasemi and Grange that order-invariant CFO contains plain FO. By combining this with a collapse result of Ghasemi and Grange, we obtain the equivalence of FO, local-order-invariant FO, and order-invariant CFO on classes of finite colored graphs of bounded degree. The proof makes use of Gaifman normal form, which allows our translation from local-order-invariant FO to order-invariant CFO to be effective. Combined with the fixed-parameter tractability of model-checking for order-invariant CFO on bounded-degree colored graph classes, this shows that model-checking for local-order-invariant FO on bounded-degree colored graph classes is fixed-parameter tractable. To generalize our collapse and model-checking results beyond colored graphs, we use a method based on first-order interpretations which also yields a collapse of order-invariant FO to FO when restricted to graph classes of bounded shrub-depth. Finally, we give an application to the database-motivated frozen-witness logic of Abiteboul, Simon, and Vianu by showing that local-order-invariant FO contains deterministic frozen-witness FO, and thus that deterministic frozen-witness FO collapses to FO on classes of finite structures of bounded degree.
papers.intro:
Finite model theory is the study of the queries on databases that can be expressed in formal languages. In particular, one tends to be interested in which queries are expressible in a given logic, and how difficult it is to compute whether a database satisfies a query defined in a given logic. In standard logics like first-order logic, fixed-point logics, or second-order logic, one can only refer to the relations of the structure itself. However, it is natural to want to make use of information like the order the data in the database is stored in, so long as the query evaluates in the same way on a database regardless of the particular order chosen. We call such a query, that is, one that uses an order but does not depend on the particular choice of order, order-invariant.

In the case of structures of arbitrary (including infinite) size, it is known that order-invariant first-order logic is equivalent in expressiveness to plain FO\mathrm{FO}, via the Craig Interpolation Theorem [8]. However, there exist properties of finite structures definable in order-invariant FO\mathrm{FO} which are not definable in FO\mathrm{FO}, the first of which was discovered by Gurevich and published in [9]. In fact, it has been shown that the weaker fragment successor-invariant FO\mathrm{FO}, in which formulae can only access the successor relation induced by the order in which the data is stored, can express properties of finite structures that cannot be expressed in FO\mathrm{FO} [21]. Based on this, it is natural to ask whether invariant logics collapse on finite structures or on particular classes of finite structures. For instance, it has been proved that successor-invariant FO\mathrm{FO} and FO\mathrm{FO} express the same queries on classes of bounded degree [16], and that order-invariant FO\mathrm{FO} collapses on trees, strings, and hollow trees [5, 15]. Our Contributions

1. Our main result is that every property expressible in local-order-invariant FO\mathrm{FO} is expressible in order-invariant CFO\mathrm{CFO}. Our translation uses Gaifman normal form, as introduced in [11], which makes it effective. Thus, our translation works on arbitrary classes of finite structures. This affirms in particular the conjecture of Ghasemi and Grange in [14] that order-invariant CFO\mathrm{CFO} contains FO\mathrm{FO}. papers.title: Variance Reduction Note 3: The Convergence of PAGE
papers.abstract: The probabilistic gradient estimator (PAGE) alternates randomly between an accurate gradient refresh and a cheap recursive correction. This third expository note on recursive variance reduction explains the algorithm and gives a self-contained convergence proof for smooth nonconvex optimization. A Lyapunov function combines objective decrease with estimation error, turning the refresh probability into an explicit contraction parameter. The resulting expected oracle complexity is $O(n+\sqrt n\,\epsilon^{-2})$ for finite sums and $O(\epsilon^{-3})$ for online problems, with the other problem parameters fixed. Initialization, refreshes, and both evaluations in each gradient difference are counted. The presentation is pedagogical and makes no claim of a new algorithm or convergence rate.

papers.title: A log-concavity criterion for finite nonnegative linearization
papers.abstract: In a 2005 survey, R. Szwarc asked for criteria, stated in the recurrence coefficients, for nonnegative linearization (property (P)) of finite orthogonal polynomial systems such as the Krawtchouk polynomials. For a finite three-term recurrence normalized to have row sums one, whose diagonal and downward coefficients have a constant nonnegative ratio, we prove that property (P) holds for every product, including products beyond the terminal degree, whenever the Newton coefficients of the profile $d_i=b_i+c_i$ are log-concave without internal zeros. The criterion contains the full positive Krawtchouk range and the dual $q$-Krawtchouk arrays, and through a quadratic decomposition of symmetric finite systems it covers Szwarc's quadratic system $Q_n$ in its sharp range $0<p_0\leq1/2$. As a limit to any such criterion, property (P) fails at coefficient distance $O((1-r^2)^N)$ from the Krawtchouk array of size $N$ with fixed ratio $c_i/d_i=r<1$. All theorems, corollaries and propositions are formalized in Lean 4.

papers.title: Haagerup vertex operator algebras at central charge eight
papers.abstract: Evans and Gannon showed that a positive vertex operator algebra of central charge eight whose representation category is the Drinfeld center $Z(\mathcal{H}_3)$ of the Haagerup fusion category has one of two character vectors, with six or nineteen currents. Call such an algebra, if strongly rational, a Haagerup algebra. We prove that a Haagerup algebra $U$ has six currents, that $U_1 \cong \mathfrak{sl}_2 \oplus \mathfrak{sl}_2$ embeds into $V_{E_6 \oplus A_2}$ in one of two explicit ways, with levels $(1,39)$ or $(3,13)$, and we determine the lowest weight spaces of its modules and $U_2$ as $U_1$-modules. For the levels $(3,13)$, $U_2$ is one of four Galois conjugate subspaces, and the algebra it generates is unitary, $C_2$-cofinite and isomorphic to the algebra constructed by Jiao; for the levels $(1,39)$, $U$ contains the algebra announced by Riesen. The associated lattice of $U$ is that of the form $x^2+xy+10y^2$, resp. $3x^2+3xy+4y^2$, the two classes of the principal genus of discriminant $-39$. Exchanging them in the decomposition of $U$ over its Heisenberg commutant gives a Haagerup algebra $U^\natural$ of the other levels, and $U \mapsto U^\natural$ is a bijection between the isomorphism classes of the two cases. Consequently, if either explicit algebra of Jiao or Riesen is positive and strongly rational with representation category braided equivalent to $Z(\mathcal{H}_3)$, there are exactly two Haagerup algebras up to isomorphism, forming a single hyperbolic genus. The explicit algebras of Jiao and Riesen have rational forms. The proofs combine exact trace relations given by vector-valued modular forms, exact computations in a model of $V_{E_6 \oplus A_2}$, and genera of vertex operator algebras.

papers.title: What reviewers call a Long Method is a length: A pre-registered test of coupling divergence as a god-unit signal, and what it settled instead
papers.abstract: A companion study found that a complexity outlier rule shows where complexity concentrates but cannot tell a god unit from a complex algorithm. This paper pre-registered a test of one way to tell them apart: weight a unit's complexity by its coupling divergence, the data it hands on minus the data it receives, so that a leaf is set aside. Coupling was measured by resolving every call in 520 MLCQ repositories, 500 fresh Java repositories and 73 Qualitas Corpus systems. The claim fails: the primary, the pooled MCC of the weighted form minus complexity alone against MLCQ's human Blob, is -0.041 [-0.130, +0.054], no difference resolved and underpowered, and the resolved readings go against it. What the data settle is at method level. What MLCQ's reviewers call a Long Method is an absolute length: a constant of 26 lines or more, chosen on the explore half, reaches MCC 0.777 on the confirm half, +0.080 [+0.016, +0.145] over the best per-repository form; every reviewer with ten or more positives, on their non-leaf reviews, has a best cutoff between 17 and 34 lines; and nothing measured inside a method, its calls, variables, data flow or the cost of cutting it, refines the constant. The constant is a limit of human reading. The next form of the construct is the cost of bringing a long method under it, which is where the construct meets architecture.
papers.intro:
A companion study [15] tested a god-class and god-method detector with no raw-scale constant: a unit is flagged when its complexity is a robust outlier for its own codebase, a modified z-score of 3.5 or more on a scale fitted to that codebase [8]. The rule found where the complexity concentrates, and its extra flags were small classes doing the work they were written to do. The difference between a god unit and a complex algorithm, that study concluded, is in the coupling, and it named this study as the test.

The rule found where the complexity concentrates, and its extra flags were small classes doing the work they were written to do. The difference between a god unit and a complex algorithm, that study concluded, is in the coupling, and it named this study as the test.

The construct tested here is coupling divergence: what a unit hands on minus what it receives. A unit that receives more than it sends is a catchment, a leaf that processes what it is given, where the complexity of an algorithm belongs; one that sends more than it receives is a junction, and a unit that directs the data and also holds the logic is what people call a god unit. The pre-registered claim was that multiplying complexity by a factor that is zero for a catchment and grows with the divergence of a junction recovers god classes and methods better than complexity alone; its estimand, decision rule, sample and bootstrap were committed before any coupling had been measured on the confirmatory material.

papers.title: Stein Criteria for Holomorphic Fibre Bundles
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study Steinness of holomorphic fibre bundles. Over a compact Riemann surface, we prove that every holomorphic ball bundle is weakly $1$-complete and that its total space is Stein if and only if it admits no holomorphic section. We also obtain higher-dimensional Stein criteria for reductive ball bundles and affine bundles in terms of positivity of the canonical class. A topological obstruction to the $1$-convexity of holomorphic fibre bundles is also established.

papers.title: Replayable Monte Carlo MRI: From Persistent Tissue Microphysics to Queryable Virtual Phantoms
papers.abstract: Multiphysics Monte Carlo simulation is the reference method for diffusion MRI in idealized tissue: walkers diffuse through a numerical substrate with relaxation, permeability, susceptibility and magnetization transfer, and accumulate the signal of a prescribed acquisition. Yet walker histories are massive, petabytes for a tractography-scale phantom, so current simulators treat them as transient. They are regenerated for every new acquisition, field strength or relaxation rate, although identical for all of them. I propose to keep these histories instead as a replay pack, compressed into persistent, shareable tissue microphysics, so that any such query is a cheap inner product against the pack. By storing each path as a Brownian bridge cut to the band a scanner class can play, transform coding its coefficients and contracting them into time segments, a replay pack is up to 5000 times smaller than the histories it keeps, while staying within the Monte-Carlo floor for every waveform of that class. It matches analytical solutions in pores, and MC/DC and MCMRSimulator on realistic axon meshes. At the scale of the field's largest benchmark, I re-simulate DiSCo, the billion-walker Monte Carlo tractography phantom, as a multiphysics replay phantom. It reproduces the published protocol's signal to one percent, and any waveform, relaxation or susceptibility up to 100 ms is a query of the same replay pack. I release every replay pack of this paper on the SubstrateCommons Hugging Face Hub and deploy replayable DiSCo as a public Hugging Face Space (https://huggingface.co/spaces/rfick/disco-replay), where anyone can choose an acquisition type (PGSE, OGSE, PGSTE or tensor encoding) and the tissue's parameters, and within two minutes receive their multiphysics Monte Carlo diffusion-weighted image volumes. With replay, a Monte Carlo simulation becomes an instrument anyone can query, at scale.
papers.intro:
Diffusion MRI measures the thermal motion of water over micrometres. The motion is independent of the scanner, but the signal depends entirely on its encoding: the method “is not a single biomarker but an acquisition-and-model framework” (Le Bihan, 2026), in which “two very different tissues can produce similar ADC values”. The response has been to diversify the acquisition and to make the biophysical description of tissue more explicit, and the demand for validation of what those descriptions mean has grown with them (Jelescu and Budde, 2017; Novikov et al., 2019; Le Bihan, 2026). Monte Carlo simulation is one of the few settings where both the microscopic tissue state and the signal are known (Hall and Alexander, 2009; Fieremans and Lee, 2018). Walkers are propagated through a numerical substrate and their magnetization evolved under a sequence, with few assumptions about the substrate, and a generation of simulators has made that routine: Camino (Hall and Alexander, 2009), MC/DC (Rafael-Patino et al., 2020), Disimpy (Kerkelä et al., 2020), the Realistic Microstructure Simulator (Lee et al., 2021), and SpinDoctor by finite elements (Li et al., 2019). The substrates have grown with them: axons packed by growth (Callaghan et al., 2020) or from spheres (Ginsburger et al., 2019), bundles with dispersion, crossings and myelin (Villarreal-Haro et al., 2023) and the glia between them (Nguyen-Duc et al., 2026), axons traced from electron microscopy with their caliber variation and undulation (Lee et al., 2020b; Lee et al., 2020a; Andersson et al., 2020), permeable membranes (Nedjati-Gilani et al., 2017), up to phantoms at the scale of a tractography benchmark (Rafael-Patiño et al., 2021a; Girard et al., 2023); and a current simulator evolves spins through an arbitrary sequence with diffusion, relaxation, permeability, susceptibility, surface relaxation and magnetization transfer active in one substrate at once (Cottaar et al., 2026). A microscopic simulation is now a numerical experiment on tissue rather than a generator of one diffusion-weighted signal.

That completeness exposes an asymmetry. Generating the stochastic histories is the expensive step, and almost nothing asked afterwards changes them. A different gradient waveform does not move the membranes a walker has already met; a different field orientation does not alter a trajectory generated in a fixed substrate; a different surface relaxivity does not change where and when a walker touched a wall. Yet the histories are either discarded once a signal is produced or kept as trajectories too large and simulator-specific to serve as a scientific object. Precomputation is well established elsewhere in microstructure imaging: matrix formalisms evaluate restricted diffusion under arbitrary waveforms from a tractable pore’s eigenmodes (Callaghan, 1997; Grebenkov, 2007; Özarslan et al., 2009; Drobnjak et al., 2011), and dictionaries make model fitting linear (Daducci et al., 2015). Monte Carlo itself has been precomputed as a signal library (Rensonnet et al., 2019; Nedjati-Gilani et al., 2017), which keeps the acquisition with it: a new sequence is a new library. Monte Carlo poses a different question: its value lies in substrates and physics with no compact analytical object, so the object kept must come from the stochastic simulation itself and be the physics, not one of its signals.

This sounds like caching, but a simulation is not easily cached. If keeping the histories were enough, DiSCo would have shared its trajectories with its meshes, and a multiphysics simulator would ship each spin’s path and what it met beside its signals (Cottaar et al., 2026); neither does, because a trajectory dump is neither small (DiSCo’s own walk, kept at every step, would be 1.2 PB; Table 4), nor readable by anyone else, nor scalable to a brain. A persistent object others can reuse needs three contributions, two theoretical and one infrastructural, and this paper makes them: 1. Encoding. Which quantities of the simulation an acquisition can never change, so that they and only they are stored, and how to compress them into a dense form without losing accuracy for the questions asked of them afterwards, with a certificate that says so. 2. Replaying. How every later question, another sequence, another scanner, a rotated substrate, a different tissue, is posed in that same compressed space, so that the dense object is queried without ever being expanded back into the trajectories it came from. 3. Sharing. How such objects are certified, shared, queried by anyone and extended in place, so a substrate’s persistent microphysics is computed once and never again.

These contributions rest on a contract. A stored microphysics is reusable only inside a precise vocabulary of what was simulated: which pools of which substrate a walker can occupy, which walls it can meet and with what properties, and which sources produce the field it samples, so that the simulation is set up in exactly one way from its description; how that record is represented, so that every later question knows what it holds and what may be done with it; and the same again one level up, from one stored substrate to an image built of many. I write these contracts down as an open specification independent of any simulator, one document each for the substrate, the stored microphysics, the acquisition and the image (Fick, 2026g); what follows is one implementation of it. This paper is therefore not another simulator. A replay pack sits after the simulation: any engine that saves its walkers’ paths can write one, and the engine of Sec. 3.2 is the one whose channels could be checked one by one against closed forms and two other simulators (Cottaar et al., 2026; Rafael-Patino et al., 2020).

papers.title: Uniqueness results for the exterior Dirichlet and Neumann problem in two dimensions for the Euler-Lagrange equations of variational integrals with linear growth
papers.abstract: We consider solutions $u, v:\Omega\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{N}$ of the Euler-Lagrange equations associated to the variational integral $\int_{\Omega}f(\nabla u)dx$, where $\Omega$ is an exterior domain in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ e.g., the complement of a disk or a half plane, and the density $f$ is of linear growth. Among other things we show that $u|_{\partial\Omega}=v|_{\partial\Omega}$ together with the boundedness of $u-v$ yields that $u=v$ on the entire domain.

papers.title: Another Application of the Alternating Map: Time-and-Band Limiting
papers.abstract: We use Castillo's dual formulation of classicality for the alternating map to reduce polynomial time-and-band limiting to two scalar problems. The reconstruction preserves polynomial cutoffs, multipliers and concentration forms. It recovers the symmetric Dunkl constructions of Castro and Gr\"unbaum and applies to continuous and discrete inputs. Scalar recurrences avoid moment factorizations; positive integrals and residual bounds control the accuracy of the concentration values.

papers.title: A Self-Generated Floor on Adam's $\varepsilon$: Evidence from Power-Law Matrix Sensing
papers.abstract: In nonconvex Burer--Monteiro low-rank matrix sensing of $U^\ast \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times D}$ under power-law covariance $\Sigma = \mathrm{diag}(j^{-s})_{j=1}^V$, the precision-wall approximation predicts that Adam stalls when the smallest non-gauge Hessian eigenvalue drops below its denominator floor, giving $s^\ast(V,D) = [\log(1/\varepsilon_{\mathrm{eff}}) - \log V]/\log(VD) + \delta_{\mathrm{Adam}}$. If $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{eff}}$ were set by $\varepsilon_0$, lowering $\varepsilon_0$ from $10^{-10}$ to $10^{-12}$ would raise $s^\ast$ by $0.95\text{--}1.33$. Instead, across six values of $\varepsilon_0$ two decades apart, $10^{-2}$ to $10^{-12}$, the boundary follows the $\varepsilon_0$ slope down to $10^{-6}$, bends near $10^{-8}$, and is flat below $10^{-8}$, while warm-started L-BFGS and Gauss--Newton reach machine precision on stalled instances. We trace this saturation to a self-generated dynamical floor $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{dyn}} \propto \alpha$: high-curvature modes oscillate persistently near the adaptive edge of stability with amplitude $\propto \alpha(1-\beta_1)/(1+\beta_1)$ and leak gradient fluctuations of scale $\kappa\alpha$ into rare modes via measurement coupling, pinning $\sqrt{\hat{v}_V} \approx \kappa\alpha \gg \varepsilon_0$. Fitting a single threshold-crossing wall parameter $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{dyn}} = 4.76\times 10^{-9}$ (with the detection lag frozen at its companion calibration) predicts the saturated failure boundary for $D \ge 4$ across five $(V,D)$ scales to RMS $0.098$ (breaking down at $D = 2$), while shrinking $\varepsilon_0$ below $10^{-8}$ is ineffective and lowering the step size $\alpha$ reduces the floor directly.

papers.title: Efficient Lempel-Ziv Prediction with the Run-Length BWT
papers.abstract: Lempel-Ziv Plurality (LZP) is an algorithm of Kosoy that predicts the next symbol of a string by using its Lempel-Ziv factorization, and makes at most $O(z\log n)$ mistakes on every string of length $n$ with $z$ LZ77 phrases. We give efficient online implementations of LZP and of a new variant of it. Our first implementation maintains a run-length encoded Burrows-Wheeler transform (RLBWT) of the reversed history. It implements LZP, uses $O(z\log z\log^2 n)$ bits, and has worst-case update and prediction times $O(\log z+\log\log n)$ and $O(\sigma(\log z+\log\log n))$, respectively, where $\sigma$ is the size of the alphabet. This is an exponential improvement over Kosoy's implementation, whose update time is $O(z\log^7 n)$. We then introduce the Lempel-Ziv Majority (LZM) predictor, which has the same mistake bound and update time, and predicts in $O(1)$ time independently of $\sigma$. These two predictors accept new symbols at any time, without knowing the alphabet in advance. For an alphabet known in advance, a different data structure gives $O(\sigma(1+\log z/\log\log n))$ time per symbol, which is constant when $\sigma=O(1)$ and $z=\mathrm{polylog}(n)$.

Online sequence prediction is a classical problem in machine learning and algorithms. A predictor reads a sequence one symbol at a time, each time guessing the next symbol, then reading the true symbol and updating its state. What one would like is a single algorithm that is at once computationally efficient, general-purpose (able to learn a wide range of patterns from many domains), and equipped with a formal mistake bound that guarantees a small number of prediction mistakes for the sequences we care about. Unfortunately, we do not know of any predictor that satisfies all three properties.

A predictor reads a sequence one symbol at a time, each time guessing the next symbol, then reading the true symbol and updating its state. What one would like is a single algorithm that is at once computationally efficient, general-purpose (able to learn a wide range of patterns from many domains), and equipped with a formal mistake bound that guarantees a small number of prediction mistakes for the sequences we care about. Unfortunately, we do not know of any predictor that satisfies all three properties.

The theoretical gold standard for sequence prediction is Solomonoff induction (Hutter et al., 2024), which gives higher weight to sequences with small Kolmogorov complexity: those generated by short computer programs. This predictor satisfies the second and third requirements, with guaranteed mistake bounds on all computable data; however, Solomonoff induction is itself uncomputable, as is the notion of Kolmogorov complexity it is based on. In order to build efficient predictors, we should relax the notion of string complexity to simpler patterns that are easier to recognize efficiently.

A natural repetitiveness measure is the size of the LZ77 parse: for a string xx, z⁡(x)z(x) is defined to be the number of phrases in its LZ77 factorization. This measure captures highly repetitive strings, which can be built by reusing and copying previous terms. The broader Lempel-Ziv approach was in fact first proposed as a computationally tractable stand-in for Kolmogorov complexity (Lempel & Ziv, 1976), and it has considerable expressive power: many rich families of deterministic sequences studied in combinatorics on words (Allouche & Shallit, 2003), such as automatic sequences, Sturmian words and many morphic sequences, have LZ77 parse size only logarithmic in their length (Kosoy, 2026; Navarro, 2022), and are therefore well-predicted by any algorithm whose error scales with zz. Predicting strings with small z⁡(x)z(x) well can thus serve as a computable toy analogue of the Solomonoff ideal.

Our first contribution removes this cost. Rather than storing the LZ77 factorization explicitly, we maintain a run-length encoded Burrows-Wheeler transform (RLBWT) of the reversed history. In this representation, all occurrences of a given phrase form a single contiguous interval, and the symbols that follow them can be counted efficiently using rank queries. Extending the current phrase by one symbol is a single incremental update. This implements LZP, while reducing the time of a single update to O⁡(log⁡z+log⁡log⁡n)O(\log z+\log\log n).

Our second contribution changes the prediction rule itself to make prediction faster. LZP prediction calculates the exact plurality in a range by iterating over all distinct symbols, costing an extra factor of the alphabet size σ\sigma. We define a weaker prediction rule that is only guaranteed to predict a symbol if it has over half of the votes. This allows prediction to run as fast as updates, and precalculating prediction makes prediction time O⁡(1)O(1).

Universal prediction of individual sequences has long been connected to Lempel-Ziv parsing. Feder et al. (1992) give a randomized LZ78-based predictor and bound its asymptotic expected fraction of mistakes on every infinite binary sequence. We instead consider finite mistake bounds in terms of the number of LZ77 phrases. Kosoy (2026) introduced LZP and proved such a bound, within a framework of stringological sequence prediction that is developed further in Kosoy (2026a); Kosoy (2026b).

papers.title: Graphs Have Structure: Declarative Manifolds, 3D Z-Order Monoid Roll-ups, and Zero-Simulation Visual Analytics in a Graph DBMS
papers.abstract: Every real-world graph is embedded in an ambient structural manifold: proteins fold in Euclidean space ($R^3$), telecom networks sit on a planetary surface ($S^2 \times R$), and ontologies and calendars form discrete subsumption posets ($(V, \sqsubseteq)$). Yet property graph databases treat node coordinates as opaque payload scalars, leave spatial proximity edges unindexed, and force visualizers into $O(V^2)$ client-side force-directed simulations that destroy true geometry and truncate hierarchy roll-ups. We elevate ambient manifold structure to a first-class primitive in Samyama Graph. First, we introduce a declarative and auto-detected structural convention contract (samyama.structure/1) persisted in .sgsnap headers that binds node labels to Euclidean 3D, Geo-Spherical, Causal Spacetime, or Poset Hierarchy manifolds. Second, we show that both discrete posets (via Order-Embedded Hierarchy $[tin, tout]$ DFS intervals) and continuous 3D manifolds (via a 63-bit 3D Morton Z-order Structural-Geometric Index, SGI) reduce regional aggregation to 1D rank-interval monoid folds answered directly from index-resident Fenwick trees (SUM, COUNT) and Segment Trees (MIN, MAX). At $100,000$ 3D nodes, SGI builds in $28.14$ ms and answers Morton-interval SUM and MAX roll-ups in $0.048\,\mu$s and $0.104\,\mu$s---$8,345.1\times$ and $3,824.4\times$ faster than property scans. Third, we introduce 3D voxel-hashed virtual contact edges weighted by Topological--Geometric Stress $\sigma(u,v) = d_{graph}(u,v) / d_{manifold}(u,v)$ to isolate long-range tertiary folds, plus manifold-guided $A^*$ shortest-path search that cuts explored states by up to $3.80\times$ over Dijkstra. Fourth, we replace client layout simulation with server-computed 3D Cone-Tree/Ribbon coordinates and a non-WebGL 2.5D Isometric projection with painter's-order depth sorting and sub-millisecond Level-of-Detail (LoD) macro-cuts.

papers.title: Improved lower bounds for the kissing number in dimensions 49 to 61
papers.abstract: We give explicit kissing configurations in R^d for every d = 49, ..., 61. The lower bound is improved over the best previously published value in all thirteen dimensions, by margins from 232 to 159,220 points and by 506,461 points in total. The configurations are obtained from the antipodal block lift of Yang et al. applied to the 52,416,000-point minimal shell of the extremal even unimodular lattice P_48p, using a class of 7,193 minimal lines and, in each dimension, a kissing configuration of R^k (k <= 15) with the largest available number of antipodal pairs. Two ingredients are new. The published class of 7,077 lines is grown to 7,193 by local search in three stages, as a sequence of exchanges between candidate lines and class lines; and the point count, which equals 52,416,000 + 2S + 2t with t the number of antipodal pairs and S the size of the union of t isometric images of the class, is maximised as a maximum-coverage problem by greedy search with iterated local search over pools of 4,000 automorphic images, reaching 92-100% of the trivial bound 7,193t. All results are verified in exact integer arithmetic, and the certificates are distributed with the code. Code and data: https://github.com/dimkadimon/KissingNumbers
papers.intro:
How many equal spheres can touch a given sphere, all of the same size and without overlapping? This question was put to Isaac Newton by David Gregory in 1694. Newton held that the answer is 1212; Gregory suspected 1313. Newton was right, but a complete proof took more than three centuries [Sch53]. The quantity is now called the kissing number K⁡(d)K(d): the largest number of non-overlapping unit spheres in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} that can all touch one central unit sphere, an arrangement of points on the unit sphere with pairwise distances at least one.

papers.title: Conditional Calibration Contracts under Coupled Load: A Branch-Aware Audit of Switched Inference
papers.abstract: Bursty serving changes both queue states and the population selected for each model. We study conditional calibration contracts as a specification to be validated, rather than a certified property of an existing router. CA-MHD combines load-coupled distillation, closed-loop replay and a cost-informed Schmitt router in a discrete-event simulator with a hardware service table. Across 40 cells (ten training seeds and four content-load coupling levels), we distinguish the original teacher, frozen wide heads on an adapted trunk, and the narrow student. A common teacher-trajectory audit has median absolute student-teacher deficit 0.06 percentage points, but does not certify the student-selected deployment support. Historical results use a kernel correctness gap, not the published SmoothECE; we separately prove selected-branch composition for a residual functional at a common fixed scale. The deployed wide branch has lower ordinal accuracy than the original teacher in all 40 cells. Same-checkpoint student-only serving has lower historical ordinal gap in 27/40 cells; routing also exposes violation tails up to 17.5 percent. Student p99 latency remains above the 1.5 ms target. Retrospective temporal recalibration improves the ordinal gap in 39/40 cells, but causal delayed-label availability is unverified and no incremental per-mode benefit is detected after multiplicity adjustment. An in-sample CUSUM detects 30/40 checkpoint changes at five historical false alarms, with no prospective false-alarm guarantee. These findings support a branch-aware audit and a scoped negative result, not demonstrated routing superiority. Independent budgets, selected-support validation and net utility under a satisfied SLA remain open.
papers.intro:
Elastic inference trades predictive performance against serving cost (Crankshaw et al., 2017; Romero et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2023). Under bursty load, the serving policy also changes queue history, batch sizes and which events reach each predictor. A training-time calibration audit need not describe that selected population. Moreover, a branch named “teacher” need not retain the original teacher when distillation updates a shared trunk. These are specification and measurement problems before they are arguments for switching.

The existing campaign provides descriptive audits, not a validated prospective contract. Calibration, accuracy, ordinal utility and latency are separate obligations: equal accuracy does not imply equal probability quality, and lower latency than the teacher does not imply SLA compliance.

papers.title: Bounded Retained History in a Proxy Flow Replay: A Mixed Predictive Pilot and an Allocation Study
papers.abstract: We examine bounded retained history through a frozen predictive pilot and a subsequent allocation study on a curated UNSW-NB15 flow mirror. Both use an artificial release-order replay based on raw ltime ticks, with equal-tick records querying a shared prior-group state. In the pilot, the model with added retained relational features had lower reconnaissance recall than the current-flow-plus-counters baseline (43.66% versus 47.84%) and lower benign false-positive rate (3.63% versus 6.68%) at separately frozen operating thresholds, together with lower AUROC. This mixed result did not establish a predictive advantage. A development-only audit subsequently found that capacity eviction dominated expiration in the 256-record, 300-tick FIFO state, with a median completed record lifetime of 11 ticks. A protocol specified before its single execution, but after the pilot and post-hoc mechanism audit, compared five label-blind retention arms on the already-used development trace. Its primary equal-source endpoint averaged retained/reference ratios for service-expanded source out-degree and source-destination service diversity. Source-balanced retention at 256 records exceeded FIFO-256 by a pooled endpoint difference of 0.440738 and met the prespecified materiality and subblock rule. Crucially, the event-weighted ratios for both quantities decreased relative to FIFO-256: the result is specific to the equal-source weighting objective and does not establish uniformly improved retention. The study supplies neither evidence of detection improvement nor an explanation of the pilot result. Reused data, concentrated reconnaissance support, proxy timing, and the absence of a qualified independent corpus bound the interpretation.

papers.title: The Ehrlich--Aberth root finder is not generally convergent
papers.abstract:
We show that the well-known Ehrlich--Aberth root finding method is not generally convergent. More precisely, we show that there is an open subset of polynomials of any degree $d\ge 7$, and an open subset of initial conditions, such that the iteration of the Ehrlich--Aberth method converges to an attracting periodic cycle of period $4$, rather than to a vector of roots. The proof is constructive in the sense that we present explicit values for the polynomial and the $4$-cycle.
  The search is highly non-trivial: we found no attracting cycles for lower degrees/periods, and the size of the attracting domain relative to a ``unit cube'' in the space of polynomials and starting vectors is on the order of $10^{-127}$.

papers.title: Detailed Derivation of The Backpropagation Algorithm
papers.abstract: Backpropagation is the standard method for computing the gradients that train neural networks, but it is usually presented in a compact vector form that skips the intermediate steps. This tutorial derives backpropagation step by step for a fully connected feedforward network with sigmoid activations and a squared-error loss. Using a running example with three layers, we first differentiate the error with respect to a single weight by following its path through the network with the chain rule. We then show how summing over all paths leads to the error terms $\delta$ and to the four general backpropagation equations in matrix form. Every term is annotated with its dimensions, so each equation can be checked for consistency. The derivation is then extended to $m$ training examples, where the weight gradients become a single matrix product and the bias term corresponds to broadcasting. It is also extended to mini-batch gradient descent, including why the gradient of a mini-batch estimates the full gradient. Batch and mini-batch training are both given as algorithms. Finally, each equation is linked to the corresponding line of a NumPy implementation trained on the AHDBase dataset of handwritten Arabic digits, and the complete code is included.

papers.title: Fiber-Connectivity of Almost-Toric Systems in Four-Dimension
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study the fiber connectivity of proper almost-toric systems $\Phi$ on connected four-dimensional symplectic manifolds. Using Morse--Kirwan theory, we establish three sufficient conditions for fiber connectivity. These results generalize and extend the fiber connectivity results of Pelayo, Ratiu, and Vu Ngoc (2015) by relaxing some of their hypotheses.

papers.title: Concise-9B: Removing the Slack from a Reasoning Model's Thinking
papers.abstract: Reasoning models answer better when they think longer, but a thinking trace keeps going well after its answer has formed. We measure this slack in Qwen3.5-9B and remove most of it with concise self-training: two rounds of on-policy rejection-sampling fine-tuning that keep the shortest correct samples, plus a small share of answer-synthesis targets, giving Concise-9B. On 8,983 held-out problems (competition and hard mathematics, SuperGPQA, a five-area confirmation set and MMLU-Pro), Concise-9B generates 0.66x the tokens of Qwen3.5-9B at a 32K thinking budget, with accuracy equivalent within +/-1 point (-0.20 [-0.77, +0.36] points). Forcing each trace on the hard and confirmation sets to answer every 2,048 thinking tokens, we find that 54-64% of Qwen3.5-9B's thinking tokens come after the point from which every forced answer equals the final one (41-48% for Concise-9B). Stopping there would keep every answer at 0.35-0.44x the base model's tokens, but finding that point takes hindsight: stopping when three consecutive forced answers agree costs the base model 2.4-9.2 points. Concise self-training removes slack without that cost: 86% [83, 90] of the thinking tokens it saves come after the answer has formed. It has a limit: with traces continued to 80K tokens, Concise-9B solves 25 fewer of 1,276 hard problems (-25 [-49, -1]), mostly in competition mathematics. The measurement also yields a cheap commit signal for adaptive sampling that matched two-sample escalation within +/-1 point at 0.67x its tokens in a pre-registered test. Results on Qwen3.5-4B, on which the recipe was developed, and a replication on Olmo-3-7B-Think suggest that the saving depends on how verbose the base model is.
papers.intro:
Reasoning models trade tokens for accuracy. A longer thinking budget lets a model keep reasoning where it would otherwise stop, often correcting itself, and this sequential test-time scaling is a large part of why thinking models are strong [24, 13]; more generally, test-time compute spent well can let a model outperform a much larger one [34]. It is also expensive, and much of the expense may buy nothing: thinking models are known to keep reasoning on problems they have already solved [8, 35], and within a problem their shorter chains are more often right [14]. Two questions follow. How much of a thinking trace comes after its answer is already fixed? And can a model be trained to drop that part without losing the reasoning that the rest of the trace does?

papers.title: Two teams that cancel: a didactic analysis of a teaching progression for signed numbers from Grade 5 to Grade 7
papers.abstract: Signed numbers make learners revise what addition, subtraction and the minus sign meant for whole numbers. This paper presents the design rationale and a critical analysis of a three-level source progression for signed numbers (Grades 5-7, nominal ages 10-13), from which French-curriculum and International Baccalaureate chapters published at https://commeunjeu.org are assembled. One representation is presented first and taken up throughout: an integer is drawn as a collection of positive and negative units, a positive and a negative unit forming a zero pair that leaves nothing. An integer therefore has many drawings, which makes visible the construction of the integers as classes of pairs of natural numbers. The design hypothesis is that the gesture pupils perform with the units, inserting a zero in the form a + (-a), is shared by the subtraction of a negative number, by the worked examples that accompany the 2026 French programme, and by the derivation of the sign of a product of two negatives through distributivity; the progression does not model that product, it derives it from the zero pair, a derivation that holds only if distributivity is kept. The number line supports position, order and distance; contexts provide applications. The choices are related to the epistemological obstacles described by Glaeser, to studies of counter and number-line models, including a classroom comparison in which a path model gave better results than chips, immediately and five weeks later, and to the French and IB curricula. A block-level audit of the dated source documents found the representation absent from the first level, no exercise asking pupils to draw, and the decisive subtraction never drawn; the revisions made after the audit are recorded. No empirical evaluation is reported; hypotheses for one are stated.
papers.intro:
Signed numbers are a turning point of school arithmetic. With them, a subtraction is always possible, adding can make a number smaller and subtracting can make it larger, the order of the magnitudes reverses below zero (−5<−2-5<-2 although 5>25>2), and the minus sign takes three roles: the operation of subtraction, the sign of a number, and the opposite of a number (Vlassis, 2004; Vlassis, 2008; Lamb et al., 2012). According to the abstract of Glaeser’s study, mathematicians needed more than fifteen centuries before the rule of signs seemed trivial (Glaeser, 1981). Research on learners is comparatively thin: a review found 47 research-journal publications on integers between 1980 and 2012 (Bishop et al., 2014).

A curriculum author meets a design problem specific to this domain. The first representation chosen for negative numbers must carry their existence, their order, addition and subtraction, and it must not stand in the way of multiplication. The didactic literature diagnoses a recurring difficulty at that last point: concrete additive models (gains and debts, rising and falling temperatures, moves along a line) serve addition, but extending them to the product of two negatives requires additional conventions and may create difficulties, up to blocking the product (Glaeser, 1981; Groupe Didactique des mathématiques, IREM d’Aquitaine, 2008; Ministère de l’Éducation nationale, de l’Enseignement supérieur et de la Recherche, 2016; Matheron et al., 2016; Glière, 2025).

This paper documents and analyses one answer to that problem, a three-level progression written as bilingual (English and French) lessons and exercise sets. One representation is presented first and taken up throughout: an integer is a collection of units of two kinds, positive and negative, and one positive unit with one negative unit forms a zero pair that leaves nothing. The paper’s thesis is not that this representation shows everything; it is that it makes one gesture available to the pupil, inserting a zero in the form a+(−a)a+(-a), and that the same gesture underlies the subtraction of a negative number and the derivation of the sign of a product of two negatives by distributivity (Figure 6). The design rests on five principles: (i) an integer has several drawings, and every balanced collection represents zero; the opposite is the same units of the other kind (Section 4); (ii) adding and subtracting are gestures on the units, and subtracting a number that is not there begins by inserting a zero (Section 5); (iii) the sign of a product of two negatives is derived from the zero pair by distributivity, not read on a model of the product (Section 6); (iv) each representation is kept for what it carries: situations for the encounter, the number line for position, order and distance, the units for equivalence and compensation; and the drawing is abandoned when the rules can stand alone (Section 7); (v) the drawing comes first, then the chain of equalities, written line for line under it (Section 8).

The paper is a design rationale and a curriculum analysis, the companion of a study of a fraction progression by the same author (Tariel-Adam, 2026), whose method it shares. Like a hypothetical learning trajectory (Simon, 1995; Clements and Sarama, 2004), the progression embodies learning goals, an order of activities and hypotheses about learning; the paper makes them explicit and confronts them with the literature and with the documents that implement them. Its method borrows the a priori analysis of didactic engineering (Artigue, 1990; Artigue, 1992) at the level of global choices (the representation, the order of meanings) and, in Section 5.3, at the level of one task and its didactic variables. No classroom experiment is reported; statements about learners are taken from the cited literature or presented as design hypotheses. None of the five principles is new taken alone: the counter or “charge” model is classical (Battista, 1983), and the derivation of the sign rule by distributivity is the route of the French official documents (Ministère de l’Éducation nationale, de l’Enseignement supérieur et de la Recherche, 2016; Ministère de l’Éducation nationale, 2026b). What the paper contributes is the articulation of one representation across three levels, the identification of the gesture that links its additive and multiplicative uses, the explicit statement of where the drawing stops, and a confrontation of the stated design with the materials, which led to revisions made before this paper was written (Section 11.3).

papers.title: On the exponential Diophantine equation $\left(P_{n}^{(k)}\right)^{x}+\left(P_{r}^{(k)}\right)^{x}=P_{m}^{(k)}$
papers.abstract: The Pell numbers satisfy $P_n^2+P_{n+1}^2=P_{2n+1}$, and Bravo, Luca and Pomeo recently found all the cases in which the sum of the $x$-th powers of two consecutive $k$-generalized Pell numbers is again a $k$-generalized Pell number. We ask what happens when the two indices are arbitrary, that is, we solve $\big(P_n^{(k)}\big)^x+\big(P_r^{(k)}\big)^x=P_m^{(k)}$ in positive integers $k\ge2$, $n\ge r$, $m$ and $x$. The answer is that nothing new appears: apart from $1^x+1^x=2$, every solution has consecutive indices. The proof combines linear forms in logarithms with an auxiliary Fibonacci equation which does not depend on $k$, and, for large $k$, with the fact that the dominant root of the sequence is very close to $\varphi^2$. For the reduction step, the method of Dujella and Peth\H{o} fails for large indices and has to be replaced by a criterion of Legendre type.

papers.title: Improved criteria for geometric properties of confluent hypergeometric functions
papers.abstract: In this paper, we establish sufficient conditions for several geometric properties of confluent hypergeometric functions. Using differential subordination techniques, we derive parameter conditions ensuring lower bounds for the real part of the confluent hypergeometric function and sectorial subordination of its derivative. We also obtain criteria for strong convexity and strong starlikeness of prescribed order. In addition, we investigate the close-to-convexity and starlikeness of the confluent hypergeometric functions. Particular cases yield corresponding results for generalized Laguerre polynomials. The obtained criteria are compared with existing sufficient conditions, and their implications for the geometric theory of special functions are discussed.

The geometric properties of confluent hypergeometric functions have been investigated using differential subordination and coefficient techniques. Merkes and Scott [12] studied starlikeness properties of hypergeometric functions, while Miller and Mocanu [14] derived sufficient conditions for confluent hypergeometric functions to have positive real part, starlike, and convex in Δ\Delta. Ponnusamy and Vuorinen [15] obtained parameter conditions for univalence, convexity, and close-to-convexity. Bohra and Ravichandran [3] investigated strong starlikeness and strong convexity. Confluent hypergeometric functions also arise in problems from mathematical physics, engineering, and applied sciences; see [1, 2, 9, 10, 11, 19]. Further results on their geometric properties and related hypergeometric functions can be found in [5, 15, 18].
