papers.title: On the exponential Diophantine equation $\left(P_{n+1}^{(k)}\right)^{x}-\left(P_{n-1}^{(k)}\right)^{x}=2P_{m}^{(k)}$
papers.abstract: For the Pell numbers one has $P_{n+1}-P_{n-1}=2P_n$ and $P_{n+1}^2-P_{n-1}^2=2P_{2n}$. We look for all the solutions of $\big(P_{n+1}^{(k)}\big)^x-\big(P_{n-1}^{(k)}\big)^x=2P_m^{(k)}$ in positive integers $k\ge2$, $n$, $m$, $x$, where $P^{(k)}$ is the $k$-generalized Pell sequence. We prove that for $k=2$ the two identities above give all the solutions, and that for $k\ge3$ the only solutions are $(n,m,x)=(1,1,1),(1,2,2),(2,2,1)$. In contrast with the analogous equation for $k$-generalized Fibonacci numbers, there are no parametric families of solutions. The proof uses an auxiliary equation with Fibonacci numbers which does not depend on $k$, Matveev's lower bound for linear forms in logarithms, the reduction of Dujella and Peth\H{o}, and, for large $k$, the fact that the dominant root of $P^{(k)}$ is very close to $\varphi^2$.

papers.title: On a certain system of discrete equations with the Laurent property
papers.abstract: We consider a system of two bilinear discrete equations with four parameters. It defines a certain discrete dynamical system. Each of its solutions is represented as a pair of sequences. It is proved that for arbitrary initial data all terms of both sequences are Laurent polynomials in the initial data with integer coefficients. This property is called the Laurent property. The proof relies on an established connection between the system and the Somos-5 equation. It is shown that both components of the solution satisfy the same equation with the same parameters. To prove the main theorem, the strong Laurent property for the Somos-5 equation is used, which makes it possible to control negative powers of the initial data. An analogue of this property is obtained directly for the system under study. As corollaries, sufficient conditions for the integrality of solutions are found. An example of a pair of integer sequences illustrating the theorem on the strong Laurent property is given.

papers.title: Does a Norwegian further-trained model give more outdated legal values than its base model? A preregistered paired comparison of Borealis 2 and Gemma 4
papers.abstract: We compare how often two released language models give outdated numeric values from Norwegian statutes and regulations: NbAiLab/borealis2-26b-a4b-preview (Borealis 2), which the National Library of Norway further trained from google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it (Gemma 4), and Gemma 4 itself. The study was preregistered (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23858965) and uses the closed norregel benchmark, scored deterministically against a value history. On the 411 of 503 primary items where both models gave an interpretable answer, Borealis 2 alone was outdated on 10 items and Gemma 4 alone on 11 (d = -0.2 percentage points, 95% cluster bootstrap interval [-2.7, +2.5], exact one-sided McNemar p = 0.668). By the preregistered rule this is no effect of interest: the whole interval lies within the smallest effect of interest of +/-10 percentage points. Among the secondary measures, only the share of answers giving a value that took effect after the question date differs after Holm correction; Gemma 4 gave such answers more often. An exploratory comparison of two smaller Borealis models had no discordant pairs and is not informative. The design compares released models and does not isolate the effect of any part of their training.
papers.intro:
The Simula CAISS audit of Borealis 1, which is built on Gemma 3, points to outdated legal values without measuring them [9]. On printed p. 11 (PDF page 12) of the report dated 25 June 2026 it states: “Part of the advantage is parametric knowledge of Norwegian rules and thresholds, which drift as the rules change; the rubric scores confident correct recall as a pass, yet the same behaviour becomes the confident-hallucination failure mode 3 (§4.1) once a recalled fact is stale, so the comparative ranking is a snapshot.” The present study measures one part of this for Borealis 2: on the same dated questions, does the further-trained model give outdated values more often than the model it is built on?

papers.title: A Sharp Mutual Information Bound for Binary Pairs
papers.abstract: We prove a sharp upper bound on the mutual information between two binary random variables in terms of their distribution-dependent KL contraction coefficient. This resolves the binary-pair conjecture of Anantharam, Gohari, Kamath, and Nair. Equality holds if and only if the variables are independent or form a doubly symmetric binary source. The proof uses supporting tangents of an entropy curve to vary the input distribution and the channel while preserving the contraction coefficient. Together with tensorization and data processing, the result also bounds the mutual information between binary outputs obtained separately from two correlated observation sequences. When the observation pairs are independent copies of a finite-alphabet pair, this bound depends only on the law of one pair and not on the number of observations.

papers.title: Dynamics of Transversal Matroids
papers.abstract: We propose a way of generating matroids by randomly picking indicator vectors, and since we will see that it mostly gives uniform matroids, which are transversal, we then look at randomly generated transversal matroids. In both models we also investigate threshold phenomena of certain monotone increasing properties. Non-monotone properties of transversal matroids will also be investigated. Moreover, we are going to see how to spot circuits of a transversal matroid from its bipartite graph presentation. In the last Chapter, we have a survey of the characterization of transversal matroids that admit acyclic bipartite presentations. We will also investigate when we can simplify a presentation for a transversal matroid.

papers.title: Right Ranking, Wrong Scale: Reproducing the Robotic World Model's Dynamics Model and Testing the Uncertainty of Its Follow-up
papers.abstract: We reimplement the dynamics model of the Robotic World Model (RWM) and test the uncertainty estimate that its follow-up, RWM-U, uses to penalize reward in offline policy optimization. Our implementation matches the released model's gradients. On held-out data, training on the model's own rollouts beats one-step training at the preregistered long horizon for all ten episodes, but loses on short one-step windows. RWM-U's ensemble disagreement ranks rollout errors better than forecast step (Spearman rho = 0.90 at 100 steps), yet its spread substantially understates error: one-sigma coverage on the released checkpoint is 4.6% at 100 steps, versus 68% for a calibrated Gaussian. Rolling ensemble members on their own predictions raises coverage to 33%. The implemented squared-error loss on sampled predictions drives each member's variance toward zero. A horizon-specific rescaling restores one-sigma coverage under leave-one-episode-out evaluation, but not two-sigma coverage. We also identify two defects in the released evaluation pipeline. The study covers one robot, one gait and one dataset; it trains no policy.
papers.intro:
Offline model-based reinforcement learning trains a robot’s policy inside a learned simulator. The Robotic World Model (RWM; Li, Krause and Hutter) learns such a simulator for a quadruped from recorded robot data, and its follow-up, RWM-U, adds an ensemble of predictors whose disagreement penalises the reward, in the manner of MOPO (Yu et al., 2020). A policy can be trusted inside the simulator only as far as the simulator’s errors are known, so the penalty has two jobs: to rank where the model is more likely to be wrong, and to say by how much. We test whether it does either, on the released code and checkpoint and on models we rebuilt from the papers’ descriptions.

papers.title: Risk-Constrained Evaluation of Financial Document Recognition: A Formal Framework for Evidence, Critical Errors, and Selective Automation
papers.abstract: Financial document recognition is commonly evaluated using character and word error rates, which do not adequately represent the consequences of errors in financial workflows. This paper formalizes financial document recognition as a risk-constrained evidence-recovery problem. It defines typed, evidence-linked financial facts and a multi-layer quality model spanning text, layout, tables, fields, semantic relations, calibration, robustness, and operational performance. It introduces non-compensatory acceptance gates based on upper confidence bounds for critical-field errors, and formulates selective automation as a constrained risk-coverage problem with review-capacity limits. The paper also specifies annotation requirements, leakage-resistant benchmark splits, statistical estimands, and a reproducibility card. Formal propositions establish why aggregate scores cannot certify critical-field reliability and why zero observed errors do not imply zero risk. A synthetic example illustrates the decision rule. The work is theoretical; no empirical benchmark or model performance claim is presented.
papers.intro:
Financial institutions and enterprises process documents whose content is both visually heterogeneous and semantically consequential. A bank statement may contain transaction dates, descriptions, debit and credit columns, balances, account identifiers, and running-balance relationships. An invoice may contain supplier identity, tax identifiers, line items, tax rates, discounts, currency, payment terms, and a payable total. A financial report may combine narrative disclosures, multi-level tables, footnotes, units, comparative periods, and negative values represented with parentheses. OCR is frequently the first machine-readable transformation in these workflows.

The common practice of reporting a single character error rate (CER) or word error rate (WER) is insufficient for this domain. Edit-distance metrics treat all character substitutions similarly, whereas the operational impact of an error depends on its semantic role and downstream use. Confusing a letter in a narrative paragraph is not equivalent to changing ‘1,250.00’ to ‘12,500.00’, dropping a minus sign, shifting a value from the debit column to the credit column, or associating a tax amount with the wrong invoice. Document understanding research has established the importance of layout, relations, and visual context in addition to text recognition [2, 5, 6, 7]. Recent financial-specific work has also highlighted fact-level evaluation for numerical, temporal, entity, and financial-concept fidelity [22].

A system is useful only to the extent that it faithfully recovers information visible in the source, preserves the structure that gives the information meaning, expresses uncertainty when evidence is inadequate, and supports safe downstream processing. The proposed framework therefore evaluates a sequence of increasingly semantic capabilities while retaining component-level diagnostics.

The framework is designed to answer six questions: 1. How accurately does a system detect and transcribe all visible text, including financial symbols and low-frequency identifiers? 2. Does it preserve spatial and logical structure, particularly tables, merged headers, row associations, and reading order? 3. Does it recover typed financial fields with correct values, units, signs, dates, currencies, and entity associations? 4. Can it distinguish what is visually supported from what is inferred, normalised, or unavailable? 5. Are its confidence estimates meaningful enough to support abstention, escalation, and human review? 6. Does its quality remain acceptable across document categories, acquisition conditions, languages, institutions, and operational loads?

The paper makes five methodological contributions. First, it specifies a typed, evidence-linked representation of financial facts that separates what is visible from what is normalized or inferred. Second, it defines a layered evaluation vector and a risk functional that preserve diagnostic information rather than collapsing all errors into a single lexical score. Third, it formalizes a non-compensatory acceptance rule based on prespecified critical-field constraints and uncertainty bounds. Fourth, it casts abstention and human review as a selective-automation problem with explicit risk, coverage, and review-capacity constraints. Fifth, it specifies a benchmark protocol designed to make these quantities estimable and reproducible. These are formalizations and design principles, not claims of a new OCR model or a validated empirical benchmark. The framework applies to OCR-dependent pipelines and OCR-free document models; both must provide output that can be evaluated against the same visual evidence contract [7].

papers.title: McKean-Vlasov flights without moments: well-posedness, propagation of chaos and a critical threshold for law-dependent jumps
papers.abstract: We study McKean-Vlasov equations driven by an isotropic $2s$-stable L{\'e}vy noise, $s\in(0,1)$, whose solutions may have no finite mean, with coefficients that are Lipschitz with respect to a bounded Wasserstein-type distance. When the jump noise is additive, we prove strong well-posedness for every initial law and every $s$, without any moment assumption, and propagation of chaos at the rate $N^{-1/2}$ for kernel interactions. When the size of the jumps depends on the law, we prove the same results for $s>1/2$, and we show by an example that uniqueness fails for every $s<1/2$. The value $s=1/2$ thus separates well-posedness from non-uniqueness; the critical case itself remains open. These results answer, for stable noise, the question of uniqueness without moments raised by Jourdain, M{\'e}l{\'e}ard and Woyczy{\'n}ski and by Cavallazzi.

papers.title: Zero-shot time-series foundation models against the Khepri v1.5 baselines for 96-hour carbon-intensity forecasts in nine Nordic bidding zones: a preregistered comparison
papers.abstract: We compare three zero-shot time-series foundation models (Timestral-5M, Timestral-209M and Chronos-2, 8192-hour context, no covariates) with the Khepri v1.5 SARIMA and GBM baselines, with their code and hyperparameters unchanged, for 96-hour forecasts of hourly carbon intensity in the Nordic bidding zones NO1-NO5 and SE1-SE4. The design, the analysis code and a minimum detectable effect (MDE) were timestamped before any foundation-model forecast by an OpenTimestamps proof (Bitcoin-confirmed) and the GPG-signed tag prereg-v1; the proofs are archived in Zenodo (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23881315). The preregistration was also submitted to OSF Registries 2026-11-02 07:49 UTC (osf.io/hncz5; embargo requested, pending OSF approval). On the 2025 test (361 daily origins, contamination not ruled out) all three models have a lower zone-averaged MAPE than both baselines, by 0.952 to 1.347 percentage points (Diebold-Mariano with the Harvey-Leybourne-Newbold correction, all p < 0.0001), and each beats SARIMA in 9 of 9 zones. On a post-release holdout of 14 origins from 2026-10-16 the point estimates have the same sign (0.729 to 1.326 percentage points lower), but all lie within the preregistered MDE of 2.989 points and are reported as not determined. For calibration (RQ4) the preregistration locked a Diebold-Mariano-HLN test on CRPS; the MDE applies to MAPE only. Holdout CRPS point estimates (n = 14) are 1.1114 (Timestral-5M), 1.0733 (Timestral-209M) and 1.1198 (Chronos-2) against 1.4165 gCO2-eq/kWh for SARIMA (each p < 0.0001). The SARIMA quantiles are constructed from the fitted model's Gaussian predictive distribution (deviation D-03), not taken from a native v1.5 forecast, so the difference may partly reflect the SARIMA intervals. The contamination indicator does not exceed its preregistered threshold for any comparison; with 14 holdout origins it has low power (HAC standard errors 0.124 to 0.360 pp).
papers.intro:
Forecasts of the carbon intensity (CI) of electricity, in grams of CO2-equivalent per kWh, have been proposed as a building block for shifting flexible electricity use to hours with lower emissions (Maji et al. 2022a).

papers.title: Buildings governed by twisted Bruhat orders
papers.abstract: This paper introduces the notion of a twisted building associated to a Coxeter system and an initial section of a reflection order. These are pairs of buildings and a map between them which depends on a twisted Bruhat order. It is proved that projection maps exist between components and that the common apartment property holds for a suitable notion of an apartment, generalising what is known for twin buildings. Several well-known examples are given, including a family of twisted buildings associated to an affine building and its fa\c{c}ades.

papers.intro:
The notion of a building was introduced by Tits in the 1950s with the aim to construct a space upon which a complex simple Lie group acts; specifically, those of exceptional type. In this context, the space is built from the parabolic subgroups and behaves locally with respect to the finite Weyl group. Examples of this kind are called spherical buildings and have numerous applications, such as Serre’s notion of GG-complete reducibility [16]. In general, one can associate a building to any Coxeter system. Most, but not all, are realised using parabolic-like subgroups of an appropriate group, e.g. parahoric subgroups for Bruhat-Tits buildings [4]. Since their inception, the definition has been recast several times, each with a different emphasis, be it apartments [18], chambers [19], or metrics [5]. A more recent formulation is the WW-metric approach [20], which focusses on a Weyl-distance map δ:X×X→W\delta:X\times X\rightarrow W satisfying some natural axioms with respect to a standard length function on the Coxeter group WW. These axioms allow one to define projection maps quickly, while apartments become trickier to establish, cf. [1, §5].

In the 1980s, twin buildings were defined and studied by Ronan and Tits. As explained in [20], one motivation for this work was the emerging theory of Kac-Moody groups. Roughly speaking, a Kac-Moody group is to an arbitrary Weyl group what a simple algebraic group is to a finite Weyl group. For infinite Weyl groups, the corresponding Kac-Moody group admits two classes of parabolic subgroup. This reflects the fact that the ambient root system admits two distinct conjugacy classes of standard positive systems. A twin building encodes these conjugacy classes with two buildings X+X_{+} and X−X_{-} of the same type, along with a map δ∗:(X+×X−)∪(X−×X+)→W\delta^{*}:(X_{+}\times X_{-})\cup(X_{-}\times X_{+})\rightarrow W satisfying a similar set of axioms as before, after replacing the standard length function with its negation. In particular, the buildings are governed by a length function opposite to the one controlling how they relate.

This article introduces a new object called a twisted building (see §3.1) which generalises the two examples above. A twisted building comprises a building XX and a satellite building XAX_{A} whose type is a Coxeter system (WA,SA)(W_{A},S_{A}) associated to an initial section AA, cf. §2.2. The buildings are related by a map δ∗:(X×XA)∪(XA×X)→W\delta^{*}:(X\times X_{A})\cup(X_{A}\times X)\rightarrow W which satisfies the same axioms again, this time replacing the standard (resp. opposite) length function with Dyer’s twisted length function [10]. Both the length function and the type of XAX_{A} depend on AA. At the extremes, when AA is empty or is the set of all reflections, one retrieves the definition of a building and a twin building, respectively. New examples appear when XX is not spherical. In particular, if XX is an affine building and XAX_{A} is a façade of XX, then a twisted building can be defined using the chimney retractions of [14]. This construction is made explicit in §4.

Twisted buildings admit projection maps just like ordinary and twin buildings. This is proved by adapting well-known arguments, first for panels (Lemma 3.8) and then to all spherical residues (Proposition 3.12). In buildings, projections exist no matter the type of the target residue. By contrast, projections between components of twin buildings are well-defined only if the target is spherical. The twisted buildings lie somewhere in the middle. They may, but not necessarily, admit projections onto non-spherical residues. A precise characterisation for existence is given with respect to the ambient initial section (Proposition 3.14). Remarkably, this sometimes allows for projections onto the whole of a non-spherical satellite building (see Corollary 4.10). The analogue of a twin apartment is defined in §3.3. It is proved that apartments are convex in a suitable sense (Lemma 3.23) and can be produced by extending a building isometry in XX (Theorem 3.25). This implies that any two chambers that lie in different components share a common twisted apartment (Corollary 3.26). The same is not true for arbitrary pairs of chambers (see Example 3.27).

papers.title: Are habitable-zone TESS Objects of Interest really there? Period resolution from the full archive
papers.abstract: TESS Objects of Interest (TOIs) seen as single or duo transits carry a catalogue period that is undefined or equal to the separation of the two events, and their insolation and any habitable-zone label inherit it. We reanalyse all 187 TOIs catalogued with P = 0 or P >= 200 d using all public TESS data through Sector 107, with a flux-based method that weights each alias by per-epoch transit likelihoods, the transit duration and a geometric prior, and tests for coherence, data edges, contamination by other planets and instrumental artefacts. It recovers 12 published periods blindly and, in injection-recovery tests, 71 per cent of periods constrained by a new transit, with no wrong period. It resolves 28 periods and fixes 8 more by exclusion. Are habitable-zone TOIs really there? Mostly not: of the 28 duo-transits that a catalogue-period criterion places in the conservative habitable zone, about two are expected to lie there, both giants, and none of the 12 planet-sized ones; those resolved are aliases of hotter planets. Conversely, habitable-zone planets hide behind missing or wrong periods: we recover three published M-dwarf examples and validate four planets with new periods, including TOI-2298 b, a 3.0 Earth-radius sub-Neptune at 146.58 d in the conservative habitable zone of a K dwarf, and TOI-6075 b, a 1.7 Earth-radius planet at 416.5 d (833 d not excluded), the second validated transiting planet smaller than 2 Earth radii with P > 1 yr. We release alias-marginalised habitable-zone probabilities for the whole sample.
papers.intro:
Transiting planets on orbits of months to years are scarce but disproportionately valuable. They probe the cool end of the sub-Neptune population, the region where atmospheres are expected to retain volatiles, and the habitable zones of Sun-like and K-type stars. Because the transit probability falls as P−2/3P^{-2/3} and the number of transits per observing window falls as P−1P^{-1}, these planets are found at a low rate and are the hardest to characterise (see the recent review by Ulmer-Moll et al. 2026).

The Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (Ricker et al., 2015, TESS;) observes most of the sky in 27-d sectors and revisits fields at intervals of roughly two years. A planet with a period of a few months is therefore often seen once (a mono-transit) or twice in non-consecutive sectors (a duo-transit), and such objects were predicted to be numerous (Villanueva et al., 2019; Cooke et al., 2019; Cooke et al., 2021). For a duo-transit, the true period is one of a discrete set of aliases Δ/n\Delta/n, where Δ\Delta is the separation between the two events; for a mono-transit, it is constrained only by the transit duration and by the absence of further events in the data. The TOI catalogue (Guerrero et al., 2021) records such objects with P=0P=0 or with P=ΔP=\Delta, the longest alias.

Resolving these aliases has motivated a growing body of work. Probabilistic alias ranking from TESS data and stellar density, as implemented in MonoTools, prioritises follow-up of the most likely periods (Osborn et al., 2022). Dedicated programmes have characterised samples of TESS duo-transits and pursued them from the ground and with CHEOPS (Hawthorn et al., 2024); the young sub-Neptunes of TOI-2076, whose outer periods had 11 and 7 allowed aliases, are a canonical example (Osborn et al., 2022). Individual periods have also been recovered from later TESS sectors, sometimes revealing that the catalogue value was a harmonic of the true one (Fukui, 2025). Most recently, uniform reanalyses of TOI host samples have resolved several long-period candidates around M dwarfs (Tschudi, 2026a; Tschudi, 2026b), and ground-based networks have confirmed long-period TESS planets and identified eclipsing binaries among them (Rea et al., 2026).

The closest precedent to this work is Bass & Fabrycky (2025), who searched every available TESS reduction at the alias epochs of the 266 TOIs with catalogue periods longer than 27 d released up to Sector 62 (code: Bass 2024). They found unrecorded transits at aliases of eight TOIs, confirmed long periods for nine more, and concluded that most TOIs with catalogue periods above 500 d are duo-transits with almost no data at their aliases. Their search excludes mono-transits, which have no catalogue period; it identifies transits by χ2\chi^{2} fits above a signal threshold rather than weighting the aliases probabilistically; and it predates most of the second extended mission. Since then the TESS archive has kept growing. By the end of the second extended mission many fields have been observed in four or more years, and a substantial number of catalogued duo- and mono-transits already have additional, unrecorded transits in public data. Their catalogue periods, and therefore their insolations, may be wrong. This matters beyond bookkeeping: lists of habitable-zone TOIs and demographic studies of long-period planets inherit these errors. The Revised TESS Habitable Zone Catalog (Kaltenegger et al., 2021), an update of Kaltenegger et al. (2019), for example, recomputed the insolation of every TOI with TIC-8 stellar parameters but adopted the catalogue periods, and listed three TOIs in the habitable zone: TOI-203.01, TOI-715.01 and TOI-2298.01. The authors themselves noted that TOI-2298.01 had a single transit and a catalogued period of 165.2 d, and that the 164-d catalogue period of TOI-793.01 was in fact 54 d, too hot for the habitable zone. To our knowledge no habitable-zone list of TOIs has since been built that accounts for period aliases. Habitable-zone catalogues exist for confirmed planets (Hill et al., 2023), and the Kepler Habitable Zone Working Group catalogued the Kepler candidates in the habitable zone (Kane et al., 2016), whose periods were well determined by four years of continuous coverage. TESS has no equivalent maintained list of candidates, and its long-period TOIs, observed in separate sectors, are exactly those whose catalogue periods are least reliable.

Habitable-zone catalogues exist for confirmed planets (Hill et al., 2023), and the Kepler Habitable Zone Working Group catalogued the Kepler candidates in the habitable zone (Kane et al., 2016), whose periods were well determined by four years of continuous coverage. TESS has no equivalent maintained list of candidates, and its long-period TOIs, observed in separate sectors, are exactly those whose catalogue periods are least reliable.

In this paper we perform a systematic, full-archive reanalysis of every TOI catalogued with P=0P=0 or P≥200P\geq 200 d, with two aims: to test whether TOIs catalogued in the habitable zone are really there, and to find habitable-zone planets hidden behind incorrect catalogue periods. We develop a flux-based alias analysis designed to be robust against the failure modes we encountered (systematics at data edges, contamination by other planets in the same system, and duos whose two events do not share a period), validate it blindly on published periods, and apply it to the full sample (Sections 2–5). We then characterise and statistically validate four planets whose periods we determine for the first time, including a sub-Neptune in the conservative habitable zone of a K dwarf (Section 6), and discuss the implications for TESS habitable-zone catalogues and for follow-up (Section 7). Relative to Bass & Fabrycky (2025), we add mono-transits, use data through Sector 107, weight the aliases with the transit duration, the stellar density and a geometric prior in the spirit of MonoTools (Osborn et al., 2022), introduce coherence and contamination tests, validate the method blindly on published periods, and carry the strongest cases through statistical validation.

papers.title: Limiting properties of Hermitian-Einstein metrics under variation of the K\"ahler class
papers.abstract: We study the behaviour of Hermitian-Einstein metrics on a holomorphic vector bundle over a compact K\"ahler manifold, as the underlying K\"ahler metric varies and its K\"ahler class changes. In particular, if the bundle stops being stable at some point, the Hermitian-Einstein metrics blow up, and their rescaling can be used to construct a destabilizing subsheaf, following the argument of Uhlenbeck and Yau. Furthermore, we study the behaviour of Chern connections of these metrics, and show, that after passing to a subsequence, and applying suitable gauge transforms these connections converge, and identify the blow-up locus of their Uhlenbeck limit.
papers.intro:
The relationship between the existence of Hermitian-Einstein metrics and the stability of holomorphic vector bundles has a long and profound history. Starting with the work of Narasimhan and Seshadri, this culminated in the works of Donaldson [15, 16] and Uhlenbeck-Yau [46], where it was proved that the slope (poly)stability of a holomorphic vector bundle is a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of the Hermitian-Einstein metric. This result was extended by many other authors, most notably by Simpson in [42] to Higgs bundles, and Bando and Siu [4] for stable sheaves on compact manifolds. Furthermore, Li and Yau [29] extended the original Donaldson-Uhlenbeck-Yau theorem to non-Kähler manifolds.

papers.title: On Higher Order Elliptic Differential Operators
papers.abstract: In this note we examine the positive preserving properties, or the lack thereof, for Green's operators of elliptic differential operators on smooth, closed Riemannian manifolds. We will obtain the existence of elliptic differential operators on closed manifolds whose lowest eigenvalue is not simple, and the existence of a large family of elliptic differential operators on closed manifolds that only have signed eigenfunctions associated with the lowest eigenvalue. That is, we will see that there is both "good news" and "bad news" when one studies the positivity preserving properties of Green's operators associated with higher order elliptic differential operators on smooth, closed Riemannian manifolds and the eigenproblem for higher order elliptic differential operators on smooth, closed Riemannian manifolds.
papers.intro:
Let UU be a smooth, bounded domain in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}. Let PP be the biharmonic operator on UU, augmented with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions. Then one has a Green’s operator associated with PP, but it doesn’t have to be positive preserving. In fact the eigenfunctions asociated with the lowest eigenvalue of PP do not have to be signed, and the solution of P​u=1Pu=1 does not have to be positive. Given this, one has to wonder ”can this happen on a smooth, closed Riemannian manifold?” This question led the author to investigate elliptic differential operators on smooth, closed Riemannian manifolds, and the results suggest that the absence of a boundary does not make the situation much better. That is, the Green’s operator associated with a coercive formally self-adjoint elliptic differential operator on a smooth, closed Riemannian manifold does not have to be positive preserving; the eigenfunctions associated with the lowest eigenvalue do not have to be signed; and the lowest eigenvalue does not have to be simple. At the same time there are some nice properties of the Green’s operator if one has that PP is a coercive operator. For example, if ff is positive, u=P−1​fu=P^{-1}f has to be positive somewhere. Given this, we will review the bad news below, and we will review the good news afterwards.

This is a joint Hausdorff moment problem. Without $C$, it holds if and only if $AB=BA$. In dimension two we give a complete criterion for noncommuting pairs. In higher finite dimensions, nonexistence is generic. Under certain spectral and cyclicity assumptions, we obtain a necessary and sufficient condition on arbitrary Hilbert spaces. The completion is unique in this case. We also classify these pairs up to unitary equivalence. The class includes irreducible infinite-dimensional examples, even with continuous spectrum.

Positive moment matrices, flat extensions, and dimensional extensions give other ways of approaching the multivariable problem [13, 22, 29]. These theories generally start with an unknown measure or an arbitrary moment functional. Our moments are already fixed, apart from one coefficient inside the inverse. This is what makes their positivity an operator problem rather than an unrestricted moment problem.

Positive operator-valued measures appear in the dilation theory of Naimark and the operator extensions of Halmos [20, 16]. Stinespring’s representation theorem and Arveson’s work put positive operator-valued measures in the setting of completely positive maps [27, 6]. Choi’s matrix criteria are central to that setting [11]. Andô’s theorem provides commuting dilations for pairs of commuting contractions [4]. None of these results by itself produces a bilinear inverse pencil with given resolvent marginals. In particular, compatibility of positive operator-valued marginals is a weaker requirement than the one imposed here.

Positive operator-valued measures appear in the dilation theory of Naimark and the operator extensions of Halmos [20, 16]. Stinespring’s representation theorem and Arveson’s work put positive operator-valued measures in the setting of completely positive maps [27, 6]. Choi’s matrix criteria are central to that setting [11]. Andô’s theorem provides commuting dilations for pairs of commuting contractions [4]. None of these results by itself produces a bilinear inverse pencil with given resolvent marginals. In particular, compatibility of positive operator-valued marginals is a weaker requirement than the one imposed here.

Moment positivity also has a long connection with subnormal operators and commuting tuples. The classical subnormality criterion and its operator-theoretic development may be found in [10, 12]. The several-operator setting is represented, for example, by joint isometries [7]. Positive kernels give another language for the same underlying positivity, starting with the reproducing kernel theory of Aronszajn [5] and its operator-valued and several-variable developments [21, 8]. The literature on multivariable operator monotone functions and Pick functions is related through positivity of analytic operator functions [1, 2]. These connections explain why joint moment positivity matters, but they do not determine which resolvent pencils have it.

papers.title: Non-simple Arrangements of Lines and Pseudolines with Many Triangles
papers.abstract:
We study affine arrangements of an even number $n$ of lines and pseudolines with many triangles. For simple ones, Blanc's bound limits the number of triangular faces to $\lfloor n(n-5/2)/3\rfloor$. Adapting the Bartholdi-Blanc-Loisel doubling to the even case, we construct an infinite series of arrangements of $n=6\cdot2^t+2$ ($8,14,26,50,\ldots$) straight lines with two triple points and $(n(n-5/2)+1)/3$ triangles, one more than the simple bound allows.
  We obtain exhaustive enumerations of triangle-maximal pseudoline arrangements, simple or not, for even $n\le12$. For $n=6,8,10,12,14$ the maximum number of triangles, for both lines and pseudolines, is $7,15,25,38,54$; for $n=8,12,14$ every optimal arrangement has multiple points. All optimal arrangements for even $n\le12$ are realizable by straight lines, except two arrangements of 10 pseudolines, which are not stretchable. For the odd value $n=11$, no arrangement with $33$ triangles exists even with multiple points.
  We also obtain even arrangements by adding a line to odd ones. For $n\equiv2\pmod 6$ this again gives one triangle more than the simple bound, in pseudolines up to $n=44$ and in straight lines for $n=20$ and $n=32$. Doubling these pseudoline arrangements gives members of the series $18\cdot2^t+2$ and $30\cdot2^t+2$ with the same excess, up to $n=146$ and $n=242$, respectively; those with $n=38$ and $n=74$ are realizable by straight lines.
  These results lead us to conjecture that an arrangement of an even number $n$ of pseudolines has at most $\lfloor n(n-2)/3\rfloor-\lfloor n/6\rfloor$ triangles.

papers.title: COVE: A Task-Adaptive, Code-Based Ensemble for Proactive Verification of LLM Outputs
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are now embedded in enterprise workflows, yet their outputs remain prone to hallucinations: plausible-sounding but factually incorrect or malformed content. Most verification approaches are reactive, detecting errors only after generation and often spending additional expensive LLM calls to do so. We present COVE, a task-adaptive, code-based ensemble that takes the opposite stance: it prevents errors before generation and validates structure and consistency afterwards using six deterministic, pure-Python innovations that add no extra LLM calls. On an internal evaluation spanning 11 text datasets (1,020 examples) and 4 image datasets (200 examples), COVE lifts text accuracy from a 45.2% unverified baseline to 82.1% (an 81.7% relative improvement), improves image accuracy by 69.5%, and reduces token usage by 48 to 96% (simulated cost model), at a measured verification overhead of 0.26 ms per output (excluding the LLM call). This article describes the engineering design of each innovation (with pseudocode and the exact parameters we use), the measured impact, an ablation of every component, and the practical lessons learned from deploying code-based verification in enterprise pipelines.

papers.title: ComplianceAtlas: A Taxonomy-Driven Agentic AI Framework for Automated AI Act Gap Analysis and Remediation
papers.abstract: Assessing regulatory compliance for high-risk AI systems requires systematic identification of technical gaps such as missing controls, in- adequate processes, or shallow evaluation of practices. Compliance officers typically admin- ister structured questionnaires collecting evi- dence of current practices, where organizations respond with descriptions of their existing pro- cesses, technical capabilities, and architectural choices. However, translating these compli- ance questionnaire responses into typed, ac- tionable gap diagnoses remains unsystematic. In this paper, we present a literature-grounded taxonomy of technical compliance gaps cover- ing areas such as accuracy, robustness, logging, and human oversight, and embed it in GapTo- Compliance, a two-stage agentic framework coordinating two specialized agents: a Gap Extraction Agent that performs hierarchical rea- soning from compliance areas to specific gap types, and a Remediation Planning Agent that ranks remediation actions from a remediation catalog via multi-signal scoring combining se- mantic similarity, regulatory alignment, and effort estimation. We evaluate this framework against four automatic compliance gap detec- tion baselines across 9 AI systems and 6 AI families. Our approach achieves a gap-type F1 of 0.831 (vs. 0.533 for the strongest baseline) and remediation P@5 of 0.872 (vs. 0.635 for retrieval methods), demonstrating promising potential for automated compliance workflows. The structured agent coordination reveals a path toward human-in-the-loop compliance systems where automated gap extraction reduces expert burden while maintaining auditability, and the taxonomy-driven design enables extension to emerging regulatory frameworks beyond

The EU AI Act European Parliament and Council of the European Union (2024) introduces binding obligations for providers of high risk AI systems across areas such as accuracy, robustness, logging, and human oversight. Organizations commonly operationalize these obligations through structured compliance questionnaires that transform regulatory requirements into observable assessment items.

Although these questionnaires are useful for identifying missing controls or incomplete practices, they rarely explain the precise technical nature of the problem. Two systems may receive similar questionnaire answers while suffering from fundamentally different operational deficiencies. One system may lack formal evaluation metrics, another may evaluate correctly but lack production monitoring, while a third may monitor runtime behavior without defining acceptable thresholds. These situations require different remediation strategies, technical expertise, and implementation effort. This distinction is important because modern ML systems fail in many operationally distinct ways. Previous work on ML production systems has highlighted issues such as monitoring gaps, training serving skew, concept drift, fairness instability, and insufficient observability Sculley et al. papers.title: Beyond Surface Metrics: Multi-Condition Requirements in Enterprise Maintenance and AI Coding Benchmarks
papers.abstract:
Repository-level AI coding benchmarks measure task success but do not directly capture the conditions required for software maintenance completion. We study multi-condition fulfillment, where a maintenance task must satisfy multiple operational conditions, sometimes with directional dependencies. Using a fixed 18-criterion taxonomy, we analyze 2,925 Apache Fineract issues and 944 tasks from SWE-bench Pro, SWE-PolyBench Java, and SWE-EVO. We examine condition breadth, corpus-level co-occurrence, and source-grounded directional requirement relationships.
  Among 1,177 benchmark task pairs matched on issue classification, modified-file count, and code churn, the mean fulfillment-set Jaccard distance is 0.8138, and 57.4% have disjoint condition sets. Condition count alone does not explain this contrast: SWE-bench Pro averages 2.47 conditions per task, versus 1.78 for Fineract. Temporal (B4) and numerical (B2) conditions have a phi coefficient of +0.430 in Fineract versus -0.013 in the pooled benchmark corpus. Among temporally tagged tasks, numerical conditions are also specified in 48.85% (254/520) of Fineract cases versus 5.81% (5/86) of benchmark cases.
  We document 16 directional relationships in Fineract requirements involving time, calculation, and state preservation, and inspect four benchmark cases to illustrate how relevant conditions appear in evaluation assertions. These examples do not quantify benchmark-wide oracle omissions. The results show that similar surface task profiles can mask substantially different fulfillment-condition sets. We recommend reporting condition breadth, co-occurrence, and directional relationships separately. The corpus comparisons are descriptive and may reflect domain differences; they do not establish causality or production failure rates.

Benchmarks such as SWE-bench [1], SWE-bench Pro [2], SWE-PolyBench [3], and SWE-EVO [4] evaluate coding agents on tasks derived from software issues, repository changes, or evolution histories. Although coding-agent benchmarks provide quantitative performance measurements, their leaderboard scores do not directly establish readiness for enterprise software maintenance.

A fundamental question precedes test adequacy: what combination of conditions defines completion of a maintenance task? In enterprise services, a single change can entail temporally ordered recalculation, preservation of prior data, and consistent downstream state. These are not necessarily independent checklist items: one operation can trigger another, and the task is complete only when the applicable conditions hold together. We call this multi-condition fulfillment, distinguishing the number of conditions from their relationships. Apache Fineract backdating requirements provide concrete instances of such linked obligations; whether comparable structures are visible in benchmark task descriptions is an empirical question.

papers.title: Hammock coordinates for silting subcategories of derived-discrete algebras
papers.abstract: We introduce hammock coordinates to study the combinatorial structure of partial silting configurations in the bounded derived category of a derived-discrete algebra $\Lambda(r,n,m)$. By extracting exact integer inequalities from the Bobi\'nski--Gei\ss{}--Skowro\'nski Hom-hammock formula, we establish a closed-form criterion for pairwise partial silting both within any $\mathcal Z$-component and across distinct components. Using this coordinate framework, we establish three primary results. First, we prove the universal upper bound $|S| \le n+m$ on the cardinality of any partial silting configuration $S$ of $\mathcal Z$-objects ---both globally via Bongartz completion in the silting-discrete setting, and combinatorially within a single component via a $\Sigma^r$-invariant staircase argument. Second, we prove that this bound is universally sharp by constructing an explicit L-shaped partial silting configuration of size $n+m$ for every $\Lambda(r,n,m)$, alongside specialized diagonal configurations. Third, we show that the configuration lattice carries a faithful action of the cyclic group $\mathbb Z/g$ where $g = \gcd(r+m, n-r)$. We conclude by showing a structural obstruction to local determination: pairwise partial silting of consecutive objects in the lattice ordering does not imply global partial silting, due to the strict additivity of a coordinate defect along chains.

papers.title: Conformal dimension of Bedford-McMullen carpets
papers.abstract: We show that the Hausdorff dimension of a Bedford-McMullen carpet with non-uniform fibres can be lowered with a quasisymmetry, provided that the defining iterated function system does not have a full column. We prove this by constructing explicit dimension lowering metrics which are quasisymmetrically equivalent to the Euclidean metric.

Quasisymmetric mappings are generalisations of bi-Lipshcitz maps, which roughly preserve shapes of sets but may distort their sizes; see Section 2 for a precise definition. These mappings originate in geometric function theory, particularly the work of Beurling and Ahlfors [6], but they are also ubiquitous in many seemingly unrelated fields of mathematics. In dynamical systems, one encounters them when studying post-critically finite rational maps, in geometric group theory they arise as boundary extensions of quasi-isometries on hyperbolic groups, and they play an important role when developing analysis on metric spaces with no a priori differentiable structure; we refer to the book of Mackay and Tyson [17] for an overview of these connections and a comprehensive introduction.

An especially important problem across different fields is characterising spaces up to quasisymmetric equivalence, and in this effort quasisymmetric invariants play a vital role. Some of the most useful quasisymmetric invariants come from fractal geometry, and the notion most relevant to this article is the classical Hausdorff dimension, denoted by dim_H\dimh. Hausdorff dimension itself is invariant under bi-Lipschitz maps, but not under quasisymmetric deformations. In fact, since the identity map from a metric space (X,d)(X,d) to the snowflaked space (X,dε)(X,d^{\varepsilon}) is a quasisymmetry for any 0<ε<10<\varepsilon<1, and since snowflaking the metric changes the Hausdorff dimension by a factor of 1/ε1/\varepsilon, any metric space with positive Hausdorff dimension can be mapped to a space with arbitrarily large Hausdorff dimension by a quasisymmetry [17, Corollary 1.4.18]. On the other hand, lowering the Hausdorff dimension by a quasisymmetry is not always possible, for instance, any quasisymmetric image of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} always has Hausdorff dimension at least dd for purely topological reasons [17, Theorem 1.4.12]. papers.title: EventGPT: Next-Event Pretraining on Banking Customer Histories
papers.abstract: A model pretrained to predict a customer's next event can estimate the probability of future events without training on their labels and provide a reusable representation for supervised downstream banking tasks. We pretrain EventGPT, a hierarchical causal transformer, by next-token maximum likelihood estimation on the public Multimodal Banking Dataset (MBD-mini: 100,224 clients, 38.8 million transactions and 66.3 million geolocation pings). Keeping one state per event, EventGPT trains in about two hours on one L4 GPU at windows up to 8,192 tokens. From its next-event distribution, with no labels, EventGPT scores five targets of the form "the client makes a transaction of a given kind for the first time next month" at ROC-AUC 0.79 to 0.92. Gradient boosting on 114 engineered features needs 10,000 to 300,000 labeled client-months to match it on four targets and stays below it on the fifth. For product prediction, frozen EventGPT embeddings score below the engineered features (mean ROC-AUC 0.787 against 0.808 over five test folds), and a rank-averaged ensemble of EventGPT, profile fields and token counts with the engineered features adds 0.014 to 0.017, of which 0.007 to 0.016 is EventGPT's own. The code and pretrained weights are released.

A model pretrained to predict a customer’s next event can be useful in two ways. It can answer questions about future events directly from its own predictions and give one representation per customer that supervised downstream banking tasks can reuse. EventGPT11 1 It is unrelated to EventGPT for event-camera streams [9] and to Event Stream GPT for medical records [11]. is trained by predicting each next event token of a customer’s event stream. This paper describes the architecture, training recipe, and measures both uses on a public banking benchmark.

The usual starting point of modeling bank outcomes is a feature table including counts, sums and recencies computed per customer and window that is fed into a machine learning algorithm. Building the table requires business knowledge (which field is the amount, which event types to include, which windows), and that work is repeated for every new event source. Each new question also needs labels and a model of its own. When events of many kinds with different fields are combined, as in a lender’s applications, repayments and account charges, there is often no obvious table to build. A pretrained event model needs neither the table nor (for questions about events) the labels.

Several financial institutions describe foundation models of this kind. Nubank’s nuFormer is a flat causal decoder over customer transaction tokens [4], Revolut’s PRAGMA is a masked model with separate encoders for profile state, single events and history [15], and Visa’s TransactionGPT encodes the aspects of each transaction before modeling across transactions [6]. Starling Bank has announced a transactional foundation model trained on 15 billion of its transactions, to be deployed in 2027 [20]. None of these releases checkpoints or evaluates on publicly available data. Even if a checkpoint were released, however, it would be of little use to another institution: its vocabulary is the company’s own event nomenclature, so each institution pretrains its own backbone (Section 8). EventGPT combines elements of existing approaches: a per-event encoder, as in PRAGMA and TransactionGPT, with the causal pretraining objective of nuFormer. It is designed for pretraining on consumer-lender product histories. Here, we train and evaluate it exclusively on publicly available data to make the results reproducible.

The weights read MBD’s schema, so another institution reruns the code on its own events (Section 8). CatBoost on the engineered features reaches the same ROC-AUC after 10,000 to 300,000 randomly sampled client-months on four targets and stays below it on the fifth at 300,000. A Markov chain over event kinds scaled by the client’s recent activity, which also needs no labels, scores 0.79 to 0.88. EventGPT scores above it on two of the five targets and on 48 of the 74 kinds with at least 50 test positives, and below it on 7 (Section 7.1). 4. The embedding is below both tables and exceeds token counts only inside its own window. We add the profile fields and full-history token counts to the embedding. The gap then falls to 0.004, averaged over five test folds, and is not statistically significant on any fold. Late fusion of the profile fields adds 0.013 to 0.019 to the ROC-AUC of the product targets and brings target_4 level with the engineered features (Sections 6–7). 5. The embedding as a second ranker beside a feature table: averaging its ranks with those of the engineered features adds 0.014 to 0.017 to their ROC-AUC on each of five test folds (intervals excluding zero, weights fixed in advance). The same ensemble built without EventGPT, from the profile fields and token counts alone, adds 0.001 to 0.008, so 0.007 to 0.016 of the gain is EventGPT’s own (p<0.01p<0.01 on each of ten fold and seed pairs). papers.title: The Universal Nilpotent Cone and a Canonical 1-form
papers.abstract: We construct a canonical Du Bois 1-form on the nilpotent cone in the dual Lie algebra of any reductive group. Using this 1-form we give an intrinsic construction of Nadler and Yun's universal global nilpotent cone. In particular, we obtain a moduli interpretation of the universal nilpotent cone.

papers.title: Same Outputs, Different Scores: Auditing the Unchecked Graders of Multimodal LLM Benchmarks
papers.abstract: Every multimodal-LLM multiple-choice benchmark ends with a scoring rule that converts a model's response, often free-form text rather than a clean option letter, into a right/wrong verdict, buried in its code. Unlike the dataset, this rule is chosen without justification and left unexamined, yet it sets the published number. We reproduce the official scorers of eight peer-reviewed benchmarks on five open vision-language models (VLMs) that fit a single 16 GB GPU, and introduce a blinded human-plus-LLM-judge adjudication (Cohen's kappa=0.956) that recovers what the model actually answered. The scoring rule alone moves accuracy by up to 22 points on identical outputs, yet exactly 0 wherever a model emits clean option letters, so it hides on strong-model leaderboards. It is the fallback and not the rambling that does the damage: the benchmark with the highest non-compliance we measure has an artifact of exactly zero, because its scorer abstains instead of guessing; a reasoning model with non-compliance 0.000 still swings 9.5 points with which regex match of its trace the parser keeps. No standard rule is reliable: snapping a non-answer to its closest option credits answers never given yet buries correct ones, abstention discards answers stated in words, and likelihood scoring follows answer-token priors, so a single grade conflates capability with luck rather than measuring either. We release all code, labels, and the protocol, and argue benchmarks should report a non-compliance rate and at least two rules, not one unexamined grade.
papers.intro:
Consider a vision-language model asked whether an industrial part is defective, with options “(A) Yes” and “(B) No.” It replies: “The object is a nail.” The model never answered the question. Yet MMAD [15], an ICLR’25 benchmark, scores this response correct: its grader calls difflib.get_close_matches(response, options, cutoff=0.0), which with a zero threshold snaps any string to the lexically nearest option: here “Yes,” by character overlap, not base rate. An abstaining grader scores the same response wrong. A likelihood grader returns whatever the model’s logits prefer. A human reading it records that the model gave no answer. Four graders, four verdicts, one output (Fig. 1). The grade came from the grader, not the model.

This is not a quirk of one benchmark. Every multimodal-LLM multiple-choice benchmark must decide what to do when a model’s free-form text does not cleanly name an option, and that decision, a few lines at the bottom of a scoring script, is made differently across the field: a no-threshold snap (MMAD [15], OmniMedVQA [14], PMC-VQA [36]), a random fallback (MMMU [33], ScienceQA [20]), a default class (POPE [18]), abstention, or likelihood scoring. These benchmarks cleared top-tier peer review and are cited widely, but reviewers judged the datasets; the grader was an unexamined implementation detail that produced numbers which looked reasonable, so it went unopened. This paper opens it.

“Just parse the letter and mark the rest wrong” (abstention) is one choice among several, and it is not obviously right: a model that answers “No.” in words, or reasons correctly and is then cut off before emitting a letter, is marked wrong. Conversely, the no-threshold snap rewards rambles that never commit. The rules are not interchangeable, and which one a benchmark ships changes its leaderboard. We scope this audit to the locally deployable regime (open models of ≤13{\leq}13B on one consumer GPU), the binding constraint for the applications these benchmarks target: privacy-bound medical VQA and air-gapped industrial inspection, where a frontier API model is not an option. Where a model emits clean letters the rules coincide, so the choice is invisible there; in the regime practitioners are confined to, the scores that guide deployment inherit it.

A line of work studies the format sensitivity of multimodal-LLM scoring: first-token logits versus decoded text on answers the model did give in parseable form [23, 37], and whether models should be allowed to abstain on unanswerable inputs [24]. Standardized harnesses do not dissolve the problem: VLMEvalKit [9], which powers the OpenVLM leaderboard, falls back to random.choice once its extraction retries fail and to a fixed sentinel under its parse-only policy: the two idioms we audit, shipped as defaults. The closest prior work anchors answer extraction to human judgment for text LLMs and does annotate non-answers, refusals and truncation among them [25, App. A.3]; what it does not do is grade them, recording a miss instead, and it varies prompt format at a fixed extractor rather than the scorer at fixed outputs. We audit what the released scorer credits when no answer is extractable, a different contrast, and find 2121–2222 points. The reason ours can be this large is mechanical. Text LLMs mostly emit a parseable letter; on the open VLMs practitioners can actually deploy, the fallback fires on 2929–37%37\% of items. Multimodal is where the fallback stops being a rounding error and starts setting the number, which is why this audit had to be done here, in the spirit of evaluation reality-checks in other subfields [22, 26].

That no rule reliably recovers what the model answered is a stronger claim, demonstrated where we have human ground truth: binary MMAD and four-option medical PMC-VQA. We anchor it on binary MMAD by design, not by limitation: yes/no is where blinded readers agree almost perfectly on what a model said (inter-annotator κ=0.91\kappa=0.91), so it is where the grader’s fabrication is certifiable rather than asserted. Breadth is carried by the field-wide survey, proof by the binary anchor.

papers.title: Zeta functions of quasi-split reductive algebraic groups over local fields
papers.abstract: We calculate zeta functions of quasi-split reductive algebraic groups over local fields using the classification of Tits and prove a functional equation. We give explicit exam- ples of these zeta functions for non-split unitary and orthogonal groups.

papers.title: Hyperplane Furstenberg Sets in Higher Dimensions
papers.abstract: The hyperplane Furstenberg problem asks how small the Hausdorff dimension of $E\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ can be when a $t$-dimensional family of affine $(n-1)$-dimensional hyperplanes meets $E$ in sets of dimension at least $s$. For $0<s\le n-1$ and $0<t\le n$, we prove the sharp bound in $\mathbb{R}^n$ $\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E\ge\mathbf{F}(s,t;n,n-1)$, where $\mathbf{F}$ is Gan's Furstenberg index proposed in prime fields. We also construct examples attaining this bound for all parameters. Our main reduction theorem, Theorem 3.1, states that for $n\ge3$, $0<s\le n-2$, and $1<t\le n$, every weighted $(s,t)$ configuration $(E,H)$ at scale $\delta$ produces a dual weighted $(s,t-1)$ configuration $(P,\mathcal{T})$ inside a hyperplane $H_{y_0}\cong\mathbb{R}^{n-1}$. The reduction uses radial projection and energy estimates for Frostman measures. Iterating this reduction and applying the Cs\"ornyei--Stull incidence theorem yields the bound.

It therefore turns the hyperplane Furstenberg problem into an equivalent problem about families of hyperplanes through points. This symmetry makes hyperplanes a natural setting in which to extend the planar problem to higher dimensions.

papers.title: Haagerup symmetries of the $E_8$ theory and conformal nets at central charge eight
papers.abstract: A Haagerup algebra is a positive strongly rational vertex operator algebra $U$ of central charge eight with $\mathrm{Rep}(U)$ braided equivalent to the Drinfeld center $Z(\cal H_3)$ of the Haagerup fusion category. Such an algebra has been proposed by Jiao, with a computer-assisted proof, and announced by Riesen and by Huang. We show that $U$ has exactly three holomorphic extensions, each isomorphic to $V_{E_8}$, and that the categories of modules over the corresponding Lagrangian algebras are the three Haagerup fusion categories of Grossman and Snyder. The extensions attached to $\cal H_2$ and $\cal H_3$ are the two lattice extensions of $V_{E_6 \oplus A_2}$. Along a strategy outlined by Huang, we prove a recognition theorem for $\cal H_2$ and $\cal H_3$ among unitary fusion categories of rank six with three invertible objects. For regular unitary vertex operator algebras with Tener's bounded localized vertex operators, we prove that the fusion product of two unitary modules is unitarizable when one of them integrates to the conformal net. The explicit unitary algebra $S \subset V_{E_6 \oplus A_2}$ of our previous work, isomorphic to Jiao's algebra, is strongly local. Granting that Jiao's algebra is a Haagerup algebra, we deduce that the conformal net $\cal A_S$ is completely rational with $\mathrm{Rep}(\cal A_S) \cong Z(\cal H_3)$, that the Haagerup subfactor arises from $\cal A_S$, and that $\cal A_S$ solves a problem of Bischoff on generalized orbifolds. Under the same hypothesis, using a unitary structure on $V_{E_8 \oplus E_8}$ found by exact computer calculations, we prove that $S$ is completely unitary and that $\mathrm{Rep}(\cal A_S) \cong \mathrm{Rep}(S)$ through the correspondence given by smeared vertex operators. The diagonal construction and the passage to the twin algebra also show that every Haagerup algebra is completely unitary and satisfies Condition I+.

papers.title: ufakzeka-kulak: Building and Evaluating a 31.6M-Parameter Turkish Speech Recognizer from Scratch
papers.abstract: ufakzeka-kulak is an open Turkish speech-to-text model of 31.6M parameters, a FastConformer encoder with a token-and-duration transducer (TDT) and a CTC head, trained from scratch and released under Apache-2.0. It writes cased, punctuated Turkish with numbers as words. Its 4,977 training hours come from sources whose licences allow commercial use; 281 hours are human-transcribed, and for the other 4,696 the training text is an uploader subtitle or a machine transcript, kept only where a second, independent reading of the audio agrees with it. The recipe, checkpoint, labelling and export choices were made on development data, and the test sets were scored once, in a release gate fixed before training. With greedy TDT decoding the normalised word error rate (WER) is 0.0921 (95 percent interval 0.0792 to 0.1055) on FLEURS Turkish test and 0.0916 (0.0873 to 0.0958) on Common Voice 27.0 Turkish test, lower than Whisper base and Whisper small on both sets with paired intervals wholly below zero; Whisper large-v3 (greedy) scores 0.0604 and 0.0767. On conversational speech the WER is 0.3807. We also report punctuation and casing, degraded audio, and how closely each shipped export reproduces the trained model.
papers.intro:
Speech recognition for Turkish is available from large multilingual models such as Whisper [3], OWSM [5] and Omnilingual ASR [6]. ufakzeka-kulak (kulak is Turkish for ear) is a small model for one language, meant to run offline on a laptop, a server or in a browser page, with a licence that allows commercial use and a published list of every training source. It follows the lab’s language model ufakzeka-1 [1] and decision model ufakzeka-karar [2].

The model is a FastConformer [8] with a TDT decoder [9] and a CTC head [10] on the same encoder, trained from scratch with NVIDIA NeMo [38]. We make four contributions: (i) the model, with exports for transformers [39], sherpa-onnx [40], parakeet.cpp [42] and parakeet-mlx [43], each measured against NeMo; (ii) a labelling pipeline for speech without trusted transcripts, in which one open recogniser writes the text and an independent one checks it, with both models and the agreement threshold chosen on human-transcribed speech that is not trained on; (iii) a recipe chosen by design pilots read by rules fixed before the runs, and a release gate fixed before any training; and (iv) reports beyond the gate on punctuation and casing, degraded audio, a media test set and the runtime differences we found. Every number for the released model traces to a result file committed in the project’s repository. Square brackets give 95 percent intervals from a blockwise percentile bootstrap [20] with 2,000 resamples (seed 0), in blocks of speakers for Common Voice and Real-TurnTurk, of sentences for FLEURS, which publishes no speaker ids, and of clips for ISSAI TSC dev and MediaSpeech, which have none; a difference between two systems is paired, with the same draws for both.

papers.title: Associated Varieties of Finite-Group Orbifolds
papers.abstract: Let $V$ be a simple, strongly finitely generated vertex algebra with a connected nonnegative integer grading, and let $G$ be a finite group of grading-preserving automorphisms. In this paper, we prove that $X_{V^G}\cong X_V/G$ as reduced Poisson varieties. More precisely, the canonical surjection $R_{V^G}\longrightarrow (R_V)^G $ has nilpotent kernel. The proof uses a uniform derivative bound in a relative $C_2$-quotient, which also implies that $V^G$ is strongly finitely generated. Consequently, quasi-lisseness and $C_2$-cofiniteness descend to finite-group orbifolds, and hence, by existing results, so does strong rationality.
papers.intro:
A central theme in invariant theory is understanding which properties of an algebraic object are preserved under taking invariants. The setting of interest in this paper is that of a finite group GG acting on a vertex algebra VV, an algebraic structure arising naturally in two-dimensional conformal field theory. The invariant subalgebra VGV^{G}, also sometimes called an orbifold (although this differs from the meaning of the term in physics), gives rise to several fundamental questions. For example, if the representation theory of VV is semisimple and has only finitely many irreducible modules, does the same hold for VGV^{G}? Similarly, if VV is strongly finitely generated, must VGV^{G} also be strongly finitely generated? The latter is a vertex-algebra analogue of Hilbert’s classical theorem on finite generation of invariants. These and related questions have been the subject of substantial work over the years [2, 4, 5, 11, 12, 21, 25, 30, 36, 37, 43]. In this paper, we continue this work by describing the associated variety of VGV^{G} in terms of the associated variety of VV and the action of GG, as well as showing strong finite generation descends.

A vertex algebra is strongly finitely generated if it is spanned by normally ordered products of derivatives of finitely many fields. As mentioned above, the descent of strong finite generation is a vertex-algebra analogue of Hilbert’s theorem. Linshaw and collaborators have studied this problem extensively, establishing strong finite generation and related derivative-order bounds for several important families of orbifolds by arbitrary complex reductive groups, including free-field algebras, affine vertex (super)algebras, generic-level 𝒲\mathcal{W}-(super)algebras, and their tensor products [31, 32, 33, 34, 6, 7]. The following theorem establishes strong finite generation uniformly for finite-group orbifolds under our hypotheses.

Building on the work of Zhu and Li [44, 28, 29], Arakawa introduced the associated variety XVX_{V} of a vertex algebra and gave a geometric interpretation of C2C_{2}-cofiniteness [1]. Namely, for a strongly finitely generated vertex algebra with a connected nonnegative integer grading, C2C_{2}-cofiniteness is equivalent to the associated variety being a point. Generalizing this condition, Arakawa and Kawasetsu introduced the notion of a quasi-lisse vertex algebra: a strongly finitely generated vertex algebra whose associated variety, viewed as an affine Poisson variety, has finitely many symplectic leaves [3]. They showed that a simple quasi-lisse VOA of CFT type has only finitely many simple ordinary modules, and that their normalized characters satisfy a common modular linear differential equation [3]. Following a suggestion of Dražen Adamović, Arakawa, Dai, Fasquel, Li, and Moreau conjectured that the quasi-lisse property descends to orbifolds by finite solvable groups [2, Conjecture B].
